## To My Most Honored Friend Mr. Francis Godolphin of Godolphin

Honored Sir,

While he lived, your most worthy brother, Mr. Sidney Godolphin, was kind enough to think my studies of some value. As you know, he also obliged me in other ways, with real tokens of his good opinion. These were considerable in themselves, and all the more so because of the worth of the man who gave them. There is no virtue that inclines a person to the service of God or of his country, to civil society or to private friendship, that did not plainly show itself in his conduct and conversation. None of these virtues was acquired out of necessity or put on for the occasion. They were inherent in him, shining out of a generous nature. It is therefore in honor of him and gratitude to him, and in devotion to you, that I humbly dedicate to you this discourse of mine on the commonwealth.

I do not know how the world will receive it, nor how it may reflect on those who seem to favor it. My path is beset on one side by those who argue for too much liberty and on the other by those who argue for too much authority, and it is hard to pass between the points of both without being wounded. Yet it seems to me that an effort to strengthen the civil power ought not to be condemned by the civil power itself. Nor should private persons, by censuring that effort, declare that they think that power too great. Besides, I am not speaking of the particular men who hold power but, in the abstract, of the seat of power itself. In this I resemble those simple and impartial creatures, the sacred geese kept in the Roman Capitol, whose noise defended the people inside not because of who they were but because they happened to be there. I offend no one, I think, except those outside, or those inside (if there are any such) who sympathize with them.

What may give the most offense are certain passages of Holy Scripture that I cite for purposes other than those for which others ordinarily use them. But I have done so with due submission, and also out of necessity, given my subject. Those passages are the outworks of the enemy, the outer fortifications from which they attack the civil power. If, despite all this, you find my work generally condemned, you may excuse yourself by saying that I am a man who loves his own opinions and believes everything he says to be true; that I honored your brother and honor you; and that on the strength of this I presumed, without your knowledge, to claim the title of being, as I truly am,

Sir,

Your most humble and most obedient servant,
Thomas Hobbes

Paris, April 15/25, 1651

## The Introduction

Nature, the art by which God has made and governs the world, is imitated by human art in many things, and in this one as well: human art can make an artificial animal. Since life is nothing more than a motion of the limbs, beginning in some principal part within, why should we not say that all automata, machines that move themselves by springs and wheels as a watch does, have an artificial life? What is the heart but a spring, the nerves but so many strings, and the joints but so many wheels, giving motion to the whole body as its maker intended?

Art goes further still, imitating the rational and most excellent work of nature, which is man. By art is created that great LEVIATHAN called a COMMONWEALTH, or STATE (in Latin, CIVITAS), which is nothing but an artificial man. It is larger and stronger than the natural man, whose protection and defense it was designed to secure. In this artificial man, sovereignty is an artificial soul, giving life and motion to the whole body. The magistrates and the other officers who judge and enforce the law are its artificial joints. Reward and punishment are its nerves: fastened to the seat of sovereignty, they move every joint and limb to perform its duty, just as nerves do in the natural body. The wealth and riches of all its individual members are its strength, and *salus populi*, the safety of the people, is its business. Its counselors, who put before it everything it needs to know, are its memory. Equity and laws are an artificial reason and will. Concord is its health, sedition its sickness, and civil war its death. Finally, the pacts and covenants by which the parts of this body politic were first made, assembled, and united resemble that *fiat*, the "Let us make man," that God pronounced at the Creation.

To describe the nature of this artificial man, I will consider four things.

First, its matter and its maker, both of which are man.

Second, how it is made and by what covenants; what the rights and the just power or authority of a sovereign are; and what preserves it and what dissolves it.

Third, what a Christian commonwealth is.

Finally, what the Kingdom of Darkness is.

Concerning the first, there is a saying much repeated lately: that wisdom is acquired by reading not books but men. Taking this to heart, people who for the most part can offer no other proof of their wisdom take great pleasure in displaying what they think they have read in men, by passing uncharitable judgments on one another behind their backs. But there is another saying, one not properly understood in recent times, by which they might truly learn to read one another if they would take the trouble. It is *nosce teipsum*: read yourself. It was not meant, as it is now used, to excuse the barbarous conduct of those in power toward their inferiors, or to encourage people of low rank to behave insolently toward their betters. It was meant to teach us something else. Because the thoughts and passions of one man are similar to the thoughts and passions of another, whoever looks into himself and considers what he does when he thinks, forms opinions, reasons, hopes, fears, and so on, and on what grounds he does so, will thereby read and know the thoughts and passions of all other men on similar occasions.

I mean the similarity of the passions themselves, such as desire, fear, and hope, which are the same in all people. I do not mean the similarity of their objects, the things desired, feared, or hoped for. These vary so widely with each person's constitution and upbringing, and are so easily hidden from us, that the characters written in a man's heart, blotted and confused as they are by dissembling, lying, counterfeiting, and false doctrines, are legible only to Him who searches hearts. We do sometimes discover people's designs through their actions. Yet to attempt this without comparing their actions with our own, and without distinguishing every circumstance that might alter the case, is to decipher a code without a key. Whoever tries it will usually be deceived, either by too much trust or by too much suspicion, depending on whether the reader is himself a good man or an evil one.

However perfectly one man may read another by his actions, the skill helps him only with his acquaintances, and they are few. Whoever is to govern a whole nation must read within himself not this or that particular man, but mankind. This is hard to do, harder than learning any language or science. But once I have set down my own reading in an orderly and clear way, the only labor left to anyone else will be to consider whether he does not find the same in himself. This kind of doctrine admits no other demonstration.

## Part I. Of Man

## Chapter I. Of Sense

I will consider human thoughts first singly, and afterward in sequence, as they follow from and depend upon one another. Taken singly, every thought is a representation or appearance of some quality or other attribute (what philosophers call an "accident") of a body outside us, which we commonly call an object. This object acts upon the eyes, the ears, and other parts of the human body, and because it acts on them in different ways, it produces different appearances.

The origin of all of them is what we call sense. There is no conception in the human mind that was not first produced, wholly or in parts, in the organs of sense. All our other thoughts are derived from that origin.

Knowing the natural cause of sense is not strictly necessary for the business at hand, and I have written about it at length elsewhere. Still, so that every part of my present method is complete, I will set it out briefly here.

The cause of sense is the external body, or object, which presses upon the organ proper to each sense. It does so either directly, as in taste and touch, or through some intervening medium, as in sight, hearing, and smell. The nerves and the other strings and membranes of the body carry this pressure inward to the brain and the heart, and there it provokes a resistance, or counter-pressure: an effort of the heart to push itself outward. Because this effort is directed outward, it seems to be some matter outside us. This seeming, or fancy, is what people call sense. To the eye it consists of light, or of color with shape; to the ear, of sound; to the nostril, of odor; to the tongue and palate, of flavor; and to the rest of the body, of heat, cold, hardness, softness, and the other qualities we discern by touch. All these so-called sensible qualities are, in the object that causes them, nothing but so many different motions of matter, by which the object presses on our organs in different ways. Nor are they anything else in us who receive the pressure; they are simply various motions, since motion produces nothing but motion. Their appearance to us, however, is fancy, and it is the same whether we are awake or dreaming.

Pressing, rubbing, or striking the eye makes us imagine a light, and pressing on the ear produces a ringing din. In the same way, the bodies we see or hear produce light and sound through their own strong, though unnoticed, action. If colors and sounds were actually in the bodies or objects that cause them, they could not be separated from those objects. Yet we see that they are separated, by mirrors and lenses, and by reflection in echoes. In such cases we know that the thing we see is in one place and its appearance is in another. At a certain distance the real object may seem to be clothed in the fancy it produces in us, but the object is still one thing and the image or fancy another. Sense, then, is in every case nothing but original fancy, caused, as I have said, by the pressure (that is, the motion) of external things upon our eyes, ears, and the other organs designed for that purpose.

The philosophy schools in all the universities of Christendom, however, build on certain texts of Aristotle and teach a different doctrine. To explain vision, they say that the thing seen sends out in every direction a "visible species." The Latin term means, in English, a visible show, apparition, or aspect, a "being seen." Receiving this into the eye, they claim, is seeing. To explain hearing, they say that the thing heard sends out an "audible species," that is, an audible aspect, or an audible "being seen," which enters the ear and produces hearing. They go further still. To explain understanding itself, they say that the thing understood sends out "intelligible species," that is, an intelligible "being seen," which enters the understanding and makes us understand. I do not say this to condemn the use of universities. But since I will later discuss their proper function in a commonwealth, I must point out along the way, whenever the occasion arises, what in them ought to be reformed. Among those things is their habit of frequently using speech that signifies nothing.

## Chapter II. Of Imagination

That a thing lying still will lie still forever, unless something else moves it, is a truth no one doubts. But that a thing in motion will stay in motion forever, unless something else stops it, is not so readily accepted, even though the reason is the same in both cases: nothing can change itself. People measure not only other people but everything else by themselves. Because they find that motion leaves them in pain and weariness, they assume that everything else tires of motion and seeks rest of its own accord. They rarely consider whether the desire for rest they feel in themselves might itself consist of some other motion. This is why the Schoolmen, the scholastic philosophers of the universities, say that heavy bodies fall downward out of an appetite for rest, and in order to preserve their nature in the place most proper to them. In doing so they absurdly attribute to inanimate things both appetite and a knowledge of what is good for their own preservation, which is more than man himself possesses.

Once a body is in motion, it moves forever unless something hinders it. Whatever hinders it cannot extinguish that motion in an instant, but only over time and by degrees. On the water, the waves keep rolling long after the wind has died, and the same thing happens with the motion produced in a man's internal parts when he sees, dreams, and so on. After the object is removed, or the eye is shut, we still retain an image of the thing seen, though a dimmer one than when we were looking at it. This is what the Latins call *imagination*, from the image formed in seeing, and they apply the word, though improperly, to all the other senses as well. The Greeks call it *fancy*, which means appearance, a word as fitting for one sense as for any other. Imagination, therefore, is nothing but decaying sense, and it is found in men and in many other living creatures, asleep as well as awake.

### Memory

In a waking man, the decay of sense is not a decay of the motion made in sensing but an obscuring of it, much as the light of the sun obscures the light of the stars. The stars exercise the power that makes them visible no less by day than by night. But of the many impacts our eyes, ears, and other organs receive from external bodies, only the dominant one is perceived. Because the sun's light is dominant, we are not affected by the action of the stars. In the same way, when an object is removed from our sight, the impression it made in us remains. Yet as other, more immediate objects follow and act upon us, the imagination of the past one is obscured and weakened, as a man's voice is drowned in the noise of the day. It follows that the longer it has been since we saw or sensed an object, the weaker our imagination of it becomes. The continual change of the human body destroys, over time, the very parts that were moved in sensing, so that distance in time and distance in place have one and the same effect on us. At a distance in place, what we look at appears dim, its smaller parts indistinct, and voices grow faint and inarticulate. So too, after a great distance in time, our imagination of the past grows weak, and we lose many particular streets of cities we have seen, for example, and many particular circumstances of actions. When we wish to express this decaying sense as the thing itself (I mean fancy itself), we call it imagination, as I said before. But when we wish to express the decay, and to signify that the sense is fading, old, and past, we call it memory. Imagination and memory are therefore one thing, which goes by different names according to the aspect under which it is considered.

Much memory, or the memory of many things, is called experience. Imagination deals only with things previously perceived by sense, either all at once or in parts at different times, and so it takes two forms. The first, which imagines the whole object just as it was presented to the senses, is simple imagination, as when one imagines a man or a horse one has seen before. The second is compound, as when, having seen a man at one time and a horse at another, we conceive a centaur in our minds. So when a man combines the image of his own person with the image of another man's deeds, as when he imagines himself a Hercules or an Alexander, it is a compound imagination, and properly nothing more than a fiction of the mind. This often happens to those who are much taken with reading romances. Still other imaginations arise in men, even while awake, from some powerful impression made on the senses. After gazing at the sun, the impression leaves an image of the sun before our eyes long afterward. A man who has been long and intensely absorbed in geometrical figures will, in the dark and though awake, see images of lines and angles before his eyes. This kind of fancy has no particular name, since it does not commonly come up in ordinary conversation.

### Dreams

The imaginations of those who sleep are what we call dreams. These too, like all other imaginations, were previously present in sense, either wholly or in pieces. In sleep, the brain and nerves, which are the necessary organs of sense, are so numbed that the action of external objects does not easily move them. There can therefore be no imagination in sleep, and so no dream, except what proceeds from the agitation of the body's inward parts. These inward parts are connected with the brain and the other organs, and when they are disordered they keep those organs in motion, so that the imaginations formerly made there appear as if the man were awake. The organs of sense, however, are now numbed, and there is no new object to overpower and obscure these images with a more vigorous impression. In this silence of the senses, a dream must therefore be clearer than our waking thoughts. Hence it is a hard matter, and one many consider impossible, to distinguish exactly between sense and dreaming. For my part, I observe that in dreams I do not often or consistently think of the same persons, places, objects, and actions that I do when awake, and that I do not remember so long a train of coherent thoughts when dreaming as at other times. I also notice that while awake I often see the absurdity of my dreams, but I never dream of the absurdities of my waking thoughts. On these grounds I am well satisfied that when I am awake I know I am not dreaming, even though when I dream I think myself awake.

Since dreams are caused by the disorder of some of the body's inward parts, different disorders must cause different dreams. This is why lying cold breeds dreams of fear and raises the thought and image of some frightening object, for the motion from the brain to the inner parts, and from the inner parts back to the brain, runs in both directions. When we are awake, anger causes heat in certain parts of the body; so when we sleep, overheating of those same parts causes anger and raises in the brain the imagination of an enemy. In the same manner, natural affection causes desire when we are awake, and desire produces heat in certain other parts of the body; so too, excessive heat in those parts during sleep raises in the brain an imagination of some affection shown. In sum, our dreams are the reverse of our waking imaginations. When we are awake the motion begins at one end, and when we dream it begins at the other.

### Apparitions or Visions

It is hardest to tell a dream from waking thoughts when, through some accident, we do not notice that we have slept. This easily happens to a man full of fearful thoughts, whose conscience is deeply troubled, and who falls asleep without the usual routine of going to bed or undressing, as when someone nods off in a chair. A man who deliberately takes pains to settle himself to sleep, by contrast, will hardly take any strange or extravagant fancy that comes to him for anything other than a dream. We read of Marcus Brutus, who owed his life to Julius Caesar, was also his favorite, and murdered him nonetheless. At Philippi, on the night before he gave battle to Augustus Caesar, Brutus saw a fearful apparition. Historians commonly report it as a vision, but given the circumstances one may easily judge it to have been only a short dream. Sitting in his tent, brooding and troubled by the horror of his rash act, he could readily dream of what frightened him most while dozing in the cold. As that fear gradually woke him, it must also have made the apparition gradually vanish. Having no assurance that he had slept, he had no reason to think it a dream, or anything but a vision. Nor is this a very rare occurrence. Even people who are fully awake, if they are timid and superstitious, filled with frightening tales, and alone in the dark, are subject to similar fancies, and believe they see spirits and the ghosts of the dead walking in churchyards. In fact these are either their own fancy alone or else the trickery of people who exploit such superstitious fear to move about disguised at night, going to places they would not want to be known to frequent.

From this ignorance of how to distinguish dreams and other strong fancies from vision and sense arose the greater part of the religion of the pagans of former times, who worshipped satyrs, fauns, nymphs, and the like. From it arise, too, the beliefs that uneducated people hold today about fairies, ghosts, and goblins, and about the power of witches. As for witches, I do not think their witchcraft is any real power. Yet they are justly punished for their false belief that they can do such harm, joined with their intention to do it if they can; their trade is closer to a new religion than to a craft or science. As for fairies and walking ghosts, I think the belief in them has been deliberately taught, or at least left unrefuted, in order to keep up the credit of exorcism, crosses, holy water, and other such inventions of the clergy. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that God can produce unnatural apparitions. But it is no article of Christian faith that he does so often enough for people to fear such things more than they fear a halt or change in the course of nature, which he can likewise halt and change. Wicked men, however, on the pretext that God can do anything, are bold enough to say anything when it serves their purpose, even when they believe it untrue. A wise man believes them only so far as right reason makes what they say appear credible. If this superstitious fear of spirits were removed, and along with it the predictions drawn from dreams, false prophecies, and the many other things that depend on them, by which crafty and ambitious people abuse the simple, men would be far better fitted than they are for civil obedience.

This ought to be the work of the schools, but they instead nourish such doctrine. Not knowing what imagination or the senses are, they teach whatever they have received. Some say that imaginations arise of themselves and have no cause. Others say they arise most commonly from the will, and that good thoughts are blown into a man by God and evil thoughts by the Devil, which is all that "inspired" means; or that good thoughts are poured into a man by God and evil ones by the Devil, which is all that "infused" means. Some say that the senses receive the "species" of things, the forms supposedly given off by objects, and deliver them to the common sense; the common sense hands them over to the fancy, the fancy to the memory, and the memory to the judgment. It is like passing things from hand to hand, with many words that make nothing understood.

### Understanding

The imagination raised in a man, or in any other creature endowed with the faculty of imagining, by words or other voluntary signs, is what we generally call understanding, and it is common to man and beast. A dog, through habit, will understand its master's call or scolding, and so will many other animals. The understanding peculiar to man is the understanding not only of another's will but of his conceptions and thoughts, conveyed through the sequence and arrangement of the names of things into affirmations, negations, and other forms of speech. Of this kind of understanding I shall speak later.

## Chapter III. Of the Consequence or Train of Imaginations

By the consequence, or train, of thoughts I mean the succession of one thought after another. To distinguish it from discourse carried on in words, it is called mental discourse.

When a man thinks about anything at all, the thought that comes next is not quite as random as it appears. Thoughts do not follow one another indiscriminately. We have no imagination of anything that we have not previously sensed, either whole or in parts. In the same way, we have no passage from one imagination to another unless we have experienced a similar passage in our senses before. The reason is this. All fancies are motions within us, remnants of the motions made in sense, and motions that immediately followed one another in sense continue together after the sensation is over. So when the earlier motion returns and becomes dominant, the later one follows it because the matter that is moved holds together, much as water spread on a flat table is drawn along in whatever direction a finger leads any one part of it. But in sense, one and the same perceived thing is sometimes followed by one thing and sometimes by another. So over time it comes about that when we imagine anything, there is no certainty what we will imagine next. Only this is certain: it will be something that followed it before, at one time or another.

### Unguided Trains of Thought

This train of thoughts, or mental discourse, is of two kinds. The first is unguided, without design, and inconstant. In it no passionate thought governs the thoughts that follow or draws them toward itself as the goal of some desire or other passion. In that case the thoughts are said to wander, and they seem unrelated to one another, as in a dream. Such are commonly the thoughts of men who are not only alone but also free of any concern. Even then their thoughts are as busy as at any other time, but they lack harmony, like the sound of a lute out of tune in anyone's hands, or of a lute in tune in the hands of someone who cannot play. And yet even in this wild ranging of the mind, a man can often trace its course and see how one thought depends on another. In a conversation about our present civil war, what could seem more irrelevant than to ask, as one person did, what a Roman penny was worth? Yet the connection was obvious enough to me. The thought of the war brought in the thought of the King being handed over to his enemies. That thought brought in the thought of Christ being handed over, and that in turn the thought of the thirty pence that were the price of that betrayal. From there the malicious question followed easily, and all of this happened in a moment, for thought is quick.

### Regulated Trains of Thought

The second kind is more constant, because it is regulated by some desire and design. The impression made by things we desire or fear is strong and lasting, or, if it lapses for a while, quick to return. At times it is strong enough to disturb and break our sleep. From desire arises the thought of some means we have seen produce something like what we aim at. From the thought of that means comes the thought of the means to reach it, and so on continually, until we arrive at some starting point within our own power. Because the impression of the end is so strong, the end often comes back to mind, and if our thoughts begin to wander, they are quickly brought back to the path. One of the Seven Wise Men of ancient Greece observed this and gave men a precept that is now worn threadbare: *Respice finem*, "look to the end." In all your actions, look often at what you want to achieve, since that is what directs all your thoughts along the way to attaining it.

### Remembrance

The train of regulated thoughts is itself of two kinds. In the first, we start from an imagined effect and seek the causes or means that produce it, and this is common to man and beast. In the second, we imagine something and seek all the possible effects it can produce. We imagine what we could do with it once we have it. I have never seen any sign of this in any creature but man, because this kind of curiosity hardly belongs to a living creature whose only passions are sensual ones, such as hunger, thirst, lust, and anger. In sum, the discourse of the mind, when governed by design, is nothing but seeking, or the faculty of invention, which the Romans called *sagacitas* and *solertia*. It is a hunting out of the causes of some effect, present or past, or of the effects of some present or past cause. Sometimes a man looks for something he has lost. Starting from the place and time at which he notices it is missing, his mind runs back from place to place and from time to time to find where and when he last had it. He is trying to fix some definite and limited time and place from which to begin a methodical search. Then, from that point, his thoughts run over the same places and times again to find what action or other occasion might have caused him to lose it. This we call remembrance, or calling to mind. The Romans called it *reminiscentia*, as though it were a re-conning, a reckoning over again, of our former actions.

Sometimes a man knows a definite area within whose bounds he must search, and then his thoughts run over every part of it. He goes about it the way one would sweep a room to find a jewel, or the way a spaniel ranges a field until it picks up a scent, or the way a man runs through the alphabet to hit upon a rhyme.

### Prudence

Sometimes a man wants to know the outcome of an action. He then thinks of some similar action in the past and the outcomes that followed it, one after another, supposing that like outcomes will follow like actions. Someone foreseeing what will become of a criminal goes back over what he has seen follow similar crimes before, and his thoughts run in this order: the crime, the officer, the prison, the judge, and the gallows. This kind of thinking is called foresight, prudence, or providence, and sometimes wisdom. Yet such conjecture is highly fallible, because it is so difficult to observe every circumstance. But this much is certain: the more experience of past things one man has compared with another, the more prudent he is, and the less often his expectations fail him.

Only the present has any existence in nature. Things past exist only in memory, and things to come do not exist at all. The future is merely a fiction of the mind, which takes the consequences that followed past actions and applies them to the actions of the present. The man with the most experience does this with the most certainty, but not with certainty enough. And though we call it prudence when the outcome matches our expectation, in its own nature it is only presumption. True foresight of things to come, which is providence, belongs only to him by whose will they are to come, and from him alone, supernaturally, comes prophecy. The best natural prophet is the best guesser, and the best guesser is the one most practiced and studied in the matters he guesses about, for he has the most signs to guess by.

### Signs

A sign is the event that comes before a consequence, and conversely the consequence that comes after an antecedent, when similar sequences have been observed before. The more often they have been observed, the less uncertain the sign. Therefore the man with the most experience in any kind of business has the most signs by which to guess at the future, and he is consequently the most prudent. He is so much more prudent than a newcomer to that business that no advantage of natural talent or quick improvisation can make up the difference, though many young men perhaps think otherwise.

Nevertheless, it is not prudence that distinguishes man from beast. There are animals that at one year old observe more, and pursue their own good more prudently, than a child can at ten.

### Conjecture of Past Time

Prudence is a presumption about the future drawn from experience of the past. In the same way, there is a presumption about past things drawn from other things that are also past rather than future. Suppose a man has seen the course and stages by which a flourishing state first fell into civil war and then into ruin. On seeing the ruins of any other state, he will guess that a similar war and a similar course of events took place there too. But his conjecture is nearly as uncertain as a conjecture about the future, since both rest on experience alone.

I can recall no other act of the human mind that is planted in man by nature, so that nothing more is needed to exercise it than to be born a man and live with the use of his five senses. The other faculties, which I will discuss shortly and which seem to belong to man alone, are acquired and increased by study and effort. Most men learn them through instruction and discipline, and all of them come from the invention of words and speech. Apart from sense, thoughts, and the train of thoughts, the human mind has no other motion. Yet with the help of speech and method these same faculties can be developed to such a height that they set men apart from all other living creatures.

Whatever we imagine is finite. Therefore we have no idea or conception of anything we call infinite. No one can hold in his mind an image of infinite magnitude, or conceive the ends and limits of the thing so named. We have no conception of the thing itself, only of our own inability to conceive it. And so the name of God is used not to make us conceive him, for he is incomprehensible and his greatness and power are inconceivable, but so that we may honor him. Moreover, as I said before, whatever we conceive has first been perceived by sense, either all at once or in parts. A man can therefore have no thought representing anything that is not subject to sense. It follows that no one can conceive of anything without conceiving it in some place, as having some definite size, and as capable of being divided into parts. Nor can anyone conceive that a thing is wholly in this place and wholly in another place at the same time, or that two or more things can be in one and the same place at once. None of these things has ever been presented to sense, and none ever could be. They are absurd expressions with no meaning at all, accepted on trust from deceived philosophers and from deceived or deceiving Schoolmen, the scholastic theologians of the universities.

## Chapter IV. Of Speech

### The Origin of Speech

The invention of printing, ingenious as it was, is no great achievement when set beside the invention of letters. Who first discovered the use of letters is not known. The man said to have first brought them into Greece was Cadmus, son of Agenor, King of Phoenicia. It was a profitable invention, both for preserving the memory of past ages and for joining together a humanity scattered across so many distant regions of the earth. It was also a difficult one, since it required careful observation of the different motions of the tongue, palate, lips, and other organs of speech, so that a distinct written character could be devised for each sound and then remembered. But the noblest and most profitable invention of all was speech itself. Speech consists of names, or appellations, and the ways in which they are connected. By it men record their thoughts, recall them once they have passed, and declare them to one another for mutual benefit and conversation. Without it there would have been among men no commonwealth, no society, no contract, and no peace, any more than there is among lions, bears, and wolves.

The first author of speech was God himself, who instructed Adam how to name the creatures He brought before his sight. Scripture goes no further on the matter. Yet this was enough to set Adam on his way: he could add more names as his experience of the creatures and his use of them gave him occasion, and he could gradually join those names together so as to make himself understood. In this way, over the course of time, he could acquire as much language as he found a use for, though not as abundant a stock as an orator or a philosopher requires. For I find nothing in Scripture from which it can be concluded, either directly or by inference, that Adam was taught the names of all figures, numbers, measures, colors, sounds, fancies, and relations. Still less was he taught the names of words and kinds of speech, such as *general*, *special*, *affirmative*, *negative*, *interrogative*, *optative*, and *infinitive*, all of which are useful. And least of all was he taught *entity*, *intentionality*, *quiddity*, and the other supposedly significant words of the Schoolmen.

But all the language that Adam and his descendants had acquired and enlarged was lost again at the Tower of Babel, when God struck every man, as punishment for his rebellion, with forgetfulness of the language he had spoken before. Forced by this to scatter into different parts of the world, they must have developed by degrees the diversity of tongues that exists today, as need, the mother of all invention, taught them. And in the course of time these languages everywhere grew richer.

### The Use of Speech

The general use of speech is to convert our mental discourse into verbal discourse, the train of our thoughts into a train of words. This brings two advantages. The first is the recording of the consequences of our thoughts. Thoughts are apt to slip from memory and put us to the labor of working them out again, but they can be recalled through the words by which they were marked. The first use of names, therefore, is to act as marks, or notes of remembrance. The second advantage arises when many people use the same words: by the connection and order of those words they can signify to one another what they conceive or think about any matter, and also what they desire, fear, or feel any other passion toward. In this use, words are called signs.

The special uses of speech are four. The first is to record what we have discovered by thinking to be the cause of anything, present or past, and what we find that present or past things may produce or bring about. This, in sum, is the acquiring of arts. The second is to show others the knowledge we have gained, which is to counsel and teach one another. The third is to make our wills and purposes known to others, so that we may have each other's help. The fourth is to please and delight ourselves and others by playing with words, innocently, for pleasure or for ornament.

### The Abuses of Speech

To these four uses correspond four abuses. The first occurs when men record their thoughts wrongly because their words shift in meaning. They then set down, as their conceptions, things they never actually conceived, and so deceive themselves. The second occurs when they use words metaphorically, that is, in some sense other than the one the words were established for, and so deceive others. The third occurs when they use words to declare as their will something that is not their will. The fourth occurs when they use words to wound one another. Nature has armed living creatures to injure an enemy, some with teeth, some with horns, and some with hands; to wound someone with the tongue is therefore nothing but an abuse of speech, unless he is someone we are obliged to govern. In that case the purpose is not to wound him but to correct and improve him.

The way speech helps us remember the connections between causes and effects lies in the assigning of names and in the connecting of them.

### Proper and Common Names; Universals

Some names are proper, belonging singularly to one thing only, such as *Peter*, *John*, *this man*, *this tree*. Others are common to many things, such as *man*, *horse*, *tree*. Each of these, though only one name, is nonetheless the name of many particular things, and considered with respect to all of them together it is called a *universal*. Nothing in the world is universal except names, for the things named are every one of them individual and singular.

A single universal name is given to many things because they resemble one another in some quality or other attribute. And whereas a proper name brings to mind only one thing, a universal brings to mind any one of the many things it covers.

Among universal names, some have a wider extent and some a narrower, the wider containing the narrower. Others are of equal extent, each containing the other. The name *body*, for example, has a broader meaning than the word *man* and contains it, while the names *man* and *rational* are of equal extent and contain each other. We should note, however, that a name is not always, as in grammar, a single word. Sometimes it is several words taken together in a roundabout phrase. The words *he that in his actions observes the laws of his country* make up a single name, equivalent to the one word *just*.

By assigning names, some of broader and some of narrower meaning, we convert the reckoning of the consequences of things imagined in the mind into a reckoning of the consequences of names. Consider a man who has no use of speech at all, such as one born and remaining entirely deaf and mute. If he sets a triangle before his eyes, and beside it two right angles, like the corners of a square, he may by careful thought compare them and discover that the three angles of the triangle are equal to the two right angles beside it. But if he is shown another triangle, different in shape from the first, he cannot know without fresh labor whether its three angles are also equal to two right angles. The man who has the use of words proceeds differently. He observes that the equality followed not from the length of the sides, nor from anything else peculiar to his particular triangle, but only from the fact that its sides were straight and its angles three, and that this was all he meant when he called it a triangle. He will then confidently conclude, universally, that this equality of angles holds in every triangle whatever, and he will record his discovery in general terms: *every triangle has its three angles equal to two right angles*. In this way a consequence discovered in one particular case comes to be recorded and remembered as a universal rule. It frees our mental reckoning from any particular time and place, spares us all mental labor except the first, and makes what was found true here and now true at all times and in all places.

Nowhere is the use of words in recording our thoughts so evident as in counting. A man simple from birth, who could never learn by heart the order of the number words *one*, *two*, *three*, may notice every stroke of the clock and nod at each, or say "one, one, one," but he can never know what hour it strikes. It appears that there was once a time when these names of numbers were not in use, and men were obliged to apply the fingers of one hand or both to whatever they wished to keep count of. From this, it seems, comes the fact that in every nation the number words go no further than ten, and in some only to five, before they begin again. A man who can count to ten will lose his place if he recites the numbers out of order, and will not know when he has finished; still less will he be able to add, subtract, and perform the other operations of arithmetic. Without words, then, there is no possibility of reckoning numbers, and still less of reckoning magnitudes, speeds, forces, and the other quantities whose calculation is necessary to the existence, or the well-being, of mankind.

When two names are joined together into a consequence or affirmation, as in *a man is a living creature*, or *if he is a man, he is a living creature*, the affirmation or consequence is true if the second name, *living creature*, signifies everything the first name, *man*, signifies. Otherwise it is false. For *true* and *false* are attributes of speech, not of things, and where there is no speech there is neither truth nor falsehood. There may be error, as when we expect something that will not happen or suspect something that has not happened, but in neither case can a man be charged with untruth.

Since truth consists in the correct ordering of names in our affirmations, a man who seeks precise truth must remember what each name he uses stands for and place it accordingly. Otherwise he will find himself entangled in words like a bird caught on lime-twigs, the branches that bird-catchers smear with a sticky paste: the more it struggles, the more thoroughly it is stuck. This is why in geometry, the only science that God has so far been pleased to grant mankind, men begin by settling the meanings of their words. These settled meanings they call *definitions*, and they place them at the beginning of their reckoning.

It is clear from this how necessary it is for anyone who aspires to true knowledge to examine the definitions of earlier authors, and either to correct them where they have been carelessly set down or to frame them himself. For errors in definitions multiply as the reckoning proceeds, and lead men into absurdities that they eventually recognize but cannot escape without reckoning anew from the beginning, where the source of their errors lies. Those who trust in books are therefore like people who add many small sums into a larger total without checking whether the small sums were correctly added in the first place. When at last the error becomes visible, they do not suspect their original foundations, and so they cannot see how to extricate themselves. Instead they spend their time fluttering over their books, like birds that have come in by the chimney and, finding themselves shut in a room, beat against the false light of a glass window because they lack the wit to consider which way they came in.

The first use of speech, then, lies in the correct definition of names, and this is the acquisition of science. The first abuse lies in wrong definitions, or in none at all, and from this proceed all false and senseless doctrines. These doctrines place those who take their instruction from the authority of books, rather than from their own reflection, as far beneath the condition of ignorant men as men endowed with true science are above it. For ignorance stands midway between true science and erroneous doctrine. Natural sense and imagination are not subject to absurdity. Nature itself cannot err. But as men grow abundant in language, they become either wiser or more foolish than ordinary men. Nor is it possible, without letters, for any man to become either exceptionally wise or, unless his memory has been damaged by disease or by some defect in his bodily organs, exceptionally foolish. For words are the counters of wise men, like the tokens a merchant moves on a counting board to work out a sum, which have no value in themselves; the wise only reckon with them. But words are the money of fools, who value them by the authority of an Aristotle, a Cicero, or a Thomas Aquinas, or of any other learned doctor whatever, so long as he is a man.

### What Can Be Named

Whatever can enter into an account or be considered in one, whatever can be added to something else to make a sum or subtracted from something else to leave a remainder, can be the subject of a name. The Romans called accounts of money *rationes* and the act of accounting *ratiocinatio*, and what we call *items* in bills and account books they called *nomina*, that is, names. It seems to follow that they extended the word *ratio* to the faculty of reckoning in all other things. The Greeks have a single word, *logos*, for both speech and reason. This was not because they thought there could be no speech without reason, but because there could be no reasoning without speech. The act of reasoning they called *syllogism*, which signifies the summing up of the consequences of one statement with another. And because the same things may enter into an account by virtue of different attributes, their names are bent and varied in different ways to show that difference. This diversity of names can be reduced to four general headings.

First, a thing may enter into account as matter, or body, as when we call it *living*, *sensible*, *rational*, *hot*, *cold*, *moved*, or *at rest*. With all these names the word *matter* or *body* is understood, since they are all names of matter.

Second, a thing may enter into account, or be considered, for some attribute or quality we conceive to be in it, such as being moved, being of a certain length, or being hot. We then make a name for the attribute under consideration by slightly altering or bending the name of the thing itself. For *living* we put into the account *life*; for *moved*, *motion*; for *hot*, *heat*; for *long*, *length*; and so on. All such names are names of the attributes and properties by which one piece of matter, or one body, is distinguished from another. These are called *abstract names*, because they are separated not from matter itself but from the reckoning of matter.

Third, we bring into account the properties of our own bodies by which we make such distinctions. When something is seen by us, we reckon not the thing itself but the sight, the color, the image of it in our imagination. When something is heard, we reckon not the thing but only the hearing, or the sound, which is our imagination or conception of it received through the ear. Such names are names of fancies.

Fourth, we bring into account, consider, and name names themselves, and speeches. *General*, *universal*, *special*, and *equivocal* are names of names. *Affirmation*, *interrogation*, *commandment*, *narration*, *syllogism*, *sermon*, *oration*, and many others like them are names of speeches.

### The Use of Positive Names

This is the full variety of positive names. They are used to mark something that exists in nature or that can be imagined by the mind of man: bodies that exist or can be conceived to exist; the properties of bodies that exist or can be imagined to exist; or words and speech.

### Negative Names and Their Uses

There are also other names, called *negative*, which are signs indicating that a word is not the name of the thing in question. Examples are *nothing*, *no man*, *infinite*, *unteachable*, *three lacking four*, and the like. Although these are not names of anything, they are nonetheless useful in reckoning, or in correcting a reckoning, and they call our past thoughts to mind, because they make us refuse to accept names that have not been rightly used.

### Insignificant Words

All other names are merely meaningless sounds, and they are of two kinds. The first kind consists of new words whose meaning has never been explained by definition. The Schoolmen and muddled philosophers have coined an abundance of these.

The second kind arises when men make a single name out of two names whose meanings are contradictory and inconsistent, such as *an incorporeal body*, or, what amounts to the same thing, *an incorporeal substance*, along with a great many others. For whenever an affirmation is false, the two names of which it is composed, when put together and made into one, signify nothing at all. If it is a false affirmation to say *a quadrangle is round*, then the phrase *round quadrangle* signifies nothing; it is a mere sound. Likewise, if it is false to say that virtue can be poured, or blown, up and down, then the expressions *in-poured virtue* and *in-blown virtue* are as absurd and meaningless as a round quadrangle. You will therefore rarely meet with a senseless and meaningless word that is not built from Latin or Greek names. A Frenchman seldom hears our Savior called by the name *Parole*, but often by the name *Verbe*; yet *Verbe* and *Parole* differ in nothing except that one is Latin and the other French.

### Understanding

When a man, on hearing any speech, has the thoughts that the words of that speech and their connection were established and designed to signify, he is said to understand it. Understanding is nothing other than conception caused by speech. If speech is peculiar to man, as for all I know it is, then understanding is peculiar to him as well. It follows that absurd and false affirmations, when they are universal, cannot be understood at all, though many people think they understand them when they are merely repeating the words under their breath or going over them in their minds.

What kinds of speech signify the appetites, aversions, and passions of the human mind, and what their uses and abuses are, I shall discuss once I have treated the passions.

### Inconstant Names

The names of things that affect us, that is, things that please or displease us, have an inconstant meaning in men's ordinary conversation, because not all men are affected alike by the same thing, nor is the same man affected alike at all times. All names are assigned to signify our conceptions, and all our feelings are nothing but conceptions; so when we conceive the same things differently, we can hardly avoid naming them differently. Though the nature of what we conceive remains the same, the variety in how we receive it, owing to differences in bodily constitution and in the prejudices of opinion, gives everything a tint of our different passions. In reasoning, therefore, a man must be wary of words that, besides signifying what we imagine of the nature of things, also signify the nature, disposition, and interest of the speaker. Such are the names of virtues and vices. One man calls *wisdom* what another calls *fear*; one calls *cruelty* what another calls *justice*; one calls *prodigality* what another calls *magnanimity*; one calls *gravity* what another calls *stupidity*; and so on. Such names can therefore never be sound foundations for any reasoning. Nor can metaphors and figures of speech. These, however, are less dangerous, because they openly declare their inconstancy, which the others do not.

## Chapter V. Of Reason, and Science

### What Reason Is

When a man reasons, he does nothing more than conceive a total from the addition of parts, or conceive a remainder from the subtraction of one sum from another. If this is done in words, it means grasping how the names of all the parts lead to the name of the whole, or how the names of the whole and of one part lead to the name of the remaining part. In some subjects, such as numbers, people name other operations besides adding and subtracting, namely multiplying and dividing. Yet these are the same operations, since multiplication is simply the adding together of equal things, and division is simply the subtracting of one thing as many times as we can. Nor are these operations confined to numbers. They apply to every kind of thing that can be added together or taken away from another. Just as arithmeticians teach addition and subtraction with numbers, geometers teach the same with lines, figures both solid and plane, angles, proportions, times, degrees of speed, force, power, and the like. Logicians teach the same with the consequences of words. They add two names together to make an affirmation, two affirmations to make a syllogism, and many syllogisms to make a demonstration; and from the sum, or conclusion, of a syllogism they subtract one proposition to find the other. Writers on politics add together pacts to find men's duties, and lawyers add together laws and facts to find what is right and wrong in the actions of private persons. Wherever there is room for addition and subtraction, there is room for reason; and wherever these have no place, reason has nothing whatever to do.

### Reason Defined

From all this we can define, that is, determine, what is meant by the word "reason" when we count it among the faculties of the mind. Reason, in this sense, is nothing but reckoning, which is to say adding and subtracting, the consequences of general names that have been agreed upon for marking and signifying our thoughts. I say "marking" them when we reckon by ourselves, and "signifying" them when we demonstrate our reckonings to other people or seek their approval of them.

### Where Right Reason Lies

In arithmetic, unpracticed people are bound to err, and even professors of the art may often miscalculate and arrive at a false total. The same is true in every other subject of reasoning: the ablest, most attentive, and most practiced people may deceive themselves and infer false conclusions. This is not because reason itself is ever anything but right reason, any more than arithmetic is anything but a certain and infallible art. It is because no one man's reason, nor the reason of any number of men, creates certainty, just as an account is not correctly totaled merely because a great many people have unanimously approved it. So when there is a dispute over an account, the parties must by their own agreement set up the reason of some arbitrator or judge as right reason and abide by that person's verdict. Otherwise their dispute must either come to blows or remain undecided, since nature has established no right reason of its own to settle it. The same holds in every kind of debate whatsoever. Some men think themselves wiser than everyone else and loudly demand that right reason be the judge, yet want nothing more than to have matters decided by their own reason and no one else's. This is as intolerable in human society as it would be in a card game, once the trump suit has been turned up, for a player to declare as trumps, at every turn, whichever suit he happens to hold the most of. Such people do nothing else than insist that each of their passions, as it comes to dominate them, be accepted as right reason, and in their own disputes no less. They betray their lack of right reason by the very claim they lay to it.

### The Use of Reason

The use and purpose of reason is not to find the sum and truth of one or a few consequences far removed from the first definitions and the settled meanings of names. It is to begin from these and to proceed from one consequence to the next. There can be no certainty about the final conclusion without certainty about all the affirmations and negations on which it was based and from which it was inferred. Consider the head of a household who, in settling his accounts, adds up the totals of all the bills of expense into one sum, without checking how each bill was totaled by those who submitted it, or what exactly he is paying for. He gains no more by this than if he had accepted the whole account at once, relying on each accountant's skill and honesty. So too in reasoning about anything else. Whoever accepts conclusions on the trust of authors, without deriving them from the first items in every reckoning, which are the meanings of names fixed by definitions, wastes his effort. He does not know anything; he merely believes.

### Of Error and Absurdity

A man can reckon without words when dealing with particular things, as when, on seeing some object, we guess what probably came before it or what is likely to follow. If what he expected to follow does not follow, or what he supposed had come before did not come before, this is called ERROR, and even the most prudent people are liable to it. But when we reason in words of general meaning and arrive at a general inference that is false, it is commonly called error, but it is really ABSURDITY, or senseless speech. Error is only a mistake in presuming that something has happened or will happen; even if it did not or will not, there was no discoverable impossibility in it. When we make a general assertion, however, unless it is true, its possibility cannot be conceived at all. Words through which we conceive nothing but the sound are what we call absurd, insignificant, and nonsense. So if someone were to talk to me of a round quadrangle, or of the accidents of bread existing in cheese (that is, the qualities of bread present in some other substance), or of immaterial substances, or of a free subject, a free will, or anything "free" except in the sense of free from being hindered by opposition, I would not say he was in error. I would say that his words had no meaning, that they were absurd.

I said earlier, in the second chapter, that man excels all other animals in this faculty: whenever he conceives anything at all, he is inclined to inquire into its consequences and into what effects he could produce with it. Now I add a further degree of the same excellence. By means of words he can reduce the consequences he discovers to general rules, called theorems or aphorisms. He can reason, or reckon, not only with numbers but with everything else in which one thing can be added to or subtracted from another.

But this privilege is offset by another, the privilege of absurdity, to which no living creature is subject except man alone. And of all men, those most subject to it are the ones who profess philosophy. Cicero says truly of them somewhere that there is nothing so absurd that it cannot be found in the books of philosophers. The reason is plain. Not one of them begins his reasoning from the definitions, or explanations, of the names he is going to use. That method has been used only in geometry, and its conclusions have thereby been made indisputable.

### The Causes of Absurdity

The first cause of absurd conclusions I attribute to a lack of method: these thinkers do not begin their reasoning from definitions, that is, from the settled meanings of their words. It is as if they tried to keep accounts without knowing the value of the number words one, two, and three.

All bodies enter into our reckoning under various aspects, as I noted in the previous chapter. Since these aspects are named in various ways, various absurdities arise from confusing these names and joining them unsuitably into assertions. Accordingly:

The second cause of absurd assertions I attribute to giving the names of bodies to accidents, that is, to qualities, or the names of accidents to bodies. This is what people do when they say that faith is "infused" or "inspired," though nothing can be poured or breathed into anything except a body; or that extension is body; or that phantasms, the images in the mind, are spirits; and so on.

The third I attribute to giving the names of the accidents of bodies outside us to the accidents of our own bodies, as people do when they say that color is in the body we look at, or that sound is in the air, and so on.

The fourth comes from giving the names of bodies to names or speeches, as people do when they say that there are universal things, or that a living creature is a genus, or a general thing, and so on.

The fifth comes from giving the names of accidents to names and speeches, as people do when they say that the nature of a thing is in its definition, or that a man's command is his will, and the like.

The sixth comes from using metaphors, tropes, and other rhetorical figures in place of proper words. In ordinary speech it is acceptable to say, for example, that the road goes or leads here or there, or that the proverb says this or that, though roads cannot go and proverbs cannot speak. Yet in reckoning and in the search for truth, such expressions must not be admitted.

The seventh comes from names that signify nothing but are picked up and learned by rote from the Schools, the scholastic philosophy of the universities: words such as *hypostatical*, *transubstantiate*, *consubstantiate*, *eternal-now*, and similar jargon of the Schoolmen.

Anyone who can avoid these things will not easily fall into absurdity, except through the sheer length of a calculation, in the course of which he may forget what came earlier. For all men by nature reason alike, and reason well, when they have good principles. Who is so stupid as both to make a mistake in geometry and to persist in it once someone else has pointed out the error to him?

### Science

From this it is clear that reason is not, like sense and memory, born with us, nor acquired by experience alone, as prudence is. It is attained through diligent effort: first, by the apt assigning of names; and second, by acquiring a good and orderly method of proceeding from the elements, which are names, to assertions formed by connecting one name with another, and from there to syllogisms, which connect one assertion with another, until we arrive at a knowledge of all the consequences of the names belonging to the subject at hand. This is what people call SCIENCE. Sense and memory are only knowledge of fact, which is something past and irrevocable. Science, by contrast, is knowledge of consequences, and of the dependence of one fact on another. Through it, from what we can do at present, we learn how to do something else whenever we wish, or to do the same again at another time. For when we see how something comes about, from what causes and in what manner, then whenever similar causes come within our power, we see how to make them produce similar effects.

Children, therefore, have no reason at all until they have acquired the use of speech. They are called rational creatures because of the evident possibility that they will have the use of reason in time. And most people, though they can reason a little way, as in counting up to a point, get little use from it in everyday life. There they govern themselves, some better and some worse, according to differences in experience, quickness of memory, and their inclinations toward various ends, but above all according to good or bad fortune and the errors of one another. As for science, or certain rules for their actions, they are so far from it that they do not know what it is. Geometry they have taken for conjuring. As for the other sciences, those who have not been taught their beginnings, and made some progress in them so as to see how they are acquired and generated, are in this respect like children who, having no notion of how children are begotten, are told by the women that their brothers and sisters were not born but found in the garden.

Yet those who have no science, relying on their natural prudence, are in a better and nobler condition than those who, by faulty reasoning or by trusting others who reason badly, arrive at false and absurd general rules. Ignorance of causes and of rules does not lead people so far astray as relying on false rules, and taking for the causes of what they aim at things that are not its causes, but rather causes of the opposite.

To conclude: the light of human minds is clear words, but only after they have first been trimmed and purged of ambiguity by exact definitions, as the charred wick of a candle is snuffed so that it burns bright. Reason is the pace; the growth of science, the path; and the benefit of mankind, the destination. Metaphors and senseless, ambiguous words, by contrast, are like *ignes fatui*, the will-o'-the-wisps, those flickering lights over marshland that lead night travelers astray. To reason upon such words is to wander among countless absurdities, and their end is quarreling and sedition, or contempt.

### Prudence and Sapience, and the Difference Between Them

Just as much experience is prudence, so much science is sapience. Although we usually have a single name, wisdom, for both, the Romans always distinguished between *prudentia* and *sapientia*, attributing the former to experience and the latter to science. To make the difference clearer, suppose one man has excellent natural skill and dexterity in handling his weapons, and another has added to that same dexterity an acquired science of where he can strike his opponent, or be struck by him, in every possible stance or guard. The ability of the first would stand to that of the second as prudence stands to sapience: both are useful, but the latter is infallible. Those who trust solely in the authority of books, and so follow the blind blindly, are like a man who trusts the false rules of a fencing master and presumptuously takes on an opponent who either kills or disgraces him.

### The Signs of Science

Some signs of science are certain and infallible; others are uncertain. They are certain when someone who claims the science of a thing can teach it, that is, can demonstrate its truth clearly to another. They are uncertain when only some particular events bear out his claim, and on many occasions things turn out as he says they must. The signs of prudence are all uncertain, because it is impossible to observe through experience, and to remember, every circumstance that may alter the outcome. But in any business where a person lacks infallible science to guide him, to abandon his own natural judgment and be steered by general maxims read in authors, maxims subject to many exceptions, is a sign of folly, commonly scorned under the name of pedantry. Even among those who, in the councils of the commonwealth, love to display their reading in politics and history, very few do the same in their domestic affairs, where their own particular interest is at stake; they have prudence enough for their private business. In public matters, however, they care more about the reputation of their own wit than about the success of another's business.

## Chapter VI. Of the Interior Beginnings of Voluntary Motions Commonly Called the Passions, and the Speeches by Which They Are Expressed

**Vital and Animal Motion**

Animals have two kinds of motion peculiar to them. The first is called vital motion. It begins at conception and continues without interruption throughout the whole of life, and it includes the circulation of the blood, the pulse, breathing, digestion, nutrition, excretion, and the like. These motions need no help from the imagination. The second is animal motion, otherwise called voluntary motion: walking, speaking, or moving any of our limbs in the manner we have first pictured in our minds. I have already explained in the first and second chapters that sense is motion in the organs and inner parts of the human body, caused by the action of the things we see, hear, and so on, and that imagination is nothing but the remnant of that same motion, lingering after the sensation itself has passed. Since walking, speaking, and other voluntary motions always depend on a prior thought of where, which way, and what, it is evident that imagination is the first internal beginning of all voluntary motion. Unlearned people do not believe there is any motion at all when the thing moved is invisible, or when the distance it travels is too short to be perceived. That does not prevent such motions from existing. However small a space may be, anything that moves across a larger space, of which the small one is a part, must first move across the small one. These tiny beginnings of motion within the human body, before they show themselves in walking, speaking, striking, and other visible actions, are commonly called ENDEAVOUR.

**Endeavour; Appetite; Desire; Hunger; Thirst; Aversion**

When this endeavour is directed toward the thing that causes it, it is called APPETITE or DESIRE. Desire is the general name, while appetite is often restricted to the desire for food, namely hunger and thirst. When the endeavour is directed away from something, it is generally called AVERSION. We have the words *appetite* and *aversion* from Latin, and both describe motions: the one of approaching, the other of withdrawing. The corresponding Greek words, *hormē* and *aphormē*, mean the same. Nature itself often presses upon people truths at which they later stumble, once they go looking for something beyond nature. The scholastic philosophers, for example, find no actual motion at all in a mere appetite to walk or move. Yet since they must admit some kind of motion, they call it "metaphorical motion," which is an absurd expression. Words may be called metaphorical; bodies and motions cannot.

**Love; Hate**

What people desire, they are also said to LOVE, and they are said to HATE the things for which they have an aversion. Desire and love are therefore the same thing, except that by desire we always signify that the object is absent, and by love, most commonly, that it is present. In the same way, aversion signifies the absence of the object, and hate its presence.

Some appetites and aversions are born with us. These include the appetite for food and the appetite for excretion and relief, which might more properly be called aversions, since they arise from something we feel in our bodies and wish to be rid of, along with a few other appetites, though not many. The rest, which are appetites for particular things, come from experience and from observing the effects of those things on ourselves or on others. Of things we know nothing about, or do not believe exist, we can have no further desire than to taste and try them. But we feel aversion not only toward things we know have hurt us, but also toward things that we do not know will hurt us or not.

**Contempt**

Things we neither desire nor hate, we are said to CONTEMN. CONTEMPT is nothing other than a stillness, or stubborn resistance, of the heart against the action of certain things. It arises either because the heart is already moved in another direction by more powerful objects, or because it has no experience of the things in question.

And because the constitution of the human body is in constant change, it is impossible for the same things always to produce the same appetites and aversions in the same person. Still less can all people agree in desiring almost any single object.

**Good; Evil**

Whatever is the object of a person's appetite or desire is what he, for his part, calls *good*. The object of his hate and aversion he calls *evil*, and the object of his contempt he calls *vile* and *inconsiderable*. These words, *good*, *evil*, and *contemptible*, are always used in relation to the person who uses them. Nothing is simply and absolutely good or evil, and no common rule of good and evil can be drawn from the nature of the objects themselves. That rule comes instead from the person of the individual, where there is no commonwealth; or, within a commonwealth, from the person who represents it; or from an arbitrator or judge whom people who disagree set up by mutual consent, agreeing to make his verdict the rule.

**Pulchrum and Turpe; Delightful and Profitable; Unpleasant and Unprofitable**

Latin has two words whose meanings come close to those of *good* and *evil*, though they are not precisely the same: *pulchrum* and *turpe*. The first signifies something that promises good through some visible signs; the second, something that promises evil. English has no names quite so general for these ideas. In place of *pulchrum* we say, depending on the thing, *fair*, *beautiful*, *handsome*, *gallant*, *honourable*, *comely*, or *amiable*; and in place of *turpe*, *foul*, *deformed*, *ugly*, *base*, *nauseous*, and so on, as the subject requires. In their proper contexts, all these words signify nothing but the outward look or bearing that promises good or evil. There are, then, three kinds of good: good in promise, which is *pulchrum*; good in effect, as the end desired, which is called *jucundum*, delightful; and good as a means, which is called *utile*, profitable. There are as many kinds of evil. Evil in promise is what is called *turpe*; evil in effect and as an end is *molestum*, unpleasant or troublesome; and evil as a means is *inutile*, unprofitable or harmful.

**Delight; Displeasure**

In sensation, as I have said before, what really exists within us is only motion caused by the action of external objects, though it appears to the eye as light and colour, to the ear as sound, to the nose as odour, and so on. In the same way, when the action of an object is carried onward from the eyes, ears, and other organs to the heart, the real effect produced there is nothing but motion, or endeavour, which consists in appetite toward the object or aversion from it. But the appearance or feeling of that motion is what we call either DELIGHT or TROUBLE OF MIND.

**Pleasure; Offence**

This motion, which is called appetite, and which in its appearance is called delight and pleasure, seems to be a strengthening of vital motion and an aid to it. Things that caused delight were therefore not improperly called *jucunda*, from *juvando*, meaning helping or fortifying. Their opposites were called *molesta*, offensive, because they hinder and disturb the vital motion.

Pleasure, or delight, is therefore the appearance or feeling of good, and molestation, or displeasure, the appearance or feeling of evil. It follows that every appetite, desire, and love is accompanied by some degree of delight, and every hatred and aversion by some degree of displeasure and offence.

**Pleasures of Sense; Pleasures of the Mind; Joy; Pain; Grief**

Some pleasures, or delights, arise from sensing an object that is present, and these may be called *pleasures of sense*. The word *sensual*, used only by those who condemn such pleasures, has no place until there are laws. Of this kind are all the bodily pleasures of taking in and discharging, as well as everything pleasant to sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch. Other pleasures arise from expectation, which proceeds from foreseeing the end or consequences of things, whether those things please or displease the senses. These are *pleasures of the mind* belonging to the person who draws those consequences, and they are generally called JOY. In the same way, some displeasures lie in the senses and are called PAIN, while others lie in the expectation of consequences and are called GRIEF.

These simple passions, namely appetite, desire, love, aversion, hate, joy, and grief, receive different names according to different considerations. First, when they follow one another, they are named according to people's opinion of how likely they are to attain what they desire. Second, they are named from the object loved or hated. Third, they are named from considering several of them together. Fourth, they are named from the change or succession itself.

Appetite joined with an opinion that one will attain its object is called **HOPE**.

The same appetite without such an opinion is called **DESPAIR**.

Aversion joined with an opinion that the object will cause harm is called **FEAR**.

The same fear joined with hope of avoiding that harm by resistance is called **COURAGE**.

Sudden courage is called **ANGER**.

Constant hope is called **CONFIDENCE** in ourselves.

Constant despair is called **DIFFIDENCE** in ourselves.

Anger at great harm done to another, when we judge that harm to have been done wrongfully, is called **INDIGNATION**.

Desire for the good of another is called **BENEVOLENCE**, **GOOD WILL**, or **CHARITY**. If it is directed toward humanity in general, it is called **GOOD NATURE**.

Desire for riches is called **COVETOUSNESS**. The name is always used as a term of blame, because people who compete for riches resent one another's success in getting them. Yet the desire in itself deserves blame or approval according to the means by which those riches are pursued.

Desire for office or precedence is called **AMBITION**, a name likewise used in the worse sense, for the reason just given.

Desire for things that contribute only a little to our ends, and fear of things that are only slight hindrances, is called **PUSILLANIMITY**.

Contempt for small helps and hindrances is called **MAGNANIMITY**.

Magnanimity in the face of death or wounds is called **VALOUR** or **FORTITUDE**.

Magnanimity in the use of riches is called **LIBERALITY**.

Pusillanimity in the use of riches is called **WRETCHEDNESS** or **MISERABLENESS**, in the old sense of miserliness, or else **PARSIMONY**, depending on whether it is disliked or liked.
