Love of persons for the sake of their company is called **KINDNESS**.

Love of persons only for the gratification of the senses is called **NATURAL LUST**.

The same love, when acquired through rumination, that is, through imagining pleasures already past, is called **LUXURY**, in the older sense of lechery.

Love of one person exclusively, together with a desire to be exclusively loved in return, is called **THE PASSION OF LOVE**. The same love, joined with fear that it is not returned, is called **JEALOUSY**.

Desire to make another person condemn some act of his own by doing him harm is called **REVENGEFULNESS**.

Desire to know why and how is called **CURIOSITY**. It is found in no living creature except man, so that man is distinguished from the other animals not only by his reason but also by this singular passion. In other animals, the appetite for food and the other pleasures of sense dominate so completely that they crowd out any concern with knowing causes. Curiosity is a lust of the mind which, through the persistent delight it takes in the continual and tireless generation of knowledge, surpasses the brief intensity of any carnal pleasure.

Fear of an invisible power, either invented by the mind or imagined from tales that are publicly sanctioned, is called **RELIGION**. If the tales are not publicly sanctioned, it is called **SUPERSTITION**. And when the power imagined truly is as we imagine it, it is called **TRUE RELIGION**.

Fear without any grasp of why or of what is called **PANIC TERROR**. It takes its name from the fables that make the god Pan its author. In truth, though, someone in the crowd who feels this fear always has some initial grasp of its cause, while the rest run away by following his example, each supposing that his neighbour knows the reason. This passion therefore occurs only in a crowd or multitude of people.

Joy arising from the perception of something new is called **ADMIRATION**, in the sense of wonder. It is proper to man, because it stirs up the appetite to know the cause.

Joy arising from a person's imagining his own power and ability is the exultation of mind called **GLORYING**. If it is founded on the experience of his own past actions, it is the same as confidence. But if it is founded on the flattery of others, or is merely supposed by himself for the pleasure of contemplating its consequences, it is called **VAINGLORY**. The name is well chosen, because well-founded confidence leads to action, whereas merely supposing that one has power does not, and so it is rightly called vain.

Grief arising from an opinion that one lacks power is called **DEJECTION** of mind.

The vainglory that consists in pretending or supposing that we have abilities we know we lack is most common in young men. It is nourished by histories and fictions about gallant heroes, and it is often corrected by age and by practical employment.

Sudden glory is the passion that produces the grimaces called **LAUGHTER**. It is caused either by some sudden act of one's own that gives pleasure, or by perceiving some deformity in another person, in comparison with which one suddenly applauds oneself. It is most common in those who are aware of having the fewest abilities, and who are therefore forced to maintain their good opinion of themselves by noticing the imperfections of others. Much laughter at the defects of others is accordingly a sign of pusillanimity. For one of the proper works of great minds is to help others and free them from scorn, and to compare themselves only with the most able.

On the other hand, sudden dejection is the passion that causes **WEEPING**. It is brought on by events that suddenly take away some intense hope or some support of one's power, and those most subject to it are the people who rely chiefly on external help, such as women and children. So some weep for the loss of friends, others for their friends' unkindness, and others for the sudden check that a reconciliation puts on their thoughts of revenge. In every case, however, both laughter and weeping are sudden motions, and custom removes them both. No one laughs at old jokes or weeps over an old calamity.

Grief at the discovery of some deficiency in one's ability is **SHAME**, the passion that reveals itself in **BLUSHING**. It consists in perceiving something dishonourable. In young men it is a sign of a love of good reputation, and it is commendable. In old men it is a sign of the same thing, but because it comes too late, it is not commendable.

Contempt for good reputation is called **IMPUDENCE**.

Grief at another's calamity is called **PITY**. It arises from imagining that a similar calamity might befall oneself, and it is therefore also called **COMPASSION**, or, in the phrase current at present, **FELLOW-FEELING**. For this reason, the best people feel the least pity for calamities that arise from great wickedness, and, for any given calamity, those who think themselves least exposed to it feel the least pity.

Contempt for the calamities of others, or little feeling for them, is what people call **CRUELTY**, and it proceeds from security in one's own fortune. For I do not think it possible that anyone should take pleasure in great harm to others with no further purpose of his own.

Grief at the success of a competitor in wealth, honour, or any other good, when it is joined with an effort to strengthen our own abilities so as to equal or surpass him, is called **EMULATION**. When it is joined with an effort to supplant or obstruct the competitor, it is called **ENVY**.

**Deliberation**

Sometimes, in a person's mind, appetites and aversions, hopes and fears concerning one and the same thing arise in alternation, and the various good and evil consequences of doing or not doing the proposed thing come into our thoughts one after another. At one moment we have an appetite for it, at another an aversion; at one moment hope of being able to do it, at another despair, or fear of attempting it. The whole sum of these desires, aversions, hopes, and fears, continuing until the thing is either done or judged impossible, is what we call DELIBERATION.

There is therefore no deliberation about things past, because they plainly cannot be changed. Nor is there deliberation about things known, or believed, to be impossible, because people know or think that such deliberation would be pointless. But we may deliberate about impossible things that we believe possible, not knowing that the effort is in vain. And the process is called *de-liberation* because it puts an end to the liberty we had of doing or not doing the thing, according to our own appetite or aversion.

This alternating succession of appetites, aversions, hopes, and fears is no less present in other living creatures than in man. Beasts, therefore, also deliberate.

Every deliberation is said to end when the thing under deliberation is either done or judged impossible, because until then we keep the liberty of doing or not doing it, according to our appetite or aversion.

**The Will**

In deliberation, the last appetite or aversion, the one immediately attached to the action or to its omission, is what we call the WILL. By this I mean the act of willing, not the faculty. Beasts that deliberate must therefore also have will. The definition commonly given by the scholastics, that the will is a *rational appetite*, is not a good one. If it were correct, there could be no voluntary act contrary to reason, since a voluntary act is one that proceeds from the will and from nothing else. But if, instead of "rational appetite," we say "an appetite resulting from a preceding deliberation," then the definition is the same as the one I have given here. The will, therefore, *is the last appetite in deliberating*. In ordinary speech we sometimes say that a man once had a will to do something which he nevertheless refrained from doing. Properly speaking, however, that was only an inclination, and an inclination does not make any action voluntary, because the action depends not on it but on the last inclination or appetite. If the intervening appetites made an action voluntary, then by the same reasoning all the intervening aversions would make the same action involuntary, and one and the same action would then be both voluntary and involuntary.

It is clear from this that voluntary actions include not only those that begin from covetousness, ambition, lust, or some other appetite for the thing proposed, but also those that begin from aversion, or from fear of the consequences that would follow if the action were not taken.

**Forms of Speech in Passion**

The forms of speech by which the passions are expressed are partly the same as, and partly different from, those by which we express our thoughts. In general, to begin with, all passions can be expressed in the indicative mood, as in *I love*, *I fear*, *I rejoice*, *I deliberate*, *I will*, *I command*. But some passions have particular expressions of their own. These are nevertheless not affirmations, except when they are used to support other inferences beyond the passion from which they proceed. Deliberation is expressed in the subjunctive, a form of speech suited to signifying suppositions and their consequences, as in *if this is done, then this will follow*. It differs from the language of reasoning only in that reasoning deals in general terms, whereas deliberation is mostly concerned with particulars. The language of desire and aversion is imperative, as in *do this* or *refrain from that*. When the person addressed is obliged to do or refrain, this is a command; otherwise it is a prayer, or else counsel. The language of vainglory, indignation, pity, and revengefulness is optative, the mood of wishing. The desire to know, however, has a peculiar form of expression of its own, called the interrogative, as in *What is it?*, *When will it be?*, *How is it done?*, and *Why so?* I find no other language of the passions. Cursing, swearing, reviling, and the like do not signify anything in the way that speech does; they are merely the habitual actions of a practised tongue.

These forms of speech, I maintain, are expressions or voluntary signs of our passions, but they are not certain signs, because people may use them at will, whether or not they actually feel the passions in question. The best signs of passions actually present lie in a person's face, in the movements of his body, in his actions, and in the ends or aims that we know by other means he has.

**Apparent Good and Evil**

In deliberation, our appetites and aversions are aroused by foreseeing the good and evil consequences and results of the action under consideration. Whether that action turns out well or badly therefore depends on foreseeing a long chain of consequences, a chain that hardly anyone is ever able to follow to its end. But so far as a person can see, if the good in those consequences outweighs the evil, the whole chain is what writers call an *apparent* or *seeming good*. Conversely, when the evil outweighs the good, the whole is an *apparent* or *seeming evil*. It follows that the person who, through experience or reason, has the widest and surest view of consequences deliberates best for himself, and is able, when he chooses, to give the best counsel to others.

**Felicity**

Continual success in obtaining the things a person desires from time to time, that is, continual prospering, is what people call FELICITY. I mean the felicity of this life. For there is no such thing as perpetual tranquillity of mind while we live here, because life itself is nothing but motion, and it can no more exist without desire and fear than without sensation. What kind of felicity God has ordained for those who devoutly honour him, no one will know until he enjoys it. Those joys are at present as incomprehensible as the scholastics' term "beatific vision" is unintelligible.

**Praise; Magnification**

The form of speech by which people signify their opinion of the goodness of anything is PRAISE. The form by which they signify its power and greatness is MAGNIFYING. And the form by which they signify their opinion of a person's felicity is called by the Greeks *makarismos*, for which we have no name in our language. This is enough to have said about the passions for the present purpose.

## Chapter VII. Of the Ends or Resolutions of Discourse

Every train of reasoning that is driven by the desire for knowledge comes at last to an end, either because it reaches what it sought or because it gives up the search. And wherever the chain of reasoning is broken off, there is an end for the time being.

If the reasoning is purely mental, it consists of thoughts that alternate: the thing will be, and it will not be; or it has been, and it has not been. So wherever you interrupt the chain of a person's reasoning, you leave him in a presumption that it will be or will not be, that it has been or has not been. All of this is opinion. What alternating appetite is in deliberating about good and evil, alternating opinion is in inquiring into the truth of the past and the future. And just as the last appetite in deliberation is called the will, so the last opinion in the search for truth about past and future is called the JUDGMENT, the resolute and final sentence of the person who reasons. Likewise, as the whole chain of alternating appetites on a question of good or bad is called deliberation, so the whole chain of alternating opinions on a question of true or false is called DOUBT.

No reasoning of any kind can end in absolute knowledge of fact, whether past or future. Knowledge of fact comes originally from sense, and ever afterward from memory. Knowledge of consequence, which I have already said is called science, is not absolute but conditional. No one can know by reasoning that this or that is, has been, or will be, for that would be to know absolutely. One can know only that if this is, that is; if this has been, that has been; if this shall be, that shall be. That is to know conditionally. And even then, what one knows is not how one thing follows from another, but how one name of a thing follows from another name of the same thing.

When reasoning is put into speech, begins with the definitions of words, proceeds by connecting those definitions into general affirmations, and connects those affirmations in turn into syllogisms, the end or final sum is called the conclusion. The thought it signifies in the mind is conditional knowledge, the knowledge of how words follow from one another, which is commonly called science. But if the first foundation of such reasoning is not definitions, or if the definitions are not correctly joined together into syllogisms, then the end or conclusion is once again OPINION: an opinion that something said is true, though it is sometimes expressed in absurd and senseless words that cannot possibly be understood. When two or more people know one and the same fact, they are said to be CONSCIOUS of it to one another, which amounts to knowing it together. Because such people are the fittest witnesses to one another's deeds, or to the deeds of a third person, it has always been, and always will be, considered a very evil act for anyone to speak against his conscience, or to corrupt or compel another to do so. For this reason the plea of conscience has in every age been listened to with great care. Later, people began to use the same word metaphorically for the knowledge of their own secret deeds and secret thoughts, and so it is said, as a figure of rhetoric, that conscience is a thousand witnesses. Last of all, people who were passionately in love with their own new opinions, however absurd, and stubbornly determined to defend them, gave those opinions as well the revered name of conscience. They did so as if to make it seem unlawful to change those opinions or to speak against them, and so they claim to know that their opinions are true, when at most they know only that they think so.

When a person's reasoning does not begin from definitions, it begins in one of two ways. It may begin from some other reflection of his own, and then it is still called opinion. Or it may begin from something said by another person, whose ability to know the truth and whose honesty in not deceiving he does not doubt. In that case the reasoning concerns not so much the thing as the person, and its resolution is called BELIEF and FAITH: faith in the man, and belief both of the man and in the truth of what he says. Belief, then, contains two opinions: one about what the man has said, and the other about his virtue. To have faith in a man, to trust him, and to believe him all signify the same thing, namely an opinion that the man is truthful. But to believe what is said signifies only an opinion that the statement is true. We should observe, however, that the phrase "I believe in," like the Latin *credo in* and the Greek *pisteuō eis*, is never used except in the writings of theologians. In other writings we find instead "I believe him," "I have faith in him," "I rely on him," and in Latin *credo illi* and *fido illi*, and in Greek *pisteuō autō*. This peculiarity in the Church's use of the word has given rise to many disputes about the proper object of Christian faith.

When the Creed speaks of believing in, it means not trust in the person but the confession and acknowledgment of the doctrine. For not only Christians but people of every kind believe in God in the sense of holding as true everything they hear him say, whether they understand it or not, and that is all the faith and trust that can possibly be placed in any person whatever. Yet they do not all believe the doctrine of the Creed.

From this we may infer that whenever we believe any statement whatever to be true, on grounds drawn not from the thing itself or from the principles of natural reason, but from the authority and good opinion we have of the person who said it, then the speaker, the person we believe in or trust and whose word we take, is the object of our faith, and the honor done in believing is done to him alone. It follows that when we believe the Scriptures to be the word of God, without any direct revelation from God himself, our belief, faith, and trust rest in the Church, whose word we take and accept. Those who believe what a prophet tells them in the name of God take the word of the prophet, honor him, and trust and believe in him concerning the truth of what he reports, whether he is a true prophet or a false one. The same holds for all other history. If I should refuse to believe everything the historians have written about the glorious deeds of Alexander or Caesar, I do not think the ghost of Alexander or Caesar would have any just reason to be offended, nor would anyone else but the historian. If Livy says that the gods once made a cow speak, and we do not believe it, it is not God we distrust but Livy. It is evident, then, that whatever we believe for no other reason than the authority of men and their writings, whether or not those men were sent by God, is faith in men alone.

## Chapter VIII. Of the Virtues Commonly Called Intellectual, and Their Contrary Defects

Virtue in general, whatever its subject, is something valued for its excellence, and it consists in comparison. If everyone possessed every quality in equal measure, nothing would be prized. By intellectual virtues, then, we always mean those abilities of the mind that people praise, value, and wish to have themselves. They commonly go by the name of "a good wit," though the same word, *wit*, is also used to single out one particular ability from the rest.

These virtues are of two kinds: natural and acquired. By natural I do not mean what a person has from birth, for that is nothing but sense. In sense, people differ so little from one another, and from brute animals, that it cannot be counted among the virtues. I mean the wit that is gained through use and experience alone, without method, cultivation, or instruction. This natural wit consists chiefly in two things: quickness of imagination, which is the swift succession of one thought upon another, and steady direction toward some approved end. A slow imagination, by contrast, produces the defect of mind commonly called dullness or stupidity, and sometimes by other names that signify slowness of motion or difficulty in being moved.

This difference in quickness is caused by differences in people's passions. Some love or dislike one thing, some another. As a result, some people's thoughts run one way and others' another, and they fasten upon and notice differently the things that pass through their imagination. In this succession of thoughts there are only four things to observe about the objects of thought: in what respects they are like one another, in what respects they are unlike, what they are good for, and how they serve a given purpose. Those who notice resemblances, when these are of a kind that others rarely notice, are said to have a good wit, by which is meant, in this context, a good fancy. Those who notice differences and dissimilarities, which is called distinguishing, discerning, and judging between one thing and another, are said to have good judgment, provided such discernment is not easy. In matters of conversation and business in particular, where times, places, and persons must be discerned, this virtue is called discretion. Fancy without the help of judgment is not praised as a virtue, but judgment and discretion are praised for their own sake, even without the help of fancy. Besides the discretion about times, places, and persons that a good fancy requires, a person must also frequently apply his thoughts to their end, that is, to some use to be made of them. Once this is done, whoever has this virtue will readily find comparisons that please, not only because they illustrate his discourse and adorn it with new and apt metaphors, but also because of the rarity of their invention. Without steadiness and direction toward some end, however, a great fancy is a kind of madness. People who suffer from it begin a discussion and are snatched away from their purpose by everything that comes into their heads, falling into so many and such long digressions and parentheses that they lose themselves entirely. I know of no particular name for this kind of folly. Its cause is sometimes lack of experience, which makes something seem new and rare to a person when it does not seem so to others, and sometimes pusillanimity, or smallness of mind, which makes something seem important to him that others consider a trifle. Whatever is new or important, and therefore seems worth telling, draws a person step by step away from the intended path of his discourse.

In a good poem, whether epic or dramatic, as well as in sonnets, epigrams, and other pieces, both judgment and fancy are required, but fancy must be the more prominent. Such works please by their extravagance, though they ought not to displease by indiscretion.

In a good history, judgment must be prominent, because the merit of a history lies in its method, its truth, and its choice of the actions most profitable to know. Fancy has no place there except in adorning the style.

In speeches of praise and in invectives, fancy predominates, because the aim is not truth but honor or dishonor, which is achieved through noble or vile comparisons. Judgment merely suggests which circumstances make an action praiseworthy or blameworthy.

In exhortations and legal pleadings, judgment or fancy is most needed according to whether truth or disguise better suits the purpose at hand.

In demonstration, in counsel, and in every rigorous search for truth, judgment does all the work, except that the understanding sometimes needs to be opened by some apt comparison, and to that extent fancy has a use. Metaphors, however, are excluded here altogether. Since they openly profess deception, to admit them into counsel or reasoning would be plain folly.

And in any discourse whatever, if a lack of discretion is evident, then however extravagant the fancy, the whole discourse will be taken as a sign of a want of wit. That will never happen where discretion is evident, however ordinary the fancy.

A person's private thoughts range over all things, holy and profane, clean and obscene, grave and light, without shame or blame. Spoken discourse cannot do the same, except so far as judgment approves of the time, the place, and the persons present. An anatomist or a physician may speak or write his judgment on unclean things, because his aim is not to please but to be useful. But for anyone else to write down his extravagant and amusing fancies on the same subjects is like a man who has been tumbled in the dirt coming to present himself before good company, and it is the lack of discretion that makes the difference. Again, when the mind is openly at ease and among familiar company, a person may play with the sounds and double meanings of words, often with flashes of extraordinary fancy. But in a sermon, or in public, or before strangers or people we ought to respect, any such jingling of words will be counted folly, and the difference lies only in the lack of discretion. So where wit is lacking, it is not fancy that is lacking but discretion. Judgment without fancy, therefore, is wit, but fancy without judgment is not.

Suppose a person has some design in hand, and his thoughts range over a multitude of things, observing how they contribute to that design or what design they might contribute to. If his observations are of a kind that are not easy or usual, this wit of his is called prudence. It depends on long experience and on the memory of similar things and of what followed from them in the past. In prudence, people differ less than they do in fancy and judgment, because the experience of people of the same age is not very unequal in quantity. It differs rather in its occasions, since each person has his own private designs. Governing a household well and governing a kingdom well are not different degrees of prudence but different kinds of business, just as painting a picture in miniature, at life size, or larger than life are not different degrees of art. A plain farmer is more prudent in the affairs of his own house than a privy councillor is in the affairs of another man.

Add to prudence the use of unjust or dishonest means, of the sort that fear or want usually prompt people to use, and you have the crooked wisdom called craft. Craft is a sign of pusillanimity, for magnanimity is contempt for unjust or dishonest aids. What the Latins called *versutia*, rendered in English as "shifting," is the putting off of a present danger or inconvenience by taking on a greater one, as when a man robs one person to pay another. It is merely a more short-sighted kind of craft, and it takes its name from *versura*, which means borrowing money at interest in order to pay interest that is presently due.

As for acquired wit, by which I mean wit acquired through method and instruction, there is none but reason, which is grounded on the right use of speech and produces the sciences. But I have already discussed reason and science in the fifth and sixth chapters.

The causes of this difference in wits lie in the passions, and the difference in passions arises partly from differences in bodily constitution and partly from differences in education. If the difference arose from the temper of the brain and the organs of sense, whether external or internal, people would differ no less in their sight, hearing, and other senses than in their fancy and discretion. It arises, therefore, from the passions, which differ not only according to people's complexions, meaning the physical makeup of their bodies, but also according to their customs and upbringing.

The passions that chiefly cause differences in wit are a greater or lesser desire for power, for riches, for knowledge, and for honor. All of these may be reduced to the first, the desire for power, since riches, knowledge, and honor are only different kinds of power.

A person who has no great passion for any of these things, but is, as people say, indifferent, may be good to the extent of giving no offense. Yet he cannot possibly have either a great fancy or much judgment. The thoughts are to the desires what scouts and spies are to an army, ranging abroad to find the way to the things desired, and all the steadiness of the mind's motion, and all its quickness, come from this source. To have no desire is to be dead. To have weak passions is dullness. To have passions indiscriminately for everything is giddiness and distraction. And to have stronger and more vehement passions for anything than is ordinarily seen in others is what people call madness.

Of madness there are almost as many kinds as there are passions. Sometimes the extraordinary and extravagant passion comes from a bad constitution of the bodily organs, or from damage done to them, and sometimes the damage and disorder of the organs is caused by the vehemence or long continuance of the passion. In either case the madness is of one and the same nature.

The passion whose violence or persistence produces madness is either great vainglory, commonly called pride and self-conceit, or great dejection of mind.

Pride makes a person subject to anger, and the excess of anger is the madness called rage and fury. So it happens that an excessive desire for revenge, once it becomes habitual, damages the organs and turns into rage. Excessive love combined with jealousy also becomes rage. An excessive opinion of oneself, whether for divine inspiration, wisdom, learning, beauty, or the like, becomes distraction and giddiness, and the same opinion joined with envy becomes rage. And a vehement conviction of the truth of anything, when others contradict it, becomes rage.

Dejection makes a person subject to groundless fears, a madness commonly called melancholy. It shows itself in various ways: in haunting lonely places and graves, in superstitious behavior, and in fearing some particular thing, one person this and another that. In sum, all passions that produce strange and unusual behavior are called by the general name of madness. As for its several kinds, anyone willing to take the trouble could enroll a legion of them. And if the excesses are madness, there is no doubt that the passions themselves, when they tend toward evil, are degrees of the same thing.

Take, for example, those possessed by the belief that they are inspired. Their folly is not always visible in any one individual through some very extravagant action arising from that passion. Yet when many of them band together, the rage of the whole multitude is plain enough. What greater evidence of madness could there be than to shout at, strike, and throw stones at our best friends? Yet this is somewhat less than such a multitude will do, for they will clamor against, fight, and destroy those by whom they have been protected and secured from injury all their lives. And if this is madness in the multitude, it is the same in each individual. In the middle of the sea, a person hears no sound from the water immediately beside him, yet he is well assured that this part contributes as much to the roaring of the sea as any other part of equal quantity. In the same way, though we perceive no great unrest in one or two people, we may be well assured that their individual passions are parts of the seditious roaring of a troubled nation. And if nothing else betrayed their madness, the very act of claiming such inspiration for themselves would be evidence enough. Suppose some inmate of Bedlam, the London hospital for the insane, should entertain you with sober conversation. As you take your leave, you ask who he is, so that you might return his courtesy another time, and he tells you that he is God the Father. I think you would need no extravagant action as proof of his madness.

This belief in inspiration, commonly called the private spirit, very often begins with some lucky discovery of an error generally held by others. Such people do not know, or do not remember, by what course of reasoning they arrived at so singular a truth, as they consider it, though it is often an untruth they have stumbled upon. So they immediately admire themselves as being in the special favor of Almighty God, who has revealed it to them supernaturally by his Spirit.

Again, that madness is nothing other than passion displayed to excess may be inferred from the effects of wine, which are the same as those of a disordered constitution of the organs. The variety of behavior among people who have drunk too much is the same as among madmen: some rage, others love, others laugh, all extravagantly, but each according to his own dominant passions. The effect of wine is only to remove dissimulation and to take from them the sight of how ugly their passions are. I believe that even the most sober people, when they walk alone, free of cares and with nothing to occupy their minds, would be unwilling to have the vanity and extravagance of their thoughts at that moment exposed to public view, which is a confession that passions left unguided are, for the most part, sheer madness.

The opinions of the world, in ancient and in more recent times alike, concerning the cause of madness have been of two kinds. Some have traced it to the passions; others to demons or spirits, good or bad, which they believed could enter a man, take possession of him, and move his organs in the strange and uncouth manner typical of madmen. Those of the first opinion accordingly called such people madmen. Those of the second called them sometimes *daemoniacs*, meaning possessed by spirits, and sometimes *energumeni*, meaning agitated or driven by spirits. In Italy today they are called not only *pazzi*, or madmen, but also *spiritati*, men possessed.

There was once a great gathering of people in Abdera, a Greek city, for a performance of the tragedy of *Andromeda* on an extremely hot day. Many of the spectators fell into fevers, and from the heat and the tragedy together they suffered this peculiar effect: they did nothing but recite iambic verses, calling out the names of Perseus and Andromeda. This condition, along with the fever, was cured by the arrival of winter, and the madness was thought to have arisen from the passion the tragedy had stamped upon their minds. Likewise, a fit of madness once prevailed in another Greek city that seized only the young unmarried women, and it drove many of them to hang themselves. Most people at the time thought this the work of the Devil. But one man suspected that their contempt for life might spring from some passion of the mind, and, supposing that they did not also hold their honor in contempt, he advised the magistrates to strip those who had hanged themselves and leave them hanging naked. According to the story, this cured the madness.

On the other hand, these same Greeks often attributed madness to the workings of the Eumenides, or Furies, and sometimes to Ceres, Phoebus, and other gods. So much did people credit to phantasms, the images of the mind, that they took them for living bodies made of air and called them, in general, spirits. In this the Romans held the same opinion as the Greeks, and so did the Jews. The Jews called madmen either prophets or demoniacs, according to whether they judged the spirits good or bad; some of them called both prophets and demoniacs madmen; and some called the same man both demoniac and madman.

In the Gentiles this is no surprise, since among them disease and health, vice and virtue, and many natural occurrences were named and worshipped as demons, so that by "demon" one might sometimes understand an ague, a recurring fever, as readily as a devil. But that the Jews should hold such an opinion is somewhat strange. Neither Moses nor Abraham claimed to prophesy through possession by a spirit, but rather from the voice of God, or by a vision or a dream. Nor is there anything in the Law of Moses, moral or ceremonial, that taught them there was any such thing as divine inspiration of this kind, or any possession. When God is said, in the eleventh chapter of Numbers, to take of the spirit that was in Moses and give it to the seventy elders, the Spirit of God, if we take that phrase to mean the substance of God, is not thereby divided. By the Spirit of God in a man, the Scriptures mean a man's own spirit inclined toward godliness. And where the twenty-eighth chapter of Exodus speaks of those "whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom to make garments for Aaron," it does not mean that a spirit capable of making garments was put into them, but rather the wisdom of their own spirits in that kind of work. In the same sense, a man's spirit is ordinarily called an unclean spirit when it produces unclean actions; and other spirits are named in the same fashion, not always, but whenever the virtue or vice so described is extraordinary and conspicuous. Nor did the other prophets of the Old Testament claim to be possessed, or say that God spoke *in* them. He spoke *to* them, by voice, vision, or dream, and "the burden of the Lord" was not possession but command.

How, then, could the Jews have fallen into this belief in possession? I can imagine no reason except one common to all mankind: a lack of curiosity to search out natural causes, together with the habit of placing happiness in the gross pleasures of the senses and in whatever most directly procures them. When people see some strange and unusual ability or defect in a man's mind, unless they can also see the cause from which it probably arises, they can hardly believe it natural. And if it is not natural, they must conclude that it is supernatural; and then what can it be, except that either God or the Devil is in him? This is why, as the third chapter of Mark relates, when our Saviour was surrounded by the multitude, those of his household suspected he was mad and went out to restrain him, while the scribes said he had Beelzebub and that it was by Beelzebub that he cast out devils, as if the greater madman had cowed the lesser. And in the tenth chapter of John, some said, "He hath a devil, and is mad," while others, who took him for a prophet, said, "These are not the words of one that hath a devil." So too in the Old Testament, as the ninth chapter of the Second Book of Kings records, the man who came to anoint Jehu was a prophet, yet some of the company asked Jehu, "Wherefore came this mad fellow to thee?" In sum, it is plain that anyone who behaved in an extraordinary manner was thought by the Jews to be possessed by either a good or an evil spirit. The exception was the Sadducees, who erred so far in the opposite direction as to deny that there were any spirits at all, a position very close to outright atheism, and who thereby perhaps provoked others all the more to call such people demoniacs rather than madmen.

Why, then, does our Saviour go about curing them as if they were possessed, and not as if they were mad? To this I can give no answer other than the one given to those who cite Scripture in the same way against the opinion that the Earth moves. Scripture was written to show men the kingdom of God and to prepare their minds to become His obedient subjects, leaving the world and its philosophy to the disputes of men, for the exercise of their natural reason. Whether it is the motion of the Earth or of the Sun that makes day and night, and whether the wild and extravagant actions of men proceed from passion or from the Devil, so long as we do not worship him, makes no difference to our obedience and subjection to God Almighty, which is the purpose for which Scripture was written. As for our Saviour's addressing the disease as though it were a person, this is the usual manner of speaking among all who heal by words alone, as Christ did, and as enchanters claim to do, whether or not they are speaking to a devil. Is not Christ also said, in the eighth chapter of Matthew, to have rebuked the winds? Is he not also said, in the fourth chapter of Luke, to have rebuked a fever? Yet that does not prove a fever is a devil. And where many of these devils are said to have acknowledged Christ, there is no need to read those passages as meaning anything other than that the madmen themselves acknowledged him. And where our Saviour, in the twelfth chapter of Matthew, speaks of an unclean spirit that, having gone out of a man, wanders through dry places seeking rest and finding none, and then returns to the same man with seven other spirits worse than itself, this is plainly a parable. It refers to a man who, after a feeble effort to give up his lusts, is overcome by their strength and becomes seven times worse than he was before. I therefore see nothing whatever in Scripture that requires us to believe that demoniacs were anything other than madmen.

### Insignificant Speech

There is yet another fault in the reasoning of some men that may also be counted among the kinds of madness: the abuse of words I discussed earlier, in the fifth chapter, under the name of absurdity. This occurs when people utter words that, put together, carry no meaning at all. Some fall into it by misunderstanding words they have received and repeat by rote; others do it deliberately, intending to deceive by obscurity. It afflicts only those who occupy themselves with questions about incomprehensible matters, as the Schoolmen, the scholastic theologians, do, or with questions of abstruse philosophy. Ordinary people seldom speak without meaning, and for that reason those other distinguished persons regard them as idiots.

To be certain that such words have nothing corresponding to them in the mind, one would need examples. If anyone wants them, let him take up a Schoolman and see whether he can translate a single chapter on any difficult point, such as the Trinity, the Deity, the nature of Christ, transubstantiation, or free will, into any modern language in a way that makes it intelligible, or even into passable Latin of the sort familiar to those who lived when Latin was the everyday spoken tongue. What is the meaning of these words: "The first cause does not necessarily inflow anything into the second, by force of the essential subordination of the second causes, by which it may help it to work"? They are a translation of the title of the sixth chapter of the first book of Suárez's treatise *On the Concourse, Motion, and Help of God*. When men write whole volumes of such stuff, are they not mad, or else trying to make others so?

Consider in particular the question of transubstantiation. Those who say that, after certain words are spoken, the whiteness, roundness, magnitude, quality, corruptibility, and the rest, all of which are incorporeal, pass out of the wafer and into the body of our blessed Saviour: do they not make those "-nesses," "-tudes," and "-ties" into so many spirits possessing his body? For by spirits they always mean things that, though incorporeal, can nevertheless move from one place to another. This kind of absurdity, then, may rightly be counted among the many sorts of madness; and all the time during which such men, guided by clear thoughts of their worldly desires, refrain from disputing or writing in this way are nothing but lucid intervals. And this is all I have to say concerning the intellectual virtues and their defects.

## Chapter IX. Of the Several Subjects of Knowledge

There are two kinds of knowledge. The first is knowledge of fact; the second is knowledge of how one affirmation follows from another. Knowledge of fact is nothing more than sense and memory, and it is absolute knowledge: we have it when we see something happening or remember that it happened. This is the kind of knowledge we require of a witness. The second kind is called science, and it is conditional. We have it when we know, for instance, that *if* the figure shown is a circle, *then* any straight line drawn through its center will divide it into two equal parts. This is the kind of knowledge we require of a philosopher, meaning anyone who lays claim to reasoning.

The record of knowledge of fact is called history, and it comes in two sorts. The first is natural history, the history of those facts or effects of nature that do not depend on human will, such as the histories of metals, plants, animals, regions, and the like. The second is civil history, the history of the voluntary actions of people living in commonwealths.

The records of science are the books that contain demonstrations of how one affirmation follows from another, and they are commonly called books of philosophy. There are many sorts of these, according to the diversity of their subject matter, and they may be divided in the manner shown in the following table. Throughout, "accidents" means the properties or attributes that bodies possess.

- **I. Science, that is, knowledge of consequences, which is also called PHILOSOPHY**
  - **A. Consequences from the accidents of natural bodies, which is called NATURAL PHILOSOPHY**
    - **1. Consequences from the accidents common to all natural bodies, namely quantity and motion**
      - **a.** Consequences from quantity and motion in general, left undetermined. Because these are the principles, or first foundation, of philosophy, this branch is called PHILOSOPHIA PRIMA, or "first philosophy."
      - **b.** Consequences from motion and quantity when they are determined
        - **1)** Consequences from quantity and motion determined by figure and by number, which constitute MATHEMATICS: GEOMETRY and ARITHMETIC
        - **2)** Consequences from the motion and quantity of particular bodies
          - **a)** Consequences from the motion and quantity of the great parts of the world, such as the earth and the stars, which constitute COSMOGRAPHY: ASTRONOMY and GEOGRAPHY
          - **b)** Consequences from the motion of particular kinds and shapes of body, which constitute MECHANICS, the doctrine of weight: the science of ENGINEERS, ARCHITECTURE, and NAVIGATION
    - **2. PHYSICS, or consequences from qualities**
      - **a.** Consequences from the qualities of transient bodies, those that sometimes appear and sometimes vanish: METEOROLOGY
      - **b.** Consequences from the qualities of permanent bodies
        - **1)** Consequences from the qualities of the stars
          - **a)** Consequences from the light of the stars. From this, together with the motion of the sun, comes the science of SCIOGRAPHY, the study of shadows and the art of making sundials.
          - **b)** Consequences from the influence of the stars: ASTROLOGY
        - **2)** Consequences from the qualities of the liquid bodies that fill the space between the stars, such as the air or the ethereal substance
        - **3)** Consequences from the qualities of terrestrial bodies
          - **a)** Consequences from those parts of the earth that lack sense
            - **1]** Consequences from the qualities of minerals, such as stones, metals, and so on
            - **2]** Consequences from the qualities of plants
          - **b)** Consequences from the qualities of animals
            - **1]** Consequences from the qualities of animals in general
              - **a]** Consequences from vision: OPTICS
              - **b]** Consequences from sounds: MUSIC
              - **c]** Consequences from the rest of the senses
            - **2]** Consequences from the qualities of human beings in particular
              - **a]** Consequences from the passions of men: ETHICS
              - **b]** Consequences from speech
                - **i)** In praising and disparaging and the like: POETRY
                - **ii)** In persuading: RHETORIC
                - **iii)** In reasoning: LOGIC
                - **iv)** In making contracts: the science of the JUST and the UNJUST
  - **B. Consequences from the accidents of political bodies, which is called POLITICS, or CIVIL PHILOSOPHY**
    - **1.** Consequences from the founding of COMMONWEALTHS for the rights and duties of the body politic, or sovereign
    - **2.** Consequences from the same founding for the duties and rights of the subjects

## Chapter X. Of Power, Worth, Dignity, Honour and Worthiness

### Power

A man's power, taken in its most general sense, is the means he presently has to obtain some apparent good in the future. Power is either original or instrumental.

Natural, or original, power is the superiority of the faculties of body or mind: extraordinary strength, physical beauty, prudence, skill in the arts, eloquence, generosity, noble birth. Instrumental powers are those acquired through these natural gifts, or by fortune, which then become the means and instruments for acquiring still more: wealth, reputation, friends, and the secret working of God that men call good luck. In this respect power resembles fame, which grows as it travels. It also resembles the motion of heavy bodies, which fall faster the farther they fall.

The greatest of human powers is the one compounded from the powers of the greatest number of men, united by consent in one person, whether a natural person or a civil one. The use of all their powers may depend on the will of that single person, as it does in a commonwealth, or on the wills of each individual member, as it does in a faction, or in several factions allied together. To have servants, therefore, is power, and to have friends is power, because they are strengths united.

Wealth joined with generosity is also power, because it wins friends and servants. Without generosity it is not, because then it offers no defence; instead it exposes its owner to envy, like a prey.

A reputation for power is itself power, because it draws to its possessor the allegiance of those who need protection.

The same holds, and for the same reason, of a reputation for loving one's country, which is called popularity.

Likewise, any quality that makes a man loved or feared by many, or merely the reputation for such a quality, is power, because it is a means of obtaining the help and service of many.

Success is power, because it creates a reputation for wisdom or good fortune, which makes men either fear the successful man or rely on him.

Courtesy in men who already hold power increases their power, because it gains them love.

A reputation for prudence in the conduct of peace or war is power, because we entrust the government of ourselves to prudent men more willingly than to others.

Noble birth is power, though not everywhere: only in those commonwealths where it carries privileges, since its power consists in those privileges.

Eloquence is power, because it has the appearance of prudence.

Physical beauty is power, because, being a promise of good, it recommends a man to the favour of women and strangers.

The sciences are only a small power. They are not conspicuous, and so are not recognized in anyone who has them. Indeed they exist in only a few men, and in those few only with respect to a few things. For science is of such a nature that no one can perceive it in another unless he has himself attained a good measure of it.

The practical arts of public use, such as fortification and the making of siege engines and other instruments of war, are power, because they contribute to defence and victory. Their true mother is science, namely mathematics. Yet because they are brought into the light by the hands of the craftsman, they are regarded as his offspring, in the same way that common people take the midwife for the mother.

### Worth

The value or worth of a man, as of all other things, is his price: that is, the amount that would be paid for the use of his power. It is therefore not absolute, but depends on the need and judgement of someone else. A capable commander of soldiers commands a high price when war is under way or imminent, but not in peacetime. A learned and incorruptible judge is worth a great deal in peace, but much less in war. And with men, as with other things, it is not the seller but the buyer who sets the price. A man may rate himself at the highest value he can, as most men do; yet his true value is no more than others judge it to be.

The outward expression of the value we set on one another is what is commonly called honouring and dishonouring. To value a man at a high rate is to honour him; to value him at a low rate is to dishonour him. But high and low must be understood here by comparison with the rate at which each man values himself.

### Dignity

A man's public worth, the value the commonwealth sets on him, is what men commonly call dignity. The commonwealth expresses this valuation through offices of command, judicial posts, and public employment, or through names and titles introduced to mark distinctions of such value.

### To Honour and Dishonour

To ask another for help of any kind is to honour him, because it is a sign that we believe he has the power to help; and the more difficult the help, the greater the honour.

To obey is to honour, because no one obeys those whom he believes have no power to help or hurt him. Consequently, to disobey is to dishonour.

To give a man great gifts is to honour him, because it amounts to buying protection and acknowledging power. To give him small gifts is to dishonour him, because that is merely alms, and signals the opinion that he needs only small help. To be diligent in promoting another's good, and also to flatter him, is to honour him, as a sign that we seek his protection or aid. To neglect him is to dishonour him.

To yield place or give way to another in pursuit of any advantage is to honour him, since it is a confession of his greater power. To claim precedence for oneself is to dishonour him.

To show any sign of love or fear toward another is to honour him, for both loving and fearing are forms of valuing. To treat him with contempt, or to love or fear him less than he expects, is to dishonour him, for that is to undervalue him.

To praise a man, to extol him, or to call him happy is to honour him, because nothing is valued but goodness, power, and happiness. To revile him, mock him, or pity him is to dishonour him.

To speak to another with consideration, and to appear before him with decency and humility, is to honour him, since these are signs of a fear of giving offence. To speak to him rashly, or to do anything in his presence that is obscene, slovenly, or impudent, is to dishonour him.

To believe, trust, and rely on another is to honour him, as a sign of our opinion of his virtue and power. To distrust him or disbelieve him is to dishonour him.

To listen attentively to a man's counsel or conversation, of whatever kind, is to honour him, as a sign that we think him wise, eloquent, or witty. To fall asleep, walk out, or talk while he is speaking is to dishonour him.

To do for another those things that he takes as signs of honour, or that law or custom has made such, is to honour him, because in approving the honour others pay him, we acknowledge the power they acknowledge. To refuse to do them is to dishonour him.

To agree with a man's opinion is to honour him, as a sign that we approve his judgement and wisdom. To disagree is to dishonour him, and to reproach him with error; and if the disagreement covers many things, to reproach him with folly.

To imitate a man is to honour him, for imitation is the strongest form of approval. To imitate his enemy is to dishonour him.

To honour those whom another honours is to honour him, as a sign that we approve his judgement. To honour his enemies is to dishonour him.

To employ a man in giving counsel, or in difficult undertakings, is to honour him, as a sign of our opinion of his wisdom or some other power. To deny such employment to those who seek it is to dishonour them.

All these ways of honouring are natural, and they exist both inside commonwealths and outside them. But within commonwealths, where the person or persons holding supreme authority can make anything they please stand as a sign of honour, there are other honours as well.

A sovereign honours a subject with whatever title, office, employment, or action he chooses to have taken as a sign of his will to honour him.

The King of Persia honoured Mordecai by ordering that he be led through the streets in the king's own garment, on one of the king's horses, with a crown on his head and a prince walking before him proclaiming, "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honour." Yet another King of Persia, or perhaps the same king on another occasion, when a man asked, as a reward for some great service, to wear one of the king's robes, gave him permission to do so, but added that he should wear it as the king's fool; and then it was a dishonour. Such, then, is civil honour: magistracies, offices, titles, and in some places painted coats of arms and escutcheons. Men honour those who possess them as having so many signs of favour in the commonwealth, and that favour is power.

Whatever possession, action, or quality is evidence and a sign of power is honourable.

Therefore to be honoured, loved, or feared by many is honourable, as evidence of power. To be honoured by few or none is dishonourable.

Good fortune, if it lasts, is honourable, as a sign of the favour of God. Bad fortune and losses are dishonourable. Wealth is honourable, for it is power; poverty is dishonourable. Magnanimity, generosity, hope, courage, and confidence are honourable, because they spring from a consciousness of one's own power. Faintheartedness, stinginess, fear, and self-distrust are dishonourable.

Timely resolution, deciding promptly what one is to do, is honourable, because it shows contempt for small difficulties and dangers. Irresolution is dishonourable, as a sign that a man places too much value on small obstacles and small advantages. When a man has weighed his options for as long as time allows and still cannot decide, the difference in weight between them must be slight; if he still does not resolve, he is overvaluing little things, and that is faintheartedness.

All actions and speech that spring, or appear to spring, from great experience, knowledge, discretion, or wit are honourable, for all these are powers. Actions or words that spring from error, ignorance, or folly are dishonourable.

Gravity of manner is honourable so far as it seems to come from a mind occupied with something else, because being occupied is a sign of power. But if it seems to come from a deliberate wish to appear grave, it is dishonourable. The gravity of the first kind is like the steadiness of a ship laden with merchandise, which rides steady because it carries valuable cargo; the gravity of the second is like the steadiness of a ship ballasted with sand and other rubbish, which rides steady only because it has been weighted down with worthless material.

To be conspicuous, that is, to be known for wealth, office, great deeds, or any other eminent good, is honourable, as a sign of the power for which one is conspicuous. Obscurity, on the contrary, is dishonourable.

To be descended from conspicuous parents is honourable, because such descendants more easily obtain the help and the friends of their ancestors. To be descended from obscure parents, on the contrary, is dishonourable.

Actions that spring from fairness and involve a loss to oneself are honourable, as signs of magnanimity, for magnanimity is a sign of power. On the contrary, craftiness, evasion, and disregard of fairness are dishonourable.

Nor does it make any difference to honour whether an action is just or unjust, provided it is great and difficult and therefore a sign of much power, for honour consists solely in the opinion of power. That is why the ancient pagans did not believe they were dishonouring their gods, but greatly honouring them, when they portrayed them in their poems committing rapes, thefts, and other great but unjust or unclean acts. Nothing is so much celebrated in Jupiter as his adulteries, nor in Mercury as his frauds and thefts. In a hymn of Homer, the greatest of the praises bestowed on Mercury is that, having been born in the morning, he had invented music by noon, and before nightfall had stolen the cattle of Apollo from his herdsmen.

Among men, likewise, until great commonwealths had been established, it was considered no dishonour to be a pirate or a highway robber. These were regarded rather as lawful trades, not only among the Greeks but among all other nations, as the histories of ancient times make plain. And at the present day, in this part of the world, private duels are honourable, though unlawful, and always will be until honour is decreed for those who refuse a challenge and disgrace for those who issue one. For duels are often the effects of courage, and the ground of courage is always strength or skill, both of which are power. Even so, most duels arise from rash speech and from the fear of dishonour in one or both of the combatants, who, having committed themselves through rashness, are driven into the lists, the enclosed field of combat, to avoid disgrace.

Hereditary escutcheons and coats of arms are honourable where they carry significant privileges, and otherwise are not, for their power consists either in such privileges, or in wealth, or in something of the kind that is equally honoured in other men. This kind of honour, commonly called gentry, derives from the ancient Germans. Nothing of the sort was ever known where German customs were unknown, and it is not in use anywhere today where Germans have not settled. The ancient Greek commanders, when they went to war, had their shields painted with whatever designs they pleased, so that an unpainted shield was a mark of poverty and of a common soldier; but they did not pass these designs down by inheritance. The Romans did pass down the marks of their families, but these were the portrait images of their ancestors, not their emblems. Among the peoples of Asia, Africa, and America there is not, and never was, any such custom. The Germans alone had it, and from them it passed into England, France, Spain, and Italy, when they came in great numbers either to aid the Romans or to make their own conquests in these western parts of the world.

Germany, like every other country in its beginnings, was anciently divided among an infinite number of petty lords, or heads of families, who were continually at war with one another. These lords painted their armour, their escutcheon, or their coat with the picture of some beast or other object, and also placed some prominent, visible mark on the crest of their helmets. They did so chiefly so that, when they were covered in armour, their followers could recognize them, and partly for ornament. These decorations of arms and crest passed by inheritance to their children: to the eldest son unaltered, and to the others with some mark of difference, as the old master, in Dutch the *Here-alt*, saw fit. But when many such families joined together to form a greater monarchy, this duty of the herald, to distinguish escutcheons, was made into a separate office of its own. The descendants of these lords make up the great and ancient gentry, whose arms for the most part bear living creatures known for courage and predation, or castles, battlements, belts, weapons, bars, palisades, and other emblems of war, since at that time nothing was held in honour but military virtue. Later, not only kings but popular commonwealths granted various kinds of escutcheons to those who went to war or returned from it, as encouragement or as reward for their service. An observant reader may find all this in those ancient Greek and Latin histories that mention the German nation and its customs in their day.

### Titles of Honour

Titles of honour, such as duke, count, marquis, and baron, are honourable, as signifying the value set on their holders by the sovereign power of the commonwealth. In former times these were titles of office and command, some derived from the Romans, others from the Germans and the French. Dukes, in Latin *duces*, were generals in war. Counts, *comites*, were those who accompanied the general out of friendship and were left behind to govern and defend places that had been conquered and pacified. Marquises, *marchiones*, were counts who governed the marches, or borders, of the empire. These titles of duke, count, and marquis entered the Roman Empire around the time of Constantine the Great, from the customs of the German military. Baron, however, seems to have been a title of the Gauls, signifying a great man, such as the men whom kings or princes employed in war about their own persons. It appears to derive from the Latin *vir*, which became *ber* and *bar*, words that meant the same in the language of the Gauls as *vir* meant in Latin, and from these came *bero* and *baro*; so that such men were called *berones*, later *barones*, and in Spanish *varones*. Anyone who wishes to know the origin of titles of honour in more detail may find it, as I have, in Mr. Selden's most excellent treatise on the subject. Over time these offices of honour, prompted by periods of disorder and for the sake of good and peaceable government, were converted into mere titles, which served for the most part to distinguish the precedence, rank, and order of subjects within the commonwealth. Men were made dukes, counts, marquises, and barons of places in which they had neither possessions nor command, and other titles were devised for the same purpose.

### Worthiness and Fitness

Worthiness is something different from a man's worth or value, and different also from his merit or desert. It consists in a particular power or ability for the thing of which he is said to be worthy, and this particular ability is usually called fitness, or aptitude.

The man most worthy to be a commander, a judge, or to hold any other charge is the one best equipped with the qualities needed to perform it well; and the man most worthy of wealth is the one who has the qualities most necessary for using it well. Even if any one of these qualities is lacking, a man may nonetheless be a worthy man, and valuable for something else. Again, a man may be worthy of wealth, office, and employment and yet be unable to claim any right to them ahead of another, and therefore cannot be said to merit or deserve them. For merit presupposes a right, and presupposes that the thing deserved is owed by promise. I shall say more of this later, when I come to speak of contracts.

## Chapter XI. Of the Difference of Manners

### What Is Meant Here by Manners

By "manners" I do not mean decency of behavior: how one person should greet another, how one should rinse one's mouth or pick one's teeth in company, or any of the other points of what might be called the minor morals. I mean those qualities of humankind that bear on living together in peace and unity. To that end, we must recognize that happiness in this life does not consist in the repose of a satisfied mind. There is no such thing as the *finis ultimus* (the ultimate aim) or the *summum bonum* (the greatest good) described in the books of the old moral philosophers. A man whose desires have come to an end can no more live than one whose senses and imagination have come to a standstill. Happiness is a continual progress of desire from one object to another, and attaining the first is only the path to the next. The reason is that the object of a person's desire is not to enjoy something once, for a single instant, but to secure forever the path to his future desires. Consequently, the voluntary actions and inclinations of all men aim not only at obtaining a contented life but also at securing it. They differ only in method. That difference arises partly from the diversity of passions in different people, and partly from differences in the knowledge or opinion each person has of the causes that produce the effect he desires.

### A Restless Desire for Power in All Men

So I put forward, in the first place, as a general inclination of all mankind, a perpetual and restless desire for power after power, which ceases only in death. The cause of this is not always that a person hopes for a more intense pleasure than he has already attained, or that he cannot be content with moderate power. It is that he cannot secure the power and means to live well that he already has without acquiring more. This is why kings, whose power is greatest, direct their efforts toward securing it at home through laws and abroad through wars. And when that is done, a new desire follows: in some, a desire for fame from fresh conquests; in others, for ease and sensual pleasure; in others, for admiration, or for being flattered for excellence in some art or other ability of the mind.

### Love of Contention, from Competition

Competition for riches, honor, command, or any other form of power inclines men to contention, enmity, and war, because the way for one competitor to attain his desire is to kill, subdue, supplant, or drive off the other. Competition for praise in particular inclines men to revere antiquity. Men compete with the living, not with the dead, and so they credit the dead with more than they are due in order to obscure the glory of their living rivals.

### Civil Obedience, from Love of Ease

The desire for ease and sensual delight disposes men to obey a common power, because anyone with such desires gives up the protection he might have hoped to win through his own industry and labor.

### From Fear of Death or Wounds

Fear of death and of wounds disposes men in the same direction, and for the same reason. By contrast, needy and hardy men who are discontented with their present condition, along with all men ambitious for military command, are inclined to keep the causes of war alive and to stir up trouble and sedition. There is no military honor except through war, and no better hope of mending a losing hand at cards than by forcing a new shuffle.

### And from Love of the Arts

The desire for knowledge and for the arts of peace inclines men to obey a common power. Such a desire includes a desire for leisure, and therefore for protection by some power other than their own.

### Love of Virtue, from Love of Praise

The desire for praise disposes men to praiseworthy actions, meaning those that please the people whose judgment they value, for we scorn the praise of those we scorn. The desire for fame after death has the same effect. After death, it is true, we have no sense of the praise given us on earth, since such joys are either swallowed up in the unspeakable joys of Heaven or extinguished in the extreme torments of Hell. Yet such fame is not worthless. Men take present delight in foreseeing it, and in foreseeing the benefit it may bring to their descendants. Though they do not see these things now, they imagine them, and whatever gives pleasure to the senses also gives pleasure to the imagination.

### Hatred, from the Difficulty of Repaying Great Benefits

To have received from someone we consider our equal greater benefits than we can hope to repay disposes us to counterfeit love while in reality harboring a secret hatred. It places a man in the position of a desperate debtor who avoids the sight of his creditor and silently wishes him somewhere he would never have to see him again. Benefits create obligation, and obligation is a form of bondage, which is hateful when it is owed to an equal. To receive benefits from someone we acknowledge as our superior, however, inclines us to love, because the obligation does not lower us any further than we already stood. Cheerful acceptance, which men call gratitude, is regarded as so great an honor to the benefactor that it is generally taken as repayment. To receive benefits even from an equal or an inferior also disposes us to love, so long as there is hope of repaying them. In the receiver's mind the obligation is one of mutual aid and service, and from it arises a rivalry over who can outdo the other in kindness. This is the noblest and most profitable contest possible, in which the victor is pleased with his victory and the loser takes his revenge by acknowledging it.

### And from Consciousness of Deserving to Be Hated

To have done someone more harm than one can or will make amends for inclines the wrongdoer to hate his victim. He must expect either revenge or forgiveness, and both are hateful.

### Readiness to Harm, from Fear

Fear of oppression disposes a man either to strike first or to seek help through alliance with others, since there is no other way for him to secure his life and liberty.

### And from Distrust of One's Own Wit

Men who distrust their own cleverness are better placed to win in times of tumult and sedition than those who think themselves wise or cunning. The clever love to deliberate, while the others, fearing to be outmaneuvered, strike first. And in sedition, where men are always on the edge of battle, holding together and using every advantage of force is a better strategy than anything cleverness can devise.

### Vain Undertakings, from Vainglory

Some vainglorious men enjoy imagining themselves as gallant figures without any real awareness of great ability in themselves. These men are inclined only to display, not to action, because when danger or difficulty appears, they expect nothing except to have their inadequacy exposed.

Other vainglorious men estimate their ability by the flattery of others, or by the good fortune of some earlier action, without any solid ground for hope in a true knowledge of themselves. These men are inclined to rush into engagements and then, as danger or difficulty approaches, to withdraw if they can. Seeing no safe way through, they would rather risk their honor, which can be patched up with an excuse, than their lives, for which no remedy suffices.

### Ambition, from an Opinion of One's Own Ability

Men who hold a high opinion of their own wisdom in matters of government are disposed to ambition, because without public employment as counselors or magistrates, the honor due to their wisdom is lost. Eloquent speakers are therefore inclined to ambition, since eloquence looks like wisdom, both to themselves and to others.

### Irresolution, from Valuing Small Matters Too Highly

Pusillanimity, or smallness of mind, disposes men to irresolution, and consequently to miss the occasions and most fitting opportunities for action. If men have deliberated until the moment for action arrives and it is still not clear what is best to do, that is a sign that the motives on either side differ only slightly. To fail to decide at that point is therefore to lose the opportunity by weighing trifles, and that is pusillanimity.

Frugality, though a virtue in poor men, makes a man unfit to accomplish actions that require the strength of many people at once. It weakens their effort, which needs to be nourished and kept vigorous by reward.

### Confidence in Others, from Ignorance of the Marks of Wisdom and Kindness

Eloquence combined with flattery disposes men to trust those who possess them, because the first is apparent wisdom and the second apparent kindness. Add military reputation to these, and men are disposed to attach themselves and submit to those who have all three. The first two reassure them against danger from the man himself, and the last reassures them against danger from others.

### And from Ignorance of Natural Causes

A lack of science, that is, ignorance of causes, disposes, or rather compels, a man to rely on the advice and authority of others. Everyone concerned with the truth of a matter must, if he does not rely on his own opinion, rely on the opinion of someone else whom he believes wiser than himself and who, as far as he can see, has no reason to deceive him.

### And from Lack of Understanding

Ignorance of the meaning of words, which is a lack of understanding, disposes men to accept on trust not only the truths they do not know but also the errors, and worse still, the nonsense of those they trust. Without a thorough understanding of words, neither error nor nonsense can be detected.

The same ignorance explains why men give different names to one and the same thing according to their own passions. Those who approve of a private opinion call it opinion, and those who dislike it call it heresy. Yet "heresy" means nothing more than private opinion, only with a stronger tinge of anger.

It also explains why men cannot distinguish, without study and great understanding, between one action performed by many men and many actions performed by a multitude. An example is the difference between the single action of the entire Roman Senate in killing Catiline and the many separate actions of a number of senators in killing Caesar. Men are therefore disposed to treat as the action of the people what is really a multitude of actions done by a multitude of men, led perhaps by the persuasion of a single one.

### Adherence to Custom, from Ignorance of the Nature of Right and Wrong

Ignorance of the causes and original constitution of right, equity, law, and justice disposes a man to make custom and example the rule of his actions. He comes to think unjust whatever it has been customary to punish, and just whatever he can cite an example of going unpunished and approved. Lawyers, who use only this false measure of justice, barbarously call such an example a "precedent." Such men are like small children who have no rule of good and bad behavior except the correction they receive from their parents and teachers, with one difference: children are constant to their rule, while men are not. Having grown strong and stubborn, men appeal from custom to reason and from reason to custom, whichever suits their purpose. They abandon custom when their interest requires it and set themselves against reason whenever reason is against them. This is why the doctrine of right and wrong is perpetually disputed, both by the pen and by the sword, while the doctrine of lines and figures is not. In geometry men do not care what the truth is, because it crosses no one's ambition, profit, or lust. I have no doubt that if it had been contrary to any man's right of dominion, or to the interest of those who hold dominion, that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two angles of a square, which is to say two right angles, then that doctrine would have been suppressed by the burning of every book of geometry, as far as the interested party was able, even if it had not been disputed.

### Adherence to Private Men, from Ignorance of the Causes of Peace

Ignorance of remote causes disposes men to attribute every event to its immediate and instrumental causes, since these are the only causes they perceive. Hence everywhere, men who resent their payments to the state vent their anger on the publicans. These are the tax farmers, private contractors who bought the right to collect revenue, along with the collectors and other officers of the public revenue. Such men attach themselves to those who find fault with the government.
