Then, having committed themselves beyond any hope of justification, they turn on the supreme authority itself, out of fear of punishment or shame at receiving a pardon.

### Credulity, from Ignorance of Nature

Ignorance of natural causes disposes a man to credulity, so that he often believes impossible things. Such people know nothing to the contrary, and since they cannot detect the impossibility, for all they know the thing may be true. Credulity in turn disposes men to lie, because men love to be listened to in company. So ignorance by itself, without any malice, can make a man both believe lies and tell them, and sometimes invent them as well.

### Curiosity to Know, from Concern for the Future

Anxiety about the future disposes men to inquire into the causes of things, because knowing them makes men better able to arrange the present to their best advantage.

### Natural Religion, from the Same

Curiosity, or love of the knowledge of causes, draws a man from considering an effect to seeking its cause, and then the cause of that cause, until he must finally arrive at the thought that there is some cause which has no prior cause but is eternal. This is what men call God. It is therefore impossible to make any deep inquiry into natural causes without being inclined to believe that there is one eternal God, even though men cannot hold in their minds any idea of him that corresponds to his nature. Consider a man born blind who hears others talk of warming themselves by the fire and is brought to warm himself by it. He can easily conceive, and assure himself, that there is something there that people call fire and that causes the heat he feels. Yet he cannot imagine what it looks like, nor have an idea of it in his mind such as those who see it possess. In the same way, from the visible things of this world and their admirable order, a man may conceive that there is a cause of them, which men call God, and yet have no idea or image of him in his mind.

Those who make little or no inquiry into the natural causes of things are still inclined to suppose and invent for themselves various kinds of invisible powers. They do so out of the fear that arises from their very ignorance of what has the power to do them great good or harm. They stand in awe of their own imaginations, invoke these powers in times of distress, and thank them when they expect success, making the creatures of their own fancy into their gods. In this way, out of the endless variety of fancy, men have created endless sorts of gods in the world. This fear of invisible things is the natural seed of what each person calls religion in himself, and superstition in those who worship or fear that power differently than he does.

This seed of religion has been observed by many. Some of those who observed it have been inclined to nourish it, cultivate it, and shape it into laws. To it they have added, of their own invention, whatever opinions about the causes of future events they thought would best enable them to govern others and make the greatest use of their own powers.

## Chapter XII. Of Religion

### Religion Exists in Humans Alone

Since the signs and fruits of religion appear in human beings and nowhere else, there is no reason to doubt that its seed also lies in humans alone. It must consist in some quality peculiar to us, or at least in some exceptional degree of a quality, that no other living creature possesses.

### First, From the Desire to Know Causes

First, it is peculiar to human nature to inquire into the causes of the events we witness. Some people do this more and some less, but all do it at least enough to be curious about the causes of their own good and bad fortune.

### From Reflecting on the Beginnings of Things

Second, whenever a person sees something that has a beginning, he also assumes it had a cause, which determined it to begin when it did rather than sooner or later.

### From Observing the Sequence of Things

Third, the only happiness of animals lies in enjoying their daily food, rest, and appetites. They have little or no foresight of the future, because they lack the observation and memory needed to grasp the order, sequence, and dependence of the things they see. A human being, by contrast, notices how one event has been produced by another and remembers what came before and what followed. When he cannot be certain of the true causes of things (for the causes of good and bad fortune are for the most part invisible), he supposes causes for them. These are either causes his own imagination suggests, or causes vouched for by others whom he takes to be his friends and wiser than himself.

### The Natural Cause of Religion: Anxiety About the Future

The first two of these produce anxiety. A person who is convinced that everything that has happened, or will happen, has a cause, and who is constantly striving to protect himself against the evils he fears and to secure the good he desires, cannot help living in perpetual concern about the future. Everyone, then, and especially those who are overly cautious about what lies ahead, is in a condition like that of Prometheus. Prometheus, whose name may be interpreted as "the Prudent Man," was chained to Mount Caucasus, a place commanding a wide view, where an eagle fed on his liver, devouring each day as much as grew back during the night. In the same way, the person who looks too far ahead, preoccupied with future time, has his heart gnawed all day long by the fear of death, poverty, or some other calamity, and finds no rest or pause from his anxiety except in sleep.

### Which Makes People Fear the Power of Invisible Things

This perpetual fear always accompanies humankind in its ignorance of causes, as if it were groping in the dark, and it must necessarily fix on some object. So when there is nothing visible to blame for their good or bad fortune, people blame some invisible power or agent. It was perhaps in this sense that some of the ancient poets said the gods were first created by human fear. Applied to the gods, meaning the many gods of the pagans, that statement is entirely true. But the acknowledgment of one God, eternal, infinite, and omnipotent, can more readily be traced to people's desire to know the causes of natural bodies, with their various properties and operations, than to their fear of what might befall them in the future. Suppose someone reasons from an effect he sees occur back to its next and immediate cause, and from there to the cause of that cause, plunging deep into the pursuit of causes. He will finally arrive at the conclusion that there must be (as even the pagan philosophers admitted) one First Mover: a first and eternal cause of all things, which is what people mean by the name of God. And he will reach it without any thought of his own fortune. Anxiety about fortune both inclines people to fear and keeps them from investigating the causes of other things, and so it gives rise to the invention of as many gods as there are people to invent them.

### And Suppose Them to Be Incorporeal

As for the matter or substance of these imagined invisible agents, natural reasoning could lead people to only one notion. They concluded that it was the same as the substance of the human soul, and that the human soul was made of the same substance as what appears in a dream to someone asleep, or in a mirror to someone awake. Not knowing that such apparitions are nothing but creatures of the imagination, people take them to be real, external substances. They therefore call them ghosts, just as the Romans called them *imagines* and *umbrae*, images and shades, and they consider them spirits, meaning thin, airy bodies. They supposed the invisible agents they feared to be like these, except that such agents could appear and vanish at will. But the opinion that such spirits were incorporeal, or immaterial, could never enter anyone's mind by nature. People can put together words of contradictory meaning, such as *spirit* and *incorporeal*, but they can never form an image of anything that corresponds to them. For this reason, those who arrive through their own reflection at the acknowledgment of one infinite, omnipotent, and eternal God prefer to confess that he is incomprehensible and beyond their understanding. They would rather do that than define his nature as "incorporeal spirit" and then admit that their definition is unintelligible. If they do give him such a title, they do so not dogmatically, intending to make the divine nature understood, but piously. Their aim is to honor him with attributes whose meanings lie as far as possible from the grossness of visible bodies.

### But Do Not Know How These Powers Bring Anything About

Next, there is the question of how people think these invisible agents produce their effects, that is, what immediate causes they use to bring things about. Those who do not understand what we call causation (which is to say, almost everyone) have only one rule to guess by. They observe and remember what they have seen precede a similar effect on some earlier occasion or occasions, without perceiving any dependence or connection at all between the earlier event and the later one. And so, from similar things in the past, they expect similar things in the future, and they hope for good or bad luck, superstitiously, from things that play no part whatever in causing it. Thus the Athenians, in their war at Lepanto, demanded another Phormio, the commander who had once won victories for them in those waters. The Pompeian faction, in their war in Africa, demanded another Scipio, because a Scipio had once conquered there. Others have done the same on many occasions since. In the same way, people attribute their fortune to a bystander, to a lucky or unlucky place, or to words spoken. They are especially inclined to do so if the name of God is among the words, as in charms and conjurations, the liturgy of witches. They go so far as to believe that such words have the power to turn a stone into bread, bread into a man, or anything into anything.

### But Honor Them as They Honor Men

Third, the worship that people naturally offer to invisible powers can consist only of the same expressions of reverence they would use toward other human beings. These include gifts, petitions, thanks, bodily submission, respectful forms of address, sober behavior, carefully considered words, and swearing by them, which means invoking them when assuring one another of their promises. Beyond this, reason suggests nothing. It leaves people either to stop there or, for any further ceremonies, to rely on those they believe to be wiser than themselves.

### And Attribute All Extraordinary Events to Them

Finally, people are naturally at a loss to say how these invisible powers reveal what will happen in the future, especially their good or bad fortune in general, or their success or failure in a particular undertaking. They have only one resource. Being accustomed to predict the future from the past, they are very prone to take chance occurrences, after one or two coincidences, as omens of the same outcome forever after. They are equally prone to believe similar omens from other people of whom they have once formed a good opinion.

### Four Things: The Natural Seeds of Religion

The natural seed of religion, then, consists in these four things: belief in ghosts, ignorance of secondary causes, devotion toward what people fear, and taking chance events for omens. Different people have different imaginations, judgments, and passions, and so this seed has grown into ceremonies so various that those practiced by one person are, for the most part, ridiculous to another.

### Made Different by Cultivation

These seeds have been cultivated by two kinds of people. The first kind have nourished and arranged them according to their own invention. The second have done so by God's command and direction. Both have done it with the aim of making those who relied on them more inclined to obedience, law, peace, charity, and civil society. The religion of the first kind is therefore a part of human politics, and teaches part of the duty that earthly kings require of their subjects. The religion of the second kind is divine politics, and contains precepts for those who have given themselves as subjects in the Kingdom of God. To the first kind belonged all the founders of commonwealths and the lawgivers of the pagans. To the second belonged Abraham, Moses, and our Blessed Saviour, through whom the laws of the Kingdom of God have come down to us.

### The Absurd Opinions of Paganism

Consider next that part of religion which consists of opinions about the nature of invisible powers. Almost nothing with a name has escaped being regarded by the pagans, in one place or another, as a god or a devil, or being imagined by their poets as animated, inhabited, or possessed by some spirit or other.

The unformed matter of the world was a god, called Chaos.

The heavens, the ocean, the planets, fire, the earth, and the winds were all so many gods.

Men, women, a bird, a crocodile, a calf, a dog, a snake, an onion, and a leek were deified. Besides this, they filled nearly every place with spirits called daemons. They filled the plains with Pan and his kind, the Panises or satyrs; the woods with fauns and nymphs; the sea with tritons and other nymphs; and every river and spring with a ghost bearing its name, and with nymphs. Every house had its *lares*, or household spirits, and every man his *genius*, or guardian spirit. Hell held ghosts and spiritual officers such as Charon, Cerberus, and the Furies. At night every place was haunted by *larvae* and *lemures*, the ghosts of the dead, along with a whole kingdom of fairies and bugbears. They also ascribed divinity to, and built temples for, mere accidents and qualities, such as Time, Night, Day, Peace, Concord, Love, Strife, Virtue, Honor, Health, Rust, Fever, and the like. When they prayed for or against these things, they prayed to them, as if ghosts of those names hovered over their heads, letting fall or withholding the good or evil for which, or against which, they prayed. They invoked their own wit under the name of the Muses, their own ignorance under the name of Fortune, their own lust under the name of Cupid, their own rage under the name of the Furies, and their own private parts under the name of Priapus. They attributed their nocturnal emissions to incubi and succubi. In short, there was nothing a poet could introduce as a character in his poem that they did not make into either a god or a devil.

The same founders of pagan religion noticed the second ground of religion: people's ignorance of causes, and their consequent readiness to attribute their fortune to causes on which it plainly did not depend. They took the opportunity to impose on that ignorance, in place of secondary causes, a kind of secondary and subordinate gods. They ascribed the cause of fertility to Venus; the cause of the arts to Apollo; of cunning and craft to Mercury; of tempests and storms to Aeolus; and of other effects to other gods. As a result, there was among the pagans almost as great a variety of gods as of occupations.

People naturally considered certain forms of worship fitting toward their gods, namely offerings, prayers, thanks, and the rest already named. To these, the same pagan legislators added images, both painted and sculpted. Their purpose was that the more ignorant sort, which is to say the great majority of the people, would believe the gods these images represented were actually enclosed and, as it were, housed within them, and so would fear them all the more. They also endowed these idols with lands, houses, officers, and revenues, set apart from every other human use, which means consecrated and made holy to them. Such holdings included caverns, groves, woods, mountains, and entire islands. They attributed to the idols not only shapes, some of men, some of beasts, some of monsters, but also the faculties and passions of men and beasts: sense, speech, sex, lust, and procreation. This procreation took place among the gods themselves, propagating the race of gods. It also took place through unions with men and women, begetting hybrid gods who were mere lodgers in heaven, such as Bacchus, Hercules, and others. They attributed to them, besides, anger, revenge, and the other passions of living creatures, together with the actions that spring from them. These included fraud, theft, adultery, sodomy, and any vice that might be taken as an effect of power or a source of pleasure, indeed all those vices that among men are considered offenses against law rather than against honor.

Finally, there are the methods of foretelling the future. Natural foretelling is nothing but conjecture drawn from the experience of the past, and supernatural foretelling is divine revelation. To these, the same founders of pagan religion added countless other superstitious methods of divination, partly on the basis of pretended experience and partly on pretended revelation. They made people believe they could discover their fortunes in many places. Sometimes they sought them in the ambiguous or senseless answers of the priests at Delphi, Delos, Ammon, and other famous oracles. These answers were made ambiguous by design, so that the oracle could claim to be right whichever way events turned out. Or they were absurd because of the intoxicating vapors of the place, which are very common in sulfurous caverns. Sometimes people sought their fortunes in the leaves of the Sibyls, whose books of prophecy were held in high regard in the time of the Roman Republic. These prophecies were perhaps like those of Nostradamus, since the fragments that survive today seem to be the invention of later times. Sometimes they sought them in the meaningless speech of madmen, who were supposed to be possessed by a divine spirit. This possession they called enthusiasm, and these kinds of foretelling were called theomancy, or prophecy. Sometimes they looked to the position of the stars at the time of their birth, which was called horoscopy and considered part of judicial astrology. Sometimes they looked to their own hopes and fears, which was called thumomancy, or presage. Sometimes they relied on the predictions of witches who claimed to converse with the dead. This is called necromancy, conjuring, and witchcraft, and it is nothing but trickery and conspiring fraud. Sometimes they looked to the chance flight or feeding of birds, which was called augury; sometimes to the entrails of a sacrificed animal, which was haruspicy; sometimes to dreams; sometimes to the croaking of ravens or the chattering of birds. Sometimes they read the features of the face, which was called metoposcopy, or the lines of the hand, by palmistry. They also read chance remarks, called *omina*. Sometimes they looked to monsters and unusual occurrences, such as eclipses, comets, rare meteors, earthquakes, floods, deformed births, and the like. These they called *portenta* and *ostenta*, because they thought such things portended, or foreshowed, some great calamity to come. And sometimes they relied on pure chance: tossing a coin for heads or tails, counting the holes in a sieve, opening Homer or Virgil at random to a verse, and countless other such empty devices. So easily are people drawn to believe anything from those who have gained their trust and who can, with gentleness and skill, take hold of their fear and ignorance.

**The Designs of the Founders of Pagan Religion**

For this reason the first founders and lawgivers of commonwealths among the Gentiles, whose only aim was to keep the people obedient and at peace, everywhere took care to do three things. First, they impressed on the people the belief that the religious precepts they laid down did not spring from their own invention but were dictated by some god or other spirit, or else that they themselves were of a higher nature than ordinary mortals, so that their laws might be accepted more readily. Thus Numa Pompilius claimed to have received from the nymph Egeria the ceremonies he instituted among the Romans; the first king and founder of the kingdom of Peru claimed that he and his wife were children of the Sun; and Muhammad, to establish his new religion, claimed to hold conversations with the Holy Ghost in the form of a dove. Second, they made the people believe that the very things forbidden by the laws were also displeasing to the gods. Third, they prescribed ceremonies, prayers, sacrifices, and festivals by which, the people were to believe, the anger of the gods could be appeased. They taught that defeat in war, great epidemics, earthquakes, and every private misery came from the anger of the gods, and that this anger arose from neglect of their worship, or from forgetting or mistaking some point of the required ceremonies. Among the ancient Romans, it is true, no one was forbidden to deny what the poets wrote about punishments and rewards after this life, and several men of great authority and seriousness in that state openly mocked such stories in their public speeches. Yet that belief was always more encouraged than its opposite.

Through these and similar institutions they achieved their purpose, which was the peace of the commonwealth. When misfortune struck, the common people blamed it on neglect or error in their ceremonies, or on their own disobedience to the laws, and so were less inclined to rise up against their rulers. And entertained as they were by the pomp and amusement of festivals and public games held in honor of the gods, they needed nothing more than bread to keep them from discontent, grumbling, and agitation against the state. This is why the Romans, who had conquered most of the world then known, had no hesitation in tolerating any religion whatever in the city of Rome itself, unless it contained something incompatible with their civil government. Nor do we read that any religion was forbidden there except that of the Jews, who, being God's own particular kingdom, held it unlawful to acknowledge subjection to any mortal king or state at all. So it is plain that the religion of the Gentiles was a part of their statecraft.

**The True Religion and the Laws of God's Kingdom Are the Same**

But where God himself planted religion by supernatural revelation, he also established a kingdom peculiarly his own, and gave laws governing not only men's conduct toward himself but also their conduct toward one another. In the kingdom of God, therefore, statecraft and civil law are a part of religion, and the distinction between temporal and spiritual power has no place there. It is true that God is king of all the earth; yet he may also be king of a particular, chosen nation. There is no more inconsistency in this than in a general who commands an entire army also keeping a regiment or company of his own. God is king of all the earth by his power, but of his chosen people he is king by covenant. I have reserved a fuller treatment of the kingdom of God, both by nature and by covenant, for a later part of this discourse.

**The Causes of Change in Religion**

Once we understand how religion propagates, it is not hard to see what causes it to dissolve back into its first seeds, or principles. These are nothing more than the belief in a deity and in invisible, supernatural powers, a belief that can never be so thoroughly rooted out of human nature that new religions cannot spring from it again, cultivated by men who enjoy the reputation needed for that purpose.

Every established religion is founded, at the outset, on the faith that a multitude places in some one person, whom they believe to be not only wise and devoted to securing their happiness, but also holy, a man to whom God himself condescends to reveal his will by supernatural means. It follows necessarily that when those who govern a religion come to be suspected in their wisdom, their sincerity, or their love, or when they can show no plausible sign of divine revelation, the religion they wish to uphold will fall under suspicion as well, and, unless the fear of the civil sword restrains them, men will contradict and reject it.

**Commanding Belief in Impossibilities**

What destroys the reputation for wisdom of a man who founds a religion, or who adds to one already founded, is requiring belief in contradictions. Both halves of a contradiction cannot possibly be true, and so to command belief in both is a mark of ignorance. It exposes the author's ignorance on that point and discredits him in everything else he puts forward as supernatural revelation. A man may indeed receive revelation of many things above natural reason, but of nothing against it.

**Acting Contrary to the Religion They Establish**

What destroys the reputation for sincerity is doing or saying things that appear to be signs that the teachers do not themselves believe what they require others to believe. All such deeds and words are therefore called scandalous, because they are stumbling blocks that make men fall on the road of religion: injustice, cruelty, profanity, greed, and luxury. For who can believe that a man who habitually commits acts springing from any of these roots believes in any such invisible power to be feared as the one he uses to frighten other men over lesser faults?

What destroys the reputation for love is being caught pursuing private ends: when the belief they require of others leads, or seems to lead, to the acquisition of power, wealth, rank, or secure pleasure for themselves alone, or for themselves above all. For whatever men profit from personally, they are assumed to do for their own sake and not out of love for others.

**Lack of the Testimony of Miracles**

Finally, the only evidence men can give of a divine calling is the working of miracles, or true prophecy (which is itself a miracle), or extraordinary good fortune. Consequently, when certain points of religion have been received from those who worked such miracles, any further points added by people who do not prove their calling by some miracle win no greater belief than custom and the laws of the places where men are raised have instilled in them. For just as in natural matters men of judgment require natural signs and arguments, so in supernatural matters they require supernatural signs, that is, miracles, before they give their inward and heartfelt consent.

All these causes of the weakening of men's faith appear clearly in the following examples. First, there is the example of the children of Israel. Moses had proved his calling to them by miracles and by leading them safely out of Egypt; yet when he was absent for only forty days, they revolted from the worship of the true God whom he had commended to them and, as the Book of Exodus records, set up a golden calf as their god, relapsing into the idolatry of the Egyptians from whom they had so recently been delivered. And again, as the Book of Judges tells, after Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and the whole generation that had witnessed God's great works in Israel had died, another generation arose and served Baal. So when miracles failed, faith failed too.

Again, as the First Book of Samuel relates, when Samuel's sons, whom their father had appointed judges in Beersheba, took bribes and judged unjustly, the people of Israel refused to have God as their king any longer, except in the way he was king of other peoples, and they cried out to Samuel to choose them a king like those of the other nations. So when justice failed, faith failed too, so completely that they deposed their God from reigning over them.

When the Christian religion was first being planted, the oracles fell silent throughout the Roman Empire, and the number of Christians grew astonishingly, every day and in every place, through the preaching of the apostles and evangelists. A large part of that success may reasonably be attributed to the contempt into which the pagan priests of the time had brought themselves by their impurity, their greed, and their double-dealing among princes. The religion of the Church of Rome was likewise abolished in England and many other parts of Christendom partly for the same reason, since the failure of virtue in the pastors makes faith fail in the people. It was abolished partly, too, because the Schoolmen brought the philosophy and doctrine of Aristotle into religion, giving rise to so many contradictions and absurdities that the clergy acquired a reputation for both ignorance and fraudulent intent. This inclined people to revolt from them, either against the will of their own princes, as in France and Holland, or with their princes' consent, as in England.

Lastly, among the doctrines the Church of Rome has declared necessary for salvation, so many plainly work to the advantage of the Pope and of his spiritual subjects living in the territories of other Christian princes that, were it not for the rivalry among those princes, they could shut out all foreign authority without war or disturbance, as easily as it has been shut out in England. For who does not see whom it benefits to have people believe that a king does not hold his authority from Christ unless a bishop crowns him? That a king who is also a priest may not marry? That whether a prince was born in lawful marriage must be decided by authority from Rome? That subjects may be released from their allegiance if the court of Rome judges their king a heretic? That a king, like Chilperic of France, may be deposed by a pope, like Pope Zachary, for no cause at all, and his kingdom given to one of his subjects? That clergy and members of religious orders, in whatever country they live, shall be exempt from their king's jurisdiction in criminal cases? Or who does not see whose profit is advanced by the fees for private Masses and the payments for souls in purgatory, along with other signs of private interest that would be enough to deaden the most lively faith, if, as I said, the civil magistrate and custom did not sustain it more than any opinion people hold of the holiness, wisdom, or integrity of their teachers? I may therefore attribute all the changes of religion in the world to one and the same cause, and that is priests who have made themselves displeasing to the people, and not only among Catholics, but even in the church that has most presumed to call itself reformed.

## Chapter XIII. Of the Natural Condition of Mankind, as Concerning Their Felicity, and Misery

Nature has made human beings so equal in their faculties of body and mind that, although one person is sometimes plainly stronger in body or quicker in mind than another, the difference between them, taken all together, is not great enough for anyone to claim some advantage that another could not claim just as well. As for bodily strength, even the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest, either by secret plotting or by joining with others who face the same danger.

As for the faculties of the mind, I find an even greater equality among people than in strength. Here I set aside the arts that are built on words, and especially that skill of reasoning from general and infallible rules which we call science. Very few people possess it, and only in a few subjects, because it is neither a native faculty we are born with nor something we pick up, as we do prudence, while attending to other things. Prudence, by contrast, is simply experience, and equal stretches of time give experience equally to everyone in whatever they equally apply themselves to. What may make this equality seem incredible is nothing but a vain conceit of one's own wisdom. Almost everyone believes he has more of it than the common run of people, by which he means everyone except himself and a few others whom he approves of, either because of their reputation or because they agree with him. Such is human nature that, however readily people may admit that many others are wittier, more eloquent, or more learned, they will hardly believe that many are as wise as they are, since they see their own intelligence up close and other people's only from a distance. Yet this proves that people are equal on this point rather than unequal, for there is usually no better sign that something has been evenly distributed than that everyone is content with his share.

### From Equality Comes Distrust

From this equality of ability arises an equality of hope in reaching our goals. If two people therefore desire the same thing, which they cannot both enjoy, they become enemies. On the way to their goal, which is chiefly their own preservation and sometimes merely their pleasure, each tries to destroy or subdue the other. It follows that wherever an invader has nothing more to fear than the power of a single person, anyone who plants, sows, builds, or holds a desirable piece of land can expect others to arrive with combined forces to dispossess him, robbing him not only of the fruit of his labor but of his life or liberty as well. And the invader, in turn, stands in the same danger from someone else.

### From Distrust Comes War

Given this mutual distrust, no way of securing oneself is so reasonable as anticipation: that is, using force or cunning to master the persons of as many others as one can, until one sees no other power great enough to threaten oneself. This is no more than self-preservation requires, and it is generally permitted. Moreover, some people take pleasure in contemplating their own power in acts of conquest and pursue those acts further than their safety requires. Consequently, others who would gladly live at ease within modest limits could not survive for long by standing only on the defensive; they too must increase their power by invasion. And since such an increase of dominion over others is necessary for a person's preservation, it ought to be permitted him.

Furthermore, people take no pleasure, and on the contrary a great deal of grief, in keeping company where there is no power able to overawe them all. Every person expects his companion to value him at the same rate he sets on himself. At every sign of contempt or undervaluing, he naturally tries, as far as he dares, to extort a higher valuation: from those who scorn him, by doing them harm, and from everyone else, by the example. Among people who have no common power to keep them quiet, "as far as he dares" is far enough to make them destroy one another.

So in human nature we find three principal causes of quarrel: first, competition; second, distrust; third, glory.

The first makes people attack for gain, the second for safety, and the third for reputation. The first use violence to make themselves masters of other people's persons, wives, children, and livestock; the second, to defend these things; the third, over trifles, such as a word, a smile, a difference of opinion, or any other sign of undervaluing, whether aimed directly at themselves or reflected onto their relatives, friends, nation, profession, or name.

### Outside Civil States There Is Always War of Everyone Against Everyone

It is plain from this that as long as people live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in the condition called war, and it is a war of every person against every person. War does not consist only in battle or the act of fighting. It consists in a stretch of time during which the will to settle matters by battle is sufficiently known. The notion of time must therefore be considered in the nature of war, as it is in the nature of weather. Foul weather does not lie in a shower or two of rain but in a tendency toward rain over many days together. In the same way, the nature of war consists not in actual fighting but in the known disposition to fight, throughout all the time that there is no assurance to the contrary. All other time is peace.

### The Hardships of Such a War

Whatever follows from a time of war, when every person is the enemy of every other, follows equally from a time when people live with no security except what their own strength and ingenuity can provide. In such a condition there is no room for industry, because its fruits are uncertain. Consequently there is no cultivation of the land; no navigation, and no use of goods that might be imported by sea; no comfortable buildings; no machinery for moving and lifting things that require great force; no knowledge of the face of the earth; no reckoning of time; no arts; no letters; no society; and, worst of all, continual fear and danger of violent death. And the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.

Someone who has not weighed these matters carefully may find it strange that nature should set people apart in this way and make them inclined to attack and destroy one another. Not trusting an inference drawn from the passions, he may want to see it confirmed by experience. Let him, then, consider his own conduct. When he sets out on a journey, he arms himself and tries to travel in good company. When he goes to sleep, he locks his doors. Even inside his own house, he locks his chests. And he does all this knowing that there are laws, and armed public officers, to avenge any injury done to him. What opinion does he hold of his fellow subjects when he rides armed, of his fellow citizens when he locks his doors, and of his children and servants when he locks his chests? Does he not accuse mankind as much by his actions as I do by my words? Yet neither of us accuses human nature itself. The desires and other passions of human beings are not in themselves sins. Neither are the actions that spring from those passions, until people know of a law that forbids them. They cannot know of such a law until laws have been made, and no law can be made until they have agreed on the person who is to make it.

It may perhaps be thought that there never was such a time or condition of war as this. I believe it was never generally so throughout the whole world, but there are many places where people live this way now. The native peoples in many parts of America, apart from the governance of small families, whose harmony depends on natural desire, have no government at all and live to this day in the brutish manner I have described. In any case, one can see what sort of life there would be where there was no common power to fear by observing the life into which people who once lived under a peaceful government tend to degenerate during a civil war.

But even if there had never been a time when individual people were in a condition of war against one another, kings and other holders of sovereign authority have, in every age, lived in continual jealousy because of their independence. They stand in the posture of gladiators, weapons drawn and eyes fixed on one another: that is, with their forts, garrisons, and guns on the frontiers of their kingdoms and their spies constantly watching their neighbors. This is a posture of war. Yet because they thereby protect the industry of their subjects, it does not bring with it the misery that accompanies the unchecked liberty of individuals.

### In Such a War, Nothing Is Unjust

A further consequence follows from this war of every person against every person: nothing can be unjust. The notions of right and wrong, justice and injustice, have no place there. Where there is no common power, there is no law, and where there is no law, there is no injustice. In war, force and fraud are the two cardinal virtues. Justice and injustice are not faculties of either the body or the mind. If they were, they could exist in a person who was alone in the world, just as his senses and passions do. They are qualities that belong to people living in society, not in solitude. It is a further consequence of this same condition that there is no property, no dominion, no clear distinction between mine and yours; each person owns only what he can seize, and only for as long as he can keep it. So much, then, for the wretched condition in which mere nature actually places human beings, though they have the possibility of escaping it, a possibility that rests partly on their passions and partly on their reason.

### The Passions That Incline People Toward Peace

The passions that incline people toward peace are fear of death, desire for the things necessary to a comfortable life, and hope of obtaining them through their own industry. And reason suggests suitable articles of peace on which people may be brought to agree. These articles are what are otherwise called the laws of nature, which I shall discuss in more detail in the next two chapters.

## Chapter XIV. Of the First and Second Natural Laws, and of Contracts

### What the Right of Nature Is

The right of nature, which writers commonly call *jus naturale*, is the liberty each man has to use his own power as he himself wills for the preservation of his own nature, that is, of his own life. It follows that he has the liberty to do anything that, in his own judgment and reason, he conceives to be the most suitable means to that end.

### What Liberty Is

By liberty, in the proper sense of the word, is meant the absence of external impediments. Such impediments may often take away part of a man's power to do what he wants, but they cannot prevent him from using whatever power remains to him, as his judgment and reason direct.

### What a Law of Nature Is

A law of nature (*lex naturalis*) is a precept, or general rule, discovered by reason. It forbids a man to do what is destructive of his life or what takes away the means of preserving it, and it forbids him to neglect what he thinks will best preserve it. Those who write on this subject tend to confuse *jus* and *lex*, right and law, but the two ought to be kept distinct. Right consists in the liberty to do or to refrain from doing, whereas law determines and binds a man to one or the other. Law and right therefore differ as much as obligation and liberty, which cannot coexist with respect to one and the same matter.

### By Nature Every Man Has a Right to Everything

As the previous chapter showed, the natural condition of mankind is a war of every man against every man. In that condition each person is governed by his own reason, and there is nothing he can make use of that might not help him preserve his life against his enemies. It follows that in such a condition every man has a right to everything, even to another man's body. So for as long as this natural right of every man to everything endures, no man can be secure of living out the span of life that nature ordinarily allows, however strong or wise he may be.

### The Fundamental Law of Nature

It is therefore a precept, or general rule of reason, "that every man ought to strive for peace, so far as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek and use all the help and advantages of war." The first branch of this rule contains the first and fundamental law of nature, which is "to seek peace, and follow it." The second branch contains the sum of the right of nature, which is "by all means we can, to defend ourselves."

### The Second Law of Nature

From this fundamental law of nature, which commands men to strive for peace, a second law is derived: "that a man be willing, when others are willing too, to lay down this right to all things, so far as he judges necessary for peace and for his own defense, and to be content with as much liberty against other men as he would allow other men against himself." For as long as every man holds on to his right to do whatever he pleases, all men remain in the condition of war. But if other men will not lay down their right as he does, then there is no reason for anyone to strip himself of his own. That would be to offer himself up as prey, which no man is obliged to do, rather than to dispose himself toward peace. This is the law of the Gospel: "Whatsoever you require that others should do to you, that do ye to them." It is also the law recognized by all mankind: *Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris*, "What you would not have done to you, do not do to another."

### What It Is to Lay Down a Right

To lay down one's right to something is to give up the liberty of hindering another from enjoying the benefit of his own right to that same thing. A man who renounces or passes away his right does not give anyone a right he did not already have, since by nature every man has a right to everything. He merely stands out of the other's way, so that the other may enjoy his own original right without hindrance from him, though not without hindrance from anyone else. The only effect one man gains from another man's surrender of right is therefore a corresponding reduction in the obstacles to the use of his own original right.

### Renouncing and Transferring Right; Obligation, Duty, Injustice

A right is set aside either by simply renouncing it or by transferring it to another. A man simply renounces a right when he does not care who receives the benefit of it, and he transfers it when he intends the benefit for some particular person or persons. When a man has abandoned or granted away his right in either manner, he is said to be obliged, or bound, not to hinder those to whom the right has been granted or abandoned from enjoying its benefit. He ought not, and it is his duty not to, nullify that voluntary act of his own. Any such hindrance is injustice and injury, because it is done *sine jure*, without right, the right having already been renounced or transferred. Injury or injustice in the disputes of the world is thus something like what scholars in their debates call absurdity. In debate it is called an absurdity to contradict what one maintained at the outset, and in the same way it is called injustice and injury in the world to voluntarily undo what one had voluntarily done at the outset. A man simply renounces or transfers his right by declaring or signifying, through some voluntary and sufficient sign or signs, that he does so renounce or transfer it, or has done so, to the one who accepts it. These signs consist of words alone, or of actions alone, or, as most often happens, of both words and actions. They are the bonds by which men are bound and obligated. The strength of these bonds comes not from their own nature, since nothing is more easily broken than a man's word, but from fear of some harmful consequence should they be broken.

### Not All Rights Are Alienable

Whenever a man transfers or renounces his right, he does so either in return for some right transferred reciprocally to himself or for some other good he hopes to gain by it. It is a voluntary act, and the object of every man's voluntary acts is some good to himself. There are therefore some rights that no man can be understood, by any words or other signs, to have abandoned or transferred. First, a man cannot lay down the right to resist those who attack him by force to take his life, because he cannot be understood to aim at any good to himself by doing so. The same may be said of wounds, chains, and imprisonment, for two reasons. No benefit follows from submitting to such treatment oneself, as benefit may follow from patiently allowing someone else to be wounded or imprisoned. And when a man sees others proceeding against him with violence, he cannot tell whether they intend his death or not. Finally, the motive and purpose for which this renouncing and transferring of right was introduced is nothing other than the security of a man's person: the security of his life, and of the means of preserving that life in such a way that he does not grow weary of it. So if a man, by words or other signs, seems to strip himself of the very end those signs were meant to serve, he is not to be understood as having meant it or willed it. He is to be understood as having been ignorant of how such words and actions would be interpreted.

### What a Contract Is

The mutual transferring of right is what men call contract.

There is a difference between transferring the right to a thing and transferring, or "tradition," meaning the delivery of the thing itself. The thing may be delivered at the same moment the right is transferred, as in buying and selling with ready money, or in exchanging goods or lands. Or it may be delivered some time afterward.

### What a Covenant Is

Again, one of the contracting parties may deliver the thing contracted for on his side and leave the other to perform his part at some fixed later time, trusting him in the meantime. In that case the contract, on the part of the one who is trusted, is called a pact, or covenant. Or both parties may contract now to perform later. In these cases the one who is to perform in the future is being trusted, and so his performance is called keeping of promise, or faith, and his failure to perform, if it is voluntary, is called violation of faith.

### Free Gift

The transfer of right is sometimes not mutual. One party may transfer his right in hope of gaining friendship or service from another, or from that person's friends. He may do it in hope of earning a reputation for charity or magnanimity, or to relieve his mind of the pain of compassion, or in hope of a reward in heaven. This is not contract but gift, free gift, or grace, and these words all signify one and the same thing.

### Express Signs of Contract

Signs of contract are either express or by inference. Express signs are words spoken with an understanding of what they mean. Such words are either in the present or past tense, as in "I give," "I grant," "I have given," "I have granted," "I will that this be yours," or in the future tense, as in "I will give," "I will grant." Words in the future tense are called a promise.

### Signs of Contract by Inference

Signs by inference are sometimes a consequence of words, sometimes of silence, sometimes of actions, and sometimes of refraining from an action. In general, a sign by inference of any contract is whatever sufficiently demonstrates the will of the contracting party.

### A Free Gift Passes by Words of the Present or Past

Words alone, if they refer to the future and contain a bare promise, are an insufficient sign of a free gift, and they are therefore not binding. If they refer to the future, as in "tomorrow I will give," they signify that I have not yet given. My right has consequently not been transferred, and it remains mine until I transfer it by some other act. But if the words are in the present or past tense, as in "I have given" or "I do give, to be delivered tomorrow," then my right for tomorrow is given away today. It is given away by virtue of the words alone, even if there were no other evidence of my will. There is a great difference in meaning between *Volo hoc tuum esse cras* and *Cras dabo*, that is, between "I will that this be yours tomorrow" and "I will give it to you tomorrow." In the first expression, "I will" signifies a present act of the will. In the second, it signifies a promise of a future act of the will. The first, being in the present, transfers a future right, while the second, being in the future, transfers nothing. If, however, there are signs besides words of a will to transfer a right, then the right may be understood to pass by words of the future tense, even though the gift is free. Suppose a man offers a prize to whoever reaches the end of a race first. The gift is free, and the words are in the future tense, yet the right still passes. If he did not want his words understood that way, he should not have let them run.

### In Contracts, the Right Passes by Words of Past, Present, and Future

In contracts, the right passes not only when the words are present or past but also when they are future. All contract is a mutual transfer or exchange of right. A man who only promises, because he has already received the benefit in return for which he promises, must therefore be understood to intend that the right should pass. Unless he had been content to have his words understood that way, the other party would not have performed his part first. For that reason, in buying and selling and in other contractual acts, a promise is equivalent to a covenant and is therefore binding.

### What Merit Is

In a contract, the party who performs first is said to merit what he is to receive through the other's performance, and he holds it as his due. Likewise, a prize may be offered to many people, to be given only to the one who wins, or money may be thrown among a crowd, to be kept by whoever catches it. Although this is a free gift, to win or to catch in this way is to merit, and to have the thing as due. The right is transferred in the offering of the prize or the throwing of the money, even though the person to whom it passes is not determined until the outcome of the contest.

There is, however, a difference between these two kinds of merit. In contract, I merit by virtue of my own power and the other party's need, whereas in the case of a free gift, I am enabled to merit only by the goodwill of the giver. In contract, I merit at the other party's hands that he should part with his right. In the case of a gift, I do not merit that the giver should part with his right, but only that, once he has parted with it, it should be mine rather than someone else's. This, I think, is what the Schoolmen mean by their distinction between *meritum congrui* and *meritum condigni*, merit of congruity and merit of condignity. God Almighty has promised Paradise to those men, blindfolded as they are by fleshly desires, who can walk through this world according to the precepts and limits he has prescribed. The Schoolmen say that whoever walks in this way will merit Paradise *ex congruo*, as something fitting. But no man can claim a right to Paradise by his own righteousness or by any other power within himself, but only by the free grace of God. For that reason they say that no man can merit Paradise *ex condigno*, as something strictly owed. This, I say, is what I think the distinction means. But disputants agree on the meaning of their own technical terms only for as long as it serves their purpose, so I will not affirm anything about what they mean. I say only this: when a gift is offered without a designated recipient, as a prize to be competed for, whoever wins it merits it and may claim the prize as his due.

### When Covenants of Mutual Trust Are Invalid

If a covenant is made in which neither party performs immediately, but each trusts the other, then in the condition of mere nature, which is a condition of war of every man against every man, the covenant is void upon any reasonable suspicion. But if a common power is set over both parties, with the right and the force to compel performance, it is not void. Whoever performs first has no assurance that the other will perform afterward, because the bonds of words are too weak to restrain men's ambition, greed, anger, and other passions without the fear of some coercive power. In the condition of mere nature, where all men are equal and each judges for himself whether his fears are justified, no such power can be assumed to exist. The one who performs first therefore only betrays himself to his enemy, contrary to the right, which he can never abandon, of defending his life and his means of living.

In a civil state, however, where a power has been established to restrain those who would otherwise break their word, that fear is no longer reasonable. For that reason, the party whom the covenant requires to perform first is obliged to do so.

The fear that makes such a covenant invalid must always arise from something that happens after the covenant was made, such as some new act or other sign of an intention not to perform. Otherwise it cannot make the covenant void. Whatever could not prevent a man from promising ought not to be accepted as preventing him from performing.

### The Right to an End Includes the Right to the Means

Whoever transfers a right also transfers, as far as lies in his power, the means of enjoying it. A man who sells land is understood to transfer the grass and whatever else grows on it, and a man who sells a mill cannot divert the stream that drives it. In the same way, those who give a man the right of sovereign government are understood to give him also the right to raise money to maintain soldiers and to appoint magistrates for the administration of justice.

### No Covenant with Animals

It is impossible to make a covenant with brute beasts. Because they do not understand our speech, they neither understand nor accept any transfer of right, nor can they transfer any right to another; and without mutual acceptance there is no covenant.

### Nor with God, Except Through Special Revelation

It is impossible to make a covenant with God except through the mediation of those to whom God speaks, either by supernatural revelation or through his lieutenants, who govern under him and in his name. Otherwise we cannot know whether our covenants have been accepted. Those who vow anything contrary to a law of nature therefore vow in vain, since it would be unjust to fulfill such a vow. And if the thing vowed is already commanded by the law of nature, it is the law, not the vow, that binds them.

### Covenants Concern Only What Is Possible and Future

The matter, or subject, of a covenant is always something that falls under deliberation, because to covenant is an act of the will, and an act of the will is the final act of deliberation. The subject of a covenant is therefore always understood to be something still to come, and something the person covenanting judges himself able to perform.

To promise what is known to be impossible is therefore no covenant. But if something that was thought possible later proves impossible, the covenant remains valid and binding. It no longer binds to the thing itself but to its value. If even that is impossible, it binds to a sincere effort to perform as much as can be done, since no man can be obliged to more.

### How Covenants Are Dissolved

Men are released from their covenants in two ways: by performing them, or by being forgiven. Performance is the natural end of an obligation. Forgiveness is the restoration of liberty, since it transfers back the right in which the obligation consisted.

### Covenants Extracted by Fear Are Valid

In the condition of mere nature, covenants entered into out of fear are binding. If, for example, I covenant to pay an enemy a ransom, or to serve him, in exchange for my life, I am bound by it. It is a contract in which one party receives the benefit of life and the other is to receive money or service for it. Where no other law forbids performance, as none does in the condition of mere nature, the covenant is therefore valid. Prisoners of war who are trusted to pay their ransom are obliged to pay it. If a weaker prince makes a disadvantageous peace with a stronger one out of fear, he is bound to keep it, unless, as was said before, some new and just cause of fear arises to renew the war. Even within commonwealths, if I am forced to buy my freedom from a thief by promising him money, I am bound to pay it until the civil law releases me. Whatever I may lawfully do without obligation, I may lawfully covenant to do out of fear; and what I lawfully covenant, I cannot lawfully break.

### An Earlier Covenant with One Party Voids a Later One with Another

An earlier covenant makes a later one void. A man who has given his right to one person today no longer has it to give to another tomorrow. The later promise therefore transfers no right and is null.

### A Man's Covenant Not to Defend Himself Is Void

A covenant not to defend myself against force by force is always void. As I have shown before, no man can transfer or give up his right to save himself from death, wounds, and imprisonment, since avoiding these is the only purpose of giving up any right at all. In no covenant, therefore, does a promise not to resist force transfer any right or create any obligation. A man may covenant, "Unless I do such and such, kill me," but he cannot covenant, "Unless I do such and such, I will not resist you when you come to kill me." By nature a man chooses the lesser evil, which is the risk of death in resisting, over the greater evil, which is certain and immediate death in not resisting. Everyone acknowledges this, since criminals are led to execution and to prison by armed men, even though those criminals have consented to the law under which they are condemned.

### No Man Is Obliged to Accuse Himself

A covenant to accuse oneself, without assurance of pardon, is likewise invalid. In the condition of nature, where every man is his own judge, there is no place for accusation. In the civil state, accusation is followed by punishment, and since punishment is force, a man is not obliged to refrain from resisting it. The same holds for accusing those whose condemnation would bring a man into misery, such as a father, a wife, or a benefactor. If the testimony of such an accuser is not given willingly, it is presumed to be corrupted by nature and is therefore not to be accepted; and where a man's testimony is not to be believed, he is not bound to give it. Accusations made under torture, likewise, are not to be regarded as testimony. Torture should be used only as a means of conjecture, a source of leads for further examination and the search for truth. What is confessed under it serves to relieve the one being tortured, not to inform the torturers, and it should therefore not be credited as sufficient testimony. Whether the victim frees himself by a true accusation or a false one, he does so by his right to preserve his own life.

### The Purpose of an Oath; the Form of an Oath

As I noted earlier, the force of words is too weak to hold men to the performance of their covenants, and human nature offers only two conceivable aids to strengthen it. One is fear of the consequences of breaking one's word; the other is glory, or pride, in appearing not to need to break it. The second is a generosity too rarely found to be relied upon, especially among those who pursue wealth, power, or sensual pleasure, who make up the greatest part of mankind. The passion to be counted on is fear, which has two very general objects. One is the power of invisible spirits; the other is the power of the men one would offend by breaking faith. Although the first is the greater power, the second is commonly the greater fear. In every man, fear of the first is his own religion, and it exists in human nature before civil society. Fear of the second does not, or at least not strongly enough to keep men to their promises, because in the condition of mere nature, inequality of power is revealed only by the outcome of battle. Before civil society exists, then, or when war interrupts it, only one thing can strengthen an agreed covenant of peace against the temptations of greed, ambition, lust, or any other strong desire: the fear of that invisible power which each party worships as God and fears as an avenger of treachery. All that can be done between two men who are not subject to a civil power, therefore, is for each to make the other swear by the God he fears. This swearing, or oath, is a form of speech added to a promise, by which the one who promises declares that unless he performs, he renounces the mercy of his God or calls on him for vengeance upon himself. The pagan form was "Let Jupiter kill me otherwise, as I kill this beast." Our form is "I will do thus and thus, so help me God." To these words each person adds the rites and ceremonies of his own religion, so that the fear of breaking faith may be all the greater.

### No Oath Except by God

It follows that an oath taken by any form or rite other than that of the person swearing is in vain and is no oath at all. Nor can anyone swear by anything he does not consider to be God. Men have sometimes sworn by their kings, out of fear or flattery, but in doing so they meant it to be understood that they attributed divine honor to them. It follows, too, that swearing by God unnecessarily is merely a profanation of his name, and that swearing by other things, as men do in ordinary conversation, is not swearing at all but an impious habit acquired through excessive vehemence in talking.

### An Oath Adds Nothing to the Obligation

It also follows that an oath adds nothing to the obligation. A lawful covenant binds in the sight of God as much without an oath as with one. An unlawful covenant does not bind at all, even when an oath confirms it.

## Chapter XV. Of Other Laws of Nature

### The Third Law of Nature: Justice

From the law of nature that obliges us to transfer to others those rights which, if we kept them, would obstruct the peace of mankind, there follows a third: that people perform the covenants they have made. Without this law, covenants are pointless, nothing but empty words; and since everyone's right to everything would remain in force, we would still be in the condition of war.

### What Justice and Injustice Are

In this law of nature lies the source and origin of justice. Where no covenant has come before, no right has been transferred, and every person has a right to everything. It follows that no action can be unjust. But once a covenant is made, breaking it is unjust. Indeed, the definition of injustice is nothing other than the failure to perform a covenant. And whatever is not unjust is just.

### Justice and Property Begin with the Founding of a Commonwealth

But as the previous chapter showed, covenants of mutual trust are invalid wherever either party has reason to fear that the other will not perform. So although justice originates in the making of covenants, there can be no actual injustice until the cause of that fear is removed, and this cannot be done while people remain in the natural condition of war. Before the words "just" and "unjust" can apply at all, therefore, there must be some coercive power to compel everyone equally to perform their covenants, through the threat of a punishment greater than whatever benefit they expect from breaking them. That same power must also secure the property that people acquire by mutual contract in exchange for the universal right they give up. No such power exists before a commonwealth is established. The same conclusion can be drawn from the standard definition of justice taught in the Schools, the scholastic philosophers of the universities, who say that "justice is the constant will to give every man his own." Where there is no "own," that is, no property, there is no injustice. And where no coercive power has been set up, where there is no commonwealth, there is no property, since all people have a right to all things. Therefore, where there is no commonwealth, nothing is unjust. The nature of justice consists in keeping valid covenants, but covenants become valid only when a civil power is constituted that is strong enough to compel people to keep them. And that is also when property begins.

### Justice Is Not Contrary to Reason

The fool has said in his heart that there is no such thing as justice, and sometimes he says it aloud as well. His serious argument runs like this: since every person's preservation and contentment are entrusted to his own care, there can be no reason why anyone should not do whatever he thinks will advance those ends. So making or not making, keeping or not keeping covenants is not against reason when it works to one's advantage. He does not deny that covenants exist, or that they are sometimes broken and sometimes kept, or that breaking them may be called injustice and keeping them justice. What he questions is whether injustice might not sometimes be consistent with the reason that directs every person toward his own good, once the fear of God is set aside, for the same fool has also said in his heart that there is no God. He has in mind especially those cases where injustice brings such an advantage that a man is placed beyond caring not only about the blame and abuse of others but also about their power. Scripture says that the kingdom of God is taken by violence; but what if it could be taken by unjust violence? Would it be against reason to seize it that way, when no harm could possibly come of it? And if it is not against reason, it is not against justice, or else justice is not worth approving as a good.

Reasoning of this kind is how successful wickedness has come to be called virtue, and how some who in every other case condemn the violation of faith have nevertheless permitted it when a kingdom is the prize. The pagans, who believed that Saturn was overthrown by his son Jupiter, nonetheless believed that this same Jupiter was the avenger of injustice. There is something similar in a point of law in Sir Edward Coke's *Commentaries on Littleton*, his celebrated commentary on Thomas Littleton's treatise on English land law. Coke says that if the rightful heir to the Crown has been attainted of treason, meaning legally condemned and stripped of his rights, including his right to inherit, the Crown shall still descend to him, and at that very instant the attainder becomes void. From such examples a person will be strongly inclined to infer the following. When the heir apparent to a kingdom kills the one who holds the throne, even if it is his own father, you may call it injustice or whatever else you like, but it can never be against reason, since all voluntary human actions aim at the actor's own benefit, and the most reasonable actions are those that best achieve one's ends. This reasoning is plausible, but it is false.

The question does not concern mutual promises where neither side has any guarantee that the other will perform, as when no civil power has been set up over the parties making the promises, because such promises are not covenants at all. The question concerns cases where one party has already performed, or where there is a power that can compel him to perform. In those cases, the question is whether it is against reason, that is, against the interest of the other party, to perform his side. And I say it is not against reason. To show this, we must consider two things. First, when a person does something that, as far as anything can be foreseen and calculated, tends toward his own destruction, then even if some unexpected accident turns it to his advantage, that outcome does not make the action reasonable or wise. Second, in a condition of war, where every person is an enemy to every other for lack of a common power to keep them all in awe, no one can hope to defend himself from destruction by his own strength or cleverness alone, without the help of allies. In such an alliance each member expects the same protection from it as every other. So anyone who declares that he thinks it reasonable to deceive those who help him can reasonably expect no means of safety beyond what his own solitary strength provides.

The person who breaks his covenant, and in doing so declares that he thinks he may reasonably do so, cannot be admitted into any society that people form for peace and defense except through the error of those who admit him. Nor, once admitted, can he be kept in it unless they fail to see the danger of their mistake. And no one can reasonably count on other people's errors as the basis of his security. If he is left out or cast out of society, he perishes. If he lives in society, it is only through other people's errors, which he could neither foresee nor count on. His conduct is therefore contrary to the reason of his own preservation. Indeed, all those who refrain from contributing to his destruction spare him only because they do not understand what is good for themselves.

The example of gaining the secure and eternal happiness of heaven by any means whatever is frivolous, since only one way to it can be imagined, and that is not by breaking covenants but by keeping them.

The other example, gaining sovereignty by rebellion, fails as well. Even if success follows, the attempt is still against reason. Success cannot reasonably be expected, and the opposite is far more likely. Gaining power in that way also teaches others to gain it in the same way. Justice, then, which is to say the keeping of covenants, is a rule of reason by which we are forbidden to do anything destructive to our own life, and is consequently a law of nature.

Some go further. They hold that the laws of nature are not the rules that promote the preservation of human life on earth but the rules for attaining eternal happiness after death, and they believe that breaking a covenant may help attain it and may therefore be just and reasonable. Such are those who think it a meritorious deed to kill, depose, or rebel against the sovereign power established over them by their own consent. But we have no natural knowledge of the human condition after death, still less of any reward to be given then for breaking faith. We have only a belief resting on the word of others who say they know it supernaturally, or that they know people who knew people who knew others who knew it supernaturally. Breaking faith, therefore, cannot be called a precept of reason or of nature.

### Covenants Are Not Cancelled by the Vices of the Person to Whom They Are Made

Others accept the keeping of faith as a law of nature but make exceptions for certain persons, such as heretics and those who habitually fail to perform their covenants with others. This too is against reason. If some fault in a person were enough to release us from a covenant made with him, it should, by the same reasoning, have been enough to prevent us from making the covenant in the first place.

### What the Justice of Persons and the Justice of Actions Are

The words "just" and "unjust" mean one thing when applied to people and another when applied to actions. Applied to people, they signify whether a person's character, his manners or settled way of life, conforms to reason or not. Applied to actions, they signify whether particular actions conform to reason, not whether a person's whole manner of life does. A just man, therefore, is one who takes all the care he can that his actions may all be just, and an unjust man is one who neglects to do so. In our language such people are more often called righteous and unrighteous than just and unjust, though the meaning is the same. A righteous man does not lose that title through one or a few unjust actions that arise from sudden passion or from a mistake about things or persons. Nor does an unrighteous man lose his character because of what he does or refrains from doing out of fear, since his will is shaped not by justice but by the apparent advantage of what he is about to do. What gives human actions the savor of justice is a certain nobility or gallantry of spirit, rarely found, by which a man scorns to owe the contentment of his life to fraud or broken promises. This justice of character is what is meant when justice is called a virtue and injustice a vice.

The justice of actions, by contrast, does not make people just but only guiltless. The injustice of actions, which is also called injury, makes them only guilty.

### Justice of Character and Justice of Actions

Again, injustice of character is the disposition or inclination to do injury. It is injustice even before it issues in any act, and it does not presuppose that any particular person has been injured. But the injustice of an action, that is, an injury, does presuppose a particular injured person, namely the one to whom the covenant was made. For this reason, the injury is often done to one person while the damage falls on another. Suppose a master orders his servant to give money to a stranger, and the servant fails to do it. The injury is done to the master, whom the servant had previously covenanted to obey. The damage, however, falls on the stranger, to whom the servant had no obligation and whom he therefore could not injure. Similarly, in commonwealths, private persons may forgive one another their debts, but not robberies or other acts of violence by which they have been harmed. Withholding a debt is an injury to the creditors themselves, whereas robbery and violence are injuries to the person of the commonwealth.

### Nothing Done to a Person with His Own Consent Can Be an Injury

Whatever is done to a person in accordance with his own will, made known to the one who does it, is no injury to him. If the doer has not, by some prior covenant, given up his original right to do as he pleases, there is no breach of covenant and therefore no injury. And if he has, then the other person's expressed wish to have it done releases him from that covenant, and so, once again, no injury is done.

### Commutative and Distributive Justice

Writers divide the justice of actions into commutative and distributive. The first, they say, consists in arithmetical proportion and the second in geometrical proportion. By this they mean that commutative justice requires a simple equality between the things exchanged, while distributive justice requires shares proportioned to the worth of the recipients. Accordingly, they locate commutative justice in the equal value of the things contracted for, and distributive justice in the distribution of equal benefits to people of equal merit, as if it were unjust to sell for more than we paid, or to give a man more than he deserves. But the value of anything contracted for is measured by the desire of the contracting parties, and so the just value is whatever they are content to give. And merit is not owed as a matter of justice but is rewarded only as a matter of grace. The one exception is merit by covenant, where performance on one side earns the performance of the other, and this falls under commutative rather than distributive justice. This distinction, therefore, in the sense in which it is usually explained, is mistaken. Properly speaking, commutative justice is the justice of a contracting party: the performance of covenants in buying and selling, hiring and letting for hire, lending and borrowing, exchanging, bartering, and other contractual acts.

Distributive justice, by contrast, is the justice of an arbitrator, that is, the act of determining what is just. If the arbitrator, having been trusted by those who appointed him, fulfills that trust, he is said to distribute to every man his own. This is indeed just distribution, and may be called distributive justice, though improperly. It is more properly called equity, which is also a law of nature, as will be shown in its place.

### The Fourth Law of Nature: Gratitude

Just as justice depends on a prior covenant, gratitude depends on prior grace, that is, a prior free gift. It is the fourth law of nature, which may be stated in this form: "That a man who receives a benefit from another out of pure grace should endeavor that the giver have no reasonable cause to regret his goodwill." No one gives except with the intention of some good to himself, since a gift is voluntary, and the object of every voluntary act is the actor's own good. If people see that this aim will be frustrated, there will be no beginning of benevolence or trust, and consequently none of mutual help or of reconciliation between one person and another.
