They will therefore remain in the condition of war, which is contrary to the first and fundamental law of nature, the law commanding men to seek peace. The breach of this law is called ingratitude, and it bears the same relation to grace that injustice bears to obligation by covenant.

### The Fifth: Mutual Accommodation, or Complaisance

A fifth law of nature is complaisance: "That every man strive to accommodate himself to the rest." To understand this, we may consider that people's fitness for society varies according to the diversity of their natures, which arises from the diversity of their passions. This is not unlike what we see in stones gathered for building a house. A stone whose rough and irregular shape takes up more room than it fills, and whose hardness makes it difficult to dress smooth, obstructs the building, and the builders throw it aside as useless and troublesome. In the same way, some people are so harsh by nature that they hold on to things that are superfluous to themselves but necessary to others, and their passions are too stubborn to be corrected. Such a person is to be left out or cast out of society as a burden to it. Every person is supposed to strive, not only by right but by necessity of nature, to obtain everything needed for his own preservation. Whoever opposes this for the sake of superfluous things is therefore guilty of the war that follows, and so acts contrary to the fundamental law of nature, which commands us to seek peace. Those who observe this law may be called sociable (the Latin writers call them *commodi*); the opposite are called stubborn, unsociable, perverse, and intractable.

### The Sixth: Readiness to Pardon

A sixth law of nature is this: "That upon security for the future, a man ought to pardon the past offenses of those who repent and ask for pardon." Pardon is nothing but the granting of peace. Granted to those who persist in their hostility, it is not peace but fear. But refusing it to those who give security for the future is a sign of aversion to peace, and is therefore contrary to the law of nature.

### The Seventh: That in Revenge, People Consider Only the Future Good

The seventh law is "that in acts of revenge (that is, in returning evil for evil), people look not to the greatness of the past evil but to the greatness of the good to follow." This forbids us to inflict punishment for any purpose other than correcting the offender or guiding others by example. The law follows from the one before it, which commands pardon once security for the future has been given. Revenge that has no regard for example or future benefit is a triumph, a glorying in another's injury that tends toward no end, since an end is always something still to come. Glorying that aims at no end is vainglory and contrary to reason. To inflict harm without reason tends to bring on war, which is against the law of nature, and such harm is commonly called cruelty.

### The Eighth, Against Contumely

Every sign of hatred or contempt provokes people to fight, so much so that most would rather risk their lives than leave such an insult unavenged. We may therefore set down as the eighth law of nature this precept: "That no one, by deed, word, facial expression, or gesture, declare hatred or contempt of another." The breach of this law is commonly called contumely, meaning insolent abuse.

### The Ninth, Against Pride

The question of who is the better man has no place in the pure state of nature, where, as I have already shown, all men are equal. The inequality that exists now was introduced by civil laws. I know that Aristotle, in the first book of his *Politics*, lays as the foundation of his doctrine the claim that some men are by nature more fit to command and others to serve. By the first he means the wiser sort, among whom he counted himself on account of his philosophy. By the second he means those who had strong bodies but were not philosophers as he was. He writes as if master and servant were established not by human consent but by differences in intelligence, which is contrary not only to reason but also to experience. For very few people are so foolish that they would not rather govern themselves than be governed by others. Nor, when those who are wise in their own estimation contend by force against those who distrust their own wisdom, do they win always, or often, or almost ever. If nature has made men equal, then that equality must be acknowledged. And if nature has made men unequal, equality must still be granted, because men who think themselves equal will not enter into peace except on equal terms. For the ninth law of nature, therefore, I set down this: "That every man acknowledge every other as his equal by nature." The breach of this precept is pride.

### The Tenth, Against Arrogance

On this law depends another: "That on entering into terms of peace, no one require to reserve for himself any right that he is not content to see reserved to everyone else." All who seek peace must lay down certain rights of nature, which is to say they must give up the liberty to do whatever they please. Yet human life also requires that some rights be kept, such as the right to govern one's own body and to enjoy air, water, movement, roads by which to travel from place to place, and everything else without which a person cannot live, or cannot live well. If, in making peace, people demand for themselves what they would not have granted to others, they violate the preceding law, which commands the acknowledgment of natural equality, and so they also act against the law of nature. Those who observe this law we call modest, and those who break it arrogant. The Greeks called the violation of this law *pleonexia*, a desire for more than one's share.

### The Eleventh, Equity

It is also a precept of the law of nature that "if someone is entrusted to judge between one person and another, he deal equally between them." Without this, human disputes can be settled only by war. Whoever is partial in judgment therefore does all in his power to discourage people from using judges and arbitrators, and so, against the fundamental law of nature, he becomes a cause of war.

The observance of this law, which consists in distributing equally to each person what belongs to him by reason, is called equity and, as I said earlier, distributive justice. Its violation is called respect of persons, or in Greek *prosopolepsia*, which means favoritism toward one party.

### The Twelfth, Equal Use of Things Held in Common

From this follows another law: "That things which cannot be divided be enjoyed in common, if that is possible; without limit, if the quantity of the thing allows; and otherwise in proportion to the number of those who have a right to it." Any other arrangement makes the distribution unequal and contrary to equity.

### The Thirteenth, Of Lot

Some things, however, can be neither divided nor enjoyed in common. In such cases the law of nature, which prescribes equity, requires "that the entire right, or else (if use is to alternate) the first possession, be determined by lot." Equal distribution belongs to the law of nature, and no other means of distributing equally can be imagined.

### The Fourteenth, Of Primogeniture and First Seizure

There are two kinds of lot: arbitrary and natural. An arbitrary lot is one agreed upon by the competitors. A natural lot is either primogeniture, the right of the firstborn (which the Greeks called *kleronomia*, meaning "given by lot"), or first seizure.

Accordingly, things that can be neither enjoyed in common nor divided ought to be awarded to the first possessor, and in some cases to the firstborn, as acquired by lot.

### The Fifteenth, Of Mediators

It is also a law of nature "that all who mediate peace be allowed safe conduct." The law that commands peace as the end commands intercession as the means, and the means to intercession is safe conduct.

### The Sixteenth, Of Submission to Arbitration

However willing people may be to observe these laws, questions may still arise about a person's action. The first is whether it was done or not done. The second, if it was done, is whether it was against the law or not. The first is called a question of fact, the second a question of right. Unless the parties to the dispute mutually agree to abide by the judgment of someone else, they remain as far from peace as ever. This other person, to whose judgment they submit, is called an arbitrator. It is therefore a law of nature "that those in dispute submit their right to the judgment of an arbitrator."

### The Seventeenth, No One Is His Own Judge

Since everyone is presumed to do all things for his own benefit, no one is a fit arbitrator in his own cause. And even if he were perfectly fit, equity grants each party an equal benefit. If one party is admitted as judge, then the other must be admitted too, and so the controversy, which is the cause of war, remains, against the law of nature.

### The Eighteenth, No One to Be Judge Who Has in Him a Cause of Partiality

For the same reason, no one ought to be accepted as arbitrator in any cause if he plainly stands to gain more profit, honor, or pleasure from the victory of one party than from that of the other. He has taken a bribe, an unavoidable one but a bribe nonetheless, and no one can be obliged to trust him. Here too the controversy, and with it the condition of war, remains, contrary to the law of nature.

### The Nineteenth, Of Witnesses

In a dispute over a matter of fact, the judge must give no more credit to one party than to the other. If there are no other grounds for decision, he must therefore give credit to a third person, or to a third and a fourth, or to more. Otherwise the question goes undecided and is left to force, contrary to the law of nature.

These are the laws of nature that dictate peace as a means of preserving people who live together in multitudes, and they concern only the doctrine of civil society. Other things tend to destroy particular individuals, such as drunkenness and every other form of intemperance, and these too may be counted among the things the law of nature forbids. But they need not be mentioned here, nor are they relevant enough to this place.

### A Rule by Which the Laws of Nature May Easily Be Examined

This may seem too subtle a deduction of the laws of nature for everyone to grasp, since most people are too busy getting food and the rest too careless to understand. Yet so that no one may be left without excuse, the laws have been condensed into one simple sum, intelligible even to the humblest capacity: "Do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself." This shows that learning the laws of nature requires only one thing. When a person weighs the actions of others against his own and finds theirs too heavy, he should put theirs on the other side of the balance and his own in their place, so that his own passions and self-love add nothing to the weight. Then every one of these laws of nature will appear entirely reasonable to him.

### The Laws of Nature Always Oblige in Conscience, but in Effect Only When There Is Security

The laws of nature oblige *in foro interno*, in the inner court of conscience, which is to say they bind us to desire that they take effect. But *in foro externo*, in the outer court of action, they do not always bind us to put them into practice. Anyone who was modest and accommodating and kept every promise at a time and place where no one else did so would only make himself prey to others and bring about his own certain ruin. That would be contrary to the very basis of all the laws of nature, which aim at preserving nature. On the other hand, anyone who has sufficient assurance that others will observe these same laws toward him, yet does not observe them himself, seeks not peace but war, and consequently the violent destruction of his own nature.

Whatever laws bind *in foro interno* may be broken not only by an act contrary to the law but also by an act in accordance with it, if the person believes it to be contrary. Although in that case his action conforms to the law, his purpose was against it, and where the obligation lies in conscience, that is a breach.

### The Laws of Nature Are Eternal

The laws of nature are unchangeable and eternal. Injustice, ingratitude, arrogance, pride, iniquity, respect of persons, and the rest can never be made lawful, for it can never be that war will preserve life and peace destroy it.

### And Yet Easy

These same laws are easy to observe, because they oblige only to a desire and an endeavor, by which I mean a sincere and constant endeavor. Since they require nothing but endeavor, whoever strives to perform them fulfills them, and whoever fulfills the law is just.

### The Science of These Laws Is the True Moral Philosophy

The science of these laws is the true and only moral philosophy. For moral philosophy is nothing other than the science of what is good and evil in the dealings and society of humankind. "Good" and "evil" are names that signify our appetites and aversions, which differ according to people's temperaments, customs, and doctrines. Different people differ not only in their judgment of what is pleasant or unpleasant to taste, smell, hearing, touch, and sight, but also in their judgment of what agrees or disagrees with reason in the actions of everyday life. Indeed, the same person differs from himself at different times: at one time he praises, or calls good, what at another time he condemns and calls evil. From this arise disputes, controversies, and in the end war. So long as people remain in the pure state of nature, which is a condition of war, private appetite is the measure of good and evil. Consequently, all agree that peace is good. It follows that the way or means to peace is also good, and those means, as I have shown, are justice, gratitude, modesty, equity, mercy, and the rest of the laws of nature. They are the moral virtues, and their opposites, the vices, are evil. Now the science of virtue and vice is moral philosophy, and therefore the true doctrine of the laws of nature is the true moral philosophy. The writers on moral philosophy acknowledge the same virtues and vices. Yet they did not see wherein the goodness of the virtues consisted, nor that the virtues are praised as the means to peaceful, sociable, and comfortable living. Instead they placed the virtues in a moderate degree of the passions, a mean between extremes, as if it were not the cause but the degree of daring that made courage, or not the cause but the size of a gift that made generosity.

People customarily call these dictates of reason laws, but the term is improper. They are only conclusions, or theorems, about what contributes to people's preservation and defense, whereas law, properly speaking, is the word of one who by right has command over others. Yet if we consider these same theorems as delivered in the word of God, who by right commands all things, then they are properly called laws.

## Chapter XVI. Of Persons, Authors, and Things Personated

A person is one "whose words or actions are considered either as his own, or as representing the words or actions of another man, or of any other thing to which they are attributed, whether truly or by fiction."

When those words and actions are considered his own, he is called a natural person. When they are considered as representing the words and actions of another, he is a feigned, or artificial, person.

The word *person* is Latin. The Greeks used *prosopon*, which means "face," just as the Latin *persona* signifies the disguise or outward appearance a man counterfeits on the stage, and sometimes, more narrowly, the part of that disguise that conceals the face, such as a mask or visor. From the stage the word was carried over to anyone who represents speech and action, in courts of law as well as in theaters. A person, then, is the same thing as an actor, both on the stage and in ordinary affairs, and to personate is to act, or represent, either oneself or another. Whoever acts for another is said to bear his person, or to act in his name. Cicero uses the word in this sense when he says, *"Unus sustineo tres personas; mei, adversarii, et judicis"*: "I alone bear three persons: my own, my adversary's, and the judge's." Such a person goes by different names on different occasions: a representer or representative, a lieutenant, a vicar, an attorney, a deputy, a procurator, an actor, and the like.

Some artificial persons have their words and actions owned by those whom they represent. In that case the person is the actor, and the one who owns his words and actions is the author, and the actor acts by authority. What is called an owner when we speak of goods and possessions (in Latin *dominus*, in Greek *kurios*) is called an author when we speak of actions. And just as the right of possession is called dominion, the right of performing any action is called authority. By authority, therefore, we always mean a right to do some act, and an act done by authority is one done by commission, or license, from the person whose right it is.

It follows that when an actor makes a covenant by authority, he binds the author just as fully as if the author had made it himself, and subjects him to all of its consequences. Everything said earlier about the nature of covenants between men in their natural capacity therefore holds equally for covenants made by their actors, representatives, or procurators who have authority from them, so far as that authority extends under their commission, and no further.

Consequently, anyone who makes a covenant with an actor or representative without knowing what authority he has does so at his own peril. No man is bound by a covenant of which he is not the author, and so no man is bound by a covenant made against, or outside of, the authority he gave.

When an actor, at the author's command, does something contrary to the law of nature, and is bound by a prior covenant to obey him, it is the author and not the actor who breaks the law of nature. The action, though contrary to the law of nature, is not the actor's own. On the contrary, for him to refuse it would violate the law of nature that forbids the breaking of covenants.

Suppose someone makes a covenant with an author through the mediation of an actor, not knowing what authority the actor holds but simply taking him at his word. If that authority is not made plain to him when he asks for it, he is no longer bound, for a covenant made with the author is not valid without the author's own counter-assurance. If, however, the person making the covenant knew beforehand that he could expect no other assurance than the actor's word, then the covenant is valid, because in that case the actor makes himself the author. Accordingly, when the authority is evident, the covenant binds the author and not the actor; and when the authority is feigned, it binds the actor alone, since there is no author but himself.

There are few things that cannot be represented by fiction. Inanimate things, such as a church, a hospital, or a bridge, may be personated by a rector, a master, or an overseer. But inanimate things cannot be authors, and so cannot give authority to their actors. The actors may nonetheless hold authority to provide for the upkeep of these things, granted to them by whoever owns or governs them. For that reason, such things cannot be personated until some form of civil government exists.

Likewise, children, fools, and madmen, who have no use of reason, may be personated by guardians or curators. During that time, however, they cannot be the authors of any action done on their behalf, except insofar as they judge it reasonable once they recover the use of reason. While their incapacity lasts, the one who has the right to govern them may give authority to the guardian. But this too has no place except in a civil state, because before such a state exists there is no dominion over persons.

An idol, or a mere figment of the brain, may also be personated, as the gods of the heathen were. Officers appointed by the state personated these gods and held, in their name, the possessions, goods, and rights that men from time to time dedicated and consecrated to them. Idols, however, cannot be authors, for an idol is nothing. The authority came from the state, and therefore, before civil government was introduced, the gods of the heathen could not be personated.

The true God may be personated, and has been. He was personated first by Moses, who governed the Israelites, a people that belonged not to him but to God, not in his own name, saying *"Hoc dicit Moses"* ("Thus says Moses"), but in God's name, saying *"Hoc dicit Dominus"* ("Thus says the Lord"). He was personated second by the Son of Man, His own Son, our blessed Savior Jesus Christ, who came to bring the Jews back and to draw all nations into His Father's kingdom, not on His own account but as one sent by the Father. And He was personated third by the Holy Ghost, the Comforter, speaking and working in the apostles, a Comforter who did not come of Himself but was sent by, and proceeded from, both the Father and the Son.

A multitude of men becomes one person when it is represented by one man, or one person, provided this is done with the consent of every member of that multitude individually. It is the unity of the representer, not the unity of the represented, that makes the person one. It is the representer who bears the person, and only one person; unity in a multitude cannot be understood in any other way.

Because a multitude is by nature not one but many, its members cannot be understood as a single author. They are many authors of everything their representative says or does in their name, each man giving their common representer authority from himself individually. Each owns all the actions the representer performs, if they have given him authority without limit. If instead they restrict what he may represent them in, and how far, then none of them owns more than he commissioned him to do.

If the representative consists of many men, the voice of the greater number must be taken as the voice of them all. If, for example, the smaller number votes in the affirmative and the greater number in the negative, there will be more than enough negatives to cancel the affirmatives, and the surplus of negatives, standing uncontradicted, is the only voice the representative has.

A representative made up of an even number, especially a small one, will often find its opposing votes equal, and for that reason it is often mute and incapable of action. In some cases, however, an equal division can still settle a question. In deciding whether to condemn or acquit, a tie acquits, since by failing to condemn it absolves; but it does not, conversely, condemn by failing to absolve. When a case has been heard, not to condemn is to acquit, whereas to say that not acquitting is condemning would be false. The same holds in deliberating whether to carry out a sentence immediately or postpone it: when the votes are equal, the failure to decree execution amounts to a decree of delay.

Or suppose the number is odd, three or more, whether of men or of assemblies, and each one holds a negative voice, that is, the authority to cancel the effect of all the affirmative votes of the rest. Such a body is no representative at all. Given the diversity of men's opinions and interests, it will often become a mute person, and frequently in matters of the greatest consequence, unfit for many things, and above all for governing a multitude, especially in time of war.

There are two kinds of authors. The first, called an author simply, I have already defined as one who owns the action of another without condition. The second is one who owns the action or covenant of another conditionally; that is, he undertakes to perform it himself if the other fails to do so at or before a certain time. Conditional authors of this kind are generally called sureties, in Latin *fidejussores* and *sponsores*; more specifically, sureties for a debt are called *praedes*, and sureties for someone's appearance before a judge or magistrate are called *vades*.

## Part II. Of Commonwealth

## Chapter XVII. Of the Causes, Generation, and Definition of a Commonwealth

The End of the Commonwealth: Particular Security

Human beings naturally love liberty and love to have dominion over others. Yet we see them living in commonwealths, under restraints they have placed upon themselves. The final cause, end, or purpose of those restraints is foresight of their own preservation and of a more contented life. They are trying to escape the miserable condition of war that, as has already been shown, follows necessarily from the natural passions of men whenever there is no visible power to keep them in awe. Such a power binds them, through fear of punishment, to perform their covenants and to observe the laws of nature set down in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

Which Is Not to Be Had from the Law of Nature

The laws of nature include justice, equity, modesty, mercy, and, in sum, doing to others as we would have done to us. Without the terror of some power to enforce them, these laws run contrary to our natural passions, which carry us toward partiality, pride, revenge, and the like. Covenants without the sword are nothing but words, and they have no strength to secure anyone at all. Every person keeps the laws of nature only when he has the will to keep them and can do so safely. Therefore, whatever the laws of nature say, if no power has been erected, or if the power erected is not great enough for our security, every man will rely on his own strength and skill to guard himself against all other men, and he may lawfully do so. Wherever men have lived in small families, robbing and plundering one another has been a trade. Far from being regarded as contrary to the law of nature, it brought honor, and the greater the spoils a man gained, the greater his honor. In this trade men observed no laws but the laws of honor, which meant abstaining from cruelty and leaving their victims their lives and their farming tools. What small families did then, cities and kingdoms, which are only larger families, do now. For their own security they enlarge their dominions on every pretext of danger, whether fear of invasion or fear of aid that might be given to invaders. They strive as far as they can to subdue or weaken their neighbors by open force and secret stratagems. Since they have no other safeguard, they act justly in doing so, and later ages remember them for it with honor.

Nor from the Union of a Few Men or Families

Nor can a small number of men gain this security by joining together. Among small numbers, a small addition to one side or the other creates an advantage of strength great enough to decide the victory, and that advantage encourages invasion. No fixed number defines a multitude large enough to rely on for our security. The measure is always the enemy we fear. Our numbers are sufficient when the enemy's advantage is not so visible and so clearly decisive for the outcome of a war that it tempts him to attack.

Nor from a Great Multitude, Unless Directed by One Judgment

However great a multitude may be, if its members act according to their individual judgments and individual appetites, they can expect from it no defense or protection, either against a common enemy or against injuries from one another. Divided in their opinions about how best to use and apply their strength, they hinder one another instead of helping, and through mutual opposition they reduce their strength to nothing. As a result, a very few who agree among themselves can easily subdue them, and when there is no common enemy, they make war on each other for their private interests. Suppose a great multitude of men could agree to observe justice and the other laws of nature without a common power to keep them all in awe. Then we might just as well suppose that all mankind could do the same. In that case there would be no civil government or commonwealth at all, and no need for one, because there would be peace without subjection.

And That Continually

Men want their security to last their whole lives. For that purpose it is not enough to be governed and directed by one judgment for a limited time, as in a single battle or a single war. A united effort may win them a victory over a foreign enemy. Afterward, however, they may have no common enemy, or some may regard as an enemy the very man whom others regard as a friend. Then their differing interests will inevitably break them apart, and they will fall back into war among themselves.

Why Certain Creatures Without Reason or Speech Nevertheless Live in Society Without Any Coercive Power

It is true that certain living creatures, such as bees and ants, live sociably with one another, and for this reason Aristotle counted them among the political creatures. Yet they have no direction other than their individual judgments and appetites. Nor do they have speech by which one of them can tell another what it thinks advantageous for the common benefit. Someone may therefore ask why mankind cannot live as they do. To this I answer as follows.

First, men are continually competing for honor and dignity, and these creatures are not. Among men, envy and hatred arise from this competition, and finally war. Among these creatures, they do not.

Second, among these creatures the common good does not differ from the private good. Their nature inclines them to pursue their private good, and in doing so they secure the common benefit. But man takes his joy in comparing himself with other men, and so he can enjoy nothing except what raises him above others.

Third, these creatures lack the reason that man possesses, and so they neither see, nor think they see, any fault in the management of their common business. Among men, however, there are very many who think themselves wiser and better able to govern the public than the rest. These men strive to reform and innovate, one in this direction and another in that, and in doing so they bring the commonwealth into disorder and civil war.

Fourth, these creatures do make some use of their voices to make their desires and other feelings known to one another. Yet they lack the art of words. With that art, some men can make good appear to others as evil and evil appear as good. They can also make good and evil seem greater or smaller than they are, and so they make men discontented and disturb their peace whenever they please.

Fifth, irrational creatures cannot distinguish between injury and damage, that is, between a wrong deliberately done to them and mere harm. So long as they are at ease, therefore, they take no offense at their fellows. Man, by contrast, is most troublesome when he is most at ease. That is when he loves to display his wisdom and to call to account the actions of those who govern the commonwealth.

Last, the agreement of these creatures is natural, while the agreement of men comes by covenant alone, and covenant is artificial. It is no wonder, then, that men need something beyond covenant to make their agreement constant and lasting. They need a common power to keep them in awe and to direct their actions toward the common benefit.

The Generation of a Commonwealth

Men need a common power that can defend them from foreign invasion and from injuries done by one another. With that protection, they can feed themselves by their own labor and the fruits of the earth and live contentedly. There is only one way to erect such a power. They must confer all their power and strength upon one man, or upon one assembly of men, that can reduce all their wills, by majority vote, to a single will. In effect, they appoint one man or assembly of men to bear their person. Each one owns and acknowledges himself as the author of whatever the bearer of their person does, or causes to be done, in matters concerning the common peace and safety. In those matters each submits his will to that one's will and his judgment to that one's judgment. This is more than consent or concord. It is a real unity of them all in one and the same person, made by the covenant of every man with every man. It is as if every man said to every other: "I authorize this man, or this assembly of men, and give up to him my right of governing myself, on this condition: that you give up your right to him in the same way and authorize all his actions likewise." Once this is done, the multitude so united in one person is called a COMMONWEALTH, in Latin CIVITAS. This is the generation of that great LEVIATHAN. To speak more reverently, it is the generation of that mortal god to which we owe, under the immortal God, our peace and defense. Every individual in the commonwealth has given him this authority. It confers on him the use of so much power and strength that, through the terror of it, he can shape the wills of them all toward peace at home and mutual aid against their enemies abroad.

The Definition of a Commonwealth

In him lies the essence of the commonwealth. To define it, a commonwealth is "one person, of whose acts a great multitude, by mutual covenants with one another, have each made themselves the author, so that he may use the strength and means of them all as he thinks expedient for their peace and common defense."

Sovereign and Subject Defined

Whoever carries this person is called SOVEREIGN and is said to have sovereign power. Everyone else is his SUBJECT.

There are two ways of attaining this sovereign power. One is by natural force. A man may compel his children to submit themselves and their children to his government, since he is able to destroy them if they refuse. Or he may subdue his enemies by war and grant them their lives on condition that they submit to his will. The other way is for men to agree among themselves to submit voluntarily to some man or assembly of men, trusting him to protect them against all others. This second kind may be called a political commonwealth, or a commonwealth by institution, and the first a commonwealth by acquisition. I shall speak first of a commonwealth by institution.

## Chapter XVIII. Of the Rights of Sovereigns by Institution

### What It Means to Institute a Commonwealth

A commonwealth is said to be *instituted* when a multitude of people agree and covenant, each one with each one, that the majority shall give some man or assembly of men the right to *present the person* of them all, that is, to be their representative. Every one of them, whether he voted for that choice or against it, shall then authorize all the actions and judgments of that man or assembly exactly as if they were his own. Their purpose is to live peaceably among themselves and to be protected against other men.

### The Consequences of Such an Institution

#### 1. Subjects Cannot Change the Form of Government

From this institution of a commonwealth come all the rights and powers of the person or persons on whom sovereign power is conferred by the consent of the assembled people.

First, because they make a covenant, it must be understood that they are not already bound by some earlier covenant to anything that contradicts it. People who have already instituted a commonwealth are bound by covenant to own the actions and judgments of one sovereign. They therefore cannot lawfully make a new covenant among themselves to obey anyone else, in anything whatsoever, without that sovereign's permission. Subjects of a monarch cannot, without his leave, cast off monarchy and return to the confusion of a disunited multitude. Nor can they transfer their person from the one who bears it to another man or another assembly. They are bound, every man to every man, to own and to be regarded as the author of everything their existing sovereign shall do and judge fit to be done. If even one man dissents, all the rest would be breaking the covenant they made with him, which is injustice.

Moreover, each of them has given the sovereignty to the one who bears their person. If they depose him, they take from him what is his own, and that again is injustice. Besides, if someone who attempts to depose his sovereign is killed or punished by him for the attempt, he is the author of his own punishment, since by the institution he is the author of everything his sovereign does. And because it is unjust for a man to do anything for which he may be punished by his own authority, he is unjust on that ground as well.

Some men have justified their disobedience to their sovereign by appealing to a new covenant made not with men but with God. This too is unjust. There is no covenant with God except through the mediation of someone who represents God's person, and no one does that except God's lieutenant, his deputy on earth, who holds the sovereignty under God. But this pretended covenant with God is so obvious a lie, even in the consciences of those who claim it, that it shows a disposition not only unjust but vile and unmanly.

#### 2. Sovereign Power Cannot Be Forfeited

Second, the subjects give the right of bearing the person of them all to the one they make sovereign by a covenant made only among themselves, one to another. The sovereign makes no covenant with any of them. There can therefore be no breach of covenant on the sovereign's part, and no subject can be released from subjection by any claim that the sovereign has forfeited his right.

That the sovereign makes no covenant with his subjects beforehand is plain. He would have to make it either with the whole multitude as one party, or separately with every individual. A covenant with the whole as one party is impossible, because they are not yet one person. If instead he makes as many separate covenants as there are men, those covenants become void once he holds the sovereignty. Any act that one of them might call a breach is the act both of that man himself and of all the rest, because it was done in the person, and by the right, of each of them individually.

Further, suppose one or more subjects claim that the sovereign broke a covenant made at his institution, while others, or a single other subject, or the sovereign alone, maintain that there was no breach. Then there is no judge to decide the dispute. It returns to the sword, and every man recovers the right to protect himself by his own strength, which defeats the very purpose for which they instituted the sovereign. It is therefore pointless to grant sovereignty by way of a prior covenant.

The opinion that a monarch receives his power by covenant, that is, on conditions, comes from failing to grasp a simple truth. Covenants are only words and breath. They have no power to oblige, contain, constrain, or protect anyone beyond the power they draw from the public sword. That sword is the untied hands of the man or assembly that holds the sovereignty, whose actions are vouched for by all and carried out by the strength of all, united in him.

When an assembly is made sovereign, however, no one imagines that any such covenant passed at the institution. No one is so dull as to say, for example, that the People of Rome made a covenant with the Romans to hold the sovereignty on such and such conditions, so that if the conditions were not met the Romans might lawfully depose the Roman People. Men fail to see that the reasoning is the same in a monarchy as in a popular government because some of them are ambitious. They look more kindly on government by an assembly, in which they may hope to take part, than on monarchy, which they despair of ever enjoying.

#### 3. No One Can Without Injustice Protest Against the Institution of a Sovereign Declared by the Majority

Third, because the majority has by consenting voices declared a sovereign, the man who dissented must now consent with the rest. He must be content to own all the actions the sovereign will perform, or else be justly destroyed by the others. If he entered voluntarily into the congregation of those assembled, he thereby declared his will clearly enough, and so tacitly covenanted, to abide by whatever the majority should ordain. If he then refuses to abide by it, or protests against any of their decrees, he acts contrary to his covenant and therefore unjustly. And whether he belongs to the congregation or not, and whether or not his consent is asked, he must either submit to their decrees or be left in the condition of war he was in before. In that condition any man whatever might destroy him without injustice.

#### 4. The Sovereign's Actions Cannot Justly Be Accused by the Subject

Fourth, every subject is by this institution the author of all the actions and judgments of the sovereign so instituted. It follows that nothing the sovereign does can injure any of his subjects, and none of them ought to accuse him of injustice. Whoever acts by another's authority does no injury to the one by whose authority he acts. By this institution of a commonwealth, every individual is the author of everything the sovereign does. Anyone who complains of injury from his sovereign therefore complains of something he himself authored. He ought to accuse no one but himself, and not even himself of injury, since it is impossible to injure oneself. Those who hold sovereign power may indeed commit iniquity, that is, act against equity and the law of nature. But they cannot commit injustice or injury in the proper sense of those words.

#### 5. Whatever the Sovereign Does Is Unpunishable by the Subject

Fifth, and as a consequence of what was just said, no one who holds sovereign power can justly be put to death, or punished in any other way, by his subjects. Since every subject is the author of his sovereign's actions, he would be punishing another for actions he himself committed.

#### 6. The Sovereign Is Judge of What Is Necessary for the Peace and Defense of His Subjects

The end of this institution is the peace and defense of them all, and whoever has a right to the end has a right to the means. It therefore belongs by right to whatever man or assembly holds the sovereignty to judge both the means of peace and defense and whatever hinders or disturbs them. The sovereign may do whatever he thinks necessary to preserve peace and security beforehand, by preventing discord at home and hostility from abroad, and to recover them once they have been lost. And therefore:

#### And Judge of What Doctrines Are Fit to Be Taught Them

Sixth, it belongs to the sovereignty to judge which opinions and doctrines are hostile to peace and which conduce to it. The sovereign therefore decides on what occasions, to what extent, and with what matters men may be trusted when they speak to multitudes of people, and who shall examine the doctrines of all books before they are published. Men's actions proceed from their opinions, and governing their actions well, for the sake of peace and concord, consists in governing their opinions well. In matters of doctrine nothing ought to be regarded but the truth. Yet regulating doctrine for the sake of peace does not conflict with this, because a doctrine contrary to peace can no more be true than peace and concord can be contrary to the law of nature.

Through the negligence or incompetence of governors and teachers, false doctrines may over time come to be generally accepted in a commonwealth, and there the contrary truths may give general offense. Yet even the most sudden and rough forcing-in of a new truth never breaks the peace. At most it sometimes awakens the war. People so loosely governed that they dare take up arms to defend or introduce an opinion are still at war. Their condition is not peace but merely a cessation of arms out of fear of one another, and they live, as it were, continually drawn up on the edge of battle. It therefore belongs to whoever holds sovereign power to be the judge of opinions and doctrines, or to appoint all such judges, because this is necessary to peace and prevents discord and civil war.

#### 7. The Right of Making Rules by Which Every Subject May Know What Is His Own, So That No Other Subject Can Take It from Him Without Injustice

Seventh, the sovereignty holds the whole power of prescribing the rules by which every man may know what goods he may enjoy and what actions he may perform without being molested by any of his fellow subjects. This is what men call *propriety*, or property. Before sovereign power was constituted, as has already been shown, all men had a right to all things, which necessarily causes war. Property is therefore necessary to peace and depends on sovereign power, and it is the act of that power for the sake of public peace. These rules of property, of *meum* and *tuum*, "mine" and "yours," together with the rules of what is good, evil, lawful, and unlawful in the actions of subjects, are the civil laws, meaning the laws of each particular commonwealth. The term "civil law" is now, however, confined to the ancient civil laws of the city of Rome. Rome was then the capital of a great part of the world, and so in those days its laws were the civil law of these regions.

#### 8. To Him Also Belongs the Right of All Judicature and Decision of Controversies

Eighth, the sovereignty holds the right of judicature: the right of hearing and deciding all controversies that may arise over law, whether civil or natural, or over fact. Without the decision of controversies, no subject is protected against the injuries of another, the laws concerning *meum* and *tuum* are useless, and every man is left, by the natural and necessary appetite for his own preservation, with the right to protect himself by his private strength. That is the condition of war, and it is contrary to the end for which every commonwealth is instituted.

#### 9. And of Making War and Peace as He Shall Think Best

Ninth, the sovereignty holds the right of making war and peace with other nations and commonwealths. This means judging when war serves the public good and how large a force must be assembled, armed, and paid for that purpose, and levying money on the subjects to cover the expense. The power by which the people are defended consists in their armies, and the strength of an army consists in the union of its strength under a single command. The instituted sovereign therefore holds that command, because command of the militia, even without any other institution, makes whoever holds it sovereign. Accordingly, whoever is made general of an army, the holder of sovereign power is always generalissimo, the commander over all commanders.

#### 10. And of Choosing All Counselors and Ministers, in Both Peace and War

Tenth, the sovereignty holds the choice of all counselors, ministers, magistrates, and officers, in peace and in war. The sovereign is charged with the end, which is the common peace and defense. He is therefore understood to have the power to use whatever means he thinks most fit for carrying out that charge.

#### 11. And of Rewarding and Punishing, and That Arbitrarily Where No Prior Law Has Fixed the Measure

Eleventh, the sovereign has the power to reward any subject with riches or honor, and to punish any subject with bodily or monetary penalties or with disgrace. He does so according to the law he has previously made. If no law has been made, he does so according to what he judges will best encourage men to serve the commonwealth or deter them from doing it disservice.

#### 12. And of Honor and Rank

Lastly, consider how highly men are naturally inclined to value themselves, how much respect they expect from others, and how little they value other men. From these traits continually arise rivalry, quarrels, factions, and at last war, which destroys men and weakens their strength against a common enemy. It is therefore necessary to have laws of honor and a public scale of worth for those who have deserved well of the commonwealth, or are able to. It is also necessary that someone hold the force to carry out those laws. But it has already been shown that the sovereignty holds not only the entire militia, or armed forces, of the commonwealth, but also the judicature of all controversies. The sovereign therefore also has the right to confer titles of honor, to appoint the rank and dignity each man shall hold, and to determine what signs of respect men shall show one another in public or private gatherings.

### These Rights Are Indivisible

These are the rights that make up the essence of sovereignty. They are the marks by which one may tell in what man or assembly sovereign power is placed and resides, for they cannot be shared out or separated. Some powers the sovereign may transfer while still keeping the power to protect his subjects. These include the power to coin money, the power to manage the estates and persons of heirs who are still minors, the right of pre-emption, or first purchase, in markets, and all other prerogatives granted by statute. The essential rights are different. If the sovereign transfers the militia, he keeps the judicature in vain, because the laws cannot be enforced. If he grants away the power of raising money, the militia is useless. If he gives away the government of doctrines, men will be frightened into rebellion by fear of spirits. Take any one of these rights away, and holding all the rest will do nothing to preserve peace and justice, which is the end for which all commonwealths are instituted.

This is the division meant by the saying, "A kingdom divided in itself cannot stand." Division into opposing armies can never happen unless this division comes first. The greater part of England first accepted the opinion that these powers were divided among the King, the Lords, and the House of Commons. Had they not, the people would never have been divided and fallen into the present civil war. That war was fought first between those who disagreed in politics, and afterward between those who dissented over religious liberty. These events have taught men so much on this point of sovereign right that few in England now fail to see that these rights are inseparable. This will be generally acknowledged at the next return of peace, and will remain so until their miseries are forgotten, and no longer, unless the common people are better taught than they have been up to now.

### And They Cannot Pass Away by Any Grant Without Direct Renunciation of the Sovereign Power

Because these rights are essential and inseparable, a grant that seems to give any of them away is void unless two things happen. The sovereign power itself must be renounced in direct terms, and those receiving the grant must no longer give the name of sovereign to the one who grants it. When he has granted away all he can, if we grant the sovereignty back to him, everything is restored, because it is inseparably attached to the sovereignty.

### The Power and Honor of Subjects Vanish in the Presence of Sovereign Power

Since this great authority is indivisible and inseparably attached to the sovereignty, there is little basis for a certain opinion about sovereign kings. Some say that kings are *singulis majores*, of greater power than each of their subjects individually, but nonetheless *universis minores*, of less power than all of them together. If by "all together" they do not mean the collective body as one person, then "all together" and "each one" mean the same thing, and the statement is absurd. If by "all together" they mean the subjects considered as one person, the person the sovereign bears, then the power of all together is the same as the sovereign's power, and the statement is again absurd. They see this absurdity clearly enough when sovereignty lies in an assembly of the people, but in a monarch they fail to see it. Yet the power of sovereignty is the same in whomever it is placed.

As with power, so with honor: the sovereign's honor ought to be greater than that of any or all of the subjects, for sovereignty is the fountain of honor. The dignities of lord, earl, duke, and prince are its creations. Servants are equal in their master's presence and have no honor at all, and so are subjects in the presence of the sovereign. Out of his sight, some shine more and some less, but in his presence they shine no more than the stars in the presence of the sun.

### Sovereign Power Is Not as Harmful as the Lack of It, and the Harm Comes Mostly from Not Submitting Readily to a Lesser Burden

Here someone may object that the condition of subjects is very wretched, since they are exposed to the lusts and other unruly passions of whoever holds such unlimited power. Those who live under a monarch commonly think this the fault of monarchy. Those who live under a democracy or another sovereign assembly blame every inconvenience on that form of commonwealth. Yet power in all forms, provided they are complete enough to protect their subjects, is the same.

Such people do not consider that the human condition can never be free of some inconvenience or other. The greatest inconvenience that can befall the people at large under any form of government is scarcely felt in comparison with the miseries and horrible calamities of civil war. It is equally slight beside the lawless condition of masterless men, who are subject to no laws and to no coercive power to tie their hands from plunder and revenge. Nor do these people consider where the heaviest burdens imposed by sovereign rulers come from. They do not arise from any pleasure or profit the rulers expect from harming or weakening their subjects, on whose vigor the rulers' own strength depends. They arise from the subjects themselves, who contribute unwillingly to their own defense. This unwillingness forces their governors to draw from them what they can in time of peace, so that in any emergency or sudden need they have the means to resist their enemies or gain an advantage over them.

All men are naturally equipped with powerful multiplying glasses, lenses that magnify, namely their passions and self-love, through which every small payment looks like a great grievance. But they lack prospective glasses, the telescopes of moral and civil science, through which they might see from far off the miseries that hang over them and that cannot be avoided without such payments.

## Chapter XIX. Of the Several Kinds of Commonwealth by Institution, and of Succession to the Sovereigne Power

### There Are Only Three Forms of Commonwealth

Commonwealths differ according to the difference in their sovereign, the person who represents each and every member of the multitude. Sovereignty resides either in one man or in an assembly of more than one, and that assembly is open either to every man or only to certain men distinguished from the rest. It follows that there can be only three kinds of commonwealth. The representative must be either one man or more than one, and if more, the assembly must consist either of all or of only a part. When the representative is one man, the commonwealth is a MONARCHY. When it is an assembly of all who choose to come together, it is a DEMOCRACY, or popular commonwealth. When it is an assembly of only a part, it is called an ARISTOCRACY. No other kind of commonwealth is possible, because either one, or several, or all must hold the sovereign power entire, and I have already shown that power to be indivisible.

### Tyranny and Oligarchy Are Only Different Names for Monarchy and Aristocracy

The histories and books of politics contain other names of government, such as tyranny and oligarchy. These are not the names of other forms of government, however, but of the same forms when people dislike them. Those who are discontented under a monarchy call it tyranny, and those who are displeased with an aristocracy call it oligarchy. In the same way, those who feel aggrieved under a democracy call it anarchy, which means the absence of government. Yet no one, I think, believes that the absence of government is a new kind of government. By the same reasoning, no one ought to believe that a government is of one kind when he likes it and of another when he dislikes it or is oppressed by those who govern.

### Subordinate Representatives Are Dangerous

Men who are in absolute liberty may, if they please, give one man the authority to represent each of them, just as they may give that authority to any assembly whatsoever. Consequently, they may subject themselves to a monarch, if they think it good, as absolutely as to any other representative. Where a sovereign power has already been established, therefore, there can be no other representative of the same people, except for particular purposes limited by the sovereign. Anything more would set up two sovereigns, and every man would have his person represented by two actors. By opposing one another, these two would necessarily divide a power that, if men are to live in peace, must remain indivisible, and so they would reduce the multitude to a condition of war, which defeats the very purpose for which sovereignty is instituted.

It would be absurd to think that a sovereign assembly, by inviting the people of its dominion to send up deputies empowered to make their advice or desires known, should therefore regard those deputies, rather than itself, as the absolute representative of the people. It is equally absurd to think the same in a monarchy. I do not know how so obvious a truth has lately come to be so little observed. In a monarchy, the man who held the sovereignty by a descent of six hundred years was alone called sovereign, received the title of Majesty from every one of his subjects, and was unquestionably accepted by them as their king; yet he was never considered their representative. That title passed without contradiction to the men who, at his command, were sent up by the people to carry their petitions and to give him their advice, if he allowed it. This should stand as a warning to those who are the true and absolute representative of a people: they ought to instruct men in the nature of that office, and take care how they admit any other general representation on any occasion whatsoever, if they mean to discharge the trust committed to them.

### Monarchy Compared with Sovereign Assemblies

These three kinds of commonwealth do not differ in power. They differ in convenience, that is, in their fitness to produce the peace and security of the people, which is the end for which they were instituted. In comparing monarchy with the other two, we may observe the following.

First, whoever bears the person of the people, or belongs to the assembly that bears it, also bears his own natural person. However careful he may be, in his political capacity, to advance the common interest, he is more careful, or at least no less careful, to advance the private good of himself, his family, his kindred, and his friends. And for the most part, if the public interest happens to cross his private interest, he prefers the private, because men's passions are commonly more powerful than their reason. It follows that the public interest is best advanced where public and private interest are most closely united. In a monarchy, the private interest is identical with the public. A monarch's riches, power, and honor arise solely from the riches, strength, and reputation of his subjects. No king can be rich, glorious, or secure if his subjects are poor, or contemptible, or too weak from want or dissension to sustain a war against their enemies. In a democracy or an aristocracy, by contrast, public prosperity contributes less to the private fortune of a corrupt or ambitious man than, very often, a piece of perfidious advice, a treacherous act, or a civil war.

Second, a monarch takes counsel from whomever he pleases, whenever and wherever he pleases. He can therefore hear the opinions of men versed in the matter under deliberation, whatever their rank or station, and he can hear them as long before the time of action and with as much secrecy as he wishes. When a sovereign assembly needs counsel, however, no one is admitted except those who have held a right to it from the beginning. For the most part, these are men more practiced in acquiring wealth than in acquiring knowledge, and they deliver their advice in long speeches, which may stir men to action, and commonly do, but cannot guide them in it. The flame of the passions never enlightens the understanding; it only dazzles it. Nor is there any place or time at which an assembly can receive counsel in secret, simply because of the number of its members.

Third, the resolutions of a monarch are subject to no inconstancy beyond what belongs to human nature. In assemblies, however, a further inconstancy arises from their numbers. A few members who would have kept a resolution firm may be absent, whether from overconfidence, negligence, or private obstacles, or a few of the contrary opinion may diligently attend, and either event undoes today everything that was concluded yesterday.

Fourth, a monarch cannot disagree with himself out of envy or self-interest. An assembly can, and to such a degree that it may produce a civil war.

Fifth, monarchy does have this drawback: any subject may be stripped of everything he owns by the power of one man, in order to enrich a favorite or a flatterer. I admit that this is a great and unavoidable drawback. But the same thing can happen just as well where the sovereign power lies in an assembly. Their power is the same, and they are as liable to bad counsel, and to being led astray by orators, as a monarch is by flatterers. Indeed, by becoming one another's flatterers, the members of an assembly serve one another's greed and ambition in turn. Moreover, the favorites of an assembly are many, and their kindred far more numerous than those of any monarch. Besides, there is no favorite of a monarch who cannot help his friends as readily as he can harm his enemies. Orators, however, who are the favorites of sovereign assemblies, have great power to harm but little power to save. Such is human nature that accusing requires less eloquence than excusing, and a condemnation looks more like justice than an acquittal does.

Sixth, it is a drawback of monarchy that the sovereignty may descend to an infant, or to someone who cannot tell good from evil. The drawback consists in this: the use of his power must then rest in the hands of another man, or of some assembly of men, who govern by his right and in his name as the curators and protectors of his person and authority. But to say that there is something harmful in placing the use of sovereign power in the hands of a man or an assembly is to say that all government is more harmful than confusion and civil war. All the danger that can be alleged, therefore, must arise from rivalry among those who may compete for an office of such great honor and profit.

To show that this drawback does not proceed from the form of government we call monarchy, we must consider two cases. In the first, the preceding monarch has appointed who shall have the guardianship of his infant successor, either expressly by his will or tacitly by not overruling the custom accepted in such cases. Then any harm that follows must be attributed not to monarchy but to the ambition and injustice of the subjects, and these are the same under every kind of government where the people are not well instructed in their duty and in the rights of sovereignty. In the second case, the preceding monarch has made no arrangement for guardianship at all. Here the law of nature supplies a sufficient rule: the guardianship belongs to the person who has, by nature, the greatest interest in preserving the infant's authority and the least to gain from his death or diminishment. Since every man naturally seeks his own benefit and advancement, to place an infant in the power of those who could advance themselves by his destruction or injury is not guardianship but treachery. Sufficient provision having thus been made against every legitimate quarrel over government under a child, any dispute that disturbs the public peace must be attributed not to the monarchical form but to the ambition of subjects and their ignorance of their duty.

On the other side, there is no great commonwealth whose sovereignty lies in a large assembly that is not, in its deliberations on peace and war and in the making of laws, in the same condition as if the government were in the hands of a child. A child lacks the judgment to dissent from the counsel given him, and is therefore compelled to take the advice of the person or persons in whose care he has been placed. In the same way, an assembly lacks the freedom to dissent from the counsel of the majority, whether that counsel is good or bad. And just as a child needs a tutor or protector to preserve his person and authority, so too, in great commonwealths, the sovereign assembly in every time of great danger and trouble needs *custodes libertatis*, guardians of liberty, which is to say dictators or protectors of its authority. These are in effect temporary monarchs, to whom the assembly may entrust the entire exercise of its power for a time; and at the end of that time, assemblies have more often been deprived of their power by such men than infant kings have been by their protectors, regents, or any other guardians.

Although there are, as I have now shown, only three kinds of sovereignty, namely monarchy, where one man holds it; democracy, where the general assembly of the subjects holds it; and aristocracy, where it rests in an assembly of certain persons who are named or otherwise distinguished from the rest, anyone who considers the particular commonwealths that have existed and still exist in the world may not find it easy to reduce them to three. He may therefore be inclined to think that there are other forms, arising from mixtures of these. Examples include elective kingdoms, where kings have the sovereign power placed in their hands for a time, and kingdoms in which the king's power is limited; most writers nevertheless call such governments monarchies. Likewise, if a popular or aristocratic commonwealth conquers an enemy's country and governs it through a president, a procurator, or some other magistrate, this may at first sight appear to be a democratic or aristocratic government. But it is not. Elective kings are not sovereigns but ministers of the sovereign. Limited kings are not sovereigns but ministers of those who hold the sovereign power. And provinces subject to the democracy or aristocracy of another commonwealth are governed not democratically or aristocratically but monarchically.

Consider first an elective king, whose power is limited to his lifetime, as it is in many parts of Christendom today, or to a certain number of years or months, as the dictator's power was among the Romans. If he has the right to appoint his successor, he is no longer elective but hereditary. If he has no power to choose his successor, then either some other known man or assembly may elect a new one after his death, or else the commonwealth dies and dissolves with him and returns to the condition of war. If it is known who has the power to confer the sovereignty after his death, then it is also known that the sovereignty lay in them all along, for no one has the right to give what he has no right to possess and keep for himself if he so chooses. But if there is no one who can confer the sovereignty after the death of the man first elected, then he has the power, and is indeed obliged by the law of nature, to establish a successor, so as to keep those who entrusted him with the government from relapsing into the miserable condition of civil war. Consequently, at the moment of his election he was an absolute sovereign.

Second, a king whose power is limited is not superior to the person or persons who have the power to limit it, and one who is not superior is not supreme, which is to say not sovereign. The sovereignty, therefore, always lay in the assembly that had the right to limit him, and so the government was not a monarchy but either a democracy or an aristocracy. Such was the case in ancient Sparta, where the kings had the privilege of leading the armies but the sovereignty belonged to the ephors, the city's board of elected magistrates.

Third, when the Roman people formerly governed the land of Judea, for example, through a president, Judea was not on that account a democracy, because its people were not governed by any assembly that any of them had the right to enter. Nor was it an aristocracy, because they were not governed by any assembly that anyone could enter by their election. They were governed by one person, which, with respect to the people of Rome, was an assembly of the people, or a democracy, but which, with respect to the people of Judea, who had no right whatever to take part in the government, was a monarch. Where a people is governed by an assembly chosen by themselves from among their own number, the government is called a democracy or an aristocracy. But where they are governed by an assembly not of their own choosing, it is a monarchy: not of one man over another man, but of one people over another people.

### Of the Right of Succession

In all these forms of government the material is mortal, since not only monarchs but entire assemblies die. For the preservation of peace among men, therefore, just as provision was made for an artificial man, so provision must also be made for an artificial eternity of life. Without it, men governed by an assembly would return to the condition of war in every generation, and those governed by one man would return to it as soon as their ruler died. This artificial eternity is what men call the right of succession.

No form of government is complete unless the disposal of the succession lies with the present sovereign. If it lies with some other particular man or private assembly, it lies with a subject, and the sovereign may take it over at his pleasure, so that the right is really his own. And if it lies with no particular man but is left to a fresh choice, then the commonwealth is dissolved and the right belongs to whoever can seize it, which defeats the intention of those who instituted the commonwealth for their permanent, not their temporary, security.

In a democracy the assembly as a whole cannot fail unless the multitude that is governed fails. Questions about the right of succession, therefore, have no place at all in that form of government.

In an aristocracy, when any member of the assembly dies, the election of another in his place belongs to the assembly itself, as the sovereign to whom the choice of all counselors and officers belongs. For whatever the representative does as actor, every one of the subjects does as author. And although the sovereign assembly may give others the power to elect new members to fill its ranks, the election is still made by the assembly's authority, and by the same authority it may be revoked whenever the public good requires.

### The Present Monarch Has the Right to Dispose of the Succession

The greatest difficulty concerning the right of succession arises in monarchy. It comes from the fact that, at first sight, it is not obvious who is to appoint the successor, nor, in many cases, whom he has appointed. Both questions demand more exact reasoning than most men are accustomed to use.

On the first question, who shall appoint the successor of a monarch who holds sovereign authority (I specify this because elective kings and princes hold the sovereign power not as their property but only in use), we must recognize that either the man in possession has the right to dispose of the succession, or else that right reverts to the dissolved multitude. The death of one who holds sovereign power as his property leaves the multitude with no sovereign at all, that is, with no representative in whom they are united and through whom they are capable of performing any single action. They are therefore incapable of electing a new monarch. Every man has an equal right to submit himself to whomever he thinks best able to protect him, or, if he can, to protect himself with his own sword, and this is a return to confusion and to the condition of a war of every man against every man, contrary to the end for which monarchy was first instituted. It is evident, therefore, that by the very institution of monarchy, the choice of a successor is always left to the judgment and will of the present possessor.

As for the second question, which sometimes arises, namely whom the reigning monarch has designated to succeed to and inherit his power, it is settled by his express words and testament, or by other sufficient tacit signs.

### Succession Passes by Express Words;

Succession passes by express words or testament when the monarch declares it during his lifetime, either *viva voce*, by word of mouth, or in writing, as the first emperors of Rome declared who should be their heirs. The word "heir" does not in itself mean a man's children or nearest relatives, but whomever he declares, in any manner, that he wishes to succeed him in his estate. If a monarch therefore declares expressly, by word or in writing, that a certain man shall be his heir, that man is invested with the right of being monarch immediately upon the death of his predecessor.

### Or by Not Overruling a Custom;

Where a testament and express words are lacking, other natural signs of the monarch's will must be followed, and one of these is custom. Where the custom is that the next of kin succeeds without qualification, the next of kin has the right of succession, because if the will of the man in possession had been otherwise, he could easily have declared it during his lifetime. Likewise, where the custom is that the next male relative succeeds, the right of succession lies with the next male relative, for the same reason. The same holds if the custom were to advance the female line. Whatever custom a man could overrule with a word, and does not, is a natural sign that he wishes it to stand.

### Or by Presumption of Natural Affection

Where neither custom nor testament has gone before, it is to be understood, first, that the monarch's will is for the government to remain monarchical, since he has approved that form of government in his own person. Second, it is to be understood that a child of his own, male or female, is to be preferred before anyone else, because men are presumed to be naturally more inclined to advance their own children than the children of others; and that among his own children a male is to be preferred to a female, because men are naturally better suited than women to undertakings of labor and danger. Third, where his own line fails, a brother is to be preferred to a stranger, and in every case the nearer in blood to the more remote, because it is always presumed that those nearer in kinship are nearer in affection, and it is evident that a man always receives the greatest honor, by reflection, from the greatness of his nearest kindred.

### Disposing of the Succession, Even to a King of Another Nation, Is Not Unlawful

If it is lawful for a monarch to dispose of the succession by words of contract or by testament, some may object that a great harm could follow: he might sell or give away his right of governing to a foreigner. Because foreigners, meaning men not accustomed to living under the same government or speaking the same language, commonly undervalue one another, this could lead to the oppression of his subjects. That is indeed a great harm. But it does not necessarily proceed from subjection to a foreign ruler; it proceeds from the lack of skill of governors who are ignorant of the true rules of politics. For this reason the Romans, after they had subdued many nations, made their rule easier to accept by removing that grievance as far as they thought necessary. Sometimes to entire nations, and sometimes to the leading men of every nation they conquered, they granted not only the privileges but also the name of Romans, and they admitted many of them into the Senate and into offices of responsibility, even in the city of Rome itself. This is what our most wise King, King James, aimed at in his efforts to unite his two realms of England and Scotland. Had he achieved it, he would in all likelihood have prevented the civil wars that now make both kingdoms miserable.

It is therefore no injury to the people for a monarch to dispose of the succession by will, even though, through the fault of many princes, it has sometimes proved harmful. A further argument for its lawfulness is this: whatever harm can come from giving a kingdom to a foreigner can also come from marrying foreigners in such a way that the right of succession descends to them, and yet everyone regards such marriages as lawful.

## Chapter XX. Of Dominion Paternal and Despotical

A commonwealth by acquisition is one in which sovereign power is gained by force. It is gained by force when men, either individually or collectively by majority vote, authorize all the actions of the man or assembly that holds their lives and liberty in his power, and do so out of fear of death or imprisonment.

This kind of dominion, or sovereignty, differs from sovereignty by institution in only one respect. Men who choose their sovereign do so out of fear of one another, not of the one they institute, whereas in this case they subject themselves to the very one they fear. In both cases, then, they act from fear. Those who hold that every covenant arising from fear of death or violence is void should take note of this, for if they were right, no one in any kind of commonwealth could be bound to obey. It is true that once a commonwealth has been instituted or acquired, promises made out of fear of death or violence are not covenants and do not bind when the thing promised is contrary to the laws. But the reason is not that the promise was made in fear; it is that the person promising has no right to the thing he promised. Likewise, when a man could lawfully perform what he promised and fails to, it is not any defect in the covenant that releases him, but the sentence of the sovereign. Otherwise, whenever a man promised lawfully, he would break his promise unlawfully. When the sovereign, who acts on behalf of all, acquits him, he is in effect acquitted by the very person who extorted the promise, since that person, as a subject, is the author of the sovereign's act of release.

The rights and consequences of sovereignty, however, are the same in both kinds of commonwealth. The sovereign's power cannot be transferred to another without his consent. He cannot forfeit it. He cannot be accused by any of his subjects of doing them injury, and he cannot be punished by them. He is the judge of what is necessary for peace, and the judge of doctrines. He is the sole legislator, and the supreme judge of controversies and of the times and occasions for war and peace. It belongs to him to choose magistrates, counselors, commanders, and all other officers and ministers, and to determine rewards and punishments, honor and rank.
