The reasons for all this are the same as those given in the previous chapter for the same rights and consequences of sovereignty by institution.

Dominion is acquired in two ways: by generation and by conquest. The right of dominion by generation is the right a parent has over his children, and it is called paternal. It does not derive from generation itself, as though a parent had dominion over a child simply because he begot it. It derives instead from the child's consent, given either expressly or through other sufficient signs. As far as generation is concerned, God ordained a helper for man, and there are always two who are equally parents. If dominion came from generation, it would therefore belong equally to both, and the child would be equally subject to both, which is impossible, since no one can obey two masters. Some have assigned dominion to the man alone, on the grounds that he belongs to the more excellent sex, but they miscalculate. There is not always such a difference of strength or prudence between a man and a woman that the right could be settled without war. In commonwealths, the dispute is decided by civil law, and in most cases, though not all, the ruling favors the father, because commonwealths have for the most part been founded by the fathers of families rather than the mothers. But the question here concerns the pure state of nature, in which there are assumed to be no laws of marriage and no laws for the education of children, only the law of nature and the natural inclination of the sexes toward each other and toward their children. In this pure state of nature, the parents either settle dominion over the child between themselves by contract, or they do not settle it at all. If they settle it, the right passes according to the contract. History records that the Amazons made a contract with the men of neighboring countries, to whom they turned for offspring, that male children would be sent back to the fathers while female children would remain with the mothers. Dominion over the daughters thus lay with the mother.

If there is no contract, dominion belongs to the mother. In the pure state of nature, where there are no marriage laws, no one can know who the father is unless the mother declares it, so the right of dominion over the child depends on her will and is therefore hers. Moreover, the infant is first in the mother's power, so that she may either nurse it or abandon it. If she nurses it, the child owes its life to her and is therefore obliged to obey her rather than anyone else, and dominion over it is consequently hers. But if she abandons it and someone else finds it and raises it, dominion belongs to the one who raises it. The child ought to obey the one who preserves it, because the preservation of life is the purpose for which one person becomes subject to another, and every person is presumed to promise obedience to whoever has the power to save or destroy him.

If the mother is the father's subject, the child is in the father's power. If the father is the mother's subject, as when a sovereign queen marries one of her subjects, the child is subject to the mother, since the father too is her subject.

If a man and a woman who are monarchs of two separate kingdoms have a child and make a contract about who shall have dominion over him, the right of dominion passes according to that contract. If they make no contract, dominion follows the sovereignty of the place where the child lives, for the sovereign of each country has dominion over everyone who resides there.

Whoever has dominion over a child also has dominion over that child's children, and over their children in turn. Whoever has dominion over a person has dominion over everything that belongs to him; without this, dominion would be a mere title without effect.

The right of succession to paternal dominion proceeds in the same way as the right of succession to monarchy, which I have already discussed sufficiently in the previous chapter.

Dominion acquired by conquest, or victory in war, is what some writers call despotical, from the Greek *despotes*, meaning a lord or master. It is the dominion of a master over his servant. The victor acquires this dominion when the vanquished, to escape the immediate stroke of death, covenants, either in express words or by other sufficient signs of his will, that for as long as he is allowed his life and the liberty of his body, the victor may make use of them as he pleases. Once this covenant is made, the vanquished man is a servant, and not before. Whether the word "servant" comes from the Latin *servire*, to serve, or *servare*, to save, I leave to the grammarians to dispute. In either case it does not mean a captive kept in prison or in chains until the man who took him, or who bought him from the man who took him, decides what to do with him. Such men, commonly called slaves, are under no obligation at all; they may justly break their chains or escape their prison, and kill their master or carry him off as a captive. A servant, by contrast, is someone who, having been taken, is allowed his bodily liberty and is trusted by his master on his promise not to run away or do him violence.

It is not the victory, therefore, that gives the right of dominion over the vanquished, but the vanquished man's own covenant. He is not obliged because he has been conquered, that is, beaten and captured or put to flight, but because he comes in and submits to the victor. Nor is the victor obliged to spare an enemy who surrenders without a promise of life. Such a surrender is made at the victor's discretion, and it binds him no longer than his own discretion sees fit.

What men do when they ask for what is now called quarter, which the Greeks called *zogria*, "taking alive," is to escape the victor's immediate fury by submitting, and to bargain for their lives with ransom or service. A man granted quarter, therefore, has not been given his life; its fate has only been postponed for further deliberation, since he has surrendered not on condition of life but at the victor's discretion. Only when the victor has entrusted him with his bodily liberty is his life secure and his service owed. Slaves who work in prisons or in fetters do so not out of duty but to avoid the cruelty of their taskmasters.

The master of a servant is also master of everything the servant has, and may demand the use of it, whether his goods, his labor, his own servants, or his children, as often as he sees fit. For the servant holds his life from his master by a covenant of obedience, which means owning and authorizing whatever the master does. If the servant refuses and the master kills him, puts him in chains, or otherwise punishes him for his disobedience, the servant is himself the author of that punishment and cannot accuse his master of injury.

In sum, the rights and consequences of both paternal and despotical dominion are exactly the same as those of a sovereign by institution, and for the same reasons, which are set out in the previous chapter. Consider a monarch who rules several nations, holding sovereignty in one by institution, through the assembled people, and in another by conquest, through the submission of each individual to avoid death or chains. For such a monarch to demand more of one nation than of the other, on the strength of his title by conquest, as though it were a conquered nation, is to show ignorance of the rights of sovereignty. The sovereign is absolute over both alike, or else there is no sovereignty at all, and then every man may lawfully protect himself, if he can, with his own sword, which is the condition of war.

It follows that a large family, if it is not part of some commonwealth, is in itself, so far as the rights of sovereignty are concerned, a small monarchy, whether the family consists of a man and his children, a man and his servants, or a man together with both his children and his servants. In it, the father or master is the sovereign. Yet a family is not properly a commonwealth unless it has enough power, through its numbers or other advantages, that it cannot be subdued without the risk of war. Where a group of men is plainly too weak to defend itself even when united, each may use his own judgment in time of danger to save his life, whether by flight or by submitting to the enemy, as he thinks best. In the same way, a very small company of soldiers surprised by an army may throw down their arms and ask for quarter, or run away, rather than be put to the sword. This is enough concerning what I have found, by reasoning and deduction, about the rights of sovereigns, drawn from the nature, needs, and purposes of men in establishing commonwealths and placing themselves under monarchs or assemblies entrusted with enough power to protect them.

Let us now consider what Scripture teaches on the same point. In Exodus, the children of Israel say to Moses: "Speak to us yourself, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, or we will die." This is absolute obedience to Moses. Concerning the rights of kings, God himself, speaking through Samuel in the first book of Samuel, says: "This will be the right of the king who will reign over you. He will take your sons and set them to drive his chariots, to be his horsemen, and to run before his chariots; to gather in his harvest; and to make his engines of war and the equipment of his chariots. He will take your daughters to make perfumes and to be his cooks and bakers. He will take your fields, your vineyards, and your olive groves, and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of your grain and wine and give it to the men of his household and to his other servants. He will take your menservants and maidservants and the best of your young men and put them to work in his affairs. He will take a tenth of your flocks; and you will be his servants." This is absolute power, summed up in the final words, "you will be his servants." Moreover, when the people had heard what power their king was to have, they consented to it, saying: "We will be like all the other nations, and our king will judge our cases and go out before us to fight our wars." This confirms the sovereign's right both to the militia and to all judicial authority, which together contain as absolute a power as one man can possibly transfer to another. Again, King Solomon prayed to God in the first book of Kings: "Give your servant understanding to judge your people, and to discern between good and evil." It belongs, therefore, to the sovereign to be judge and to prescribe the rules for discerning good and evil; those rules are laws, and so the legislative power lies in him. Saul sought David's life, yet when David had Saul in his power and his servants would have killed him, David forbade them, saying, as the first book of Samuel records: "God forbid that I should do such a thing against my lord, the anointed of God." On the obedience of servants, St. Paul says in his letter to the Colossians, "Servants, obey your masters in all things," and, a few verses earlier, "Children, obey your parents in all things." This is simple obedience in those subject to paternal or despotical dominion. Again, in Matthew: "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do." Here again is simple obedience. And St. Paul writes to Titus: "Remind them to submit to rulers and to those in authority, and to obey them." This obedience, too, is simple. Finally, our Savior himself acknowledges that men ought to pay the taxes kings impose, when he says, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's," and he paid such taxes himself. He also acknowledges that the king's word is enough to take anything from any subject when there is need, and that the king is the judge of that need. For he himself, as King of the Jews, commanded his disciples to take a donkey and its colt to carry him into Jerusalem, saying, in Matthew: "Go into the village ahead of you, and you will find a donkey tied there, and her colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. And if anyone asks you what you are doing, say, 'The Lord has need of them,' and they will let them go." The owners would not ask whether his need was a sufficient claim, or whether he was the judge of that need, but would simply yield to the will of the Lord.

To these passages may be added one from Genesis: "You will be like gods, knowing good and evil," and, a few verses later, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?" The power of judging good and evil had been forbidden under the name of the fruit of the tree of knowledge, as a test of Adam's obedience. The Devil, to inflame the ambition of the woman, to whom that fruit already seemed beautiful, told her that by tasting it they would become like gods, knowing good and evil. When both had eaten, they did indeed take upon themselves God's office, which is the judging of good and evil, but they acquired no new ability to tell the two apart correctly. As for the statement that after eating they saw they were naked, no one has ever interpreted it to mean that they had previously been blind and unable to see their own skin. The meaning is plain: it was then that they first judged their nakedness, the condition in which it had been God's will to create them, to be indecent, and by being ashamed they tacitly passed judgment on God himself. That is why God says, "Have you eaten," and so on, as if to say: Do you, who owe me obedience, take it upon yourself to judge my commandments? This signifies clearly, though allegorically, that the commands of those who have the right to command are not to be criticized or disputed by their subjects.

It is plain to me, then, from both reason and Scripture, that sovereign power, whether it is placed in one man, as in a monarchy, or in one assembly of men, as in popular and aristocratic commonwealths, is as great as men can possibly be imagined to make it. Men may imagine many evil consequences of so unlimited a power, but the consequences of lacking it, which are the perpetual war of every man against his neighbor, are far worse. Human life in this world will never be free of hardships, but no great hardship arises in any commonwealth except from the disobedience of subjects and their breach of the covenants from which the commonwealth took its existence. And whoever thinks sovereign power too great and seeks to reduce it must subject himself to a power capable of limiting it, which is to say, to a greater one.

The strongest objection is the one drawn from practice: people ask where and when such power has ever been acknowledged by subjects. One may ask them in turn when or where there has ever been a kingdom long free of sedition and civil war. In those nations whose commonwealths have been long-lived, and have been destroyed only by foreign war, the subjects never disputed the sovereign power. In any case, an argument drawn from the practice of men who have never examined the causes and nature of commonwealths thoroughly, never weighed them with exact reason, and who daily suffer the miseries that arise from this ignorance, carries no weight. Even if men everywhere in the world laid the foundations of their houses on sand, it would not follow that this is how it ought to be done. The skill of making and maintaining commonwealths rests on definite rules, like arithmetic and geometry, and not on practice alone, as with a game of tennis. These are rules that poor men have lacked the leisure to discover, and that men who had the leisure have so far lacked the curiosity or the method to find out.

## Chapter XXI. Of the Liberty of Subjects

### What Liberty Is

Liberty, or freedom, properly means the absence of opposition, and by opposition I mean external impediments to motion. In this sense the word applies to irrational and inanimate things no less than to rational ones. Whatever is so tied down or hemmed in that it can move only within a certain space, a space fixed by the resistance of some external body, we say has no liberty to go further. So it is with any living creature while walls or chains imprison or restrain it, and with water while banks or vessels hold it in when it would otherwise spread into a larger space. We say they are not at liberty to move as they would without those external impediments. But when the obstacle to motion lies in the constitution of the thing itself, we do not say it lacks liberty. We say it lacks the power to move, as when a stone lies still or a man is confined to his bed by sickness.

### What It Is to Be Free

According to this proper and generally accepted meaning of the word, a free man is one who, in those things he is able to do by his strength and wits, is not hindered from doing what he has a will to do. But when the words *free* and *liberty* are applied to anything other than bodies, they are misused, for what is not subject to motion is not subject to impediment. When we say, for example, that the way is free, we mean no liberty belonging to the road itself, but the liberty of those who walk along it without being stopped. When we say a gift is free, we mean not any liberty of the gift but of the giver, who was bound by no law or covenant to give it. When we speak freely, the liberty belongs not to the voice or to pronunciation but to the man, whom no law obliged to speak otherwise than he did. Finally, the phrase *free will* allows us to infer no liberty in the will, desire, or inclination itself, but only in the man. His liberty consists in this: he meets no obstacle in doing what he has the will, desire, or inclination to do.

### Fear and Liberty Are Compatible

Fear and liberty are compatible. When a man throws his goods into the sea for fear that the ship will sink, he nevertheless does it quite willingly, and he could refuse if he chose. It is therefore the act of someone who was free. In the same way a man sometimes pays a debt only for fear of prison, and since nobody prevented him from keeping the money, it was the act of a man at liberty. And generally, all the actions that men perform in commonwealths out of fear of the law are actions that the doers had the liberty to leave undone.

### Liberty and Necessity Are Compatible

Liberty and necessity are compatible. Water flowing down a channel has not only the liberty but the necessity of descending along it, and the same holds for the actions men perform voluntarily. Because these actions proceed from their will, they proceed from liberty. Yet every act of a man's will, and every desire and inclination, proceeds from some cause, and that cause from another, in a continuous chain whose first link is in the hand of God, the first of all causes. So these actions also proceed from necessity. To anyone who could see the connection of those causes, the necessity of all men's voluntary actions would be plain. God, therefore, who sees and disposes all things, sees also that man's liberty in doing what he wills is accompanied by the necessity of doing what God wills, no more and no less. For although men may do many things that God does not command, and of which He is therefore not the author, they can have no passion or appetite for anything unless God's will is the cause of that appetite. If His will did not secure the necessity of man's will, and consequently of everything that depends on man's will, then human liberty would contradict and obstruct the omnipotence and liberty of God. This is enough, for the matter at hand, about natural liberty, which alone is properly called liberty.

### Artificial Bonds, or Covenants

But just as men, to attain peace and thereby preserve themselves, have made an artificial man, which we call a commonwealth, so too have they made artificial chains, called civil laws. By mutual covenants they have fastened these chains at one end to the lips of the man or assembly to whom they have given sovereign power, and at the other end to their own ears. These bonds are weak in themselves, yet they can be made to hold, not by the difficulty of breaking them but by the danger of doing so.

### The Liberty of Subjects Consists in Liberty from Covenants

It is only in relation to these bonds that I now intend to speak of the liberty of subjects. No commonwealth in the world regulates all the actions and words of men, since that is impossible. It follows necessarily that in every kind of action the laws have passed over, men have the liberty to do whatever their own reason suggests is most profitable to themselves. If we take liberty in its proper sense, as bodily liberty, meaning freedom from chains and prison, it would be quite absurd for men to clamor, as they do, for a liberty they so evidently enjoy. And if we take liberty to mean exemption from the laws, it is no less absurd for men to demand, as they do, a liberty by which every other man could become master of their lives. Yet absurd as it is, this is what they demand. They do not know that the laws have no power to protect them unless a sword in the hands of a man, or men, enforces those laws. The liberty of a subject, therefore, lies only in those things that the sovereign, in regulating their actions, has passed over. These include the liberty to buy and sell and otherwise make contracts with one another; to choose their own place of residence, their own diet, and their own trade or way of life; to bring up their children as they themselves think fit; and the like.

### The Liberty of the Subject Is Compatible with the Unlimited Power of the Sovereign

We are not to understand, however, that such liberty abolishes or limits the sovereign's power over life and death. It has already been shown that nothing the sovereign representative can do to a subject, under any pretext whatever, can properly be called injustice or injury, because every subject is the author of every act the sovereign performs. The sovereign therefore never lacks the right to anything, except insofar as he is himself the subject of God and so bound to observe the laws of nature. It can happen, then, and often does happen in commonwealths, that a subject is put to death by command of the sovereign power and yet neither does the other wrong. Such was the case when Jephthah, bound by his vow, caused his daughter to be sacrificed. In this and similar cases, the one who dies had the liberty to do the action for which he is nonetheless put to death without injury.

The same holds for a sovereign prince who puts an innocent subject to death. The act violates the law of nature, being contrary to equity, as did David's killing of Uriah, whom he sent to die in battle so that he might take Uriah's wife. Yet it was an injury not to Uriah but to God. It was no injury to Uriah, because Uriah himself had given David the right to do as he pleased. It was an injury to God, because David was God's subject and forbidden all iniquity by the law of nature. David himself plainly confirmed this distinction when he repented of the deed, saying, "To thee only have I sinned."

In the same way the people of Athens believed they committed no injustice when they banished the most powerful man in their commonwealth for ten years. Yet they never asked what crime he had committed, only what harm he might do. They even ordered banishments without knowing whom they would banish. Each citizen brought into the marketplace an oyster shell on which he had written the name of the man he wished to see banished. With no actual accusation, they sometimes banished an Aristides for his reputation for justice, and sometimes a scurrilous jester like Hyperbolus, as a joke. And yet no one can say that the sovereign people of Athens lacked the right to banish them, or that an Athenian lacked the liberty to jest, or to be just.

### The Liberty Writers Praise Is the Liberty of Sovereigns, Not of Private Men

The histories and philosophy of the ancient Greeks and Romans mention liberty often and with honor, as do the writings and discourse of those who have drawn all their political learning from them. That liberty belongs not to individual men but to the commonwealth. It is the same liberty every man would have if there were no civil laws and no commonwealth at all, and its effects are the same as well. Among men without a master there is perpetual war of every man against his neighbor. There is no inheritance to pass on to the son or to expect from the father, no ownership of goods or land, and no security, only a full and absolute liberty in every individual. In the same way, among states and commonwealths that do not depend on one another, every commonwealth (not every man) has an absolute liberty to do whatever it judges most conducive to its benefit, meaning whatever the man or assembly representing it judges. But along with this, they live in a condition of perpetual war, on the verge of battle, their frontiers armed and their cannon trained on the neighbors all around them. The Athenians and Romans were free in the sense that they were free commonwealths. No private man among them had the liberty to resist his own representative; rather, their representative had the liberty to resist or invade other peoples. To this day the word LIBERTAS is written in large letters on the towers of the city of Lucca. Yet no one can infer from this that an individual there has more liberty, or more exemption from service to the commonwealth, than one in Constantinople. Whether a commonwealth is a monarchy or a popular state, the freedom is still the same.

But men are easily deceived by the attractive name of liberty. Lacking the judgment to draw distinctions, they mistake for their private inheritance and birthright what is in fact a right belonging only to the public. When writers renowned on the subject confirm the same error with their authority, it is no wonder that it produces sedition and changes of government. In these western parts of the world we are taught to receive our opinions on the institution and rights of commonwealths from Aristotle, Cicero, and other Greeks and Romans. Because they lived under popular states, they did not derive those rights from the principles of nature. They copied them into their books from the practice of their own commonwealths, which were popular, much as grammarians describe the rules of language from the usage of their time, or the rules of poetry from the poems of Homer and Virgil. The Athenians were taught, to keep them from wanting to change their government, that they were free men and that everyone living under a monarchy was a slave. Aristotle accordingly sets down in his *Politics*: "In democracy liberty is to be presupposed, for it is commonly held that no man is free under any other form of government." Cicero and other writers followed Aristotle's example and grounded their civil doctrine on the opinions of the Romans. The Romans were taught to hate monarchy first by those who deposed their sovereign and divided the sovereignty of Rome among themselves, and afterward by their successors. From reading these Greek and Latin authors, men have acquired from childhood a habit, under a false show of liberty, of favoring tumults and of presumptuously controlling the actions of their sovereigns. They have then controlled those controllers in turn, at the cost of so much bloodshed that I think I may truly say nothing was ever so dearly bought as the learning of the Greek and Latin tongues has been bought by these western parts of the world.

### How the Liberty of the Subject Is to Be Measured

To come now to the particulars of the true liberty of a subject: what things may he refuse to do without injustice, even though the sovereign commands them? We must consider what rights we give away when we make a commonwealth, or, what comes to the same thing, what liberty we deny ourselves by owning all the actions, without exception, of the man or assembly we make our sovereign. Both our obligation and our liberty consist in the act of our submission, and they must therefore be inferred by arguments drawn from that act. No man is under any obligation that does not arise from some act of his own, since by nature all men are equally free. Such arguments must be drawn either from the express words "I authorize all his actions," or from the intention of the one who submits himself to that power, and that intention is to be understood by the end for which he submits. The obligation and liberty of the subject, therefore, are to be derived either from those words, or others equivalent to them, or else from the purpose for which sovereignty is instituted: namely, the peace of the subjects among themselves and their defense against a common enemy.

### Subjects Have Liberty to Defend Their Own Bodies, Even Against Those Who Lawfully Attack Them

First, then: sovereignty by institution rests on a covenant of every one with every one, and sovereignty by acquisition rests on covenants of the vanquished with the victor, or of the child with the parent. It is therefore evident that every subject has liberty in all those things the right to which cannot be transferred by covenant. I showed earlier, in chapter fourteen, that covenants not to defend one's own body are void.

### Subjects Are Not Bound to Harm Themselves

The sovereign may command a man, even one justly condemned, to kill, wound, or maim himself; or not to resist those who assault him; or to abstain from food, air, medicine, or anything else without which he cannot live. That man nevertheless has the liberty to disobey.

If the sovereign, or anyone acting with his authority, questions a man about a crime he himself has committed, he is not bound to confess it unless he is assured of pardon. As I showed in the same chapter, no man can be obliged by covenant to accuse himself.

Again, a subject's consent to sovereign power is contained in the words "I authorize, or take upon myself, all his actions," and these words place no restriction at all on his own former natural liberty. By allowing the sovereign to kill me, I am not bound to kill myself when he commands it. It is one thing to say, "Kill me, or my fellow, if you please"; it is another to say, "I will kill myself, or my fellow." It follows, therefore, that no man is bound by the words themselves either to kill himself or to kill any other man. A man may sometimes be obliged, at the sovereign's command, to carry out some dangerous or dishonorable duty, but that obligation does not depend on the words of our submission. It depends on the intention behind them, which is to be understood by its purpose. When our refusal to obey would defeat the purpose for which sovereignty was established, there is no liberty to refuse; otherwise there is.

### Nor Are They Bound to Go to War, Unless They Undertake It Voluntarily

On this basis, a man commanded as a soldier to fight against the enemy may in many cases refuse without injustice, even though his sovereign has right enough to punish the refusal with death. He may do so, for example, when he provides a capable soldier to take his place, since in that case he does not desert the service of the commonwealth. Allowance must also be made for natural timidity, not only in women, from whom no such dangerous duty is expected, but also in men of womanish courage. When armies fight, there is running away on one side or both. Yet when men flee not out of treachery but out of fear, they are judged to act not unjustly but dishonorably. For the same reason, avoiding battle is not injustice but cowardice. But a man who enlists as a soldier, or accepts the enlistment money paid in advance to recruits, gives up the excuse of a timid nature. He is obliged not only to go into battle but also not to run from it without his captain's permission. And when the defense of the commonwealth requires the help of everyone able to bear arms at once, every one of them is obliged, because otherwise the institution of the commonwealth, which they lack the will or the courage to preserve, was in vain.

No man has the liberty to resist the sword of the commonwealth in defense of another man, whether guilty or innocent. Such a liberty takes away from the sovereign the means of protecting us and is therefore destructive of the very essence of government. But suppose a great many men together have already resisted the sovereign power unjustly, or committed some capital crime for which each of them expects death. Do they not then have the liberty to join together and assist and defend one another? Certainly they do, for they are only defending their lives, which the guilty may do as well as the innocent. There was indeed injustice in their first breach of duty. But their taking up arms afterward, even to maintain what they have done, is no new unjust act, and if they act only to defend their persons, it is not unjust at all. The offer of a pardon, however, takes away the plea of self-defense from those to whom it is offered, and makes it unlawful for them to persist in assisting or defending the rest.

### The Greatest Liberty of Subjects Depends on the Silence of the Law

As for the other liberties, they depend on the silence of the law. Where the sovereign has prescribed no rule, the subject has the liberty to act or to refrain, at his own discretion. Such liberty is therefore greater in some places and smaller in others, greater at some times and smaller at others, according to what those who hold sovereignty think most convenient. For example, there was a time in England when a man could enter his own land by force and eject those who were wrongfully occupying it. In later times a statute made by the king in Parliament took away that liberty of forcible entry. Likewise, in some places in the world men have the liberty of having many wives, while in other places such liberty is not allowed.

A subject may have a dispute with his sovereign over a debt, or over the right to possess lands or goods, or over some service required of him, or over some bodily or monetary penalty. If the dispute rests on an existing law, he has the same liberty to sue for his right as he would against a fellow subject, before such judges as the sovereign has appointed. The sovereign in such a case makes his demand on the strength of a prior law and not by virtue of his power, and he thereby declares that he requires no more than what that law shows to be due. The suit is therefore not contrary to the sovereign's will, and consequently the subject has the liberty to demand a hearing of his case and a judgment according to that law. But if the sovereign demands or takes anything on the strength of his power, no legal action lies in that case. Everything he does by virtue of his power is done by the authority of every subject, and so whoever brings an action against the sovereign brings it against himself.

A monarch or sovereign assembly may grant a liberty to all or any of its subjects. If that grant, while it stands, disables the sovereign from providing for their safety, the grant is void, unless the sovereign directly renounces sovereignty or transfers it to another. He could have renounced or transferred it openly and in plain terms, had that been his will, and he did not; it is therefore to be understood that it was not his will. The grant must instead have proceeded from ignorance of the conflict between such a liberty and sovereign power. Sovereignty is therefore still retained, and with it all the powers necessary to exercise it: the power of war and peace, of judging, of appointing officers and counselors, of levying money, and the rest listed in chapter eighteen.

### In What Cases Subjects Are Released from Obedience to Their Sovereign

The obligation of subjects to the sovereign is understood to last as long as, and no longer than, the power by which he is able to protect them. Men have by nature the right to protect themselves when no one else can protect them, and no covenant can give that right up. Sovereignty is the soul of the commonwealth, and once it has departed from the body, the members no longer receive their motion from it. The end of obedience is protection. Wherever a man sees protection, whether in his own sword or in another's, nature directs his obedience to it and his efforts to maintain it. Those who create sovereignty intend it to be immortal. Yet by its own nature it is subject to violent death through foreign war, and through the ignorance and passions of men it also carries within it, from its very institution, many seeds of natural mortality through internal discord.

### In Case of Captivity

A subject may be taken prisoner in war, or his person or his means of livelihood may fall within the enemy's guard. If he is then granted his life and bodily liberty on condition that he become subject to the victor, he has the liberty to accept that condition. Having accepted it, he is the subject of the one who captured him, because he had no other way to preserve himself. The case is the same if he is detained on the same terms in a foreign country. But if a man is held in prison or in chains, or is not trusted with the liberty of his body, he cannot be understood to be bound by covenant to subjection, and may therefore escape, if he can, by any means whatever.

### In Case the Sovereign Renounces the Government for Himself and His Heirs

If a monarch relinquishes sovereignty for both himself and his heirs, his subjects return to the absolute liberty of nature. Nature may declare who his sons are and who his nearest kin are, but, as I said in the preceding chapter, it depends on his own will who shall be his heir. If, therefore, he wills to have no heir, there is no sovereignty and no subjection. The case is the same if he dies without known kin and without naming an heir, for then no heir can be known, and consequently no subjection is due.

### In Case of Banishment

If the sovereign banishes a subject, then for the duration of the banishment he is not a subject. But a man sent abroad on a mission, or given leave to travel, is still a subject. This, however, is by contract between sovereigns, not by virtue of the covenant of subjection. Whoever enters another's dominion is subject to all its laws, unless he has a privilege through the friendship of the sovereigns or by special license.

### In Case the Sovereign Makes Himself Subject to Another

If a monarch conquered in war makes himself subject to the victor, his subjects are released from their former obligation and become obliged to the victor. But if he is held prisoner, or does not have the liberty of his own body, he is not understood to have given up the right of sovereignty. His subjects are therefore obliged to obey the magistrates previously installed, who govern not in their own name but in his. Since his right remains, the question concerns only the administration, that is, the magistrates and officers. If he has no means of naming them, he is presumed to approve those he himself had appointed before.

## Chapter XXII. Of Systems Subject, Political, and Private

Having discussed how a commonwealth comes into being, its form, and its power, I turn next to its parts. I begin with systems, which resemble what anatomists call the "similar parts" of a natural body: the muscles, which are made of the same tissue throughout. By *systems* I mean any number of people joined together in one interest or one business. Some systems are regular, and some are irregular. Regular systems are those in which one man, or one assembly of men, is appointed to represent the whole number. All others are irregular.

Among regular systems, some are absolute and independent, subject to no one but their own representative. Only commonwealths are of this kind, and I have dealt with them in the five preceding chapters. Others are dependent, meaning that they are subordinate to some sovereign power, to which every member, and their representative as well, is subject.

Subordinate systems are either political or private. Political systems, also called bodies politic or persons in law, are those created by authority of the sovereign power of the commonwealth. Private systems are those that subjects form among themselves, or that are formed by authority from a foreigner. No authority derived from a foreign power is public within another sovereign's dominion. There, it is private.

Private systems are in turn either lawful or unlawful. They are lawful if the commonwealth allows them, and unlawful otherwise. Irregular systems are those that have no representative and consist only of a gathering of people. If such a gathering is not forbidden by the commonwealth and has no evil design, as when people flock to markets, to shows, or for any other harmless purpose, it is lawful. But when its intention is evil, or when the crowd is sizable and its intention unknown, it is unlawful.

In a body politic, the power of the representative is always limited, and the sovereign power sets those limits. Unlimited power is absolute sovereignty. In every commonwealth the sovereign is the absolute representative of all the subjects, so no one else can represent any part of them except so far as the sovereign permits. To permit a body politic made up of subjects to have an absolute representative for every purpose would be to abandon the government of that portion of the commonwealth and to divide dominion, contrary to the subjects' peace and defense. The sovereign cannot be understood to have done this by any grant that does not plainly and directly release them from their subjection. When the implications of a sovereign's words point one way and other evidence points the opposite way, those implications are not signs of his will. They are rather signs of error and miscalculation, to which all mankind is too prone.

The limits of the power given to the representative of a body politic can be learned from two sources. One is its writ, or letters from the sovereign. The other is the law of the commonwealth.

When an independent commonwealth is instituted or acquired, no writing is needed, because there the representative's power has no bounds except those set by the unwritten law of nature. Subordinate bodies are different. They require so many different limitations, concerning their business, their times, and their places, that these could neither be remembered without written letters nor made known unless the letters were patent. Letters patent are open documents that can be read aloud to the members and that are sealed or attested with the seals or other permanent marks of sovereign authority.

Such limitations are not always easy, and perhaps not even possible, to set down in writing. The ordinary laws common to all subjects must therefore determine what the representative may lawfully do in every case where the letters themselves are silent. It follows that in a body politic whose representative is one man, whatever he does in the person of the body that is warranted neither by his letters nor by the laws is his own act. It is not the act of the body, nor of any member but himself, because beyond what his letters or the laws allow, he represents no one's person but his own. What he does in accordance with them, however, is the act of every member. Every subject is the author of the sovereign's acts, because the sovereign is their unlimited representative. The act of anyone who keeps within the sovereign's letters is therefore the act of the sovereign, and every member of the body is its author.

If the representative is an assembly, whatever it decrees without warrant from its letters or the laws is the act of the assembly, or body politic, and the act of every member whose vote helped pass the decree. It is not the act of anyone who was present and voted against it, nor of anyone absent, unless he voted for it by proxy. It is the act of the assembly because the majority voted for it. If it is a crime, the assembly may be punished so far as it is capable of punishment. It may be dissolved or made to forfeit its letters, which for such artificial and fictitious bodies amounts to capital punishment. Or, if the assembly has a common fund in which none of the innocent members holds any property, it may be fined, for nature has exempted all bodies politic from bodily punishment. Those who did not vote for the decree are innocent, because the assembly cannot represent anyone in matters its letters do not warrant, and so the dissenters are not implicated in its votes.

Suppose the person of the body politic rests in one man and he borrows money from a stranger, that is, from someone who is not a member of the same body. No letters need to limit borrowing, since the limit on lending is left to each lender's own inclinations. In that case the debt is the representative's own. If his letters gave him authority to make the members repay what he borrows, he would by implication hold sovereignty over them. The grant would then be void, as arising from an error to which human nature is commonly liable and therefore an insufficient sign of the grantor's will. Or, if the grantor stood by it, the representative would be a sovereign and would fall outside the present question, which concerns only subordinate bodies. No member, then, is obliged to pay a debt so borrowed. Only the representative is. The lender knows nothing of the letters or of how the body is constituted, so he regards as his debtors only those who have bound themselves. Since the representative can bind himself and no one else, the lender has him alone as his debtor. The representative must therefore repay him from the common fund if there is one, or from his own estate if there is none.

If he incurs a debt by contract or by fine, the case is the same.

When the representative is an assembly and the debt is owed to a stranger, all those who voted for the borrowing, or for the contract that made the money due, or for the act for which the fine was imposed, are responsible for the debt, and only they are. Each of them, in voting, bound himself to payment. Whoever is an author of the borrowing is obliged to pay, even the whole debt, though once any one of them has paid it, he is discharged.

If the debt is owed to a member of the assembly, the assembly alone is obliged to pay it, out of its common fund if it has one. Since the member is free to vote, if he votes that the money should be borrowed, he votes that it should be repaid. If he votes against the borrowing, or is absent, he nonetheless votes for the borrowing by the act of lending. He contradicts his earlier vote, is bound by the later one, and becomes both borrower and lender. Consequently he cannot demand repayment from any particular man, but only from the common treasury. If that fails, he has no remedy and no complaint except against himself. He knew the assembly's proceedings and its means of payment, he was under no compulsion, and yet through his own folly he lent his money.

It is clear from this that in bodies politic that are subordinate and subject to a sovereign power, it is sometimes not only lawful but advisable for an individual member to protest openly against the decrees of the representative assembly, and to have his dissent recorded or witnessed. Otherwise he may be held liable for debts contracted, and responsible for crimes committed, by other men. In a sovereign assembly, however, that liberty is taken away, for two reasons. First, whoever protests there denies its sovereignty. Second, whatever the sovereign power commands is justified by the command itself, at least as far as the subject is concerned, though not always in the sight of God, because every subject is the author of such a command.

The variety of bodies politic is almost infinite. They differ in the affairs for which they are established, where the diversity is beyond description, and also in their times, places, and numbers, all of which are subject to many limitations. As to their affairs, some are established for government. The government of a province, for example, may be entrusted to an assembly in which every resolution depends on a majority vote. Such an assembly is a body politic, and its power is limited by its commission. The word *province* means a charge, or the care of some business, which the person whose business it is entrusts to another to administer on his behalf and under his authority. So when a single commonwealth contains several countries that have laws distinct from one another, or that lie far apart, and the administration of government is entrusted to different persons, the countries where the sovereign does not reside but governs by commission are called provinces. Yet there are few examples of a province governed by an assembly residing in the province itself. The Romans held sovereignty over many provinces, but they always governed them through presidents and praetors, not through assemblies as they governed the city of Rome and its neighboring territories. Likewise, when colonies were sent from England to settle Virginia and the Somers Isles, now called Bermuda, the government of those colonies was entrusted at home to assemblies in London. Yet those assemblies never delegated the government under them to any assembly in the colonies. Instead they sent each plantation a single governor. Wherever people can be present, they naturally desire a share in government. Where they cannot be present, they are just as naturally inclined to entrust the government of their common interest to a monarchical rather than a popular form. The same is evident among men with large private estates. When they do not wish to take the trouble of managing their own affairs, they would rather trust one servant than an assembly of their friends or servants. But whatever the practice in fact, we may suppose that the government of a province or colony has been entrusted to an assembly. In that case, I have the following to say. Whatever debt that assembly contracts, and whatever unlawful act it decrees, is the act only of those who assented. It is not the act of those who dissented or were absent, for the reasons already given. Further, an assembly sitting outside the bounds of the colony it governs cannot exercise any power over the persons or goods of any colonist anywhere outside the colony itself, whether to seize them for debt or for any other obligation. It has no jurisdiction or authority elsewhere and is left to whatever remedy the law of that place allows. And although the assembly has the right to fine any of its members who break the laws it makes, it has no right to enforce that fine outside the colony. What is said here about the rights of an assembly governing a province or colony applies equally to an assembly governing a town, a university, a college, a church, or any other government over the persons of men.

In general, in all bodies politic, if a member believes himself injured by the body itself, his case belongs to the sovereign and to those whom the sovereign has appointed, or shall appoint, as judges in such cases or in that particular case. It does not belong to the body itself, because in this situation the whole body is his fellow subject. In a sovereign assembly it is otherwise. There, if the sovereign is not the judge, even in its own cause, there can be no judge at all.

In a body politic established for the regulation of foreign trade, the most suitable representative is an assembly of all the members. In such an assembly, everyone who ventures his money may attend all the body's deliberations and resolutions if he chooses. To prove this, we must consider why merchants, who are free to buy and sell, export and import their goods at their own discretion, nonetheless bind themselves together in a single corporation. It is true that few merchants can fill a ship with the goods they buy at home for export, or with the goods they buy abroad to bring home. They therefore need to join together in one society. In such a society each man may either share in the profit in proportion to his investment, or take his own goods and sell what he carries out or brings back at whatever prices he thinks fit. But such a society is no body politic, because it has no common representative to bind its members to any law other than the one common to all subjects. The purpose of incorporation is to increase their profit, which is done in two ways: by being sole buyers and by being sole sellers, both at home and abroad. To make a company of merchants a corporation, or body politic, is therefore to grant them a double monopoly, one as sole buyers and the other as sole sellers. When a company is incorporated for trade with a particular foreign country, only its members export the goods that sell in that country, which makes them the sole buyers at home and the sole sellers abroad. At home there is only one buyer, and abroad only one seller. Both conditions profit the merchant, since he buys at home at lower prices and sells abroad at higher ones. And abroad there is only one buyer of foreign goods, and at home only one seller of them. Both conditions, again, profit the merchant-adventurers who have staked their money in the trade.

Of this double monopoly, one part works to the disadvantage of the people at home and the other to the disadvantage of foreigners. At home, as sole exporters, the merchants set whatever price they please on the produce of the people's farming and handicrafts, and as sole importers, they set whatever price they please on all the foreign commodities the people need. Both are bad for the people. Abroad, by contrast, as the only sellers of native commodities and the only buyers of foreign commodities on the spot, they raise the price of the first and lower the price of the second, to the foreigner's disadvantage. Where only one sells, goods are dearer, and where only one buys, they are cheaper. Such corporations, therefore, are nothing other than monopolies. Yet they would be very profitable to a commonwealth if they were bound together into one body in foreign markets while leaving every man at home free to buy and sell at whatever price he could get.

The purpose of these bodies of merchants, then, is not a common benefit to the whole body, which in this case has no common stock beyond what is deducted from the individual ventures for building, buying, provisioning, and crewing ships. Their purpose is the private gain of each adventurer, each man who has put his money into the venture. It is reasonable, therefore, that every member should know how his own money is employed. That means every member should belong to the assembly that has power to direct its use and should be acquainted with its accounts. The representative of such a body must accordingly be an assembly at whose consultations every member may be present if he chooses.

If a political body of merchants contracts a debt to an outsider by act of its representative assembly, each member is individually liable for the whole of it. An outsider can take no notice of their private rules. He regards them simply as so many individual men, each obliged for the entire payment, until payment by any one of them discharges all the rest. But if the debt is owed to a member of the company, the creditor is himself a debtor to himself for the whole amount, and so he cannot demand his debt except from the common stock, if there is one.

If the commonwealth imposes a tax on the body, it is understood to fall on each member in proportion to his individual stake in the company, since in this case there is no common stock other than the one made up of those individual stakes.

If a fine is imposed on the body for some unlawful act, only those members are liable by whose votes the act was decreed or by whose help it was carried out. None of the rest is guilty of any crime except belonging to the body, and even if that is a crime, it is not his own, because the body was established by the authority of the commonwealth.

If a member owes money to the body, the body may sue him. But his goods cannot be seized, nor his person imprisoned, on the body's own authority, only on the authority of the commonwealth. If the members could do this on their own authority, they could on their own authority also give judgment that the debt is due, which would make them judges in their own cause.

### A Political Body for Giving Counsel to the Sovereign

These bodies formed for governing men or for conducting trade are either perpetual or last for a period fixed in writing. There are also bodies whose duration is limited only by the nature of their business. Suppose a sovereign monarch or sovereign assembly sees fit to order the towns and other parts of the territory to send deputies: to inform the sovereign of the condition and needs of the subjects, to advise on making good laws, or for any other purpose, treating those deputies as one person representing the whole country. Once a place and time of meeting have been appointed, these deputies form, at that place and at that time, a political body representing every subject of the dominion. But they represent the subjects only in the matters put before them by the man or assembly that summoned them by sovereign authority, and when it is declared that nothing further will be put before them or debated, the body is dissolved. If they were the absolute representative of the people, they would be the sovereign assembly. There would then be two sovereign assemblies, or two sovereigns, over the same people, and that cannot be reconciled with their peace. Therefore, wherever a sovereignty exists, there can be no absolute representation of the people except by that sovereignty. As for how far such a body represents the whole people, the limits are set out in the writ that summoned it, for the people cannot choose their deputies for any purpose other than the one expressed in the writ their sovereign has directed to them.

### A Regular Private Body That Is Lawful, Such as a Family

Regular and lawful private bodies are those formed without letters patent or any other written authority beyond the laws common to all subjects. Because they are united in one representative person, they count as regular. All families are of this kind, since in each the father or master directs the whole household. He binds his children and servants as far as the law permits, but no further, because none of them is bound to obey in actions the law has forbidden. In all other actions, for as long as they live under household government, they are subject to their fathers and masters as to their immediate sovereigns. Before the commonwealth was instituted, fathers and masters were absolute sovereigns in their own families, and afterward they lose no more of that authority than the law of the commonwealth takes from them.

### Private Bodies That Are Regular but Unlawful

Regular but unlawful private bodies are those that unite into one representative person without any public authority at all. Such are the corporations of beggars, thieves, and gypsies, organized to manage their trades of begging and stealing more effectively. Such also are the corporations of men who, on the authority of some foreign person, unite within another sovereign's dominion to spread their doctrines more easily and to build a party against the power of the commonwealth.

### Irregular Systems, Such as Private Leagues

Irregular systems are by nature nothing more than leagues, or sometimes a mere gathering of people united toward no particular design. They arise not from any obligation of one person to another but only from a likeness of wills and inclinations. They become lawful or unlawful according to the lawfulness or unlawfulness of each individual's design in joining them, and that design is to be inferred from the occasion.

Because leagues are commonly made for mutual defense, leagues among subjects are for the most part unnecessary within a commonwealth, which is itself nothing more than a league of all the subjects together. Such leagues smack of unlawful design, and for that reason they are unlawful and commonly go by the name of factions or conspiracies. A league is a bond among men created by covenants. Where no man or assembly has been given power to compel them to perform their covenants, as in the condition of mere nature, a league remains valid only so long as no just cause for distrust arises. Leagues between commonwealths, over which no human power has been established to keep them all in awe, are therefore not only lawful but profitable for as long as they last. Leagues among subjects of one and the same commonwealth are a different matter. There, everyone can obtain his rights through the sovereign power, so such leagues are unnecessary for maintaining peace and justice, and they are unlawful whenever their design is evil or unknown to the commonwealth. Any pooling of strength by private men is unjust if its intent is evil; if its intent is unknown, it is dangerous to the public and unjustly concealed.

### Secret Cabals

Suppose the sovereign power lies in a large assembly, and a number of its members, without authority, consult apart to engineer the direction of the rest. This is a faction, an unlawful conspiracy, because it is a fraudulent manipulation of the assembly for the conspirators' private interest. But if a man whose private interest is to be debated and judged in the assembly gathers as many friends as he can, there is no injustice in it, because in this case he is not part of the assembly. Even if he hires such friends with money, it is not injustice unless an express law forbids it. Given how men behave, justice sometimes cannot be had without money, and every man may consider his own cause just until it has been heard and judged.

### Feuds of Private Families

In every commonwealth, a private man who keeps more servants than the management of his estate and his lawful business require is engaged in faction, which is unlawful. Since he enjoys the protection of the commonwealth, he has no need of defense by private force. In nations not thoroughly civilized, numerous great families have lived in continual hostility and attacked one another with private force. Yet it is evident enough that either they acted unjustly or they had no commonwealth.

### Factions for Government

Factions of kindred are unjust, and so are factions concerning the government of religion, such as Papists and Protestants, or the government of the state, such as the patricians and plebeians of ancient Rome and the aristocratic and democratic parties of ancient Greece. They run contrary to the peace and safety of the people, and they amount to taking the sword out of the sovereign's hand.

A gathering of people is an irregular system whose lawfulness depends on the occasion and on the number assembled. If the occasion is lawful and evident, the gathering is lawful, as with the customary meeting of people at church or at a public spectacle in customary numbers. If the numbers are extraordinarily large, however, the occasion is no longer evident. Anyone who cannot then give a specific and satisfactory account of why he is among the crowd is to be judged aware of an unlawful and riotous design. It may be lawful for a thousand men to sign a petition to be delivered to a judge or magistrate, yet if a thousand men come to present it, the gathering is a tumultuous assembly, since one or two would serve the purpose. In such cases, though, no fixed number makes the assembly unlawful. What makes it unlawful is a number so large that the officers on hand cannot suppress it and bring it to justice.

When an unusual number of men assemble against someone they are accusing, the assembly is an unlawful tumult, because they could deliver their accusation to the magistrate through a few men, or through one. Such was the case of Saint Paul at Ephesus. There Demetrius and a great number of others brought two of Paul's companions before the magistrate, crying with one voice, "Great is Diana of the Ephesians!" This was their way of demanding justice against the two men for teaching the people a doctrine contrary to their religion and their trade. Given the laws of that people, the occasion was just. Even so, their assembly was judged unlawful, and the magistrate rebuked them for it in these words, recorded in the nineteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles: "If Demetrius and the other workmen have a charge against anyone, the courts are open and there are deputies; let them bring charges against one another. If you have any other demand, it may be settled in a lawfully called assembly. For we are in danger of being accused of sedition over this day's events, since there is no cause anyone can give to account for this gathering of people." Here the magistrate calls an assembly for which men can give no just account a sedition, and one they could not answer for.

This is all I shall say concerning systems and assemblies of people. As I said earlier, they may be compared to the "similar parts" of the human body, the tissues of uniform substance as distinct from its organs. The lawful ones resemble the muscles. The unlawful ones resemble wens, boils, and abscesses, bred by the unnatural flowing-together of evil humors, the corrupt bodily fluids that the medicine of the day held responsible for such swellings.

## Chapter XXIII. Of the Public Ministers of Sovereign Power

In the last chapter I discussed the similar parts of a commonwealth, the uniform tissues of the political body, as an anatomist would call them. In this chapter I turn to its organic parts, its organs, which are the public ministers.

A public minister is a person whom the sovereign, whether a monarch or an assembly, employs in some affair with authority to represent, in that employment, the person of the commonwealth. Every man or assembly holding sovereignty represents two persons, or, as it is more commonly put, has two capacities, one natural and the other political. A monarch bears not only the person of the commonwealth but also that of a man, and a sovereign assembly bears not only the person of the commonwealth but also that of the assembly. Those who serve the sovereign in his natural capacity are therefore not public ministers. Only those who serve him in administering the public business are. In an aristocracy or a democracy, then, the ushers, the sergeants, and the other officers who attend the assembly solely for the convenience of the men assembled are not public ministers. Nor, in a monarchy, are the stewards, the chamberlains, the cofferers who keep the household's money, or any other officers of the royal household.

Some public ministers are entrusted with a general administration, either of the whole dominion or of a part of it. The whole may be entrusted to a protector or regent, as when the predecessor of an infant king commits to such a person the entire administration of the kingdom during the king's minority. In that case every subject is bound to obey, so long as the ordinances the regent makes and the commands he gives are issued in the king's name and are consistent with the king's sovereign power. A part, or province, may be entrusted to a governor, lieutenant, prefect, or viceroy, when a monarch or a sovereign assembly gives that person general charge of it. Here too, everyone in the province is bound by whatever he does in the sovereign's name, provided it does not conflict with the sovereign's right. Protectors, viceroys, and governors have no right except what depends on the sovereign's will, and no commission given to them can be read as a declaration of the sovereign's will to transfer sovereignty unless it contains express and unmistakable words to that effect. This kind of public minister resembles the nerves and tendons that move the various limbs of a natural body.

Other public ministers have a special administration, meaning charge of some particular business, either at home or abroad. At home, the first such business is the economy of the commonwealth. Those who have authority over the treasury, whether to collect, receive, disburse, or audit tributes, levies, rents, fines, or any other public revenue, are public ministers. They are ministers because they serve the representative person and can do nothing against his command or without his authority. They are public because they serve him in his political capacity.

Second, those who have authority over the militia are public ministers: those who keep custody of arms, forts, and ports; who raise, pay, or lead soldiers; or who provide anything necessary for war, whether on land or at sea. A soldier without a command, however, does not represent the person of the commonwealth merely because he fights for it, since there is no one to whom he could represent it. Everyone who holds a command represents the commonwealth only to those whom he commands.

Those who have authority to teach the people, or to enable others to teach them, are also public ministers. Their task is to teach the people their duty to the sovereign power and to instruct them in the knowledge of what is just and unjust, so that they become better fitted to live in godliness and in peace with one another and to resist the public enemy. They are ministers because they act not by their own authority but by another's, and public because they act, or ought to act, by no authority but the sovereign's. Only the monarch or the sovereign assembly holds authority to teach and instruct the people directly from God. No one but the sovereign receives his power *Dei Gratia* simply, that is, by the grace of God alone. Everyone else receives his power from the grace and providence of God together with that of his sovereign. In a monarchy the formula is *Dei Gratia et Regis*, by the grace of God and of the King, or *Dei Providentia et Voluntate Regis*, by the providence of God and the will of the King.

Those to whom jurisdiction is given are also public ministers. In their seats of justice they represent the person of the sovereign, and their sentence is his sentence. As I have already shown, all judicial power is essentially attached to sovereignty, and so every other judge is only a minister of the one man or the assembly that holds sovereign power. Controversies are of two kinds, those of fact and those of law, and judgments are accordingly of two kinds as well. It follows that in a single controversy there may be two judges, one of fact and another of law.

In either kind of controversy a further dispute may arise between the party being judged and the judge. Since both are subjects of the sovereign, equity requires that this dispute be decided by men chosen with the consent of both, because no one may be judge in his own cause. But both parties have already agreed on the sovereign as their judge, and so the sovereign must either hear and decide the cause himself or appoint as judges such men as both parties accept. This agreement is understood to be made in several ways. First, if the defendant is allowed to object to any of his judges whose interests give him reason to suspect them, then those he does not object to are judges he has himself agreed to. The plaintiff needs no such allowance, since he has already chosen his judge by bringing his suit before him. Second, if the defendant appeals to some other judge, he can appeal no further, because the appeal was his own choice. Third, if he appeals to the sovereign himself, and the sovereign gives sentence either in person or through delegates on whom the parties agree, that sentence is final, because the defendant has been judged by his own judges, that is, by himself.

With these properties of just and rational adjudication in view, I cannot refrain from remarking on the excellent constitution of the English courts of justice, both for common pleas and for public pleas. By common pleas I mean cases in which both plaintiff and defendant are subjects. By public pleas, also called pleas of the Crown, I mean cases in which the plaintiff is the sovereign. England had two orders of men, the Lords and the Commons. The Lords enjoyed the privilege of being tried in all capital crimes by none but Lords, and by as many of them as chose to attend. Since this was always acknowledged as a privilege granted in their favor, their judges were exactly those they had themselves desired. In all controversies, every subject, and in civil controversies the Lords as well, was tried by men from the district where the matter in dispute had arisen. The party could object to these men until at last twelve were agreed on against whom he raised no objection, and he was then judged by those twelve. Since he had in this way his own judges, he could allege no reason why the sentence should not be final. These public persons, who hold authority from the sovereign power either to instruct or to judge the people, are members of the commonwealth that may fitly be compared to the organs of voice in a natural body.

Public ministers also include all those who have authority from the sovereign to carry out the judgments that have been given, to publish the sovereign's commands, to suppress riots, to arrest and imprison wrongdoers, and to perform any other acts that tend to preserve the peace. Every act they perform by such authority is an act of the commonwealth, and their service corresponds to that of the hands in a natural body.

Public ministers abroad are those who represent the person of their own sovereign to foreign states. Such are ambassadors, messengers, agents, and heralds sent by public authority on public business.

Those sent by the authority of some private faction within a state torn by internal conflict, even if they are received abroad, are neither public nor private ministers of the commonwealth, because none of their actions has the commonwealth as its author. Likewise, an ambassador sent by a prince to offer congratulations or condolences, or to attend some ceremony, is a private person. The authority that sends him is public, but the business is private, since it belongs to the prince in his natural capacity. Again, a man sent secretly into another country to spy out its plans and its strength is only a private minister, even though both the authority and the business are public, because no one there recognizes any person in him but his own. He is nonetheless a minister of the commonwealth, and may be compared to an eye in the natural body. Those appointed to receive the petitions and other reports of the people serve, as it were, as the public ear. They are public ministers and represent their sovereign in that office.

Neither a counselor nor a council of state is a public person, if we consider it as having no authority to judge or command but only to give advice to the sovereign when asked, or to offer it when not asked. Such advice is addressed to the sovereign alone, and the sovereign's person cannot be represented to him by another while he himself is present. In practice, however, a body of counselors always holds some other authority as well, either judicial or administrative. In a monarchy, the counselors represent the monarch when they deliver his commands to the public ministers. In a democracy, the council or senate presents the results of its deliberations to the people in its capacity as a council, but when it appoints judges, hears cases, or receives ambassadors, it acts as a minister of the people. And in an aristocracy, the council of state is the sovereign assembly itself, and gives counsel to no one but its own members.

## Chapter XXIV. Of the Nutrition, and Procreation of a Commonwealth

### The Nourishment of a Commonwealth Consists in the Commodities of Sea and Land

The nutrition of a commonwealth consists in three things: the plenty and distribution of the materials that sustain life; their concoction, or preparation (concoction being the old physicians' word for digestion); and, once they have been concocted, their conveyance through suitable channels to public use.

The plenty of this matter is limited by nature to those commodities that God draws from the two breasts of our common mother, the land and the sea, and that he usually either gives freely to mankind or sells to it in exchange for labor.

The matter of this nourishment consists of animals, plants, and minerals, and God has freely laid them before us on or near the surface of the earth, so that nothing more is needed than the labor and industry of gathering them. Plenty therefore depends, next to God's favor, simply on the labor and industry of human beings.

This matter, commonly called commodities, is partly native and partly foreign. Native commodities are those to be had within the territory of the commonwealth; foreign commodities are those imported from outside it. No territory under the dominion of a single commonwealth, unless it is of enormous extent, produces everything needed to maintain and move the whole body, and few territories fail to produce something beyond what they need. The surplus at home therefore ceases to be surplus, because it supplies the country's shortages by bringing in what can be had abroad, whether by exchange, by just war, or by labor. A man's labor, after all, is a commodity that can be exchanged for benefit just like anything else. There have been commonwealths with no more territory than they needed to live on that have nonetheless not only maintained their power but increased it, partly through the labor of carrying trade from one place to another, and partly by selling manufactured goods made from materials brought in from elsewhere.

### And the Right of Distributing Them

The distribution of the materials of this nourishment is the establishment of mine, yours, and his: in a word, of property. In every kind of commonwealth, it belongs to the sovereign power. Where there is no commonwealth, there is, as has already been shown, a perpetual war of every man against his neighbor, and so everything belongs to whoever takes it and keeps it by force. That is neither property nor common ownership; it is uncertainty. This is so evident that even Cicero, a passionate defender of liberty, attributed all property to the civil law in one of his public speeches. "Let the civil law be once abandoned," he said, "or even carelessly guarded, not to say suppressed, and there is nothing that any man can be sure of receiving from his ancestors or leaving to his children." And again: "Take away the civil law, and no one knows what is his own and what is another's." Since the introduction of property is therefore an effect of the commonwealth, and since the commonwealth can do nothing except through the person who represents it, establishing property is the act of the sovereign alone. It consists in the laws, which no one can make who does not hold the sovereign power. The ancients understood this well. They gave the name *nomos*, meaning distribution, to what we call law, and they defined justice as distributing to every man his own.

### All Private Estates in Land Derive Originally from the Discretionary Distribution of the Sovereign

In this distribution, the first law concerns the division of the land itself.
