Here the sovereign assigns each man a portion according to what he, and not any subject or any number of subjects, judges consistent with equity and the common good. The children of Israel were a commonwealth in the wilderness, but they lacked the commodities of the earth until they became masters of the Promised Land. That land was afterward divided among them, not at their own discretion, but at the discretion of Eleazar the priest and Joshua their general. There were twelve tribes, which these two made thirteen by dividing the tribe of Joseph; even so, they made only twelve portions of land. They assigned no land to the tribe of Levi, granting it instead a tenth of all the produce. That division was therefore discretionary. And when a people gains possession of a country by war, it does not always wipe out the original inhabitants, as the Jews did. It may leave many, most, or all of them their estates. Yet it is plain that they hold those estates afterward as the victor's grant, just as the people of England held all of theirs from William the Conqueror.

### A Subject's Property Excludes the Claims of Other Subjects, Not the Dominion of the Sovereign

From this we can conclude that a subject's property in his land consists in a right to exclude all other subjects from using it, not a right to exclude his sovereign, whether that sovereign is an assembly or a monarch. The sovereign, which is to say the commonwealth whose person he represents, is understood to do nothing except for the sake of common peace and security. This distribution of land must therefore be understood as made for the same purpose. Consequently, any distribution he makes to the detriment of peace and security runs contrary to the will of every subject who entrusted his peace and safety to the sovereign's discretion and conscience, and by the will of every one of them it must be regarded as void. It is true that a sovereign monarch, or the majority of a sovereign assembly, may order many things in pursuit of their passions and against their own consciences, which is a breach of trust and of the law of nature. But this is not enough to entitle any subject to make war on his sovereign, or even to accuse him of injustice, or to speak ill of him in any way. The subjects have authorized all his actions, and in conferring the sovereign power on him they made those actions their own. In what cases the commands of sovereigns are contrary to equity and the law of nature will be considered later, in another place.

### The Public Cannot Be Put on a Fixed Diet

One might imagine that in the distribution of land the commonwealth itself could take a portion, holding and improving it through its representative, and that this portion could be made large enough to cover the whole expense required for common peace and defense. That would be entirely true if one could conceive of a representative free from human passions and weaknesses. But human nature being what it is, setting aside public land, or any fixed revenue, for the commonwealth is futile. It tends toward the dissolution of government and a return to the condition of mere nature and war as soon as the sovereign power falls into the hands of a monarch or an assembly that is either too careless with money or too reckless in committing the public stock to a long or costly war. Commonwealths cannot endure a fixed diet. Their expenses are set not by their own appetite but by outside events and the appetites of their neighbors, and so the public wealth can have no limits other than those that emergencies require. In England, the Conqueror reserved various lands for his own use, apart from the forests and chases (unenclosed hunting grounds) he kept either for recreation or to preserve the woods, and he also reserved various services owed from the land he granted his subjects. Yet these appear to have been reserved for his maintenance not in his public capacity but in his natural one, as a private man. For all that, he and his successors still imposed taxes at their discretion on all their subjects' land whenever they judged it necessary. Or, if those public lands and services were intended as a sufficient maintenance for the commonwealth, the arrangement defeated the purpose of its institution. As the taxes that followed showed, those resources were insufficient, and as the recent revenue of the Crown shows, they were liable to be sold off and diminished. It is therefore futile to assign a portion to the commonwealth, since the commonwealth may sell it or give it away, and in fact does sell it and give it away whenever its representative does so.

### The Places and Goods of Trade Depend, Like Their Distribution, on the Sovereign

Just as the distribution of land at home belongs to the sovereign, so does the power to decide in what places, and in what commodities, the subject may trade abroad. If private persons were left to their own discretion in this, some of them would be drawn by profit to supply the enemy with the means of harming the commonwealth, and would harm it themselves by importing goods that please people's appetites but are nonetheless harmful, or at least useless, to them. It therefore belongs to the commonwealth, that is, to the sovereign alone, to approve or disapprove both the places and the goods of foreign trade.

### The Laws of Transferring Property Also Belong to the Sovereign

Furthermore, it is not enough for the sustenance of a commonwealth that every man should own a portion of land, or a few commodities, or possess by nature some useful skill. There is no skill in the world that is not necessary to the existence, or at least the well-being, of almost every individual. Men must therefore distribute what they can spare and transfer their property in it to one another through exchange and mutual contract. It accordingly belongs to the commonwealth, that is, to the sovereign, to determine how every kind of contract between subjects is to be made, whether buying, selling, exchanging, borrowing, lending, leasing, or hiring, and by what words and signs such contracts are to be recognized as valid. As for the matter of this nourishment and its distribution to the various members of the commonwealth, this much is sufficient, given the plan of the whole work.

### Money, the Blood of a Commonwealth

By concoction I mean the reduction of all commodities that are not consumed immediately but are kept as nourishment for the future into something of equal value, and something portable enough not to hinder people as they move from place to place, so that a person may have, wherever he goes, whatever nourishment that place provides. This is nothing other than gold, silver, and money. Gold and silver happen to be highly valued in almost every country in the world, and so they serve as a convenient measure of the value of everything else between nations. Money, of whatever material the sovereign of a commonwealth coins it, is a sufficient measure of the value of everything else among the subjects of that commonwealth. By means of these measures, all commodities, movable and immovable alike, can accompany a man to every place he goes, both within and beyond the place where he ordinarily lives. Money also passes from hand to hand within the commonwealth and circulates throughout it, nourishing every part as it goes. This concoction is, so to speak, the sanguification of the commonwealth, the making of its blood. Natural blood is made in the same way from the fruits of the earth, and as it circulates it nourishes every member of the human body along the way.

Because silver and gold derive their value from the metal itself, they have two advantages. First, their value cannot be altered by the power of one commonwealth or of a few, since they are a common measure of the commodities of every place, whereas money of base metal can easily be raised or lowered in value. Second, they enable commonwealths to move and stretch out their arms into foreign countries when necessary, supplying not only private subjects who travel but entire armies with provisions. Coin whose worth lies not in its material but in the stamp of the place that issued it cannot survive a change of air. It has its effect only at home, and even there it is subject to changes in the law that can reduce its value, often to the detriment of those who hold it.

### The Channels and Routes of Money to Public Use

The channels and routes by which money is conveyed to public use are of two kinds: one carries it into the public coffers, and the other issues it out again for public payments. To the first kind belong collectors, receivers, and treasurers; to the second belong the treasurers again, along with the officers appointed to pay the various public or private ministers. Here too the artificial man keeps his resemblance to the natural one. In the natural body, the veins collect the blood from its various parts and carry it to the heart, where it is made vital, and the heart then sends it out again through the arteries to enliven all the members of the body and enable them to move.

### Colonies, the Children of a Commonwealth

The procreation, or children, of a commonwealth are what we call plantations, or colonies. These are bodies of people sent out from the commonwealth under a leader or governor to inhabit a foreign country, one either previously empty of inhabitants or emptied at that time by war. Once a colony is settled, one of two things follows. Either it becomes a commonwealth in its own right, released from subjection to the sovereign who sent it, as many commonwealths of ancient times did. In that case the commonwealth it came from was called its metropolis, or mother, and demands no more of it than fathers demand of children whom they emancipate and free from their household government, namely honor and friendship. Or else the colonists remain united to their metropolis, as the colonies of the Roman people were, and then they are not commonwealths themselves but provinces and parts of the commonwealth that sent them. The rights of colonies, apart from the honor and alliance they owe their metropolis, therefore depend entirely on the license, or letters, by which their sovereign authorized them to settle.

## Chapter XXV. Of Counsel

How misleading it is to judge the nature of things by the ordinary and inconsistent use of words appears nowhere more plainly than in the confusion of counsel with command. That confusion arises because both are expressed in the imperative mood, as are many other kinds of speech besides. The words "Do this" belong not only to someone who commands, but also to someone who gives counsel, and to someone who exhorts. Few people fail to see that these are very different things, and few cannot tell them apart once they know who is speaking, to whom, and on what occasion. But when people find such phrases in what others have written, and are unable or unwilling to consider the circumstances, they sometimes mistake the precepts of counselors for the precepts of those who command, and sometimes the reverse, depending on which reading better suits the conclusions they want to draw or the actions they approve. To prevent these mistakes, and to restore to the terms *commanding*, *counseling*, and *exhorting* their proper and distinct meanings, I define them as follows.

A *command* is when someone says "Do this" or "Do not do this" and expects no reason for it other than the will of the person who says it. From this it plainly follows that whoever commands is aiming at his own benefit. The reason for his command is his will alone, and the proper object of every person's will is some good to himself.

*Counsel* is when someone says "Do this" or "Do not do this" and derives his reasons from the benefit that will come of it to the person he is addressing. From this it is evident that whoever gives counsel professes to aim only at the good of the person he advises, whatever he may privately intend.

One great difference between counsel and command, therefore, is that command is directed to the speaker's own benefit, and counsel to the benefit of someone else. A second difference follows from the first. A person may be obliged to do what he is commanded, as when he has covenanted to obey; but he cannot be obliged to do what he is counseled, because the harm of not following the advice falls on himself alone. And if he were to covenant to follow it, the counsel would thereby be converted into a command. A third difference is that no one can claim a right to be another person's counselor, since a counselor is not supposed to seek any benefit for himself from the role. To demand the right to counsel another betrays a wish to learn that person's plans, or to gain some other good for oneself, which, as I said before, is the proper object of every person's will.

It also belongs to the nature of counsel that, whatever it may be, the person who asked for it cannot fairly accuse or punish the one who gave it. To ask another for counsel is to permit him to give whatever counsel he thinks best. Consequently, anyone who counsels his sovereign, whether a monarch or an assembly, at the sovereign's request, cannot in fairness be punished for it, whether or not his advice agrees with the opinion of the majority, so long as it bears on the proposal under debate. If the mind of the assembly could be known before the debate was over, there would be no reason to ask for or receive any further counsel, since the mind of the assembly is the resolution of the debate and the end of all deliberation. In general, whoever asks for counsel is its author, and therefore cannot punish it; and what the sovereign cannot punish, no one else can. But if one subject counsels another to do something contrary to the laws, that counsel is punishable by the commonwealth, whether it springs from evil intention or from mere ignorance. Ignorance of the law is no adequate excuse where everyone is bound to take notice of the laws to which he is subject.

*Exhortation* and *dehortation* are counsel accompanied by signs, in the person who gives it, of an intense desire to have it followed; or, more briefly, counsel vehemently pressed. Someone who exhorts does not trace out the consequences of what he advises and hold himself to the rigor of sound reasoning. Instead he urges the person he is counseling toward action, just as one who dehorts, arguing someone out of a course, frightens him away from it. Such speakers therefore frame their reasons with an eye to the common passions and opinions of mankind, and make use of similes, metaphors, examples, and the other tools of oratory to persuade their hearers of the usefulness, honor, or justice of following their advice.

Several things may be inferred from this. First, exhortation and dehortation are directed to the good of the person who gives the counsel, not of the person who asks for it. This runs contrary to the duty of a counselor, who by the very definition of counsel ought to consider not his own benefit but that of the person he advises. That the exhorter directs his counsel to his own benefit is plain enough from the length and vehemence of his urging, or from the artfulness of his delivery. Since no one asked these things of him, they proceed from his own motives, and so they aim principally at his own benefit, and only incidentally at the good of the person being counseled, if they aim at it at all.

Second, exhortation and dehortation have their use only when a speaker must address a multitude. When speech is directed to one person, that person can interrupt and examine the speaker's reasons more rigorously than is possible in a crowd, whose members are too many to enter into argument and dialogue with someone addressing all of them at once. Third, those who exhort and dehort when they have been asked to give counsel are corrupt counselors, bribed, as it were, by their own interest. However good the counsel they give may be, the person who gives it is no more a good counselor than a man who hands down a just verdict in exchange for a reward is a just judge. Where a person may lawfully command, however, as a father in his family or a commander in an army, his exhortations and dehortations are not only lawful but necessary and praiseworthy. In that case they are no longer counsels but commands. And when such commands call for the performance of hard and disagreeable labor, sometimes necessity, and always humanity, requires that they be sweetened in the delivery with encouragement, and couched in the tone and phrasing of counsel rather than in the harsher language of command.

Examples of the difference between command and counsel can be taken from the forms of speech that express them in Holy Scripture. "Have no other gods but me; make for yourself no graven image; take not God's name in vain; sanctify the Sabbath; honor your parents; do not kill; do not steal," and the rest, are commands, because the reason we are to obey them is drawn from the will of God our King, whom we are obliged to obey. But the words "Sell all you have, give it to the poor, and follow me" are counsel, because the reason we are to do so is drawn from our own benefit, namely that we shall have "treasure in heaven." The words "Go into the village opposite you, and you will find an ass tied, and her colt with her; untie her and bring her to me" are a command, because the reason for the disciples' action is drawn from the will of their Master. But the words "Repent, and be baptized in the name of Jesus" are counsel, because the reason we should do so tends to no benefit for God Almighty, who will remain King however we may rebel, but to our own, since we have no other means of escaping the punishment that hangs over us for our sins.

The difference between counsel and command has now been derived from the nature of counsel, which consists in showing the benefit or harm that may come to the person being counseled from the necessary or probable consequences of the action the counselor proposes. The differences between fit and unfit counselors can be derived from the same source. Experience is nothing more than the memory of the consequences of similar actions observed in the past, and counsel is nothing more than the speech by which that experience is made known to another. It follows that the virtues and defects of counsel are the same as the virtues and defects of the intellect. To the person of a commonwealth, its counselors stand in place of memory and of mental discourse, the connected train of reasoning by which a mind works from one thought to the next. But alongside this resemblance between a commonwealth and a natural man there is one difference of great importance. A natural man receives his experience from the natural objects of sense, which act upon him without any passion or interest of their own; whereas those who counsel the representative person of a commonwealth may have, and often do have, their own particular ends and passions, which make their counsels always suspect and frequently unfaithful. We may therefore set down as the first condition of a good counselor *that his ends and interests not be inconsistent with the ends and interests of the person he counsels*.

Second, when an action comes up for deliberation, a counselor's office is to make its consequences plain, in such a way that the person counseled may be truly and clearly informed. He ought therefore to present his advice in whatever form of speech will make the truth appear most clearly: that is, with reasoning as firm, language as meaningful and precise, and expression as brief as the evidence will allow. Accordingly, *rash and unsupported inferences* (such as those drawn only from examples or from the authority of books, which are not arguments about what is good or evil but merely testimony to fact or to opinion), *obscure, confused, and ambiguous expressions, and all metaphorical speech designed to stir up the passions, are contrary to the office of a counselor*. Such reasoning and such expressions are useful only to deceive, or to lead the person we counsel toward ends other than his own.

Third, the ability to give counsel proceeds from experience and long study, and no one is presumed to have experience in everything that must be known to administer a great commonwealth. Therefore *no one is presumed to be a good counselor except in matters in which he has not only been well practiced, but on which he has also reflected and deliberated at length*. The business of a commonwealth is to preserve the people at home and defend them against foreign invasion. We shall find that this requires a deep knowledge of the disposition of mankind, of the rights of government, and of the nature of equity, law, justice, and honor, none of which can be attained without study. It also requires knowledge of the strength, resources, and geography both of one's own country and of its neighbors, and of the inclinations and designs of every nation that might in any way trouble it; and this cannot be attained without much experience. Not only the whole of this knowledge, but every particular part of it, requires the maturity and observation of a man advanced in years and of more than ordinary study. The kind of intelligence counsel requires, as I have said before, is judgment; and the differences among men on that score come from their different educations, some having been trained to one kind of study or business and others to another. Where there are infallible rules for doing something, as the rules of geometry are for machines and buildings, all the experience in the world cannot match the counsel of someone who has learned or discovered the rule. Where there is no such rule, the person with the most experience in that particular kind of business has the best judgment in it, and is the best counselor.

Fourth, to be able to counsel a commonwealth on any business that concerns another commonwealth, *one must be acquainted with the intelligence reports and dispatches that come from there, and with all the records of treaties and other transactions of state between the two*. No one can do this except those whom the representative sees fit to admit. From this we can see that people who are not called to give counsel can have no good counsel to press on the sovereign in such matters.

Fifth, assuming the number of counselors is the same, a person is better counseled by hearing them separately than in an assembly, and for many reasons. First, when you hear them separately, you get each one's advice; but in an assembly many of them deliver their advice with an "Aye" or a "No," or by a show of hands, or by rising from their seats, moved not by their own understanding but by the eloquence of someone else, or by fear of displeasing those who have already spoken, or the whole assembly, by contradicting them, or by fear of seeming slower of understanding than those who have applauded the opposite opinion. Second, in an assembly of many there cannot fail to be some whose interests are contrary to the public's. Their interests make them passionate, passion makes them eloquent, and eloquence draws others to the same advice. The passions of men, which are moderate when they are apart, like the heat of a single burning stick, become in an assembly like many burning sticks that set one another alight, especially when they fan one another with speeches, until they set the commonwealth on fire under the pretense of counseling it. Third, when you hear each person separately, you can test the truth or probability of his reasons, and of the grounds of the advice he gives, by frequent interruptions and objections where necessary. This cannot be done in an assembly, where, on any difficult question, a person is more likely to be stunned and dazzled by the variety of speeches about it than informed of the course he ought to take. Besides, no assembly of many called together for advice can fail to include some who are ambitious to be thought eloquent and learned in politics, and who give their advice with an eye not to the business before them but to the applause their speeches will win, motley speeches stitched together from the many-colored threads and scraps of various authors. This is at the very least an irrelevance that eats up the time meant for serious consultation, and it is easily avoided by the private method of counseling men separately. Fourth, in deliberations that ought to be kept secret, of which there are many occasions in public business, the counsel of many, and especially of assemblies, is dangerous. Great assemblies are therefore compelled to commit such affairs to smaller groups, made up of those who are most experienced and in whose loyalty they have the most confidence.

To conclude: who approves so far of taking counsel from a great assembly of counselors that he would wish for their help, or even accept it, when the question is how to marry off his children, dispose of his land, govern his household, or manage his private estate, especially if there are some among them who do not wish him to prosper? A person who conducts his business with the help of many prudent counselors, each consulted separately in his own field, does it best, like a tennis player who has able partners, each posted at his proper station on the court. The person who relies on his own judgment alone does next best, like a player who has no partner at all. But the person who is carried back and forth to his business by a formal council, which cannot move except by a majority of agreeing opinions, and whose decisions are usually delayed in execution by the dissenting party out of envy or self-interest, does it worst of all. He is like a player who is carried to the ball, even by good players, in a wheelbarrow or some other contraption, heavy in itself and slowed further by the conflicting judgments and efforts of those pushing it. The more hands there are on it, the worse it goes, and worst of all when one or more of those pushing want him to lose. It is true that many eyes see more than one. But this should not be understood of many counselors, except when the final decision rests with one man. Otherwise, because many eyes see the same thing from different angles and are prone to squint toward their own private advantage, those who do not wish to miss their mark, though they look about with two eyes, always take aim with one. For this reason no great popular commonwealth has ever been sustained except by a foreign enemy that united its people, or by the reputation of some one eminent man among them, or by the secret counsel of a few, or by the mutual fear of evenly matched factions, and never by the open deliberations of the assembly. As for very small commonwealths, whether popular or monarchical, no human wisdom can preserve them any longer than the mutual jealousy of their powerful neighbors lasts.

## Chapter XXVI. Of Civil Laws

### What Civil Law Is

By civil laws I mean the laws that people are bound to observe because they are members not of this or that particular commonwealth, but of a commonwealth as such. Knowledge of particular laws belongs to those who make the laws of their own countries their professional study, but knowledge of civil law in general belongs to anyone. The ancient law of Rome was called its civil law, from the word *civitas*, which means a commonwealth. Those countries that were once under the Roman Empire and governed by its law still retain whatever parts of it they see fit, and they call that portion "the civil law" to distinguish it from the rest of their own civil laws. That is not what I intend to discuss here. My aim is to show not what the law is in this place or that, but what law *is*, as Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and various others have done without claiming to be professional students of the law.

It is clear, first, that law in general is not counsel but command. Nor is it a command of any person to any person, but only of one whose command is addressed to someone already obliged to obey him. Civil law adds only the name of the person commanding, which is *persona civitatis*, the person of the commonwealth.

With this in mind, I define civil law as follows: "Civil law is, for every subject, those rules which the commonwealth has commanded him, by word, by writing, or by some other sufficient sign of its will, to use in distinguishing right from wrong; that is, in distinguishing what is contrary to the rule from what is not."

Everything in this definition is evident at first sight. Anyone can see that some laws are addressed to all subjects in general, some to particular provinces, some to particular occupations, and some to particular individuals, and that each is therefore law to those to whom the command is directed and to no one else. It is equally plain that laws are the rules of just and unjust, since nothing is considered unjust that is not contrary to some law. It is plain, too, that no one can make laws but the commonwealth, because our subjection is to the commonwealth alone, and that commands must be conveyed by sufficient signs, because otherwise a person would not know how to obey them. Whatever can be deduced from this definition by necessary consequence must therefore be accepted as true. From it I deduce the following.

### The Sovereign Is the Legislator

1. In every commonwealth the legislator is the sovereign alone, whether that sovereign is one man, as in a monarchy, or one assembly of men, as in a democracy or an aristocracy. The legislator is the one who makes the law. Only the commonwealth prescribes and commands the observance of the rules we call law; therefore the commonwealth is the legislator. But the commonwealth is not a person, and it has no capacity to do anything except through its representative, that is, the sovereign. The sovereign is therefore the sole legislator. For the same reason, no one but the sovereign can repeal a law once made, because a law is repealed only by another law that forbids it to be put into effect.

### And Is Not Subject to Civil Law

2. The sovereign of a commonwealth, whether an assembly or one man, is not subject to the civil laws. Having the power to make and repeal laws, the sovereign may free himself from that subjection whenever he pleases, by repealing the laws that trouble him and making new ones. He was therefore free all along, for whoever can be free when he wishes is free. Nor is it possible for anyone to be bound to himself, because whoever can bind can also release; and so one who is bound only to himself is not bound at all.

### Custom Becomes Law Not by Length of Time but by the Sovereign's Consent

3. When long usage acquires the authority of law, it is not the length of time that confers that authority but the will of the sovereign, signified by his silence, since silence is sometimes evidence of consent. The custom remains law only so long as the sovereign remains silent about it. Therefore, if the sovereign has a question of right that rests not on his present will but on laws made in the past, the length of time does no damage to his right, and the question is to be judged by equity. Many unjust actions and unjust sentences go unchecked for longer than anyone can remember. Our lawyers, moreover, count no custom as law unless it is reasonable, and they hold that evil customs ought to be abolished. But the judgment of what is reasonable, and of what ought to be abolished, belongs to the one who makes the law, which is the sovereign assembly or monarch.

### The Law of Nature and the Civil Law Contain Each Other

4. The law of nature and the civil law contain each other and are of equal extent. The laws of nature consist in equity, justice, gratitude, and the other moral virtues that depend on these. In the condition of mere nature, as I said at the end of the fifteenth chapter, they are not properly laws at all, but qualities that dispose people toward peace and obedience. Only once a commonwealth is settled do they become actual laws, and not before, because they are then the commands of the commonwealth and therefore also civil laws; it is the sovereign power that obliges people to obey them. In disputes between private individuals, declaring what is equity, what is justice, and what is moral virtue, and making these binding, requires the ordinances of sovereign power, together with punishments ordained for those who break them. Those ordinances are therefore part of the civil law, and so the law of nature is part of the civil law in every commonwealth in the world.

Conversely, the civil law is part of the dictates of nature. Justice, which is the keeping of covenants and the giving to every person of what is his own, is a dictate of the law of nature. Every subject in a commonwealth has covenanted to obey the civil law. Subjects make this covenant either with one another, as when they assemble to create a common representative, or individually with the representative itself, as when, conquered by the sword, they promise obedience in order to be granted their lives. Obedience to the civil law is therefore also part of the law of nature. Civil and natural law are not different kinds of law but different parts of it: the written part is called civil, and the unwritten part natural. The right of nature, however, which is the natural liberty of human beings, may be curtailed and restrained by the civil law. Indeed, the whole purpose of making laws is such restraint, and without it there can be no peace. Law was brought into the world for no other reason than to limit the natural liberty of individuals in such a way that they would not harm but help one another, and would join together against a common enemy.

### Provincial Laws Are Made Not by Custom but by Sovereign Power

5. Suppose the sovereign of one commonwealth conquers a people that has lived under other written laws, and afterward governs them by the same laws they lived under before. Those laws are nonetheless the civil laws of the victor, not of the vanquished commonwealth. The legislator is not the one by whose authority the laws were first made, but the one by whose authority they now continue to be laws. Accordingly, where a commonwealth's dominion includes various provinces, and those provinces have differing laws, commonly called the customs of each province, we should not suppose that these customs draw their force merely from length of time. They were, in former times, written laws, or were otherwise made known as the constitutions and statutes of their sovereigns. They are laws now not by virtue of prescription, the authority that long continuance is supposed to confer, but by the constitutions of their present sovereigns. If, however, an unwritten law is generally observed in every province of a dominion, and no injustice appears in its use, that law can be nothing other than a law of nature, binding all mankind equally.

### Some Foolish Opinions of Lawyers Concerning the Making of Laws

6. All laws, written and unwritten, derive their authority and force from the will of the commonwealth, that is, from the will of its representative, which in a monarchy is the monarch and in other commonwealths the sovereign assembly. One may therefore wonder where certain opinions come from that appear in the books of eminent lawyers in various commonwealths, opinions that, directly or by implication, make legislative power depend on private persons or subordinate judges. One example is the maxim "that the common law has no controller but Parliament." This is true only where a parliament holds sovereign power and can be assembled or dissolved at no one's discretion but its own. If anyone else has a right to dissolve it, that person also has a right to control it, and consequently to control its controlling. And if no one else has such a right, then the controller of the laws is not *Parlamentum*, Parliament, but *Rex in Parlamento*, the king in Parliament. Where a parliament is sovereign, it might summon any number of men, however wise, from the regions subject to it, and for whatever purpose; yet no one would believe that the assembly so gathered had thereby acquired legislative power for itself. Another example is the saying that "the two arms of a commonwealth are force and justice, the first of which is in the king, while the other is deposited in the hands of Parliament," as if a commonwealth could exist where force lay in any hand that justice lacked the authority to command and govern.

7. Our lawyers agree that law can never be contrary to reason, and that the law is not the letter, meaning every possible construction of the words, but whatever accords with the intention of the legislator. This is true. The question, however, is whose reason is to be accepted as law. It cannot mean any private reason, for then there would be as much contradiction in the laws as there is in the schools of philosophy. Nor can it mean, as Sir Edward Coke would have it, "an artificial perfection of reason, gotten by long study, observation, and experience," such as his own was. Long study may well multiply and entrench mistaken judgments, and where people build on false foundations, the more they build, the greater the ruin. Moreover, among those who study and observe with equal time and diligence, the reasonings and conclusions are, and must remain, at odds. It is therefore not the jurisprudence, or wisdom, of subordinate judges that makes law, but the reason of this artificial man of ours, the commonwealth, together with his command. And since the commonwealth, in its representative, is only one person, contradictions in the laws cannot easily arise; when they do, the same reason can remove them by interpretation or by alteration. In all courts of justice, it is the sovereign, as the person of the commonwealth, who judges. The subordinate judge ought to attend to the reason that moved his sovereign to make the law in question, so that his sentence accords with it, and his sentence is then his sovereign's sentence. Otherwise it is his own, and an unjust one.

### A Law Made but Not Made Known Is No Law

8. Law is a command, and a command consists in declaring or making manifest the will of the one commanding, by voice, by writing, or by some other sufficient evidence of that will. It follows that the command of the commonwealth is law only to those who have the means of learning of it. Over natural fools, children, and madmen there is no law, any more than there is over brute beasts. Nor can they be called just or unjust, because they never had the power to make any covenant or to understand its consequences, and so they never undertook to authorize the actions of any sovereign, as those who create a commonwealth for themselves must do. Those whom nature or accident has deprived of all awareness of laws in general are excused, and in the same way, anyone whom some accident, not arising from his own fault, has deprived of the means of learning a particular law is excused if he fails to observe it. Properly speaking, that law is no law to him. It is necessary, then, to consider at this point what evidence and signs are sufficient for knowing what the law is, that is, what the will of the sovereign is, in monarchies and in other forms of government alike.

### All Unwritten Laws Are Laws of Nature

First, if a law binds all subjects without exception and is neither written nor otherwise published in places where they can take notice of it, it is a law of nature. Whatever people are to recognize as law, not on the word of others but each through his own reason, must be agreeable to the reason of all, and no law can meet that standard except the law of nature. The laws of nature therefore need no publication or proclamation, since they are contained in a single sentence approved by the whole world: "Do not do to another what you would think it unreasonable for another to do to you."

Second, if a law binds only some class of people, or one particular person, and is neither written nor published by word of mouth, it too is a law of nature, and it is known by the same evidence and signs that distinguish those in that condition from other subjects. Any law that is not written, or in some way published by the one who makes it law, can be known only through the reason of the one who is to obey it, and it is therefore not only a civil law but a natural one. If, for example, the sovereign employs a public minister without written instructions about what to do, the minister is obliged to take the dictates of reason as his instructions. If the sovereign appoints a judge, the judge must understand that his sentence ought to accord with the reason of his sovereign; since that reason is always understood to be equity, he is bound to it by the law of nature. If the sovereign appoints an ambassador, the ambassador must, in everything not covered by his written instructions, take as his instruction whatever reason shows to be most conducive to his sovereign's interest. The same holds for all other ministers of the sovereign power, public and private. All these instructions of natural reason can be gathered under the single name of fidelity, which is a branch of natural justice.

With the exception of the law of nature, it belongs to the essence of all other laws that they be made known to everyone obliged to obey them, by word, by writing, or by some other act known to proceed from the sovereign authority. The will of another cannot be understood except through his own word or act, or by inference from his aims and purpose, and in the person of the commonwealth those aims are always to be presumed consistent with equity and reason. In ancient times, before writing was in common use, laws were often set in verse, so that uneducated people, taking pleasure in singing or reciting them, might more easily keep them in memory. For the same reason Solomon advises a man to bind the Ten Commandments upon his ten fingers. And of the law that Moses gave to the people of Israel at the renewal of the covenant, Moses commands them to teach it to their children, speaking of it at home and on the road, on going to bed and on rising; to write it on the doorposts and doors of their houses; and to assemble the people, men, women, and children, to hear it read aloud.

### Nothing Is Law Where the Legislator Cannot Be Known

Nor is it enough that the law be written and published; there must also be clear signs that it proceeds from the will of the sovereign. Private individuals who have, or believe they have, enough force to secure their unjust designs and carry them safely through to their ambitious ends may publish as law whatever they please, without the legislative authority or against it. What is required, therefore, is not only a declaration of the law but also sufficient signs of its author and its authority. In every commonwealth the author, or legislator, is presumed to be evident, because he is the sovereign, who, having been established by the consent of every person, is presumed to be sufficiently known to every person. It is true that people are, for the most part, so ignorant and so complacent that once the memory of their commonwealth's original founding has faded, they no longer consider by whose power they are customarily defended against their enemies, have their labor protected, and have their wrongs redressed. Yet because no one who does consider the matter can doubt it, no excuse can be drawn from ignorance of where sovereignty lies. It is a dictate of natural reason, and consequently an evident law of nature, that no one ought to weaken the power whose protection he has himself sought, or knowingly received, against others. No one, therefore, can doubt who is sovereign except through his own fault, whatever wicked men may suggest. The difficulty lies in the evidence of the authority derived from the sovereign, and removing that difficulty depends on knowledge of the public registers, public councils, public ministers, and public seals, by which all laws are sufficiently verified.

### The Difference Between Verifying and Authorizing

Verified, I say, not authorized. Verification is only testimony and record. It is not the authority of the law, which consists solely in the command of the sovereign.

### Law Verified by the Subordinate Judge

If, then, someone has a case of injury that depends on the law of nature, that is, on common equity, the sentence of the judge who holds a commission giving him authority to hear such cases is sufficient verification of the law of nature in that individual case. The advice of someone who makes a profession of studying the law is useful for avoiding disputes, but it is only advice. It is the judge who must tell people what the law is, after hearing the controversy.

### By the Public Registers

But when the question concerns an injury or a crime under a written law, anyone may, if he chooses, consult the registers himself or through others, and so be sufficiently informed, before he commits the injury or the crime, whether it is an injury or not. Indeed, he ought to do so. When someone doubts whether the act he is about to commit is just or unjust, and could inform himself if he wished, the act is unlawful. In the same way, a person who believes himself injured in a matter settled by written law, which he could examine and consider himself or through others, acts unjustly if he complains before consulting the law, and he reveals a disposition more inclined to harass other people than to claim his own right.

### By Letters Patent and the Public Seal

If the question concerns obedience to a public officer, it is sufficient verification of his authority to have seen his commission under the public seal and heard it read, or to have had the means of learning of it had one wished to. Everyone is obliged to do his best to inform himself of all written laws that may bear on his own future actions.

### The Interpretation of Law Depends on the Sovereign Power

Once the legislator is known, and the laws have been sufficiently published, whether in writing or by the light of nature, one further and very important condition is still needed to make them binding. The nature of a law lies not in its letter but in its intent or meaning, that is, in its authentic interpretation, which is the sense the legislator intended. The interpretation of all laws therefore depends on the sovereign authority, and the only interpreters can be those whom the sovereign, to whom alone the subject owes obedience, appoints. Otherwise, through an interpreter's cunning, the law could be made to bear a sense contrary to the sovereign's, and by that means the interpreter would become the legislator.

### All Laws Need Interpretation

All laws, written and unwritten, require interpretation. The unwritten law of nature is easy for those who use their natural reason without partiality or passion, and it therefore leaves those who violate it without excuse. Yet since very few people, perhaps none, are not in some cases blinded by self-love or some other passion, it has now become the most obscure of all laws, and consequently has the greatest need of able interpreters. Written laws, if they are short, are easily misinterpreted because a word or two may carry different meanings; if they are long, they grow more obscure through the different meanings of many words. No written law, then, whether expressed in few words or many, can be properly understood without a thorough understanding of the final causes, the ends for which the law was made, and the knowledge of those final causes lies with the legislator. For him, therefore, there can be no knot in the law that cannot be undone. Either he finds the ends by which to untie it, or else, by his legislative power, he makes whatever ends he wishes, as Alexander did when, faced with the Gordian knot, he cut through it with his sword. No other interpreter can do this.

### The Authentic Interpretation of Law Is Not That of Writers

In a commonwealth, the interpretation of the laws of nature does not depend on books of moral philosophy. The authority of writers, without the authority of the commonwealth, does not make their opinions law, however true those opinions may be. What I have written in this treatise about the moral virtues, and about their necessity for securing and maintaining peace, is evident truth, but it is not law for that reason. It is law because, in every commonwealth in the world, it is part of the civil law. Though it is naturally reasonable, it becomes law through the sovereign power. Otherwise it would be a serious error to call the laws of nature unwritten law, when we see so many volumes published about them, filled with so many contradictions of one another and of themselves.

### The Interpreter of the Law Is the Judge Giving Sentence by Word of Mouth in Each Particular Case

The interpretation of the law of nature is the sentence of the judge appointed by sovereign authority to hear and decide the controversies that depend on that law, and it consists in applying the law to the case at hand. In the act of judging, the judge does no more than consider whether the claim of the party before him agrees with natural reason and equity, and the sentence he gives is therefore the interpretation of the law of nature. That interpretation is authentic not because it is his private judgment, but because he gives it by the authority of the sovereign, through which it becomes the sovereign's sentence; and that sentence is law, for the time being, to the parties in the case.

### The Sentence of a Judge Does Not Bind Him, or Another Judge, to Give the Same Sentence in Similar Cases Ever After

But since no judge, whether subordinate or sovereign, is immune from error in a judgment of equity, a judge who later finds, in a similar case, that a contrary sentence agrees better with equity is obliged to give it. No man's error becomes his own law, and no error binds him to persist in it. For the same reason, his error does not become law for other judges, even if they are sworn to follow it. In laws that are changeable, a wrong sentence given by the sovereign's authority, if the sovereign knows of it and allows it, does establish a new law for cases in which every small circumstance is the same. But in laws that are unchangeable, such as the laws of nature, such sentences are not law for the same judge or for any other judge in similar cases ever afterward. Princes succeed one another; one judge passes away and another comes; indeed, heaven and earth shall pass away, but not one tittle of the law of nature shall pass, for it is the eternal law of God. Therefore all the sentences of all the judges who have ever lived cannot together make a law contrary to natural equity. Nor can any precedent set by former judges justify an unreasonable sentence, or relieve the present judge of the labor of working out, from the principles of his own natural reason, what equity requires in the case before him. For example, it is against the law of nature to punish the innocent, and an innocent person is one who clears himself in a court of law and is acknowledged as innocent by the judge. Suppose a man is accused of a capital crime. Seeing the power and malice of some enemy, and the frequent corruption and partiality of judges, he runs away for fear of the outcome. Later he is caught and brought to a lawful trial, where he shows convincingly that he was not guilty of the crime. He is acquitted, yet he is nevertheless sentenced to forfeit his goods. This is a plain condemnation of the innocent. I say, therefore, that there is no place in the world where this can count as an interpretation of a law of nature, or be made law by the sentences of earlier judges who did the same thing. Whoever first judged this way judged unjustly, and no injustice can be a model for the judgments of later judges. A written law may forbid innocent men to flee, and they may then be punished for fleeing. But to treat flight from fear of injury as a presumption of guilt, after a man has already been cleared of the crime in court, contradicts the very nature of a presumption, which has no place once judgment has been given. Yet a great lawyer has set this down as the common law of England. "If a man who is innocent," he writes, "is accused of felony and flees for fear of the charge, then even though he judicially acquits himself of the felony, if it is found that he fled because of the felony, he shall, notwithstanding his innocence, forfeit all his goods and chattels, and all debts and dues owed to him. For as to the forfeiture of these, the law will admit no proof against the presumption in law that is grounded upon his flight." Here, then, is an innocent man, acquitted in court, who is nevertheless condemned, after his acquittal and upon a presumption in law, to lose everything he owns, even though no written law forbade him to flee. If the law grounded on his flight a presumption that he had committed the act, which was a capital crime, the sentence ought to have been death. If the presumption was not that he had committed the act, then why should he lose his goods? This, therefore, is no law of England, and the condemnation is grounded not on a presumption of law but on the presumption of the judges. It is also against law to say that no proof shall be admitted against a presumption of law. All judges, sovereign and subordinate, who refuse to hear proof refuse to do justice. Even if their sentence happens to be just, judges who condemn without hearing the proofs offered are unjust judges, and their presumption is nothing but prejudice, which no one ought to bring with him to the seat of justice, whatever earlier judgments or examples he may claim to be following. There are other matters of this kind in which men's judgments have been corrupted by trusting to precedents, but this one is enough to show that although a judge's sentence is law to the party pleading, it is no law to any judge who succeeds him in that office.

In the same way, when the question concerns the meaning of written laws, the interpreter is not the person who writes a commentary on them. Commentaries are generally more open to quibbling than the text itself, so they need further commentaries of their own, and such interpretation would never end. Therefore, unless the sovereign has authorized an interpreter from whom subordinate judges may not depart, the interpreter can be none other than the ordinary judges, just as they are in cases of unwritten law. Those who plead before them are to accept their sentences as law in that particular case, but those sentences do not bind other judges to give the same judgments in similar cases. A judge may err in interpreting even written laws, and no error of a subordinate judge can change the law, which is the general sentence of the sovereign.

### The Difference Between the Letter and the Sense of the Law

With written laws, people customarily distinguish between the letter of the law and its sense. If by "the letter" is meant whatever can be extracted from the bare words, the distinction is sound. The meanings of nearly all words are ambiguous, either in themselves or in their metaphorical use, and can be stretched in argument to yield many senses, but a law has only one sense. If, however, by "the letter" is meant the literal sense, then the letter and the sense, or intention, of the law are one and the same. The literal sense is what the legislator intended the letter of the law to signify, and the legislator's intention is always presumed to be equity, since it would be a grave insult for a judge to think otherwise of the sovereign. If the words of the law do not fully authorize a reasonable sentence, therefore, the judge ought to supply what is lacking from the law of nature; or, if the case is difficult, he ought to postpone judgment until he has received fuller authority. For example, a written law ordains that a man who is forcibly thrown out of his house shall be restored to it by force. Now suppose a man carelessly leaves his house empty and, on returning, is kept out by force, a case for which no specific law has been made. Clearly this case falls under the same law, since otherwise he would have no remedy at all, which must be presumed contrary to the legislator's intention. Again, the words of the law command the judge to decide according to the evidence. Suppose a man is falsely accused of an act that the judge himself saw committed by someone other than the accused. In this case the judge should neither follow the letter of the law so far as to condemn the innocent, nor give sentence against the evidence of the witnesses, since the letter of the law forbids that. Instead, he should arrange with the sovereign for someone else to be made judge, while he himself becomes a witness. Thus the harm that follows from the bare words of a written law may lead the judge to the law's intention and help him interpret it better, though no harm of that kind can justify a sentence against the law. For a judge of right and wrong is not thereby a judge of what is advantageous or disadvantageous to the commonwealth.

### The Abilities Required in a Judge

The abilities required in a good interpreter of the law, which is to say a good judge, are not the same as those of an advocate, whose ability lies in the study of the laws. Just as a judge should learn the facts only from the witnesses, he should learn the law only from the statutes and constitutions of the sovereign, either cited in the pleadings or declared to him by those whom the sovereign power has authorized to declare them. He need not concern himself in advance with what he will decide, because what he is to say about the facts will be supplied by the witnesses, and what he is to say on points of law will be supplied by those who set it out in their pleadings and interpret it with authority on the spot. The Lords of Parliament in England were judges, and the most difficult cases have been heard and decided by them; yet few of them were deeply versed in the study of the laws, and fewer still had made law their profession. Although they consulted lawyers appointed to attend for that purpose, the authority to give sentence was theirs alone. Similarly, in ordinary trials of right, twelve men of the common people are the judges. They give sentence not only on the facts but on the right, pronouncing simply for the plaintiff or for the defendant, so that they judge not only the fact but also the right. In a criminal case they determine not only whether the act was done but also whether it is murder, homicide, felony, assault, or the like, which are determinations of law. Because they are not supposed to know the law on their own, someone with authority informs them of it in the particular case they are to judge. Yet if they do not decide according to what he tells them, they are not liable to any penalty for it, unless it is shown that they acted against their consciences or had been bribed. The qualities that make a good judge, or a good interpreter of the laws, are these. First, a right understanding of that principal law of nature called equity. Since it depends not on reading other men's writings but on the soundness of a man's own natural reason and reflection, it is presumed to be strongest in those who have had the most leisure and the greatest inclination to reflect on it. Second, contempt for unnecessary riches and advancement. Third, the ability, when judging, to strip himself of all fear, anger, hatred, love, and compassion. Fourth and last, patience to hear, diligent attention in hearing, and the memory to retain, digest, and apply what he has heard.

### Divisions of Law

The laws have been distinguished and divided in various ways, according to the different methods of those who have written about them. Classification depends not on nature but on the purpose of the writer, and it follows each man's own method. In the Institutes of Justinian we find seven kinds of civil law.

1. The edicts, constitutions, and letters of the prince, that is, of the emperor, since the whole power of the people was vested in him. The proclamations of the kings of England resemble these.

2. The decrees of the whole people of Rome, including the Senate, when the Senate put a question to them. These were laws at first by virtue of the sovereign power that resided in the people, and those the emperors did not repeal remained laws by imperial authority. For all laws that bind are understood to be laws by the authority of whoever has the power to repeal them. The acts of Parliament in England are somewhat like these laws.

3. The decrees of the common people, excluding the Senate, when the question was put to them by the tribune of the people. Those the emperors did not repeal likewise remained laws by imperial authority. The orders of the House of Commons in England were like these.

4. The *senatus consulta*, or orders of the Senate. When the people of Rome grew so numerous that it was inconvenient to assemble them, the emperor thought it fit that the Senate should be consulted instead of the people. These bear some resemblance to the acts of the Council.

5. The edicts of the praetors, the Roman magistrates who administered justice, and in some cases of the aediles. These correspond to the chief justices in the courts of England.

6. The *responsa prudentum*, the sentences and opinions of those lawyers whom the emperor had authorized to interpret the law and to answer anyone who sought their advice on a point of law. The emperor's constitutions obliged judges to observe these answers when giving judgment. They would be like the reports of decided cases in England, if other judges are bound by English law to observe those reports. For the judges of the common law of England are not properly judges but *juris consulti*, legal advisers, whom the true judges, either the Lords or the twelve men of the country, are to consult on points of law.

7. Finally, unwritten customs, which by their nature imitate law, are true laws by the tacit consent of the emperor, provided they are not contrary to the law of nature.

Another division of laws is into natural and positive. Natural laws are those that have been laws from all eternity. They are called not only natural but also moral laws, and they consist in the moral virtues, such as justice, equity, and all habits of mind that lead to peace and charity, which I have already discussed in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

Positive laws are those that have not existed from eternity but have been made laws by the will of those who have held sovereign power over others. They are either written down or made known to people by some other evidence of their legislator's will.

### Another Division of Law

Again, some positive laws are human and some divine; and of human positive laws, some are distributive and some penal. Distributive laws determine the rights of subjects, declaring to every man the grounds on which he acquires and holds property in land or goods, and a right or liberty of action. These are addressed to all subjects. Penal laws declare what penalty shall be inflicted on those who violate the law, and they are addressed to the ministers and officers appointed to carry them out. Although everyone ought to be informed in advance of the punishments ordained for transgression, the command is addressed not to the offender, who cannot be expected to punish himself faithfully, but to the public ministers appointed to see that the penalty is carried out. These penal laws are for the most part written together with the distributive laws and are sometimes called judgments. For all laws are general judgments, or sentences, of the legislator, just as every particular judgment is a law to the person whose case is judged.

### How Divine Positive Law Is Made Known to Be Law

Divine positive laws are commandments of God that do not date from all eternity and are not addressed universally to all men, but only to a certain people or to certain persons; they are declared to be divine by those whom God has authorized to declare them. Natural laws, being eternal and universal, are all divine. But how can anyone know that a man has the authority to declare what God's positive laws are? God may command a man in a supernatural way to deliver laws to other men. But it is of the essence of law that the person to be obliged be assured of the authority of the one who declares it, and we cannot know by natural means that this authority comes from God. Two questions therefore arise. How can a man, without supernatural revelation, be assured of the revelation received by the one who declares the law? And how can he be bound to obey such laws? The first, how a man can be assured of another's revelation without a revelation made to himself, is evidently impossible to answer. A man may be led to believe in such a revelation by the miracles he sees the other perform, or by the extraordinary holiness of his life, or by the extraordinary wisdom or extraordinary success of his actions, all of which are signs of God's extraordinary favor. Yet none of these is sure evidence of a special revelation. Miracles are marvelous works, but what is marvelous to one man may not be so to another. Holiness may be feigned, and the visible successes of this world are most often God's work through natural and ordinary causes. No man, therefore, can know infallibly by natural reason that another has received a supernatural revelation of God's will. He can only believe it, and his belief will be firmer or weaker as the signs appear greater or lesser.

The second question, how he can be bound to obey such laws, is not so hard. If the law declared is not against the law of nature, which is undoubtedly God's law, and he undertakes to obey it, then he is bound by his own act. He is bound, I say, to obey it, but not bound to believe it, for men's beliefs and inner thoughts are not subject to commands, but only to the operation of God, whether ordinary or extraordinary. Faith in a supernatural law is not a fulfillment of it but only an assent to it; it is not a duty we render to God but a gift that God freely gives to whomever he pleases. Likewise, unbelief is not a breach of any of God's laws but a rejection of all of them except the natural laws. The examples and testimonies of holy Scripture on this point make what I say clearer still. The covenant God made with Abraham, in a supernatural manner, is set out in the seventeenth chapter of Genesis: "This is the covenant which you shall keep between me and you and your seed after you." Abraham's descendants did not receive this revelation, nor did they yet exist. Yet they are a party to the covenant and bound to obey whatever Abraham should declare to them as God's law. They could be bound only by virtue of the obedience they owed to their parents, who, when they are subject to no other earthly power, as in Abraham's case, have sovereign power over their children and servants. Again, where God says to Abraham, "In you shall all nations of the earth be blessed, for I know that you will command your children and your household after you to keep the way of the Lord and to observe righteousness and judgment," it is plain that the obedience of his family, who had received no revelation, depended on their prior obligation to obey their sovereign. At Mount Sinai only Moses went up to God; the people were forbidden to approach on pain of death. Yet they were bound to obey everything Moses declared to them as God's law. On what ground, if not on their own act of submission: "Speak to us yourself, and we will hear you; but let not God speak to us, lest we die"? These two passages show clearly enough that in a commonwealth, a subject who has received no certain and assured revelation of God's will is to obey the command of the commonwealth as that will. If men were free to take as God's commandments their own dreams and fancies, or the dreams and fancies of private men, scarcely two men would agree on what God commands, and every man, holding to such dreams, would despise the commandments of the commonwealth. I conclude, therefore, that in all things not contrary to the moral law, that is, to the law of nature, all subjects are bound to obey as divine law whatever the laws of the commonwealth declare to be so. This is also evident to any man's reason. Whatever is not against the law of nature may be made law in the name of those who hold sovereign power, and there is no reason men should be less obliged by it when it is put forward in the name of God. Besides, there is no place in the world where men are permitted to claim any commandments of God other than those the commonwealth declares to be such. Christian states punish those who revolt from the Christian religion, and all other states punish those who set up any religion they have forbidden. In whatever the commonwealth does not regulate, equity, which is the law of nature and therefore an eternal law of God, requires that every man enjoy his liberty equally.

### Another Division of Laws

There is also another distinction of laws, into fundamental and not fundamental, but I have never been able to find in any author what a fundamental law means. Nevertheless, one may very reasonably distinguish laws in that way.

### What a Fundamental Law Is

A fundamental law in every commonwealth is one whose removal causes the commonwealth to fail and be utterly dissolved, like a building whose foundation is destroyed. A fundamental law, therefore, is one by which subjects are bound to uphold whatever power is given to the sovereign, whether a monarch or a sovereign assembly, without which the commonwealth cannot stand: such as the power of war and peace, of judicature, of the appointment of officers, and of doing whatever he thinks necessary for the public good. A law that is not fundamental is one whose repeal does not bring with it the dissolution of the commonwealth, such as the laws concerning disputes between one subject and another. So much for the division of laws.

### The Difference Between Law and Right

I find the words *lex civilis* and *jus civile*, that is, civil law and civil right, used interchangeably for the same thing, even by the most learned authors, yet this ought not to be so. For right is liberty, namely the liberty that the civil law leaves us, while civil law is an obligation that takes from us the liberty the law of nature gave us. Nature gave every man a right to secure himself by his own strength and to attack a neighbor he suspected, as a preventive measure. But the civil law takes away that liberty in all cases where it is safe to wait for the protection of the law. *Lex* and *jus*, therefore, are as different as obligation and liberty.

### And Between a Law and a Charter

Likewise, laws and charters are treated interchangeably as the same thing. Yet charters are gifts of the sovereign; they are not laws but exemptions from law. The language of a law is *jubeo, injungo*: I command, I enjoin. The language of a charter is *dedi, concessi*: I have given, I have granted. But what is given or granted to a man is not forced upon him by a law. A law may be made to bind all the subjects of a commonwealth, whereas a liberty, or charter, is granted only to one man or to some one part of the people. To say that all the people of a commonwealth have liberty in some case is to say that in that case no law has been made, or else that one was made and has since been repealed.

## Chapter XXVII. Of Crimes, Excuses, and Extenuations

*What Sin Is*

A sin is not only the transgression of a law but also any contempt for the lawgiver, since such contempt breaks all of his laws at once. Sin can therefore consist not only in committing a deed, in speaking words the laws forbid, or in omitting what the law commands, but also in the intention or purpose to transgress. The purpose to break the law is already a degree of contempt for the one whose responsibility it is to see the law carried out. Merely taking pleasure in imagining that one possesses another man's goods, servants, or wife, without any intention of taking them from him by force or fraud, is no breach of the law that says, "Thou shalt not covet." Nor is it a sin to take pleasure in imagining or dreaming of the death of someone from whose life one expects nothing but harm and annoyance. The sin lies in resolving to carry out some act that tends toward that end. To be pleased by the fiction of something that would please us if it were real is a passion so deeply rooted in the nature of human beings, and of every other living creature, that to call it a sin would be to make it a sin to be human. Reflecting on this, I have come to think that those who maintain that the first stirrings of the mind are sins, even when checked by the fear of God, are too severe, both toward themselves and toward others. Still, I confess it is safer to err in that direction than in the other.

*What a Crime Is*

A crime is a sin that consists in committing, by deed or by word, what the law forbids, or in omitting what the law has commanded. Every crime is therefore a sin, but not every sin is a crime. To intend to steal or to kill is a sin even if the intention never shows itself in word or deed, for God, who sees the thoughts of men, can hold a person accountable for it. But until the intention appears through something done or said, from which a human judge could infer it, it does not bear the name of crime. The Greeks observed this distinction in their words *hamartema* on the one hand and *enklema* or *aitia* on the other. The first, which is translated as "sin," signifies any departure from the law whatever. The latter two, translated as "crime," signify only those sins of which one person may accuse another, and intentions that never appear in any outward act leave no room for human accusation. In the same way, the Romans used *peccatum*, meaning sin, for every kind of deviation from the law. By *crimen*, a word they derived from *cerno*, "to perceive," they meant only those sins that could be made evident before a judge, and which were therefore not mere intentions.

*Where There Is No Civil Law, There Is No Crime*

Several conclusions follow from this relationship of sin to law, and of crime to civil law. First, where law ceases, sin ceases. But because the law of nature is eternal, the violation of covenants, ingratitude, arrogance, and every act contrary to any moral virtue can never cease to be sin. Second, when the civil law ceases, crimes cease. With no law left but the law of nature, there is no room for accusation: each person is his own judge, accused only by his own conscience and cleared by the uprightness of his own intention. When his intention is right, his act is no sin; when it is not, his act is a sin, but not a crime. Third, when sovereign power ceases, crime ceases as well. Where no such power exists, the law offers no protection, and everyone may therefore protect himself by his own strength. No one, in establishing a sovereign power, can be supposed to have surrendered the right to preserve his own body, since the safety of the body is the very purpose for which all sovereignty was instituted. This applies, however, only to those who have not themselves helped to destroy the power that protected them, for that act was a crime from the start.

*Ignorance of the Law of Nature Excuses No One*

Every crime springs from some defect of understanding, some error in reasoning, or some sudden force of the passions. A defect of understanding is ignorance; a defect of reasoning is erroneous opinion. Ignorance, in turn, is of three kinds: ignorance of the law, ignorance of the sovereign, and ignorance of the penalty. Ignorance of the law of nature excuses no one, because everyone who has reached the use of reason is presumed to know that he ought not to do to another what he would not have done to himself. Wherever a person goes, then, if he does anything contrary to that law, he commits a crime. Suppose a man comes here from the Indies and persuades people to accept a new religion, or teaches them anything that tends toward disobedience of this country's laws. However firmly he believes in the truth of what he teaches, he commits a crime and may justly be punished for it. He may be punished not only because his doctrine is false but also because he is doing what he would not approve in another, namely, that someone from here should travel to his country and try to change its religion. Ignorance of the civil law, by contrast, will excuse a person in a foreign country until that law has been declared to him, because until then no civil law binds him.

*Ignorance of the Civil Law Sometimes Excuses*

Likewise, suppose the civil law of a person's own country has not been declared clearly enough that he could know it if he wished, and the act in question is not against the law of nature. In that case his ignorance is a good excuse. In other cases, ignorance of the civil law does not excuse.

*Ignorance of the Sovereign Does Not Excuse*

Ignorance of who holds sovereign power in the place where a person ordinarily lives does not excuse him, because he ought to take notice of the power that has protected him there.

*Ignorance of the Penalty Does Not Excuse*

Where the law has been declared, ignorance of the penalty excuses no one. A law without the fear of a penalty to follow would not be a law at all, only empty words, so whoever breaks it incurs the penalty even without knowing what that penalty is. Anyone who voluntarily performs an action accepts all of its known consequences, and punishment is a known consequence of breaking the laws in every commonwealth. If the punishment has already been fixed by law, the offender is subject to that; if not, he is subject to punishment at the discretion of the sovereign. It is reasonable that a person who commits an injury limited by nothing but his own will should suffer a punishment limited by nothing but the will of the one whose law he has violated.

*Penalties Declared Before the Act Excuse from Greater Penalties After It*

When a penalty has either been attached to the crime in the law itself or has customarily been inflicted in similar cases, the offender is excused from any greater penalty. A known punishment that is not severe enough to deter people from an action is in effect an invitation to commit it. When people weigh the benefit of their injustice against the harm of their punishment, they choose, by necessity of nature, whatever appears best for themselves. So when they are punished more severely than the law had previously laid down, or more severely than others have been punished for the same crime, it is the law that has tempted and deceived them.

*No Law Made After the Act Can Make It a Crime*

No law made after an act has been done can make that act a crime. If the act was against the law of nature, the law existed before the act. A positive law, one enacted by human authority, cannot be known before it is made, and so cannot be binding.
