But when the law forbidding an act was made before the act was done, the person who does it is liable to a penalty fixed afterward, provided that no lesser penalty had been made known beforehand, either in writing or by precedent. The reason is the one given just above.

*False Principles of Right and Wrong as Causes of Crime*

From defects in reasoning, which is to say from error, people are prone to break the laws in three ways. The first is by presuming false principles. People observe that in every place and every age unjust actions have been sanctioned by the force and victories of those who committed them. They see that powerful men have broken through the laws of their country as easily as through cobwebs, which hold only small flies, while the weaker sort, and those whose enterprises failed, have been regarded as the only criminals. From this they take as the principles and foundations of their reasoning such propositions as these: "Justice is an empty word"; "Whatever a man can obtain by his own effort and risk is his own"; "The practice of all nations cannot be unjust"; "Precedents from former times are good arguments for doing the same again"; and many more of the same kind. If these are granted, no act can be a crime in itself. It must be made one not by the law but by the success of those who commit it, and the same deed will be virtuous or vicious as fortune pleases. What Marius makes a crime, Sulla will make meritorious, and Caesar, with the same laws still standing, will turn into a crime again, to the perpetual disturbance of the commonwealth's peace.

*False Teachers Misinterpreting the Law of Nature*

The second way is through false teachers. Some misinterpret the law of nature and thereby set it against the civil law. Others teach as laws their own doctrines, or traditions of former times, that are inconsistent with the duty of a subject.

*And False Inferences from True Principles, by Teachers*

The third way is through erroneous inferences from true principles. This commonly happens to people who are hasty and rash in drawing conclusions and deciding what to do. They hold a high opinion of their own understanding and believe that matters of this kind require no time or study, only ordinary experience and good natural wit, of which no one thinks himself short. Yet there are other kinds of knowledge, no more difficult than the knowledge of right and wrong, that no one would claim to possess without long and serious study. None of these defects in reasoning can excuse a crime, though some may mitigate it, in anyone who claims competence to manage his own private affairs, and still less in those who take on a public office. Such people lay claim to the very reason whose absence they would plead as their excuse.

*By Their Passions*

Among the passions that most often cause crime, one is vainglory, a foolish overestimation of one's own worth. The vainglorious suppose that differences of worth arise from wit, wealth, birth, or some other natural quality, when in fact they depend on the will of those who hold sovereign authority. From this arises the presumption that the punishments ordained by law, which extend to all subjects generally, ought not to be inflicted on them with the same rigor as on the poor, obscure, and simple people grouped together under the name of "the vulgar."

*Presumption of Riches*

So it commonly happens that people who value themselves for the greatness of their wealth venture on crimes in the hope of escaping punishment, either by corrupting public justice or by buying a pardon with money or other rewards.

*And of Friends*

Likewise, people with many powerful relatives, and popular figures who have won a reputation among the multitude, take courage to break the laws in the hope of overpowering the authority responsible for enforcing them.

*And of Wisdom*

Those with a high but false opinion of their own wisdom take it upon themselves to criticize the actions and question the authority of those who govern. Through their public talk they so unsettle the laws that nothing is to count as a crime except what their own designs require. The same people are prone to every crime that consists in cunning and in deceiving their neighbors, because they think their schemes too subtle to be detected. These, I say, are the effects of a false presumption of their own wisdom. Of those who first set in motion the disturbance of a commonwealth, which can never happen without civil war, very few live long enough to see their new designs established. The benefit of their crimes passes to posterity, and to the people who would least have wished it, which shows that they were not as wise as they thought. And those who deceive in the hope of not being observed commonly deceive themselves. The darkness in which they believe they lie hidden is nothing but their own blindness, and they are no wiser than children who think everything is hidden because they have covered their own eyes.

In general, all vainglorious people, unless they are also timid, are subject to anger, since they are more inclined than others to interpret the ordinary freedom of conversation as contempt. And there are few crimes that anger cannot produce.

*Hatred, Lust, Ambition, and Covetousness as Causes of Crime*

As for the passions of hatred, lust, ambition, and covetousness, the crimes they tend to produce are so obvious to everyone's experience and understanding that nothing needs to be said of them. They are infirmities so bound up with the nature of human beings, and of all other living creatures, that their effects can be prevented only by an extraordinary exercise of reason or by constant severity in punishing them. In the things people hate they find a continual and unavoidable vexation. Either their patience must last forever, or they must find relief by removing the power of whatever vexes them. The first is difficult, and the second is often impossible without some breach of the law. Ambition and covetousness are likewise passions that press upon us constantly, whereas reason is not constantly present to resist them, so whenever the hope of impunity appears, they produce their effects. As for lust, what it lacks in duration it makes up in intensity, and that intensity is enough to outweigh the fear of any light or uncertain punishment.

*Fear Is Sometimes a Cause of Crime, as When the Danger Is Neither Present nor Bodily*

Of all the passions, the one that least inclines people to break the laws is fear. Indeed, setting aside some generous natures, fear is the only thing that makes people keep the laws when there appears to be profit or pleasure in breaking them. And yet in many cases a crime may be committed out of fear.

Not every fear justifies the action it produces. Only the fear of bodily harm does so, what we call bodily fear, and only when a person can see no way to be delivered from that harm except by the action. Suppose a man is assaulted, fears immediate death, and sees no way to escape except by wounding his attacker. If he wounds him fatally, this is no crime, because no one is supposed, in the making of a commonwealth, to have given up the defense of his life or limbs in situations where the law cannot arrive in time to help him. But suppose I infer from a man's actions or threats that he will kill me when he can. If I kill him for that reason, when I have the time and means to seek protection from the sovereign power, I commit a crime. Again, suppose a man receives insulting words or some small injuries, for which the lawmakers assigned no punishment and which they thought unworthy of the notice of anyone with the use of reason. He fears that unless he takes revenge he will fall into contempt and so be exposed to similar injuries from others. To avoid this, he breaks the law and protects himself for the future through the terror of his private revenge. This is a crime. The harm he suffered is not bodily but imaginary. In this corner of the world it has been made to seem real by a custom begun only a few years ago among young and vain men, yet it is so slight that a man of honor, assured of his own courage, cannot take notice of it.

A man may also stand in fear of spirits, whether through his own superstition or through placing too much faith in others who tell him of strange dreams and visions. He may thereby be made to believe that these spirits will harm him for doing or omitting various things, even though the laws forbid him to do or omit them. Whatever he does or omits on this account is not excused by his fear; it is a crime. As I showed earlier, dreams are by nature nothing but the images that remain during sleep from the impressions our senses received while we were awake, and when people are for some reason unsure whether they have slept, those images seem to be real visions. Anyone who presumes to break the law on the strength of his own or another's dream or claimed vision, or on any other notion of the power of invisible spirits than the commonwealth permits, abandons the law of nature, which is a certain offense. He follows instead the imagery of his own brain, or of some other private person's, and he can never know whether that imagery signifies anything or nothing, nor whether the one who reports the dream is telling the truth or lying. If every private person were permitted to do this, as all must be under the law of nature if any one is, no law could hold, and every commonwealth would dissolve.

*Crimes Are Not Equal*

These different sources of crime already make clear that crimes are not all, as the Stoics of ancient times maintained, of the same alloy, like coins struck from metal of a single uniform purity. There is room not only for excuse, by which something that seemed a crime is shown to be none at all, but also for extenuation, by which a crime that seemed great is made less. All crimes equally deserve the name of injustice, just as every deviation from a straight line is equally crookedness, as the Stoics rightly observed. But it does not follow that all crimes are equally unjust, any more than it follows that all crooked lines are equally crooked. Failing to observe this, the Stoics held that killing a hen against the law was as great a crime as killing one's father.

*Total Excuses*

The only thing that can wholly excuse an act and strip it of the character of a crime is something that, at the same moment, removes the obligation of the law. An act committed against the law, if the person who committed it is bound by that law, can be nothing other than a crime.

The lack of any means to know the law excuses an act entirely, because a law that a man has no way of learning cannot bind him. A lack of diligence in inquiring, however, will not be treated as a lack of means. Nor will any man who claims enough reason to manage his own affairs be supposed to lack the means of knowing the laws of nature, since those laws are known by the very reason he claims to possess. Only children and madmen are excused from offenses against the natural law.

When a man is a captive, or otherwise in the power of the enemy, through no fault of his own, the obligation of the law ceases. A man is in the enemy's power whenever either his person or his means of living is in that power. He must then obey the enemy or die, and so his obedience is no crime, for when the protection of the law fails, no one is obliged to refrain from protecting himself by the best means he can find.

If a man is compelled by the terror of immediate death to commit an act against the law, he is entirely excused, because no law can oblige a man to abandon his own preservation. And even supposing such a law were binding, a man would still reason this way: "If I do not do it, I die now; if I do it, I die later; so by doing it, I gain time to live." Nature itself, therefore, compels him to the act.

When a man is destitute of food or of anything else necessary to his life, and cannot preserve himself in any way except by breaking the law, he is entirely excused for the same reason. This would be the case if, in a great famine, he took by force or by stealth the food he could not obtain either by money or by charity, or if, to defend his life, he snatched away another man's sword.

Again, acts done against the law on the authority of another person are excused as far as that person, the author of the act, is concerned, because no one ought to accuse his own act when it is carried out by another who is merely his instrument. But the act is not thereby excused with respect to a third party who has been injured by it, because in the violation of the law both the author and the agent are criminals. From this it follows that when the man or assembly holding sovereign power commands someone to do something contrary to an earlier law, the act is entirely excused. The sovereign ought not to condemn it himself, since he is its author, and what the sovereign cannot justly condemn, no one else can justly punish. Moreover, when the sovereign commands something to be done against his own earlier law, that command, with respect to that particular act, amounts to a repeal of the law.

Suppose the man or assembly holding sovereign power renounces some right essential to sovereignty, so that the subject acquires a liberty inconsistent with sovereign power, which is to say, inconsistent with the very existence of a commonwealth. If the subject then refuses to obey a command on the ground that it contradicts the liberty granted, his refusal is nevertheless a sin and contrary to his duty as a subject. He ought to recognize what is inconsistent with sovereignty, because sovereignty was established by his own consent and for his own defense, and he ought to understand that any liberty inconsistent with it was granted out of ignorance of its harmful consequences. And if he not only disobeys but also resists a public official in carrying out the command, then his act is a crime, because he could have obtained redress, without any breach of the peace, by lodging a complaint.

The degrees of crime are measured on several scales: first, by the malignity of their source or cause; second, by the contagion of their example; third, by the harm of their effect; and fourth, by the coincidence of times, places, and persons.

The same unlawful act is a greater crime when it springs from a presumption that one's strength, wealth, or friends will allow one to resist those charged with enforcing the law than when it springs from a hope of going undiscovered or of escaping by flight. Presuming that force will secure one's impunity is a root from which grows, at all times and under every temptation, contempt for all laws; whereas in the second case, the fear of danger that makes a man flee renders him more obedient in the future. Likewise, a crime committed in the knowledge that it is a crime is greater than the same crime committed under the mistaken belief that it was lawful. The man who acts against his own conscience is relying on his force or some other power, and that reliance encourages him to offend again; but the man who acts in error will conform to the law once his error is shown to him.

A man whose error comes from the authority of a teacher or an interpreter of the law who has been publicly authorized is less at fault than one whose error comes from stubbornly pursuing his own principles and reasoning. Whatever is taught by someone teaching under public authority is taught by the commonwealth itself, and it carries something of the character of law until that same authority corrects it. In all crimes that do not involve a denial of sovereign power and do not violate an evident law, such teaching excuses entirely. The man who bases his actions on his private judgment, by contrast, must stand or fall according to whether that judgment is right or wrong.

The same act is a greater crime if it has been consistently punished in others than if there have been many previous examples of its going unpunished. Those examples are so many hopes of impunity held out by the sovereign himself, and because whoever gives a man a hope and presumption of mercy that encourages him to offend has a share in the offense, the sovereign cannot reasonably charge the offender with the whole of it.

A crime arising from sudden passion is not as great as the same crime arising from long deliberation. In the first case there is room for extenuation in the common weakness of human nature. But the man who acts with premeditation has taken care to look at the law, at the punishment, and at the consequences for human society, and in committing the crime he has held all of these in contempt and set them below his own appetite. Still, no suddenness of passion is enough to excuse an act entirely. All the time between a man's first learning of the law and his committing the act is to be counted as time for deliberation, because he ought, by reflecting on the law, to have corrected the irregularity of his passions.

Where the law is read and interpreted publicly and regularly before all the people, an act against it is a greater crime than where people are left without such instruction and must inquire into the law with difficulty and uncertainty, interrupting their occupations to learn it from private individuals. In the latter case, part of the fault can be attributed to common human weakness; in the former, there is evident negligence, which is not without some contempt for sovereign power.

Acts that the law expressly condemns, but that the lawmaker tacitly approves through other clear signs of his will, are lesser crimes than the same acts condemned by both the law and the lawmaker. Since the will of the lawmaker is itself law, there appear in such a case to be two contradictory laws. This would excuse the act entirely if people were obliged to take notice of the sovereign's approval through signs other than those expressed in his command. They are not; but because penalties follow not only from breaking his law but also from keeping it, the sovereign is partly a cause of the transgression and therefore cannot reasonably lay the whole crime on the offender. Consider dueling. The law condemns it, and the penalty is death. On the other side, a man who refuses a duel is exposed to contempt and scorn with no remedy, and the sovereign himself sometimes considers him unworthy of any command or promotion in war. If such a man then accepts a duel, he ought not in reason to be punished severely, considering that all men legitimately try to win the good opinion of those who hold sovereign power, and that part of the fault may be laid on the one who punishes. I say this not because I wish to permit private revenge or any other kind of disobedience, but because I want rulers to take care not to encourage indirectly what they directly forbid. The examples set by princes have always had more power to govern the actions of those who observe them than the laws themselves. And although it is our duty to do not what rulers do but what they say, that duty will never be performed until it pleases God to give men an extraordinary and supernatural grace to follow that precept.

If we compare crimes by the harm of their effects, then, first, the same act is greater when it damages many people than when it hurts only a few. It follows that when an act does harm not only in the present but also, through its example, in the future, it is a greater crime than one that harms only in the present. The first is a fertile crime that multiplies to the injury of many; the second is barren. To maintain doctrines contrary to the religion established in the commonwealth is a greater fault in an authorized preacher than in a private person, and the same is true of living profanely or unchastely, or of committing any irreligious act whatever. Likewise, for a professor of law to defend any position, or to do any act, that tends to weaken sovereign power is a greater crime than for another man to do the same. So too, when a man has such a reputation for wisdom that many follow his counsel or imitate his actions, his breach of the law is a greater crime than the same breach by another, because such men do not merely commit a crime; they teach it as law to everyone else. In general, all crimes are made greater by the scandal they give, that is, by becoming stumbling blocks to the weak, who look less at the road they are walking than at the light that others carry ahead of them.

Acts of hostility against the existing state of the commonwealth are also greater crimes than the same acts done against private persons, because the damage extends to everyone. Among these are betraying the commonwealth's defenses or revealing its secrets to an enemy; every attempt against the representative of the commonwealth, whether a monarch or an assembly; and every effort, by word or deed, to diminish that representative's authority, whether in the present or in its succession. The Romans understood these crimes under the name *crimina laesae majestatis*, crimes of injured majesty, and they consist in a design or an act contrary to a fundamental law.

Likewise, crimes that render judgments ineffective are greater than injuries done to one or a few persons. Taking money to give a false judgment or false testimony, for instance, is a greater crime than cheating a man out of the same or a larger sum by other means, because it wrongs not only the person who suffers by such judgments: it makes all judgments useless and gives occasion to force and private revenge.

Robbery and embezzlement of the public treasury or public revenues is likewise a greater crime than robbing or defrauding a private man, because to rob the public is to rob many people at once.

So too, it is a greater crime to usurp a public office fraudulently, or to counterfeit public seals or the public coinage, than to impersonate a private man or counterfeit his seal, because the fraud extends to the damage of many.

Among unlawful acts done to private persons, the greater crime is the one whose damage is most keenly felt in the common opinion of mankind. Accordingly, to kill unlawfully is a greater crime than any other injury in which life is spared. To kill with torture is greater than simply to kill. To mutilate a limb is greater than to strip a man of his goods. To strip a man of his goods by the terror of death or wounds is greater than to take them by secret theft, and secret theft is greater than obtaining his consent by fraud. The violation of chastity by force is greater than by seduction, and the violation of a married woman is greater than that of an unmarried one. All these things are commonly valued in this order, though some people feel a given offense more and some less. The law, however, considers not the particular person but the general inclination of mankind.

For this reason, the offense people take at insults in word or gesture, when these cause no other harm than the immediate distress of the person insulted, has been disregarded in the laws of the Greeks, the Romans, and other commonwealths both ancient and modern. Those laws assumed that the true cause of such distress lies not in the insult, which takes no hold on men conscious of their own virtue, but in the faintheartedness of the one who is offended by it.

A crime against a private person is also greatly aggravated by the person, the time, and the place. To kill one's parent is a greater crime than to kill someone else, because a parent ought to receive the honor due to a sovereign, even though he has surrendered his power to the civil law, since he held that power originally by nature. And to rob a poor man is a greater crime than to rob a rich one, because to the poor the loss is more keenly felt.

A crime committed at a time or in a place set apart for worship is greater than one committed at another time or place, because it proceeds from a greater contempt for the law.

Many other cases of aggravation and extenuation could be added. But from those I have set down, anyone can see how to take the measure of any other crime put before him.

Finally, because almost every crime does injury not only to some private person but also to the commonwealth, the same crime is called a public crime when the accusation is brought in the name of the commonwealth, and a private crime when it is brought in the name of a private person. The corresponding proceedings are called public pleas, *judicia publica*, or pleas of the Crown, on the one hand, and private pleas on the other. In an accusation of murder, for example, if the accuser is a private person, the plea is a private plea; if the accuser is the sovereign, it is a public plea.

## Chapter XXVIII. Of Punishments, and Rewards

### The Definition of Punishment

"A punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on someone who has done, or failed to do, what that same authority has judged to be a transgression of the law, with the aim that people's wills may thereby be better disposed to obedience."

### Where the Right to Punish Comes From

Before I draw any conclusions from this definition, there is a question of great importance to be answered: through what door did the right, or authority, to punish in any case first come in? From what I have said earlier, no one is understood to be bound by covenant not to resist violence, and it follows that no one can be supposed to have given another person the right to lay violent hands on him. In making a commonwealth, each person gives up the right of defending someone else, but not the right of defending himself. He also obliges himself to help the sovereign in punishing another person, but not in punishing himself. Yet an agreement to help the sovereign harm someone else does not give the sovereign a right to punish, unless the person who makes that agreement already has the right to do the harm himself. It is clear, then, that the right to punish held by the commonwealth (that is, by the person or persons who represent it) does not rest on any concession or gift from the subjects. But I have also shown that before the commonwealth was instituted, every person had a right to everything, and a right to do whatever he thought necessary for his own preservation, including subduing, hurting, or killing anyone to that end. This is the foundation of the right to punish that is exercised in every commonwealth. The subjects did not give the sovereign that right. They only strengthened him to use his own as he thought fit for the preservation of them all, by laying down theirs. The right was therefore not given to him. It was left to him, and to him alone, and it remains as complete as it was in the condition of mere nature, the war of every one against his neighbour, apart from the limits that natural law sets upon it.

### Private Injuries and Revenge Are Not Punishments

From the definition of punishment I conclude, first, that neither private revenge nor injuries done by private persons can properly be called punishment, because they do not come from public authority.

### Nor Is Being Passed Over for Advancement

Second, being neglected and passed over by public favour is not a punishment, because no new evil is inflicted on anyone by it. The person is simply left in the condition he was already in.

### Nor Is Pain Inflicted Without a Public Hearing

Third, an evil inflicted by public authority without a prior public condemnation should not be called punishment but an act of hostility. The deed for which a person is punished must first be judged by public authority to be a transgression of the law.

### Nor Is Pain Inflicted by Usurped Power

Fourth, an evil inflicted by usurped power, or by judges who lack authority from the sovereign, is not punishment but an act of hostility. The person condemned is not the author of acts done by usurped power, and those acts are therefore not acts of public authority.

### Nor Is Pain Inflicted Without Regard to Future Good

Fifth, any evil inflicted without the intention or the possibility of disposing the offender, or other people through his example, to obey the laws is not punishment but an act of hostility. Without that purpose, no harm done falls under the name of punishment.

### Natural Evil Consequences Are Not Punishments

Sixth, nature attaches various harmful consequences to certain actions. A man who assaults another may himself be killed or wounded, and a man may fall sick from doing some unlawful act. Such harm may be said to be inflicted by God, who is the author of nature, and in that sense it is a divine punishment. In relation to human beings, however, it does not fall under the name of punishment, because no human authority inflicted it.

### Harm Less Than the Benefit of Transgressing Is Not Punishment

Seventh, if the harm inflicted is less than the benefit or satisfaction that naturally follows from committing the crime, that harm falls outside the definition. It is the price of the crime, or the sum that buys it off, rather than its punishment. The purpose of punishment is to dispose people to obey the law, and when the harm is smaller than the gain from the transgression, it fails in that purpose and has the opposite effect.

### Where the Law Fixes the Punishment, a Greater Harm Is Not Punishment but Hostility

Eighth, if a punishment is fixed and prescribed in the law itself, and a greater punishment is inflicted after the crime has been committed, the excess is not punishment but an act of hostility. The aim of punishment is not revenge but deterrence through fear. When the law declares a lesser penalty, it removes the fear that an unknown and greater one would have inspired, so the unexpected addition forms no part of the punishment. Where the law fixes no punishment at all, however, whatever is inflicted has the nature of punishment, because someone who sets out to break a law that specifies no penalty expects an undetermined, that is, an arbitrary, punishment.

### Harm Inflicted for a Deed Done Before the Law Is Not Punishment

Ninth, harm inflicted for a deed done before there was any law forbidding it is not punishment but an act of hostility. Before the law exists, there can be no transgression of it, and punishment presupposes a deed judged to have been a transgression of the law. Harm inflicted for what was done before the law was made is therefore not punishment but an act of hostility.

### The Representative of the Commonwealth Cannot Be Punished

Tenth, harm inflicted on the representative of the commonwealth is not punishment but an act of hostility, because punishment by its nature is inflicted by public authority, and public authority belongs to the representative alone.

### Harm to Rebellious Subjects Is Done by Right of War, Not as Punishment

Last, harm inflicted on a declared enemy does not count as punishment. Such enemies either were never subject to the law, and so cannot transgress it, or were once subject to it and now profess to be so no longer, and so deny that they can transgress it. All harm that can be done to them must therefore be taken as acts of hostility, and in declared hostility every infliction of evil is lawful. It follows that if a subject, by deed or by word, knowingly and deliberately denies the authority of the representative of the commonwealth, he may lawfully be made to suffer whatever the representative wills, whatever penalty may previously have been set down for treason. In denying his subjection, he denies the punishment that the law has prescribed, and he therefore suffers as an enemy of the commonwealth, which is to say according to the will of the representative. The punishments set down in the law are meant for subjects, not for enemies, and enemies include those who became subjects by their own act and then deliberately revolted and denied the sovereign power.

The first and most general division of punishments is into divine and human. I will have occasion to speak of divine punishment later, in a more suitable place.

Human punishments are those inflicted by the command of man. They are corporal, pecuniary, ignominious, imprisonment, or exile, or some mixture of these.

### Corporal Punishments

A corporal punishment is one inflicted directly on the body, and intentionally so by the person who inflicts it. Examples are lashes, wounds, or the loss of bodily pleasures that were previously enjoyed lawfully.

### Capital Punishment

Some corporal punishments are capital, and some are less than capital. A capital punishment is the infliction of death, either simply or with torment. Punishments less than capital include lashes, wounds, chains, and any other bodily pain that is not deadly by its own nature. If death follows a punishment without having been intended by the person who inflicted it, the punishment is not to be regarded as capital, even though the harm proved fatal through some accident that could not be foreseen. In that case death is not inflicted but hastened.

### Pecuniary Punishment

A pecuniary punishment is the loss not only of a sum of money but also of land or any other goods usually bought and sold for money. If the law that imposes such a punishment is framed with the design of collecting money from those who break it, it is not properly a punishment. It is the price of a privilege, a purchased exemption from the law, since such a law does not forbid the act absolutely but forbids it only to those who cannot pay. The exception is a law that belongs to natural law or to religion. In that case payment does not buy an exemption from the law; the act remains a transgression of it. Where a law imposes a fine on those who take the name of God in vain, for example, paying the fine is not the price of a license to swear but the punishment for breaking a law from which no one can be released. Similarly, if the law requires a sum of money to be paid to the person who has been injured, this is only compensation for the harm done to him. It extinguishes the injured party's accusation, but not the offender's crime.

### Ignominy

Ignominy is the infliction of an evil that the commonwealth has made dishonourable, or the removal of a good that the commonwealth has made honourable. Some things are honourable by nature, such as the effects of courage, magnanimity, strength, wisdom, and other abilities of body and mind. Others are made honourable by the commonwealth, such as badges, titles, offices, or any other special mark of the sovereign's favour. The first kind may fail through nature or accident, but no law can take them away, and so their loss is not a punishment. The second kind can be taken away by the public authority that made them honourable, and their removal is properly a punishment. Examples are stripping condemned men of their badges, titles, and offices, or declaring them incapable of holding such honours in the future.

### Imprisonment

Imprisonment is the deprivation of a person's liberty by public authority. It may serve two different ends: the safe custody of someone accused, or the infliction of pain on someone condemned. The first is not punishment, because no one is supposed to be punished before he has been heard in court and declared guilty. Any harm a person is made to suffer through bonds or restraint before his case is heard, beyond what is necessary to secure his custody, is therefore contrary to the law of nature. The second is punishment, because it is an evil inflicted by public authority for something that the same authority has judged a transgression of the law. Under the word imprisonment I include every restraint of movement caused by an external obstacle. That obstacle may be a building, which goes by the general name of a prison; an island, as when people are said to be confined to one; a place where people are set to work, as in ancient times men were condemned to the quarries, and in our own time to row in the galleys; or a chain, or any other such impediment.

### Exile

Exile, or banishment, is when a person is condemned for a crime to leave the territory of the commonwealth, or some part of it, and not to return, either for a fixed period or forever. In its own nature, without other circumstances, it does not seem to be a punishment at all. It looks more like an escape, or a public order to avoid punishment by flight. Cicero says that no such punishment was ever established in the city of Rome, and calls exile a refuge for men in danger. If a banished man is still allowed to keep his goods and the income of his lands, the mere change of air is no punishment. Nor does it serve the benefit for which all punishments are established, namely the shaping of people's wills toward keeping the law. Often it actually damages the commonwealth, since a banished man is no longer a member of the commonwealth that banished him, and is therefore its lawful enemy. If he is also deprived of his lands or goods, then the punishment lies not in the exile itself but in the loss, and it is to be counted among pecuniary punishments.

### Punishing Innocent Subjects Is Contrary to the Law of Nature

Every punishment of innocent subjects, great or small, is against the law of nature. Punishment applies only to transgression of the law, and so there can be no punishment of the innocent. Punishing them therefore violates, first, the law of nature that forbids all people, in taking revenge, to aim at anything but some future good, since no good can come to the commonwealth from punishing the innocent. Second, it violates the law that forbids ingratitude. All sovereign power was originally given by the consent of each of the subjects, so that they would be protected by it for as long as they remained obedient, and punishing the innocent is therefore a return of evil for good. Third, it violates the law that commands equity, that is, an equal distribution of justice, which is not observed when the innocent are punished.

### But Harm Done to the Innocent in War Is Not

The infliction of any evil whatever on an innocent person who is not a subject, however, is no breach of the law of nature, provided it is for the benefit of the commonwealth and violates no previous covenant. Everyone who is not a subject is either an enemy, or else has ceased to be one by some earlier covenant. Against enemies whom the commonwealth judges capable of harming it, it is lawful to make war by the original right of nature. In war the sword does not judge, and the victor does not distinguish between the guilty and the innocent with respect to what is past, nor does he show mercy except so far as it serves the good of his own people. On this same ground, in the case of subjects who deliberately deny the authority of the established commonwealth, vengeance may lawfully be extended not only to the fathers but also to the third and fourth generations not yet born, who are therefore innocent of the deed for which they suffer. The nature of this offence consists in renouncing subjection, which is a relapse into the condition of war, commonly called rebellion. Those who commit it suffer not as subjects but as enemies, for rebellion is simply war renewed.

### Reward Is Either Salary or Grace

A reward is given either as a gift or under a contract. When it is under a contract, it is called salary or wages, which is a benefit owed for service performed or promised. When it is a gift, it is a benefit that comes from the goodwill of those who bestow it, meant to encourage or enable people to serve them. When the sovereign of a commonwealth attaches a salary to a public office, the person who receives it is bound in justice to perform the office. Otherwise he is bound only in honour, to acknowledge the favour and to try to repay it. People have no lawful remedy when they are commanded to leave their private business and serve the public without reward or salary. Even so, neither the law of nature nor the institution of the commonwealth binds them to do so, unless the service cannot be performed in any other way. For it is presumed that the sovereign can draw on all their resources to pay for such service, so much so that even the most common soldier may claim the wages of his service as a debt.

### Benefits Given Out of Fear Are Not Rewards

The benefits a sovereign bestows on a subject out of fear of some power or capacity that subject has to harm the commonwealth are not properly rewards. They are not salaries, because no contract is supposed in such a case, every person being already obliged not to do the commonwealth any disservice. Nor are they acts of grace, because they are extorted by fear, and fear ought never to touch the sovereign power. They are rather sacrifices, which the sovereign, considered in his natural person and not as the person of the commonwealth, makes to appease the discontent of someone he thinks more powerful than himself. Such benefits do not encourage obedience. On the contrary, they encourage further extortion and its continued increase.

### Fixed and Variable Salaries

Some salaries are fixed and paid from the public treasury. Others are uncertain and variable, arising from the performance of the office to which they are attached, such as fees. The latter are in some cases harmful to the commonwealth, as in the administration of justice. Where the income of judges and officers of a court depends on the number of cases brought before them, two problems necessarily follow. One is the encouragement of lawsuits, since the more suits there are, the greater the profit. The other, which depends on the first, is rivalry over jurisdiction, as each court draws to itself as many cases as it can. Offices of execution do not suffer from these problems, because the officers cannot increase their own business by any effort of theirs. This is enough on the nature of punishment and reward, which are, so to speak, the sinews and tendons that move the limbs and joints of a commonwealth.

So far I have set out the nature of man, whose pride and other passions have compelled him to submit to government, together with the great power of his governor. I have compared that governor to Leviathan, taking the comparison from the last two verses of the forty-first chapter of Job, where God, having described the great power of Leviathan, calls him the King of the Proud. "There is nothing on earth," he says, "to be compared with him. He is made so as not to be afraid. He sees every high thing below him, and is king of all the children of pride." But because he is mortal and subject to decay, like every other earthly creature, and because there is something in heaven, though not on earth, that he ought to fear and whose laws he ought to obey, I will speak in the chapters that follow of his diseases and the causes of his mortality, and of the laws of nature he is bound to obey.

## Chapter XXIX. Of Those Things That Weaken, or Tend to the Dissolution of a Commonwealth

### The Dissolution of Commonwealths Proceeds from Imperfect Institution

Nothing that mortals make can be immortal. Yet if men had the use of the reason they claim to possess, their commonwealths could at least be secured from perishing by internal diseases. By the nature of their institution, commonwealths are designed to live as long as mankind itself, or as long as the laws of nature, or as justice, which gives them life. When they are dissolved, then, not by external violence but by internal disorder, the fault lies in men not as the material of which commonwealths are made, but as their makers and arrangers. Men eventually grow weary of jostling and hacking at one another without rule, and they desire with all their hearts to fit themselves together into one firm and lasting structure. But they lack the art of making suitable laws by which to square their actions, as a mason trues his stones against his square. They also lack the humility and patience to let the rough and awkward edges of their present greatness be trimmed away. For these reasons, without the help of a very able architect, they cannot be assembled into anything but a rickety building, one that will hardly outlast their own lifetime and will surely fall on the heads of their descendants.

Among the infirmities of a commonwealth, therefore, I will count first those that arise from an imperfect institution. These resemble the diseases of a natural body that come from defective procreation.

### Want of Absolute Power

One of these is this: "that a man, in order to obtain a kingdom, is sometimes content with less power than the peace and defense of the commonwealth necessarily require." As a result, when the power he set aside must be taken up again for the sake of public safety, the act looks unjust, and this disposes great numbers of men to rebel when the occasion presents itself. The case resembles that of children conceived by diseased parents, whose bodies are liable either to die young or to purge the bad quality inherited from their unhealthy conception by breaking out in boils and scabs. When kings deny themselves some such necessary power, it is not always, though it is sometimes, out of ignorance of what their office requires. Often it is in the hope of recovering that power whenever they please. In this they reason badly, because those who hold them to their promises will be supported against them by foreign commonwealths, which, for the good of their own subjects, let few opportunities slip to weaken the states of their neighbors. In this way Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, was supported by the Pope against Henry II. The subjection of churchmen to the commonwealth had been waived by William the Conqueror at his accession, when he swore an oath not to infringe the liberty of the Church. In the same way, the barons, whose power William Rufus had increased to a degree inconsistent with sovereign power in order to gain their help in transferring the succession from his elder brother to himself, were supported by the French in their rebellion against King John. Nor does this happen only in monarchy. The formal title of the ancient Roman commonwealth was "the Senate and People of Rome," and since neither the Senate nor the people claimed the whole power, this division first caused the seditions of Tiberius Gracchus, Gaius Gracchus, Lucius Saturninus, and others. It later caused the wars between the Senate and the people under Marius and Sulla, and again under Pompey and Caesar, which ended in the extinction of their democracy and the establishment of monarchy.

The people of Athens bound themselves against only a single action: no one, on pain of death, was to propose renewing the war for the island of Salamis. Yet even this one restriction would have left them with an enemy permanently poised at the very gates of their city, had not Solon spread the word that he had gone mad and then, with the gestures and dress of a madman, proposed the war in verse to the people who flocked around him. Such are the damages, or the desperate expedients, forced on every commonwealth whose power is limited in even the slightest degree.

### Private Judgment of Good and Evil

In the second place, I observe the diseases of a commonwealth that come from the poison of seditious doctrines. One of these is "that every private man is judge of good and evil actions." This is true in the condition of mere nature, where there are no civil laws, and also under civil government in cases the law has not settled. Otherwise, it is evident that the measure of good and evil actions is the civil law, and that the judge is the legislator, who is always the representative of the commonwealth. This false doctrine disposes men to debate with themselves and to dispute the commands of the commonwealth, and afterward to obey or disobey them as their private judgment sees fit. By this the commonwealth is distracted and weakened.

### Erroneous Conscience

Another doctrine opposed to civil society is that "whatever a man does against his conscience is sin." It depends on the presumption of making oneself the judge of good and evil. A man's conscience and his judgment are the same thing, and conscience, like judgment, may be mistaken. A man who is subject to no civil law sins in everything he does against his conscience, because he has no other rule to follow but his own reason. It is not so, however, with a man who lives in a commonwealth, because the law is the public conscience, by which he has already undertaken to be guided. Were it otherwise, given the great diversity of private consciences, which are nothing but private opinions, the commonwealth would necessarily be distracted, and no one would dare to obey the sovereign power any further than seemed good in his own eyes.

### Pretense of Inspiration

It has also been commonly taught "that faith and sanctity are not to be attained by study and reason, but by supernatural inspiration or infusion." If this is granted, I do not see why anyone should give a reason for his faith, or why every Christian should not also be a prophet, or why anyone should take the law of his country rather than his own inspiration as the rule of his conduct. And so we fall once more into the fault of taking it upon ourselves to judge good and evil, or of making judges of it out of private men who claim to be supernaturally inspired, to the dissolution of all civil government. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing comes by those chance events that bring us into the presence of the people who speak to us. All these events are arranged by Almighty God, and yet they are not supernatural; they are merely unobservable, because so great a number of them combine to produce every effect. Faith and sanctity are certainly not common, but they are not miracles either. They are brought about by education, discipline, correction, and other natural means, through which God works them in his elect at such time as he thinks fit. These three opinions, so harmful to peace and government, have come in this part of the world chiefly from the tongues and pens of unlearned divines, who string together the words of Holy Scripture in ways that do not agree with reason, and do all they can to make men believe that sanctity and natural reason cannot coexist.

### Subjecting the Sovereign Power to Civil Laws

A fourth opinion contrary to the nature of a commonwealth is "that he who holds the sovereign power is subject to the civil laws." It is true that all sovereigns are subject to the laws of nature, because those laws are divine and cannot be abolished by any man or any commonwealth. But the sovereign is not subject to the laws that he himself makes, which is to say, the laws the commonwealth makes. To be subject to laws is to be subject to the commonwealth, that is, to the sovereign representative, that is, to himself; and that is not subjection but freedom from the laws. Because this error sets the laws above the sovereign, it also sets a judge above him, together with a power to punish him, and that amounts to making a new sovereign. For the same reason, a third sovereign would be needed to punish the second, and so on without end, to the confusion and dissolution of the commonwealth.

### Attributing Absolute Property to the Subjects

A fifth doctrine that tends to the dissolution of a commonwealth is "that every private man has an absolute property in his goods, such as excludes the right of the sovereign." Every man does indeed have a property that excludes the right of every other subject, and he has it only from the sovereign power. Without the protection of that power, every other man would have an equal right to the same things. But if the right of the sovereign is excluded as well, he cannot perform the office in which they have placed him, which is to defend them both from foreign enemies and from injuring one another; and consequently there is no longer a commonwealth.

And if the property of subjects does not exclude the sovereign representative's right to their goods, still less does it exclude his right to their offices of judgment or execution, in which they represent the sovereign himself.

### Dividing the Sovereign Power

There is a sixth doctrine, plainly and directly opposed to the essence of a commonwealth: "that the sovereign power may be divided." To divide the power of a commonwealth is nothing other than to dissolve it, for divided powers destroy each other. For these doctrines, men are chiefly indebted to certain members of the legal profession, who try to make the laws depend on their own learning rather than on the legislative power.

### Imitation of Neighboring Nations

Like false doctrine, the example of a different government in a neighboring nation often disposes men to alter the form of government already settled among them. In this way the Jewish people were stirred up to reject God and to call on the prophet Samuel for a king after the manner of the other nations. So too the lesser cities of Greece were continually disturbed by seditions between aristocratic and democratic factions, one party in almost every commonwealth wishing to imitate the Lacedaemonians, or Spartans, and the other the Athenians. I do not doubt that many men were glad to see the recent troubles in England out of imitation of the Low Countries, supposing that nothing more was needed to grow rich than to change the form of their government as the Dutch had done. Human nature is, of itself, inclined to desire novelty. When men are further provoked to it by living near those who have grown rich through change, it is almost impossible for them not to welcome whoever urges them to change, and to love the first beginnings of it, even though they come to be pained by the disorder that follows. They are like people of hot blood who, having caught the itch, the skin disease of that name, tear at themselves with their own nails until they can no longer bear the smart.

### Imitation of the Greeks and Romans

As for rebellion against monarchy in particular, one of its most frequent causes is the reading of the political books and histories of the ancient Greeks and Romans. Young men, and all others who lack the antidote of solid reason, take from these books a strong and delightful impression of the great feats of war achieved by the commanders of those armies, and along with it a pleasing idea of everything else those peoples did. They imagine that their great prosperity came not from the rivalry of particular men but from the virtue of their popular form of government, without considering the frequent seditions and civil wars produced by the imperfection of their political order. From the reading of such books, I say, men have undertaken to kill their kings, because the Greek and Latin writers, in their books and discourses on politics, make it lawful and praiseworthy for any man to do so, provided that before he does it he calls the king a tyrant. They do not say that regicide, the killing of a king, is lawful, but that tyrannicide, the killing of a tyrant, is. From the same books, those who live under a monarch form the opinion that the subjects of a popular commonwealth enjoy liberty, while in a monarchy all are slaves. I say that those who live under a monarchy form this opinion, not those who live under a popular government, for they find no such thing. In sum, I cannot imagine anything more damaging to a monarchy than allowing such books to be read publicly without at once applying the correctives of discreet teachers, such as are fit to remove their venom. I will not hesitate to compare this venom to the bite of a mad dog, which causes a disease physicians call hydrophobia, or fear of water. Whoever is so bitten suffers a continual torment of thirst and yet abhors water, and is in such a state that it seems as if the poison were trying to turn him into a dog. In the same way, when a monarchy has once been bitten to the quick by those democratic writers who continually snarl at that form of state, it needs nothing more than a strong monarch; and yet, out of a certain tyrannophobia, or fear of being strongly governed, its people abhor him once they have him.

As there have been learned doctors who hold that a person has three souls, so there are also those who think a commonwealth may have more than one soul, which is to say more than one sovereign. They set up a Supremacy against the Sovereignty, canons against laws, and a spiritual authority against the civil. They work on people's minds with words and distinctions that mean nothing in themselves, though their very obscurity reveals that another kingdom walks abroad in the dark, invisibly as some believe, like a kingdom of fairies. Yet it is plain that the civil power and the power of the commonwealth are the same thing, and that supremacy, the power of making canons, and the power of granting ecclesiastical licenses all imply a commonwealth. It follows that wherever one party is sovereign and another supreme, wherever one can make laws and another can make canons, there must be two commonwealths over one and the same subjects. That is a kingdom divided against itself, and it cannot stand.

The empty distinction between temporal and spiritual changes nothing: they are still two kingdoms, and every subject is subject to two masters. The spiritual power claims the right to declare what is sin, and since sin is nothing but the transgression of law, it thereby claims the right to declare what is law. The civil power also claims the right to declare what is law. Every subject must therefore obey two masters, each of whom insists that his commands be observed as law, and that is impossible. Alternatively, if there is only one kingdom, then either the civil power, which is the power of the commonwealth, must be subordinate to the spiritual, or the spiritual must be subordinate to the temporal, in which case there is no supremacy but the temporal.

When these two powers oppose each other, the commonwealth is necessarily in great danger of civil war and dissolution. The civil authority is more visible and stands in the clearer light of natural reason, so it will always draw a very considerable part of the people to its side. The spiritual authority stands in the darkness of scholastic distinctions and difficult words, yet because the fear of darkness and ghosts is greater than other fears, it will never lack a party large enough to trouble a commonwealth, and sometimes to destroy it.

This disease may fairly be compared to epilepsy, the "falling sickness," which the Jews regarded as a kind of possession by spirits, in the natural body. In epilepsy, an unnatural spirit or wind in the head obstructs the roots of the nerves and moves them violently. It takes from them the motion they should naturally receive from the power of the soul in the brain, and so produces violent, irregular movements in the limbs, which people call convulsions. The person seized by the fit sometimes falls into water and sometimes into fire, like someone deprived of his senses. So it is in the body politic. The nerves of a commonwealth are the terror of punishment and the hope of reward. When the spiritual power moves the members of the commonwealth through these nerves otherwise than the civil power, which is the soul of the commonwealth, ought to move them, and when it suffocates the people with strange and difficult words, it either overwhelms the commonwealth with oppression or casts it into the fire of civil war.

### Mixed Government

Sometimes, even in a purely civil government, there is more than one soul. This happens when the power of raising money, which corresponds to the nutritive faculty, depends on a general assembly; the power of direction and command, which corresponds to the motive faculty, rests with one man; and the power of making laws, which corresponds to the rational faculty, depends on the chance agreement not only of those two but of a third party as well. Such an arrangement endangers the commonwealth, sometimes because the parties fail to agree on good laws, but most often because it lacks the nourishment necessary for life and motion. Few people perceive that this is not government at all, but the division of the commonwealth into three factions, and they call it mixed monarchy. The truth is that it is not one independent commonwealth but three independent factions, not one representative person but three. In the kingdom of God there may be three independent persons without any breach in the unity of the God who reigns. Where men reign, however, subject as they are to differences of opinion, this cannot be. If the king bears the person of the people, and the general assembly also bears the person of the people, and a further assembly bears the person of a part of the people, then they are not one person or one sovereign, but three persons and three sovereigns.

I do not know of any disease in the natural human body to which I could exactly compare this irregularity in a commonwealth. But I have seen a man who had another man growing out of his side, with a head, arms, chest, and stomach of his own. If he had had a third man growing out of his other side, the comparison would have been exact.

### Want of Money

So far I have named the diseases of a commonwealth that pose the greatest and most immediate danger. There are others, less grave, that are nonetheless worth noting. The first is the difficulty of raising money for the necessary purposes of the commonwealth, especially when war approaches. This difficulty arises from the belief every subject holds that he has a property in his lands and goods that excludes the sovereign's right to make use of them. As a result, the sovereign power, which foresees the needs and dangers of the commonwealth, finds the flow of money into the public treasury blocked by the people's tight grip. Where it ought to expand itself to meet and forestall such dangers at their outset, it contracts itself for as long as it can. When it can hold out no longer, it struggles with the people through legal stratagems to obtain small sums, and when these prove insufficient, it is forced at last to open the way violently for immediate supply, or else perish. Driven often to such extremities, it eventually brings the people back to their proper disposition; otherwise the commonwealth must perish.

This disorder may very aptly be compared to an ague, a fever marked by alternating chills and heat. In an ague, the fleshy parts of the body are congealed or obstructed by poisonous matter, so the veins, which by their natural course empty into the heart, are not supplied from the arteries as they should be. First comes a cold contraction and trembling of the limbs, and afterward a hot and powerful effort of the heart to force a passage for the blood. Until it can do so, the heart makes do with the small relief of things that cool it for a time, until at last, if nature is strong enough, it breaks the resistance of the obstructed parts and disperses the poison as sweat, or, if nature is too weak, the patient dies.

### Monopolies and the Abuses of Tax Farmers

There is sometimes a disease in a commonwealth that resembles pleurisy. It occurs when the treasure of the commonwealth flows out of its proper course and collects in too great abundance in one or a few private men, through monopolies or through the farming out of public revenues to private collectors. In the same way, in pleurisy, blood gets into the membrane lining the chest and breeds an inflammation there, accompanied by fever and painful stitches in the side.

### Popular Men

The popularity of a powerful subject is also a dangerous disease, unless the commonwealth has very good assurance of his loyalty. The people ought to take their direction from the authority of the sovereign, but through the flattery and reputation of an ambitious man they are drawn away from their obedience to the laws to follow someone whose virtues and intentions they know nothing about. This is usually more dangerous in a popular government than in a monarchy, because in a popular government a crowd can easily be persuaded that it is the people. It was by this means that Julius Caesar, who had been raised up by the people against the Senate, won the affection of his army and made himself master of both Senate and people. Such conduct by popular and ambitious men is plain rebellion, and its effects may be likened to those of witchcraft.

### Excessive Size of a Town, and a Multitude of Corporations

Another infirmity of a commonwealth is the excessive size of a town, when it can supply from within its own bounds both the men and the funds for a great army. So too is a large number of corporations, which are like many lesser commonwealths in the bowels of a greater one, like worms in the entrails of a human body.

### Liberty of Disputing Against Sovereign Power

To these may be added the liberty of disputing against absolute power, exercised by people who lay claim to political wisdom. Though they are bred for the most part among the dregs of the populace, they are spurred on by false doctrines and are forever meddling with the fundamental laws, to the harassment of the commonwealth, like the small intestinal worms that physicians call ascarides.

We may add further the insatiable appetite, or bulimia, for enlarging dominion, together with the incurable wounds that the enemy often inflicts as a result; the swollen growths, like wens on the body, of conquests never properly united to the commonwealth, which are often a burden and less dangerous to lose than to keep; and also the lethargy of ease, and the wasting consumption of riot and extravagant spending.

### Dissolution of the Commonwealth

Finally, when in a war, whether foreign or civil, the enemy wins a final victory, so that the forces of the commonwealth no longer hold the field and subjects who remain loyal have no further protection, then the commonwealth is dissolved, and every man is free to protect himself by whatever means his own judgment suggests. For the sovereign is the public soul that gives life and motion to the commonwealth. When it expires, the members are no more governed by it than the corpse of a man is governed by his departed, though immortal, soul. The right of a sovereign monarch cannot be extinguished by the act of another, but the obligation of his subjects can be. A man who lacks protection may seek it wherever he can find it, and once he has it, he is obliged to defend his protector for as long as he is able, without the fraudulent excuse that he submitted only out of fear. When the power of an assembly is once suppressed, however, its right perishes entirely, because the assembly itself no longer exists, and so there is no possibility for the sovereignty to return.

## Chapter XXX. Of the Office of the Sovereign Representative

### Securing the Good of the People

The office of the sovereign, whether a monarch or an assembly, consists in the purpose for which sovereign power was entrusted to it: securing the safety of the people. The sovereign is bound to this by the law of nature, and must answer for it to God, the author of that law, and to no one else. By "safety," however, I do not mean bare survival. I mean also all the other satisfactions of life that each person may acquire for himself through lawful industry, without danger or harm to the commonwealth.

### By Instruction and by Laws

This is meant to be accomplished not through attention to individuals, beyond protecting them from injuries when they bring complaints, but through a general provision for all. That provision consists of public instruction, both by doctrine and by example, and of making and enforcing good laws, to which individuals may apply their own cases.

### It Is Against the Sovereign's Duty to Give Up Any Essential Right of Sovereignty, or to Leave the People Untaught in Its Grounds

If the essential rights of sovereignty, which I set out in the eighteenth chapter, are taken away, the commonwealth is dissolved, and every man returns to the condition and misery of a war of each against all, which is the greatest evil that can happen in this life. It is therefore the sovereign's office to keep those rights intact. It follows, first, that it is against his duty to transfer any of them to another or to lay any of them aside. Whoever abandons the means abandons the end. And a sovereign abandons the means when he acknowledges himself subject to the civil laws, or renounces any of the following powers: the power of supreme judgment; the power to make war or peace on his own authority; the power to judge what the commonwealth needs; the power to raise money and soldiers whenever, and in whatever amount, his own conscience judges necessary; the power to appoint officers and ministers of both war and peace; and the power to appoint teachers and to examine which doctrines agree with, and which oppose, the defense, peace, and good of the people. Second, it is against his duty to leave the people ignorant of, or misinformed about, the grounds and reasons for these essential rights. People in that condition are easily seduced and drawn into resisting him at the very moment the commonwealth requires those rights to be used and exercised.

The grounds of these rights need to be taught diligently and truthfully all the more because no civil law, and no fear of legal punishment, can uphold them. A civil law forbidding rebellion, and all resistance to the essential rights of sovereignty is rebellion, creates no obligation in its capacity as civil law. It binds only by virtue of the law of nature, which forbids the breaking of faith. If men do not understand that natural obligation, they cannot understand the authority of any law the sovereign makes. As for punishment, they will regard it merely as an act of hostility, and when they believe themselves strong enough, they will try to escape it by acts of hostility of their own.

### The Objection That No Principles of Reason Support Absolute Sovereignty

I have heard some people say that justice is only a word without substance, and that whatever a man can acquire by force or cunning is his own, not only in the condition of war but also within a commonwealth. I have already shown that this is false. In the same way, there are those who maintain that no grounds or principles of reason support the essential rights that make sovereignty absolute. If such principles existed, they say, someone somewhere would have discovered them, yet we see that there has never been a commonwealth in which those rights were acknowledged or asserted. This argument is as poor as it would be for the native peoples of America to deny that there are any principles of reason by which a house can be built to last as long as its materials, simply because they had never seen one built so well. Time and industry produce new knowledge every day. The art of sound building derives from principles of reason, worked out by diligent men who studied for a long time the nature of materials and the various effects of shape and proportion, and they did so long after mankind had begun, however crudely, to build. In the same way, long after men began to found commonwealths that were imperfect and prone to relapse into disorder, principles of reason may be discovered through diligent thought that would make those commonwealths everlasting, barring violence from outside. Such are the principles I have set out in this discourse. Whether or not they ever come to the attention of those who have the power to put them to use, or are neglected by them, concerns my own private interest very little at present. But even supposing that my principles are not principles of reason, I am certain that they are principles grounded in the authority of Scripture. I will demonstrate this when I come to speak of the kingdom of God, administered by Moses, over the Jews, His own people by covenant.

### The Objection That Ordinary People Cannot Understand

They say further that even if the principles are correct, ordinary people lack the capacity to be made to understand them. I would be glad if the rich and powerful subjects of a kingdom, and those considered most learned, were no more capable of resisting them than the common people are. But everyone knows that the obstacles to this kind of teaching arise less from the difficulty of the subject than from the interests of those who are to learn it. Powerful men can hardly stomach anything that sets up a power to restrain their desires, and learned men can hardly stomach anything that exposes their errors and so diminishes their authority. The minds of ordinary people, by contrast, unless they have been tainted by dependence on the powerful or scribbled over with the opinions of their teachers, are like clean paper, ready to receive whatever public authority chooses to imprint on them. Whole nations have been brought to accept the great mysteries of the Christian religion, which are above reason, and millions of people have been made to believe that the same body can be in countless places at one and the same time, which is against reason. Shall men, then, be unable through teaching and preaching, protected by law, to win acceptance for something so consistent with reason that any unprejudiced person needs only to hear it in order to learn it? I conclude, therefore, that so long as a sovereign holds his power intact, there is no difficulty in instructing the people in the essential rights of sovereignty, which are the natural and fundamental laws, except what arises from his own fault or the fault of those he entrusts with administering the commonwealth. Consequently, it is his duty to have the people so instructed. It is not only his duty but also to his benefit, and a safeguard against the danger of rebellion to himself in his own natural person.

### Subjects Are to Be Taught Not to Desire a Change of Government

To come to particulars, the people are to be taught, first, that they should not be more enamored of any form of government they see in neighboring nations than of their own, nor desire change, whatever present prosperity they may observe in nations governed differently from theirs. The prosperity of a people ruled by an aristocratic or democratic assembly does not come from aristocracy or from democracy, but from the obedience and concord of the subjects. Nor do people flourish under a monarchy because one man has the right to rule them, but because they obey him. Take away obedience, and with it the concord of the people, in any kind of state, and the people will not only fail to flourish but will soon be dissolved. Those who set out through disobedience to do no more than reform the commonwealth will find that they destroy it instead. They are like the foolish daughters of Peleus in the old fable, who wished to restore their aged father's youth. On the advice of the sorceress Medea, they cut him into pieces and boiled him with strange herbs, but they did not make a new man of him. This desire for change resembles a breach of the first of God's commandments. For there God says, *Non habebis deos alienos*, "You shall not have the gods of other nations," and in another place He says of kings that they are gods.

### Nor to Side with Popular Men Against the Sovereign

Second, they are to be taught that they should not be so carried away by admiration for the virtue of any fellow subject, however high he stands or however brightly he shines in the commonwealth, or for any assembly other than the sovereign assembly, as to give it any obedience or honor that belongs to the sovereign alone. Such persons represent the sovereign in their particular stations, and the people should accept no influence from them except what they convey from the sovereign authority. A sovereign cannot be supposed to love his people as he ought unless he is jealous of them, and does not allow them to be lured away from their loyalty by the flattery of popular men. This has often happened, not only in secret but openly, to the point where preachers have proclaimed the people's marriage to such men *in facie ecclesiae*, "in the face of the Church," as a wedding is solemnly announced before the congregation, and the match has been published in the open streets. This may fitly be compared to a violation of the second of the Ten Commandments, which forbids the worship of images.

### Nor to Dispute the Sovereign Power

Third, and following from this, they should be shown how great a fault it is to speak ill of the sovereign representative, whether one man or an assembly of men, or to argue about and dispute his power, or to use his name irreverently in any way. Such conduct may bring him into contempt among his people and weaken their obedience, in which the safety of the commonwealth consists. The third commandment, by analogy, points to this doctrine.

### And to Have Days Set Apart for Learning Their Duty

Fourth, people cannot be taught these things, nor remember them once taught, nor even know after a single generation has passed in whom sovereign power resides, unless certain times are set apart from their ordinary labor during which they may attend those appointed to instruct them. It is therefore necessary that such times be fixed, when they may assemble together and, after offering prayers and praises to God, the sovereign of sovereigns, hear their duties explained to them. At these times the positive laws that generally concern them all should be read aloud and interpreted, and the people reminded of the authority that makes them laws. For this purpose the Jews had a Sabbath every seventh day, on which the Law was read and interpreted. In its observance they were reminded that their king was God; that having created the world in six days, He rested on the seventh; and, by their own rest from labor on that day, that their king was the same God who had redeemed them from their servile and painful labor in Egypt, and who gave them a time, after they had rejoiced in God, to take pleasure in themselves as well through lawful recreation. The whole of the first table of the commandments is thus devoted to setting out the sum of God's absolute power, not only as God but as king, by a particular covenant, of the Jews. It may therefore shed light for those on whom sovereign power has been conferred by human consent, showing them what doctrine they ought to teach their subjects.

### And to Honor Their Parents

Because the first instruction of children depends on the care of their parents, children must obey their parents while under their guardianship. Beyond that, as gratitude requires, they must afterward acknowledge the benefit of their upbringing through outward signs of honor. To this end they are to be taught that originally every man's father was also his sovereign lord, with power over him of life and death. When the fathers of families gave up that absolute power by founding a commonwealth, it was never intended that they should lose the honor owed to them for raising their children. Surrendering that right was not necessary to establish sovereign power. Nor would anyone have reason to want children, or to take the trouble of feeding and educating them, if he were to receive no more benefit from them afterward than from any other man.
