This agrees with the fifth commandment.

### And to Refrain from Doing Injury

Every sovereign ought also to have justice taught. Justice consists in taking from no one what is his, which amounts to teaching men not to deprive their neighbor, by violence or fraud, of anything that the sovereign authority has made his. Of the things a man holds as his own, the dearest are his life and limbs. Next, for most men, come those that concern the affection of marriage, and after these, wealth and the means of living. The people are therefore to be taught to refrain from violence against one another's persons through private revenge, from violating the honor of marriage, and from seizing one another's goods by force or taking them by stealth and fraud. For the same purpose they must be shown the evil consequences of false judgment, whether through corrupt judges or corrupt witnesses, by which the distinction between what belongs to one person and what belongs to another is erased, and justice is rendered ineffective. All of these things are indicated in the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth commandments.

### And to Do All This Sincerely, from the Heart

Finally, they are to be taught that not only unjust acts but also the plans and intentions to commit them, even when accidentally prevented, are injustice. Injustice lies in the corruption of the will as well as in the irregularity of the act. This is the meaning of the tenth commandment and the sum of the second table, which is reduced entirely to the single commandment of mutual charity, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," just as the sum of the first table is reduced to the love of God, whom the Jews had then newly accepted as their king.

### The Use of Universities

As for the means and channels through which the people may receive this instruction, we must inquire how so many opinions hostile to the peace of mankind, resting on weak and false principles, have nonetheless taken such deep root in them. I mean the opinions I specified in the preceding chapter: that men should judge what is lawful and unlawful not by the law itself but by their own private judgment; that subjects sin in obeying the commands of the commonwealth unless they have first judged those commands to be lawful; that their ownership of their wealth is such as to exclude the commonwealth's authority over it; that it is lawful for subjects to kill those they call tyrants; that the sovereign power may be divided; and others of the same kind. These are instilled in the people in the following way. Some men are kept bent on their trades and labor by necessity or greed; others are carried off after their sensual pleasures by excess wealth or idleness. These two sorts make up the greater part of mankind. Being diverted from the deep reflection that learning the truth requires, not only in matters of natural justice but in every other science, they take their notions of duty chiefly from clergymen in the pulpit, and partly from those neighbors or acquaintances who speak readily and plausibly and so seem wiser and better versed in questions of law and conscience than themselves. The clergy, and others who make a show of learning, draw their knowledge from the universities and the schools of law, or from books published by men prominent in those schools and universities. It is clear, therefore, that the instruction of the people depends entirely on the right teaching of young men in the universities.

But, some may ask, are not the universities of England learned enough already to do this? Or do you propose to teach the universities? These are hard questions. To the first, I do not hesitate to answer that until toward the end of the reign of Henry the Eighth, the power of the Pope was always upheld against the power of the commonwealth, chiefly by the universities. And the doctrines maintained against the sovereign power of the king by so many preachers, and by so many lawyers and others educated there, are sufficient proof that, although the universities did not originate those false doctrines, they did not know how to plant the true ones. Where opinions are so contradictory, it is certain that the teachers have not been adequately instructed. It is no wonder if they still retain a taste of that subtle liquor with which they were first seasoned against the civil authority, as a cask keeps the flavor of the first wine stored in it. As to the second question, it is neither fitting nor necessary for me to answer yes or no, for anyone who sees what I am doing can easily tell what I think.

### Equal Justice

The safety of the people further requires of whoever holds sovereign power that justice be administered equally to people of every rank. The rich and powerful, as well as the poor and obscure, must be able to obtain redress for injuries done to them, so that the great have no greater hope of going unpunished when they commit violence, dishonor, or any injury against people of lower standing than a commoner would have in doing the same to one of them. Equity consists in this, and since equity is a precept of the law of nature, a sovereign is as much subject to it as the humblest of his people. Every breach of the law is an offense against the commonwealth, but some offenses are also against private persons. Those that concern the commonwealth alone may be pardoned without any breach of equity, since every man may pardon at his own discretion what is done against himself. But an offense against a private person cannot in equity be pardoned without the consent of the injured party, or without reasonable compensation.

The inequality among subjects arises from acts of sovereign power. It therefore has no more place in the presence of the sovereign, that is, in a court of justice, than the inequality between kings and their subjects has in the presence of the King of Kings. The honor of great persons is to be valued according to their generosity and the help they give to people of lower rank, or not at all. The acts of violence, oppression, and injury they commit are not lessened but made worse by their eminence, since they have the least need to commit them. The consequences of partiality toward the great unfold in this sequence: impunity breeds insolence; insolence breeds hatred; and hatred breeds an effort to pull down all oppressive and contemptuous greatness, even at the cost of ruining the commonwealth.

### Equal Taxes

To equal justice also belongs the equal imposition of taxes. That equality depends not on equality of wealth but on equality of the debt that every person owes the commonwealth for his defense. It is not enough for a man to labor to sustain his life; he must also be ready to fight, if need be, to secure the fruits of that labor. People must either do as the Jews did after their return from captivity, when they rebuilt the Temple, building with one hand and holding the sword in the other, or else they must hire others to fight for them. The taxes that the sovereign power lays on the people are nothing other than the wages owed to those who bear the public sword and defend private individuals as they pursue their various trades and callings. The benefit each person receives from this defense is the enjoyment of life, which is equally dear to poor and rich. The debt a poor man owes to those who defend his life is therefore the same as the debt a rich man owes for the defense of his, except that the rich, who command the service of the poor, may be debtors not only for their own persons but for many others besides. On this view, equality of taxation consists in the equality of what is consumed rather than in the wealth of the persons who consume it. What reason is there that a man who works hard, saves the fruits of his labor, and consumes little should be charged more than one who lives idly, earns little, and spends everything he gets, when the one receives no more protection from the commonwealth than the other? But when taxes are laid on the things people consume, everyone pays equally for what he uses, and the commonwealth is not cheated by the extravagant waste of private individuals.

### Public Charity

Many people, through misfortune they could not have avoided, become unable to support themselves by their labor. They ought not to be left to the charity of private persons. Instead, the laws of the commonwealth should provide for them, so far as the necessities of nature require. For just as it is uncharitable in any individual to neglect the helpless, so it is uncharitable in the sovereign of a commonwealth to leave them exposed to the hazards of such uncertain charity.

### The Prevention of Idleness

With those who have strong bodies, the case is different: they are to be compelled to work. To remove the excuse that no employment can be found, there ought to be laws that encourage every kind of skilled occupation, such as navigation, agriculture, fishing, and every sort of manufacture that requires labor. If the number of poor but able-bodied people keeps increasing, they are to be transplanted to countries that are not sufficiently inhabited. There, however, they are not to exterminate the people they find. Rather, they are to constrain them to live closer together, so that they no longer range over a great expanse of ground to snatch whatever they come across, but tend each small plot with skill and labor until it yields their sustenance in due season. And when the whole world is overburdened with inhabitants, the last remedy of all is war, which provides for every man, either by victory or by death.

### What a Good Law Is

The making of good laws belongs to the sovereign's care. But what is a good law? By a good law I do not mean a just law, for no law can be unjust. Law is made by the sovereign power, and everything done by that power is authorized and owned by every one of the people; and what every man wills to be so, no man can call unjust. The laws of a commonwealth are like the rules of a game: whatever all the players agree on is an injustice to none of them. A good law is one that is necessary for the good of the people and, in addition, clear.

### Laws That Are Necessary

Laws are simply authorized rules, and their purpose is not to restrain people from all voluntary action. Their purpose is to direct people and keep them moving in such a way that they do not harm themselves through their own headlong desires, rashness, or lack of judgment, much as hedges are planted not to stop travelers but to keep them on the road. A law that is not necessary therefore lacks the true purpose of a law, and is not good. It might be supposed that a law is good when it benefits the sovereign, even if it is not necessary for the people, but this is not so, for the good of the sovereign and the good of the people cannot be separated. A sovereign with weak subjects is a weak sovereign, and a people whose sovereign lacks the power to rule them at his will is a weak people. Unnecessary laws are not good laws but traps for money. Where the right of sovereign power is acknowledged, such laws are superfluous; where it is not acknowledged, they are insufficient to defend the people.

### Laws That Are Clear

The clarity of a law lies not so much in the wording of the law itself as in a declaration of the causes and motives for which it was made. That declaration reveals the intent of the legislator, and once his intent is known, the law is more easily understood in few words than in many. All words are subject to ambiguity, so to multiply words in the body of a law is to multiply its ambiguity. Moreover, so much diligence in the wording seems to imply that whoever can evade the words lies outside the reach of the law, and this gives rise to many unnecessary lawsuits. When I consider how short the laws of ancient times were, and how they grew gradually longer and longer, I seem to see a contest between those who draft the law and those who plead it, the drafters trying to hem in the pleaders, and the pleaders trying to slip past every restriction the drafters set. And the pleaders have won. It therefore belongs to the office of the legislator, who in every commonwealth is the supreme representative, whether one man or an assembly, to make plain why the law was made, and to keep the body of the law itself as short as possible while framing it in terms as precise and meaningful as can be found.

### Punishments

It also belongs to the office of the sovereign to apply punishments and rewards rightly. The purpose of punishment is not revenge or the venting of anger. Its purpose is correction, either of the offender or of others through his example. The severest punishments, then, are to be inflicted for the crimes that pose the greatest danger to the public. These include crimes that spring from malice toward the established government, crimes that spring from contempt of justice, crimes that provoke indignation in the multitude, and crimes that, if left unpunished, seem to be authorized, as when they are committed by the sons, servants, or favorites of men in authority. Indignation carries people not only against those who commit and instigate an injustice but against every power likely to protect them. Such was the case with Tarquin, the last king of Rome, who was driven from the city for the insolent act of one of his sons, and the monarchy itself was dissolved. Crimes of weakness are different: those that arise from great provocation, great fear, or great need, or from ignorance of whether the deed is a serious crime at all. For these there is often room for leniency without harm to the commonwealth, and where there is such room, the law of nature requires leniency. When there has been an uprising, it is the punishment of the leaders and teachers, not of the poor people they misled, that can benefit the commonwealth by its example. To be severe with the common people is to punish an ignorance that can largely be laid at the door of the sovereign, whose fault it was that they were not better instructed.

### Rewards

In the same way, it belongs to the office and duty of the sovereign always to apply his rewards so that the commonwealth benefits from them, for in that benefit lie their use and their purpose. This is achieved when those who have served the commonwealth well are rewarded, at the least possible expense to the common treasury, generously enough that others are encouraged both to serve it as faithfully as they can and to study the skills that will enable them to serve it better. To buy off an ambitious subject who is popular with the people, paying him with money or with promotion to keep quiet and stop stirring up bad feeling in the people's minds, has nothing of the nature of a reward, which is meant for past service and not for disservice. Nor is it a sign of gratitude; it is a sign of fear. And it tends not to the benefit of the public but to its damage. It is a struggle against ambition like Hercules's struggle with the Hydra, the many-headed monster that grew three new heads for every one he cut off. In the same way, when the stubbornness of one popular man is overcome with a reward, many more arise who, following his example, make the same mischief in hope of the same benefit; for malice, like every kind of manufactured goods, multiplies once it can be sold. Such methods may sometimes postpone a civil war, but the danger keeps growing all the while, and the ruin of the public becomes all the more certain. It is therefore contrary to the duty of the sovereign, to whom the public safety is entrusted, to reward those who seek greatness by disturbing the peace of their country. He ought instead to oppose such men at their beginnings, at small risk, rather than later on, at greater risk.

### Counselors

Another business of the sovereign is to choose good counselors, by which I mean those whose advice he is to take in governing the commonwealth. The word *counsel* comes from the Latin *consilium*, which is itself a corruption of *considium*, a sitting together. It has a broad meaning, covering every assembly of people who sit together, whether to deliberate on what should be done in the future, to judge past facts, or to determine what the law is at present. I use it here only in the first of these senses. In that sense, there is no choosing of counsel in a democracy or an aristocracy, because those who give counsel are themselves members of the body that receives it. The choice of counselors therefore belongs to monarchy, and a monarch who does not try to choose those most able in every field fails to discharge his office as he ought. The most able counselors are those who have the least hope of profiting from giving bad counsel and the most knowledge of the things that make for the peace and defense of the commonwealth. It is hard to know who expects to profit from public troubles. But the signs that justify suspicion can easily be observed by anyone whose business it is to know: they appear when men whose estates are not large enough to cover their customary expenses flatter the people in their unreasonable or irremediable grievances. To know who has the most knowledge of public affairs is harder still, and those who can tell need such advisers a great deal less. For to know who knows the rules of almost any art is already to possess a large part of that art, since no one can be sure that another's rules are true unless he has first been taught to understand them. The best signs of knowledge in any art are long practice in it and consistently good results. Good counsel does not come by lot or by inheritance. There is therefore no more reason to expect good advice from the rich or the noble in matters of state than in drawing up the plans and measurements of a fortress, unless we suppose that the study of politics, unlike the study of geometry, requires no method and only the experience of looking on. That is not the case, for politics is the harder study of the two. In these parts of Europe, certain persons have been held to have a right, by inheritance, to a seat in the highest council of state. This custom derives from the conquests of the ancient Germans. Many independent lords joined together to conquer other nations, and they would not enter the confederacy without privileges that would mark a distinction, in times to come, between their descendants and the descendants of their subjects. Because such privileges are inconsistent with sovereign power, those who hold them may appear to keep them by the sovereign's favor. But if they contend for them as a matter of right, they must gradually lose them, and in the end retain no more honor than naturally attaches to their abilities.

However able the counselors may be in any matter, their counsel is of greater benefit when each gives his advice and his reasons separately than when they deliver it in an assembly by way of speeches, and when they have considered it beforehand than when they speak on the spur of the moment. They then have more time to survey the consequences of an action, and they are less likely to be carried into contradiction by envy, rivalry, or the other passions that arise from differences of opinion.

The best counsel on matters that concern not other nations but only the ease and benefit the subjects may enjoy under laws that look solely inward is to be drawn from the general reports and complaints of the people of each province. They know their own needs best, and so, as long as they demand nothing that would undermine the essential rights of sovereignty, their reports and complaints ought to be attended to diligently. Without those essential rights, as I have often said before, the commonwealth cannot survive at all.

### Commanders

A commander-in-chief of an army who is not popular will be neither loved nor feared by his army as he ought to be, and consequently cannot carry out his office successfully. He must therefore be industrious, brave, approachable, generous, and fortunate, so that he may earn a reputation both for competence and for caring about his soldiers. This is popularity. It breeds in the soldiers both the desire and the courage to win his favor, and it protects the general's severity when he must punish mutinous or negligent soldiers. But unless there is some guarantee of the commander's loyalty, this love of soldiers for their general is dangerous to sovereign power, especially when that power lies in the hands of an assembly that is not itself popular. It is essential to the safety of the people, then, that those to whom the sovereign entrusts his armies be both good leaders and faithful subjects.

When the sovereign himself is popular, however, which is to say revered and loved by his people, there is no danger at all from the popularity of a subject. For soldiers are never so generally unjust as to side with their captain against their sovereign, however much they love the captain, when they love not only the sovereign's person but also his cause. This is why those who have at any time overthrown the power of their lawful sovereign by violence have always had to go to the trouble of contriving titles for themselves before they could settle into his place, so as to spare the people the shame of accepting them. To have a known right to sovereign power is so popular a quality that the one who possesses it needs nothing more, on his own side, to turn his subjects' hearts toward him than that they see him able to govern his own household absolutely; nor does he need anything more, on his enemies' side, than that their armies be disbanded. For the greatest and most active part of mankind has never yet been content with things as they are.

Concerning the duties of one sovereign to another, which fall under what is commonly called the law of nations, I need say nothing here, because the law of nations and the law of nature are the same thing. Every sovereign has the same right in securing the safety of his people that any private individual has in securing the safety of his own body. The same law that dictates to people living without civil government what they ought to do and what they ought to avoid in their dealings with one another dictates the same to commonwealths, that is, to the consciences of sovereign princes and sovereign assemblies. For there is no court of natural justice except in the conscience alone, where not man but God reigns. God's laws, those of them that bind all mankind, are natural laws insofar as God is the author of nature, and they are laws in the full sense insofar as the same God is King of Kings. But of the Kingdom of God, both as King of Kings and as King of a particular people, I shall speak in the rest of this discourse.

## Chapter XXXI. Of the Kingdom of God by Nature

### The Scope of the Following Chapters

In what I have already written, I have sufficiently proved four things. First, the condition of mere nature, meaning the absolute liberty of those who are neither sovereigns nor subjects, is anarchy and a state of war. Second, the precepts that guide men to avoid that condition are the laws of nature. Third, a commonwealth without sovereign power is only a word without substance, and it cannot stand. Fourth, subjects owe their sovereigns simple obedience in all things where that obedience does not conflict with the laws of God. Only one thing is still needed for a complete knowledge of civil duty: to know what those laws of God are. Without that knowledge, a man who receives a command from the civil power cannot tell whether it is contrary to the law of God. He will then either offend the Divine Majesty through too much civil obedience, or break the commandments of the commonwealth through fear of offending God. To steer clear of both these rocks, we must know what the divine laws are. And since the knowledge of all law depends on the knowledge of the sovereign power, I shall say something in what follows about the kingdom of God.

### Who Are Subjects in the Kingdom of God

"God is King, let the earth rejoice," says the Psalmist in the ninety-sixth Psalm. And again, in the ninety-eighth: "God is King, though the nations be angry; and he that sits upon the cherubim, though the earth be moved." Whether men will it or not, they must always be subject to the divine power. By denying the existence or the providence of God, men may throw off their peace of mind, but not their yoke. Yet to call this power of God a "kingdom," when it extends not only to man but also to beasts, plants, and inanimate bodies, is only a metaphorical use of the word. For properly speaking, only he reigns who governs his subjects by his word, promising rewards to those who obey it and threatening punishment to those who do not. The subjects in the kingdom of God, therefore, are not inanimate bodies or irrational creatures, because they understand no precepts as his. Nor are they atheists, or those who do not believe that God has any concern for the actions of mankind, because these acknowledge no word as his and have neither hope of his rewards nor fear of his threats. Those who believe that there is a God who governs the world, who has given precepts to mankind and set forth rewards and punishments, are God's subjects. All the rest are to be understood as enemies.

### A Threefold Word of God: Reason, Revelation, Prophecy

To rule by words requires that those words be made plainly known, for otherwise they are not laws. It belongs to the nature of law that it be promulgated sufficiently and clearly enough to remove the excuse of ignorance. Among the laws of men there is only one kind of promulgation, namely proclamation, or announcement by the voice of a man. But God declares his laws in three ways: by the dictates of natural reason, by revelation, and by the voice of some man to whom, by working miracles, he secures the belief of everyone else. From this arises a threefold word of God, which may be called rational, sensible, and prophetic. To these correspond three kinds of hearing: right reason, supernatural sense, and faith. As for supernatural sense, which consists in revelation or inspiration, no universal laws have ever been given in that way, because God does not speak in that manner except to particular persons, and he tells different things to different men.

### A Twofold Kingdom of God, Natural and Prophetic

From the difference between the other two kinds of God's word, the rational and the prophetic, we may attribute to God a twofold kingdom, natural and prophetic. In his natural kingdom he governs, by the natural dictates of right reason, as many of mankind as acknowledge his providence. In his prophetic kingdom, having chosen one particular nation, the Jews, for his subjects, he governed them, and none but them, not only by natural reason but also by positive laws, which he gave them through the mouths of his holy prophets. In this chapter I intend to speak of the natural kingdom of God.

### The Right of God's Sovereignty Is Derived from His Omnipotence

The natural right by which God reigns over men and punishes those who break his laws is to be derived not from his having created them, as though he required obedience out of gratitude for his benefits, but from his irresistible power. I have already shown how sovereign right arises from a pact. To show how the same right may arise from nature requires only showing in what case it is never surrendered. Since all men by nature had a right to all things, each of them had a right to reign over all the rest. But because no one could obtain this right by force, it was in the interest of everyone's safety to lay that right aside and, by common consent, to set up men with sovereign authority to rule and defend them. If, however, there had been any man of irresistible power, there would have been no reason why he should not have used that power to rule and defend both himself and them at his own discretion. Dominion over all men therefore belongs naturally to those whose power is irresistible, by virtue of the superiority of that power. Consequently, it is from that power that the kingdom over men, and the right to afflict men as he pleases, belongs naturally to God Almighty: not as Creator and as gracious, but as omnipotent. And although punishment is due only for sin, since the word "punishment" means affliction for sin, the right of afflicting is not always derived from men's sin. It is derived from God's power.

### Sin Is Not the Cause of All Affliction

The question "Why do evil men often prosper, while good men suffer adversity?" was much debated by the ancients. It is the same as our question, "By what right does God distribute the prosperities and adversities of this life?" Its difficulty is such that it has shaken faith in divine providence, not only among the common people but among philosophers and, what is more, among the saints. "How good," says David, "is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart; and yet my feet had almost given way, my steps had all but slipped; for I was grieved at the wicked when I saw the ungodly in such prosperity." And how earnestly Job remonstrates with God over the many afflictions he suffered despite his righteousness! In Job's case the question is settled by God himself, and not by arguments drawn from Job's sin, but by arguments drawn from God's own power. Job's friends reasoned from his affliction to his sin, while he defended himself by the testimony of his conscience to his innocence. Then God himself took up the matter. Having justified the affliction by arguments drawn from his power, such as "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?", he both approved Job's innocence and rebuked the mistaken doctrine of his friends. The judgment of our Saviour about the man who was born blind agrees with this teaching: "Neither has this man sinned, nor his parents; but that the works of God might be made manifest in him." It is also said that "death entered into the world by sin," meaning that if Adam had never sinned, he would never have died, that is, his soul would never have been separated from his body. But it does not follow that God could not justly have afflicted him even if he had not sinned, just as he afflicts other living creatures that cannot sin.

### Divine Laws

Having spoken of the right of God's sovereignty as grounded on nature alone, we must next consider what the divine laws, or dictates of natural reason, are. These laws concern either the natural duties of one man to another or the honour naturally due to our divine sovereign. The first kind are the same laws of nature I have already discussed in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters of this treatise: equity, justice, mercy, humility, and the rest of the moral virtues. It remains, then, to consider what precepts men's natural reason alone, without any other word of God, dictates to them concerning the honour and worship of the Divine Majesty.

### What Honour and Worship Are

Honour consists in the inward thought and opinion of another's power and goodness. To honour God, therefore, is to think as highly of his power and goodness as is possible. The outward signs of that opinion, appearing in men's words and actions, are called worship, which is one part of what the Romans meant by the word *cultus*. Properly and consistently, *cultus* means the labour a man spends on anything with the aim of profiting from it. The things we profit from are of two kinds. Some are subject to us, and the profit they yield follows from the labour we spend on them as a natural effect. Others are not subject to us, and they respond to our labour according to their own wills. In the first sense, labour spent on the earth is called culture, or cultivation, and the education of children is called a cultivation of their minds. In the second sense, where other men's wills are to be bent to our purpose not by force but by obliging behaviour, the word means courting, that is, winning favour by good services: by praise, by acknowledging their power, and by whatever pleases those from whom we expect some benefit. This is worship in the proper sense. In this sense the Roman surname Publicola was understood to mean a worshipper of the people, and *cultus Dei* to mean the worship of God.

### The Several Signs of Honour

From inward honour, which consists in the opinion of power and goodness, arise three passions. One is love, which relates to goodness. The other two are hope and fear, which relate to power. There also arise three parts of outward worship: praising, magnifying, and blessing. The object of praise is goodness, while the object of magnifying and blessing is power and its effect, which is happiness. Praising and magnifying can be expressed both by words and by actions. We express them by words when we say that a man is good or great, and by actions when we thank him for his generosity and obey his power. The opinion that another is happy, however, can only be expressed by words.

### Natural and Arbitrary Worship

Some signs of honour, whether attributes or actions, are honourable by nature. Among attributes these include good, just, generous, and the like. Among actions they include prayers, thanks, and obedience. Other signs are honourable by human institution or custom. These are honourable in some times and places, dishonourable in others, and indifferent in others still. Examples are the gestures used in greeting, prayer, and thanksgiving, which differ from one time and place to another. The first kind is natural worship, and the second is arbitrary worship.

### Commanded and Free Worship

Arbitrary worship is of two kinds, for it is sometimes commanded and sometimes voluntary. It is commanded when it is the kind of worship required by the one who is worshipped. It is free when it is the kind the worshipper himself thinks fit. When worship is commanded, the worship lies not in the words or gestures but in the obedience. When it is free, the worship depends on the opinion of those who witness it. If the words or actions by which we intend honour seem ridiculous or insulting to them, then they are not worship, because a sign is not a sign to the one who gives it. It is a sign to the one to whom it is made, that is, to the spectator.

### Public and Private Worship

There is also a distinction between public and private worship. Public worship is the worship a commonwealth performs as one person. Private worship is that which a private person offers. Public worship is free with respect to the commonwealth as a whole, but not with respect to particular men. Private worship is free when done in secret. In the sight of the multitude, however, it is never without some restraint, either from the laws or from the opinion of men, and restraint is contrary to the nature of liberty.

### The End of Worship

Among men, the end of worship is power. When a man sees another being worshipped, he assumes that the other is powerful and becomes more ready to obey him, which makes that man's power greater still. But God has no ends. The worship we give him comes from our duty. It is guided, as far as our capacity allows, by those rules of honour that reason tells the weak to observe toward more powerful men, whether in hope of benefit, in fear of harm, or in gratitude for good already received from them.

### The Attributes of Divine Honour

To learn what worship of God the light of nature teaches us, I will begin with his attributes. First, it is plain that we ought to attribute existence to him, for no one can have the will to honour something he believes has no being.

Second, those philosophers who said that the world, or the soul of the world, was God spoke unworthily of him and denied his existence. By God is meant the cause of the world, and to say that the world is God is to say that the world has no cause, which is to say that there is no God.

Third, to say that the world was not created but is eternal is to deny that there is a God, since what is eternal has no cause.

Fourth, those who think they are attributing ease to God when they deny that he cares for mankind are in fact taking his honour from him. They take away men's love and fear of him, which are the root of honour.

Fifth, in matters that signify greatness and power, to say that he is finite is not to honour him. It is no sign of a will to honour God to attribute less to him than we can, and the finite is less than we can attribute, because to anything finite it is easy to add more.

Therefore it is not honour to attribute shape to him, for every shape is finite.

Nor is it honour to say that we conceive or imagine him, or have an idea of him in our minds, for whatever we conceive is finite.

Nor is it honour to attribute parts or wholeness to him, for these are attributes only of finite things.

Nor is it honour to say that he is in this place or that, for whatever is in a place is bounded and finite.

Nor is it honour to say that he moves or is at rest, for both of these attributes assign him a place.

Nor is it honour to say that there is more than one God, because that implies that all of them are finite, and there cannot be more than one infinite.

Nor is it honour to ascribe to him passions that involve grief, such as repentance, anger, and mercy, or that involve want, such as appetite, hope, and desire, or any passive faculty at all, unless we speak metaphorically and mean not the passion but its effect. For passion is power limited by something else.

And so when we ascribe a will to God, we must not understand it as we understand will in human beings, as a rational appetite. We must understand it as the power by which he brings everything about.

The same holds when we attribute to him sight and the other acts of sense, or knowledge and understanding. In us these are nothing but a commotion of the mind, stirred up by external things pressing on the organs of the body. There is nothing of this kind in God, and since such things depend on natural causes, they cannot be attributed to him.

Whoever would attribute to God nothing beyond what natural reason warrants must use one of three kinds of attribute. The first is negative, such as infinite, eternal, or incomprehensible. The second is superlative, such as most high or most great. The third is indefinite, such as good, just, holy, or creator. He must use them not as if he meant to declare what God is, for that would confine God within the limits of our imagination, but to express how much we admire him and how ready we would be to obey him. This is a sign of humility, and of a will to honor him as fully as we can. For there is only one name that signifies our conception of his nature, and that is I AM. There is only one name for his relation to us, and that is God, a name that contains within it Father, King, and Lord.

### Actions That Are Signs of Divine Honor

Concerning the actions of divine worship, the most general precept of reason is that they be signs of an intention to honor God. The first of these is prayer. When carvers made images, no one thought that the carvers had made them into gods. It was the people who prayed to those images who made them gods.

Second, thanksgiving. In divine worship it differs from prayer only in timing: prayers come before a benefit, and thanks come after it. Both have the same purpose, which is to acknowledge God as the author of all benefits, past as well as future.

Third, gifts, that is, sacrifices and oblations (offerings presented to God), are signs of honor, provided they are of the best, because they are a form of thanksgiving.

Fourth, to swear by no one but God is naturally a sign of honor. It admits that God alone knows the heart, and that no man's cleverness or strength can protect anyone from God's vengeance on those who swear falsely.

Fifth, it is part of rational worship to speak of God with deliberation and care. Such care shows that we fear him, and fear is an acknowledgment of his power. It follows that the name of God must not be used rashly and to no purpose, which is the same as using it in vain. The only purposes for which it may be used are an oath, by order of the commonwealth, to make judgments certain, or an oath between commonwealths, to avoid war. It follows, too, that disputing about God's nature is contrary to his honor. In this natural kingdom of God, it is assumed that the only way to know anything is by natural reason, that is, from the principles of natural science. Those principles cannot teach us anything about God's nature. They cannot even teach us our own nature, or the nature of the smallest living creature. When men dispute about the attributes of God on the basis of natural reason, therefore, they only dishonor him. In the attributes we give to God, we should consider not what they mean as philosophical truth but what they mean as pious intention: the wish to do him the greatest honor we are able. Because men have neglected this, whole volumes of disputation about the nature of God have been written. They tend not to his honor but to the honor of our own wit and learning, and they are nothing but thoughtless and empty abuses of his sacred name.

Sixth, natural reason dictates that prayers, thanksgivings, offerings, and sacrifices each be the best of its kind and the most expressive of honor. Prayers and thanksgivings, for example, should be made in words and phrases that are not hasty, frivolous, or vulgar, but beautiful and well composed. Otherwise we do not honor God as much as we can. The heathens, then, acted absurdly in worshiping images as gods, but their doing so in verse, and with music both of voice and of instruments, was reasonable. It was likewise reasonable that the beasts they sacrificed, the gifts they presented, and their gestures in worship were full of submission and commemorated the benefits they had received. All of this proceeded from an intention to honor him.

Seventh, reason directs us to worship God not only in private but also, and especially, in public and in the sight of others. Without public worship, we lose the part of honor that is most acceptable, which is the bringing of others to honor him as well.

Finally, obedience to his laws, which in this case means the laws of nature, is the greatest worship of all. Just as obedience is more acceptable to God than sacrifice, so making light of his commandments is the greatest of all insults. These, then, are the laws of the divine worship that natural reason dictates to private individuals.

### Public Worship Consists in Uniformity

But since a commonwealth is a single person, it ought also to offer God a single worship. It does so when it commands private individuals to offer that worship publicly. This is public worship, and its defining property is uniformity, because actions performed differently by different people cannot be called a public worship. Where many kinds of worship are permitted, arising from the different religions of private individuals, there is no public worship at all, and the commonwealth cannot be said to have any religion whatsoever.

### All Attributes Depend on the Civil Laws

Words, and consequently the attributes of God, take their meaning from human agreement and decision. Those attributes are therefore to be taken as signs of honor which men intend to be signs of honor. Moreover, whatever individuals may do by their own wills, where there is no law but reason, the commonwealth may do by its will through civil laws. A commonwealth has no will and makes no laws except those made by the will of the person or persons who hold sovereign power. It follows that whatever attributes the sovereign ordains as signs of honor in the worship of God ought to be accepted and used as such by private individuals in their public worship.

### Not All Actions

Not all actions, however, are signs by convention. Some are naturally signs of honor, and others are naturally signs of contempt. The latter are the actions people are ashamed to perform in front of anyone they revere, and no human power can make them part of divine worship. Nor can the former, such as decent, modest, and humble behavior, ever be separated from it. But there are countless actions and gestures that are indifferent by nature. When the commonwealth ordains that any of these be used publicly and universally as signs of honor and as part of God's worship, its subjects must accept and use them as such. As for the saying of Scripture, "It is better to obey God than men," it applies in the kingdom of God by covenant, not in the kingdom of God by nature.

### Natural Punishments

Having spoken briefly of the natural kingdom of God and his natural laws, I will add to this chapter only a short account of his natural punishments. Every human action in this life begins a chain of consequences, and the chain is so long that no human foresight can see to its end. In this chain, pleasing and unpleasing events are linked together, so that whoever does something for his pleasure commits himself to suffering all the pains attached to it. These pains are the natural punishments of those actions that set in motion more harm than good. So it comes about that intemperance is naturally punished with disease, rashness with misfortune, injustice with the violence of enemies, pride with ruin, cowardice with oppression, the negligent government of princes with rebellion, and rebellion with slaughter. Since punishments follow upon the breaking of laws, natural punishments must naturally follow upon the breaking of the laws of nature. They follow as natural effects, not as arbitrary ones.

### The Conclusion of the Second Part

So much, then, for the constitution, nature, and rights of sovereigns, and for the duty of subjects, as derived from the principles of natural reason. This doctrine differs greatly from the practice of most of the world, especially of these Western regions, which received their moral learning from Rome and Athens. Those who administer sovereign power would also need great depth in moral philosophy to follow it. When I consider these things, I come close to believing that my labor is as useless as Plato's *Republic*. Plato, too, held that the disorders of the state and the overthrow of governments by civil war could never be ended until sovereigns became philosophers.

But then I consider other things. The science of natural justice is the only science that sovereigns and their principal ministers need. They need not be burdened with the mathematical sciences, as Plato would have them be, beyond encouraging their subjects through good laws to study them. And neither Plato nor any other philosopher has yet set in order, and sufficiently or even plausibly proved, all the theorems of moral doctrine from which people might learn both how to govern and how to obey. With these thoughts I recover some hope. Some day this writing of mine may fall into the hands of a sovereign who will consider it for himself, since it is short and, I think, clear, without the help of any self-interested or envious interpreter. By using his full sovereignty to protect the public teaching of it, he may convert this truth of speculation into the utility of practice.

## Part III. Of a Christian Commonwealth

## Chapter XXXII: Of the Principles of Christian Politics

### The Word of God Delivered by Prophets Is the Main Principle of Christian Politics

So far I have derived the rights of sovereign power and the duties of subjects from the principles of nature alone. These are principles that experience has found to be true, or that agreement about the use of words has made true. I have reasoned, in other terms, from human nature as experience reveals it, and from universally accepted definitions of the words essential to all political reasoning. But the subject I turn to next, the nature and rights of a Christian commonwealth, depends heavily on supernatural revelations of God's will. My discussion must therefore rest not only on the natural word of God, which is reason, but also on his prophetic word.

We are not, however, to renounce our senses and our experience, nor our natural reason, which is beyond doubt the word of God. These are the talents he has placed in our hands to trade with until our blessed Savior returns, like the sums of money that the master in the Gospel parable entrusts to his servants to invest while he is away. They are therefore not to be wrapped up and laid aside, as the unprofitable servant hid his master's money in a napkin, in an implicit faith that accepts doctrines without understanding them. They are to be put to work in acquiring justice, peace, and true religion. For although many things in God's word are above reason, meaning that natural reason can neither prove nor disprove them, nothing in it is contrary to reason. When something seems to be, the fault lies either in our unskillful interpretation or in our faulty reasoning.

Therefore, when anything written in Scripture is too difficult for us to examine, we are told to make our understanding captive to the words. We are not to labor at extracting a philosophical truth, by logic, from mysteries that lie beyond comprehension and fall under no rule of natural science. The mysteries of our religion are like wholesome pills for the sick: swallowed whole, they have the power to cure, but chewed, they are for the most part vomited back up without effect.

### What It Is to Captivate the Understanding

By the captivity of our understanding, however, I do not mean submitting our intellect to the opinion of any other man. I mean submitting our will to obedience, where obedience is due. Sense, memory, understanding, reason, and opinion are not in our power to change. They are always, and necessarily, whatever the things we see, hear, and consider make them. They are not effects of our will; our will is an effect of them. We captivate our understanding and reason, then, when we refrain from contradiction, when we speak as lawful authority commands us, and when we live accordingly. In sum, it is trust and faith placed in the one who speaks, even when the mind can form no notion at all from the words spoken.

### How God Speaks to Men

When God speaks to a man, he must do so either directly or through another man to whom he has previously spoken directly. Those to whom God has spoken directly may understand well enough how he did it. How anyone else could understand it is hard, if not impossible, to know. If a man claims to me that God has spoken to him supernaturally and directly, and I doubt it, I cannot easily see what argument he could produce to oblige me to believe him. It is true that if he is my sovereign, he may oblige me to obey, so that I do not declare by act or word that I disbelieve him. He cannot, however, oblige me to think otherwise than my reason persuades me. And if someone who holds no such authority over me makes the same claim, nothing requires either my belief or my obedience.

To say that God has spoken to him in Holy Scripture is not to say that God has spoken to him directly. It is to say that God has spoken to him through the mediation of the prophets, or the apostles, or the Church, in the same way he speaks to all other Christians. To say that God has spoken to him in a dream is no more than to say he dreamed that God spoke to him. Such a claim has no power to win belief from anyone who knows that dreams are for the most part natural and may arise from a person's earlier thoughts. Dreams of this particular kind arise from self-conceit, foolish arrogance, and a false opinion of one's own godliness or other virtue, by which a man thinks he has earned the favor of an extraordinary revelation. To say he has seen a vision or heard a voice is to say he has dreamed between sleeping and waking. In that state a man often naturally takes his dream for a vision, because he has not noticed that he was dozing. To say he speaks by supernatural inspiration is to say he feels an ardent desire to speak, or holds some strong opinion of himself for which he can offer no natural and sufficient reason. So although Almighty God can speak to a man through dreams, visions, a voice, and inspiration, he obliges no one to believe that he has done so when someone claims it. The claimant is a man, and may therefore be mistaken and, what is more, may lie.

### By What Marks Prophets Are Known

How, then, can someone to whom God has never revealed his will directly, except by way of natural reason, know when he ought to obey the word delivered by someone who says he is a prophet, and when he ought not? The First Book of Kings records that of the four hundred prophets whom the king of Israel consulted about his war against Ramoth-Gilead, only Micaiah was a true one. The same book tells of the prophet sent to prophesy against the altar that Jeroboam had set up. He was a true prophet, and two miracles performed in his presence showed that God had sent him. Yet another, older prophet deceived him, persuading him, as if speaking from the mouth of God, to eat and drink with him. If one prophet can deceive another, what certainty is there of knowing God's will by any way other than reason?

To this I answer, from Holy Scripture itself, that there are two marks by which a true prophet is to be known, and they must be taken together, not separately. One is the performing of miracles. The other is not teaching any religion besides the one already established. Separately, I say, neither is sufficient. The thirteenth chapter of Deuteronomy says: "If a prophet arises among you, or a dreamer of dreams, and claims to perform a miracle, and the miracle comes to pass, and he says, 'Let us follow strange gods, which you have not known,' you shall not listen to him. That prophet and dreamer of dreams shall be put to death, because he has spoken to you to revolt from the Lord your God." Two things are to be observed in these words. First, God does not want miracles alone to stand as proof of a prophet's calling. As the third verse puts it, they are a test of how constantly we hold to him. The works of the Egyptian sorcerers were not as great as those of Moses, but they were still great miracles. Second, however great the miracle may be, if it tends to stir up revolt against the king, or against whoever governs by the king's authority, the one who performs it is to be regarded only as someone sent to test the people's allegiance. In this passage, the words "revolt from the Lord your God" are equivalent to "revolt from your king." The Israelites had made God their king by covenant at the foot of Mount Sinai, and God ruled them through Moses alone, since only Moses spoke with God and from time to time declared God's commandments to the people. In the same way, our Savior Christ, after bringing his disciples to acknowledge him as the Messiah, did not neglect to warn them of the danger of miracles. The Messiah was God's anointed, whom the Jewish nation daily expected as its king but refused when he came. "There shall arise false Christs and false prophets," he says in Matthew's Gospel, "and they shall do great wonders and miracles, so as to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect." Plainly, then, false prophets may have the power of miracles, and still we are not to take their doctrine for God's word. St. Paul goes further, telling the Galatians that "if he himself, or an angel from heaven, preached to them any other gospel than the one he had preached, let him be accursed." That gospel was that Christ was king. As a consequence of these words, St. Paul curses all preaching against the power of the king once he has been received. His words are addressed to those who had already, through his preaching, received Jesus as the Christ, that is, as King of the Jews.

### The Marks of a Prophet Under the Old Law: Miracles, and Doctrine Conformable to the Law

Miracles without the preaching of the doctrine God has established are an insufficient argument for direct revelation, and so is preaching the true doctrine without performing miracles. If a man who teaches no false doctrine claims to be a prophet without showing any miracle, his claim gives us no greater reason to heed him. The eighteenth chapter of Deuteronomy makes this evident: "If you say in your heart, 'How shall we know that the prophet's word is not what the Lord has spoken?' When the prophet speaks in the name of the Lord something that does not come to pass, that is the word the Lord has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it out of the pride of his own heart. Do not fear him." But here again someone may ask how we are to know, when a prophet has foretold something, whether it will come to pass. He may predict it as something that will happen after a long time, longer than a human lifetime, or he may predict it indefinitely, as something that will happen at one time or another. In such cases this mark of a prophet is useless. The miracles that oblige us to believe a prophet must therefore be confirmed by an event that is immediate, or not long delayed. Teaching the religion God has established and showing a present miracle, joined together, were thus the only marks by which Scripture would have a true prophet, and with him direct revelation, acknowledged. Neither mark alone is sufficient to oblige anyone else to heed what the prophet says.

### Miracles Ceasing, Prophets Cease; the Scripture Supplies Their Place

Since miracles have now ceased, we have no sign left by which to acknowledge the claimed revelations or inspirations of any private person. Nor are we obliged to listen to any doctrine except so far as it agrees with Holy Scripture. Since the time of our Savior, Scripture has made up for the absence of all other prophecy. From it, by wise and careful reasoning, we can easily deduce all the rules and precepts necessary for knowing our duty to both God and man, without enthusiasm, meaning the conviction of being personally filled with divine inspiration, or any other supernatural inspiration. This Scripture is the source from which I am to draw the principles of my discussion concerning the rights of those who are the supreme governors on earth of Christian commonwealths, and concerning the duty of Christian subjects toward their sovereigns. To that end, I shall discuss in the next chapter the books, writers, scope, and authority of the Bible.

## Chapter XXXIII. Of the Number, Antiquity, Scope, Authority, and Interpreters of the Books of Holy Scripture

### Of the Books of Holy Scripture

By the books of Holy Scripture we mean those books that ought to be the canon, that is, the rules of Christian life. Every rule of life that people are bound in conscience to observe is a law. The question of what counts as Scripture is therefore the question of what counts as law, both natural and civil, throughout all of Christendom. Scripture does not determine what laws each Christian king shall enact in his own dominions, but it does determine what laws he shall not enact. I have already proved that sovereigns are the sole legislators within their own dominions. It follows that in every nation the only canonical books, the only books that are law, are those established as such by the sovereign authority.

It is true that God is the sovereign of all sovereigns. When he speaks to any subject, that subject ought to obey him, whatever any earthly ruler may command to the contrary. But the question is not whether we should obey God. The question is when God spoke and what he said. Subjects who have received no supernatural revelation cannot know this except by natural reason. That same reason led them, for the sake of peace and justice, to obey the authority of their several commonwealths, that is, of their lawful sovereigns.

In keeping with this obligation, I can acknowledge no books of the Old Testament as Holy Scripture except those that the authority of the Church of England has commanded to be acknowledged as such. Which books these are is well enough known that I need not list them here. They are the same ones acknowledged by St. Jerome, who classed the rest as Apocrypha: the Wisdom of Solomon, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, the first and second books of Maccabees (though he had seen the first in Hebrew), and the third and fourth books of Esdras.

Josephus, a learned Jew who wrote in the reign of the Emperor Domitian, counts twenty-two canonical books, making their number match the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. St. Jerome arrives at the same number, though the two divide the books differently. Josephus counts five books of Moses, thirteen by prophets who wrote the history of their own times, and four of hymns and moral precepts. How his thirteen agree with the prophetic writings contained in the Bible we shall see later. St. Jerome counts five books of Moses, eight of the prophets, and nine of other holy writings, which he calls the Hagiographa. The Septuagint was the work of seventy learned Jews summoned by Ptolemy, king of Egypt, to translate the Jewish law from Hebrew into Greek. These translators have left us no books as holy Scripture in the Greek tongue other than those the Church of England receives.

The books of the New Testament, for their part, are acknowledged as canonical by every Christian church alike, and by every Christian sect that admits any books as canonical at all.

### Their Antiquity

Who originally wrote the various books of Holy Scripture has not been established by sufficient testimony from other histories, which are the only proof of a matter of fact. Nor can it be established by any argument of natural reason, for reason can demonstrate the truth not of facts but only of consequences. The light that must guide us in this question, then, is the light the books themselves hold out to us. This light does not reveal the author of every book, but it does show us when they were written.

### The Pentateuch Not Written by Moses

To begin with the Pentateuch: the fact that its books are called the five books of Moses is no proof that Moses wrote them. The titles the Book of Joshua, the Book of Judges, the Book of Ruth, and the Books of the Kings likewise do not prove that they were written by Joshua, by the judges, by Ruth, and by the kings. A book's title names its subject as often as its author. The History of Livy names the writer, while the History of Scanderbeg is named for its subject, the Albanian commander.

In the last chapter of Deuteronomy, at the sixth verse, we read of Moses's grave that "no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day," meaning the day on which those words were written. These words were therefore written after his burial. It would be a strange reading to suppose that Moses, while still alive, said of his own grave, even by prophecy, that it had not been found to that day. It may be objected that someone else wrote only the last chapter and that Moses wrote the rest. Let us therefore consider Genesis 12:6: "And Abraham passed through the land to the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh, and the Canaanite was then in the land." These must be the words of someone writing at a time when the Canaanite was no longer in the land. They cannot be the words of Moses, who died before he ever entered it. Likewise, in Numbers 21:14 the writer cites an older book called The Book of the Wars of the Lord, which recorded the deeds of Moses at the Red Sea and at the brook of Arnon. The five books of Moses were evidently written after his time, though how long after is less clear.

Moses did not compile those books entirely, nor in the form we now have them. He did, however, write everything that they say he wrote. One example is the Volume of the Law, which appears to be contained in Deuteronomy from chapter 11 through chapter 27. The Israelites were also commanded to write it on stones when they entered the land of Canaan. As Deuteronomy 31 records, Moses wrote this law himself and delivered it to the priests and elders of Israel. It was to be read to all Israel every seventh year, when they assembled for the Feast of Tabernacles. God commanded that their kings, once they had established that form of government, should take a copy of this law from the priests and Levites, and that it be laid in the side of the Ark. This same law was later lost, and long afterward Hilkiah found it again and sent it to King Josiah. As told in the second book of Kings, chapters 22 and 23, Josiah had it read to the people and so renewed the covenant between God and them.

### The Book of Joshua Written After His Time

Many passages in the Book of Joshua show that it, too, was written long after Joshua's time. Joshua set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan as a monument to the Israelites' crossing. Of these the writer says, "they are there unto this day," a phrase that signifies a time already past, beyond living memory. Similarly, after the Lord declared that he had rolled away from the people the reproach of Egypt, the writer adds, "the place is called Gilgal unto this day." It would have been odd to say this in Joshua's own time. The Valley of Achor was named for the trouble Achan stirred up in the camp, and its name, the writer says, "remaineth unto this day." This too must have been written long after Joshua. There are many other arguments of this kind, as in Joshua 8:29, 13:13, 14:14, and 15:63.

### The Books of Judges and Ruth Written Long After the Captivity

Similar arguments make the same point about the Book of Judges, at 1:21 and 26, 6:24, 10:4, 15:19, and 17:6, and about Ruth 1:1. The clearest case is Judges 18:30, which says that Jonathan "and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land."

### The Like of the Books of Samuel

There are like arguments that the Books of Samuel were also written after Samuel's own time, at 1 Samuel 5:5, 7:13 and 15, 27:6, and 30:25. In the last of these, David rules that those who guarded the supplies should receive an equal share of the spoils with those who fought. The writer then says, "he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel unto this day." In another passage, the Lord strikes down Uzzah for reaching out his hand to steady the Ark. David, displeased, names the place Perez-Uzzah, and the writer says it is called so "to this day." The book must therefore have been written long after these events, which is to say long after the time of David.

### The Books of the Kings, and the Chronicles

The two books of Kings and the two books of Chronicles contain many passages mentioning monuments that, the writer says, remained until his own day. Examples include 1 Kings 9:13, 9:21, 10:12, and 12:19; 2 Kings 2:22, 8:22, 10:27, 14:7, 16:6, 17:23, 17:34, and 17:41; and 1 Chronicles 4:41 and 5:26. Beyond these passages, the fact that their history continues down to the captivity in Babylon is sufficient proof that they were written after it. The events recorded in a register are always older than any book that mentions and quotes that register. These books do so in many places. They refer the reader to the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel, and the books of the prophets Samuel, Nathan, and Ahijah. They also cite the vision of Iddo the seer and the books of the prophet Shemaiah and the prophet Iddo.

### Ezra and Nehemiah

The books of Ezra and Nehemiah were certainly written after the return from captivity. They contain the account of that return, the rebuilding of the walls and houses of Jerusalem, the renewal of the covenant, and the ordering of the people's government.

### Esther

The history of Queen Esther belongs to the time of the captivity, so its writer must have lived then or afterward.

### Job

The Book of Job bears no mark of when it was written. Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11 make it clear enough that Job was not an invented person. Yet the book itself seems to be not a history but a treatise on a question much debated in ancient times: why the wicked have often prospered in this world while the good have suffered.

The form of the text makes this reading the most probable. As St. Jerome attests, the Hebrew is in prose from the beginning up to the third verse of the third chapter, where Job's lament begins. From there to the sixth verse of the last chapter it is in hexameter verse, and the remainder of that chapter is again prose. The whole dispute, then, is in verse, and the prose is added only as a preface at the beginning and an epilogue at the end. Verse is not the usual way of speaking for people in great pain, as Job was, nor for those who come to comfort them, as his friends did. In ancient times, however, it was a common form for philosophy, and especially for moral philosophy.

### The Psalter

David wrote most of the Psalms for the use of the choir. To these were added some songs of Moses and of other holy men. Some psalms were composed after the return from captivity, such as Psalms 137 and 126. The Psalter must therefore have been compiled and given its present form after the Jews returned from Babylon.

### The Proverbs

The Proverbs are a collection of wise and godly sayings. Some are by Solomon, some by Agur the son of Jakeh, and some by the mother of King Lemuel. It is no more probable that Solomon collected them than that Agur or Lemuel's mother did. The sayings are theirs, but the work of gathering them into this one book was most likely done by some other godly man who lived after them all.

### Ecclesiastes and the Canticles

The books of Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs contain nothing that is not Solomon's, except perhaps their titles or inscriptions. The first is headed "The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem," and the second "The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's." These titles seem to have been added for the sake of distinction when the books of Scripture were gathered into one body of law. Their purpose was to preserve not only the doctrine but also the names of the authors.

### The Prophets

The most ancient of the prophets are Zephaniah, Jonah, Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, and Micah, who lived in the reigns of Amaziah and Azariah, also called Uzziah, kings of Judah. The Book of Jonah, however, is not properly a record of his prophecy, which consists of a few words: "Forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed." It is instead a history of his stubbornness and his disputing of God's commandments. Since Jonah is the subject of the book, he is unlikely to have been its author. The Book of Amos, on the other hand, is his prophecy.

Jeremiah, Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk prophesied in the time of Josiah.

Ezekiel, Daniel, Haggai, and Zechariah prophesied during the captivity.

When Joel and Malachi prophesied is not evident from their writings. The inscriptions or titles of their books, however, make one thing clear enough. The whole Scripture of the Old Testament was set out in the form we have it after the Jews returned from captivity in Babylon. This happened before the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, who had it translated into Greek by seventy men sent to him from Judea for that purpose.

The Church commends the books of the Apocrypha to us as profitable for our instruction, though not as canonical. If they may be trusted on this point, Esdras set out the Scripture in the form we have it. His own words in the second book of Esdras, chapter 14, verses 21 and following, show this. Speaking to God, he says: "Thy law is burnt; therefore no man knoweth the things which thou hast done, or the works that are to begin. But if I have found grace before thee, send down the Holy Spirit into me, and I shall write all that hath been done in the world since the beginning, which were written in thy law, that men may find thy path, and that they which will live in the latter days may live." And at verse 45: "And it came to pass, when the forty days were fulfilled, that the Highest spake, saying, 'The first that thou hast written, publish openly, that the worthy and unworthy may read it; but keep the seventy last, that thou mayest deliver them only to such as be wise among the people.'" So much, then, for the time at which the books of the Old Testament were written.

### The New Testament

The writers of the New Testament all lived within a single generation after Christ's ascension. All of them, except St. Paul and St. Luke, had either seen our Savior or been his disciples. Whatever they wrote is therefore as old as the time of the apostles. The Church's acceptance of these books as the apostles' writings, however, came somewhat later. The books of the Old Testament come down to us from no earlier a time than that of Esdras, who recovered them by the direction of God's Spirit after they had been lost. In the same way, the books of the New Testament cannot be traced to an earlier time than when the governors of the Church collected them. These governors approved the books and recommended them to us as the writings of the apostles and disciples whose names they bear. Copies of these books were few, and no single private person could easily have held them all.

The first list of all the books of both the Old and New Testaments appears in the Canons of the Apostles. That collection was supposedly compiled by Clement, the first bishop of Rome after St. Peter. But the attribution is only supposed, and many have questioned it. The first body we know of that recommended the Bible to the Christian churches as the writings of the prophets and apostles is the Council of Laodicea, held in the year 364 after Christ.

By that time, ambition had so far overtaken the great doctors of the Church that they no longer regarded emperors, even Christian ones, as shepherds of the people. They regarded them instead as sheep, and non-Christian emperors as wolves. They sought to pass off their doctrine not as the counsel and instruction of preachers but as the law of absolute governors. They even considered pious any deception that tended to make the people more obedient to Christian doctrine. Even so, I am persuaded that they did not falsify the Scriptures, although the copies of the New Testament were in the hands of the clergy alone. Had they intended to falsify them, they would surely have made those books more favorable than they are to their own power over Christian princes and over civil sovereignty.

I therefore see no reason to doubt that the Old and New Testaments as we now have them are true records of what the prophets and apostles did and said. The same may be true of some of the books called Apocrypha, if they were left out of the canon only because they are not found in Hebrew and not because their doctrine disagreed with the rest. After Alexander the Great conquered Asia, few learned Jews were not fluent in Greek. The seventy translators who rendered the Bible into Greek were all Hebrews, and we still have the works of Philo and Josephus, both Jews, written eloquently in Greek. But it is not the writer that makes a book canonical. It is the authority of the Church.

### Their Scope

These books were written by many different men, yet the writers were evidently all endowed with one and the same Spirit. They all work toward a single end: setting forth the rights of the Kingdom of God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

The Book of Genesis traces the genealogy of God's people from the creation of the world to their going down into Egypt. The other four books of Moses record the people's choice of God as their king and the laws he prescribed for their government. The books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and Samuel, up to the time of Saul, describe the acts of God's people until they cast off God's yoke and demanded a king like the neighboring nations. The rest of the Old Testament history traces the succession of David's line down to the captivity. From that line the restorer of the Kingdom of God was to spring, our blessed Savior, God the Son. The books of the prophets foretold his coming, and after him the evangelists wrote of his life and actions and of his claim to the kingdom while he lived on earth. Lastly, the Acts and Epistles of the apostles declare the coming of God the Holy Ghost. They also declare the authority he left with the apostles and their successors for guiding the Jews and inviting the Gentiles.

In sum, the histories and prophecies of the Old Testament and the Gospels and Epistles of the New Testament have had one and the same aim, which is to bring men to obedience to God. That obedience was owed first in Moses and the priests, second in the man Christ, and third in the apostles and the successors to apostolic power. These three, at different times, represented the person of God. In the Old Testament it was Moses and his successors, the high priests and kings of Judah. Then it was Christ himself during his life on earth. Finally it was the apostles and their successors, from the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Ghost descended on them, to the present day.

### The Question of the Authority of the Scriptures Stated

The various sects of the Christian religion have much disputed where the Scriptures derive their authority. The question is sometimes posed in other terms: how we know them to be the Word of God, or why we believe them to be so. The difficulty of resolving it arises chiefly from the imprecise words in which the question itself is framed.

Everyone believes that God is the first and original author of the Scriptures, so that is not what is in dispute. Again, no one can know they are God's Word, though all true Christians believe it, except those to whom God himself has revealed it supernaturally. The question is therefore wrongly posed when it asks about our knowledge. Finally, when the question is posed about our belief, no single general answer can be given, because some are moved to believe for one reason and others for another. The question, properly stated, is this: by what authority are the Scriptures made law?

### Their Authority and Interpretation

Insofar as the Scriptures do not differ from the laws of nature, they are without doubt the law of God. They carry their authority with them, legible to everyone who has the use of natural reason. But this is the same authority held by any moral doctrine consistent with reason, whose dictates are laws that were never made but are eternal.

If God himself makes them law, they are of the nature of written law. Written law binds only those to whom God has published it so sufficiently that no one can excuse himself by saying he did not know it was God's.

Some people have had no supernatural revelation that these books are God's, or that those who published them were sent by him. Such people are obliged to obey the books only by the authority of one whose commands already have the force of law. That authority is the authority of the commonwealth, residing in the sovereign, who alone has legislative power.

If it is not the legislative authority of the commonwealth that gives the Scriptures the force of law, it must be some other authority derived from God, either private or public. A private authority obliges only the person to whom God has been pleased to reveal it in particular. Many people, out of pride and ignorance, mistake their own dreams, extravagant fancies, and madness for testimonies of God's Spirit.
