Others, out of ambition, falsely claim such divine testimony against their own consciences. If everyone were obliged to accept as God's law whatever such individuals pressed upon them in the name of private inspiration or revelation, no divine law could be acknowledged at all.

A public authority must be that of either the commonwealth or the Church. If the Church is one person, it is the same thing as a commonwealth of Christians. It is called a commonwealth because it consists of men united in one person, their sovereign, and a church because it consists of Christian men united in one Christian sovereign. If the Church is not one person, then it has no authority whatsoever. It can neither command nor perform any action. It cannot have any power or right to anything, and it has no will, no reason, and no voice, for all these qualities belong to persons.

Now, if all Christians are not contained in one commonwealth, they are not one person, and no universal Church has any authority over them. In that case the universal Church does not make the Scriptures law. If, instead, all Christians do form one commonwealth, then all Christian monarchs and states are private persons. They would be liable to be judged, deposed, and punished by a universal sovereign of all Christendom. The question of the authority of the Scriptures thus comes down to this. Are Christian kings, and the sovereign assemblies in Christian commonwealths, absolute in their own territories, immediately under God? Or are they subject to one Vicar of Christ, set over the universal Church, who may judge, condemn, depose, and put them to death as he thinks expedient or necessary for the common good?

That question cannot be resolved without a closer consideration of the Kingdom of God. That same consideration will also show us where the authority to interpret Scripture lies. For whoever has the lawful power to make any writing law also has the power to approve or disapprove its interpretation.

## Chapter XXXIV. Of the Meaning of Spirit, Angel, and Inspiration in the Books of Holy Scripture

### Body and Spirit: How These Words Are Used in Scripture

All sound reasoning depends on words keeping a constant meaning. In the doctrine that follows, that meaning does not depend on the will of the writer, as it does in natural science, or on popular usage, as it does in ordinary conversation. It depends on the sense the words carry in Scripture. Before I go any further, therefore, I must establish from the Bible itself the meaning of those words whose ambiguity might make my conclusions obscure or open to dispute. I will begin with the words *body* and *spirit*, which the language of the Schools calls corporeal and incorporeal substances.

The word *body*, in its most general sense, means whatever fills or occupies some definite space or imagined place. A body does not depend on the imagination but is a real part of what we call the universe. Since the universe is the aggregate of all bodies, every real part of it is also a body, and nothing is properly a body unless it is also part of the universe, that aggregate of all bodies. Bodies are subject to change, which means they present a variety of appearances to the senses of living creatures. For this reason the same thing is also called *substance*, meaning a subject of various accidents. It sometimes moves and sometimes stands still, and to our senses it sometimes seems hot and sometimes cold, now of one color, smell, taste, or sound and now of another. This diversity of seeming is produced by the different ways bodies act on our sense organs. We attribute it to alterations in the bodies that act on us, and we call those alterations the *accidents* of those bodies. In this sense of the word, *substance* and *body* mean the same thing. When the words *incorporeal* and *substance* are joined, therefore, they cancel each other out, as if someone were to speak of an incorporeal body.

Ordinary people, however, do not call the whole universe body. They give that name only to the parts of it they can perceive by touch, as resisting their force, or by sight, as blocking their view. In common speech, therefore, air and airy substances are not usually counted as bodies. Whenever people feel their effects, they call them wind, or breath, or spirits, because the Latin word for these things is *spiritus*. So they speak of "vital and animal spirits" when they mean the airy substance inside a living creature that gives it life and motion. Then there are the idols of the brain, the images that show us bodies where there are none, as in a mirror, in a dream, or in a disordered mind while awake. These are, as the Apostle says of all idols in general, nothing. They are nothing at all in the place where they appear to be, and in the brain itself they are nothing but a commotion, caused either by the action of external objects or by the disorderly agitation of our sense organs. People whose work lies elsewhere than in searching out the causes of such images do not know on their own what to call them, and they can easily be persuaded by those whose learning they greatly respect. Some are led to call them bodies and to think them made of air condensed by a supernatural power, because the eye judges them to be corporeal. Others call them spirits, because touch finds nothing in the place where they appear to resist the fingers. The proper meaning of *spirit* in common speech, then, is either a subtle, fluid, invisible body, or a ghost or some other idol or phantasm of the imagination. Its metaphorical meanings, however, are many. Sometimes it stands for a disposition or inclination of the mind. A habit of contradicting what others say we call a spirit of contradiction; a tendency to impurity, an unclean spirit; perversity, a froward spirit; sullenness, a dumb spirit; and an inclination to godliness and the service of God, the Spirit of God. Sometimes it stands for an outstanding ability, or for some extraordinary passion or disease of the mind, as when great wisdom is called the spirit of wisdom and madmen are said to be possessed by a spirit.

I find no other meaning of *spirit* anywhere. Where none of these meanings can account for the word in Scripture, the passage lies beyond human understanding, and our faith in it consists not in holding an opinion but in submitting. This is the case wherever God is said to be a spirit, or wherever "the Spirit of God" means God himself. The nature of God is incomprehensible: we understand nothing of *what* he is, only *that* he is. The attributes we give him are therefore not meant to tell one another what he is, or to express our opinion of his nature. They express our desire to honor him with the names we consider most honorable among ourselves.

### The Spirit of God Taken in Scripture Sometimes for a Wind or Breath

Genesis 1:2 says, "The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." If the Spirit of God here means God himself, then motion is attributed to God, and with motion, place. Both are intelligible only of bodies, not of incorporeal substances. On that reading, the passage lies beyond our understanding, because we cannot conceive of anything moving that does not change place or that has no dimensions, and whatever has dimensions is body. The meaning of these words is best understood by comparing a similar passage, Genesis 8:1. There the earth was covered with water, as it had been in the beginning, and God intended to make the waters recede and uncover the dry land again. He used similar words: "I will bring my Spirit upon the earth, and the waters shall be diminished." In that passage *spirit* means a wind, that is, air or spirit in motion. It could be called the Spirit of God, as in the earlier passage, because it was God's work.

### Second, for Extraordinary Gifts of the Understanding

In Genesis 41:38, Pharaoh calls the wisdom of Joseph the Spirit of God. Joseph had advised him to find a wise and discreet man and set him over the land of Egypt, and Pharaoh replies, "Can we find such a man as this is, in whom is the Spirit of God?" In Exodus 28:3, God says, "Thou shalt speak to all that are wise-hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, to make Aaron garments, to consecrate him." Here extraordinary understanding, even if only in the making of garments, is called the Spirit of God because it is God's gift. The same usage appears again in Exodus 31:3–6 and 35:31. It also appears in Isaiah 11:2–3, where the prophet, speaking of the Messiah, says, "The Spirit of the Lord shall abide upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord." What is plainly meant is not so many ghosts but so many outstanding graces that God would give him.

### Third, for Extraordinary Passions

In the Book of Judges, extraordinary zeal and courage in defending God's people is called the Spirit of God, as when it stirred Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson to deliver Israel from servitude (Judges 3:10, 6:34, 11:29, 13:25, and 14:6 and 19). When Saul heard how insolently the Ammonites had treated the men of Jabesh-gilead, 1 Samuel 11:6 says that "the Spirit of God came upon Saul, and his anger was kindled greatly." The Latin has "his fury." A ghost is unlikely to be meant here. What is meant is an extraordinary zeal to punish the cruelty of the Ammonites. In the same way, the Spirit of God that came upon Saul when he was among the prophets who were praising God in songs and music (1 Samuel 19:20) should be understood as a sudden and unexpected zeal to join them in their devotions, not as a ghost.

### Fourth, for the Gift of Prediction by Dreams and Visions

In 1 Kings 22:24, the false prophet Zedekiah says to Micaiah, "Which way went the Spirit of the Lord from me to speak unto thee?" This cannot refer to a ghost. Micaiah had announced the outcome of the battle before the kings of Israel and Judah as something he had seen in a vision, not as a spirit speaking within him.

The books of the prophets show the same thing. The prophets spoke by the Spirit of God, that is, by a special grace of prediction. Yet their knowledge of the future came not from a ghost inside them but from some supernatural dream or vision.

### Fifth, for Life

Genesis 2:7 says, "God made man of the dust of the earth, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life," in the Latin *spiraculum vitae*, "and man became a living soul." The breath of life breathed in by God means no more than that God gave him life. Likewise, in Job 27:3, "as long as the Spirit of God is in my nostrils" means no more than "as long as I live." In Ezekiel 1:20, "the spirit of life was in the wheels" is equivalent to "the wheels were alive." And in Ezekiel 2:30, "the spirit entered into me, and set me on my feet" means "I recovered my vital strength." It does not mean that some ghost or incorporeal substance entered his body and took possession of it.

### Sixth, for a Subordination to Authority

In Numbers 11:17, God says to Moses, "I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee." "Them" means the seventy elders. Two of the seventy are then said to have prophesied in the camp. Some people complained about them, and Joshua asked Moses to stop them, which Moses refused to do. This shows that Joshua did not know they had received authority to prophesy, and that they prophesied according to the mind of Moses, that is, by a spirit, or authority, subordinate to his own.

In the same sense we read in Deuteronomy 34:9 that "Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom" because Moses had laid his hands on him, that is, because Moses had ordained him to carry on the work Moses himself had begun, namely bringing God's people into the promised land, which death had prevented Moses from finishing.

In the same sense, Romans 8:9 says, "If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." This means submission to Christ's doctrine, not the ghost of Christ. So too 1 John 4:2: "Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God." What is meant is the spirit of sincere Christianity, or submission to the central article of Christian faith, that Jesus is the Christ, and this cannot be interpreted as a ghost.

Likewise, the words of Luke 4:1, "And Jesus, full of the Holy Ghost," which Matthew 4:1 and Mark 1:12 express as "the Holy Spirit," may be understood as zeal to do the work God the Father had sent him to do. To interpret the phrase as a ghost would be to say that God himself, for that is what our Savior was, was filled with God, which is a highly improper and meaningless expression. How we came to translate *spirits* by the word *ghosts* I do not examine. That word signifies nothing in heaven or on earth except the imaginary inhabitants of the human brain. But this much I do say: the word *spirit* in the text signifies no such thing. Properly, it means a real substance. Metaphorically, it means some extraordinary ability or passion of the mind or of the body.

### Seventh, for Aerial Bodies

When Christ's disciples saw him walking on the sea (Matthew 14:26 and Mark 6:49), they supposed him to be a spirit, by which they meant an aerial body and not a phantasm. We are told that they all saw him, and that cannot be said of delusions of the brain. Such delusions are not shared by many people at once, as visible bodies are, but are peculiar to each person, because each person's imagination differs. A sight shared by all must therefore be a body. The same holds where the same apostles took him for a spirit in Luke 24:37. Something similar happens in Acts 12:15. When St. Peter was delivered from prison, the disciples would not believe it, and when the servant girl said he was at the door, they said it was his angel. Either this must mean a corporeal substance, or we must say that the disciples themselves followed the common opinion of both Jews and Gentiles that certain apparitions were not imaginary but real, and needed no human imagination in order to exist. The Jews called these spirits and angels, good or bad, just as the Greeks called the same things daemons. Some such apparitions may indeed be real and substantial. They may be subtle bodies that God can form by the same power by which he formed all things, and use as ministers and messengers (that is, angels) to declare his will and carry it out, when he pleases, in an extraordinary and supernatural manner. But once he has formed them, they are substances with dimensions. They take up room and can be moved from place to place, which is a property peculiar to bodies. They are therefore not incorporeal ghosts, meaning ghosts that are in no place, which is to say ghosts that are nowhere, which is to say things that seem to be something and are nothing. If, however, *corporeal* is taken in its most popular sense, for substances perceptible to our external senses, then an incorporeal substance is something real rather than imaginary: a thin, invisible substance that has the same dimensions as grosser bodies.

### What an Angel Is

The word *angel* means, in general, a messenger, and most often a messenger of God. A messenger of God is anything that makes known his extraordinary presence, that is, any extraordinary manifestation of his power, especially through a dream or vision.

Scripture says nothing about the creation of angels. It often repeats that they are spirits, but in Scripture and in the common usage of Jews and Gentiles alike, the word *spirit* has two meanings. Sometimes it means thin bodies, such as the air, the wind, and the vital and animal spirits of living creatures. Sometimes it means the images that arise in the imagination in dreams and visions. These images are not real substances but accidents of the brain. Yet when God raises them supernaturally to signify his will, they may properly be called God's messengers, that is, his angels.

The Gentiles commonly mistook the images of the brain for things that really existed outside themselves and did not depend on the imagination, and out of these images they formed their beliefs about daemons, good and evil. Because such things seemed really to exist, they called them substances, and because they could not touch them with their hands, they called them incorporeal. The Jews, with the exception of the sect of the Sadducees, generally held a similar opinion on the same grounds, although nothing in the Old Testament compelled them to it. God was sometimes pleased to produce apparitions in men's imaginations for his own service, and for that reason they were called his angels. The Jews believed these apparitions were substances that did not depend on the imagination and were permanent creatures of God. Those they thought were good to them they regarded as angels of God, and those they thought would harm them they called evil angels or evil spirits. Among these were the spirit of Python, that is, the spirit of divination, and the spirits that were thought to afflict madmen, lunatics, and epileptics. The Jews regarded anyone afflicted with these diseases as a demoniac.

But if we examine the passages in the Old Testament where angels are mentioned, we shall find that in most of them the word *angel* can mean nothing other than some image raised supernaturally in the imagination to signify God's presence in the performance of some supernatural work. In the remaining passages, therefore, where the nature of angels is not stated, the word may be understood in the same way.

For in the sixteenth chapter of Genesis the same apparition is called not only an angel but God. The figure that the seventh verse calls "the angel of the Lord" says to Hagar in the tenth verse, "I will multiply your descendants exceedingly." It speaks, that is, in the person of God. Nor was this apparition a figure shaped in the imagination; it was a voice. It is evident, then, that "angel" signifies nothing there but God himself, who caused Hagar to perceive, by supernatural means, a supernatural voice testifying to his special presence in that place. Why, then, may we not read the angels who appeared to Lot in the same way? In Genesis 19:13 they are called men; and although there were two of them, Lot speaks to them in verse 18 as though they were one, and addresses that one as God, for the words are, "Lot said unto them, Oh, not so, my Lord." Why should these not be understood as images of men supernaturally formed in the imagination, just as, in the earlier case, "angel" was understood to mean an imagined voice? When the angel called to Abraham out of heaven to stay his hand from slaying Isaac, in Genesis 22:11, there was no apparition at all, only a voice. That voice was nonetheless properly called a messenger, or angel, of God, because it declared God's will by supernatural means, and reading it this way spares us the labor of supposing any permanent ghosts. The angels Jacob saw on the ladder reaching to heaven, in Genesis 28:12, were a vision of his sleep, and therefore only imagination and a dream; yet because they were supernatural, and signs of God's special presence, those apparitions are not improperly called angels. The same must be understood of Genesis 31:11, where Jacob says, "The angel of the Lord appeared to me in my sleep." An apparition that comes to a man while he sleeps is what everyone calls a dream, whether the dream is natural or supernatural. And what Jacob there calls an angel was God himself, for the same angel says in verse 13, "I am the God of Bethel."

Likewise, in Exodus 14:9, the angel that went before the army of Israel to the Red Sea and then came behind it is, in verse 19, the Lord himself. He appeared not in the form of a beautiful man, but by day in the form of a pillar of cloud and by night in the form of a pillar of fire. Yet this pillar was the entire apparition, and the entire angel promised to Moses as the army's guide in Exodus 14:9. For this pillar of cloud is said to have descended, to have stood at the door of the tabernacle, and to have talked with Moses.

Here, then, motion and speech, which are commonly attributed to angels, are attributed to a cloud, because the cloud was a sign of God's presence. It was no less an angel than if it had borne the form of a man, or of a child of the greatest imaginable beauty, or had worn wings, as angels are usually painted, to the false instruction of ordinary people. It is not their shape but their function that makes them angels, and their function is to signify God's presence in supernatural operations. So when Moses, in Exodus 33:14, asked God to go along with the camp, as he had always done before the making of the golden calf, God did not answer "I will go," nor "I will send an angel in my place," but rather, "My presence shall go with you."

To mention every place in the Old Testament where the word "angel" appears would take too long. To take them all in at once, then, I say this: there is no text in that part of the Old Testament which the Church of England holds to be canonical from which we can conclude that there exists, or has ever been created, any permanent thing, understood by the name of spirit or angel, that lacks quantity. Nor is there any from which we can conclude that such a thing cannot be divided by the understanding, that is, considered as having parts, so that one part may be in one place and the next part in the place beside it. In sum, no such text shows that an angel is not corporeal, if by "body" we mean whatever is something, or is somewhere. In every place the sense will bear the interpretation of "angel" as "messenger." John the Baptist, for instance, is called an angel, and Christ is called the angel of the covenant; and, by the same analogy, the dove and the tongues of fire, being signs of God's special presence, might also be called angels. We do find two names of angels in Daniel, Gabriel and Michael. Yet it is clear from the text itself, in Daniel 12:1, that "Michael" means Christ, not as an angel but as a prince. As for Gabriel, he was nothing but a supernatural phantasm, like the apparitions shown to other holy men in their sleep, by which it seemed to Daniel in his dream that two saints were talking and one said to the other, "Gabriel, let us make this man understand his vision." God has no need to distinguish his heavenly servants by names, which are useful only to the short memories of mortals.

Nor is there any place in the New Testament from which it can be proved that angels are both permanent and incorporeal, except where the word stands for men whom God has made the messengers and ministers of his word or works. That angels are permanent may be gathered from the words of our Savior himself in Matthew 25:41, where he says that on the last day it shall be said to the wicked, "Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire prepared for the Devil and his angels." That passage plainly establishes the permanence of evil angels, unless we may take "the Devil and his angels" to mean the Church's adversaries and their agents. But it is then incompatible with their immateriality, because everlasting fire is no punishment to substances incapable of being acted upon or of suffering, and all incorporeal things are of that kind. So this text does not prove angels to be incorporeal. The same holds where Saint Paul says, in 1 Corinthians 6:3, "Do you not know that we shall judge the angels?"; where 2 Peter 2:4 says, "For if God did not spare the angels that sinned, but cast them down into hell"; and where Jude, in verse 6, says, "And the angels who did not keep their first estate, but left their own dwelling, he has reserved in everlasting chains under darkness until the judgment of the last day." Though these passages prove that the angelic nature is permanent, they confirm that it is material as well. Matthew 22:30 likewise says, "In the resurrection men neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven." But in the resurrection men will be permanent and not incorporeal, and so, therefore, are the angels.

There are various other places from which a similar conclusion may be drawn. To anyone who understands what the words "substance" and "incorporeal" mean, taking "incorporeal" not as "a thin, rarefied body" but as "not a body," the two words imply a contradiction. To say that an angel or spirit is, in that sense, an incorporeal substance is in effect to say that there is no angel or spirit at all. Considering, then, what the word "angel" means in the Old Testament, and the nature of the dreams and visions that come to men in the ordinary course of nature, I was inclined to the opinion that angels were nothing but supernatural apparitions of the imagination, raised by the special and extraordinary operation of God in order to make his presence and his commandments known to mankind, and chiefly to his own people. But the many passages of the New Testament, and our Savior's own words, in texts where there is no suspicion that Scripture has been corrupted, have extorted from my feeble reason an acknowledgment and a belief that there are also angels that are substantial and permanent. But to believe that they are in no place, which is to say nowhere, which is to say nothing, as those who would have them incorporeal are saying, however indirectly, is a belief that Scripture cannot be made to prove.

**What Inspiration Is**

The meaning of the word "inspiration" depends on the meaning of the word "spirit." If it is taken literally, inspiration is nothing but the blowing of some thin and subtle air, or wind, into a man, in the way a man fills a bladder with his breath. If, on the other hand, spirits are not corporeal and exist only in the imagination, then inspiration is nothing but the blowing in of a phantasm, which is both improper to say and impossible, since phantasms are not anything but only seem to be something. The word is therefore used in Scripture only metaphorically. When Genesis 2:7 says that God breathed into man the breath of life, nothing more is meant than that God gave him vital motion. We are not to think that God first made a living breath and then blew it into Adam after Adam was formed, whether that breath was real or only apparent. We are to understand it as Acts 17:25 puts it: "he gave him life and breath," that is, he made him a living creature. And when 2 Timothy 3:16 says that "all Scripture is given by inspiration of God," speaking there of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, it is an easy metaphor signifying that God inclined the spirit, or mind, of those writers to write what would be useful in teaching, reproving, correcting, and instructing men in the way of righteous living. But when Saint Peter says, in 2 Peter 1:21, that "prophecy came not in old times by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit," the Holy Spirit means the voice of God in a supernatural dream or vision, which is not inspiration. Nor, when our Savior breathed on his disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit," was that breath the Spirit; it was a sign of the spiritual graces he gave them. And although it is said of many, and of our Savior himself, that they were full of the Holy Spirit, that fullness is not to be understood as an infusion of the substance of God, but as an accumulation of his gifts: the gift of holiness of life, the gift of tongues, and the like, whether acquired supernaturally or through study and diligence, since in every case they are gifts of God. Likewise, where God says in Joel 2:28, "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions," we are not to take this literally, as though his Spirit were like water, capable of being poured out or poured in. We are to take it as though God had promised to give them prophetic dreams and visions. To use the word "infused" in its literal sense when speaking of the graces of God is to misuse it, for those graces are virtues, not bodies to be carried from place to place and poured into men as into barrels.

In the same way, to take inspiration in its literal sense, or to say that good spirits entered into men to make them prophesy, or that evil spirits entered into those who became frenzied, lunatic, or epileptic, is not to take the word in the sense Scripture gives it. For "spirit" there is taken to mean the power of God working through causes unknown to us. So too, in Acts 2:2, the wind said to have filled the house where the apostles were assembled on the day of Pentecost is not to be understood as the Holy Spirit, which is the Deity itself, but as an external sign of God's special working on their hearts, to produce in them the inward graces and holy virtues he judged necessary for the performance of their apostleship.

## Chapter XXXV. Of the Meaning in Scripture of Kingdom of God, of Holy, Sacred, and Sacrament

In the writings of theologians, and especially in sermons and devotional treatises, the phrase "the Kingdom of God" is most often taken to mean eternal happiness after this life in the highest heaven, which they also call the Kingdom of Glory. Sometimes it is taken to mean sanctification, which is the pledge or down payment on that happiness and which they call the Kingdom of Grace. It is never taken to mean monarchy, that is, the sovereign power of God over subjects acquired by their own consent, even though that is the proper meaning of the word "kingdom."

I find, on the contrary, that in most places of Scripture the Kingdom of God means a kingdom in the proper sense of the word. It was constituted in a special manner by the votes of the people of Israel, who chose God for their king by a covenant made with him, in return for God's promise that they would possess the land of Canaan. Only seldom is the phrase used metaphorically, and only in the New Testament. In those cases it means dominion over sin, because that kind of dominion is something every subject in the Kingdom of God will possess, and possess without any injury to the sovereign.

From the very Creation, God not only reigned over all men naturally, by his might, but also had particular subjects of his own, whom he commanded by a voice, as one man speaks to another. It was in this manner that he reigned over Adam and commanded him not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Adam did not obey. By tasting the fruit he presumed to be like God, judging between good and evil by his own sense rather than by his Creator's command, and his punishment was to be deprived of the state of eternal life in which God had first created him. Afterward God punished Adam's descendants for their vices with a universal flood that destroyed all but eight people, and in those eight consisted the Kingdom of God of that time.

After this it pleased God to speak to Abraham and to make a covenant with him, recorded in the seventeenth chapter of Genesis, in these words: "I will establish my covenant between me and you and your descendants after you, throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your descendants after you. And I will give to you and to your descendants after you the land in which you are now a stranger, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession." As a memorial and token of this covenant, God ordained in the same chapter the sacrament of circumcision. This is what is called the Old Covenant, or Old Testament, and it consists of a contract between God and Abraham, by which Abraham bound himself and his descendants to be subject, in a special manner, to God's positive law, meaning the particular laws God chose to enact for them. To the moral law Abraham was already bound, as if by an oath of allegiance. And although God is not yet given the name of king, nor are Abraham and his descendants called a kingdom, the thing itself is the same: the institution, by agreement, of God's special sovereignty over the descendants of Abraham. When Moses renewed this same covenant at Mount Sinai, it was expressly called a special kingdom of God over the Jews. Yet it is Abraham, not Moses, whom St. Paul calls in his Letter to the Romans "the father of the faithful," meaning of those who are loyal and do not violate the allegiance they swore to God, first through circumcision and later, under the New Covenant, through baptism.

At the foot of Mount Sinai, Moses renewed this covenant. In the nineteenth chapter of Exodus, the Lord commands Moses to speak to the people in these terms: "If you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, then you shall be a peculiar people to me, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a sacerdotal kingdom and a holy nation." Where the text says "a peculiar people," the Latin Vulgate has *peculium de cunctis populis*, a special possession out of all peoples. The English translation made at the beginning of the reign of King James has "a peculiar treasure unto me above all nations," and the French Geneva Bible has "the most precious jewel of all nations." The truest of these is the first, because St. Paul himself confirms it. In his Letter to Titus, alluding to this passage, he says that our blessed Saviour "gave himself for us, that he might purify us to himself, a peculiar people," meaning an extraordinary one. The Greek word there is *periousios*, which is commonly set against the word *epiousios*. Just as *epiousios* means ordinary, everyday, or, as in the Lord's Prayer, "for daily use," so *periousios* means what is surplus, stored up, and enjoyed in a special way, which the Latins call *peculium*. This reading of the passage is confirmed by the reason God gives for it in the words immediately following: "for all the earth is mine." It is as if he said, "All the nations of the world are mine, but not in the way that you are mine; you are mine in a special manner. They are all mine by reason of my power, but you shall be mine by your own consent and covenant." That covenant is an addition to the ordinary title God holds over all nations.

The same reading is confirmed in express words by the same text: "You shall be to me a sacerdotal kingdom and a holy nation." The Vulgate renders this as *Regnum Sacerdotale*, a priestly kingdom. This agrees with the translation of the parallel passage in the First Letter of Peter, *Sacerdotium Regale*, a royal priesthood. It also agrees with the institution itself, under which no one might enter the *Sanctum Sanctorum*, the Holy of Holies, except the High Priest; that is to say, no one but the High Priest might inquire God's will directly of God himself. The English translation just mentioned, following the Geneva version, reads "a kingdom of priests." Either this refers to the succession of one high priest after another, or else it agrees neither with St. Peter nor with the way the high priesthood was actually exercised. For no one except the High Priest was ever permitted to inform the people of God's will, and no assembly of priests was ever allowed to enter the Holy of Holies.

The title "a holy nation" confirms the same point. "Holy" means what belongs to God by a special right, not by a general one. As the text itself says, all the earth is God's, yet the whole earth is not called holy, but only that which is set apart for his special service, as the nation of the Jews was. It is therefore plain enough from this single passage that the Kingdom of God properly means a commonwealth, instituted by the consent of those who were to be subject to it, for their civil government. It was meant to regulate their conduct not only toward God their king, but also toward one another in matters of justice, and toward other nations in both peace and war. It was, properly speaking, a kingdom in which God was king and in which the High Priest, after the death of Moses, was to be his sole viceroy, or lieutenant.

Many other passages clearly prove the same thing. The first is in the eighth chapter of the First Book of Samuel. When the elders of Israel, aggrieved by the corruption of Samuel's sons, demanded a king, Samuel was displeased and prayed to the Lord, and the Lord answered him: "Listen to the voice of the people, for they have not rejected you; they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." From this it is evident that God himself was then their king, and that Samuel did not command the people but only conveyed to them whatever God from time to time instructed him to.

Again, in the twelfth chapter of the same book, Samuel says to the people: "When you saw that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, came against you, you said to me, 'No, a king shall reign over us,' when the Lord your God was your king." It is plain that God was their king and governed the civil affairs of their commonwealth.

After the Israelites had rejected God, the prophets foretold that his reign would be restored. Isaiah says: "Then the moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of Hosts shall reign in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem." Here he speaks expressly of God's reign in Zion and Jerusalem, that is, on earth. Micah says: "And the Lord shall reign over them in Mount Zion," and this Mount Zion is in Jerusalem, upon the earth. And in the twentieth chapter of Ezekiel, the Lord says: "As I live, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with fury poured out, I will rule over you," and a few verses later, "I will make you pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant." The meaning is: I will reign over you, and I will hold you to the covenant you made with me through Moses, which you broke when you rebelled against me in the days of Samuel and chose another king.

In the New Testament, the angel Gabriel says of our Saviour in the first chapter of Luke: "He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord shall give him the throne of his father David; and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." This, too, is a kingdom on earth. For claiming it, Jesus was put to death as an enemy of Caesar. The inscription on his cross read "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews"; he was crowned in mockery with a crown of thorns; and in the seventeenth chapter of Acts it is said of the disciples, for proclaiming him, that "they all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus." The Kingdom of God is therefore a real kingdom, not a metaphorical one, and it is understood that way not only in the Old Testament but in the New. When we say, "For thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory," it should be understood of the kingdom God holds by virtue of our covenant, not by the right of his power, since God always has a kingdom of the latter kind. It would be superfluous to pray "Thy kingdom come" unless the words referred to the restoration by Christ of the Kingdom of God, which had been interrupted by the Israelites' revolt when they elected Saul. Nor would it have been fitting to say "The kingdom of heaven is at hand," or to pray "Thy kingdom come," if that kingdom had continued without interruption.

So many other passages confirm this interpretation that it would be a wonder it has not received more attention, were it not that it sheds too much light for Christian kings on their right to govern the Church. Those who have noticed this translate "sacerdotal kingdom" as "a kingdom of priests," though by the same logic they might just as well translate "a royal priesthood," as St. Peter has it, into "a priesthood of kings." And where they render "a peculiar people" as "a precious jewel" or "treasure," one might just as well call a general's own special regiment or company his precious jewel, or his treasure.

In short, the Kingdom of God is a civil kingdom. It consisted, first, in the obligation of the people of Israel to the laws that Moses would bring them from Mount Sinai, and afterward to the laws that the High Priest of the time would deliver to them from before the cherubim in the Holy of Holies. When that kingdom was cast off with the election of Saul, the prophets foretold that Christ would restore it. We pray daily for its restoration when we say in the Lord's Prayer, "Thy kingdom come," and we acknowledge its right when we add, "For thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory, for ever and ever, Amen." The apostles' preaching was the proclamation of that kingdom, and the teachers of the Gospel prepare men to enter it. To embrace the Gospel, which is to promise obedience to God's government, is to be in the Kingdom of Grace, because God has freely given, *gratis*, to those who embrace it the power to become his subjects, that is, his children, hereafter, when Christ shall come in majesty to judge the world and actually to govern his own people, which is called the Kingdom of Glory. If the Kingdom of God, which is also called the Kingdom of Heaven because of the glory and surpassing height of its throne, were not a kingdom that God exercised on earth through his lieutenants or vicars, who deliver his commandments to the people, there would never have been so much contention and war over the question of who it is through whom God speaks to us. Nor would so many priests have troubled themselves about spiritual jurisdiction, or any king have denied it to them.

From this literal interpretation of the Kingdom of God there also follows the true interpretation of the word "holy." In God's kingdom it corresponds to what men in their own kingdoms commonly call "public," or "the king's."

The king of any country is the public person, the representative of all his subjects, and God, the King of Israel, was the Holy One of Israel. A nation subject to one earthly sovereign is the nation of that sovereign, that is, of the public person. So the Jews, who were God's nation, were called in the nineteenth chapter of Exodus "a holy nation." For "holy" always means either God himself or what belongs to God as his property, just as "public" always means either the person of the commonwealth itself or something that belongs to the commonwealth in such a way that no private person can claim any ownership of it.

Therefore the Sabbath, being God's day, is a holy day; the Temple, being God's house, is a holy house; sacrifices, tithes, and offerings, being God's tribute, are holy duties; priests, prophets, and anointed kings under Christ, being God's ministers, are holy men; the heavenly ministering spirits, being God's messengers, are holy angels; and so on. Wherever the word "holy" is used in its proper sense, it always signifies some form of ownership acquired by consent. When we say "Hallowed be thy name," we are simply praying to God for grace to keep the first commandment, to "have no other gods but him." All mankind is God's nation by ownership, yet only the Jews were a holy nation. The reason can only be that they became his property by covenant.

In Scripture the word "profane" is usually taken to mean the same as "common," and so their opposites, "holy" and "proper," must in the Kingdom of God mean the same thing as well. Figuratively, however, men are also called holy who led lives so godly that they seemed to have abandoned all worldly ambitions and devoted and given themselves wholly to God. In the proper sense, whatever God makes holy by appropriating it or setting it apart for his own use is said to be sanctified by God, as the seventh day is in the fourth commandment, and as the elect in the New Testament were said to be sanctified when they were endowed with the spirit of godliness. Whatever is made holy by the dedication of men, and given to God so as to be used only in his public service, is also called "sacred" and is said to be consecrated. Such are temples and other houses of public prayer, together with their furnishings and vessels, as well as priests and ministers, sacrificial victims, offerings, and the outward material of the sacraments.

There are degrees of holiness. Among the things set apart for the service of God, some may be set apart again for a closer and more special service. The whole nation of Israel was a people holy to God, yet among the Israelites the tribe of Levi was a holy tribe; among the Levites, the priests were holier still; and among the priests, the High Priest was the most holy. In the same way, the land of Judea was the Holy Land, but the Holy City, where God was to be worshipped, was holier; the Temple was holier than the city; and the Holy of Holies was holier than the rest of the Temple.

A sacrament is the separation of some visible thing from common use and its consecration to God's service, as a sign either of our admission into the Kingdom of God, to be counted among his special people, or as a commemoration of that admission. In the Old Testament the sign of admission was circumcision; in the New Testament it is baptism. In the Old Testament the commemoration was the eating of the Paschal lamb at a fixed time each year, which reminded the people of the night on which they were delivered from their bondage in Egypt. In the New Testament it is the celebration of the Lord's Supper, which reminds us of our deliverance from the bondage of sin through our blessed Saviour's death on the cross. The sacraments of admission are to be used only once, because only one admission is needed. But because we need to be reminded often of our deliverance and of our allegiance, the sacraments of commemoration must be repeated. These are the principal sacraments, and they are, as it were, the solemn oaths by which we pledge our allegiance. There are also other consecrations that may be called sacraments, insofar as the word implies only consecration to God's service. But insofar as it implies an oath or promise of allegiance to God, there were no others in the Old Testament besides circumcision and the Passover, and there are no others in the New Testament besides baptism and the Lord's Supper.

## Chapter XXXVI. Of the Word of God, and of Prophets

### What Is Meant by "Word"

When we speak of the Word of God, or the word of a man, we do not mean a part of speech of the kind grammarians call a noun or a verb, nor any single sound that signifies nothing until it is joined with other words. We mean a complete utterance or discourse, by which the speaker affirms, denies, commands, promises, threatens, wishes, or asks a question. In this sense the term is not *vocabulum*, the Latin for a single word, but *sermo*, or in Greek *logos*, meaning a speech, a discourse, or a saying.

### The Words Spoken by God and the Words Spoken About God Are Both Called God's Word in Scripture

The phrase "the word of God," or "the word of a man," can also refer either to the speaker or to the subject. When it refers to the speaker, it means the words that God or a man has spoken. In this sense, when we say "the Gospel of St. Matthew," we understand Matthew to be its writer. When it refers to the subject, it means what the words are about. In this sense, when the Bible speaks of "the words of the days of the kings of Israel" or "of Judah," it means that the deeds done in those days were the subject of those words. In the Greek of the Scriptures, which retains many Hebrew idioms, "the Word of God" often means not what was spoken by God but what is spoken about God and his government, which is the doctrine of religion. This usage is so established that to say *logos theou*, "word of God," is the same as to say *theologia*, the doctrine we usually call divinity. The following passages make this clear. In Acts 13:46 we read: "Then Paul and Barnabas grew bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you; but seeing you put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles." What is called the Word of God here was the doctrine of the Christian religion, as the preceding verses plainly show. In Acts 5:20, an angel says to the apostles, "Go, stand and speak in the Temple all the words of this life." By "the words of this life" is meant the doctrine of the Gospel. This is evident from what they did in the Temple, which is recorded in the last verse of the same chapter: "Daily in the Temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Christ Jesus." Jesus Christ was therefore the subject of this word of life, or, what amounts to the same thing, the subject of the words of eternal life that our Savior offered them. So too in Acts 15:7 the Word of God is called the word of the Gospel, because it contains the doctrine of the kingdom of Christ. In Romans 10:8–9 the same word is called the word of faith, which the passage itself explains as the doctrine that Christ has come and has been raised from the dead. Likewise, in Matthew 13:19, "When anyone hears the word of the kingdom" refers to the doctrine of the kingdom taught by Christ. In Acts 12:24 this same word is said "to grow and multiply." That phrase is easy to understand of the doctrine of the Gospel, but it is hard and strange to understand of the voice or speech of God. In the same sense, "the doctrine of devils" in 1 Timothy 4:1 does not mean the words of any devil. It means the doctrine of the heathen concerning daemons, and concerning those phantasms they worshipped as gods.

Given these two meanings of "the Word of God" in Scripture, the whole of Scripture is clearly the Word of God in the second sense, where the phrase means the doctrine of the Christian religion. In the first sense it is not. For example, the words from "I am the Lord thy God" to the end of the Ten Commandments were spoken by God to Moses, yet the preface, "God spoke these words, and said," must be understood as the words of the man who wrote the sacred history. The Word of God, taken as what God has spoken, is understood sometimes properly and sometimes metaphorically. Taken properly, it means the words he has spoken to his prophets. Taken metaphorically, it means his wisdom, power, and eternal decree in making the world. In this sense the *fiats*, the "let there be" commands of Genesis 1, are the Word of God: "Let there be light," "Let there be a firmament," "Let us make man," and the rest. In the same sense John 1:3 says, "All things were made by it, and without it was nothing made that was made." Hebrews 1:3 says, "He upholds all things by the word of his power," which means by the power of his word, or simply by his power. Hebrews 11:3 says, "The worlds were framed by the word of God," and many other passages speak in the same way. The Latins used their word *fate* in this same sense, for *fatum* properly means "that which has been spoken."

### Second, for the Effect of His Word

Second, the Word of God is taken for the effect of his word, meaning the very thing that his word affirms, commands, threatens, or promises. In Psalm 105:19, Joseph is said to have been kept in prison "until his word came to pass." This means until the event he had foretold to Pharaoh's butler in Genesis 40:13, the man's restoration to his office, had actually happened. "His word came" means that the thing itself had come about. Likewise in 1 Kings 18:36, Elijah says to God, "I have done all these thy words," instead of "I have done all these things at thy word," or command. In Jeremiah 17:15, "Where is the word of the Lord?" stands for "Where is the evil he threatened?" In Ezekiel 12:28, "None of my words shall be prolonged any more," the "words" are the things God had promised his people. In the New Testament, Matthew 24:35 reads: "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away." This means that nothing I have promised or foretold will fail to come to pass.

It is in this sense that St. John the Evangelist, and I believe St. John alone, calls our Savior himself, as he was in the flesh, "the Word of God." John 1:14 says, "The Word was made flesh." This was the word or promise that Christ would come into the world, he "who in the beginning was with God." In other terms, it was the purpose of God the Father from the beginning to send God the Son into the world to show men the way of eternal life, but that purpose was not carried out, and the Son was not actually made flesh, until that time. Our Savior is therefore called "the Word" not because he was the promise but because he was the thing promised. Those who take this passage as grounds for calling him the *Verb* of God only make the text more obscure. They might as well call him the Noun of God. By "verb," just as by "noun," people understand nothing but a part of speech, a voice, a sound. Such a thing neither affirms, nor denies, nor commands, nor promises, and it is no substance at all, whether bodily or spiritual. It therefore cannot be said to be either God or man, whereas our Savior is both. This Word, which St. John in his Gospel says was with God, is called "the Word of life" in the first verse of his First Epistle and "the eternal life, which was with the Father" in the second. He can therefore be called the Word in no other sense than the one in which he is called eternal life, as "he who has procured eternal life for us" by coming in the flesh. So too in Revelation 19:13 the apostle, speaking of Christ clothed in a garment dipped in blood, says that his name is "the Word of God." This should be understood as though he had said that Christ's name was "He who has come according to the purpose of God from the beginning, and according to his word and the promises delivered by the prophets." There is nothing here about the incarnation of a word. The passage concerns the incarnation of God the Son, who is called the Word because his incarnation fulfilled the promise, just as the Holy Ghost is called "the Promise" in Acts 1:4 and Luke 24:49.

### Third, for the Words of Reason and Equity

There are also places in Scripture where "the Word of God" signifies words that accord with reason and equity, even when they are spoken by someone who was neither a prophet nor a holy man. Pharaoh Necho was an idolater. Yet his words to the good King Josiah, in which he advised him through messengers not to oppose his march against Carchemish, are said to have come from the mouth of God, and Josiah, who refused to heed them, was killed in the battle. This account appears in 2 Chronicles 35:21–23. When the same history is told in the First Book of Esdras, it is not Pharaoh but Jeremiah who speaks these words to Josiah from the mouth of the Lord. But we must trust the canonical Scripture, whatever may be written in the Apocrypha.

The Word of God is also to be taken for the dictates of reason and equity when Scripture says that it is written in the human heart, as in Psalm 36:31, Jeremiah 31:33, Deuteronomy 30:11 and 14, and many similar passages.

### The Various Senses of the Word "Prophet"

In Scripture the word *prophet* sometimes means a *prolocutor*, a spokesman who speaks from God to man or from man to God. Sometimes it means a *predictor*, one who foretells things to come. And sometimes it means one who speaks incoherently, like a person out of his mind. It is most often used for one who speaks from God to the people. In this sense Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others were prophets. In this sense, too, the High Priest was a prophet, since he alone entered the *Sanctum Sanctorum*, the Holy of Holies, to inquire of God, and it was his duty to declare God's answer to the people. That is why, when Caiaphas said it was expedient that one man should die for the people, St. John says in his Gospel (11:51): "He spoke this not of himself, but being High Priest that year, he prophesied that one man should die for the nation." Those who taught the people in Christian congregations are also said to prophesy in 1 Corinthians 14:3. In the same sense, God says to Moses about Aaron in Exodus 4:16, "He shall be your spokesman to the people; he shall be to you a mouth, and you shall be to him in place of God." What is called "spokesman" here is rendered "prophet" in Exodus 7:1: "See," says God, "I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet."

In the sense of speaking from man to God, Abraham is called a prophet in Genesis 20:7, where God speaks to Abimelech in a dream: "Now therefore restore the man his wife, for he is a prophet, and shall pray for you." From this it may also be inferred that the name of prophet may fittingly be given to those in Christian churches who are called to say public prayers on behalf of the congregation. In the same sense, the prophets who came down from the high place, or hill of God, with a psaltery, a tabret (a small hand drum), a pipe, and a harp (1 Samuel 10:5–6), with Saul among them (verse 10), are said to prophesy, because they praised God publicly in that manner. In the same sense Miriam is called a prophetess in Exodus 15:20. The word must be understood the same way in 1 Corinthians 11:4–5, where St. Paul speaks of "every man praying or prophesying with his head covered" and "every woman that prays or prophesies with her head uncovered." Prophecy in that passage means no more than praising God in psalms and holy songs, which women might do in church, though it was not lawful for them to address the congregation. It is also in this sense that the heathen poets who composed hymns and other poems in honor of their gods were called *vates*, or prophets, as everyone versed in the literature of the Gentiles knows well. Titus 1:12 makes this evident as well, where St. Paul says of the Cretans that a prophet of their own called them liars. Paul did not consider their poets to be prophets. He was acknowledging that the word "prophet" was commonly used for those who celebrated the honor of God in verse.

### Prediction of Future Contingent Events Is Not Always Prophecy

When prophecy means prediction, the foretelling of future contingent events that may or may not come to pass, then the prophets include not only God's spokesmen, who foretold to others what God had foretold to them. They also include all those impostors who claim to foretell future events, either with the help of familiar spirits or by superstitiously reading past events as signs, assigning them false causes and expecting similar events to follow. As I explained earlier in Chapter 12 of this discourse, there are many kinds of these people. Among ordinary men they gain more reputation as prophets from a single chance event, twisted to suit their claims, than they can lose through any number of failures. Prophecy is not an art. Nor, when it means prediction, is it a permanent vocation. It is an extraordinary and temporary employment from God, most often given to good men but sometimes to wicked ones. The woman of Endor, who is said to have had a familiar spirit, by which she raised a phantasm of Samuel and foretold Saul's death, was not a prophetess on that account. She had no knowledge by which she could raise such a phantasm, nor does it appear that God commanded it to be raised. God merely guided that imposture so that it became a means of terrifying and discouraging Saul, and consequently of the defeat in which he fell. As for incoherent speech, the Gentiles took it for a kind of prophecy, because the prophets of their oracles were intoxicated by a spirit or vapor rising from the cave of the Pythian oracle at Delphi and were, for the time, genuinely mad and spoke like madmen. Their loose words could be made to fit any outcome whatever. In the same way, the philosophers said that all bodies are made of *materia prima*, a formless prime matter capable of taking any shape. I find the word used in this sense in Scripture as well, in 1 Samuel 18:10: "And the evil spirit came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of the house."

### How God Has Spoken to the Prophets

The word "prophet" has many meanings in Scripture, but the most frequent is a person to whom God speaks directly the message that the prophet is to deliver on God's behalf to some other man or to the people. This raises the question of how God speaks to such a prophet. Some may ask whether God can properly be said to have a voice and a language when he cannot properly be said to have a tongue or any other organs as a man has. The prophet David argues: "Shall he that made the eye not see? Shall he that made the ear not hear?" But David may have said this not to describe God's nature, which is the usual reading of such language, but to express our intention of honoring him. To see and to hear are honorable attributes, and they may be ascribed to God to declare his almighty power as far as our capacity can conceive it. If such language were taken in its strict and proper sense, one might argue that because God made every part of the human body, he must also put those parts to the same uses that we do. Many of those uses would be so unseemly that attributing them to him would be the greatest insult in the world. We must therefore interpret God's speaking directly to men as whatever means, of whatever kind, God uses to make them understand his will. Those means are many, and they are to be sought only in Holy Scripture. Scripture often says that God spoke to this or that person without describing the manner. But many passages also describe the signs by which people were to recognize his presence and his command, and from these we may understand how he spoke to many of the others.

### To the Extraordinary Prophets of the Old Testament He Spoke by Dreams or Visions

Scripture does not say how God spoke to Adam and Eve, to Cain, or to Noah. Nor does it say how he spoke to Abraham until Abraham left his own country and came to Shechem in the land of Canaan. At that point, in Genesis 12:7, God is said to have appeared to him. This is one way in which God made his presence known: by an apparition, or vision. Again, in Genesis 15:1, the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision, which means that something appeared as a sign of God's presence and spoke to him as God's messenger. The Lord appeared to Abraham again in Genesis 18:1 through an apparition of three angels; to Abimelech in Genesis 20:3 in a dream; to Lot in Genesis 19:1 through an apparition of two angels; to Hagar in Genesis 21:17 through an apparition of one angel; and to Abraham once more in Genesis 22:11 through a voice from heaven. In Genesis 26:24 he appeared to Isaac at night, that is, in his sleep, or by a dream. In Genesis 18:12 he appeared to Jacob in a dream, for the text says, "Jacob dreamed that he saw a ladder," and so on, and in Genesis 32:1 he appeared to Jacob in a vision of angels. To Moses, in Exodus 3:2, he appeared as a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. After the time of Moses, wherever the Old Testament specifies how God spoke directly to a man, he always spoke by a vision or a dream. He spoke this way to Gideon, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the rest of the prophets. He often spoke the same way in the New Testament, as to Joseph, to St. Peter, to St. Paul, and to St. John the Evangelist in the Apocalypse.

Only to Moses did God speak in a more extraordinary manner, on Mount Sinai and in the Tabernacle. He also spoke in that manner to the High Priest in the Tabernacle and in the Holy of Holies of the Temple. Moses, and the High Priests after him, were prophets of a more eminent rank and of a higher degree in God's favor. God himself declares in express words that he spoke to other prophets in dreams and visions, but to his servant Moses as a man speaks to his friend. The words are these, from Numbers 12:6–8: "If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known to him in a vision, and will speak to him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all my house; with him I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in dark speeches; and the likeness of the Lord shall he behold." And in Exodus 33:11: "The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." Yet even this speaking of God to Moses took place through the mediation of an angel or angels, as Acts 7:35 and 53 and Galatians 3:19 expressly show. It was therefore a vision, though a clearer one than other prophets received. Consistent with this, where God says in Deuteronomy 13:1, "If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams," the second phrase merely interprets the first. In Joel 2:28, "Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions," the word *prophesy* is again explained by *dream* and *vision*. God spoke to Solomon in the same manner when he promised him wisdom, riches, and honor, for the text says in 1 Kings 3:15, "And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream." In general, then, the extraordinary prophets of the Old Testament received the Word of God only through their dreams or visions, that is, through the images that came to them in sleep or in a state of ecstasy. In every true prophet these images were supernatural. In false prophets they were either natural or invented.

Yet these same prophets were also said to speak by the Spirit. In Zechariah 7:12 the prophet, speaking of the Jews, says: "They made their hearts as hard as adamant, so that they would not hear the law and the words which the Lord of Hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets." (Adamant was the old name for the hardest of all stones.) This makes it plain that speaking by the Spirit, or by inspiration, was not some particular manner of God's speaking distinct from vision. Those who were said to speak by the Spirit were extraordinary prophets, men who needed a particular commission for every new message, or, what amounts to the same thing, a new dream or vision.

### To Supreme Prophets of Permanent Calling, God Spoke in the Old Testament from the Mercy Seat, in a Manner the Scripture Does Not Describe

Among the prophets of the Old Testament who held their office by a permanent calling, some were supreme and some subordinate. The first supreme prophet was Moses. After him came the High Priest, each in his turn, for as long as the priesthood held sovereign power. When the people of the Jews later rejected God, so that he should no longer reign over them, the kings who submitted themselves to God's government became his chief prophets as well, and the office of High Priest became a ministerial one, serving under them. When God was to be consulted, the priests put on the holy vestments and inquired of the Lord as the king commanded them, and they were removed from office whenever the king saw fit. King Saul, in 1 Samuel 13:9, commanded the burnt offering to be brought to him. In 1 Samuel 14:18 he commands the priest to bring the Ark near him, and in the next verse he tells him to leave it alone, because he saw an opportunity to strike at his enemies. In the same chapter Saul asks counsel of God. In the same way King David, after he had been anointed but before he had possession of the kingdom, is said in 1 Samuel 23:2 to "inquire of the Lord" whether he should fight the Philistines at Keilah; and in verse 10 David commands the priest to bring him the ephod, the priestly garment worn when consulting God, so that he might inquire whether he should remain in Keilah or not. And King Solomon, in 1 Kings 2:27, took the priesthood from Abiathar and gave it, as verse 35 records, to Zadok. Moses, then, and the High Priests, and the pious kings, who on every extraordinary occasion inquired of God how they should conduct themselves or what outcome they were to expect, were all sovereign prophets.

But in what manner God spoke to them is not made clear. To say that when Moses went up to God on Mount Sinai he had a dream or vision like those of other prophets contradicts the distinction God himself drew between Moses and the other prophets in Numbers 12:6–8. To say that God spoke or appeared as he is in his own nature is to deny his infinity, his invisibility, and his incomprehensibility. To say that he spoke by inspiration, or by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, where the Holy Spirit means the Deity itself, is to make Moses equal with Christ, in whom alone, as St. Paul says in Colossians 2:9, the Godhead dwells bodily. And finally, to say that he spoke by the Holy Spirit in the sense of the graces or gifts of the Holy Spirit is to attribute nothing supernatural to Moses at all. For God disposes men to piety, justice, mercy, truth, faith, and every kind of virtue, both moral and intellectual, through teaching, through example, and through a variety of natural and ordinary circumstances.

Just as none of these explanations can be applied to God's speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai, so none of them can be applied to his speaking to the High Priests from the Mercy Seat, the golden covering of the Ark of the Covenant from which God was said to give his answers. The manner in which God spoke to those sovereign prophets of the Old Testament, whose office it was to inquire of him, is therefore beyond our understanding. In the time of the New Testament there was no sovereign prophet but our Savior, who was both the God who spoke and the prophet to whom he spoke.

### To Subordinate Prophets of Permanent Calling, God Spoke by the Spirit

As for subordinate prophets of permanent calling, I find no passage proving that God spoke to them supernaturally. He spoke to them only in the way he naturally inclines all other Christians to piety, to belief, to righteousness, and to the other virtues. That way consists in temperament, instruction, and upbringing, and in the occasions and encouragements men meet with toward Christian virtue; yet it is rightly attributed to the operation of the Spirit of God, or Holy Spirit, which in our language we call the Holy Ghost. For there is no good inclination that is not the work of God. But these workings are not always supernatural. So when a prophet is said to speak in the Spirit, or by the Spirit of God, we are to understand nothing more than that he speaks in accordance with God's will as declared by the supreme prophet. The most common meaning of the word *spirit* is a man's intention, mind, or disposition.

In the time of Moses there were seventy men besides himself who prophesied in the camp of the Israelites. How God spoke to them is declared in Numbers 11:25: "The Lord came down in a cloud and spoke to Moses, and took some of the Spirit that was upon him and gave it to the seventy elders. And when the Spirit rested upon them, they prophesied and did not cease." Two things are evident from this. First, their prophesying to the people was subservient and subordinate to the prophesying of Moses. God took of the Spirit of Moses to put upon them, so that they prophesied as Moses would have them prophesy; otherwise they would not have been permitted to prophesy at all. Indeed, as verse 27 records, a complaint was made to Moses against some of them, and Joshua wanted Moses to forbid them. Moses did not, but said to Joshua, "Do not be jealous on my behalf." Second, the Spirit of God in that passage means nothing but the mind and disposition to obey and assist Moses in the administration of the government. If it meant that they had the substantial Spirit of God, that is, the divine nature breathed into them, then they would have had it in no lesser degree than Christ himself, in whom alone the Spirit of God dwelt bodily. It refers, therefore, to the gift and grace of God that guided them to cooperate with Moses, from whom their spirit was derived. It also appears from verse 16 that they were men whom Moses himself was to appoint as elders and officers of the people, for the words are: "Gather to me seventy men whom you know to be elders and officers of the people." Here "whom you know" is the same as "whom you appoint," or "have appointed," to be such. We have already been told, in Exodus 18, that Moses, following the advice of his father-in-law Jethro, appointed judges and officers over the people, men who feared God. The seventy were drawn from these, and God, by putting the spirit of Moses upon them, inclined them to help Moses administer the kingdom. It is in this same sense that the Spirit of God is said, in 1 Samuel 16:13–14, to have come upon David immediately after his anointing and to have left Saul: God gave his graces to the man he had chosen to govern his people and took them away from the man he had rejected. By the Spirit, then, is meant an inclination to God's service, and not any supernatural revelation.

### God Sometimes Also Spoke by Lots

God also spoke on many occasions through the outcome of lots, which were managed by those he had placed in authority over his people. So we read in 1 Samuel 14:43 that God revealed, through the lots Saul had drawn, the fault Jonathan had committed in eating from a honeycomb in violation of the oath the people had sworn. In Joshua 18:10, God divided the land of Canaan among the Israelites by "the lots that Joshua cast before the Lord in Shiloh." And it seems to have been in the same way that God exposed the crime of Achan, in Joshua 7:16 and the verses that follow. These are the means by which God declared his will in the Old Testament.

He used every one of these means in the New Testament as well. He spoke to the Virgin Mary through the vision of an angel; to Joseph in a dream; to Paul on the road to Damascus through a vision of our Savior; and to Peter through the vision of a sheet let down from heaven, filled with the flesh of many kinds of beasts, clean and unclean, and again in prison through the vision of an angel. He spoke to all the apostles and writers of the New Testament through the graces of his Spirit, and to the apostles once more by lot, when they chose Matthias to take the place of Judas Iscariot.

### Every Man Ought to Weigh the Probability of a Professed Prophet's Calling

All prophecy, then, presupposes either a vision or a dream (which two, when they are natural, are the same thing), or else some special gift of God so rarely seen in mankind that it is marveled at wherever it appears. And such gifts, like the most extraordinary dreams and visions, may come from God not only through his supernatural and immediate action but also through his natural operation, by way of secondary causes. Reason and judgment are therefore needed to distinguish natural gifts from supernatural ones, and natural visions or dreams from supernatural ones. It follows that men need to be extremely careful and wary in obeying the voice of any man who claims to be a prophet and requires us to obey God in whatever way he, in God's name, tells us is the way to happiness. For whoever claims to teach men the way to so great a happiness claims to govern them, that is, to rule and reign over them. That is something all men naturally desire, and it is therefore rightly open to suspicion of ambition and imposture. Such a man ought accordingly to be examined and tested by every individual before he is obeyed, unless obedience has already been given him in the founding of a commonwealth, as when the prophet is the civil sovereign or has been authorized by the civil sovereign.

If this examination of prophets and spirits were not permitted to every one of the people, there would have been no point in setting out the marks by which every man might distinguish those he ought to follow from those he ought not. Such marks are in fact set out: in Deuteronomy 13:1 and the verses following, for recognizing a prophet, and in 1 John 4:1 and the verses following, for recognizing a spirit. And seeing that there is so much prophesying in the Old Testament, and so much preaching in the New Testament against prophets, and that false prophets ordinarily far outnumber true ones, every man must beware of obeying their directions, at his own peril.

That false prophets were far more numerous than true ones appears, first of all, from the fact that when Ahab consulted four hundred prophets, as recorded in 1 Kings 22, all of them were false impostors except one, Micaiah. And shortly before the time of the Babylonian captivity, the prophets were generally liars. "The prophets," says the Lord through Jeremiah in chapter 14, verse 14, "prophesy lies in my name. I did not send them, nor command them, nor speak to them. They prophesy to you a false vision, a worthless thing, and the deceit of their own hearts." So much so that God commanded the people, through the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah in chapter 23, verse 16, not to obey them: "Thus says the Lord of Hosts: Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They fill you with vain hopes; they speak a vision of their own heart, and not from the mouth of the Lord."

### All Prophecy Except That of the Sovereign Prophet Is to Be Examined by Every Subject

In the time of the Old Testament, then, there were bitter quarrels among the visionary prophets, one contending with another and asking, "Which way did the Spirit go from me to speak to you?" as happened between Micaiah and the rest of the four hundred; and there were prophets openly calling one another liars, as in Jeremiah 14:14. And there are similar controversies today, in the age of the New Testament, among the spiritual prophets. Every man, therefore, was then and is now bound to use his natural reason to apply to all prophecy the rules God has given us for telling the true from the false. In the Old Testament there were two such rules. One was that the prophet's doctrine must conform to what Moses, the sovereign prophet, had taught; the other was the miraculous power of foretelling what God would bring to pass, as I have already shown from Deuteronomy 13:1 and the verses following. In the New Testament there was only one mark, and that was the preaching of this doctrine: *that Jesus is the Christ*, that is, the King of the Jews promised in the Old Testament. Whoever denied that article was a false prophet, whatever miracles he might appear to perform, and whoever taught it was a true prophet.

St. John, in his First Epistle, chapter 4, verse 2 and following, speaks expressly of how to test spirits to see whether they are from God. After warning that false prophets would arise, he says: "By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God." That is, such a spirit is approved and accepted as a prophet of God. This does not mean that a man is godly, or one of the elect, because he confesses, professes, or preaches that Jesus is the Christ; it means only that he is an acknowledged prophet. For God sometimes speaks through prophets whose persons he has not accepted, as he did through Balaam, and as he foretold Saul's death to him through the Witch of Endor. Then, in the next verse, John says: "Every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of Christ. And this is the spirit of Antichrist." The rule is thus complete on both sides. He is a true prophet who preaches that the Messiah has already come in the person of Jesus, and he is a false one who denies that he has come and looks for him in some future impostor who will falsely claim that honor, the figure the Apostle there properly calls Antichrist.
