Every man, therefore, ought to consider who the sovereign prophet is: who it is that serves as God's viceroy on earth and holds, next under God, the authority to govern Christian men. He ought to take as his rule the doctrine which that sovereign, in the name of God, has commanded to be taught, and by that rule examine and test the truth of whatever doctrines professed prophets, with miracles or without them, may at any time put forward. If he finds them contrary to that rule, he should do what was done by those who came to Moses complaining that certain men were prophesying in the camp without any authority they could be sure of: leave it to the sovereign, as they left it to Moses, to uphold or forbid them as he sees fit. If the sovereign disowns them, they are no longer to be obeyed; if he approves them, they are to be obeyed as men to whom God has given a portion of their sovereign's spirit. For when Christian men do not take their Christian sovereign to be God's prophet, they must do one of three things. They must take their own dreams for the prophecy by which they mean to be governed, and the swelling passions of their own hearts for the Spirit of God; or they must allow themselves to be led by some foreign prince; or they must follow some of their fellow subjects who are able to bewitch them into rebellion by slandering the government, with no other miracle to confirm their calling than, now and then, an extraordinary success and escape from punishment. And by this means, destroying all laws, both divine and human, they reduce all order, government, and society to the first chaos of violence and civil war.

## Chapter XXXVII. Of Miracles, and Their Use

### A Miracle Is a Work That Causes Wonder

By miracles we mean the admirable works of God, works that excite admiration in the old sense of astonishment, and for this reason they are also called wonders. They are usually performed to make God's commands known on occasions when people, following their own private, natural reasoning, would otherwise be inclined to doubt what he has commanded and what he has not. For that reason Holy Scripture commonly calls them signs. The word carries the same sense as the Latin *ostenta* and *portenta*, terms that come from showing, and from signifying in advance, what the Almighty is about to bring to pass.

### It Must Therefore Be Rare, and Have No Known Natural Cause

To understand what a miracle is, then, we must first understand which works people wonder at and call admirable. Only two things make anyone wonder at an event. The first is that it be strange: nothing like it has ever been produced, or has been produced only very rarely. The second is that, once it has been produced, we cannot imagine it came about by natural means, but only by the immediate hand of God. When we can see some possible natural cause for it, however rarely anything like it has occurred, we no longer wonder at it or regard it as a miracle. The same holds when things like it have occurred often, however impossible it may be to imagine a natural means behind them.

If a horse or a cow were to speak, therefore, that would be a miracle, because the thing is both strange and hard to attribute to any natural cause. The same would be true of some startling departure of nature that produced a living creature of an entirely new shape. But when a human being or any other animal begets its own kind, that is no miracle, because it is common, even though we know no more about how it happens than about the other. Likewise, if a man were transformed into stone, or into a pillar, it would be a miracle, because it is strange. But if a piece of wood undergoes such a change and turns to stone, it is no miracle, because we see that happen often. And yet we know no more about the operation by which God brings about the one than the other.

The first rainbow ever seen in the world was a miracle, because it was the first and consequently strange. It was set in the heavens as a sign from God to assure his people that the world would never again be destroyed universally by water. Today, because rainbows are frequent, they are not miracles, either to those who know their natural causes or to those who do not. Human skill also produces many rare works. Yet when we know that people have made them, we also know by what means they were made, and so we do not count them as miracles, since they were brought about through human industry and not by the immediate hand of God.

### What Seems a Miracle to One Person May Seem Otherwise to Another

Furthermore, admiration and wonder depend on the knowledge and experience that people possess, some more and some less. It follows that the same thing may be a miracle to one person and not to another. That is why ignorant and superstitious people make great wonders of works that others do not marvel at at all, because they know those works proceed from nature, which is the ordinary rather than the immediate work of God. The common people, for example, have taken eclipses of the sun and moon for supernatural works, when there were nevertheless others who could have predicted the very hour of their arrival from their natural causes. Or consider a man who uses collusion and secretly gathered information to learn the private doings of some ignorant and unwary person, and then tells him what he has done in the past. To that person it seems a miraculous thing. Among wise and wary people, however, miracles of that kind are not easily performed.

### The Purpose of Miracles

It belongs, further, to the nature of a miracle that it be performed to win credit for God's messengers, ministers, and prophets. People may then know that these men are called, sent, and employed by God, and be more inclined to obey them. The creation of the world, and afterward the destruction of all living creatures in the universal flood, were admirable works. They are not customarily called miracles, however, because they were not done to win credit for any prophet or other minister of God. However admirable a work may be, the wonder does not lie in the fact that it could be done, since people naturally believe that the Almighty can do all things. It lies in the fact that he does it at the prayer or the word of a man.

The works God performed in Egypt by the hand of Moses, by contrast, were properly miracles. They were done to make the people of Israel believe that Moses came to them as one sent by God, not out of any design to serve his own interest. God commanded him to deliver the Israelites from their bondage in Egypt, and Moses objected, in the fourth chapter of Exodus, that the people would not believe him but would say that the Lord had not appeared to him. God then gave him the power to turn the rod in his hand into a serpent and back again into a rod. He also gave him the power to make his hand leprous by putting it inside his cloak, and whole again by drawing it out. According to the fifth verse, all this was done so that the children of Israel might believe that the God of their fathers had appeared to him. And in case that should not be enough, God gave him the power to turn their waters into blood. When Moses had performed these miracles before the people, the chapter concludes, "they believed him." Even so, out of fear of Pharaoh, they did not yet dare to obey him. The further works done to plague Pharaoh and the Egyptians were therefore all aimed at making the Israelites believe in Moses, and they were properly miracles. Consider all the miracles done by the hand of Moses and by all the other prophets up to the Captivity, and those done afterward by our Savior and his apostles. We shall find that their purpose was always to produce or confirm the belief that these men had not come of their own accord but had been sent by God.

We may further observe in Scripture that the purpose of miracles was to produce belief only in the elect, not in everyone, elect and reprobate alike. The elect are those whom God had determined should become his subjects. The miraculous plagues of Egypt were not aimed at converting Pharaoh, because God had told Moses beforehand that he would harden Pharaoh's heart so that he would not let the people go. When Pharaoh did let them go at last, the miracles had not persuaded him; the plagues had forced him. So too it is written of our Savior, in the thirteenth chapter of Matthew, that he did not perform many miracles in his own country because of the people's unbelief. In the sixth chapter of Mark, instead of "he did not do many," the text reads, "he could do none." This was not because he lacked the power, since to say so would be blasphemy against God. Nor was it because miracles were not meant to convert unbelievers to Christ, since all the miracles of Moses, of the prophets, of our Savior, and of his apostles were meant to add people to the Church. It was because their miracles were meant to add to the Church not everyone, but those who were to be saved, that is, those whom God had elected. Since our Savior had been sent by his Father, he could not use his power to convert those whom his Father had rejected.

Some interpret this passage in Mark by saying that "he could not" stands for "he would not." They do so without any precedent in the Greek language. In Greek, "would not" is sometimes used for "could not" when speaking of inanimate things that have no will, but "could not" is never used for "would not." These interpreters thereby put a stumbling block before weak Christians, as though Christ could perform miracles only among the credulous.

### The Definition of a Miracle

From what I have set down here about the nature and use of a miracle, we may define it as follows: a MIRACLE is a work of God, distinct from his operation through the course of nature that he ordained at the Creation, done to make known to his elect the mission of an extraordinary minister for their salvation.

From this definition we may infer, first, that in every miracle the work done is not the effect of any power in the prophet, because it is the effect of the immediate hand of God. God has done it without using the prophet as a subordinate cause.

Second, no devil, angel, or other created spirit can perform a miracle. Such a spirit would have to do it either by means of some natural knowledge or by incantation, that is, by the power of words. If enchanters did it by their own independent power, there would be some power that does not proceed from God, which everyone denies. If they did it by a power given to them, then the work would come from nature and not from the immediate hand of God, and would consequently be no miracle.

Some passages of Scripture seem to attribute to certain arts of magic and incantation the power of working wonders equal to some of the immediate miracles performed by God himself. In the seventh chapter of Exodus, for example, we read that after Moses' rod was cast on the ground and became a serpent, "the magicians of Egypt did the like by their enchantments." We read in the same chapter that after Moses had turned the waters of Egypt's streams, rivers, ponds, and pools into blood, "the magicians of Egypt did so likewise with their enchantments." And in the eighth chapter we read that after Moses had brought frogs upon the land by the power of God, "the magicians also did so with their enchantments, and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt." A reader will naturally be inclined to attribute miracles to enchantments, that is, to the power of the sound of words, and to think the point well proved by these and similar passages. And yet no passage of Scripture tells us what an enchantment is.

Suppose, then, that enchantment is not, as many believe, the working of strange effects by spells and words. Suppose it is instead imposture and delusion produced by ordinary means. In that case it is so far from supernatural that the impostors need not even study natural causes. They need only the ordinary ignorance, stupidity, and superstition of mankind. If that is so, then the passages that seem to support the power of magic, witchcraft, and enchantment must have a different meaning from the one they appear to have at first sight.

### That People Are Easily Deceived by False Miracles

It is evident enough that words have no effect except on those who understand them. Even then, their only effect is to signify the intentions or passions of the speaker, and so to produce hope, fear, or some other passion or idea in the hearer. Suppose, then, that a rod seems to become a serpent, or water seems to become blood, or some other miracle seems to be done by enchantment, and it is not done for the edification of God's people. In that case it is not the rod, the water, or any other object that is enchanted, or acted upon by the words. It is the spectator. The whole miracle consists in the enchanter's having deceived a man, and that is no miracle but a very easy thing to do.

All people are generally ignorant and prone to error, especially those with little knowledge of natural causes and of human nature and interests, and so they can be imposed upon by countless easy tricks. Before it was known that there was a science of the movements of the stars, a man who told the people that the sun would be darkened at a certain hour, or on a certain day, could have won a great reputation for miraculous power. If juggling were not common today, a juggler working his cups and other small props would be thought to perform his wonders by the power of the Devil at the very least. Some men have trained themselves to speak while drawing in their breath, and in ancient times such men were called *ventriloqui*. Such a man can make the weakness of his voice seem to come from a great distance rather than from the feeble force of his organs of speech. He can thereby persuade a great many people that whatever he chooses to tell them is a voice from Heaven. People ordinarily confide in one another about their past actions and adventures. A cunning man who has found out these secrets and private confidences can easily repeat them back to the person concerned, and yet many gain a reputation as conjurers by just such means. It would take too long to list the various kinds of men whom the Greeks called *thaumaturgi*, meaning workers of wonders, and all of these do what they do by their own individual skill.

When we turn to impostures carried out by collusion, however, nothing is so impossible to do that it cannot be believed. Two men conspiring, one to pretend to be lame and the other to cure him with a charm, will deceive many. But many men conspiring, one to pretend to be lame, another to cure him, and all the rest to bear witness, will deceive many more.

### Safeguards Against the Imposture of Miracles

Mankind is inclined to believe too quickly in pretended miracles. Against this there can be no better safeguard, and I think no other, than the one God prescribed, first through Moses, at the beginning of the thirteenth and the end of the eighteenth chapters of Deuteronomy, as I noted in the preceding chapter. We are not to accept as a prophet anyone who teaches a religion other than the one established by God's lieutenant, who at that time was Moses. Nor are we to accept anyone, even if he teaches the same religion, whose predictions we do not see come to pass. Before we give credit to any pretended miracle or prophet, therefore, we must consult the proper authority about what doctrine has been established. In his time that authority was Moses, and in theirs it was Aaron and his successors. In all times it is the sovereign governor of God's people, next under God himself, that is, the Head of the Church.

Once that is done, we must actually see the claimed miracle performed. We must use every possible means to determine whether it has really been done. We must also consider whether it is of such a kind that no one could do the like by natural power, so that it requires the immediate hand of God. In this too we must turn to God's lieutenant, to whom we have submitted our private judgments in all doubtful cases. Suppose, for example, that a man claims that after certain words have been spoken over a piece of bread, God has immediately made it no longer bread but a god, or a man, or both, and yet it still looks exactly as much like bread as it ever did. There is no reason for anyone to think the thing has really been done, or consequently to fear the man, until he has asked God, through his vicar or lieutenant, whether it has been done or not. If the lieutenant says it has not, then what Moses says in the eighteenth chapter of Deuteronomy applies: "he hath spoken it presumptuously; thou shalt not fear him." If he says it has been done, then one is not to contradict it. Likewise, if we do not see a miracle ourselves but only hear it reported, we are to consult the lawful Church, that is, its lawful head, about how far we should believe those who report it.

This is chiefly the situation of people who live today under Christian sovereigns. In our times I do not know of a single person who has ever seen a wondrous work, performed by the charm, word, or prayer of a man, that anyone with even a modest degree of reason would consider supernatural. The question is therefore no longer whether what we see done is a miracle, or whether the miracle we hear or read about was a real work and not merely the product of a tongue or a pen. In plain terms, the question is whether the report is true or a lie. None of us is to make our own private reason or conscience the judge of that question. The judge is the public reason, that is, the reason of God's supreme lieutenant. Indeed, we have already made him judge, if we have given him sovereign power to do everything necessary for our peace and defense.

A private person always has the liberty, since thought is free, to believe or disbelieve in his heart the acts that have been put forward as miracles. He may weigh what benefit people's belief in them could bring to those who claim or endorse them, and so judge for himself whether they are miracles or lies. But when it comes to professing that faith, private reason must submit to public reason, that is, to God's lieutenant. Who this lieutenant of God and Head of the Church is will be considered in its proper place hereafter.

## Chapter XXXVIII. Of the Meaning in Scripture of Eternal Life, Hell, Salvation, the World to Come, and Redemption

Civil society depends on justice, and justice depends on the power of life and death, along with lesser rewards and punishments, held by those who have sovereignty in the commonwealth. It follows that no commonwealth can stand where anyone other than the sovereign has the power to give rewards greater than life, or to inflict punishments greater than death. Eternal life is a greater reward than present life, and eternal torment a greater punishment than natural death. Everyone who wishes, by obeying authority, to avoid the calamities of confusion and civil war should therefore consider carefully what Holy Scripture means by eternal life and eternal torment: for what offenses, and against whom committed, men are to be eternally tormented, and for what actions they are to obtain eternal life.

### Where Adam's Eternal Life Would Have Been Had He Not Sinned: The Earthly Paradise

We find first that Adam was created in such a condition of life that, had he not broken God's commandment, he would have enjoyed it everlastingly in the Paradise of Eden. The Tree of Life stood there, and he was permitted to eat from it for as long as he refrained from eating of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, which was forbidden him. As soon as he had eaten of the forbidden tree, God thrust him out of Paradise, "lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and live forever," as Genesis 3:22 records. From this it seems to me that Adam, had he not sinned, would have had eternal life on earth, and that mortality came upon him and his descendants through his first sin. In this, as in every question whose resolution depends on Scripture, I nevertheless submit to the interpretation of the Bible authorized by the commonwealth of which I am a subject. It was not actual death that entered then, for in that case Adam could never have had children; in fact he lived long afterward and saw a numerous posterity before he died. When God said, "In the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die," the words must refer to his mortality, the certainty that he would die. Since eternal life was lost through Adam's forfeiture in committing sin, whoever cancelled that forfeiture would thereby recover that life again. Jesus Christ has made satisfaction for the sins of all who believe in him, and has therefore recovered for all believers the ETERNAL LIFE that Adam's sin had lost. This is the sense in which St. Paul's comparison in Romans 5:18–19 holds: "As by the offense of one, judgment came upon all men to condemnation, even so by the righteousness of one, the free gift came upon all men to justification of life." Paul states the same point more plainly in 1 Corinthians 15:21–22: "For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive."

### Texts Concerning the Place of Eternal Life for Believers

As to the place where men will enjoy the eternal life Christ has obtained for them, the texts just cited seem to locate it on earth. If, as in Adam all die (that is, have forfeited Paradise and eternal life on earth), so in Christ all shall be made alive, then all men will be made to live on earth; otherwise the comparison would not fit. The Psalmist seems to agree in Psalm 133:3: "Upon Zion God commanded the blessing, even life forevermore." Zion is in Jerusalem, on earth. St. John agrees as well in Revelation 2:7: "To him that overcomes I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the Paradise of God." This was the tree of Adam's eternal life, and his life was to have been on earth. St. John seems to confirm the same again in Revelation 21:2, where he says, "I John saw the Holy City, New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband," and again to the same effect at verse 10. It is as if he were saying that the New Jerusalem, the Paradise of God, will come down from heaven to God's people at Christ's return, and that they will not go up to it from earth. This agrees entirely with what the two men in white clothing, that is, the two angels, said to the apostles as they watched Christ ascending, in Acts 1:11: "This same Jesus, who is taken up from you into heaven, shall come in the same way as you have seen him go up into heaven." The words sound as though the angels meant that he would come down to govern the faithful eternally here, under his Father, and would not take them up to govern them in heaven. That reading is also consistent with the restoration of the Kingdom of God instituted under Moses, which was a political government of the Jews on earth.

Again, our Saviour's saying in Matthew 22:30, that "in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven," describes an eternal life resembling, in the matter of marriage, the one we lost in Adam. Had Adam and Eve not sinned, they would have lived on earth eternally in their own individual persons, and plainly they would not then have gone on reproducing their kind continually. If immortals reproduced as mankind does now, the earth would in a short time be unable to give them a place to stand. The Jews who asked our Saviour whose wife a woman who had married several brothers would be at the resurrection did not understand the consequences of immortality: that there will be no generation, and consequently no marriage, any more than there is marriage or generation among the angels. The comparison between the eternal life Adam lost and the eternal life our Saviour recovered by his victory over death holds in another respect as well. Adam lost eternal life by his sin and yet lived on for a time afterward; in the same way, the faithful Christian has recovered eternal life through Christ's passion, even though he dies a natural death and remains dead for a time, namely until the resurrection. Just as death is reckoned from Adam's condemnation rather than from its execution, so life is reckoned from the absolution of those elected in Christ, not from their resurrection.

### Ascension into Heaven

I can find no text from which it is easy to conclude that the place where men are to live eternally after the resurrection is the heavens. By "heaven" here I mean those parts of the world most remote from earth, where the stars are, or a still higher heaven above the stars called the *Caelum Empyreum*, the Empyrean Heaven, of which Scripture makes no mention and for which reason supplies no ground. By the Kingdom of Heaven is meant the kingdom of the King who dwells in heaven. His kingdom was the people of Israel, whom he ruled through the prophets as his lieutenants: first Moses, after him Eleazar, and then the sovereign priests, until in the days of Samuel the people rebelled and demanded a mortal man for their king, after the manner of other nations. When our Saviour Christ, through the preaching of his ministers, has persuaded the Jews to return and has called the Gentiles to obey him, there will be a new Kingdom of Heaven, because our King will then be God, whose throne is heaven. Nothing in Scripture shows any necessity that man must ascend to his happiness any higher than the earth, which is God's footstool. On the contrary, John 3:13 says that "no man has ascended into heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man, who is in heaven." I observe in passing that these words, unlike those immediately preceding them, are not our Saviour's but St. John's own, for Christ was at that time not in heaven but on earth. The same is said of David in Acts 2:34. There St. Peter, to prove Christ's ascension, quotes the Psalmist in Psalm 16:10, "You will not leave my soul in hell, nor suffer your Holy One to see corruption," and says that the words were spoken not of David but of Christ. As proof, he adds this reason: "For David is not ascended into heaven."

To this a man might easily reply that although their bodies were not to ascend until the general Day of Judgment, their souls were in heaven as soon as they departed from their bodies. Our Saviour's words in Luke 20:37–38 seem to confirm this reply. Proving the resurrection from the words of Moses, he says: "That the dead are raised, even Moses showed at the bush, when he calls the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living; for they all live to him." But if these words are understood only as referring to the immortality of the soul, they prove nothing at all of what our Saviour meant to prove, which was the resurrection of the body, that is, the immortality of the man. Our Saviour therefore means that the patriarchs were immortal, not by some property following from the essence and nature of mankind, but by the will of God, who was pleased out of his mere grace to bestow eternal life on the faithful. Although at that time the patriarchs and many other faithful men were dead, they nonetheless, as the text says, lived to God. They were written in the Book of Life, together with those who had been absolved of their sins and ordained to eternal life at the resurrection.

That the soul of man is by its own nature eternal, a living creature independent of the body, or that any mere man is immortal other than by the resurrection on the last day (except Enoch and Elijah), is a doctrine not evident in Scripture. The whole fourteenth chapter of Job, which is the speech of Job himself and not of his friends, is a lament over this natural mortality, and yet it does not contradict immortality at the resurrection. "There is hope for a tree," he says in verse 7, "if it be cut down. Though its root grow old, and its stock die in the ground, yet when it scents the water it will bud, and put forth boughs like a young plant. But man dies, and wastes away; yes, man gives up the ghost, and where is he?" And in verse 12: "Man lies down, and rises not, till the heavens be no more." But when will the heavens be no more? St. Peter tells us that it will be at the general resurrection. In the third chapter of his second epistle, at verse 7, he says that "the heavens and the earth that are now are reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men." At verse 12 he continues, "looking for and hastening the coming of God, wherein the heavens shall be on fire and shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat. Nevertheless we, according to the promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwells righteousness." When Job says that man rises not until the heavens are no more, then, it amounts to saying that immortal life does not begin in man until the resurrection and the Day of Judgment. In Scripture, "soul" and "life" usually signify the same thing. The cause of that life is not man's specific nature and generation but the promise. St. Peter does not say, "We look for new heavens and a new earth from nature," but "from promise."

Lastly, it has already been proved from several clear passages of Scripture, in the thirty-fifth chapter of this book, that the Kingdom of God is a civil commonwealth in which God himself is sovereign. He is sovereign first by virtue of the Old Covenant and since then by virtue of the New, under which he reigns through his vicar, or lieutenant. Those same passages therefore also prove that after our Saviour comes again in majesty and glory to reign actually and eternally, the Kingdom of God is to be on earth. But because this doctrine, though proved from passages of Scripture neither few nor obscure, will strike most men as a novelty, I only propose it. I maintain nothing in this or in any other religious paradox. I await instead the outcome of that dispute of the sword, not yet decided among my countrymen, over which authority is to approve or reject every kind of doctrine. Whatever private men may think, all who mean to be protected by that authority's laws must obey its commands, whether spoken or written. Points of doctrine concerning the Kingdom of God have so great an influence on the kingdom of man that they are not to be determined except by those who, under God, hold the sovereign power.

### The Place, After Judgment, of Those Who Were Never in the Kingdom of God, or Who Were In It and Are Cast Out

Scripture shows that God's enemies and their torments after judgment, like the Kingdom of God and eternal life, have their place on earth. All men who were either buried or swallowed up by the earth remain in a certain place until the resurrection, and Scripture usually names that place with words meaning "underground." The Latin writers generally render it *Infernus* and *Inferni*, and the Greeks *Hades*, meaning a place where men cannot see. It includes the grave as well as any deeper place. But the place of the damned after the resurrection is not fixed by any indication of location in either the Old Testament or the New. It is identified only by the company kept there: it will be where those wicked men are whom God in former times destroyed from the face of the earth in some extraordinary and miraculous manner. For example, the damned are said to be *in Inferno*, in Tartarus, or in the bottomless pit, because Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were swallowed alive by the earth. The writers of Scripture did not mean us to believe that the globe of the earth could contain a pit without a bottom, that is, a hole of infinite depth. The earth is not only finite but, compared with the height of the stars, of no considerable magnitude. The Greeks in their demonology, which is to say their doctrine concerning daemons, imagined such a pit, and the Romans after them called it Tartarus. Of it Virgil says:

*Bis patet in praeceps tantum tenditque sub umbras*
*Quantus ad aethereum caeli suspectus Olympum:*

Tartarus, that is, opens sheer downward and stretches beneath the shadows twice as far as the eye looks upward to the heavenly heights of Olympus. Such a thing is impossible given the proportion of the earth to the heavens. We are meant rather to believe, without definite location, that the damned will be wherever those men are on whom God inflicted that exemplary punishment.

### The Congregation of Giants

Again, the mighty men of the earth who lived in Noah's time, before the Flood, were destroyed by the general deluge for their wicked lives. The Greeks called them heroes and Scripture calls them giants, and both say they were begotten by the union of the children of God with the children of men. The place of the damned is therefore sometimes also marked out by the company of those dead giants. Proverbs 21:16 says, "The man who wanders out of the way of understanding shall remain in the congregation of the giants," and Job 26:5 says, "Behold, the giants groan under the water, and those who dwell with them." Here the place of the damned is under the water. Isaiah 14:9, addressing the king of Babylon, says, "Hell is troubled how to meet you, and will displace the giants for you." Here again the place of the damned, if the sense is literal, is to be under the water.

### The Lake of Fire

Third, the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah were consumed with fire and brimstone for their wickedness by the extraordinary wrath of God. Together with them, the surrounding country was made into a stinking lake of bitumen. For this reason the place of the damned is sometimes expressed as fire, or a fiery lake, as in Revelation 21:8: "But the cowardly, the unbelieving, the abominable, murderers, whoremongers, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars shall have their part in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death." It is clear, then, that hell fire, expressed here by a metaphor drawn from the real fire of Sodom, does not signify any definite kind or place of torment. It is to be taken indefinitely as destruction, as it is in chapter 20, verse 14, where it is said that "Death and Hell were cast into the lake of fire." That is to say, Death and Hell were abolished and destroyed, as though after the Day of Judgment there will be no more dying and no more going into Hell. No more going into Hell means no more going to Hades, from which word our word "Hell" is perhaps derived, and that is the same as no more dying.

### Outer Darkness

Fourth, God inflicted a plague of darkness on the Egyptians, of which Exodus 10:23 says, "They saw not one another, nor did any man rise from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings." From this plague the place of the wicked after judgment is called "utter darkness," or, as it is in the original, "darkness outside." So it is expressed in Matthew 22:13, where the king commands his servants "to bind hand and foot the man who did not have on his wedding garment, and to cast him out," *eis to skotos to exoteron*, into the outer darkness, the darkness outside. Though the phrase is translated "utter darkness," it does not signify how great that darkness is, but where it is to be: namely, outside the dwelling of God's elect.

### Gehenna and Tophet

Lastly, there was a place near Jerusalem called the Valley of the Children of Hinnom. In one part of it, called Tophet, the Jews had committed the most grievous idolatry, sacrificing their children to the idol Moloch. There too God had afflicted his enemies with the most grievous punishments, and there Josiah burned the priests of Moloch on their own altars, as the twenty-third chapter of 2 Kings recounts at length. The place was afterward used to receive the filth and garbage carried out of the city. Fires were made there from time to time to purify the air and take away the stench of carrion. From this abominable place, the Jews ever afterward called the place of the damned by the name of Gehenna, or the Valley of Hinnom. This word Gehenna is the one now usually translated as HELL. From the fires that burned there from time to time, we have the notion of everlasting and unquenchable fire.

### The Literal Sense of Scripture Concerning Hell

No one interprets Scripture to mean that after the Day of Judgment the wicked are all to be punished eternally in the Valley of Hinnom. No one holds that they will rise again only to remain ever after underground or under water, or that after the resurrection they will never again see one another or move from one place to another. It follows necessarily, I think, that what is said in this way about hell fire is spoken metaphorically. There is therefore a proper sense still to be inquired after, both of the place of hell and of the nature of hellish torment and of the tormentors, since every metaphor has some real ground that can be expressed in proper words.

### Satan and Devil Are Not Proper Names, but Appellatives

And first, the tormenters. Their nature and properties are described exactly and literally by the names they bear: the Enemy, or Satan; the Accuser, or Diabolus; the Destroyer, or Abaddon. These names, Satan, Devil, and Abaddon, each carry a meaning, and none of them identifies an individual person, as a proper name does. Each names only an office or a quality. They are therefore common nouns, descriptive titles rather than names, and they should not have been left untranslated, as they are in the Latin and modern Bibles. Left in their original form, they look like the proper names of demons, and people are all the more easily led into believing the doctrine of devils. That doctrine was, at the time, the religion of the Gentiles, and it was contrary to the religion of Moses and of Christ.

The Enemy, the Accuser, and the Destroyer means the enemy of those who will be in the Kingdom of God. If the Kingdom of God after the Resurrection is to be on earth, as I showed from Scripture in the previous chapter that it appears to be, then the Enemy and his kingdom must be on earth as well. So it was in the period before the Jews deposed God. God's kingdom was then in Palestine, and the surrounding nations were the kingdoms of the Enemy. By Satan, consequently, is meant any earthly enemy of the Church.

### Torments of Hell

Scripture expresses the torments of hell in several ways. Sometimes it speaks of "weeping and gnashing of teeth," as in Matthew 8:12, and sometimes of "the worm of conscience," as in Isaiah 66:24 and Mark 9:44, 46, and 48. Sometimes it speaks of fire, as in the passage just cited, "where the worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched," and in many other places. Sometimes it speaks of "shame and contempt," as in Daniel 12:2: "And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." All these passages describe, metaphorically, a grief and discontent of mind. It arises from seeing others enjoy that eternal happiness which the sufferers themselves have lost through their own unbelief and disobedience. Happiness in others can be felt only by comparison with one's own actual miseries. It follows that the wicked are to suffer the bodily pains and calamities that befall those who not only live under evil and cruel rulers but also have as their enemy the eternal King of the saints, God Almighty.

Among these bodily pains must also be counted, for every one of the wicked, a second death. Scripture is clear that there will be a universal resurrection, yet nowhere do we read that eternal life is promised to any of the reprobate. In 1 Corinthians 15:42–43, St. Paul answers the question of what bodies men will be raised with. He says that "the body is sown in corruption, and is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power." Glory and power cannot be applied to the bodies of the wicked. Nor can the term "second death" be applied to those who can die only once. In metaphorical speech an everlasting life of calamity might be called an everlasting death, but it cannot properly be understood as a second death.

The fire prepared for the wicked is an everlasting fire. This means that after the Resurrection there will be a condition in which no one can exist without torment of body and mind, and that this condition will last forever. In that sense the fire will be unquenchable and the torments everlasting. But it does not follow that anyone cast into that fire, or tormented with those torments, will endure and withstand them so as to be burned and tortured eternally without ever being destroyed or dying. Many passages affirm an everlasting fire and everlasting torments, into which people may be cast one after another, forever. I find none that affirms any individual person will live eternally within them. On the contrary, they speak of an everlasting death, which is the second death, as in Revelation 20:13–14: "For after Death and the Grave shall have delivered up the dead which were in them, and every man be judged according to his works, Death and the Grave shall also be cast into the Lake of Fire. This is the second death." It is evident, then, that everyone condemned on the Day of Judgment is to suffer a second death, after which he will die no more.

### The Joys of Eternal Life and Salvation Are the Same Thing; Salvation from Sin and Salvation from Misery Are One

In Scripture, all the joys of eternal life are gathered under a single name: salvation, or being saved. To be saved is to be made secure, either relatively, against particular evils, or absolutely, against all evil, including want, sickness, and death itself. Man was created immortal. He was not subject to corruption, and therefore not subject to anything that tends to break down his nature, and he fell from that happiness through the sin of Adam. It follows that to be saved from sin is to be saved from all the evils and calamities that sin has brought upon us. For this reason, in Holy Scripture, the forgiveness of sin and salvation from death and misery are the same thing.

The words of our Saviour show this. As Matthew 9:2 records, he healed a man sick with palsy by saying, "Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee." He knew that the scribes considered it blasphemy for a man to claim the power to forgive sins, and so he asked them, in verse 5, "whether is it easier to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee, or to say, Arise and walk?" He meant that, for the purpose of healing the sick man, it made no difference whether he said "Thy sins are forgiven" or "Arise and walk." He used the first form of words only to show that he had power to forgive sins. Reason makes the same point. Since death and misery were the punishments of sin, release from sin must also be release from death and misery. That release is absolute salvation, which the faithful are to enjoy after the Day of Judgment through the power and favour of Jesus Christ, who for that reason is called our Saviour.

Scripture also speaks of particular salvations. One is meant in 1 Samuel 14:39, "as the Lord liveth, which saveth Israel," that is, saves them from their enemies of the moment. Others appear in 2 Samuel 22:4, "Thou art my Saviour; thou savest me from violence," and in 2 Kings 13:5, "God gave the Israelites a Saviour, and so they were delivered from the hand of the Assyrians," and in similar passages. Of these I need say nothing, since texts of that kind present no difficulty, and no one has any interest at stake that might corrupt their interpretation.

### The Place of Eternal Salvation

The general salvation is another matter. Because it must take place in the Kingdom of Heaven, there is great difficulty about where it is to be. On one side, the word "kingdom" suggests that this salvation should be on earth, for a kingdom is a state that men establish for their lasting security against enemies and want. Salvation is presented to us as the glorious reign of our King, won by conquest. It is not presented as safety gained by escape. Wherever we look for salvation, then, we must also look for triumph. Before triumph we must look for victory, and before victory for battle, and a battle can hardly be supposed to take place in heaven. However good this reasoning may be, I will not rely on it without very clear passages of Scripture. The state of salvation is described at length in Isaiah 33:20–24:

"Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities; thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken.

But there the glorious Lord will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams, wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby.

For the Lord is our Judge, the Lord is our Lawgiver, the Lord is our King; he will save us.

Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast; they could not spread the sail. Then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey.

And the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick; the people that shall dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity."

These words give us the place from which salvation is to come: "Jerusalem, a quiet habitation." They give us its eternity: "a tabernacle that shall not be taken down," and what follows. They name its Saviour: "the Lord, their Judge, their Lawgiver, their King; he will save us." They describe the salvation itself: "the Lord shall be to them as a broad moat of swift waters," and so on. They describe the condition of their enemies: "their tacklings are loose, their masts weak, the lame shall take the spoil of them." They describe the condition of the saved: "The inhabitant shall not say, I am sick." And finally, all of this is summed up in the forgiveness of sin: "The people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity." Salvation, then, will be on earth when God reigns in Jerusalem at the second coming of Christ. From Jerusalem will come the salvation of the Gentiles who are received into God's kingdom.

The same prophet states this even more explicitly in Isaiah 66:20–21. "And they," meaning the Gentiles who held any Jew in bondage, "shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the Lord out of all nations, upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and upon mules, and upon swift beasts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, saith the Lord, as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord. And I will also take of them for priests and for Levites, saith the Lord." This makes it plain that Jerusalem will be the chief seat of God's kingdom, and the place from which the salvation of us who were Gentiles is to come.

Our Saviour confirms this in his conversation with the Samaritan woman about where God ought to be worshipped. He tells her, in John 4:22, that the Samaritans worship what they do not know, while the Jews worship what they know, "for salvation is of the Jews." The Latin is *ex Judaeis*, meaning that salvation begins with the Jews. He is saying, in effect: you worship God, but you do not know through whom he will save you. We do know, for we know it will be someone of the tribe of Judah, a Jew and not a Samaritan. The woman's reply, "We know that the Messiah shall come," was therefore entirely to the point. Our Saviour's statement that "salvation is from the Jews" means the same as Paul's words in Romans 1:16–17: "The gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith." The movement is from the faith of the Jew to the faith of the Gentile.

The prophet Joel speaks in the same sense when he describes the Day of Judgment. In chapter 2, verses 30 and 31, he says that God will "show wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord come." In verse 32 he adds: "And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved: for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be salvation." Obadiah says the same in verse 17: "Upon Mount Zion shall be deliverance, and there shall be holiness; and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions." He means the possessions of the heathen, which he lists in detail in the verses that follow: the mount of Esau, the land of the Philistines, the fields of Ephraim and of Samaria, Gilead, and the cities of the south. He closes with the words "the kingdom shall be the Lord's." All these passages support the view that salvation, and the Kingdom of God after the Day of Judgment, will be on earth.

On the other side, I have found no text from which a probable argument can be drawn for an ascension of the saints into heaven. By heaven I mean the *Coelum Empyreum*, the fiery outermost heaven of the old cosmology, or any other ethereal region. The only support is that the kingdom is called the Kingdom of Heaven, and there are other reasons it may bear that name. God, who was King of the Jews, governed them by commands sent to Moses by angels from heaven, in order to bring them back to obedience. From heaven he will send again the one who is to rule both them and all other faithful people forever, from the Day of Judgment onward. Or the name may come from the fact that the throne of our great King is in heaven, while the earth is only his footstool. But it does not seem fitting to the dignity of a king that his subjects should occupy a place as high as his throne, or higher than his footstool. Nor can I find any clear text for it in Holy Scripture.

From what has been said about the Kingdom of God and about salvation, it is not hard to interpret what is meant by the World to Come. Scripture mentions three worlds: the Old World, the Present World, and the World to Come. St. Peter speaks of the first in 2 Peter 2:5: "If God spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly," and so on. The first world, then, lasted from Adam to the universal Flood. Our Saviour speaks of the present world in John 18:36: "My kingdom is not of this world." He came only to teach men the way of salvation and to renew his Father's kingdom through his teaching. St. Peter speaks of the world to come in 2 Peter 3:13: "Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth." This is the world in which Christ will come down from heaven in the clouds with great power and glory. He will send his angels to gather his elect from the four winds and from the farthest parts of the earth, and from then on he will reign over them, under his Father, forever.

### Redemption

The salvation of a sinner presupposes a prior redemption. Whoever is once guilty of sin is liable to its penalty. He must pay, or someone else must pay for him, whatever ransom the offended party, who holds him in his power, chooses to demand. The offended party is Almighty God, in whose power all things lie, so before salvation can be obtained, the ransom paid must be whatever God has been pleased to require. This ransom does not mean a satisfaction for sin equal to the offence. No sinner could ever make such a satisfaction for himself, and no righteous man could make it for another. A man can make amends for damage he does to another by restoring what he took or by paying compensation, but sin cannot be removed by compensation. That would turn the freedom to sin into something that could be bought and sold. Sins may, however, be pardoned to those who repent. God may pardon them freely, without charge, or on payment of whatever penalty he is pleased to accept. In the Old Testament, what God usually accepted was a sacrifice or offering.

To forgive sin is no injustice, even when punishment has been threatened. Even among men, a promise of good binds the one who makes it, but threats, which are promises of evil, do not bind. Still less will they bind God, who is infinitely more merciful than men. Our Saviour Christ, therefore, did not redeem us by satisfying for the sins of men in the sense that his death, by its own power, could make it unjust for God to punish sinners with eternal death. At his first coming he offered himself as the sacrifice and offering that God was pleased to require. In return, at his second coming, those who in the meantime had repented and believed in him would be saved. Scripture does not always call this act of our redemption a sacrifice and offering. Sometimes it calls it a price. Even so, we are not to understand by "price" something whose value gave him a right to claim our pardon from his offended Father. It is only the price that God the Father, in his mercy, was pleased to demand.

## Chapter XXXIX. Of the Meaning in Scripture of the Word Church

### The Church as the Lord's House

In the books of Holy Scripture, the word *church* (*ecclesia*) carries several meanings. Sometimes, though not often, it means God's house: a temple in which Christians gather to perform their sacred duties in public. Paul uses it this way in 1 Corinthians 14:34, "Let your women keep silence in the churches." But there the word is a metaphor for the congregation assembled in the building. Only later did it come to mean the building itself, as a way of distinguishing the temples of Christians from those of idolaters. The Temple at Jerusalem was God's house and the house of prayer. In the same way, any building that Christians dedicate to the worship of Christ is Christ's house. For this reason the Greek Fathers called it *Kuriake*, "the Lord's house," and from that word our own language derived *kyrke*, and finally *church*.

### What *Ecclesia* Properly Means

When it does not refer to a building, *church* means what *ecclesia* meant in the commonwealths of ancient Greece: a congregation, an assembly of citizens called out to hear a magistrate address them. In the Roman commonwealth such an assembly was called a *concio*, and the man who spoke to it was called an *ecclesiastes* or *concionator*. When citizens were called out by lawful authority, as in Acts 19:39, the gathering was an *ecclesia legitima*, a lawful church, or in Greek an *ennomos ecclesia*. When they were stirred up and drawn together by riotous and seditious clamor, it was a confused church, an *ecclesia sugkechumene*.

The word is also sometimes used for all those who have the right to belong to the congregation, even when they are not actually assembled. In this sense it means the whole body of Christians, however widely scattered. This is its meaning in Acts 8:3, where we read that "Saul made havoc of the church," and it is in this sense that Christ is called the head of the church. Sometimes it means a particular group of Christians, as in Colossians 4:15: "Salute the church that is in his house." Sometimes it means the elect alone, as in Ephesians 5:27: "A glorious church, without spot or wrinkle, holy, and without blemish." This passage refers to the Church Triumphant, the church to come. And sometimes it means an assembled congregation of those who profess Christianity, whether that profession is sincere or counterfeit. Such is the meaning in Matthew 18:17: "Tell it to the church; and if he neglect to hear the church, let him be to thee as a Gentile or a publican."

### In What Sense the Church Is One Person, and the Church Defined

Only in this last sense can the church be regarded as a single person, that is, as a body that can be said to have the power to will, to pronounce judgment, to command, to be obeyed, to make laws, or to perform any other action whatever. Without authority from a lawful congregation, anything done in a gathering of people is the individual act of each person who was present and helped to bring it about. It is not the act of all of them together, as of one body. Still less is it the act of those who were absent, or of those who were present but did not want it done. In this sense I define a CHURCH as "a company of men professing the Christian religion, united in the person of one sovereign, at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble." And because in every commonwealth any assembly held without warrant from the civil sovereign is unlawful, a church that assembles in a commonwealth that has forbidden it to assemble is likewise an unlawful assembly.

### A Christian Commonwealth and a Church Are One and the Same

It also follows that there is no universal church on earth that all Christians are bound to obey, because there is no power on earth to which all other commonwealths are subject. There are Christians in the dominions of many different princes and states, but each of them is subject to the commonwealth of which he himself is a member, and consequently he cannot be subject to the commands of any other person. A church, then, in the sense of a body capable of commanding, judging, absolving, condemning, or performing any other act, is the same thing as a civil commonwealth made up of Christians. It is called a civil state because its subjects are men, and a church because its subjects are Christians. "Temporal" and "spiritual" government are merely two words brought into the world to make men see double and mistake their lawful sovereign. It is true that after the resurrection the bodies of the faithful will be not only spiritual but eternal; in this life, however, they are gross and corruptible. In this life, therefore, there is no government other than temporal government, whether of the state or of religion. Nor is it lawful for any subject to teach a doctrine that the governor of both the state and the religion forbids to be taught. And that governor must be one. Otherwise faction and civil war must inevitably follow within the commonwealth: between church and state, between spiritualists and temporalists, between the sword of justice and the shield of faith, and, what is worse, within every Christian's own breast, between the Christian and the man. The teachers of the church are called pastors, and so are civil sovereigns. But unless pastors are subordinate to one another, so that there is a single chief pastor, men will be taught contradictory doctrines, of which both may be false and one must be. Who that chief pastor is according to the law of nature has already been shown: it is the civil sovereign. To whom Scripture has assigned that office we shall see in the chapters that follow.

## Chapter XL. Of the Rights of the Kingdom of God, in Abraham, Moses, High Priests, and the Kings of Judah

### The Sovereign Rights of Abraham

Abraham, the father of the faithful, was the first to enter the Kingdom of God by covenant, because the covenant was first made with him. In it he bound himself and his descendants to acknowledge and obey the commands of God. These included the moral laws, which he could recognize by the light of nature, and also the commands that God would deliver to him in a special manner through dreams and visions. As for the moral law, Abraham and his descendants were already bound by it, and there was no need to secure their obedience by contract with the promise of the land of Canaan. No contract could add to or strengthen the obligation by which they, like all other people, were bound by nature to obey Almighty God. The covenant Abraham made with God was therefore an agreement to accept as God's commandment whatever was commanded him in God's name in a dream or vision, to deliver it to his family, and to make them observe it.

### Abraham Had the Sole Power of Ordering the Religion of His Own People

This contract between God and Abraham reveals three points that bear heavily on the government of God's people. The first is that when the covenant was made, God spoke only to Abraham. He did not contract with any of Abraham's family or descendants except insofar as their wills, which are the essence of every covenant, were already contained in Abraham's will before the contract was made. Abraham was therefore understood to have lawful power to make them perform everything he had covenanted on their behalf. Accordingly, in the eighteenth chapter of Genesis, God says: "All the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him. For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord." From this we may draw the first point: those to whom God has not spoken directly must receive God's positive commandments, meaning the laws He has specifically decreed as distinct from those known by natural reason, from their sovereign, just as the family and descendants of Abraham received them from Abraham, who was their father, their lord, and their civil sovereign. Consequently, in every commonwealth, those who have received no supernatural revelation to the contrary ought to obey the laws of their own sovereign in the outward acts and profession of religion. Inward thought and belief are another matter. Human governors cannot observe them, since God alone knows the heart. They are not voluntary, and they are produced by God's unrevealed will and power rather than by laws. They therefore fall outside the scope of obligation.

### No Pretense of Private Spirit Against the Religion of Abraham

The second point follows from the first. Some of Abraham's subjects might claim a private vision, a private spirit, or some other revelation from God in support of a doctrine that Abraham had forbidden, and others might follow or attach themselves to such a claimant. It was not unlawful for Abraham to punish any of them. Likewise, it is lawful today for the sovereign to punish anyone who sets his private spirit against the laws, because the sovereign holds the same place in the commonwealth that Abraham held in his own family.

### Abraham Sole Judge and Interpreter of What God Spoke

A third point arises from the same source. Just as no one but Abraham could determine within his family what was or was not the Word of God, so no one but the sovereign can make that determination in a Christian commonwealth. God spoke only to Abraham, and Abraham alone could know what God had said and interpret it to his family. Those who hold Abraham's place in a commonwealth are therefore the only interpreters of what God has spoken.

### The Authority of Moses, and Its Foundation

The same covenant was renewed with Isaac and afterward with Jacob, and then it was not renewed again until the Israelites had been freed from the Egyptians and arrived at the foot of Mount Sinai. There, as I have said before, Moses renewed it in such a way that from that time forward the Israelites became God's own peculiar kingdom, His special possession among the nations. Moses was God's lieutenant for his own lifetime, and the succession to that office was settled on Aaron and his heirs after him, so that they would be a priestly kingdom to God forever.

This arrangement acquired a kingdom for God. Moses, however, had no authority to govern the Israelites as successor to Abraham's right, because he could not claim that right by inheritance. Nothing so far shows that the people were obliged to accept him as God's lieutenant for any longer than they believed that God spoke to him. His authority, notwithstanding the covenant they had made with God, still depended entirely on their opinion of his holiness, of the reality of his conversations with God, and of the truth of his miracles. If that opinion changed, they would no longer be obliged to accept as God's law anything he set before them in God's name. We must therefore consider what other ground there was for their obligation to obey him. It could not be the command of God, because God did not speak to them directly but only through Moses himself. Our Savior says of himself, in the fifth chapter of John, "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true." Still less ought Moses' testimony to be accepted when he bears witness of himself, especially when he claims kingly power over God's people. His authority, like that of every other prince, must therefore rest on the consent of the people and their promise to obey him. And so it did. In the twentieth chapter of Exodus we read that "the people, when they saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking, removed, and stood afar off. And they said unto Moses, Speak thou with us, and we will hear; but let not God speak with us, lest we die." This was their promise of obedience, and by it they bound themselves to obey whatever Moses should deliver to them as the commandment of God.

### Moses Was, Under God, Sovereign of the Jews Throughout His Own Time, Though Aaron Held the Priesthood

The covenant did establish a priestly kingdom, a kingdom hereditary in the line of Aaron. That provision, however, must be understood to concern the succession after Moses' death. Whoever orders and establishes the constitution of a commonwealth as its first founder, whether it is a monarchy, an aristocracy, or a democracy, must necessarily hold sovereign power over the people for as long as he is engaged in that work. Scripture plainly affirms that Moses held this power throughout his lifetime. The first evidence is the passage just cited, in which the people promised obedience to Moses rather than to Aaron. The second is in the twenty-fourth chapter of Exodus: "And God said unto Moses, Come up unto the Lord, thou, and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. And Moses alone shall come near the Lord; but they shall not come nigh, neither shall the people go up with him." Moses alone was called up to God. Aaron, the other priests, and the seventy elders were not, and the people were expressly forbidden to come up. This makes it plain that Moses alone represented the person of God to the Israelites and was their sole sovereign under God. A few verses later the text does say, "Then went up Moses, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and they saw the God of Israel, and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone." But this happened only after Moses had already been with God and had brought the people the words God had spoken to him. Moses alone went on the people's business. The others were admitted as the nobles of his retinue, as an honor, to a special grace that was denied to the people, which, as the following verse shows, was to see God and live: "God laid not his hand upon them; they saw God, and did eat and drink," meaning that they lived. They carried no commandment from Him to the people.

Again, Scripture says throughout that "the Lord spake unto Moses," and it says so in every matter of government. This is equally true of the ordering of the ceremonies of religion, set out in the twenty-fifth through thirty-first chapters of Exodus and throughout Leviticus. To Aaron the Lord seldom spoke. When Aaron made the golden calf, Moses threw it into the fire. Finally, when Aaron and Miriam rebelled against Moses and the question of Aaron's authority arose, God Himself judged it in Moses' favor, as the twelfth chapter of Numbers records. The same happened in the dispute between Moses and the people, recorded in the sixteenth chapter of Numbers, when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, together with two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, "gathered themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said unto them, Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the Lord is among them: wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the Lord?" God caused the earth to swallow Korah, Dathan, and Abiram alive, together with their wives and children, and He consumed the two hundred and fifty princes with fire.

It follows that the sovereignty over the Israelites, next under God, belonged neither to Aaron, nor to the people, nor to any aristocracy of the leading princes of the people, but to Moses alone. This sovereignty extended to religion as well as to civil government, because Moses alone spoke with God and therefore he alone could tell the people what God required of them. No one, on pain of death, could be so presumptuous as to approach the mountain where God spoke with Moses. In the nineteenth chapter of Exodus the Lord says: "Thou shalt set bounds unto the people round about, saying, Take heed to yourselves, that ye go not up into the mount, or touch the border of it: whosoever toucheth the mount shall be surely put to death." A few verses later He says again: "Go down, charge the people, lest they break through unto the Lord to gaze." From this we may conclude that whoever holds the place of Moses in a Christian commonwealth is the sole messenger of God and the sole interpreter of His commandments. It follows that no one, in interpreting Scripture, ought to go beyond the bounds set by his own sovereign. Since God now speaks through the Scriptures, they are our Mount Sinai, and its boundary markers are the laws of those who represent God's person on earth. We are permitted to look upon the Scriptures, to behold in them the wondrous works of God, and to learn to fear Him. But to interpret them, which means to pry into what God says to the one He has appointed to govern under Him and to set ourselves up as judges of whether that ruler governs as God commands, is to cross the bounds God has set for us and to gaze upon God irreverently.

### All Spirits Were Subordinate to the Spirit of Moses

In Moses' time there was no prophet, and no one claiming the Spirit of God, except those whom Moses had approved and authorized. Only seventy men in his time are said to have prophesied by the Spirit of God, and Moses chose every one of them. Concerning them God says to Moses, in the eleventh chapter of Numbers: "Gather unto me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people." God imparted His Spirit to these men, but it was not a Spirit different from that of Moses, for the text says: "The Lord came down in a cloud, and took of the spirit that was upon him, and gave it unto the seventy elders." As I have shown earlier, "spirit" here means mind. The sense of the passage is simply that God gave the elders a mind that conformed and was subordinate to the mind of Moses, so that they could prophesy, meaning that they could speak to the people in God's name, and, as Moses' ministers acting under his authority, advance doctrine that agreed with his. They were only ministers. When two of them prophesied in the camp, it was regarded as something new and unlawful. As the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth verses of the same chapter relate, they were accused, and Joshua advised Moses to forbid them, not realizing that it was by Moses' spirit that they prophesied. This makes it plain that no subject ought to claim the gift of prophecy, or the Spirit, in opposition to the doctrine established by the one whom God has placed in the position of Moses.

### After Moses the Sovereignty Lay with the High Priest

After the death of Aaron, and then of Moses, the kingdom, being a priestly kingdom, passed by virtue of the covenant to Aaron's son Eleazar, the high priest. God declared Eleazar sovereign, next under Himself, at the same time that He appointed Joshua general of the army. In the twenty-seventh chapter of Numbers, God says expressly of Joshua: "He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall ask counsel for him before the Lord: at his word shall they go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he, and all the children of Israel with him." The supreme power of making war and peace therefore belonged to the priest. The supreme judicial power belonged to the high priest as well, because the Book of the Law was in the priests' keeping, and the priests and Levites alone served as the subordinate judges in civil cases, as the seventeenth chapter of Deuteronomy shows. As for the manner of God's worship, no one ever doubted that the high priest held supreme authority over it until the time of Saul. Civil and ecclesiastical power were therefore joined in one and the same person, the high priest. They ought to be joined in the same way in anyone who governs by divine right, that is, by authority received directly from God.

### Of the Sovereign Power Between the Time of Joshua and of Saul

From the death of Joshua until the time of Saul, the Book of Judges repeatedly observes that "in those days there was no king in Israel," and sometimes adds that "every man did that which was right in his own eyes." Where it says "there was no king," it means that there was no sovereign power in Israel. That was true if we consider the actual exercise of such power. For after the deaths of Joshua and Eleazar, as the second chapter of Judges records, "there arose another generation, which knew not the Lord, nor the works which he had done for Israel, but did evil in the sight of the Lord, and served Baalim," the Baals of the surrounding peoples. The Jews also had the trait that St. Paul remarks upon: they looked for a sign. They demanded signs not only before they would submit to the government of Moses but even after they had bound themselves by that submission. Yet signs and miracles were meant to produce faith, not to keep people from breaking it once they had given it, because the law of nature already obliges men to keep faith once given. If, however, we consider not the exercise of government but the right to govern, sovereign power still resided in the High Priest. The Judges were men chosen by God through extraordinary means to rescue his rebellious subjects from the hands of their enemies, and whatever obedience the people gave them cannot be used as an argument against the High Priest's right to sovereign power in all matters of both policy and religion. Neither the Judges nor Samuel himself held an ordinary calling to govern; theirs was an extraordinary one. The Israelites obeyed them not out of duty but out of reverence for the favor they evidently enjoyed with God, a favor that showed itself in their wisdom, their courage, or their good fortune. Up to this point, then, the right to regulate civil policy and the right to regulate religion were inseparable.

### Of the Rights of the Kings of Israel

Kings succeeded the Judges. Where all authority in religion and in policy had previously belonged to the High Priest, it now belonged entirely to the King. Sovereignty over the people had rested not only on God's divine power but also on a particular covenant by which the Israelites had placed themselves under God and, next under him, under the High Priest as his viceroy on earth. The people cast that sovereignty off, and God himself consented. When they said to Samuel, as recorded in the eighth chapter of the First Book of Samuel, "Make us a king to judge us, like all the nations," they declared that they would no longer be governed by commands laid upon them by the Priest in God's name, but by a ruler who would command them in the same way all other nations were commanded. In stripping the High Priest of royal authority, they consequently abolished God's own peculiar government over them. And yet God consented, saying to Samuel in the seventh verse, "Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." Having rejected God, in whose right the Priests had governed, the people left the Priests no authority except what the King chose to allow them, and that was more or less according to whether the Kings were good or evil.

As for the government of civil affairs, it plainly lay entirely in the King's hands. In the same chapter, at the twentieth verse, the people say they will be like all the nations, that their king shall judge them, go out before them, and fight their battles. That is, he would hold the whole of authority in peace and in war. That authority included the ordering of religion as well, because in that age there was no other word of God by which to regulate religion than the Law of Moses, and the Law of Moses was their civil law. Moreover, we read in the second chapter of the First Book of Kings that Solomon "thrust out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord." Solomon therefore had authority over the High Priest, as over any other subject, and that is a strong mark of supremacy in religion. We read too, in the eighth chapter of the same book, that Solomon dedicated the Temple, that he blessed the people, and that he personally offered the excellent prayer that is still used at the consecration of all churches and houses of prayer. That is another strong mark of supremacy in religion. Again, the twenty-second chapter of the Second Book of Kings relates that when a question arose about the Book of the Law found in the Temple, the High Priest did not decide it. Instead, King Josiah sent him, along with others, to inquire about it of Huldah the prophetess, which is yet another mark of supremacy in religion. Finally, the twenty-sixth chapter of the First Book of Chronicles tells us, at the thirtieth verse, that David appointed Hashabiah and his brethren, the Hebronites, as officers of Israel on the western side of the Jordan "in all the business of the Lord, and in the service of the king." Likewise, at the thirty-second verse, he appointed other Hebronites as "rulers over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh," who were the rest of Israel living beyond the Jordan, "for every matter pertaining to God, and affairs of the king." Is this not full power, both "temporal" and "spiritual," as those who would divide it call these two halves? To conclude: from the first institution of God's kingdom until the Babylonian Captivity, supremacy in religion was held by the same hand that held civil sovereignty. After the election of Saul, the Priest's office was not one of command but one of service.

### The Practice of Supremacy in Religion Did Not, in the Time of the Kings, Match the Right to It

Although government in both policy and religion was united, first in the High Priests and afterward in the Kings, as a matter of right, the same sacred history makes clear that the people did not understand this. A large part of them, and probably the larger part, gave credit to the reputation of Moses, or to the conversations reported between God and the Priests, only so long as they witnessed great miracles. Great ability, or great success in their governors' undertakings, served them as the equivalent of a miracle. Whenever their governors displeased them, they seized the occasion, blaming sometimes the policy and sometimes the religion, to change the government or to withdraw their obedience as they pleased. From this came the civil disturbances, divisions, and calamities that afflicted the nation from time to time.
