For example, after the deaths of Eleazar and Joshua, the next generation had not seen God's wonders and was left to its own weak reason. Not recognizing that they were bound by the covenant of a priestly kingdom, they no longer paid any regard to the commands of the Priest or to any law of Moses, and every man did what was right in his own eyes. In civil affairs they obeyed whatever men they believed, at any given moment, could deliver them from the neighboring nations that oppressed them. They did not consult God, as they ought to have done, but consulted men or women whom they took to be prophets because of their predictions of future events. And even if they kept an idol in their chapel, so long as they had a Levite as their chaplain, they considered themselves worshippers of the God of Israel.

Later, when they demanded a king in the manner of the nations, they did not intend to abandon the worship of God their King. They had despaired of justice from Samuel's sons and wanted a king to judge them in civil matters, but they had no intention of allowing their king to change the religion they believed Moses had commended to them. So they always kept a pretext in reserve, whether of justice or of religion, by which to release themselves from obedience whenever they had hope of succeeding. Samuel was displeased with the people for wanting a king, since God was already their King and Samuel held only an authority under him. Yet when Saul disregarded Samuel's counsel by failing to destroy Agag as God had commanded, Samuel anointed another king, David, to take the succession away from Saul's heirs. Rehoboam was no idolater, but when the people judged him an oppressor, that civil pretext carried ten tribes away from him to Jeroboam, who was an idolater. Throughout the entire history of the kings, of Judah and of Israel alike, there were prophets who continually checked the kings for transgressing in religion, and sometimes for errors of state as well. The nineteenth chapter of the Second Book of Chronicles records how the prophet Jehu rebuked Jehoshaphat for helping the King of Israel against the Syrians, and Isaiah rebuked Hezekiah for showing his treasures to the ambassadors of Babylon. All of this shows that although the power of both state and religion lay with the kings, none of them exercised it unchecked except those who were favored for their natural abilities or their good fortune. No argument can therefore be drawn from the practice of those times that the right of supremacy in religion did not belong to the kings, unless we place it in the prophets. We would then have to conclude that because Hezekiah, praying to the Lord before the cherubim, received no answer from there and at that time, but only later through the prophet Isaiah, Isaiah was the supreme head of the Church. Or we would have to conclude that because Josiah consulted Huldah the prophetess about the Book of the Law, supreme authority in matters of religion belonged neither to him nor to the High Priest but to Huldah. I do not think any learned theologian holds that opinion.

### After the Captivity the Jews Had No Settled Commonwealth

During the Captivity, the Jews had no commonwealth at all. After their return they renewed their covenant with God, yet they made no promise of obedience either to Ezra or to anyone else. Soon afterward they became subjects of the Greeks, and their religion was badly corrupted by Greek customs and Greek beliefs about demons, as well as by the doctrines of the Cabalists. Their confusion in both state and religion was such that nothing can be gathered from it about supremacy in either. So far as the Old Testament is concerned, then, we may conclude that whoever held the sovereignty of the commonwealth among the Jews also held supreme authority in matters of God's outward worship, and represented God's person, that is, the person of God the Father. God was not called by the name of Father until he sent his Son Jesus Christ into the world to redeem mankind from their sins and to bring them into his everlasting kingdom, to be saved forevermore. That is the subject of the following chapter.

## Chapter XLI. Of the Office of Our Blessed Saviour

### The Three Parts of Christ's Office

Holy Scripture describes the office of the Messiah as having three parts. The first is that of a Redeemer, or Saviour. The second is that of a Pastor, Counselor, or Teacher, which is to say a Prophet sent from God to convert those whom God has chosen for salvation. The third is that of a King, an eternal King, yet one who reigns under his Father, as Moses and the High Priests did in their respective times. These three parts correspond to three periods of time. Christ accomplished our redemption at his first coming, through the sacrifice in which he offered himself on the cross for our sins. Our conversion he accomplished partly then, in his own person, and he accomplishes it partly now through his ministers, and will continue to do so until he comes again. After his second coming his glorious reign over his elect will begin, and it will last forever.

### His Office as a Redeemer

A Redeemer is one who pays the ransom for sin, and that ransom is death. To this office it therefore belonged that he should be sacrificed, and in that way bear upon his own head and carry away from us our sins, in the manner God had required. This does not mean that the death of one man, even a man without sin, can satisfy for the offenses of all men by the strict measure of justice. It satisfies them through the mercy of God, who ordained such sacrifices for sin as he was pleased, in his mercy, to accept.

Under the old Law, as we read in the sixteenth chapter of Leviticus, the Lord required that once every year an atonement be made for the sins of all Israel, priests and people alike. To carry it out, Aaron alone was to sacrifice a young bullock for himself and the priests. For the rest of the people he was to receive two young goats. One of these he was to sacrifice. The other was the scapegoat: he was to lay his hands on its head, confess over it the sins of the people, and so place all those sins upon that head. Then he was to have the goat led into the wilderness by some man appointed for the purpose, and there let it escape, carrying the people's sins away with it.

The sacrifice of the one goat was a sufficient price for the ransom of all Israel because it was an acceptable one. In the same way, the death of the Messiah is a sufficient price for the sins of all mankind, because nothing more was required. Our Saviour's sufferings appear to be foreshadowed here as clearly as in the offering of Isaac, or in any other figure of him in the Old Testament. He was both the sacrificed goat and the scapegoat. In the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah we read: "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he did not open his mouth; he was brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep is silent before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth." Here he is the sacrificed goat. Earlier in that chapter: "He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows," and again, "The Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all." Here he is the scapegoat. "He was cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of my people": here once more he is the sacrificed goat. And again, "He shall bear their sins": he is the scapegoat. In this way the Lamb of God is the equivalent of both goats. He was sacrificed in that he died, and he escaped in his resurrection, having been raised at the appointed time by his Father and removed from the dwelling place of men in his ascension.

### Christ's Kingdom Not of This World

One who redeems has no title to the thing redeemed until the redemption is complete and the ransom paid, and this ransom was the death of the Redeemer. It is therefore plain that our Saviour, as a man, was not King of those he redeemed before he suffered death, that is, during the time he lived bodily on earth. I mean that he was not then their King in the present by virtue of the covenant the faithful make with him in baptism. Nevertheless, by renewing their covenant with God in baptism, they were bound to obey him as King, under his Father, whenever he should be pleased to take the kingdom upon himself. In keeping with this, our Saviour says expressly in the Gospel of John, "My kingdom is not of this world." Scripture mentions only two worlds: the present one, which will last until the Day of Judgment and for that reason is also called the Last Day, and the one that shall be a new heaven and a new earth. It follows that the kingdom of Christ will not begin until the general resurrection.

This is what our Saviour says in Matthew: "The Son of Man shall come in the glory of his Father, with his angels, and then he shall reward every man according to his works." To reward every man according to his works is to perform the office of a king, and this is not to happen until he comes in the glory of his Father with his angels. When our Saviour says, also in Matthew, "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore whatever they tell you to do, observe and do it," he declares plainly that for that time he assigns kingly power not to himself but to them. He does the same when he says in Luke, "Who made me a judge or a divider over you?" and in John, "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world."

And yet our Saviour came into this world so that he might be a King and a Judge in the world to come. He was the Messiah, that is, the Christ, the Anointed Priest and Sovereign Prophet of God, which means he was to hold all the power that had belonged to Moses the Prophet, to the High Priests who succeeded Moses, and to the Kings who succeeded the Priests. Saint John says expressly, "The Father judges no man, but has committed all judgment to the Son." This does not contradict the other passage, "I came not to judge the world," because one speaks of the present world and the other of the world to come. The same holds where it is said of Christ's second coming, in Matthew, "You who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you also shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel."

### The Purpose of Christ's Coming Was to Renew the Covenant of the Kingdom of God and to Persuade the Elect to Embrace It, Which Was the Second Part of His Office

If Christ had no kingdom in this world while he was on earth, what was the purpose of his first coming? It was to restore to God, by a new covenant, the kingdom that had been his under the old covenant and had been cut off by the rebellion of the Israelites when they chose Saul as king. To accomplish this, he was to preach to them that he was the Messiah, the King promised to them by the Prophets; to offer himself as a sacrifice for the sins of those who would submit to him in faith; and, if the nation as a whole refused him, to call into his obedience those among the Gentiles who would believe in him.

His office during his time on earth therefore had two parts. One was to proclaim himself the Christ. The other was to persuade and prepare men, by teaching and by working miracles, to live in such a way as to be worthy of the immortality believers were to enjoy when he came in majesty to take possession of his Father's kingdom. This is why he himself often called the time of his preaching the Regeneration. It was not properly a kingdom, and so gave no license to refuse obedience to the magistrates then in power, for he commanded his followers to obey those who then sat in Moses' chair and to pay tribute to Caesar. It was only a pledge of the kingdom of God that was to come, given to those whom God had granted the grace to be his disciples and to believe in him. For this reason the godly are said to be already in the Kingdom of Grace, as though they were naturalized citizens of that heavenly kingdom.

### The Preaching of Christ Not Contrary to the Law of the Jews of That Time, Nor to the Law of Caesar

So far, then, Christ did and taught nothing that tended to diminish the civil rights of the Jews or of Caesar. As for the commonwealth that then existed among the Jews, both those who ruled and those who were ruled were expecting the Messiah and the kingdom of God. They could not have done so if their laws had forbidden him, once he came, to reveal and declare himself. Since he did nothing except attempt to prove, by preaching and miracles, that he was that Messiah, he did nothing in this against their laws. The kingdom he claimed was to be in another world. He taught all men to obey, in the meantime, those who sat in Moses' seat. He allowed them to pay Caesar his tribute, and he refused to take on the role of a judge. How, then, could his words or actions be seditious, or tend toward the overthrow of the civil government of the day? But God, having determined on his sacrifice as the means of bringing his elect back to the obedience they had once covenanted, made use of their malice and ingratitude to bring it about.

Nor was his preaching contrary to the laws of Caesar. Pilate himself, to please the Jews, handed him over to be crucified, yet before doing so he declared openly that he found no fault in him. And for the inscription stating the cause of his condemnation, Pilate did not write what the Jews demanded, "that he claimed to be King," but simply "that he was King of the Jews." Despite their outcry, he refused to change it, saying, "What I have written, I have written."

### The Third Part of His Office Was to Be King, Under His Father, of the Elect

As for the third part of his office, which was to be King, I have already shown that his kingdom was not to begin until the resurrection. But then he will be King not only as God, in which sense he already is and always will be King of all the earth by virtue of his omnipotence, but also, in a particular way, King of his own elect, by virtue of the covenant they make with him in baptism. This is why our Saviour says in the nineteenth chapter of Matthew that his Apostles would sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel "when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his glory," by which he indicated that he would then reign in his human nature. And in the sixteenth chapter: "The Son of Man shall come in the glory of his Father, with his angels, and then he shall reward every man according to his works." The same may be read in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters of Mark, and still more explicitly as to the time in the twenty-second chapter of Luke: "I appoint to you a kingdom, as my Father has appointed one to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." From this it is plain that the kingdom appointed to Christ by his Father is not to come before the Son of Man comes in glory and makes his Apostles judges of the twelve tribes of Israel.

Someone may ask here, since there is no marriage in the kingdom of heaven, whether men will then eat and drink, and if not, what kind of eating is meant in this passage. Our Saviour explains it himself in John, where he says, "Do not labor for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to everlasting life, which the Son of Man shall give you." So to eat at Christ's table means to eat of the Tree of Life, that is, to enjoy immortality in the kingdom of the Son of Man. From these passages and many others it is evident that our Saviour's kingdom is to be exercised by him in his human nature.

### Christ's Authority in the Kingdom of God Subordinate to His Father's

Furthermore, he is to be King then only as a subordinate, or viceroy, of God the Father, as Moses was in the wilderness, as the High Priests were before the reign of Saul, and as the Kings were after it. One of the prophecies concerning Christ is that he would be like Moses in his office. "I will raise up for them a Prophet from among their brethren, like you," says the Lord in Deuteronomy, "and will put my words in his mouth." This likeness to Moses is also apparent in what our Saviour himself did while he lived on earth. Moses chose twelve princes of the tribes to govern under him; our Saviour chose twelve Apostles, who will sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel. Moses authorized seventy elders to receive the Spirit of God and to prophesy to the people, which, as I have said before, means to speak to them in the name of God; our Saviour likewise ordained seventy disciples to preach his kingdom and salvation to all nations. When a complaint was brought to Moses against some of the seventy who were prophesying in the camp of Israel, he defended them, since in doing so they were serving under his government. In the same way, when Saint John complained to our Saviour about a certain man who was casting out devils in his name, our Saviour defended him, saying, as Luke records, "Do not forbid him, for he who is not against us is on our side."

Our Saviour also resembled Moses in instituting sacraments, both of admission into the kingdom of God and of commemoration of the deliverance of his elect from their wretched condition. Before the time of Moses, the children of Israel had circumcision as the sacrament of their reception into the kingdom of God. The rite was neglected in the wilderness but restored as soon as they came into the Promised Land. Similarly, before our Saviour came, the Jews had a rite of baptism, that is, of washing with water all Gentiles who embraced the God of Israel. Saint John the Baptist used this rite to receive all those who enrolled themselves under the Christ, whom he preached as having already come into the world, and our Saviour instituted the same rite as a sacrament to be received by all who believed in him.

Scripture does not state formally where the rite of baptism originated. It may reasonably be thought to imitate the law of Moses concerning leprosy. Under that law, a leper was ordered to be kept outside the camp of Israel for a certain period, after which, if the priest judged him clean, he was admitted back into the camp after a solemn washing. This may therefore be a figure of the washing in baptism, in which those who have been cleansed by faith of the leprosy of sin are received into the Church with the solemnity of baptism. Another conjecture is drawn from the ceremonies of the Gentiles in a case that rarely occurs. When a man thought to be dead happened to recover, other people were reluctant to have dealings with him, as they would be with a ghost, unless he had been received back into the company of men by a washing, just as newborn children were washed of the uncleanness of their birth, which made it a kind of new birth. This Greek ceremony may quite plausibly have found its way into the religion of the Jews during the period when Judaea was under the rule of Alexander and his Greek successors. But since it is unlikely that our Saviour would have endorsed a heathen rite, the most probable source is the ceremony prescribed by the Law for washing after leprosy.

As for the other sacrament, the eating of the Passover lamb, it is plainly imitated in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. There the breaking of the bread and the pouring out of the wine keep in memory our deliverance from the misery of sin through Christ's Passion, just as eating the Passover lamb kept in memory the deliverance of the Jews from bondage in Egypt.

Since the authority of Moses, then, was only subordinate, and he was only a lieutenant to God, it follows that Christ, whose authority as a man was to resemble that of Moses, was likewise nothing more than subordinate to the authority of his Father. The same point is made still more explicitly by the prayer he teaches us, "Our Father, thy kingdom come," and "For thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory"; by the statement that "he shall come in the glory of his Father"; by what Saint Paul says in his First Letter to the Corinthians, "Then comes the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father"; and by many other passages that are perfectly explicit.

### One and the Same God Is the Person Represented by Moses and by Christ

Our Saviour, therefore, in both teaching and reigning, represents the person of God, as Moses did. From that time forward, but not before, this God is called the Father. Remaining always one and the same substance, he is one person as represented by Moses and another person as represented by his Son, the Christ. For since a person is defined in relation to a representer, it follows that where there are several representers there are several persons, even though they are of one and the same substance.

## Chapter XLII. Of Power Ecclesiastical

To understand ecclesiastical power, both what it is and in whom it resides, we must divide the time since our Savior's Ascension into two periods: one before the conversion of kings and others who held sovereign civil power, and the other after their conversion. For it was long after the Ascension before any king or civil sovereign embraced the Christian religion and publicly permitted it to be taught.

### Of the Holy Spirit That Fell on the Apostles

For the period in between, it is clear that ecclesiastical power lay with the apostles. After them it lay with those whom the apostles ordained to preach the gospel, to convert people to Christianity, and to guide the converted along the way to salvation. After these, it passed in turn to others whom they ordained. This transmission was carried out by the laying on of hands upon those being ordained, a gesture that signified the giving of the Holy Spirit, or Spirit of God, to those they ordained as ministers of God to advance his kingdom. The laying on of hands, then, was nothing other than the seal on their commission to preach Christ and teach his doctrine, and the giving of the Holy Ghost through that ceremony imitated what Moses had done. Moses used the same ceremony with his minister Joshua, as we read in Deuteronomy 34:9: "And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the Spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him." Between his Resurrection and his Ascension, therefore, our Savior gave his Spirit to the apostles, first by "breathing on them, and saying, Receive ye the Holy Spirit," as John 20:22 records, and then, after his Ascension, by sending down upon them "a mighty wind, and cloven tongues of fire," as Acts 2:2–3 tells us. He did not do it by laying on hands, just as God had not laid his hands on Moses. His apostles afterward transmitted the same Spirit by the laying on of hands, as Moses had done with Joshua. It is therefore evident in whom ecclesiastical power continually resided during those early times, when no Christian commonwealth yet existed: namely, in those who received it from the apostles through the successive laying on of hands.

### Of the Trinity

Here we see the person of God borne, or represented, for the third time. Just as Moses and the high priests represented God in the Old Testament, and our Savior himself did so as a man during his time on earth, so the Holy Ghost has represented him ever since. By the Holy Ghost I mean the apostles and their successors in the office of preaching and teaching, who had received the Holy Spirit. But a person, as I have shown before, is whoever is represented, each time he is represented. God, who has been represented (that is, personated) three times, may therefore quite properly be said to be three persons, even though neither the word "person" nor the word "Trinity" is applied to him anywhere in the Bible. St. John does say, in his first epistle, at 5:7, "There be three that bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one." But this does not conflict with three persons in the proper sense of the word "person," meaning that which is represented by another; on the contrary, it fits that sense well. God the Father, as represented by Moses, is one person; as represented by his Son, another person; and as represented by the apostles and by the teachers who taught with authority derived from them, a third person. And yet each of these is the person of one and the same God.

Someone might ask, however, what it was that these three bore witness to. St. John tells us in verse 11 that they bear witness that "God hath given us eternal life in his Son." And if one asks further where that testimony appears, the answer is easy. God has testified to it through the miracles he worked, first through Moses, second through his Son himself, and last through his apostles, who had received the Holy Spirit. Each of these, in its own time, represented the person of God, and each either prophesied or preached Jesus Christ. As for the apostles, the defining mark of apostleship in the first twelve great apostles was to bear witness to his Resurrection. This appears explicitly in Acts 1:21–22, where St. Peter, when a new apostle was to be chosen in place of Judas Iscariot, uses these words: "Of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out amongst us, beginning at the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection." These words explain the bearing of witness that St. John mentions.

In the same passage, John names another trinity of witnesses, this one on earth. In verse 8 he says, "there are three that bear witness in earth, the Spirit, and the water, and the blood; and these three agree in one." He means the graces of God's Spirit and the two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, which all agree in a single testimony that assures believers' consciences of eternal life. Of this testimony he says in verse 10, "He that believeth on the Son of man hath the witness in himself." In this earthly trinity the unity is not one of substance, for the Spirit, the water, and the blood are not the same thing, though they give the same testimony. In the heavenly Trinity, by contrast, the persons are the persons of one and the same God, though represented at three different times and on three different occasions.

To conclude: the doctrine of the Trinity, so far as it can be drawn directly from Scripture, comes in substance to this. God, who is always one and the same, was the person represented by Moses, the person represented by his incarnate Son, and the person represented by the apostles. As represented by the apostles, the Holy Spirit through whom they spoke is God. As represented by his Son, who was both God and man, the Son is that God. As represented by Moses and the high priests, the Father, meaning the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is that God. From this we can see why the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, used to signify the Godhead, never appear in the Old Testament. They are persons; that is, they take their names from the act of representing, and that could not happen until various men had represented God's person, either by ruling or by directing under him.

Thus we see how our Savior left ecclesiastical power to the apostles, and how they were endowed with the Holy Spirit so that they might exercise that power more effectively. For this reason the Spirit is sometimes called in the New Testament the *Paracletus*, which means an assistant, or one called upon for help, though it is commonly translated as "Comforter." Let us now consider the power itself: what it was, and over whom it extended.

### Ecclesiastical Power Is Only the Power to Teach

Cardinal Bellarmine, in his third general Controversy, has treated a great many questions concerning the ecclesiastical power of the Pope of Rome, and he begins with this one: whether that power ought to be monarchical, aristocratic, or democratic. All of these kinds of power are sovereign and coercive. Suppose, however, it should turn out that our Savior left his ministers no coercive power at all, but only a power to proclaim the kingdom of Christ and to persuade people to submit to it, and then, through precepts and sound advice, to teach those who have submitted what they must do to be received into the kingdom of God when it comes. Suppose, in short, that the apostles and other ministers of the gospel are our schoolmasters and not our commanders, and that their precepts are not laws but wholesome counsel. In that case the entire dispute would be in vain.

### An Argument from the Power of Christ Himself

I showed in the previous chapter that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world. It follows that his ministers, unless they are kings, cannot demand obedience in his name. For if the supreme King does not exercise his royal power in this world, by what authority can obedience be demanded for his officers? "As my Father sent me," says our Savior, "I send you." But our Savior was sent to persuade the Jews to return to his Father's kingdom and to invite the Gentiles to receive it, not to reign in majesty, not even as his Father's lieutenant, until the Day of Judgment.

### From the Name "Regeneration"

The time between the Ascension and the general resurrection is called not a reign but a regeneration, meaning a preparation of humanity for Christ's second and glorious coming on the Day of Judgment. This appears in our Savior's words in Matthew 19:28: "You that have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, you shall also sit upon twelve thrones." It appears as well in St. Paul's words in Ephesians 6:15: "Having your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace."

### From Its Comparison to Fishing, Leaven, and Seed

Our Savior also compares this work to fishing, which is to say, to winning people over to obedience not by coercion and punishment but by persuasion. That is why he did not tell his apostles he would make them so many Nimrods, after the "mighty hunter" of Genesis, hunters of men, but rather fishers of men. He compares it as well to leaven working through dough, to the sowing of seed, and to the growth of a grain of mustard seed. Every one of these images excludes compulsion, and consequently there can be no actual reigning during this period. The work of Christ's ministers is evangelization: a proclamation of Christ and a preparation for his second coming, just as the evangelization of John the Baptist was a preparation for his first.

### From the Nature of Faith

Again, the office of Christ's ministers in this world is to bring people to believe and to have faith in Christ. But faith has no connection to compulsion or command and does not depend on them in the least. It depends only on the certainty or probability of arguments drawn from reason, or from something people already believe. The ministers of Christ in this world therefore have no power, by that title, to punish anyone for not believing or for contradicting what they say. I repeat: they have no such power by virtue of being Christ's ministers. If, however, they also hold sovereign civil power by political institution, then they may indeed lawfully punish any contradiction of their laws whatsoever. And St. Paul, speaking of himself and the other preachers of the gospel in his day, says in plain words in 2 Corinthians 1:24: "We have no dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy."

### From the Authority Christ Has Left to Civil Princes

A further argument that Christ's ministers in this present world have no right to command can be drawn from the lawful authority that Christ has left to all princes, Christian and infidel alike. St. Paul says in Colossians 3:20, "Children, obey your parents in all things; for this is well pleasing to the Lord." And in verse 22: "Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh, not with eye-service, as men-pleasers, but in singleness of heart, as fearing the Lord." These words are addressed to people whose masters were infidels, and yet they are told to obey them in all things. On obedience to princes, Paul urges believers in the first six verses of Romans 13 to "be subject to the higher powers," declaring "that all power is ordained of God," and that we ought to be subject to them "not only for" fear of incurring their "wrath, but also for conscience sake." St. Peter, in the second chapter of his first epistle, verses 13 through 15, writes: "Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man, for the Lord's sake, whether it be to the king, as supreme, or unto governors, as to them that be sent by him for the punishment of evil-doers, and for the praise of them that do well; for so is the will of God." And St. Paul says again, in Titus 3:1: "Put men in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, and to obey magistrates." The princes and powers of which Peter and Paul speak here were all infidels. All the more, then, are we bound to obey those Christians whom God has ordained to hold sovereign power over us. How, then, can we be obliged to do anything contrary to the command of the king, or of whatever other sovereign representative governs the commonwealth of which we are members and to which we look for protection? It is therefore clear that Christ has left his ministers in this world no authority to command others, unless they are also endowed with civil authority.

### What Christians May Do to Avoid Persecution

But what, someone may object, if a king, a senate, or some other sovereign forbids us to believe in Christ? I answer that such a prohibition has no effect, because belief and unbelief never follow human commands. Faith is a gift of God, which no man can give or take away, whether by promising rewards or by threatening torture. And if it is asked further whether we must obey our lawful prince when he commands us to declare aloud that we do not believe, I answer that a profession made with the tongue is only an outward act, no different from any other gesture by which we signal our obedience. In this matter a Christian who holds the faith of Christ firmly in his heart has the same liberty that the prophet Elisha granted to Naaman the Syrian. Naaman had been converted in his heart to the God of Israel, for he says in 2 Kings 5:17: "Thy servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice unto other gods, but unto the Lord. In this thing the Lord pardon thy servant, that when my master goeth into the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leaneth on my hand, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon; when I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, the Lord pardon thy servant in this thing." The prophet approved this and told him, "Go in peace." Naaman believed in his heart; yet by bowing before the idol Rimmon he denied the true God in effect, as completely as if he had done so with his lips.

What, then, shall we answer to our Savior's words, "Whosoever denieth me before men, I will deny him before my Father which is in heaven"? We may say this: whatever a subject such as Naaman is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, and does not do of his own inclination but in conformity with the laws of his country, is not his action but his sovereign's. In such a case it is not he who denies Christ before men, but his ruler and the law of his country. If anyone condemns this doctrine as contrary to true and sincere Christianity, I put a case to him. Imagine a subject in some Christian commonwealth who is inwardly, in his heart, a Muslim, and whose sovereign commands him, on pain of death, to attend the divine service of the Christian church. Does my accuser think that Muslim is bound in conscience to suffer death rather than obey the command of his lawful prince? If he says the man ought to suffer death, he authorizes every private person to disobey his prince in defense of his religion, whether true or false. If he says the man ought to obey, he allows himself what he denies to another, contrary to our Savior's words, "Whatsoever you would that men should do unto you, that do ye unto them," and contrary to the law of nature, which is the indubitable and everlasting law of God: "Do not to another that which thou wouldest not he should do unto thee."

### Of Martyrs

What, then, shall we say of all the martyrs we read of in the history of the Church? Did they throw away their lives needlessly? To answer, we must distinguish among those who were put to death for this cause. Some had received a calling to preach and profess the kingdom of Christ openly; others had received no such calling, and nothing more was required of them than their own faith. Those of the first sort, if they were put to death for bearing witness that Jesus Christ is risen from the dead, were true martyrs. A martyr, to give the true definition of the word, is a witness of the resurrection of Jesus the Messiah, and no one can be such a witness except those who lived alongside him on earth and saw him after he had risen. A witness must have seen what he testifies to, or else his testimony is worthless. That only such people can properly be called martyrs of Christ is evident from the words of St. Peter in Acts 1:21–22: "Wherefore of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out amongst us, beginning from the baptism of John unto that same day he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a martyr," that is, a witness, "with us of his resurrection." Here we may observe that anyone who is to witness to the truth of Christ's Resurrection, and so to the truth of the fundamental article of the Christian religion, that Jesus was the Christ, must be a disciple who lived alongside him and saw him both before and after his Resurrection. He must consequently be one of his original disciples. Those who were not can testify to nothing more than that their predecessors said it. They are therefore only witnesses to other men's testimony, secondary martyrs, or martyrs of Christ's witnesses.

Whoever sets himself against the laws and authority of the civil state in order to uphold every doctrine he draws for himself from the history of our Savior's life, or from the Acts or the Epistles of the apostles, or that he believes on the authority of some private person, is very far from being a martyr of Christ, or a martyr of his martyrs. Only one article earns so honorable a name for those who die for it, and that article is this: that Jesus is the Christ, meaning he who has redeemed us and will come again to give us salvation and eternal life in his glorious kingdom. No one is required to die for every tenet that serves the ambition or profit of the clergy. Nor is it the witness's death that makes him a martyr, but the testimony itself, for the word means nothing other than one who bears witness, whether or not he is put to death for his testimony.

Moreover, a man who is not sent to preach this fundamental article, but takes it upon himself on his own private authority, may indeed be a witness, and consequently a martyr, either a primary martyr of Christ or a secondary martyr of his apostles, disciples, or their successors. Yet he is not obliged to suffer death for that cause, since he was never called to it and it is not required of him. Nor should he complain if he loses the reward he expected from those who never set him to the work. No one, therefore, can be a martyr of either the first or the second degree who lacks a warrant to preach Christ come in the flesh, which is to say, no one but those sent to convert unbelievers. For no one is a witness to a person who already believes and so needs no witness; one is a witness only to those who deny, doubt, or have never heard. Christ sent his apostles and his seventy disciples with authority to preach; he did not send everyone who believed. And he sent them to unbelievers: "I send you," he says, "as sheep amongst wolves," not as sheep to other sheep.

### An Argument from the Points of Their Commission

Finally, none of the points of their commission, as they are expressly set down in the Gospels, contains any authority over the congregation.

### To Preach

First, in Matthew 10, the twelve apostles are sent "to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" and commanded to preach "that the kingdom of God is at hand." In the original language, preaching is the act a crier, herald, or other officer performs when publicly proclaiming a king. But a crier has no right to command anyone. In Luke 10:2 the seventy disciples are sent out "as labourers, not as lords of the harvest," and in verse 9 they are told to say, "The kingdom of God is come nigh unto you." By "kingdom" here is meant not the kingdom of grace but the kingdom of glory, for in verse 11 they are told to announce it as a threat to the cities that refuse to receive them, warning that on that day it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for such a city. And in Matthew 20:28 our Savior tells his disciples, who were vying for precedence, that their office was to serve, just as the Son of man came not to be served but to serve. Preachers, then, hold not the magisterial power of a master who commands, but the ministerial power of a servant: "Be not called masters," says our Savior in Matthew 23:10, "for one is your master, even Christ."

### And to Teach

Another point of their commission is to "teach all nations," as Matthew 28:19 has it, or, in the words of Mark 16:15, "Go into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Teaching and preaching, therefore, are the same thing. Those who proclaim a king's coming must also make known by what right he comes, if they intend that people should submit to him. St. Paul did exactly this with the Jews of Thessalonica, when "three sabbath days he reasoned with them out of the scriptures, opening and alleging that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead, and that this Jesus is Christ." But to teach from the Old Testament that Jesus was the Christ, that is, the King, and that he rose from the dead, is not to say that people who come to believe it are bound to obey those who told them so, against the laws and commands of their sovereigns. It is to say that they will act wisely if they await the coming of Christ hereafter in patience and faith, while obeying their present magistrates.

### To Baptize

Another point of their commission is to baptize "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." What is baptism? Dipping in water. But what does it mean to dip a man in water in the name of something? The meaning of these words of baptism is this. The person baptized is dipped or washed as a sign that he is becoming a new man and a loyal subject, first, to the God whose person was represented in ancient times by Moses and the high priests, when he reigned over the Jews; and second, to Jesus Christ, his Son, God and man, who has redeemed us and who will, in his human nature, represent his Father's person in his eternal kingdom after the Resurrection. It is also a sign that he acknowledges the doctrine of the apostles, who were left, with the assistance of the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, as guides to bring us into that kingdom, to be the only sure way to it. This is what we promise in baptism. And the authority of earthly sovereigns is not to be put down until the Day of Judgment, as St. Paul expressly affirms in 1 Corinthians 15:22–24: "As in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive. But every man in his own order, Christ the first fruits, afterward they that are Christ's, at his coming. Then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom of God, even the Father, when he shall have put down all rule, and all authority and power." It is therefore clear that in baptism we do not set up over ourselves another authority to govern our outward actions in this life. We promise only to take the doctrine of the apostles as our direction on the way to eternal life.

### And to Forgive and Retain Sins

The power to remit and to retain sins, which is also called the power of loosing and binding, and sometimes the keys of the kingdom of heaven, follows from the authority to baptize or to refuse baptism. Baptism is the sacrament of allegiance for those who are to be received into the kingdom of God: into eternal life, and therefore into the remission of sin. Eternal life was lost by committing sins, and it is recovered when those sins are remitted. The purpose of baptism is the remission of sins. When the people converted by St. Peter's sermon on the day of Pentecost asked him what they should do, he advised them to "repent, and be baptized in the name of Jesus, for the remission of sins." To baptize is to declare that a person has been received into God's kingdom, and to refuse baptism is to declare that person excluded. It follows that the power to declare people cast out of the kingdom, or retained in it, was given to the same apostles and to their substitutes and successors. After our Savior breathed upon them, saying, "Receive the Holy Ghost" (John 20:22), he added in the next verse, "Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained."

These words do not grant an authority to forgive or retain sins simply and absolutely, as God forgives or retains them, for God knows the human heart and the truth of a person's penitence and conversion. They grant that authority conditionally, to the penitent. If the person absolved has only feigned his repentance, the forgiveness or absolution he received becomes void by that fact alone, without any further act or sentence from the one who absolved him. It does nothing toward his salvation and, on the contrary, aggravates his sin. The apostles and their successors must therefore go by the outward signs of repentance alone. Where those signs appear, they have no authority to deny absolution, and where they do not appear, they have no authority to grant it. The same rule holds for baptism: the apostles had no power to refuse baptism to a converted Jew or Gentile, nor to grant it to the unrepentant.

No one, however, can discern the truth of another person's repentance except by external signs drawn from his words and actions, and these are open to hypocrisy. A further question therefore arises: who is appointed to judge those signs? Our Savior himself settles the question in Matthew 18:15–17: "If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone; if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother. But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more. And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church; let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." These words make plain that the judgment of whether repentance was genuine belonged to no single man. It belonged to the church, meaning the assembly of the faithful or those who had authority to represent them.

Beyond the judgment, a sentence also had to be pronounced, and this always belonged to the apostle, or to some pastor of the church acting as spokesman. Our Savior speaks of this in verse 18: "Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." St. Paul's practice agreed with this. In 1 Corinthians 5:3–5 he says, "For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have determined already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed; in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one unto Satan." To deliver someone to Satan meant to cast him out of the church as a man whose sins are not forgiven. Paul pronounces the sentence here, but because he was absent, the assembly first had to hear the case and, consequently, to condemn the man. Later in the same chapter, in verses 11 and 12, the judgment in such a case is attributed to the assembly more explicitly: "But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, et cetera; with such a one no not to eat. For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? Do not ye judge them that are within?" The apostle or pastor therefore pronounced the sentence that put a man out of the church, but the judgment on the merits of the case lay with the church. In the era before kings and others holding sovereign authority in the commonwealth had been converted, the church meant the assembly of Christians living in the same city. In Corinth, for example, it was the assembly of the Christians of Corinth.

### Of Excommunication

The part of the power of the keys by which people were thrust out of the kingdom of God is called excommunication. In the original Greek, to excommunicate is *aposunagogon poiein*, "to cast out of the synagogue," that is, out of the place of divine worship. The word comes from the Jewish custom of expelling from their synagogues anyone they considered contagious in conduct or in doctrine, much as lepers, under the law of Moses, were separated from the congregation of Israel until a priest pronounced them clean.

### The Use of Excommunication Without Civil Power

Before excommunication was reinforced by civil power, its use and effect extended no further than this: those who were not excommunicated had to avoid the company of those who were. Treating the excommunicated in the same way as heathens who had never been Christians was not enough, because Christians might eat and drink with heathens, and they might not do so with excommunicated persons. St. Paul makes this clear in 1 Corinthians 5:9–10 and the verses that follow. He tells the Corinthians that he had earlier forbidden them "to company with fornicators," but because obeying that rule absolutely would require them to leave the world altogether, he restricts it to fornicators and other vicious persons who belong to the brethren. With such a one, he says, they should not keep company, "no, not to eat." This is no more than our Savior says in Matthew 18:17: "Let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." Publicans were tax farmers, men who had contracted to collect the revenues of the commonwealth, and the Jews who had to pay those revenues hated and detested them so much that "publican" and "sinner" were treated among them as the same thing. When our Savior accepted the invitation of Zacchaeus, a publican, his critics charged it against him as a crime, even though he went in order to convert the man. So when our Savior added "publican" to "heathen," he was forbidding his followers to eat with an excommunicated man.

As for keeping excommunicated people out of their synagogues or places of assembly, Christians had no power to do so beyond the power belonging to the owner of the place, whether that owner was Christian or heathen. All places are by right under the dominion of the commonwealth, so an excommunicated person, just like someone never baptized, could enter them under a commission from the civil magistrate. Paul himself, before his conversion, entered the synagogues at Damascus in this way (Acts 9:2), under a commission from the high priest, to arrest Christians, both men and women, and carry them in chains to Jerusalem.

### Of No Effect Upon an Apostate

It follows that excommunication had no effect at all on a Christian who became an apostate in a place where the civil power persecuted the church or gave it no support. It did him no harm in this world, and it caused him no fear. He felt no fear because he no longer believed, and he suffered no harm because apostasy returned him to the world's favor. In the world to come, he would be in no worse condition than those who had never believed. The harm fell rather on the church, because those it cast out were provoked to act on their malice more freely.

### But Upon the Faithful Only

Excommunication therefore took effect only on those who believed that Jesus Christ would come again in glory to reign over the living and the dead and to judge them, and that he would refuse entry into his kingdom to those whose sins were retained, which is to say those whom the church had excommunicated. This is why St. Paul calls excommunication a delivery of the excommunicated person to Satan: after the Judgment, every kingdom outside the kingdom of Christ is included in the kingdom of Satan. The faithful feared this for as long as they remained excommunicated, in a state where their sins were not forgiven. We can conclude that in the period before the Christian religion was authorized by the civil power, excommunication served only to correct conduct, never errors of opinion. It was a punishment that no one could feel except those who believed in and expected our Savior's return to judge the world, and those who held that belief needed no further opinion to be saved, only an upright life.

### For What Fault Excommunication Applies

Excommunication applies to injustice, as in Matthew 18: if your brother offends you, tell him privately, then before witnesses, and finally tell the church, and if he still does not obey, "let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." It also applies to a scandalous life, as in 1 Corinthians 5:11: "If any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or an extortioner, with such a one ye are not to eat." But Scripture gives no authority, and the apostles give no example, for excommunicating a man who holds the foundational belief that Jesus was the Christ because he differs on other points that do not undermine that foundation.

One text from St. Paul, Titus 3:10, does appear to say the contrary: "A man that is an heretic, after the first and second admonition, reject." A heretic is someone who, while a member of the church, nevertheless teaches some private opinion that the church has forbidden, and St. Paul advises Titus to reject such a person after the first and second admonition. To reject him in this passage does not mean to excommunicate him. It means to stop admonishing him, to leave him alone, and to give up disputing with him, since he can be convinced only by himself. The same apostle writes in 2 Timothy 2:23, "Foolish and unlearned questions avoid." The word translated "avoid" there and the word translated "reject" in Titus are the same in the original Greek, *paraitou*, and foolish questions can obviously be set aside without excommunicating anyone. Again, in Titus 3:9, Paul writes, "Avoid foolish questions," and the original word there, *periistaso*, meaning "set them aside," is equivalent to the word translated "reject." No other passage can be made, even plausibly, to support casting out of the church faithful people who believed the foundation, merely because they built some singular structure of their own upon it, a structure that may well have come from a good and pious conscience. On the contrary, every passage that commands the avoidance of such disputes was written as a lesson to pastors such as Timothy and Titus. They were not to create new articles of faith by settling every small controversy, because such articles lay a needless burden on people's consciences or provoke them to break the unity of the church.

The apostles themselves observed this lesson well. St. Peter and St. Paul had a serious controversy, as we read in Galatians 2:11, yet neither cast the other out of the church. Even in the apostles' time, however, some pastors did not observe it. Diotrephes, as 3 John 9 and the following verses relate, took such pride in his preeminence that he cast out of the church people whom St. John himself thought fit to be received into it. Vainglory and ambition had entered the church of Christ that early.

### Of Persons Liable to Excommunication

Several conditions must be met before a person is liable to excommunication. First, he must be a member of some community, meaning some lawful assembly, meaning some Christian church, that has power to judge the cause for which he is to be excommunicated. Where there is no community, there can be no excommunication, and where there is no power to judge, there can be no power to pronounce sentence. It follows that one church cannot excommunicate another. If the two have equal power to excommunicate each other, then excommunication is not discipline or an act of authority at all, only schism and the breaking of charity. If one is so subordinate to the other that the two have a single voice, then they are really one church, and the part that is excommunicated is no longer a church but a scattered number of individual persons.

The sentence of excommunication amounts to an instruction not to keep company with the excommunicated person, or even to eat with him. If a sovereign prince or sovereign assembly is excommunicated, the sentence therefore has no effect. By the law of nature, all subjects are bound to be in the company and presence of their own sovereign whenever he requires it. They cannot lawfully expel him from any place within his own dominion, whether that place is secular or sacred, and they cannot leave his dominion without his permission. Still less can they refuse to eat with him if he calls them to that honor. Other princes and states, for their part, are not members of one and the same congregation, so they need no sentence to keep them out of the company of the excommunicated state. The very act that founds a commonwealth unites many people into one community and, by the same stroke, separates that community from every other. Excommunication is therefore not needed to keep kings and states apart, and it has no effect beyond what lies in the nature of political relations already, unless its effect is to incite princes to make war on one another.

Nor does excommunication have any effect on a Christian subject who obeys the laws of his own sovereign, whether that sovereign is Christian or heathen. If he believes that Jesus is the Christ, "he hath the Spirit of God" (1 John 4:1), and "God dwelleth in him, and he in God" (1 John 4:15). Whoever has the Spirit of God, whoever dwells in God, and whoever has God dwelling in him can suffer no harm from being excommunicated by men. Anyone who believes Jesus to be the Christ is therefore free of every danger with which excommunicated persons are threatened, and anyone who does not believe it is no Christian. A true and sincere Christian, then, is not liable to excommunication. Neither is a professed Christian, until his hypocrisy shows itself in his conduct, that is, until his behavior runs contrary to the law of his sovereign. That law is the rule of conduct, and Christ and his apostles commanded us to be subject to it. The church can judge conduct only by external actions, and external actions can never be unlawful except when they violate the law of the commonwealth.

If a person's father, mother, or master is excommunicated, the children are still not forbidden to keep their company or to eat with them. Such a prohibition would, in most cases, oblige the children not to eat at all, since they would lack the means of getting food. It would also authorize them to disobey their parents and masters, contrary to the precept of the apostles.

In sum, the power of excommunication cannot extend beyond the purpose for which the apostles and pastors of the church received their commission from our Savior, and that purpose is not to rule by command and coercion but to teach and direct people in the way of salvation in the world to come. A master in any science may abandon a student who obstinately neglects to practice the master's rules, but he cannot accuse the student of injustice, because the student was never bound to obey him. In the same way, a teacher of Christian doctrine may abandon disciples who obstinately persist in an unchristian life, but he cannot say they wrong him, because they are not obliged to obey him. To any teacher who complained in that way, one might apply God's answer to Samuel in a similar situation (1 Samuel 8): "They have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me."

When excommunication lacks the support of the civil power, as it does when a Christian state or prince is excommunicated by a foreign authority, it has no effect and consequently ought to inspire no fear. The phrase *fulmen excommunicationis*, "the thunderbolt of excommunication," arose from a notion held by the Bishop of Rome, who first used it, that he was King of Kings. The heathens had likewise made Jupiter king of the gods and, in their poems and pictures, gave him a thunderbolt with which to subdue and punish the Giants who dared to deny his power. The Bishop's notion rested on two errors. The first was that the kingdom of Christ is of this world, which contradicts our Savior's own words: "My kingdom is not of this world." The second was that the Bishop is Christ's vicar not only over his own subjects but over all the Christians in the world. Scripture gives no ground for this claim, and the contrary will be proved in its proper place.

### Of the Interpreter of the Scriptures Before Civil Sovereigns Became Christians

When St. Paul came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue, he, "as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures, opening and alleging that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead; and that this Jesus, whom I preach unto you, is Christ" (Acts 17:2–3). The scriptures mentioned here were the scriptures of the Jews, that is, the Old Testament. The people to whom Paul had to prove that Jesus was the Christ and had risen from the dead were also Jews, and they already believed those scriptures to be the word of God. As a result, some of them believed, according to verse 4, and some did not, according to verse 5. All of them believed the scriptures, so why did they not all believe alike? Why did some accept and others reject the interpretation of the man who cited those scriptures, with each person interpreting them for himself?

The reason is this. St. Paul came to them without any legal commission, in the manner of someone who meant to persuade rather than to command. He had to persuade them in one of two ways: by miracles, as Moses did with the Israelites in Egypt, so that they might see his authority in God's works, or by reasoning from scripture they already accepted, so that they might see the truth of his doctrine in God's word. Whoever persuades by reasoning from written principles makes his listener the judge both of what those principles mean and of how much force his inferences from them carry. If the Jews of Thessalonica were not the judges of what St. Paul drew from Scripture, who was? If St. Paul himself was the judge, why did he need to cite any passages to prove his doctrine? It would have been enough to say, "I find it so in Scripture, that is, in your laws, of which I am the interpreter, sent by Christ." There was therefore no interpreter of Scripture whose interpretation the Jews of Thessalonica were bound to accept. Each of them could believe or disbelieve according to whether Paul's arguments seemed to him to agree with the meaning of the passages he cited. In general, in every case in the world, whoever offers a proof makes the person he addresses the judge of that proof. In the particular case of the Jews, it is true that the express words of Deuteronomy 17 bound them to accept the decisions of the priests and judges of Israel then in office on all hard questions. But this applies only to Jews who had not yet been converted.

For converting the Gentiles, quoting the Scriptures was useless, since the Gentiles did not believe them. The apostles therefore worked to refute their idolatry by reason and then, once that was done, to persuade them to faith in Christ through their testimony of his life and resurrection. No controversy could yet arise about the authority to interpret Scripture, because no one in his state of unbelief was obliged to follow anyone's interpretation of any scripture. The only interpretation he was bound to follow was his sovereign's interpretation of the laws of his own country.

Consider now the act of conversion itself, and whether anything in it could create such an obligation. People were converted to nothing other than belief in what the apostles preached. The apostles preached only that Jesus was the Christ, meaning the King who was to save them and reign over them eternally in the world to come. It followed that he was not dead but had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, and that he would come again one day to judge the world, which would itself rise again to be judged, and would reward every person according to his works. None of the apostles preached that he himself, or any other apostle, was an interpreter of Scripture whose interpretation all converts must take as law. To interpret the laws is part of administering a kingdom that exists in the present, and the apostles had no such kingdom. They prayed, as all pastors since have prayed, "Thy kingdom come," and they urged their converts to obey the heathen princes who then ruled.

The New Testament had not yet been published as a single body. Each of the evangelists was the interpreter of his own gospel, and each apostle of his own epistle. As for the Old Testament, our Savior himself says to the Jews in John 5:39, "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life; and they are they which testify of me." If he had not meant them to interpret the Scriptures, he would not have told them to draw from those Scriptures the proof that he was the Christ. He would either have interpreted them himself or referred the Jews to the interpretation of the priests.

When a difficulty arose, the apostles and elders of the church assembled and decided what should be preached and taught, and how the Scriptures should be interpreted to the people, but they did not take from the people the freedom to read and interpret the Scriptures for themselves. The apostles sent various letters and other writings to the churches for their instruction, and these would have been sent in vain if the recipients had not been permitted to interpret them, that is, to consider what they meant. As it was in the apostles' time, so it had to remain until there were pastors who could authorize an interpreter whose interpretation would be generally accepted. That could not happen until kings were pastors, or pastors were kings.

### Of the Power to Make Scripture Law

A writing may be called canonical in two senses. "Canon" means a rule, and a rule is a precept by which a person is guided and directed in any action whatever. Precepts of this kind are still canons when a teacher gives them to his student, or an adviser to his friend, without any power to compel their observance, because they are rules. When they are given by someone whom the recipient is bound to obey, however, those canons are not only rules but laws. The question here, therefore, concerns the power to make the Scriptures, which are the rules of Christian faith, into laws.

### Of the Ten Commandments

That part of Scripture which first became law was the Ten Commandments. They were written on two tablets of stone, delivered by God himself to Moses, and made known by Moses to the people. Before that time there was no written law of God. God had not yet chosen any people to be his own particular kingdom, so he had given humanity no law except the law of nature: the precepts of natural reason, written in every person's own heart.

Of the two tablets, the first contains the law of sovereignty. First, the people were not to obey or honor the gods of other nations. This is the meaning of the words "Non habebis Deos alienos coram me": "You shall not take as gods the gods that other nations worship, but only me." By this they were forbidden to obey or honor, as their king and governor, any god other than the one who spoke to them then through Moses, and afterward through the high priest. Second, they were not to "make any image to represent him." They were not to choose for themselves, in heaven or on earth, any representative of their own invention, but were to obey Moses and Aaron, whom God had appointed to that office. Third, they were not to "take the name of God in vain." They were not to speak rashly of their king, dispute his right, or question the commissions of Moses and Aaron, his lieutenants. Fourth, they were "to abstain from their ordinary labor every seventh day" and spend that time paying him public honor.

The second tablet contains the duties of one person toward another: "to honor parents; not to kill; not to commit adultery; not to steal; not to corrupt judgment by false witness"; and finally, "not even to plan in their hearts to do any injury to one another."

The question now is who gave these written tablets the binding force of law. There is no doubt that God himself made them laws. But a law binds no one, and indeed is no law at all, except to those who acknowledge it as the act of the sovereign. How, then, could the people of Israel be obliged to obey all the laws that Moses set before them, when they had been forbidden to approach the mountain and hear what God said to him? Some of these laws were laws of nature, such as the whole of the second tablet. These were therefore to be acknowledged as God's laws by all peoples, and not by the Israelites alone. For the laws that applied particularly to the Israelites, such as those of the first tablet, the question remains open, with one exception. Immediately after these laws were put to them, the Israelites bound themselves to obey Moses, in the words recorded in Exodus 20:19: "Speak to us yourself, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, or we will die."

It was therefore Moses alone at that time who held on earth the power to make this brief Scripture, the Decalogue, into law in the commonwealth of Israel. After him that power passed to the high priest, whom God, speaking through Moses, declared should administer this particular kingdom of his. But Moses, Aaron, and the high priests who succeeded them were the civil sovereigns. Up to this point, therefore, the canonizing of Scripture, or the making of it into law, belonged to the civil sovereign.

### Of the Judicial and Levitical Law

The judicial law consisted of the laws God prescribed to the magistrates of Israel as their rule for administering justice and for the sentences or judgments they were to pronounce in disputes between one person and another. The Levitical law was the rule God prescribed concerning the rites and ceremonies of the priests and Levites. Both were delivered to the people by Moses alone, and so they too became laws by virtue of the same promise of obedience to Moses. The text does not say whether these laws were written down at the time, or dictated to the people by Moses by word of mouth after his forty days with God on the mountain. Either way, they were all positive laws, equal in standing to holy Scripture, and made canonical by Moses, the civil sovereign.

### The Second Law

After the Israelites had come into the plains of Moab opposite Jericho and were ready to enter the promised land, Moses added various other laws to the earlier ones. These are therefore called Deuteronomy, meaning "second laws." They are, as Deuteronomy 29:1 states, "the words of a covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel, besides the covenant which he made with them in Horeb." Having explained the earlier laws at the beginning of the book of Deuteronomy, Moses adds others, which begin at the twelfth chapter and continue to the end of the twenty-sixth.

According to the twenty-seventh chapter, the people were commanded to write this law on great plastered stones when they crossed the Jordan. Moses himself also wrote it in a book, which, according to the thirty-first chapter, he delivered into the hands of "the priests and the elders of Israel," commanding that it be "put in the side of the ark." The ark itself contained nothing but the Ten Commandments. This was the law of which Moses, in the seventeenth chapter, commanded the kings of Israel to keep a copy. And this is the law which, after it had been lost for a long time, was found again in the Temple in the reign of Josiah and accepted, on his authority, as the law of God. But Moses when he wrote it, and Josiah when he recovered it, both held the civil sovereignty. Up to this point, then, the power of making Scripture canonical lay with the civil sovereign.

From the time of Moses until after the Captivity, no book other than this Book of the Law was received among the Jews as the law of God. With a few exceptions, the prophets lived during the Captivity itself, and the rest lived only a little before it. Their prophecies were not generally accepted as laws. On the contrary, the prophets themselves were persecuted, partly by false prophets and partly by kings whom those false prophets had led astray. And this very book, which Josiah had confirmed as the law of God, was lost in the Captivity and the sack of Jerusalem, together with the whole history of God's works. This appears from 2 Esdras 14:21: "Your law is burned; therefore no one knows the things that have been done by you, or the works that are about to begin."

The book had also been lost once before, prior to the Captivity. Scripture does not say when, but it was probably in the reign of Rehoboam, when Shishak, king of Egypt, carried off the treasures of the Temple, as related in the fourteenth chapter of First Kings. Between that loss and the reign of Josiah, when the book was found again, the Jews had no written word of God. They governed themselves by their own discretion, or under the direction of whomever each of them regarded as a prophet.

### The Old Testament, When Made Canonical

From this we may infer that the Scriptures of the Old Testament as we have them today were neither canonical nor law for the Jews until two events: the renewal of their covenant with God on their return from the Captivity, and the restoration of their commonwealth under Esdras, more commonly called Ezra. From that time on, however, they were regarded as the law of the Jews. As such they were translated into Greek by seventy elders of Judea, placed in the library of Ptolemy at Alexandria, and approved as the word of God. Esdras was the high priest, and the high priest was their civil sovereign. It is evident, then, that the Scriptures were never made laws except by the sovereign civil power.

### The New Testament Began to Be Canonical Under Christian Sovereigns

We can learn from the writings of the Church Fathers who lived before the Emperor Constantine accepted and authorized the Christian religion how the Christians of that time regarded the books we now have of the New Testament. They held them to be the dictates of the Holy Spirit, and consequently the canon, or rule, of faith. A few dissented, and it was in contrast to these few that the rest were called the Catholic Church and the others heretics. Such was the reverence and esteem in which Christians held their teachers; and in general, the reverence that disciples feel for their first masters, in every kind of doctrine they receive from them, is not small. There is no doubt, therefore, that when St. Paul wrote to the churches he had converted, the recipients accepted his writings as true Christian doctrine. The same held when any other apostle or disciple of Christ wrote to those who had embraced Christ. But in that period people accepted this doctrine because of the faith of the hearer, not the power and authority of the teacher. The apostles therefore did not make their own writings canonical; each convert made them canonical for himself.

The question here, however, is not what any Christian made a law or canon for himself, since he could reject it again by the same right by which he had accepted it. The question is what was made a canon for Christians in such a way that they could not act against it without injustice. For the New Testament to be canonical in this sense, that is, to be law, in any place where the law of the commonwealth had not made it so, is contrary to the very nature of law. A law, as has already been shown, is the command of the person or assembly to whom we have given sovereign authority to make whatever rules for the direction of our actions that sovereign sees fit, and to punish us when we act against them.

When anyone else offers us rules that the sovereign ruler has not prescribed, those rules are merely counsel and advice. Whether that advice is good or bad, the person counseled may refuse to follow it without injustice. When it runs contrary to laws already established, he cannot follow it without injustice, however good he may believe it to be. I mean that in such a case he cannot follow it in his actions, nor in his discourse with other people. He may still, without blame, believe his private teachers, wish that he were free to practice their advice, and wish that it were publicly accepted as law. Inner faith is by its very nature invisible, and is therefore exempt from all human jurisdiction. The words and actions that proceed from it, however, are injustice before both God and man when they amount to breaches of our civil obedience.

Our Savior denied that his kingdom is of this world, and he said that he came not to judge the world but to save it. He has therefore not subjected us to any laws other than those of the commonwealth. The Jews he left under the law of Moses, which, as he says in the fifth chapter of Matthew, he came not to destroy but to fulfill. Other nations he left under the laws of their respective sovereigns, and all people under the laws of nature. Both he and his apostles, in their teaching, commended the observance of these laws to us as a necessary condition of being admitted by him, on the last day, into his eternal kingdom, where there will be protection and everlasting life. Our Savior and his apostles thus left us no new laws to bind us in this world, only new doctrine to prepare us for the next. The books of the New Testament, which contain that doctrine, were therefore not binding canons, that is, laws, until obedience to them was commanded by those to whom God has given the power to legislate on earth. Until then they were only good and safe advice for guiding sinners on the way to salvation. Each person might take that advice or refuse it at his own peril, without injustice.

Consider, too, the commission that Christ our Savior gave his apostles and disciples. It was to proclaim his kingdom, not as present but as to come; to teach all nations; to baptize those who believed; to enter the houses of those who welcomed them; and, where they were not welcomed, to shake the dust from their feet as a testimony against them. It was not to call down fire from heaven to destroy the unwelcoming, nor to compel them to obedience by the sword. In all this there is nothing of power, only of persuasion. He sent them out as sheep among wolves, not as kings to their subjects. Their commission was not to make laws but to obey the laws already made and to teach obedience to them. Consequently, they could not make their writings binding canons without the help of the sovereign civil power.
