The Scripture of the New Testament is therefore law only where the lawful civil power has made it so. And where it has, the king or sovereign also makes it a law for himself. In doing so he subjects himself not to the teacher or apostle who converted him, but to God himself and his Son Jesus Christ, as directly as the apostles themselves did.

### Of the Power of Councils to Make Scripture Law

For those who had embraced Christian doctrine in times and places of persecution, one thing might seem to give the New Testament the force of law: the decrees Christians made among themselves in their synods. Acts 15:28 records the formula used by the council of the apostles, the elders, and the whole church: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things," and so on. This language signifies a power to lay a burden on those who had accepted their doctrine. To "lay a burden on another" seems to mean the same as "to oblige," and so the acts of that council would seem to have been laws for the Christians of that time.

Nevertheless, they were no more laws than are these other precepts: "Repent"; "Be baptized"; "Keep the commandments"; "Believe the gospel"; "Come unto me"; "Sell all that you have"; "Give it to the poor"; and "Follow me." These are not commands. They are invitations, callings of people to Christianity, like the call in Isaiah 55:1: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; come, and buy wine and milk without money." There are two reasons for this. First, the apostles' power was no different from that of our Savior: to invite people to embrace the kingdom of God. The apostles themselves acknowledged that kingdom to be not present but to come, and those who have no kingdom can make no laws. Second, if their acts of council had been laws, no one could have disobeyed them without sin. But we read nowhere that those who rejected the doctrine of Christ sinned in rejecting it. We read only that they died in their sins, meaning that their sins against the laws they were bound to obey were not pardoned. Those laws were the laws of nature and the civil laws of the state, to which every Christian had submitted himself by covenant.

The burden the apostles might lay on those they had converted is therefore to be understood not as law but as conditions proposed to those who sought salvation. These conditions could be accepted or refused at the hearer's own peril. Refusing them committed no new sin, though it carried the risk of being condemned and shut out of the kingdom of God for one's past sins. That is why St. John does not say of unbelievers that the wrath of God "shall come" upon them, but that "the wrath of God remains upon them"; and not that they shall be condemned, but that "they are condemned already." Nor can we conceive that the benefit of faith is "the remission of sins" unless we also conceive that the cost of unbelief is "the retention of those same sins."

Someone may ask why, if no one was obliged to observe their decrees, the apostles met together at all, and why the other pastors of the church did so after them, to agree on what doctrine should be taught on matters of faith and conduct. The answer is that the apostles and elders of that council were obliged, by the very act of joining it, to teach whatever doctrine it concluded and decreed should be taught, so long as no prior law they were bound to obey was contrary to it. This did not oblige all other Christians to observe what they taught. The members could deliberate about what each of them should teach, but they could not deliberate about what others should do unless their assembly had legislative power, and no one could have that except civil sovereigns. For although God is the sovereign of the whole world, we are not bound to accept as his law whatever any person puts forward in his name. Still less are we bound to accept anything contrary to the civil law, which God has expressly commanded us to obey.

The acts of the apostles' council, then, were counsels at the time and not laws. Still less are the acts of any later teachers or councils laws, if those councils met without the authority of the civil sovereign. Consequently, the books of the New Testament, though they are the most perfect rules of Christian doctrine, could not be made laws by any authority other than that of kings or sovereign assemblies.

The first council that made the Scriptures we now have into canon has not survived. The collection attributed to the first bishop of Rome after St. Peter is open to question. It does list the canonical books, but its words "Sint vobis omnibus Clericis & Laicis Libri venerandi," meaning "Let these books be held in reverence by all of you, clergy and laity," draw a distinction between clergy and laity that was not in use so close to St. Peter's time. The first surviving council to settle the canonical Scripture is the Council of Laodicea. Its fifty-ninth canon forbids reading in the churches any books other than the canonical ones. This mandate is addressed not to every Christian, but only to those who had authority to read publicly in the church, that is, to ecclesiastics alone.

### Of the Right of Appointing Ecclesiastical Officers in the Time of the Apostles

Of the ecclesiastical officers in the time of the apostles, some were magisterial and some ministerial. The magisterial offices were these: preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God to unbelievers, administering the sacraments and divine service, and teaching the rules of faith and conduct to those who had been converted. The ministerial office was that of the deacons. They were appointed to manage the secular needs of the church at a time when its members lived on a common fund of money raised from the voluntary contributions of the faithful.

Among the magisterial officers, the first and principal were the apostles. At first there were only twelve, chosen and appointed by our Savior himself. Their office was not only to preach, teach, and baptize, but also to be martyrs, in the original sense of that word: witnesses of our Savior's resurrection. This testimony was the specific and essential mark that distinguished the apostleship from the other ecclesiastical teaching offices. An apostle had to qualify as a sufficient witness, either by having seen our Savior after his resurrection, or by having kept company with him before it and seen his works and other proofs of his divinity. That is why, at the election of a new apostle to replace Judas Iscariot, St. Peter says in Acts 1:21–22: "Of these men who have accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up from us, one must be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection." The word "must" here implies a necessary qualification of an apostle: to have kept company with the first and original apostles during the time our Savior showed himself in the flesh.

### Matthias Made Apostle by the Congregation

The first apostle not appointed by Christ during his time on earth was Matthias, and he was chosen in this way. As Acts 1:15 records, about 120 Christians had gathered together in Jerusalem. They put forward two men, Joseph the Just and Matthias, and had lots drawn; "and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the apostles." Here we see that the ordination of this apostle was the act of the congregation. It was not the act of St. Peter, nor of the eleven, except insofar as they were members of the assembly.

### Paul and Barnabas Made Apostles by the Church of Antioch

After Matthias, no other apostle was ever ordained except Paul and Barnabas. Acts 13:1–3 describes how this was done: "There were in the church at Antioch certain prophets and teachers: Barnabas, and Simeon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. As they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, 'Separate for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.' And when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away."

From this it is clear that, although they were called by the Holy Spirit, their calling was declared to them, and their mission authorized, by the particular church of Antioch. That their calling was to the apostleship is evident from the fact that Acts 14:14 calls them both apostles. That they were apostles by virtue of this act of the church of Antioch, St. Paul declares plainly in Romans 1:1, where he uses the very word the Holy Spirit used at his calling. He styles himself "an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God," alluding to the Holy Spirit's words, "Separate for me Barnabas and Saul."

The work of an apostle, however, was to be a witness of Christ's resurrection. Someone may therefore ask how St. Paul, who had not kept company with our Savior before his passion, could know that he had risen. The answer is easy. After his ascension, our Savior himself appeared to Paul from heaven on the road to Damascus, "and chose him as a vessel to bear his name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel." Having seen the Lord after his passion, Paul was a competent witness of his resurrection. As for Barnabas, he had been a disciple before the passion. It is therefore evident that Paul and Barnabas were apostles, and yet that they were chosen and authorized not by the original apostles alone but by the church of Antioch, just as Matthias was chosen and authorized by the church of Jerusalem.

### What Offices in the Church Are Magisterial

"Bishop," a word formed in our language from the Greek *episkopos*, means an overseer or superintendent of any business, and in particular a pastor or shepherd. From that sense it was taken by metaphor to signify the office of a king, or of any other ruler or guide of a people, whether he ruled by laws or by doctrine. This metaphor was used not only among the Jews, who were originally shepherds, but also among the heathen. In this sense the apostles were the first Christian bishops, instituted by Christ himself, and so Acts 1:20 calls the apostleship of Judas his "bishopric." Later, elders were appointed in the Christian churches and charged with guiding Christ's flock by their doctrine and advice, and these elders were also called bishops.

Timothy was an elder, and in the New Testament "elder" names an office as well as an age; yet Timothy was also a bishop. Bishops in those days were content with the title of elder. St. John himself, the apostle whom our Lord loved, begins his second epistle with the words "The elder to the elect lady." It is evident from this that in the time of the apostles bishop, pastor, elder, and doctor, meaning teacher, were simply different names for the same office. There was then no government by coercion, only by doctrine and persuasion. The kingdom of God was yet to come, in a new world, so no church could hold any authority to compel until the commonwealth had embraced the Christian faith. Consequently, there was no diversity of authority, though there was diversity of employment.

The New Testament mentions no other offices in the Church beyond these ruling ones: apostles, bishops, elders, pastors, and teachers, whose calling was to proclaim Christ to Jews and unbelievers and to direct and teach those who already believed. The names "evangelists" and "prophets" do not signify offices. They name various gifts by which particular men were useful to the Church. Evangelists were useful by writing the life and acts of our Savior. Such were Saint Matthew and Saint John, who were apostles, and Saint Mark and Saint Luke, who were disciples, together with anyone else who wrote on that subject, as Saint Thomas and Saint Barnabas are said to have done, though the Church has not accepted the books that circulated under their names. Prophets were useful through the gift of interpreting the Old Testament, and sometimes by declaring their special revelations to the Church. None of these gifts made a man an officer in the Church, nor did the gift of tongues, the gift of casting out devils or of curing other diseases, or any other gift. Only a proper calling and election to the charge of teaching did that.

### The Ordination of Teachers

Our Savior did not personally appoint the apostles Matthias, Paul, and Barnabas. The Church elected them, meaning the assembly of Christians: the church of Jerusalem chose Matthias, and the church of Antioch chose Paul and Barnabas. In the same way, the presbyters and pastors of other cities were elected by the churches of those cities. As proof, consider first how Saint Paul went about ordaining presbyters in the cities where he had converted people to the Christian faith, immediately after he and Barnabas had received their apostleship. We read in Acts 14:23 that "they ordained elders in every church." At first glance this might be taken as evidence that Paul and Barnabas themselves chose the elders and gave them their authority. But the original Greek makes it plain that the elders were authorized and chosen by the assembly of Christians in each city. The words there are *cheirotonēsantes autois presbyterous kat' ekklēsian*, which mean "when they had ordained them elders by the holding up of hands in every congregation."

It is well known that in all those cities, magistrates and officers were chosen by majority vote. Because the ordinary way of separating the votes in favor from the votes against was a show of hands, to "ordain" an officer in any of these cities meant nothing more than to bring the people together and elect him by a majority. The majority might be counted in raised hands, in voices, or in balls, beans, or small stones, each man casting one into a vessel marked either for or against, since different cities had different customs on that point. It was the assembly, then, that elected its own elders. The apostles were only the presidents of the assembly. They called the people together for the election, announced who had been elected, and gave the newly elected the blessing that is now called consecration. For this reason, those who presided over the assemblies, as the elders did when the apostles were absent, were called *proestōtes*, and in Latin *antistites*. Both words signify the principal person of the assembly, whose office was to count the votes, declare from them who had been chosen, and, where the votes were tied, decide the question by adding his own, which is the office of the president of any council.

Since all the churches had their presbyters ordained in the same manner, the same thing must be understood where Scripture uses the word "constitute." Titus 1:5 reads *hina katastēsēs kata polin presbyterous*: "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest constitute elders in every city." Titus was to call the faithful together and ordain presbyters by majority vote. It would have been strange if the people of some town, who had perhaps never seen a magistrate chosen in any other way than by an assembly, should, on becoming Christians, have even considered any other way of electing their teachers and guides, that is, their presbyters, otherwise called bishops, than the majority vote that Saint Paul indicates in Acts 14:23 with the word *cheirotonēsantes*. Nor were bishops ever chosen except by the assemblies of Christians in each town, until the emperors found it necessary to regulate their elections in order to keep the peace among them.

The continuous practice of electing the bishops of Rome, which persists to this day, confirms the same conclusion. Suppose the bishop of some city had the right to choose his successor in the pastoral office whenever he left that city to plant the faith somewhere else. He would then have had an even stronger right to appoint his successor in the place where he last lived and died. Yet we find no bishop of Rome who ever appointed his successor. For a long time they were chosen by the people, as the riot over the disputed election between Damasus and Ursinicus shows. Ammianus Marcellinus reports that this disturbance grew so violent that Juventius, the prefect, could not keep the peace between the factions and was forced to leave the city, and that more than a hundred men were found dead in the church itself. Later the bishops of Rome were chosen first by the whole clergy of Rome and then by the cardinals, but none was ever appointed to the succession by his predecessor. If these bishops claimed no right to appoint their own successors, I think I may reasonably conclude that they had no right to appoint the new power either. No one could take that power from the Church and bestow it on them except someone with lawful authority not only to teach the Church but to command it, and no one could do that except the civil sovereign.

### What Ministers of the Church Are

The word "minister," in the original Greek *diakonos*, signifies someone who voluntarily does another man's business. A minister differs from a servant only in this: servants are bound by their condition to do whatever they are commanded, whereas ministers are bound only by what they have undertaken, and are therefore obliged to do no more than that. Both those who teach the Word of God and those who manage the worldly affairs of the Church are ministers, but they are ministers of different persons. The pastors of the Church, called in Acts 6:4 "the ministers of the word," are ministers of Christ, whose Word it is. The ministry of a deacon, called in verse 2 of the same chapter "serving tables," is a service done to the Church or congregation. Therefore no single man, and not even the whole Church, could ever say of their pastor that he was *their* minister. Of a deacon, however, the whole congregation could properly say so, whatever charge he had undertaken: to serve tables; to distribute provisions to the Christians, who in the earliest times lived in each city on a common fund or on collections; to look after the house of prayer; to manage the revenue; or to handle any other worldly business of the Church.

Their work as deacons was to serve the congregation. Even so, when the occasion arose, they did not neglect to preach the Gospel and uphold the doctrine of Christ, each according to his gifts, as Saint Stephen did, and some both preached and baptized, as Philip did. The Philip who preached the Gospel in Samaria (Acts 8:5) and baptized the eunuch (verse 38) was Philip the deacon, not Philip the apostle. Verse 1 makes this clear: when Philip preached in Samaria, the apostles were in Jerusalem. And verse 14 says that "when the apostles which were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John." Through the laying on of their hands, those who had been baptized received the Holy Ghost (verse 15), which they had not received through Philip's baptism. For the Holy Ghost to be conferred, baptism had to be administered or confirmed by a minister of the Word, not by a minister of the Church. That is why the apostles sent two of their own number, Peter and John, from Jerusalem to Samaria to confirm the baptism of those whom Philip the deacon had baptized. Peter and John conferred on these people, who until then had only been baptized, the graces that were signs of the Holy Spirit, which at that time accompanied all true believers. What those signs were can be learned from Saint Mark 16:17: "These signs shall follow them that believe; in my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover." This power Philip could not give. The apostles could, and, as this passage shows, they actually did give it to every man who truly believed and had been baptized by a minister of Christ himself. So either Christ's ministers in our age cannot confer this power, or there are very few true believers, or Christ has very few ministers.

### How Deacons Were Chosen

The first deacons were chosen not by the apostles but by a congregation of the disciples, meaning Christians of every sort. Acts 6 makes this plain. There we read that once the number of disciples had multiplied, the Twelve called them together and told them that it was not fitting for the apostles to leave the Word of God in order to serve tables. Then they said (verse 3): "Brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business." Clearly, although the apostles declared the seven elected, it was the congregation that chose them. Verse 5 says so more explicitly still: "the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose" seven men, whose names follow.

### Church Revenue Under the Law of Moses

Under the Old Testament, only the tribe of Levi was eligible for the priesthood and the other lower offices of the Church. The land was divided among the other tribes, Levi excepted, and these still numbered twelve because the tribe of Joseph had been split into Ephraim and Manasseh. The tribe of Levi was assigned certain cities to live in, with the surrounding pastureland for their cattle, but for their portion they were to receive a tenth of the produce of their brethren's land. The priests, in turn, received for their support a tenth of that tenth, together with a share of the offerings and sacrifices. For God had said to Aaron (Numbers 18:20): "Thou shalt have no inheritance in their land, neither shalt thou have any part among them: I am thy part and thine inheritance among the children of Israel." Since God was then king, and had appointed the tribe of Levi to be his public ministers, he allowed them the public revenue for their support. That revenue was the share God had reserved for himself, namely the tithes and offerings, and this is what God means when he says, "I am thine inheritance." The name "clergy" might therefore be fittingly applied to the Levites, from the Greek *klēros*, meaning a lot or an inheritance. This was not because they were heirs of the Kingdom of God any more than anyone else, but because God's inheritance was their livelihood. And since in this period God himself was their king, with Moses, Aaron, and the succeeding high priests as his lieutenants, it is clear that the right to tithes and offerings was established by the civil power.

After the Israelites rejected God by demanding a king, the Levites continued to enjoy the same revenue. But their right to it now rested on the fact that the kings never took it away from them, because the public revenue was at the disposal of the public person, and until the Babylonian Captivity that person was the king. After the return from captivity, the people again paid their tithes to the priests as before. Up to this point, then, the livings of the Church were determined by the civil sovereign.

### In Our Savior's Time and After

Of how our Savior and his apostles were supported, we read only that they kept a common purse, which Judas Iscariot carried; that those of the apostles who were fishermen sometimes went back to their trade; and that when our Savior sent the twelve apostles out to preach, he forbade them to "provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses... for the workman is worthy of his meat" (Matthew 10:9–10). From this it seems likely that their ordinary support was suited to their work. Their work was "freely ye have received, freely give" (verse 8), and their support was the free gift of those who believed the good news they carried about the coming of the Messiah, their Savior. To this we may add what was contributed out of gratitude by people whom our Savior had healed. Luke 8:2–3 mentions "certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils, and Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance."

After our Savior's ascension, the Christians of each city lived in common (Acts 4:34) on the money raised from selling their lands and possessions, which they laid at the apostles' feet out of goodwill rather than obligation. As Saint Peter said to Ananias in Acts 5:4, "Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power?" This shows that Ananias had no need to hold back his land or his money by lying, since he was not bound to contribute anything at all unless he chose to. And as it was in the time of the apostles, so it remained all the way down to the period after Constantine the Great: the support of the bishops and pastors of the Christian Church consisted of nothing but the voluntary contributions of those who had embraced their teaching. There was as yet no mention of tithes. Yet in the time of Constantine and his sons, Christians were so devoted to their pastors that Ammianus Marcellinus, describing the riot between Damasus and Ursinicus over the bishopric, says the office was worth fighting for. Thanks to the generosity of their flocks, and especially of wealthy married women, the bishops of that era lived splendidly, rode in carriages, and were lavish in their food and dress.

### The Ministers of the Gospel Lived on the Goodwill of Their Flocks

Someone may ask whether the pastor was then bound to live on voluntary contributions, as though on charity. For Saint Paul asks (1 Corinthians 9:7): "Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges? ... or who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock?" And again (1 Corinthians 9:13): "Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?" That is, they receive for their support a share of what is offered at the altar. He then concludes: "Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel."

From this passage one may indeed infer that the pastors of the Church ought to be supported by their flocks. One may not infer that the pastors were to decide the amount or the kind of their own allowance, serving themselves at the table as they pleased. Their allowance therefore had to be set either by the gratitude and generosity of each individual member of the flock or by the whole congregation. It could not be set by the whole congregation, because the congregation's decisions were not then laws. Before emperors and civil sovereigns had made laws to settle it, then, the support of pastors was nothing but goodwill. Those who served at the altar lived on what was offered there. In what court could they have sued for more, when they had no tribunals? And if they had arbitrators among themselves, who would have enforced their judgments, when they had no power to arm officers? It follows that no fixed income could be assigned to any pastors of the Church except by the whole congregation, and only once its decrees had the force not merely of church rules but of laws. Such laws could be made only by emperors, kings, or other civil sovereigns. The right to tithes under the Law of Moses could not be applied to the ministers of the Gospel in that period, because Moses and the high priests had been the civil sovereigns of the people under God, whose kingdom among the Jews was then present, whereas the Kingdom of God through Christ is yet to come.

So far I have shown what the pastors of the Church are, and what their commission includes: to preach, to teach, to baptize, and to preside over their several congregations. I have shown what ecclesiastical censure is, namely excommunication. Where the civil law forbade Christianity, excommunication meant that Christians withdrew themselves from the company of the excommunicated person; where the civil law commanded Christianity, it meant putting the excommunicated person out of the Christian congregations. I have shown who elected the pastors and ministers of the Church, which was the congregation; who consecrated and blessed them, which was the pastor; and what their proper income was, which was nothing but their own possessions, their own labor, and the voluntary contributions of devout and grateful Christians. We must now consider what office belongs to those who, being civil sovereigns, have also embraced the Christian faith.

### The Civil Sovereign, Being a Christian, Has the Right to Appoint Pastors

First, we must remember that the right to judge which doctrines are conducive to peace and fit to be taught to the subjects is, in every commonwealth, inseparably joined to the civil sovereign power, whether that power lies in one man or in one assembly of men, as I proved in Chapter 18. It is evident to even the dullest mind that men's actions arise from their opinions about the good or evil those actions will bring upon themselves. Consequently, once men are convinced that obeying the sovereign power will harm them more than disobeying it, they will break the laws, and in doing so overthrow the commonwealth and bring on confusion and civil war, which all civil government was instituted to prevent. That is why, in all the commonwealths of the heathens, sovereigns bore the title of shepherds, or pastors, of the people: no subject could lawfully teach the people except by their permission and authority.

This right of heathen kings cannot be thought to have been taken from them when they converted to the faith of Christ. Christ never decreed that kings, for believing in him, should be deposed, that is, made subject to anyone but himself, or, what amounts to the same thing, be stripped of the power needed to preserve peace among their subjects and to defend them against foreign enemies. Christian kings, therefore, are still the supreme pastors of their people, and have the power to ordain whatever pastors they please to teach the Church, that is, to teach the people committed to their charge.

Suppose, further, that the right to choose pastors lies in the Church, as it did before kings were converted, and as it did in the time of the apostles themselves, as shown earlier in this chapter. Even so, the right belongs to the Christian civil sovereign. Insofar as he is a Christian, he permits the teaching; and insofar as he is the sovereign, which is to say the Church by representation, the teachers he elects are elected by the Church. When an assembly of Christians chooses its pastor in a Christian commonwealth, it is the sovereign who elects him, because the choice is made by his authority. It is the same as when a town chooses its mayor: the choice is the act of whoever holds the sovereign power, since every act is the act of the person without whose consent it would be invalid. Therefore, whatever examples history may offer of pastors elected by the people or by the clergy, they are no argument against the right of any civil sovereign, because those who elected them did so by his authority.

In every Christian commonwealth, then, the civil sovereign is the supreme pastor, to whose charge the whole flock of his subjects is committed, and it is by his authority that all other pastors are made and empowered to teach and to perform every other pastoral function. It follows that all other pastors derive from the civil sovereign their right to teach, to preach, and to carry out the other duties of that office, and that they are only his ministers. They stand in the same relation to him as the magistrates of towns, the judges of courts, and the commanders of armies stand to the one who is magistrate of the whole commonwealth, judge of all cases, and commander of the entire armed force, which is always the civil sovereign. The reason for this is not that those who teach are his subjects, but that those who are to learn are his subjects.

Suppose a Christian king entrusts the authority to ordain pastors in his dominions to another king, as several Christian kings grant that power to the Pope. He does not thereby set up a pastor over himself, or a sovereign pastor over his people. To do so would be to strip himself of his civil power. That power depends on men's opinion of their duty to him and on their fear of punishment in the next world, and so it would come to depend on the skill and loyalty of teachers, who are no less prone than any other kind of men, not only to ambition, but also to ignorance. Where a foreigner has authority to appoint teachers, therefore, it has been given to him by the sovereign in whose dominions those teachers teach. Christian teachers are our schoolmasters in Christianity; but kings are the fathers of families, and may accept schoolmasters for their subjects on a foreigner's recommendation, but not on his command. This holds especially when bad teaching by those schoolmasters would bring great and obvious profit to the one who recommends them. Nor can kings be obliged to keep such teachers any longer than the public good requires, for the care of the public good remains their charge for as long as they retain any other essential right of sovereignty.

### The Pastoral Authority of Sovereigns Alone Is by Divine Right; That of Other Pastors Is by Civil Right

Suppose, then, that someone were to ask a pastor in the exercise of his office what the chief priests and elders of the people asked our Savior in Matthew 21:23: "By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority?" The only proper answer he could give is that he acts by the authority of the commonwealth, given to him by the king or by the assembly that represents it. All pastors except the supreme one perform their duties by the right, that is, by the authority, of the civil sovereign, which is to say *jure civili*, by civil right. But the king, and every other sovereign, performs the office of supreme pastor by authority received directly from God, that is, by God's right, *jure divino*. For this reason no one but a king may place in his title the words *Dei gratia rex*, "king by the grace of God," as a mark that he submits to God alone. Bishops ought to begin their mandates with "By the favor of the King's Majesty, Bishop of such-and-such a diocese," or, as civil ministers do, "In His Majesty's name." When they write *divina providentia*, "by divine providence," which means the same as *Dei gratia* in disguise, they deny that they received their authority from the civil state, and they slyly slip off the collar of their civil subjection, to the detriment of the unity and defense of the commonwealth.

### Christian Kings Have Power To Execute All Manner Of Pastoral Function

But if every Christian sovereign is the supreme pastor of his own subjects, it would seem that he also has the authority not only to preach, which perhaps no one will deny, but also to baptize, to administer the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, and to consecrate both temples and pastors to God's service. Most people deny this. They do so partly because kings do not customarily do these things, and partly because administering the sacraments and consecrating persons and places to holy uses is held to require the laying on of hands by men who were themselves ordained to the same ministry through the same laying on of hands, in an unbroken succession reaching back to the time of the apostles. To prove, therefore, that Christian kings have the power to baptize and to consecrate, I must explain two things: why they do not customarily do so, and how, without the ordinary ceremony of the laying on of hands, they are made capable of doing it whenever they choose.

There is no doubt that any king who was learned in the sciences could lecture on them himself, by the same right of his office through which he authorizes others to lecture on them in the universities. Nevertheless, because the care of the commonwealth's affairs as a whole occupies all his time, it would not be practical for him to devote himself personally to that particular task. A king may likewise, if he wishes, sit in judgment to hear and decide every kind of case, just as he gives others authority to do so in his name. But the burden of command and government that rests upon him compels him to remain continually at the helm and to delegate the ministerial offices to others beneath him. In the same way, our Savior, who surely had the power to baptize, baptized no one himself but sent his apostles and disciples to do it, as the fourth chapter of John records. Saint Paul, too, was compelled to preach in many widely scattered places, and so he baptized few. Among all the Corinthians, as he writes in the first chapter of his first epistle to them, he baptized only Crispus, Gaius, and Stephanas, and he gives the reason in the same passage: his principal charge was to preach. From this it is clear that the greater charge, such as the government of the Church, excuses a person from the lesser. The reason Christian kings do not customarily baptize is therefore evident, and it is the same reason why few people today are baptized by bishops, and fewer still by the pope.

As for whether the laying on of hands is necessary to authorize a king to baptize and consecrate, we may consider the matter as follows.

The laying on of hands was a very ancient public ceremony among the Jews. By it, a person or thing was designated and marked out with certainty as the object of someone's prayer, blessing, sacrifice, consecration, condemnation, or other pronouncement. When Jacob blessed the children of Joseph, as Genesis 48:14 relates, he "laid his right hand on Ephraim the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh the firstborn." He did this deliberately, in order to designate which of the two he intended to receive the greater blessing, even though Joseph had presented the boys to him in such a way that he was forced to cross his arms to do it. Similarly, in the sacrifice of the burnt offering, Aaron is commanded in Exodus 29:10 "to lay his hands on the head of the bullock," and in verse 15 "to lay his hand on the head of the ram." The same is said again in Leviticus 1:4 and 8:14. When Moses ordained Joshua as captain of the Israelites, which is to say, consecrated him to God's service, Numbers 27:23 tells us that he "laid his hands upon him, and gave him his charge," thereby designating and making certain whom the people were to obey in war. In the consecration of the Levites, God commanded in Numbers 8:10 that "the children of Israel should put their hands upon the Levites." And in the condemnation of the man who had blasphemed the Lord, God commanded in Leviticus 24:14 that "all that heard him should lay their hands on his head, and that all the congregation should stone him." Why should only those who heard him lay their hands on him, rather than a priest, a Levite, or some other minister of justice? The only reason can be that no one else was able to designate, and show to the eyes of the congregation, who it was that had blasphemed and ought to die. To designate a man, or anything else, by pointing the hand to the eye is less liable to error than to identify him by speaking a name to the ear.

So carefully was this ceremony observed that even when Aaron blessed the whole congregation at once, which cannot be done by laying on hands, he nevertheless, according to Leviticus 9:22, "lifted up his hand toward the people when he blessed them." We read also of a similar ceremony in the consecration of temples among the heathen: the priest laid his hands on some post of the temple for the whole time he was speaking the words of consecration. So natural is it, in matters of God's public service, to designate any individual thing by the hand, so as to assure the eyes, rather than by words, which only inform the ear.

This ceremony, then, was not new in our Savior's time. Jairus, whose daughter was sick, begged our Savior, as Mark 5:23 records, not to heal her, but "to lay his hands upon her, that she might be healed." And in Matthew 19:13, "they brought unto him little children, that he should put his hands on them, and pray."

Following this ancient rite, the apostles, the presbyters, and the presbytery as a body laid hands on those whom they ordained as pastors, and at the same time prayed that they might receive the Holy Ghost. They did this not only once but sometimes more often, whenever a new occasion arose. Yet the purpose was always the same: a precise and religious designation of the person being ordained, either to the pastoral charge in general or to a particular mission. Thus, in Acts 6:6, "the apostles prayed, and laid their hands" on the seven deacons. This was done not to give them the Holy Ghost, for they were full of the Holy Ghost before they were chosen, as verse 3 shows just before, but to designate them for that office. Again, after Philip the deacon had converted certain people in Samaria, Peter and John went down and, as Acts 8:17 relates, "laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Not only an apostle but a presbyter had this power, for Saint Paul advises Timothy in his first epistle, "Lay hands suddenly on no man," meaning that he should designate no one rashly to the office of pastor. We read in the fourth chapter of the same epistle that the whole presbytery laid their hands on Timothy. This should be understood to mean that someone did so by the appointment of the presbytery, most likely its proestos, or presiding speaker, who may well have been Saint Paul himself. For in his second epistle to Timothy, Paul says to him, "Stir up the gift of God which is in thee, by the laying on of my hands." Note in passing that by "the Holy Ghost" in these passages is meant not the third person of the Trinity but the gifts necessary for the pastoral office. We read also that Saint Paul received the laying on of hands twice: once from Ananias at Damascus, at the time of his baptism, as told in the ninth chapter of Acts; and again at Antioch, when he was first sent out to preach, as told in the thirteenth. The use of this ceremony in the ordination of pastors, then, was to designate the person to whom such power was being given.

But suppose there had been at that time a Christian who already possessed the power of teaching. Baptizing him, that is, making him a Christian, would have given him no new power. It would only have led him to preach true doctrine, which is to say, to use his power rightly. The laying on of hands would therefore have been unnecessary, and baptism alone would have sufficed. Now every sovereign, before Christianity, had the power of teaching and of ordaining teachers. Christianity therefore gave sovereigns no new right; it only directed them in the way of teaching the truth. Consequently, they needed no laying on of hands, beyond what is done in baptism, to authorize them to exercise any part of the pastoral function, such as baptizing and consecrating. And in the Old Testament, although the priest alone had the right to consecrate during the period when sovereignty rested with the high priest, this was not the case once sovereignty rested with the king. For we read in the eighth chapter of the First Book of Kings that Solomon blessed the people, consecrated the Temple, and pronounced the public prayer that is now the model for the consecration of all Christian churches and chapels. From this it appears that he had not only the right of ecclesiastical government but also the right to perform ecclesiastical functions.

### The Civil Sovereign, If a Christian, Is Head of the Church in His Own Dominions

From this union of political and ecclesiastical right in Christian sovereigns, it is evident that they hold every kind of power over their subjects that can be given to a man for governing people's outward actions, in both civil affairs and religion. They may make whatever laws they themselves judge most fitting for the government of their own subjects, both as those subjects constitute the commonwealth and as they constitute the Church, for state and Church are made up of the same people.

If they choose, therefore, they may, as many Christian kings now do, commit the government of their subjects in matters of religion to the pope. But in that case the pope is subordinate to them on that point. He exercises his charge in another ruler's dominion *jure civili*, by the right of the civil sovereign, not *jure divino*, by God's right, and he may therefore be dismissed from that office whenever the sovereign judges it necessary for the good of his subjects. Sovereigns may also, if they choose, commit the care of religion to one supreme pastor or to an assembly of pastors, and give them whatever power over the Church, or over one another, they think most convenient. They may confer whatever titles of honor they wish, such as bishop, archbishop, priest, or presbyter, and they may make whatever laws they please for the pastors' maintenance, whether by tithes or by other means, provided they do so out of a sincere conscience, of which God alone is the judge. It is the civil sovereign who must appoint the judges and interpreters of the canonical Scriptures, for it is he who makes the Scriptures law. It is he, too, who gives force to excommunications, which would be held in contempt were it not for laws and punishments capable of humbling obstinate libertines and bringing them back into union with the rest of the Church. In sum, he holds supreme power in all causes, ecclesiastical as well as civil, so far as they concern actions and words. These alone can be known and can be accused, and over what cannot be accused there is no judge at all except God, who knows the heart. These rights belong to every sovereign, whether a monarch or an assembly, because those who represent a Christian people are representatives of the Church. A Church and a commonwealth of Christian people are one and the same thing.

### Cardinal Bellarmine's Books De Summo Pontifice Considered

What I have said here, and elsewhere in this book, seems clear enough to establish that supreme ecclesiastical power belongs to Christian sovereigns. Yet the pope of Rome's claim to that power over all Christendom has been defended chiefly, and I think as forcefully as is possible, by Cardinal Bellarmine, in the part of his *Controversies* titled *De Summo Pontifice*, "On the Supreme Pontiff." I have therefore thought it necessary to examine, as briefly as I can, the foundations and strength of his argument.

### The First Book

Of the five books he has written on this subject, the first takes up three questions. The first asks which is simply the best form of government, monarchy, aristocracy, or democracy, and concludes in favor of none of them, but rather of a government mixed from all three. The second asks which of these is the best government for the Church, and concludes in favor of a mixed government, but one that should partake most of monarchy. The third asks whether, in this mixed monarchy, Saint Peter held the place of monarch.

As for his first conclusion, I have already sufficiently proved, in Chapter 18, that all governments which men are bound to obey are simple and absolute. In a monarchy there is only one man who is supreme, and all others who hold any kind of power in the state hold it by his commission, during his pleasure, and exercise it in his name. In an aristocracy or a democracy there is only one supreme assembly, holding the same power that in a monarchy belongs to the monarch; and this is not a mixed sovereignty but an absolute one. As for which of the three is best, that question is not to be disputed where any one of them is already established. The existing form ought always to be preferred, maintained, and regarded as the best, because it is contrary both to the law of nature and to God's positive law to do anything that tends to overthrow it. Besides, it makes no difference to the power of any pastor, unless he also holds the civil sovereignty, which kind of government is best. A pastor's calling is not to govern men by command but to teach them and persuade them by argument, leaving them to consider whether to embrace or reject the doctrine he teaches. Monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy mark out three kinds of sovereigns, not three kinds of pastors; or, as we might put it, three kinds of masters of households, not three kinds of schoolmasters for their children.

The second conclusion, then, concerning the best form of government for the Church, has no bearing on the question of the pope's power outside his own dominions. In all other commonwealths his power, if he has any at all, is only that of the schoolmaster, not that of the master of the household.

For the third conclusion, that Saint Peter was monarch of the Church, Bellarmine's chief argument is the passage in Matthew 16:18–19: "Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church," and so on, continuing, "And I will give thee the keys of heaven; whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Considered carefully, this passage proves nothing more than that the Church of Christ has for its foundation a single article of faith: namely, the one that Peter professed on behalf of all the apostles, which gave our Savior the occasion to speak the words quoted here. To see this clearly, we must recognize that our Savior, whether he preached in person, through John the Baptist, or through his apostles, preached nothing but this one article of faith: "that he was the Christ." All other articles require faith only insofar as they are founded on that one. John came first, preaching only this, as Matthew 3:2 records: "The kingdom of God is at hand." Then our Savior himself preached the same, according to Matthew 4:17. And when he gave the twelve apostles their commission, in Matthew 10:7, there is no mention of their preaching any article but that. This was the fundamental article, the foundation of the Church's faith.

Later, when the apostles had returned to him, he asked all of them, not Peter alone, "Who men said he was," and they answered, as Matthew 16:13 records, that "some said he was John the Baptist, some Elias, and others Jeremias, or one of the prophets." Then, in verse 15, he asked them all again, not Peter alone, "Whom say ye that I am?" Peter therefore answered on behalf of them all, "Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God." This, as I have said, is the foundation of the faith of the whole Church, and from it our Savior took occasion to say, "Upon this stone I will build my Church." It is clear from this that by the foundation stone of the Church was meant the fundamental article of the Church's faith.

But why then, someone will object, does our Savior insert the words "Thou art Peter"? Had the original text been translated strictly, the reason would readily have appeared. We must consider that the apostle Simon had the surname Stone, which is the meaning of the Syriac word *Cephas* and of the Greek word *Petrus*. After the confession of that fundamental article, our Savior, alluding to Simon's name, said in effect, to render it in English, "Thou art Stone, and upon this stone I will build my Church." This amounts to saying that the article "I am the Christ" is the foundation of all the faith I require of those who are to be members of my Church. Such a play on a name is nothing unusual in ordinary speech. But it would have been a strange and obscure way of speaking if our Savior, intending to build his Church on the person of Saint Peter, had said, "Thou art a stone, and upon this stone I will build my Church," when it would have been so simple, and free of all ambiguity, to say, "I will build my Church on thee," and the same allusion to his name would still have been there.

As for the words that follow, "I will give thee the keys of heaven," and so on, this is no more than what our Savior also gave to all the rest of his disciples, in Matthew 18:18: "Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." But however this is interpreted, there is no doubt that the power granted here belongs to all supreme pastors, as all Christian civil sovereigns are within their own dominions. This holds so firmly that if Saint Peter, or our Savior himself, had converted one of these sovereigns to believe in him and to acknowledge his kingdom, then, because his kingdom is not of this world, he would have left the supreme care of converting that sovereign's subjects to no one but the sovereign. Otherwise he would have had to strip him of his sovereignty, to which the right of teaching is inseparably attached. So much, then, in refutation of Bellarmine's first book, in which he tries to prove that Saint Peter was the universal monarch of the Church, that is, of all the Christians in the world.

### The Second Book

The second book draws two conclusions: first, that Saint Peter was bishop of Rome and died there; and second, that the popes of Rome are his successors. Both have been disputed by others. But even supposing them true, if by "bishop of Rome" is meant either the monarch of the Church or its supreme pastor, then the bishop in question was not Silvester but Constantine, the first Christian emperor. And like Constantine, all other Christian emperors were by right the supreme bishops of the Roman Empire. I say of the Roman Empire, not of all Christendom, because other Christian sovereigns had the same right in their several territories, as an office essentially bound up with their sovereignty. This is my answer to his second book.

### The Third Book

In the third book he takes up the question of whether the pope is Antichrist. For my part, I see no argument proving that he is, in the sense in which Scripture uses the name. Nor will I draw any argument from the nature of Antichrist to contest the authority he exercises, or has formerly exercised, in the dominions of any other prince or state.

It is evident that the prophets of the Old Testament foretold, and the Jews expected, a Messiah, that is, a Christ, who would re-establish among them the kingdom of God, which they had rejected in the time of Samuel when they demanded a king like those of other nations. This expectation left them exposed to the deceptions of anyone who had both the ambition to try to seize the kingdom and the skill to deceive the people through counterfeit miracles, a hypocritical life, or plausible speeches and doctrine. Our Savior and his apostles therefore warned men against false prophets and false Christs. False Christs are those who claim to be the Christ but are not, and they are properly called Antichrists, in the same sense in which, when a schism arises in the Church through the election of two popes, each calls the other *Antipapa*, the false pope. Antichrist, in the proper meaning of the word, therefore bears two essential marks: first, that he denies Jesus to be the Christ; and second, that he professes himself to be the Christ. The first mark is set down by Saint John in the fourth chapter of his first epistle: "Every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh, is not of God; and this is the spirit of Antichrist." The second is expressed in our Savior's words in Matthew 24:5, "Many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ," and again, "If any man shall say unto you, Lo, here is Christ, there is Christ, believe it not." Antichrist must therefore be a false Christ, one of those who shall claim to be the Christ. And from these two marks, denying Jesus to be the Christ and affirming oneself to be the Christ, it follows that he must also be an adversary of the true Christ, which is another common meaning of the word Antichrist.

But among these many Antichrists there is one in particular, *ho Antichristos*, the Antichrist: Antichrist in the definite sense, as one specific person, and not merely an Antichrist in the indefinite sense. Now, since the pope of Rome neither claims to be the Christ himself nor denies that Jesus is the Christ, I do not see how he can be called Antichrist. That word does not mean someone who falsely claims to be Christ's lieutenant or vicar general, but someone who claims to be Christ himself. Scripture also gives a mark of the time when this particular Antichrist will appear. According to Matthew 24:15, he will come when the abominable destroyer spoken of in the ninth chapter of Daniel shall stand in the holy place, and there shall be such tribulation as has not been since the beginning of the world, nor ever shall be again, so great that if it were to last long, as verse 22 says, "no flesh could be saved; but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened," that is, made fewer. But that tribulation has not yet come, for it is to be followed immediately, as verse 29 states, by a darkening of the sun and moon, a falling of the stars, a shaking of the heavens, and the glorious return of our Savior in the clouds. The Antichrist, therefore, has not yet come, whereas many popes have both come and gone. It is true that the pope, in presuming to give laws to all Christian kings and nations, usurps a kingdom in this world that Christ did not take upon himself. But he does this not as Christ but on behalf of Christ, and in that there is nothing of the Antichrist.

### The Fourth Book

In the fourth book, Bellarmine sets out to prove that the pope is the supreme judge in all questions of faith and morals, which amounts to being the absolute monarch of all Christians in the world. To this end he puts forward three propositions: first, that the pope's judgments are infallible; second, that he can make true laws and punish those who do not observe them; and third, that our Savior conferred all ecclesiastical jurisdiction on the pope of Rome.

### Texts for the Infallibility of the Pope's Judgment in Points of Faith

To establish the infallibility of the pope's judgments, Bellarmine appeals to Scripture, beginning with Luke 22:31: "Simon, Simon, Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not; and when you are converted, strengthen your brethren." On Bellarmine's reading, Christ here granted Simon Peter two privileges: first, that his faith should never fail; and second, that neither he nor any of his successors should ever define any point of faith or morals erroneously, or contrary to the definition of an earlier pope. This is a strange and badly strained interpretation. Anyone who reads that chapter attentively will find that no passage in all of Scripture tells more heavily against the pope's authority than this one. The priests and scribes were seeking to kill our Saviour at the Passover, and Judas had resolved to betray him. When the day for killing the Passover lamb arrived, our Saviour celebrated the feast with his apostles, saying that he would not celebrate it again until the Kingdom of God had come, and at the same time telling them that one of them would betray him. They began asking which of them it would be. Reasoning that the next Passover their Master celebrated would be one at which he was king, they also fell into a dispute over which of them would then be the greatest. Our Saviour therefore told them that the kings of the nations hold dominion over their subjects and are called by a name that in Hebrew means "Bountiful." He could not be that to them, he said; they must instead strive to serve one another. He was ordaining a kingdom for them, but only such a kingdom as his Father had ordained for him: one that he was now to purchase with his blood and would not possess until his second coming. Then they would eat and drink at his table and sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Turning next to St. Peter, he said, in substance: Simon, Simon, Satan is trying to weaken your faith in what is to come by tempting you with the prospect of dominion now; but I have prayed for you, that your faith shall not fail. Therefore, once you are converted (and this should be noted), and understand my kingdom as belonging to another world, confirm that same faith in your brethren. St. Peter replied as a man who no longer expected any authority in this world: "Lord, I am ready to go with you, not only to prison, but to death." It is plain from this that St. Peter was not only given no jurisdiction in this world but was charged to teach all the other apostles that they too should have none. As for the infallibility of St. Peter's final judgment in matters of faith, nothing more can be drawn from this text than that Peter would remain firm in believing one particular point: that Christ would come again and take possession of his kingdom on the Day of Judgment. And not even this was granted by the text to all his successors, for we see them claiming that kingdom in the present world.

The second text is Matthew 16: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." As I have already shown in this chapter, this proves nothing more than that the gates of hell shall not prevail against Peter's confession, which prompted the saying. That confession was that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

The third text is John 21:16–17: "Feed my sheep." This contains nothing more than a commission to teach. If we grant that the other apostles are included under the name of "sheep," then it is a commission of supreme teaching power, but one that held only for the period when there were not yet any Christian sovereigns in possession of that supremacy. I have already proved that Christian sovereigns are the supreme pastors within their own dominions, and that they are appointed to that office by virtue of their baptism, without any further laying on of hands. That ceremony is merely a means of designating the person for the office, and it is therefore unnecessary when he has already been designated to teach whatever doctrine he chooses by his appointment to absolute power over his subjects. For, as I have proved before, sovereigns are supreme teachers in general by virtue of their office, and they bind themselves by their baptism to teach the doctrine of Christ. When they allow others to teach their people, they do so at the peril of their own souls, because it is from the heads of families that God will demand an account of how his children and servants were instructed. It is of Abraham himself, and not of some hired hand, that God says (Genesis 18:19): "I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, that they keep the way of the Lord, and do justice and judgment."

The fourth text is Exodus 28:30: "You shall put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim." Bellarmine notes that the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, renders these words as *delosin kai aletheian*, "evidence and truth," and he concludes that God had given evidence and truth, which amounts almost to infallibility, to the High Priest. But whether what was given was evidence and truth itself, or merely an admonition to the priest to take pains to inform himself clearly and to judge uprightly, the fact that it was given to the High Priest means that it was given to the civil sovereign, since in the commonwealth of Israel the High Priest stood next under God. The text is therefore evidence and truth in favor of the ecclesiastical supremacy of civil sovereigns over their own subjects, and against the pretended power of the pope. These are all the texts Bellarmine brings for the infallibility of the pope's judgment in matters of faith.

### Texts for the Same in Matters of Morals

For the infallibility of the pope's judgment in matters of morals, Bellarmine brings a single text, John 16:13: "When the Spirit of truth has come, he will guide you into all truth." Here, he says, "all truth" means at the very least all truth necessary to salvation. But with this qualification he attributes no more infallibility to the pope than to any professing Christian who is not destined for damnation. If a man errs on any point where freedom from error is necessary to salvation, he cannot possibly be saved, for the only things necessary to salvation are those without which salvation is impossible. I will set out from Scripture in the following chapter which points these are. Here I will say only this: even if it were granted that the pope could not possibly teach any error at all, that would not entitle him to any jurisdiction in the dominions of another prince, unless we are also prepared to say that a man is bound in conscience always to employ the best available workman, even when he has already promised the work to someone else.

Besides this text, Bellarmine argues from reason. If the pope could err in necessary matters, he says, then Christ would not have made sufficient provision for the Church's salvation, since he has commanded the Church to follow the pope's directions. But this argument has no force unless Bellarmine can show when and where Christ gave that command, or indeed took any notice of a pope at all. Even granting that whatever was given to St. Peter was given to the pope, Scripture contains no command that anyone obey St. Peter, and so no one can act justly in obeying him when his commands conflict with those of his lawful sovereign.

Finally, neither the Church nor the pope himself has ever declared that he is the civil sovereign of all Christians in the world, and therefore not all Christians are bound to acknowledge his jurisdiction in matters of morals. Civil sovereignty and supreme judicial authority in moral disputes are one and the same thing. Those who make civil laws are not merely the declarers but also the makers of the justice and injustice of actions, since nothing in men's conduct makes it righteous or unrighteous except its conformity with the sovereign's law. When the pope claims supremacy in disputes about morals, then, he is teaching men to disobey the civil sovereign. That is an erroneous doctrine, contrary to many precepts of our Saviour and his apostles handed down to us in Scripture.

To prove that the pope has power to make laws, Bellarmine cites many passages. The first is Deuteronomy 17:12: "The man who acts presumptuously and will not listen to the priest who stands to minister there before the Lord your God, or to the judge, that man shall die; and you shall put away the evil from Israel." In answer, we must remember that the High Priest, standing next and immediately under God, was the civil sovereign, and that all judges were to be appointed by him. The words cited therefore amount to this: "The man who presumes to disobey the civil sovereign for the time being, or any of his officers in the execution of their duties, shall die," and so forth. This plainly supports civil sovereignty against the universal power of the pope.

Second, he cites Matthew 16, "Whatever you shall bind," and so forth, and interprets it as the same kind of binding attributed to the scribes and Pharisees in Matthew 23:4: "They bind heavy burdens, grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders." This binding, he says, means the making of laws, and from it he concludes that the pope can make laws. But this too supports only the legislative power of civil sovereigns. The scribes and Pharisees sat in Moses' seat, and Moses, next under God, was sovereign of the people of Israel. That is why our Saviour commanded the people to do all that the scribes and Pharisees said, but not all that they did: to obey their laws, but not to follow their example.

The third passage is John 21:16, "Feed my sheep," which confers not a power to make laws but a command to teach. Making laws belongs to the master of the household, who chooses his chaplain at his own discretion, just as he chooses a schoolmaster to teach his children.

The fourth passage, John 20:21, actually tells against him. The words are: "As my Father has sent me, so I send you." But our Saviour was sent to redeem by his death those who would believe, and, through his own preaching and that of his apostles, to prepare them for entry into his kingdom. That kingdom, he himself says, is not of this world. He taught us to pray for its coming hereafter, though he refused (Acts 1:6–7) to tell his apostles when it would come; and when it does come, the twelve apostles will sit on twelve thrones, each perhaps as high as St. Peter's, to judge the twelve tribes of Israel. Since God the Father did not send our Saviour to make laws in this present world, we may conclude from the text that our Saviour did not send St. Peter to make laws here either. He sent him to persuade men to await the second coming with steadfast faith, and in the meantime, if they were subjects, to obey their princes, and if they were princes, both to believe it themselves and to do their best to bring their subjects to believe it too. That is the office of a bishop. This passage therefore argues most strongly for uniting ecclesiastical supremacy with civil sovereignty, which is the very opposite of what Cardinal Bellarmine cites it to prove.

The fifth passage is Acts 15:28: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication." Here Bellarmine takes the phrase "lay upon you a burden" as a sign of legislative power. But who, reading this text, could deny that the apostles' manner of speaking could just as properly be used in giving counsel as in making laws? The form of a law is "We command." "We think it good" is the ordinary form used by those who merely give advice. Those who advise do lay a burden, but a conditional one, binding only if the person advised wishes to attain his ends. Such is the burden of abstaining from things strangled and from blood: it is not absolute, but applies only if the converts wish not to go astray. I showed earlier, in Chapter 25, that law is distinguished from counsel in this respect: the reason for a law is drawn from the purpose and benefit of the one who prescribes it, while the reason for a counsel is drawn from the purpose and benefit of the one who receives it. Here the apostles aim solely at the benefit of the converted Gentiles, namely their salvation, and not at any benefit of their own, for having done their part they will receive their reward whether they are obeyed or not. The acts of this council were therefore not laws but counsels.

The sixth passage is Romans 13: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, for there is no power but of God." Bellarmine says this refers not only to secular princes but also to ecclesiastical ones. My answer is, first, that there are no ecclesiastical princes except those who are also civil sovereigns, and their principalities extend no further than their civil sovereignty. Beyond those bounds they may be received as teachers, but they cannot be acknowledged as princes. If the apostle had meant that we should be subject both to our own princes and to the pope, he would have taught a doctrine that Christ himself told us is impossible: "to serve two masters." It is true that the apostle says elsewhere, "I write these things while absent, lest when present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord has given me." But he is not claiming any power to put people to death, imprison, banish, whip, or fine them, all of which are punishments. He claims only the power to excommunicate, which, without the civil power behind it, amounts to nothing more than withdrawing from someone's company and having no more to do with him than with a heathen or a publican, one of the despised tax collectors of the Gospels. On many occasions this might cause more hardship to the one who excommunicates than to the one excommunicated.

The seventh passage is 1 Corinthians 4:21: "Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and the spirit of gentleness?" Here again the "rod" does not mean a magistrate's power to punish offenders, but only the power of excommunication. Excommunication is not by nature a punishment at all. It is only the announcement of a punishment that Christ will inflict once he has taken possession of his kingdom on the Day of Judgment. Even then it will not properly be a punishment, such as is imposed on a subject who has broken the law, but an act of vengeance, such as is taken against an enemy or rebel who denies our Saviour's right to the kingdom. This passage therefore does not prove the legislative power of any bishop who does not also hold civil power.

The eighth passage is 1 Timothy 3:2: "A bishop must be the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober," and so on, which Bellarmine says was a law. I had understood that no one could make a law in the Church except its monarch, St. Peter. But suppose this precept was issued on St. Peter's authority. I still see no reason to call it a law rather than advice, since Timothy was not St. Paul's subject but his disciple, and the flock in Timothy's care were not his subjects in a kingdom but his pupils in the school of Christ. If all the precepts Paul gives Timothy are laws, then why is this not a law as well: "Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for your health's sake"? And why are the prescriptions of good physicians not so many laws? The reason is that what makes a person's precepts into laws is not the imperative form of speech, but absolute subjection to that person.

In the same way, the ninth passage, 1 Timothy 5:19, "Against an elder receive no accusation except before two or three witnesses," is a wise precept, but not a law.

The tenth passage is Luke 10:16: "He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me." There is no doubt that whoever despises the counsel of those sent by Christ despises the counsel of Christ himself. But who are those sent by Christ today, if not those ordained as pastors by lawful authority? Who is lawfully ordained, if not someone ordained by the sovereign pastor? And who in a Christian commonwealth is ordained by the sovereign pastor, if not someone ordained by the authority of its sovereign? It follows from this passage that whoever hears his sovereign, when that sovereign is a Christian, hears Christ, and that whoever despises the doctrine authorized by his Christian king despises the doctrine of Christ. That is not what Bellarmine means to prove here, but the contrary. In any case, none of this has anything to do with law. A Christian king, acting as pastor and teacher of his subjects, does not thereby turn his doctrines into laws. He cannot oblige men to believe. As civil sovereign, however, he may make laws suited to his doctrine, and these can oblige men to certain actions, sometimes to actions they would not otherwise perform and which he ought not to command. Yet once commanded, they are laws. The outward actions performed in obedience to them, without inward approval, are the actions of the sovereign and not of the subject, who in that case is merely an instrument with no impulse of his own, because God has commanded obedience to such laws.

The eleventh category takes in every passage where the apostle, in giving counsel, uses some word that ordinarily signifies command, or describes the following of his counsel as obedience. Thus 1 Corinthians 11:2 is cited: "I commend you for keeping my precepts as I delivered them to you." The Greek reads: "I commend you for keeping the things I delivered to you, as I delivered them." This is far from meaning that they were laws, or anything other than good counsel. So too with 1 Thessalonians 4:2: "You know what commandments we gave you." Here the Greek phrase *paraggelias edokamen* is equivalent to *paredokamen*, "what we delivered to you," as in the passage just cited, and it does not prove that the traditions of the apostles were anything more than counsels. This holds even though the eighth verse says that "he who despises them despises not man, but God." Our Saviour himself did not come to judge, that is, to be king in this world, but to sacrifice himself for sinners and to leave teachers in his Church who would lead men to Christ rather than drive them. Christ never accepts forced actions, which are all that law can produce. He accepts only the inward conversion of the heart, and that is the work not of laws but of counsel and doctrine.

There is also 2 Thessalonians 3:14: "If any man does not obey our word in this epistle, take note of that man and keep no company with him, that he may be ashamed." From the word "obey," Bellarmine would infer that this epistle was a law to the Thessalonians. The epistles of the emperors were indeed laws, and if St. Paul's epistle were also a law, the Thessalonians would have had to obey two masters. But the Greek word for "obey," *hupakouei*, means to listen to or put into practice, and it applies not only to what is commanded by someone with the right to punish, but also to what is offered by way of counsel for our own good. That is why St. Paul does not tell them to kill the one who disobeys, or to beat, imprison, or fine him, all of which legislators may do. He tells them only to avoid his company, so that he may be ashamed. It is evident from this that what the Christians stood in awe of was not any imperial authority belonging to an apostle, but his reputation among the faithful.

The last passage is Hebrews 13:17: "Obey your leaders, and submit yourselves to them, for they watch over your souls, as those who must give account." Here too, obedience means following their counsel. The reason given for our obedience is drawn not from the will and command of our pastors but from our own benefit, since it is the salvation of our souls that they watch over, not the exaltation of their own power and authority. If the passage meant that everything pastors teach is law, then not only the pope but every pastor in his parish would have legislative power. Moreover, those who are bound to obey their pastors would have no power to examine their commands. What, then, are we to make of St. John, who tells us (1 John 4:1) "not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world"? It is clear, therefore, that we may dispute the doctrine of our pastors, whereas no one can dispute a law. The commands of civil sovereigns are acknowledged on all sides to be laws. If anyone other than the sovereign could make a law, every commonwealth, and with it all peace and justice, would come to an end, which is contrary to all laws, both divine and human. Nothing can therefore be drawn from these or any other passages of Scripture to prove that the decrees of the pope are laws where he does not also hold the civil sovereignty.

### The Question of Superiority Between the Pope and Other Bishops

The last point Bellarmine sets out to prove is "that our Saviour Christ has committed ecclesiastical jurisdiction immediately to no one but the pope." Here he is dealing not with the question of supremacy between the pope and Christian kings, but with the question of supremacy between the pope and other bishops.
