He begins by saying it is agreed that the jurisdiction of bishops is, at least in general, *de jure divino*, that is, held by the right of God. For this he cites St. Paul in Ephesians 4:11, where Paul says that Christ, after his ascension into heaven, "gave gifts to men: some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers." From this Bellarmine infers that bishops do indeed hold their jurisdiction by God's right, but he will not grant that they receive it immediately from God; it comes to them, he says, through the pope. But if a man can be said to hold his jurisdiction by divine right and yet not immediately, then what lawful jurisdiction in a Christian commonwealth, even a purely civil one, is not also held by divine right? Christian kings receive their civil power immediately from God, and the magistrates under them carry out their various duties by virtue of the king's commission. What those magistrates do is therefore held by mediate divine right, *de jure divino mediato*, no less than what bishops do by virtue of the pope's ordination. All lawful power comes from God: immediately in the supreme governor, and mediately in those who hold authority under him. Bellarmine must therefore either grant that every constable in the state holds his office by the right of God, or deny that any bishop holds his office that way, apart from the pope himself.

This entire dispute, however, over whether Christ left jurisdiction to the pope alone or to other bishops as well, is, outside the places where the pope holds civil sovereignty, a quarrel *de lana caprina*, an argument over goat's wool, which is to say over nothing at all. Where they are not sovereigns, none of them has any jurisdiction whatever. Jurisdiction is the power of hearing and deciding cases between one person and another. It can belong only to the one who has the power to prescribe the rules of right and wrong, that is, to make laws, and who can compel men with the sword of justice to obey his decisions, whether he pronounces them himself or through the judges he appoints for the purpose. No one can lawfully do this except the civil sovereign.

Therefore, when he cites the sixth chapter of Luke, where our Savior called his disciples together and chose twelve of them whom he named apostles, he proves that Christ elected them (all except Matthias, Paul, and Barnabas) and gave them the power and command to preach. He does not prove that Christ gave them power to judge disputes between one person and another. That is a power Christ refused to take upon himself, asking, "Who made me a judge or a divider over you?" and declaring elsewhere, "My kingdom is not of this world." Whoever lacks the power to hear and decide disputes between people cannot be said to have any jurisdiction at all. None of this prevents our Savior from having given the apostles power to preach and baptize in every part of the world, provided their own lawful sovereign did not forbid it. Christ himself and his apostles have expressly commanded us, in many places, to obey our own sovereigns in all things.

The arguments by which Bellarmine tries to prove that bishops receive their jurisdiction from the pope are all futile, since the pope himself has no jurisdiction in the dominions of other princes. Yet because these arguments prove the opposite, namely that all bishops who have jurisdiction receive it from their civil sovereigns, I will not omit to recount them.

The first comes from the eleventh chapter of Numbers. Moses could not bear alone the whole burden of administering the affairs of the people of Israel, so God commanded him to choose seventy elders, and God took part of the spirit of Moses and put it upon them. Bellarmine takes this to mean, not that God weakened the spirit of Moses, which would not have eased his burden at all, but that the elders all received their authority from him. In this he interprets the passage correctly and honestly. But since Moses held the entire sovereignty in the commonwealth of the Jews, the passage plainly signifies that the elders received their authority from the civil sovereign. It therefore proves that bishops in every Christian commonwealth receive their authority from the civil sovereign, and receive it from the pope only within his own territories, not within the territories of any other state.

The second argument comes from the nature of monarchy, in which all authority resides in one man and resides in others only by derivation from him. The government of the Church, Bellarmine says, is monarchical. This argument also works in favor of Christian monarchs. They are truly monarchs of their own people, which is to say of their own church, since a church is the same thing as a Christian people. The power of the pope, by contrast, even if he were Saint Peter himself, is no monarchy at all. It contains nothing of rule, the root of the word "monarchy," and nothing of coercive force, the root of words like "aristocracy," but only the authority of a teacher. God does not accept a forced obedience, only a willing one.

The third argument rests on the fact that Saint Cyprian calls the see of Saint Peter the head, the source, the root, and the sun from which the authority of bishops is derived. But by the law of nature, which is a better principle of right and wrong than the word of any teacher who is merely a man, the civil sovereign in every commonwealth is the head, the source, the root, and the sun from which all jurisdiction is derived. The jurisdiction of bishops is therefore derived from the civil sovereign.

The fourth argument is drawn from the inequality of bishops' jurisdictions. If God had given them jurisdiction directly, Bellarmine says, he would have given them equality of jurisdiction just as he gave them equality of order. Yet we see that some are bishops of only one town, some of a hundred towns, and some of many whole provinces, and these differences were not fixed by any command of God. Their jurisdiction therefore comes not from God but from man, and one bishop has more and another less, as it pleases the prince of the Church. Had he first proved that the pope possessed universal jurisdiction over all Christians, this argument would have served his purpose. But he has not proved it, and it is well known that the pope's broad jurisdiction was granted to him by those who held it, namely the Roman emperors. The patriarch of Constantinople, claiming on the same grounds of being bishop of the empire's capital and the emperor's seat, asserted that he was the pope's equal. It follows that all other bishops receive their jurisdiction from the sovereigns of the places where they exercise it. And just as bishops do not hold their authority by divine right, neither does the pope hold his by divine right, except where he is also the civil sovereign.

His fifth argument runs as follows: "If bishops had their jurisdiction directly from God, the pope could not take it from them, for he can do nothing contrary to God's ordinance." This inference is sound and well proved. "But," he continues, "the pope can do this, and has done it." This too may be granted, so long as he does it in his own dominions, or in the dominions of some other prince who has given him that power. He cannot do it universally, by right of the papacy, for that power belongs to every Christian sovereign within the boundaries of his own realm and cannot be separated from sovereignty. Before the people of Israel, by God's command to Samuel, set a king over themselves in the manner of other nations, the high priest held the civil government, and he alone could appoint or depose a lesser priest. Afterward that power belonged to the king, as Bellarmine's own argument proves. If a priest, whether the high priest or any other, had held his jurisdiction directly from God, the king could not have taken it from him, "for he could do nothing contrary to God's ordinance." Yet it is certain that King Solomon removed Abiathar the high priest from his office, as recorded in the second chapter of First Kings, at the twenty-sixth verse, and installed Zadok in his place, at the thirty-fifth verse. Kings may therefore, in the same manner, ordain and depose bishops as they think fit for the good government of their subjects.

His sixth argument is this: if bishops have their jurisdiction by divine right, that is, directly from God, those who maintain this should produce some word of God to prove it, and they can produce none. The argument is sound, and I have nothing to say against it. But it is no less sound as proof that the pope himself has no jurisdiction in the dominion of any other prince.

Finally, he offers as evidence the testimony of two popes, Innocent and Leo. I have no doubt he could have cited, with equal justification, the testimony of nearly every pope since Saint Peter. Given the love of power that is naturally implanted in mankind, whoever became pope would be tempted to uphold the same opinion. Even so, in doing this they would only be doing what Innocent and Leo did, bearing witness on their own behalf, and such testimony carries no weight.

### Of the Pope's Temporal Power

In his fifth book Bellarmine sets out four conclusions. The first is "that the pope is not lord of all the world"; the second, "that the pope is not lord of all the Christian world"; the third, "that the pope, outside his own territory, has no temporal jurisdiction directly." These three conclusions are easily granted. The fourth is "that the pope has, in the dominions of other princes, the supreme temporal power indirectly." This I deny, unless by "indirectly" he means that the pope has acquired it by indirect, that is, underhanded, means, in which case I grant it as well. But I understand him to mean something else. When he says the pope holds this power indirectly, he means that such temporal jurisdiction belongs to the pope by right, but that this right is merely a consequence of his pastoral authority, which he could not exercise without possessing temporal jurisdiction along with it. Supreme civil power is therefore necessarily attached to the pastoral power, which he calls spiritual, and by virtue of it the pope has a right to alter kingdoms, giving them to one ruler and taking them from another, whenever he judges that doing so promotes the salvation of souls.

Before I examine the arguments by which he tries to prove this doctrine, it will be useful to set out its consequences. Princes and states that hold civil sovereignty in their several commonwealths may then consider whether it is advisable for them to accept it, and whether accepting it would promote the good of their subjects, for whom they must give an account on the Day of Judgment.

When it is said that the pope does not have the supreme civil power directly in the territories of other states, we are to understand that he does not claim it as other civil sovereigns do, on the basis of an original submission by those who are to be governed. For it is evident, and has already been sufficiently demonstrated in this treatise, that the right of every sovereign is derived originally from the consent of each of those who are to be governed. They may choose him for their common defense against an enemy, as when they agree among themselves to appoint a man or an assembly of men to protect them; or they may submit to a conquering enemy in order to save their lives. When the pope disclaims supreme civil power over other states directly, then, he denies only that his right comes to him by that route. He does not for all that stop claiming it by another route: by a right given him by God upon his elevation to the papacy, without the consent of those who are to be governed. This is what he calls holding it indirectly. But whatever route he claims, the power is the same. If it is granted to be his right, he may depose princes and states as often as the salvation of souls requires, which is to say as often as he pleases, since he also claims the sole power of judging whether a thing serves the salvation of souls or not. This is the doctrine that not only Bellarmine here, and many other doctors in their sermons and books, teach, but that certain councils have decreed, that the popes have decreed, and that the popes have accordingly put into practice whenever occasion served them. The Fourth Lateran Council, held under Pope Innocent III, includes this canon in its third chapter, *On Heretics*: "If a king, upon the pope's admonition, does not purge his kingdom of heretics, and, having been excommunicated for this, does not make satisfaction within a year, his subjects are absolved of their obedience." The canon has been put into practice on various occasions: in the deposing of Chilperic, king of France; in the transfer of the Roman Empire to Charlemagne; in the oppression of King John of England; in the transfer of the kingdom of Navarre; and in recent years, in the League formed against Henry III of France; and in many other instances besides. I think few princes fail to regard this as unjust and harmful, but I wish they would all decide to be either kings or subjects. No one can serve two masters. Princes ought therefore to relieve their subjects of this conflict, either by holding the reins of government wholly in their own hands or by handing them over wholly to the pope, so that those who are willing to obey may be protected in their obedience. The distinction between temporal and spiritual power is nothing but words. Power is divided as truly, and as dangerously in every respect, by sharing it with an indirect power as with a direct one. But now to his arguments.

The first is this: "The civil power is subject to the spiritual. Therefore whoever holds the supreme spiritual power has the right to command temporal princes and to dispose of their temporal affairs for the sake of the spiritual." As for the distinction between temporal and spiritual, let us consider in what sense it can intelligibly be said that the temporal or civil power is subject to the spiritual. There are only two ways those words can make sense. When we say that one power is subject to another, we mean either that the person who holds the one is subject to the person who holds the other, or that the one power stands to the other as a means stands to an end. We cannot understand one power to have power over another power, or to hold right or command over it, because subjection, command, right, and power are attributes of persons, not of powers. One power may be subordinate to another, as the craft of a saddle-maker is subordinate to the craft of a horseman, since saddles exist for the sake of riding. Suppose, then, it is granted that civil government is ordained as a means of bringing us to spiritual happiness. It still does not follow that a king who holds civil power is bound to obey a pope who holds spiritual power, any more than every saddle-maker is bound to obey every horseman. Just as the subjection of a practitioner cannot be inferred from the subordination of his craft, so the subjection of a governor cannot be inferred from the subordination of his government. When Bellarmine says that the civil power is subject to the spiritual, therefore, he means that the civil sovereign is subject to the spiritual sovereign. His argument then stands thus: "The civil sovereign is subject to the spiritual; therefore the spiritual prince may command temporal princes." Here the conclusion merely restates the premise he was supposed to prove. To prove it, he first offers this reasoning: "Kings and popes, clergy and laity, make up a single commonwealth, that is, a single church. In every body the members depend on one another. But spiritual things do not depend on temporal things. Therefore temporal things depend on spiritual things, and are accordingly subject to them." This reasoning contains two gross errors. The first is that all Christian kings, popes, clergy, and other Christians make up a single commonwealth. It is evident that France is one commonwealth, Spain another, Venice a third, and so on. These consist of Christians, and are therefore several bodies of Christians, that is, several churches. Their respective sovereigns represent them, and through that representation each is able to command and to obey, to act and to be acted upon, as a natural person does. No general or universal church can do so until it has a representative, and it has none on earth. If it had one, there is no doubt that all Christendom would be a single commonwealth, whose sovereign would be that representative in both spiritual and temporal matters. To make himself that representative, the pope lacks three things that our Savior never gave him: the power to command, to judge, and to punish, beyond the power, through excommunication, to withdraw from those who will not learn from him. For even if the pope were Christ's sole vicar, he could not exercise that government until our Savior's second coming; and even then it will not be the pope, but Saint Peter himself, together with the other apostles, who will judge the world.

The other error in this first argument is his claim that the members of every commonwealth, like those of a natural body, depend on one another. It is true that they hold together, but they depend only on the sovereign, who is the soul of the commonwealth. If the sovereign fails, the commonwealth dissolves into civil war, in which no one so much as holds together with anyone else, for lack of a common dependence on an acknowledged sovereign, just as the members of a natural body crumble into earth when there is no soul to hold them together. Nothing in this comparison, therefore, supports the inference that the laity depend on the clergy, or temporal officers on spiritual ones. It shows only that both depend on the civil sovereign, who ought indeed to direct his civil commands toward the salvation of souls, but who is not on that account subject to anyone but God himself. Here, then, is the elaborate fallacy of the first argument, designed to deceive those who do not distinguish between the subordination of actions along the path toward an end and the subjection of persons to one another in administering the means. For every end, the means are determined by nature, or supernaturally by God himself. But the power to make people use those means is, in every nation, surrendered to the civil sovereign by the law of nature, which forbids people to break the faith they have pledged.

His second argument is this: "Every commonwealth, because it is presumed to be complete and self-sufficient, may command any other commonwealth not subject to it, and compel it to change the administration of its government, and may even depose its prince and set another in his place, if it cannot otherwise defend itself against the injuries that prince intends to do it. All the more may a spiritual commonwealth command a temporal one to change the administration of its government, and depose princes and install others, when it cannot otherwise defend the spiritual good."

That a commonwealth may lawfully do everything he describes in order to defend itself against injury is entirely true, and has already been sufficiently demonstrated in what came before. And if it were also true that there now exists in this world a spiritual commonwealth distinct from the civil commonwealth, then its prince, upon suffering injury, or upon lacking sufficient assurance that no injury would be done him in the future, might obtain redress and secure himself by war, which amounts to deposing, killing, subduing, or committing any other act of hostility. But by the same reasoning it would be no less lawful for a civil sovereign, upon suffering or fearing similar injuries, to make war on the spiritual sovereign, which I believe is more than Cardinal Bellarmine would have wished to infer from his own proposition.

But there is no spiritual commonwealth in this world. It is the same thing as the kingdom of Christ, which he himself says is not of this world. It will exist in the next world, at the resurrection, when those who have lived justly and believed that he was the Christ will rise as spiritual bodies, even though they died as natural ones. Then our Savior will judge the world, conquer his adversaries, and establish a spiritual commonwealth. In the meantime, since no one on earth has a spiritual body, there can be no spiritual commonwealth among those who are still in the flesh, unless we call the preachers who are commissioned to teach, and to prepare people for their reception into the kingdom of Christ at the resurrection, a commonwealth; and I have proved that they are not one.

The third argument is this: "It is not lawful for Christians to tolerate an infidel or heretical king if he tries to draw them into his heresy or unbelief. But it belongs to the pope to judge whether a king is drawing his subjects into heresy or not. Therefore the pope has the right to determine whether the prince is to be deposed or not."

To this I answer that both assertions are false. Christians, or people of any religion whatever, who refuse to tolerate their king, whatever law he makes, even a law concerning religion, break their faith, contrary to divine law, both natural and positive. Nor is there any judge of heresy among subjects other than their own civil sovereign, for "heresy is nothing but a private opinion, obstinately maintained, contrary to the opinion that the public person, that is, the representative of the commonwealth, has commanded to be taught." It is plain from this that an opinion publicly appointed to be taught cannot be heresy, and that sovereign princes who authorize such opinions cannot be heretics. Heretics are only private persons who stubbornly defend some doctrine their lawful sovereigns have prohibited.

To prove that Christians must not tolerate infidel or heretical kings, he cites the seventeenth chapter of Deuteronomy, where God forbids the Jews, when they set a king over themselves, to choose a foreigner. From this he infers that it is unlawful for a Christian to choose a king who is not a Christian. And it is true that a Christian, someone who has already bound himself to receive our Savior as his king when he comes, would tempt God too far by choosing as king in this world someone he knows will try, by both terror and persuasion, to make him break his faith. But, Bellarmine says, the danger of choosing a non-Christian as king is the same as the danger of failing to depose him once he has been chosen. To this I reply that the question concerns not the danger of failing to depose him but the justice of deposing him. To choose him may in some cases be unjust; but to depose him once he has been chosen is never just. It is always a breach of faith, and therefore contrary to the law of nature, which is the eternal law of God. Nor do we read that any such doctrine was considered Christian in the time of the apostles, or in the time of the Roman emperors, until the popes acquired civil sovereignty over Rome. To this he has replied that the early Christians did not depose Nero, or Diocletian, or Julian, or Valens the Arian, only because they lacked temporal forces. Perhaps so. But did our Savior lack the forces to depose Caesar, or at least Pilate, who unjustly, without finding any fault in him, handed him over to the Jews to be crucified, when merely by asking he could have had twelve legions of immortal, invulnerable angels to assist him? Or, if the apostles lacked the temporal forces to depose Nero, did it then follow that they had to teach the newly made Christians in their epistles, as they did, to obey the powers set over them, of which Nero was one at that time, and to obey them not out of fear of their wrath but for conscience's sake? Shall we say that, for lack of strength, they not only obeyed but also taught what they did not mean? It is not, then, for lack of strength but for conscience's sake that Christians are to tolerate their heathen princes, or princes who authorize the teaching of an error; for I cannot call anyone a heretic whose doctrine is the public doctrine. He further argues, in support of the pope's temporal power, that Saint Paul, in the sixth chapter of First Corinthians, appointed judges under the heathen princes of that era who were not ordained by those princes. This is not true. Saint Paul merely advises them to choose some of their brethren to settle their differences as arbitrators, rather than go to law against one another before heathen judges. This is a sound precept, full of charity, and fit to be practiced even in the best Christian commonwealths. As for the danger that may arise to religion from subjects tolerating a heathen or an erring prince, a subject is not competent to judge it. If he were, then the pope's temporal subjects could equally judge the pope's doctrine. For every Christian prince, as I have previously proved, is just as much the supreme pastor of his own subjects as the pope is of his.

The fourth argument is drawn from the baptism of kings, in which, in order to become Christians, they submit their scepters to Christ and promise to keep and defend the Christian faith. This is true, for Christian kings are nothing more than Christ's subjects. But they may for all that be the pope's equals, for they are supreme pastors of their own subjects, and the pope is nothing more than king and pastor, even in Rome itself.

The fifth argument rests on the words our Savior spoke, "Feed my sheep." Bellarmine holds that these words conferred every power a pastor needs. The first is the power to drive away wolves, by which he means heretics. The second is the power to pen up rams that have gone mad or that butt the other sheep with their horns, by which he means wicked kings, even Christian ones. The third is the power to give the flock proper food. From this he concludes that Christ gave all three powers to St. Peter.

My answer is that the last of these powers amounts to nothing more than the power, or more accurately the command, to teach. For the first, driving away wolves, that is, heretics, the passage he cites is Matthew 7:15: "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves." But heretics are not false prophets, or prophets of any kind. And even if we grant that heretics are the wolves meant there, the apostles were not commanded to kill them, or, if they were kings, to depose them. They were told to beware of them, flee them, and avoid them. Nor was this counsel to beware of false prophets addressed to St. Peter or to any of the apostles. It was addressed to the crowd of Jews who had followed Christ up the mountain, most of whom had not yet been converted. If the counsel conferred a power to drive away kings, then that power was given not only to private men but to men who were not Christians at all.

As for the power to separate and pen up furious rams, by which Bellarmine means Christian kings who refuse to submit to the Roman pastor, our Savior declined to take that power upon himself in this world. He advised instead that the wheat and the tares be left to grow together until the Day of Judgment. Still less did he give such a power to St. Peter, and still less can St. Peter pass it on to the popes. St. Peter and all other pastors are told to regard Christians who disobey the Church, meaning those who disobey the Christian sovereign, as heathens and publicans. Since no one claims for the Pope any authority over heathen princes, no one ought to claim for him any authority over those who are to be regarded as heathens.

From the power to teach alone, Bellarmine also infers that the Pope has coercive power over kings. The pastor, he says, must give his flock proper food, and therefore the Pope may, and indeed must, compel kings to do their duty. It follows from this that the Pope, as pastor of Christian men, is King of Kings. All Christian kings ought either to admit as much, or else each of them ought to take the supreme pastoral charge upon himself within his own dominion.

His sixth and last argument is drawn from examples. I answer, first, that examples prove nothing, and second, that the examples he cites do not establish even a probability of right. When Jehoiada killed Athaliah, as told in 2 Kings 11, he acted either by the authority of King Joash or else committed a horrible crime, for from the election of King Saul onward the high priest was merely a subject. When St. Ambrose excommunicated the Emperor Theodosius, if he really did so, he committed a capital crime. As for the popes Gregory I, Gregory II, Zachary, and Leo III, their judgments are void, since each was a judge in his own cause, and the acts they performed in keeping with this doctrine are among the greatest crimes of which human nature is capable, that of Zachary above all. So much, then, for ecclesiastical power. I would have been briefer and spared myself the examination of these arguments of Bellarmine had he made them as a private man, and not as the champion of the papacy against all other Christian princes and states.

## Chapter XLIII. Of What Is Necessary for a Man's Reception into the Kingdom of Heaven

### The Difficulty of Obeying God and Man at Once

For a long time, the most common pretext for sedition and civil war in Christian commonwealths has come from a difficulty that has never been adequately resolved: how to obey both God and man at once when their commands contradict each other. It is plain enough that when someone receives two contradictory commands and knows that one of them comes from God, he ought to obey that one and not the other, even if the other is the command of his lawful sovereign (whether a monarch or a sovereign assembly) or of his own father. The difficulty lies elsewhere. When people are commanded in God's name, they often cannot tell whether the command really comes from God or whether the person giving it is merely abusing God's name for private ends of his own. The Jewish Church had many false prophets who won standing with the people through invented dreams and visions. In the same way, the Church of Christ has had false teachers in every age who win standing with the people through fantastic and false doctrines, and who then use that standing, as ambition naturally does, to govern the people for their own private benefit.

### A Difficulty That Disappears for Those Who Distinguish What Is and Is Not Necessary to Salvation

For those who can distinguish between what is necessary and what is not necessary for their admission into the Kingdom of God, this difficulty of obeying both God and the civil sovereign on earth carries no weight. If the civil sovereign's command can be obeyed without forfeiting eternal life, then disobeying it is unjust, and the Apostle's precepts apply: "Servants, obey your masters in all things," and "Children, obey your parents in all things." So does the precept of our Savior: "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore whatever they tell you, observe and do." But if the command cannot be obeyed without being damned to eternal death, it would be madness to obey it, and our Savior's counsel applies (Matthew 10:28): "Fear not those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." Anyone who wishes to avoid both the punishments inflicted in this world for disobeying an earthly sovereign and those to be inflicted in the world to come for disobeying God must therefore be taught to distinguish carefully between what is and what is not necessary to eternal salvation.

### All That Is Necessary to Salvation Is Contained in Faith and Obedience

Everything necessary to salvation is contained in two virtues: faith in Christ, and obedience to laws. If our obedience were perfect, it alone would be enough. But we are all guilty of disobedience to God's law, not only originally, through Adam, but also actually, through our own transgressions. We are therefore now required not only to obey for the rest of our lives but also to obtain forgiveness for the sins we have already committed, and that forgiveness is the reward of our faith in Christ. That nothing else is necessarily required for salvation is clear from the fact that the Kingdom of Heaven is closed to no one except sinners, meaning the disobedient, those who transgress the law. Even sinners are not shut out, provided they repent and believe all the articles of Christian faith that are necessary to salvation.

### What Obedience Is Necessary

God accepts the will for the deed in all our actions, and the obedience he requires of us is a serious effort to obey him. That effort goes by every name that signifies it. Obedience is therefore sometimes called charity and love, because these imply a will to obey, and our Savior himself makes our love of God and of one another the fulfilling of the whole law. Sometimes it is called righteousness, for righteousness is nothing but the will to give everyone his own, which is the will to obey the laws. And sometimes it is called repentance, because to repent means to turn away from sin, which is the same as the will's return to obedience. Whoever sincerely desires to fulfill God's commandments, or truly repents of his transgressions, or loves God with all his heart and his neighbor as himself, therefore has all the obedience necessary for admission into the Kingdom of God. If God required perfect innocence, no human being could be saved.

### And to What Laws

But which commandments has God given us? Are all the laws given to the Jews through Moses the commandments of God? If they are, why are Christians not taught to obey them? If they are not, what other commandments of God are there, besides the law of nature? Christ our Savior did not give us new laws. He gave us counsel to observe the laws we are already subject to, namely the laws of nature and the laws of our respective sovereigns. Nor did he make any new law for the Jews in his Sermon on the Mount; he only expounded the laws of Moses, to which they were already subject. The laws of God, then, are none other than the laws of nature. The chief of these is that we should not break faith, which amounts to a commandment to obey the civil sovereigns whom we set over ourselves by mutual agreement with one another. And this law of God, which commands obedience to the civil law, consequently commands obedience to all the precepts of the Bible. As I proved in the previous chapter, the Bible is law only where the civil sovereign has made it so. Everywhere else it is only counsel, which a person may refuse to follow without injustice, though at his own peril.

### In the Faith of a Christian, Who Is the Person Believed

Having established what obedience is necessary to salvation and to whom it is owed, we must next consider faith: whom we believe and why, and which articles or points must necessarily be believed by those who are to be saved. First, as to the person we believe: it is impossible to believe anyone before we know what he says, so that person must be someone we have heard speak. The person whom Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and the prophets believed was therefore God himself, who spoke to them supernaturally, and the person whom the apostles and disciples who lived alongside Christ believed was our Savior himself. But of those to whom neither God the Father nor our Savior ever spoke, it cannot be said that the person they believed was God. They believed the apostles, and after them the pastors and teachers of the Church, who commended to their faith the history contained in the Old and New Testaments. Ever since our Savior's time, therefore, the faith of Christians has rested first on the reputation of their pastors, and afterward on the authority of those who caused the Old and New Testaments to be accepted as the rule of faith. Only Christian sovereigns could do this. They are therefore the supreme pastors, and the only persons whom Christians now hear speaking from God, apart from those to whom God speaks supernaturally in our own day. But because many false prophets "have gone out into the world," others must test such spirits, as St. John advises in his first epistle (1 John 4:1), to see "whether they are of God." And since the examination of doctrines belongs to the supreme pastor, the person whom everyone without a special revelation is to believe is, in every commonwealth, the supreme pastor, which is to say the civil sovereign.

### The Causes of Christian Faith

People believe Christian doctrines for various reasons, since faith is the gift of God, and he produces it in each individual by whatever means seem good to him. The most common immediate cause of our belief in any point of Christian faith is that we believe the Bible to be the Word of God. But why we believe the Bible to be the Word of God is much disputed, as every badly framed question must be. People pose the question not as "Why do we believe it?" but as "How do we know it?", as though believing and knowing were the same thing. As a result, one side grounds its knowledge on the infallibility of the Church and the other on the testimony of the private spirit, and neither proves what it claims. How can anyone know the infallibility of the Church without first knowing the infallibility of Scripture? Or how can anyone know that his own private spirit is anything other than a belief grounded on the authority and arguments of his teachers, or on a presumption about his own gifts? Besides, nothing in Scripture allows us to infer the infallibility of the Church, much less of any particular church, and least of all of any particular man.

### Faith Comes by Hearing

It is clear, then, that Christians do not know but only believe that Scripture is the Word of God. The means God ordinarily provides for making them believe it follow the course of nature, which means the belief comes from their teachers. St. Paul's doctrine concerning Christian faith in general is that "faith comes by hearing" (Romans 10:17), meaning by hearing our lawful pastors. He also says, in verses 14 and 15 of the same chapter, "How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, unless they are sent?" This makes it evident that the ordinary cause of believing the Scriptures to be the Word of God is the same as the cause of believing every other article of our faith: hearing those whom the law permits and appoints to teach us, such as our parents in their households and our pastors in the churches. Experience makes this plainer still. In Christian commonwealths everyone either believes or at least professes that Scripture is the Word of God, while in other commonwealths hardly anyone does. What other reason can be given for this, except that in Christian commonwealths people are taught it from infancy, and elsewhere they are taught otherwise?

But if teaching is the cause of faith, why does not everyone believe? It is certain, therefore, that faith is the gift of God, and that he gives it to whom he will. Nevertheless, he gives it to those who receive it by means of teachers, and so the immediate cause of faith is hearing. In a school where many are taught, some make progress and others do not. The cause of learning in those who progress is the schoolmaster, yet it cannot be inferred from this that learning is not the gift of God. All good things come from God, yet not everyone who has them can claim to be inspired, for inspiration implies a supernatural gift and the direct hand of God. Whoever claims that much claims to be a prophet, and is subject to examination by the Church.

Whether people know, believe, or merely grant that the Scriptures are the Word of God, I can show from passages free of obscurity which articles of faith are necessary for salvation, and which alone are necessary. If I do, those people must likewise know, believe, or grant the same.

### The Only Necessary Article of Christian Faith

The one necessary thing, the *unum necessarium*, the only article of faith that Scripture makes simply necessary to salvation, is this: that *Jesus is the Christ*. By the name "Christ" is meant the king whom God had promised through the prophets of the Old Testament to send into the world. This king would reign eternally under God himself, over the Jews and over those of other nations who would believe in him, and would give them the eternal life that was lost through Adam's sin. Once I have proved this from Scripture, I will go on to show when, and in what sense, some other articles may also be called necessary.

### Proved from the Purpose of the Evangelists

My first argument that belief in this article, *Jesus is the Christ*, is all the faith required for salvation comes from the purpose of the evangelists, which was to establish that single article by describing the life of our Savior. The substance of St. Matthew's Gospel is as follows. Jesus was descended from David and born of a virgin, which are the marks of the true Christ. The Magi came to worship him as King of the Jews, and Herod sought to kill him for that same reason. John the Baptist proclaimed him. He preached, both personally and through his apostles, that he was that king. He taught the law not as a scribe but as a man with authority. He cured diseases by his word alone and performed many other miracles that had been foretold of the Christ. He was hailed as king when he entered Jerusalem. He warned his followers to beware of all others who would claim to be the Christ. He was arrested, accused, and put to death for saying he was a king, and the charge for which he was condemned, written on the cross, was JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. All of this aims at nothing other than leading people to believe that Jesus is the Christ. Such was the purpose of St. Matthew's Gospel. But the purpose of all the evangelists, as reading them shows, was the same. The purpose of the whole Gospel, therefore, was to establish that single article. And St. John expressly makes it his conclusion (John 20:31): "These things are written, that you may know that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God."

### From the Sermons of the Apostles

My second argument is drawn from the subject of the apostles' preaching, both while our Savior lived on earth and after his ascension. During our Savior's lifetime, the apostles were sent, according to Luke 9:2, to preach the Kingdom of God. Neither there nor in Matthew 10:7 does he give them any commission other than this: "As you go, preach, saying, The Kingdom of Heaven is at hand." That message is that Jesus is the Messiah, the Christ, the king who was to come. That their preaching after his ascension was the same is clear from Acts 17:6: "They dragged Jason and certain brethren before the rulers of the city," says St. Luke, "crying, These who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them. And they all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus." It is also clear from verses 2 and 3 of the same chapter, which tell us that St. Paul, "as his custom was, went in to them, and on three Sabbath days reasoned with them out of the Scriptures, explaining and demonstrating that the Christ must have suffered and risen again from the dead, and that this Jesus, whom he preached, is the Christ."

### From the Ease of the Doctrine

The third argument comes from those passages of Scripture that declare all the faith required for salvation to be easy. Suppose an inward assent of the mind to every doctrine of Christian faith now taught, most of which are disputed, were necessary to salvation. Then nothing in the world would be as hard as being a Christian. The thief on the cross, though repentant, could not have been saved by saying, "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom," since by those words he professed belief in no other article than this: that Jesus was the king. Nor could it be said, as it is in Matthew 11:30, that Christ's "yoke is easy, and his burden light," nor that "little children believe in him," as in Matthew 18:6. Nor could St. Paul have said (1 Corinthians 1:21), "It pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe." Nor could St. Paul himself have been saved, much less have become so great a teacher of the Church so suddenly, when he perhaps never gave a thought to transubstantiation, or purgatory, or the many other articles now forced upon believers.

### From Formal and Clear Texts

The fourth argument is drawn from passages that are explicit and admit no dispute over their interpretation. The first is John 5:39: "Search the Scriptures, for in them you think you have eternal life; and they are what testify of me." Here our Savior is speaking only of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, since the Jews of that time could not search the Scriptures of the New Testament, which had not yet been written. But the Old Testament contains nothing about Christ except the marks by which people might recognize him when he came: that he would be descended from David, be born in Bethlehem and of a virgin, perform great miracles, and the like. To believe that this Jesus was he was therefore sufficient for eternal life. But what is more than sufficient is not necessary, and consequently no other article is required.

The second is John 11:26: "Whoever lives and believes in me shall not die eternally." To believe in Christ, then, is faith sufficient for eternal life, and consequently no more faith than that is necessary. But to believe in Jesus and to believe that Jesus is the Christ are one and the same, as the verses immediately following show. When our Savior asked Martha (verse 26), "Do you believe this?" she answered (verse 27), "Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world." This article alone, therefore, is faith sufficient for eternal life, and what is more than sufficient is not necessary.

The third is John 20:31: "These things are written that you might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you might have life through his name." There, believing that Jesus is the Christ is faith sufficient to obtain life, and therefore no other article is necessary.

The fourth is 1 John 4:2: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God." To this may be added 1 John 5:1, "Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God," and verse 5 of the same chapter, "Who is it that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?"

The fifth is Acts 8:36–37: "See," said the eunuch, "here is water; what hinders me from being baptized? And Philip said, If you believe with all your heart, you may. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." Belief in this article, *Jesus is the Christ*, is therefore sufficient for baptism, which is our admission into the Kingdom of God, and consequently it is the only thing necessary. And generally, wherever our Savior says to anyone, "Your faith has saved you," he says it in response to some confession that directly or by implication contains the belief that Jesus is the Christ.

### From the Fact That It Is the Foundation of All Other Articles

The last argument comes from those passages in which this article is made the foundation of faith, for whoever holds to the foundation will be saved. The first of these is Matthew 24:23: "If anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ,' or 'There he is,' do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders." Here we see that the article *Jesus is the Christ* must be held even if the one teaching the contrary should work great miracles. The second is Galatians 1:8: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any gospel other than the one we have preached to you, let him be accursed." But the gospel that Paul and the other apostles preached was this article alone, that Jesus is the Christ. For the sake of believing this article, therefore, we are to reject the authority of an angel from heaven, and still more the authority of any mortal man who teaches the contrary. It follows that this is the fundamental article of the Christian faith. The third is 1 John 4:1: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit. By this you shall know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God." From this it is evident that this article is the measure and rule by which all other articles are to be weighed and examined, and that it alone is therefore fundamental. The fourth is Matthew 16:18. After St. Peter had professed this article, saying to our Savior, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," our Savior answered, "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church." From this I infer that this article is the one on which all the other doctrines of the Church are built, as on their foundation. The fifth is 1 Corinthians 3:11 and the verses that follow: "No one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is that Jesus is the Christ. Now if anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, each one's work will be made plain. For the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet only as through fire." These words are partly plain and easy to understand, and partly allegorical and difficult. From what is plain, we may infer that pastors who teach this foundation, that Jesus is the Christ, may still be saved even if they draw false consequences from it, as all men sometimes do. Still more may those be saved who are not pastors but hearers, and who believe what their lawful pastors have taught them. The belief in this article is therefore sufficient, and it follows that no other article of faith is necessarily required for salvation.

As for the allegorical part, such as the phrases "the fire will test each one's work" and "he will be saved, but only as by fire" (or "through fire," since the original Greek is *dia puros*), it tells in no way against the conclusion I have drawn from the plain words. Nevertheless, because this passage has been used as an argument to prove the fire of Purgatory, I will offer here my own conjecture about what this testing of doctrines, and this saving of men as by fire, means. The Apostle seems here to allude to the words of the prophet Zechariah, chapter 13, verses 8 and 9, who, speaking of the restoration of the Kingdom of God, says: "Two parts in it shall be cut off and die, but the third shall be left in it. And I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and test them as gold is tested. They shall call on the name of the Lord, and I will hear them." The Day of Judgment is the day of the restoration of the Kingdom of God, and it is on that day, as St. Peter tells us in his second epistle, chapter 3, that the world will be consumed by fire. In that conflagration the wicked will perish, but the remnant whom God will save will pass through the fire unharmed. They will be tested in it and refined of their idolatry, as silver and gold are refined of their dross, and they will be made to call upon the name of the true God. Alluding to this, St. Paul says here that the Day, meaning the Day of Judgment, the great day of our Savior's coming to restore the Kingdom of God in Israel, will test every man's doctrine by judging which of them are gold, silver, and precious stones, and which are wood, hay, and straw. Then those who have built false consequences on the true foundation will see their doctrines condemned. They themselves, however, will be saved. They will pass unharmed through this universal fire and live eternally, calling upon the name of the one true God. Read in this sense, the passage contains nothing that disagrees with the rest of Holy Scripture, and not the slightest glimpse of the fire of Purgatory.

### In What Sense Other Articles May Be Called Necessary

Someone might ask at this point whether it is not just as necessary to salvation to believe that God is omnipotent and the Creator of the world, that Jesus Christ has risen, and that all other men will rise from the dead on the last day, as it is to believe that Jesus is the Christ. My answer is that it is, and so are many other articles. But they are all contained in this one article and can be deduced from it with more or less difficulty. Who can fail to see that those who believe Jesus to be the Son of the God of Israel, and who believe that the Israelites worshiped the omnipotent Creator of all things as their God, thereby also believe that God is the omnipotent Creator of all things? Or how can anyone believe that Jesus is the King who will reign eternally unless he also believes that Jesus has risen from the dead? A dead man cannot exercise the office of a king. In sum, whoever holds this foundation, that Jesus is the Christ, holds *explicitly* everything he sees to be rightly deduced from it, and *implicitly* everything that follows from it, even if he lacks the skill to discern the connection. It therefore remains true that belief in this one article is faith sufficient to obtain forgiveness of sins for the penitent, and so to bring them into the Kingdom of Heaven.

### That Faith and Obedience Are Both Necessary to Salvation

I have now shown that all the obedience required for salvation consists in the will to obey the law of God, which is to say in repentance, and that all the faith required for it is contained in the belief in this one article, that Jesus is the Christ. I will now cite those passages of the Gospel which prove that everything necessary to salvation is contained in these two joined together. On the day of Pentecost following our Savior's ascension, the men to whom St. Peter preached asked him and the other apostles, as recorded in Acts 2:37, "Brothers, what shall we do?" St. Peter answered them in the next verse: "Repent, and be baptized every one of you for the forgiveness of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit." Repentance and baptism, which is to say believing that Jesus is the Christ, are therefore all that is necessary to salvation. Again, when a certain ruler asked our Savior, in Luke 18:18, "What shall I do to inherit eternal life?" he answered, "You know the commandments: Do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and your mother." When the man replied that he had kept all of these, our Savior added, "Sell everything you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me." This was as much as to say, "Rely on me, for I am the King." To fulfill the law, and to believe that Jesus is the King, is therefore all that is required to bring a man to eternal life. Third, St. Paul says in Romans 1:17, "The just shall live by faith." He does not say that everyone shall live by faith, but the just. Faith and justice, meaning the will to be just, or repentance, are therefore all that is necessary to eternal life. And in Mark 1:15 our Savior preached, saying, "The time is fulfilled, and the Kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel," that is, the good news that the Christ had come. To repent, and to believe that Jesus is the Christ, is therefore all that is required for salvation.

### What Each of Them Contributes to It

Since it is necessary that faith and obedience (the obedience implied in the word *repentance*) both work together toward our salvation, the dispute over which of the two justifies us is beside the point. Still, it is not beside the point to make clear how each contributes to salvation, and in what sense we are said to be justified by the one and by the other. First, if righteousness is understood to mean the justice of the works themselves, then no one can be saved, for there is no one who has not broken the law of God. When we are said to be justified by works, therefore, this must be understood to refer to the will, which God always accepts in place of the work itself, in good men and evil men alike. It is in this sense only that a man is called just or unjust, and that his justice justifies him. His justice gives him the title of "just" in God's acceptance and makes him capable of *living by his faith*, which he was not before. Justice, then, justifies in the sense in which to justify means to declare a man just, and not in the sense of fulfilling the law so completely that punishing his sins would itself be unjust.

But a man is also said to be justified when his plea is accepted even though it is insufficient in itself. This happens when we plead our will and our effort to fulfill the law, and repent of our failures, and God accepts this as if it were the performance itself. And because God accepts the will in place of the deed only in the faithful, it is faith that makes our plea good. In this sense it is said that faith alone justifies. Faith and obedience are thus both necessary to salvation, yet each is said to justify in a different sense.

### That Obedience to God and to the Civil Sovereign Are Not Inconsistent

#### Whether the Sovereign Is Christian

Having shown what is necessary to salvation, I find it not hard to reconcile our obedience to God with our obedience to the civil sovereign, who is either a Christian or an unbeliever. If he is a Christian, he permits belief in the article that Jesus is the Christ, and in all the articles contained in it or deduced from it by evident consequence, which together make up all the faith necessary to salvation. And because he is sovereign, he requires obedience to all his own laws, that is, to all the civil laws. These include all the laws of nature, which is to say all the laws of God. For apart from the laws of nature and the laws of the Church, which are part of the civil law (since the only church that can make laws is the commonwealth), there are no other divine laws. Whoever obeys his Christian sovereign is therefore not prevented either from believing in God or from obeying him. Now suppose that a Christian king should draw some false consequences from the foundation that Jesus is the Christ. Suppose, that is, that he should raise some superstructure of hay or straw on it, and order it to be taught. Since St. Paul says that such a builder will be saved, much more will the man be saved who teaches these things by the king's command, and more still the man who does not teach at all but simply believes his lawful teacher. And if a subject is forbidden by the civil sovereign to profess some of his own opinions, on what grounds can he disobey? Christian kings may err in drawing a consequence, but who is to judge? Shall a private man judge, when the question concerns his own obedience? Or shall anyone judge except the one appointed to it by the Church, that is, by the civil sovereign who represents it? And if the Pope or an apostle should judge, may he not also err in drawing a consequence? Did not one of the two, either St. Peter or St. Paul, err in a superstructure, when St. Paul opposed St. Peter to his face? There can therefore be no contradiction between the laws of God and the laws of a Christian commonwealth.

#### Or an Unbeliever

When the civil sovereign is an unbeliever, any of his own subjects who resists him sins against the laws of God, since the laws of nature are God's laws. He also rejects the counsel of the apostles, who urge all Christians to obey their rulers, and all children and servants to obey their parents and masters in all things. As for their faith, it is inward and invisible. Such subjects have the same allowance that was granted to Naaman, the Syrian commander who, after coming to believe in the God of Israel, asked leave to go on bowing in the temple of his king's idol when his duties required it, and was told by the prophet to go in peace. They need not put themselves in danger for their faith. But if they do, they should look for their reward in heaven, and not complain against their lawful sovereign, much less make war on him. For a man who is not glad of any just occasion for martyrdom does not have the faith he professes. He only pretends to it, in order to give some plausible cover to his own stubborn defiance. And what unbelieving king would be so unreasonable as to put to death or persecute a subject whom he knows to be waiting for the second coming of Christ, after the present world has been burned, and intending to obey Christ then (which is what it means to believe that Jesus is the Christ), while in the meantime considering himself bound to obey the laws of that unbelieving king, as all Christians are obliged in conscience to do?

This is enough on the subject of the Kingdom of God and ecclesiastical government. In it I claim to put forward no position of my own. I aim only to show what consequences seem to me to follow from the principles of Christian politics, which are the Holy Scriptures, in confirmation of the power of civil sovereigns and the duty of their subjects. In citing Scripture, I have tried to avoid texts whose interpretation is obscure or disputed, and to cite none except in the sense that is plainest and most consistent with the harmony and purpose of the whole Bible, which was written for the re-establishment of the Kingdom of God in Christ. It is not the bare words but the purpose of the writer that gives the true light by which any writing is to be interpreted. Those who fasten on single texts without considering the main design can draw nothing clearly from them. Instead, by throwing atoms of Scripture like dust before men's eyes, they make everything more obscure than it is, which is the usual trick of those who seek not the truth but their own advantage.

## Part IV. Of the Kingdom of Darkness

## Chapter XLIV. Of Spiritual Darkness from Misinterpretation of Scripture

#### What the Kingdom of Darkness Is

Besides the sovereign powers, divine and human, that I have discussed so far, Scripture mentions another power. Ephesians 6:12 speaks of "the rulers of the darkness of this world," Matthew 12:26 of "the kingdom of Satan," and Matthew 9:34 of "the principality of Beelzebub over demons," that is, over phantasms that appear in the air. For this reason Ephesians 2:2 also calls Satan "the prince of the power of the air," and, because he rules in the darkness of this world, John 16:11 calls him "the prince of this world." Accordingly, those under his dominion are called the children of darkness, in contrast to the faithful, who are the children of light. Since Beelzebub is the prince of phantasms, which inhabit his dominion of air and darkness, the phrases "children of darkness" and "demons, phantasms, or spirits of illusion" mean allegorically the same thing. With this in view, the kingdom of darkness, as these and other passages of Scripture describe it, is nothing other than "a confederacy of deceivers who, to obtain dominion over men in this present world, try by dark and erroneous doctrines to extinguish in them the light both of nature and of the Gospel, and so to leave them unprepared for the Kingdom of God to come."

#### The Church Not Yet Fully Freed of Darkness

Those who have been blind from birth have no idea at all of the light the bodily eye perceives, and no one can imagine a greater light than one he has at some time perceived through his outward senses. The same is true of the light of the Gospel and the light of the understanding: no one can conceive that there is any greater degree of it than what he has already reached. It follows that men have no way of recognizing their own darkness except by reasoning from the unforeseen misfortunes that overtake them along their way. The darkest part of Satan's kingdom lies outside the Church of God, among those who do not believe in Jesus Christ. But we cannot conclude from this that the Church enjoys all the light it needs to perform the work God has commanded of us, as the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, had light while the plague of darkness covered the rest of Egypt. Why else has Christendom, almost from the time of the apostles, seen men jostling one another out of their places through both foreign and civil war? Why do they stumble over every small roughness in their own fortune and every small eminence in another's? Why do they take so many different paths while running toward the same goal, happiness? It can only be night among us, or at least a fog. We are, then, still in the dark.

#### Four Causes of Spiritual Darkness

The enemy has come here in the night of our natural ignorance and sown the tares of spiritual error, the weeds of the parable scattered among the wheat. He has done so, first, by abusing and putting out the light of the Scriptures, for we err by not knowing the Scriptures. Second, he has introduced the demonology of the heathen poets: their fabulous doctrine of demons, which are nothing but idols, phantasms of the brain with no real nature of their own apart from human fancy. Such are the ghosts of the dead, fairies, and the other stuff of old wives' tales. Third, he has mixed into Scripture various relics of the religion of the Greeks, along with much of their vain and erroneous philosophy, especially Aristotle's. Fourth, he has blended into both of these false or uncertain traditions and invented or uncertain history. And so we come to err by "giving heed to seducing spirits" and to the demonology of those "who speak lies in hypocrisy," or, as the original Greek of 1 Timothy 4:1–2 has it, "of those who play the part of liars," "with a seared conscience," that is, against their own knowledge. Of the first of these, the seducing of men by the abuse of Scripture, I intend to speak briefly in this chapter.

#### Errors from Misinterpreting the Scriptures Concerning the Kingdom of God

The greatest and chief abuse of Scripture, to which nearly all the others are either consequent or subservient, is the twisting of it to prove that the Kingdom of God, so often mentioned there, is the present Church: the multitude of Christians now living, together with those who have died and are to rise again at the last day. In fact, the Kingdom of God was first instituted through the ministry of Moses, over the Jews alone, who were for that reason called his peculiar people, his own special possession. It came to an end afterward with the election of Saul, when they refused to be governed by God any longer and demanded a king like those of the other nations, and God himself consented, as I proved at greater length in Chapter 35. From that time on there was no other Kingdom of God in the world, by covenant or otherwise, except in the sense that he always was, is, and shall be King of all men and all creatures, governing them according to his will by his infinite power. Nevertheless, he promised through his prophets to restore this government to them when the time appointed in his secret counsel should fully come, and when they turned back to him in repentance and amendment of life. He also invited the Gentiles to come in and share the happiness of his reign on the same conditions of conversion and repentance. And he promised as well to send his Son into the world to atone for the sins of them all by his death, and to prepare them by his teaching to receive him at his second coming. Since that second coming has not yet happened, the Kingdom of God has not yet come, and we are not now under any kings by covenant except our civil sovereigns. The one exception is that Christians are already in the Kingdom of Grace, insofar as they already hold the promise of being received at his coming again.

#### As That the Kingdom of God Is the Present Church

If the present Church is Christ's kingdom, it follows that there must be some one man or assembly through whose mouth our Savior, now in heaven, speaks and gives law, and who represents his person to all Christians. Alternatively, there must be several men or several assemblies doing the same for different parts of Christendom. The Pope claims this royal power under Christ universally, and assemblies of the local pastors claim it in particular commonwealths, although Scripture gives it to none but civil sovereigns. The power has therefore come to be disputed so passionately that the dispute puts out the light of nature and casts such darkness over men's understanding that they cannot see to whom they have pledged their obedience.

#### And That the Pope Is His Vicar General

The Pope claims to be Christ's vicar general in the present Church, which is supposed to be the kingdom of Christ that the Gospel addresses us to. From that claim follows the doctrine that a Christian king must receive his crown from a bishop. On this view, it is from that ceremony that he derives the phrase *Dei gratia*, "by the grace of God," in his title, and he is made king by God's favor only when he is crowned by the authority of God's universal viceroy on earth. The same claim produces the practice by which every bishop, whoever his sovereign may be, swears at his consecration an oath of absolute obedience to the Pope. From the same source also comes the doctrine of the Fourth Lateran Council, held under Pope Innocent III, in its third chapter, *On Heretics*: "That if a king, at the Pope's admonition, does not purge his kingdom of heresies, and, being excommunicated for this, does not give satisfaction within a year, his subjects are absolved of the bond of their obedience." By heresies the council means every opinion the Church of Rome has forbidden men to hold. As a result, whenever the political designs of the Pope conflict with those of other Christian princes, as they very often do, such a fog arises among the subjects that they cannot tell a foreigner who thrusts himself onto the throne of their lawful prince from the prince they themselves had placed there. In this darkness of mind they are made to fight one another, unable to distinguish enemies from friends, under the leadership of another man's ambition.

#### And That the Pastors Are the Clergy

The same opinion, that the present Church is the Kingdom of God, explains why pastors, deacons, and all other ministers of the Church take for themselves the name of clergy and give other Christians the name of laity, which means simply "people." The word clergy refers to those who live on a particular revenue. During his reign over the Israelites, God reserved that revenue to himself and assigned it as an inheritance to the tribe of Levi. The Levites were to be his public ministers and, unlike their brethren, were given no portion of land to live on. The Pope claims that the present Church, like the realm of Israel, is the Kingdom of God, and on that ground he demanded a similar revenue for himself and his subordinate ministers as God's inheritance. The name of clergy suited that claim. That is why churchmen have long demanded tithes and other tributes from Christians, and taken them, *jure divino*, that is, by divine right, as the Israelites once paid them to the Levites as God's right. In this way people everywhere were bound to pay a double tribute, one to the state and another to the clergy. The clergy's share, a tenth of their income, was twice what a certain king of Athens, a man regarded as a tyrant, took from his subjects to meet all public expenses. He demanded no more than a twentieth, and with it he maintained the commonwealth abundantly. And in the kingdom of the Jews, during God's priestly reign, the tithes and offerings made up the entire public revenue.

The same confusion of the present Church with the Kingdom of God produced the distinction between civil and canon law. Civil law consists of the acts of sovereigns in their own dominions, and canon law consists of the acts of the Pope in those same dominions. At first these canons were only canons, that is, rules proposed, and Christian princes accepted them only voluntarily, up to the transfer of the empire to Charlemagne. Afterward, as the power of the Pope grew, they became rules commanded. The emperors themselves were forced to let them pass as laws in order to avoid the greater harms that a blinded people might be led into.

Hence, in every dominion where the Pope's ecclesiastical power is fully accepted, the Roman Church tolerates Jews, Turks, and Gentiles in their religion so long as they do not offend against the civil power in practicing and professing it. A Christian, however, even a foreigner, who does not belong to the Roman religion commits a capital offense, because the Pope claims that all Christians are his subjects. Without that claim, persecuting a Christian foreigner for professing the religion of his own country would violate the law of nations as much as persecuting an infidel, or rather more, since those who are not against Christ are with him.

For the same reason, every Christian state contains certain men who are exempt, by ecclesiastical liberty, from the taxes and the courts of the civil state. The secular clergy are exempt in this way, and so are the monks and friars. In many places these men are so numerous in proportion to the common people that, if need arose, an army could be raised from them alone, large enough for any war in which the Church militant might employ them, whether against their own princes or against others.

#### Error from Mistaking Consecration for Conjuration

A second general abuse of Scripture is the turning of consecration into conjuration, or enchantment. In Scripture, to consecrate is to offer, give, or dedicate a man or any other thing to God, with pious and fitting words and gestures, by setting it apart from common use. It is to sanctify the thing, to make it God's, so that only those whom God has appointed as his public ministers may use it, as I have already shown at length in Chapter 35. Consecration therefore changes not the thing consecrated but only its use, from profane and common to holy and reserved for God's service. But when such words are claimed to change the nature or quality of the thing itself, that is not consecration. It is either an extraordinary work of God or a vain and impious conjuration. And since they claim this change of nature so often in their consecrations, it cannot be regarded as an extraordinary work. It can only be a conjuration or incantation, by which they would have men believe in an alteration of nature that does not exist, contrary to the testimony of their sight and all their other senses.

The priest at the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper provides an example. He ought to consecrate the bread and wine to God's special service, which means only setting them apart from common use so that they signify, that is, remind men of, their redemption through the Passion of Christ, whose body was broken and whose blood was shed on the cross for our transgressions. Instead, he claims that by saying our Savior's words, "This is my body" and "This is my blood," he makes the nature of bread no longer present and puts Christ's very body in its place. He claims this even though nothing appears to the sight or any other sense of the receiver that did not appear before the consecration. The Egyptian magicians who are said to have turned their rods into serpents and the water into blood are thought only to have deluded the senses of the spectators by a false show, and yet they are still considered enchanters. What, then, should we have thought of them if nothing in their rods had looked like a serpent, and nothing in the enchanted water had looked like blood or like anything but water, and yet they had brazenly insisted to Pharaoh's face that these were serpents that looked like rods and blood that only seemed to be water? That would have been both enchantment and lying. Yet in this daily act the priests do the very same thing. They turn the holy words into a kind of charm that produces nothing new to the senses, and still they insist to our faces that it has turned the bread into a man, and more than that, into a God. They require men to worship it as if it were our Savior himself, present as God and man, and so lead them to commit the grossest idolatry. If it were enough to clear this practice of idolatry to say that the thing is no longer bread but God, the same excuse would serve the Egyptians, had they had the effrontery to claim that the leeks and onions they worshipped were not really leeks and onions but a divinity under their species, or outward likeness. The words "This is my body" are equivalent to "This signifies, or represents, my body," which is an ordinary figure of speech. To take them literally is an abuse. And even taken literally, they can extend no further than the bread that Christ himself consecrated with his own hands. He never said that whatever bread any priest might call "my body" or "Christ's body" would at once be transubstantiated. Nor did the Church of Rome establish this doctrine of transubstantiation until the time of Innocent III, not more than five hundred years ago. By then the power of the popes was at its height, and the darkness of the age had grown so great that men could not discern the bread they were given to eat. The bread was even stamped with the figure of Christ on the cross, as if the Church wished men to believe that it had been transubstantiated not only into the body of Christ but also into the wood of his cross, and that they ate both together in the sacrament.

#### Incantation in the Ceremonies of Baptism

The same kind of incantation takes the place of consecration in the Sacrament of Baptism. There the charm consists of the abuse of God's name, in each of the three Persons and in the whole Trinity, together with the sign of the cross made at each name. First, in making the holy water, the priest says: "I conjure you, creature of water, in the name of God the Father Almighty, and in the name of Jesus Christ his only Son our Lord, and in the power of the Holy Ghost, that you become conjured water, to drive away all the powers of the Enemy, and to root out and supplant the Enemy," and so on. He does the same in blessing the salt that is to be mixed with the water: "That you become conjured salt, so that all phantasms and knavery of the Devil's fraud may fly and depart from the place where you are sprinkled, and every unclean spirit be conjured by Him who shall come to judge the living and the dead." And he does the same in blessing the oil: "That all the power of the Enemy, all the host of the Devil, all assaults and phantasms of Satan, may be driven away by this creature of oil." The infant to be baptized undergoes many charms. First, at the church door the priest blows three times in the child's face and says, "Go out of him, unclean spirit, and give place to the Holy Ghost the Comforter," as if every child were possessed by demons until the priest blew on it. Again, before the child enters the church, the priest says, as before, "I conjure you," and so on, "to go out and depart from this servant of God." And he repeats the same exorcism once more before the child is baptized.
