These and certain other incantations take the place of consecrations in the administration of the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. In these sacraments everything those holy men use, except the priest's unhallowed spittle, has some set form of exorcism.

#### In Marriage, in Visitation of the Sick, and in Consecration of Places

Nor are the other rites free of charms: marriage, extreme unction, the visitation of the sick, the consecration of churches and churchyards, and the like. They all involve enchanted oil and water, together with the abuse of the cross and of David's holy words, *Asperges me, Domine, hyssopo*, "You will sprinkle me with hyssop, O Lord," as though these things had power to drive away phantasms and imaginary spirits.

#### Errors from Mistaking Eternal Life and Everlasting Death

Another general error arises from misinterpreting the words eternal life, everlasting death, and the second death. Holy Scripture states plainly that God created Adam in a state of living forever, and that this state was conditional: it depended on his not disobeying God's commandment. Eternal life was not essential to human nature but came from the power of the Tree of Life, from which Adam was free to eat so long as he had not sinned. Scripture states just as plainly that after he sinned he was driven out of Paradise lest he eat of that tree and live forever, and that Christ's Passion discharges the sin of all who believe in him. It follows that the Passion restores eternal life to all the faithful, and to them alone. Yet the doctrine now, and for a long time past, has been very different. It holds that every man has eternal life by nature, because his soul is immortal. On this view, the flaming sword at the entrance of Paradise keeps a man from the Tree of Life but does not keep him from the immortality God took from him for his sin, and it does not make him need the sacrifice of Christ to recover that immortality. Consequently, not only the faithful and righteous but also the wicked and the heathen will enjoy eternal life without any death at all, much less a second and everlasting death. To get around this difficulty, they say that second and everlasting death means a second and everlasting life, but in torment. That figure of speech is never used except in this one case.

All of this doctrine rests only on certain of the more obscure passages of the New Testament, and these, when the whole drift of Scripture is considered, are clear enough in a different sense and are in any case unnecessary to the Christian faith. Suppose that when a man dies, nothing remains of him but his corpse. Could not God, who by his Word raised lifeless dust and clay into a living creature, just as easily raise a dead body to life again, and then either keep it alive forever or make it die a second time by another Word? In Scripture the word *soul* always means either life or the living creature, and body and soul together mean the living body. On the fifth day of Creation God said, "Let the waters bring forth *reptile animae viventis*," the creeping thing that has in it a living soul, which the English translators render as "that hath life." Again, God created whales "*et omnem animam viventem*," which the English gives as "every living creature." The same holds for man: God made him from the dust of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, "*et factus est homo in animam viventem*," that is, "and man was made a living creature." After Noah came out of the ark, God says he will never again smite "*omnem animam viventem*," "every living creature." And Deuteronomy 12:23 says, "Eat not the blood, for the blood is the soul," meaning the life. If *soul* in these passages meant an incorporeal substance with an existence separable from the body, the same could be inferred of every other living creature as well as of man. I believe I have already proved sufficiently from Scripture, in Chapter 38, that the souls of the faithful remain in their bodies from the Resurrection to all eternity by God's special grace and not by their own nature. As for the passages in the New Testament that speak of a man being cast body and soul into hellfire, they mean no more than body and life: such men will be cast alive into the perpetual fire of Gehenna.

### Hence the Doctrines of Purgatory, Exorcism, and the Invocation of Saints

This is the window that lets in the dark doctrine of eternal torments, and after it the doctrine of purgatory. From purgatory follows the belief that the ghosts of the dead walk abroad, especially in consecrated, solitary, or dark places. That belief in turn opens the way to the pretensions of exorcism and the conjuring of phantasms, to the invocation of dead men, and to the doctrine of indulgences. An indulgence is an exemption, for a time or forever, from the fire of purgatory, in which these incorporeal substances are alleged to be cleansed by burning and made fit for heaven. Before the time of our Savior, the demonology of the Greeks had infected men generally with the opinion that human souls were substances distinct from their bodies. On this view, when the body died, every man's soul, godly or wicked, must go on existing somewhere by virtue of its own nature, and no supernatural gift of God was acknowledged in the matter. The Doctors of the Church were therefore long in doubt about where these souls were to dwell until they should be reunited with their bodies at the Resurrection. For a while they supposed that the souls lay beneath the altars. Afterward the Church of Rome found it more profitable to build them this place called purgatory, which some other churches in this latter age have torn down.

### The Texts Cited for These Doctrines Have Already Been Answered

Let us now consider which texts of Scripture seem most to confirm the three general errors I have touched on here. Cardinal Bellarmine has cited texts in support of a present Kingdom of God administered by the Pope, and none makes a better show of proof than these. I have already answered them, and have made it plain that the Kingdom of God instituted by Moses ended with the election of Saul. From that time on, no priest ever deposed a king by his own authority. What the high priest did to Athaliah was done in the right of the young King Joash, her son, and not in his own right. Solomon, by contrast, deposed the high priest Abiathar in his own right and set up another in his place. The most difficult text to answer, of all those that can be brought to prove that the Kingdom of God through Christ already exists in this world, is cited not by Bellarmine or anyone else of the Church of Rome, but by Beza, who would have that kingdom begin at the Resurrection of Christ. I do not know whether he means thereby to give supreme ecclesiastical power in the commonwealth of Geneva to the Presbytery, and consequently to every presbytery in every other commonwealth, or to give it to princes and other civil sovereigns. Wherever they have that form of church government, the presbyteries have claimed the power to excommunicate their own kings and to act as the supreme arbiters of religion, no less than the Pope claims that power universally.

### Answer to the Text from Which Beza Infers That the Kingdom of Christ Began at the Resurrection

The words are these (Mark 9:1): "Verily I say unto you, that there be some of them that stand here, which shall not taste of death, till they have seen the kingdom of God come with power." Taken grammatically, these words make it certain either that some of the men standing beside Christ at that moment are still alive, or that the Kingdom of God must exist now, in this present world. Another passage is more difficult still. After our Savior's Resurrection, and just before his Ascension, the apostles asked him (Acts 1:6), "Wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" He answered: "It is not for you to know the times and the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power; but ye shall receive power by the coming of the Holy Ghost upon you, and ye shall be my witnesses (martyrs) both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." This is as much as to say: My kingdom has not yet come, and you will not know beforehand when it will come, for it will come like a thief in the night. But I will send you the Holy Spirit, and through him you will have power to bear witness by your preaching to the whole world of my Resurrection, of the works I have done, and of the doctrine I have taught, so that men may believe in me and look for eternal life at my coming again. How does this agree with the coming of Christ's kingdom at the Resurrection? St. Paul says (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10) "that they turned from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven." To wait for his Son from heaven is to wait for him to come and reign as king in power, and that waiting would be unnecessary if the kingdom were already present. Again, if the Kingdom of God began at the Resurrection, as Beza would have it in his comment on Mark 9:1, what reason have Christians had ever since the Resurrection to say in their prayers, "Thy kingdom come"? It is therefore evident that St. Mark's words are not to be interpreted this way. "There be some of them that stand here," says our Savior, "that shall not taste of death till they have seen the kingdom of God come in power." If this kingdom were to come at the Resurrection of Christ, why does he say "some of them" rather than all? They all lived until after Christ had risen.

### An Explanation of Mark 9:1

Those who demand a precise interpretation of this text should first interpret the similar words our Savior spoke to St. Peter about St. John (John 21:22): "If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?" A report arose from these words that John would not die. Yet that report was neither confirmed as well founded on those words nor refuted as badly founded on them. It was left as a saying not understood. The same difficulty attends the passage in St. Mark. We may conjecture at its meaning from what immediately follows, both in Mark and in St. Luke, where the same saying is repeated. On that basis it is not improbable that the words refer to the Transfiguration, which is described in the verses that come right after. There it is said that "after six days Jesus taketh with him Peter, and James, and John" (not all of his disciples, but some) "and leadeth them up into an high mountain apart by themselves: and he was transfigured before them. And his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them." A fuller was a tradesman who cleaned and bleached cloth. "And there appeared unto them Elias with Moses: and they were talking with Jesus," and so on. So they saw Christ in glory and majesty, as he is to come, and "they were sore afraid." In this way our Savior's promise was fulfilled by means of a vision. That it was a vision may be inferred with probability from St. Luke, who tells the same story (Luke 9:28) and says that Peter and those with him were heavy with sleep. It may be inferred with certainty from Matthew 17:9, where the story is told again, because there our Savior charged them: "Tell the vision to no man, until the Son of man be risen again from the dead." However that may be, no argument can be drawn from the passage to prove that the Kingdom of God begins before the Day of Judgment.

### The Misuse of Certain Other Texts in Defense of the Pope's Power

Besides Bellarmine's texts, there are others offered to prove the Pope's power over civil sovereigns. It is claimed, for instance, that the two swords Christ and his apostles had among them were the spiritual sword and the temporal sword, and that Christ gave both to St. Peter. It is also claimed that of the two great lights in the heavens, the greater signifies the Pope and the lesser the king. One might as well infer from the first verse of the Bible that "heaven" means the Pope and "earth" the king. This is not arguing from Scripture. It is a wanton insult to princes, and it came into fashion once the popes had grown so secure in their greatness that they despised all Christian kings. Treading on the necks of emperors, they mocked both the emperors and Scripture in the words of the Ninety-first Psalm: "Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet."

### Consecration in Scripture Was Performed Without Exorcism

The rites of consecration depend for the most part on the discretion and judgment of the governors of the Church rather than on Scripture. Those governors are nonetheless bound by whatever the nature of the action itself requires: the ceremonies, words, and gestures must be decent and meaningful, or at least suited to the act being performed. When Moses consecrated the Tabernacle, the altar, and their vessels (Exodus 40), he anointed them with the oil God had commanded to be made for that purpose, and they were holy. Nothing was exorcised to drive away phantasms. When the same Moses, the civil sovereign of Israel, consecrated Aaron the high priest and his sons, he washed them with water (not exorcised water), put their garments on them, and anointed them with oil, and they were sanctified to minister to the Lord in the priest's office. It was a simple and decent cleansing and adorning of them before he presented them to God as his servants. When King Solomon, the civil sovereign of Israel, consecrated the Temple he had built (2 Kings 8), he stood before the whole congregation of Israel and blessed them. He then gave thanks to God for putting it into his father's heart to build the Temple, and for granting Solomon himself the grace to complete it. Next he prayed that God would accept that house, though it was unworthy of his infinite greatness, and that God would hear the prayers of his servants who should pray in it, or toward it if they were absent. Finally he offered a sacrifice of peace offerings, and the house was dedicated. There was no procession here, for the king stood still in the place where he had begun. There was no exorcised water and no *Asperges me*, the chant "Thou shalt sprinkle me," sung as holy water is sprinkled. Nor was there any other irrelevant application of words originally spoken on some different occasion. There was only a decent and reasonable speech, the one best suited to the occasion of presenting God with the gift of a newly built house. We do not read that St. John exorcised the water of the Jordan, or that Philip exorcised the water of the river in which he baptized the eunuch. Nor do we read that any pastor in the time of the apostles took his spittle, put it to the nose of the person to be baptized, and said "*In odorem suavitatis*," that is, "for a sweet savor unto the Lord." No human authority can justify either the ceremony of the spittle, because of its uncleanness, or the application of that scripture, because of its levity.

### Scripture Does Not Prove the Immortality of the Soul to Be a Matter of Nature, but of Grace

Several passages seem at first sight to prove well enough that the soul, once separated from the body, lives eternally. On this reading, eternal life would belong to the souls of the elect by special grace, through the restoration to the faithful of the eternal life that Adam lost through sin and that our Savior restored by the sacrifice of himself. But it would also belong to the souls of the reprobate, as a property following naturally from the essence of mankind, with no grace from God beyond what is given universally to all humanity. Yet when I compare these passages with what I cited earlier in Chapter 38 from the fourteenth chapter of Job, they seem to me far more open to a different interpretation than Job's words are.

First there are Solomon's words (Ecclesiastes 12:7): "Then shall the dust return to dust, as it was, and the spirit shall return to God that gave it." If no other text stands directly against it, this can quite well bear the interpretation that God alone, and not man, knows what becomes of a man's spirit when he dies. The same Solomon, in the same book (chapter 3, verses 20–21), states the same idea in the sense I have given it. His words are: "All go (man and beast) to the same place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again. Who knoweth that the spirit of man goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast goeth downward to the earth?" That is, no one knows but God. Nor is it an unusual turn of phrase to say of things we do not understand, "God knows what," or "God knows where." Then there is Genesis 5:24: "Enoch walked with God, and he was not; for God took him." This is explained in Hebrews 13:5: "He was translated, that he should not die; and was not found, because God had translated him. For before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God." To be translated here means to be carried up bodily to God. The text argues as much for the immortality of the body as for that of the soul, and it proves that Enoch's translation was peculiar to those who please God, not shared by them with the wicked, and that it depended on grace, not on nature. On the other hand, what interpretation besides the literal sense can we give to Solomon's words in Ecclesiastes 3:19: "That which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath" (that is, one spirit), "so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all is vanity"? Taken literally, these words contain no natural immortality of the soul, and yet nothing in them conflicts with the eternal life that the elect will enjoy by grace. In chapter 4, verse 3, Solomon says: "Better is he that hath not yet been, than both they," meaning better than those who live or have lived. If the souls of all who have lived were immortal, this would be a hard saying, because then to have an immortal soul would be worse than to have no soul at all. And again, in chapter 9, verse 5: "The living know that they shall die, but the dead know not any thing." This means that the dead know nothing naturally, before the resurrection of the body.

Another passage that seems to support a natural immortality of the soul is the one in which our Savior says that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are living. But this is said of God's promise and of their certainty of rising again, not of a life they were actually living at that time. It is meant in the same sense in which God told Adam that on the day he ate the forbidden fruit he would surely die. From that moment Adam was a dead man by sentence, though not by execution until nearly a thousand years later. In the same way, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were alive by promise when Christ spoke, but they will not be actually alive until the Resurrection. Nor does the story of Dives and Lazarus count against this, if we take it as what it is: a parable.

There are, however, other passages in the New Testament where immortality seems to be attributed directly to the wicked. It is evident that they will all rise to judgment. It is also said in many places that they will go into "everlasting fire, everlasting torments, everlasting punishments," and that "the worm of conscience never dieth." All of this is summed up in the phrase "everlasting death," which is commonly interpreted as everlasting life in torment. Yet I can find nowhere that any man will live in torment everlastingly. It also seems hard to say that God would punish men's transgressions without any end of time, and with every extremity of torture that men can imagine, and more. This is the God who is the Father of mercies, who does in heaven and on earth whatever he wills, and who has the hearts of all men at his disposal. He works in men both to do and to will, and without his free gift a man has neither any inclination to good nor any repentance of evil. We must therefore consider what is meant by "everlasting fire" and other such phrases in Scripture.

I have already shown that the Kingdom of God through Christ begins on the Day of Judgment. On that day the faithful will rise again with glorious and spiritual bodies and be his subjects in that kingdom, which will be eternal. They will neither marry nor be given in marriage, nor eat and drink as they did in their natural bodies, but will live forever as individual persons, without the eternity that a species gains through reproduction. The reprobate will also rise again, to receive punishment for their sins. I have shown, too, that those of the elect who are still alive in their earthly bodies on that day will have their bodies suddenly changed and made spiritual and immortal. But no passage of Scripture proves that the bodies of the reprobate, who make up the Kingdom of Satan, will also be glorious or spiritual bodies. None proves that they will be like the angels of God, neither eating, nor drinking, nor begetting offspring, or that their life will be eternal in their individual persons, as the life of every faithful man is, or as Adam's life would have been had he not sinned. The only exceptions are these passages about eternal torments, and they can be interpreted otherwise.

From this it may be inferred that the elect after the Resurrection will be restored to the state Adam was in before he sinned, and the reprobate will be in the state that Adam and his descendants were in after the sin was committed. There is one difference: God promised a Redeemer to Adam and to those of his seed who should trust in him and repent, but not to those who should die in their sins, as the reprobate do.

### What Eternal Torments Are

These things considered, the texts that speak of eternal fire, eternal torments, or the worm that never dies do not contradict the doctrine of a second and everlasting death, taking the word *death* in its proper and natural sense. The fire or torments prepared for the wicked in Gehenna, in Tophet, or in whatever place it may be, can continue forever, and there may never be a lack of wicked people to be tormented in them, even though no single one of them is tormented eternally. The wicked are left in the condition they were in after Adam's sin. They may therefore, after the Resurrection, live as they did before: they may marry and be given in marriage, and have gross and corruptible bodies, as all mankind now has. It follows that they may go on reproducing perpetually after the Resurrection, just as they did before it, for no passage of Scripture says otherwise. When St. Paul speaks of the Resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15, he means only the resurrection to eternal life, not the resurrection to punishment. Of the first he says that the body is "sown in corruption, raised in incorruption; sown in dishonor, raised in honor; sown in weakness, raised in power; sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body." Nothing of the kind can be said of the bodies of those who rise to punishment.

The decisive text, and a fertile one, is Luke 20:34–36: "The children of this world marry, and are given in marriage; but those who shall be counted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry nor are given in marriage. Neither can they die any more, for they are equal to the angels, and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." The children of this world, who remain in the condition in which Adam left them, shall marry and be given in marriage. That is, they shall decay and reproduce in succession, which is an immortality of the species but not of individual persons. They are not worthy to be counted among those who shall obtain the next world and an absolute resurrection from the dead. They are admitted to that world only for a short time, as temporary lodgers, and only so that they may receive the punishment their stubborn disobedience deserves. The elect are the only children of the Resurrection, which is to say the sole heirs of eternal life. They alone can die no more; it is they who are equal to the angels, and they who are the children of God, and not the reprobate. What remains to the reprobate after the Resurrection is a second and eternal death. Between that resurrection and their second, eternal death there is only a period of punishment and torment, and that period will be sustained by a succession of sinners for as long as the human species continues by propagation, which is eternally.

### An Answer to the Texts Cited for Purgatory

As I said before, the doctrine of Purgatory is founded on this doctrine of the natural eternity of souls separated from their bodies. If eternal life comes by grace alone, then there is no life except the life of the body, and no immortality until the Resurrection, and Purgatory loses its foundation. The texts for Purgatory that Bellarmine cites from the canonical Scripture of the Old Testament are, first, David's fasting for Saul and Jonathan, recorded in 2 Samuel 1:12 (which Bellarmine's Bible calls 2 Kings), and again his fasting for the death of Abner in 2 Samuel 3:35. Bellarmine says that David fasted in order to obtain something from God on their behalf after their deaths. His evidence is that David had fasted to win the recovery of his own child, and called for food as soon as he knew the child was dead. Bellarmine reasons as follows. The soul has an existence separate from the body. Men gain nothing by fasting for souls that are already in Heaven or in Hell. Therefore some souls of the dead must be neither in Heaven nor in Hell, and so they must be in some third place, which must be Purgatory.

By such hard straining he has twisted these passages into proof of a Purgatory. Yet the real explanation is plain. When the ceremonies of mourning and fasting are performed for the death of people whose lives brought the mourners no benefit, they are performed to honor those people. When they are performed for the death of people whose lives did benefit the mourners, they arise from the mourners' own particular loss. So David honored Saul and Abner by fasting, and at the death of his own child he consoled himself by returning to his ordinary food.

The other passages he cites from the Old Testament do not offer even the appearance or pretense of proof. He brings in every text containing the word *anger*, *fire*, *burning*, *purging*, or *cleansing*, provided that one of the Church Fathers once applied it, rhetorically and in a sermon, to the doctrine of Purgatory, which that Father already believed. Take the first verse of Psalm 38 (Psalm 37 in the numbering Bellarmine used): "O Lord, rebuke me not in your wrath, nor chasten me in your hot displeasure." What would this have to do with Purgatory if Augustine had not applied the *wrath* to the fire of Hell and the *displeasure* to the fire of Purgatory? And what has Purgatory to do with Psalm 66:12, "We went through fire and water, and you brought us out into a moist place," or with other texts like it? The doctors of those times used such verses to adorn or to lengthen their sermons and commentaries, and Bellarmine has dragged them to his purposes by sheer force of ingenuity.

### Passages of the New Testament Cited for Purgatory, Answered

But he also cites passages from the New Testament that are not so easy to answer. The first is Matthew 12:32: "Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come." He takes Purgatory to be the world to come, in which some sins may be forgiven that were not forgiven in this world. Yet there are plainly only three worlds. The first ran from the Creation to the Flood. It was destroyed by water and is called in Scripture the Old World. The second runs from the Flood to the Day of Judgment. It is the present world, and it shall be destroyed by fire. The third shall run from the Day of Judgment onward, everlasting, and it is called the World to Come. Everyone agrees that in that world there will be no Purgatory, and so the world to come and Purgatory cannot be the same thing.

What, then, can our Savior's words mean? I confess they are very hard to reconcile with all the doctrines now unanimously received. There is no shame in confessing that the depth of Scripture is too great to be measured by the short line of human understanding. Nevertheless, I may put forward for the consideration of more learned divines whatever the text itself suggests.

First, the Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity and resides in the Church, so to speak against the Holy Spirit is to speak against the Church. It seems, then, that the comparison is between the leniency of our Savior in bearing with offenses done to him while he was on earth, and the severity of the pastors who came after him toward those who denied their authority, an authority that came from the Holy Spirit. It is as if he said: "You who deny my power, and even you who will crucify me, shall be pardoned by me as often as you turn to me in repentance. But if you deny the power of those who teach you hereafter by virtue of the Holy Spirit, they will be inexorable. They will not forgive you. They will persecute you in this world and leave you without absolution, even though you turn to me, unless you turn to them as well, and so they will consign you, as far as it lies in their power, to the punishments of the world to come." Read this way, the words may be taken as a prophecy concerning the times, as those times have since unfolded in the Christian Church.

If that is not the meaning, and I am not dogmatic about such difficult passages, then perhaps some room is left after the Resurrection for the repentance of certain sinners. There is another passage that seems to agree with this. Consider the words of St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:29: "What shall they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they baptized for the dead?" From this a man may reasonably infer, as some have done, that in St. Paul's time there was a custom of receiving baptism on behalf of the dead. Believers would thereby undertake for the persons of their deceased friends that they would be ready to obey our Savior and receive him as their King at his second coming, much as believers today stand as sureties and sponsors for the faith of infants who are not yet capable of believing. In that case, the forgiveness of sins in the world to come has no need of a Purgatory.

Both of these interpretations, however, contain so much paradox that I do not trust them. I put them forward only to those who are thoroughly versed in Scripture, so that they may inquire whether some clearer passage contradicts them. Of this much, though, I see evident Scripture to persuade men: neither the word nor the thing called Purgatory appears in this text or in any other. Nor is there anything that can prove the necessity of a place for the soul apart from the body, whether for the soul of Lazarus during the four days he lay dead, or for the souls that the Roman Church claims are now being tormented in Purgatory. For God, who could give life to a piece of clay, has the same power to give life again to a dead man, and to renew his lifeless and rotten carcass into a glorious, spiritual, and immortal body.

Another passage is 1 Corinthians 3, where it is said that those who built with stubble, hay, and the like on the true foundation will see their work perish, but "they themselves shall be saved, yet as through fire." Bellarmine insists that this fire is the fire of Purgatory. As I have said before, the words allude to those of Zechariah 13:9: "I will bring the third part through the fire, and refine them as silver is refined, and will test them as gold is tested." That prophecy concerns the coming of the Messiah in power and glory, which is to say the Day of Judgment and the burning of the present world. In that fire the elect shall not be consumed but refined. They shall lay aside their erroneous doctrines and traditions, which will be, as it were, singed off them, and afterward they shall call upon the name of the true God. In the same way, the Apostle says that those who hold the foundation that *Jesus is the Christ*, and who build some other, erroneous doctrines on top of it, shall not be consumed in the fire that renews the world. They shall pass through it to salvation, but in such a way as to see their former errors and give them up. The builders are the pastors. The foundation is that Jesus is the Christ. The stubble and hay are false conclusions drawn from it through ignorance or frailty. The gold, silver, and precious stones are their true doctrines. And their refining or purging is the abandonment of their errors. In all of this there is no pretext whatever for the burning of incorporeal souls, which is to say souls incapable of suffering.

### How Baptism for the Dead Is to Be Understood

A third passage is the one from 1 Corinthians 15 already mentioned, concerning baptism for the dead. From it Bellarmine concludes, first, that prayers for the dead are not useless, and from that, that there is a fire of Purgatory. Neither conclusion is sound. Of the many interpretations of the word *baptism*, the one he ranks first is that baptism here means, metaphorically, a baptism of penance, so that people are baptized in this sense when they fast, pray, and give alms. On this reading, baptism for the dead and prayer for the dead are the same thing. But this is a metaphor for which there is no example, either in Scripture or in any other use of language, and it is also out of keeping with the harmony and purpose of Scripture. In Mark 10:38 and Luke 12:50 the word *baptism* is used for being dipped in one's own blood, as Christ was on the cross and as most of the apostles were for bearing witness to him. But it is hard to claim that prayer, fasting, and almsgiving bear any resemblance to dipping.

In Matthew 3:11 the same word is used for a purging with fire, which seems to lend some support to Purgatory. But the fire and purging mentioned there are plainly the same as those the prophet Zechariah speaks of in chapter 13, verse 9: "I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them," and so on. St. Peter speaks of them after him, in his first epistle, 1:7: "That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than gold that perishes, though it be tested with fire, might be found to praise and honor and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ." And St. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 3:13: "The fire shall try every man's work, of what sort it is." St. Peter and St. Paul speak of the fire that will come at the second appearing of Christ, and the prophet Zechariah of the Day of Judgment. This passage of St. Matthew may therefore be interpreted the same way, and then there is no need for a fire of Purgatory.

The other interpretation of baptism for the dead is the one I mentioned earlier, which Bellarmine ranks second in probability. From it, too, he infers the usefulness of prayer for the dead. If, after the Resurrection, those who never heard of Christ, or did not believe in him, may be received into Christ's kingdom, then it is not in vain for their friends to pray for them after their deaths until they rise. Let it be granted that God, at the prayers of the faithful, may convert to himself some of those who never heard Christ preached, and who therefore cannot have rejected him, and let it be granted that the charity of those who pray in this way cannot be faulted. Even so, this proves nothing for Purgatory. To rise from death to life is one thing; to rise from Purgatory to life is another, for the second is a rising from life to life, from a life in torment to a life in joy.

A fourth passage is Matthew 5:25–26: "Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him, lest at any time the adversary deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Truly I say to you, you shall by no means come out of there until you have paid the last farthing." In this allegory the offender is the sinner, and God is both the adversary and the judge. The way is this life, the prison is the grave, and the officer is death. From the grave the sinner shall not rise again to eternal life, but to a second death, until he has paid the last farthing, the smallest coin, or until Christ pays it for him by his Passion. That Passion is a full ransom for every kind of sin, the lesser sins as well as the greater crimes, since the Passion of Christ makes both equally pardonable.

The fifth passage is Matthew 5:22: "Whoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment. And whoever says to his brother, *Raca*, shall be in danger of the council. But whoever says, *You fool*, shall be in danger of hell fire." From these words Bellarmine infers three kinds of sin and three kinds of punishment. Only the last of these sins, he says, will be punished with hell fire, and so there must be punishment for lesser sins in Purgatory after this life. No interpretation yet given to these words offers any pretext for that inference. Will there be, after this life, a division among courts of justice like the one that existed among the Jews in our Savior's time, with the judges and the council each hearing and deciding different kinds of crimes? Will not all judgment belong to Christ and his apostles?

To understand this text, then, we must not consider it in isolation but together with the words that come before and after it. In this chapter our Savior is interpreting the Law of Moses. The Jews thought the Law was fulfilled so long as they had not broken its literal, grammatical sense, however much they had violated the intention or meaning of the lawgiver. They thought the Sixth Commandment was broken only by killing a man, and the Seventh only when a man lay with a woman who was not his wife. Our Savior tells them that a man's inward anger against his brother, if it lacks just cause, is homicide. "You have heard," he says, "the Law of Moses, *You shall not kill*, and *Whoever kills shall be condemned before the judges*," or before the session of the Seventy. "But I say to you that to be angry with one's brother without cause, or to say to him *Raca* or *Fool*, is homicide, and shall be punished with hell fire at the Day of Judgment, at the session of Christ and his apostles."

These words, then, were not meant to distinguish between different crimes, different courts of justice, and different punishments. They were meant to censure the distinction the Jews drew between one sin and another, which the Jews based not on the difference in the will to obey God but on the difference among their earthly courts of justice. And they were meant to show that whoever has the will to harm his brother, even if the effect appears only in insults or not at all, shall be cast into hell fire by the judges and by the session, which at the Day of Judgment will be one and the same court, not different ones. With this considered, I cannot imagine what can be drawn from this text to support Purgatory.

The sixth passage is Luke 16:9: "Make friends for yourselves by means of the unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings." Bellarmine cites this to prove the invocation of departed saints. But the sense is plain: we should use our riches to make friends of the poor, and thereby obtain their prayers while they are still alive. As the proverb says, "He who gives to the poor lends to the Lord."

The seventh is Luke 23:42, the plea of the penitent thief: "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom." Therefore, says Bellarmine, there is forgiveness of sins after this life. But the conclusion does not follow. Our Savior forgave him then and there, and at his coming again in glory he will remember to raise him to eternal life.

The eighth is Acts 2:24, where St. Peter says of Christ "that God had raised him up, having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it." Bellarmine interprets this as Christ's descent into Purgatory to release certain souls there from their torments. Yet it is evident that it was Christ who was loosed; it was he who could not be held by death or the grave, not the souls in Purgatory. And if what Beza says in his notes on this passage is carefully observed, everyone will see that in place of *pains* the word should be *bonds*, and then there is no further reason to look for Purgatory in this text.

## Chapter XLV. Of Demonology, and Other Relics of the Religion of the Gentiles

### The Origin of Demonology

When luminous bodies act on the organs of sight, whether along a single direct line or along many lines, reflected from opaque bodies or refracted as they pass through transparent ones, they produce an image of the object from which the impression comes. They do so in every living creature in which God has placed such organs, and this image is called sight. It seems to be not a mere image but the body itself, existing outside us. The same thing happens when a man presses hard on his eye: a light appears to him outside and in front of him that no one else perceives. There is in fact no such thing outside him, only a motion in the interior organs, pressing outward by resistance, that makes him think so. The motion produced by this pressure, continuing after the object that caused it has been removed, is what we call imagination and memory, and, in sleep or sometimes when the organs are badly disordered by sickness or violence, a dream. I have already spoken of these things briefly in the second and third chapters.

The ancient claimants to natural knowledge never discovered this nature of sight, and still less did those who give no thought to matters as remote from their immediate use as such knowledge is. Men therefore found it hard to conceive of the images in the fancy and in the senses as anything other than things really existing outside us. These images vanish, men know not where or how, and so some insist that they are absolutely incorporeal, that is, immaterial: forms without matter, color and shape without any colored or shaped body. These same people hold that the images can put on airy bodies like a garment, to make themselves visible to our bodily eyes whenever they choose. Others say they are bodies and living creatures, but made of air or of some other finer, more ethereal matter, which condenses when they wish to be seen. Both camps, however, agree on one general name for them: DAEMONS. It is as though the dead they dreamed of lived not in their own brains but in the air, or in heaven or hell, and were not phantasms but ghosts. There is exactly as much reason in this as if someone claimed to see his own ghost in a mirror, or the ghosts of the stars in a river, or called the ordinary appearance of the sun, which looks about a foot across, the daemon or ghost of that great sun which lights the whole visible world. In this way men came to fear these things as beings of unknown, and therefore unlimited, power to do them good or harm. This fear in turn gave the rulers of the heathen commonwealths the opportunity to regulate it by establishing a DAEMONOLOGY, in which the poets, as the principal priests of the heathen religion, were especially employed or revered. The rulers did this for the sake of public peace and of the obedience of subjects that peace requires. They made some daemons good and others evil, the first as a spur to keeping the laws, the second as reins to hold men back from breaking them.

### What the Daemons of the Ancients Were

The kinds of things to which the ancients gave the name of daemons appear partly in the genealogy of their gods written by Hesiod, one of the most ancient Greek poets, and partly in other histories, a few of which I noted earlier, in the twelfth chapter of this discourse.

### How That Doctrine Spread

Through their colonies and conquests, the Greeks carried their language and writings into Asia, Egypt, and Italy, and with them, by necessary consequence, their daemonology, which St. Paul calls their "doctrines of devils." By that means the contagion passed also to the Jews, both those of Judaea and those of Alexandria and the other places into which they had been dispersed. But the Jews did not, as the Greeks did, apply the name daemon to both good and evil spirits. They applied it to the evil ones only. To the good daemons they gave the name of the Spirit of God, and they regarded those whose bodies such spirits entered as prophets. In sum, they attributed every singularity to the Spirit of God if it was good, and if it was evil, to some daemon, but specifically a *kakodaimon*, an evil daemon, that is, a devil. Accordingly they called "demoniacs," meaning possessed by the devil, those whom we call madmen or lunatics, those who had the falling sickness, and anyone who said something that they, for want of understanding, thought absurd. In the same way they used to say of a notoriously unclean person that he had an unclean spirit, and of a mute man that he had a dumb devil. Of John the Baptist, as the eleventh chapter of Matthew records, they said he had a devil because of the singularity of his fasting. Of our Saviour, because he said that whoever keeps his sayings shall never see death, *in aeternum*, they said, according to the eighth chapter of John, "Now we know that you have a devil; Abraham is dead, and so are the prophets." And again, in the seventh chapter of John, when he said that they were seeking to kill him, the people answered, "You have a devil; who is seeking to kill you?" From all this it is plain that the Jews held the same opinions about phantasms as the Greeks did. They believed that phantasms were not phantasms at all, that is, not idols of the brain, but real things, independent of the fancy.

### Why Our Saviour Did Not Correct It

If this doctrine is not true, someone may ask, why did our Saviour not contradict it and teach the contrary? Indeed, why does he on various occasions use forms of speech that seem to confirm it? My first answer is that when Christ says, "A spirit does not have flesh and bones," he shows that spirits exist, but he does not deny that they are bodies. And when St. Paul says, "We shall rise spiritual bodies," he acknowledges the nature of spirits, but as bodily spirits, which is not hard to understand. Air and many other things are bodies, though they are not flesh and bone or any other gross body that the eye can make out.

The objector may press further. When our Saviour speaks to the devil and commands him to go out of a man, is his speech not improper, if by "the devil" is meant a disease, such as frenzy or lunacy, or else a corporeal spirit? Can diseases hear? And can there be a corporeal spirit inside a body of flesh and bone that is already full of vital and animal spirits? Must there not, then, be spirits that neither have bodies nor are mere imaginations?

To the first question I answer that directing our Saviour's command at the madness or lunacy he cures is no more improper than his rebuking a fever, or the wind and the sea, since these do not hear either. Nor is it more improper than God's command to the light, the firmament, the sun, and the stars when he commanded them to be, since they could not hear before they existed. Those speeches are not improper, because they signify the power of God's word. It is therefore no more improper to command madness or lunacy to depart out of a man's body, under the name of devils, by which such conditions were then commonly understood. To the second question, concerning their being incorporeal, I have not yet found any passage of Scripture from which it can be inferred that any man was ever possessed by any corporeal spirit other than his own, the spirit by which his body is naturally moved.

### The Scriptures Do Not Teach That Spirits Are Incorporeal

Immediately after the Holy Ghost descended on our Saviour in the form of a dove, St. Matthew says in his fourth chapter that he was "led up by the Spirit into the wilderness." St. Luke, also in his fourth chapter, recounts the same event in these words: "Jesus, being full of the Holy Ghost, was led in the Spirit into the wilderness." It is evident from this that "Spirit" there means the Holy Ghost. This cannot be interpreted as a possession, for Christ and the Holy Ghost are one and the same substance, and one substance or body cannot possess another that it already is. In the verses that follow, he is said "to have been taken up by the devil into the holy city and set upon a pinnacle of the temple." Are we to conclude from this that he was possessed by the devil, or carried there by force? Again, he was "carried from there by the devil into an exceedingly high mountain," from which the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world. We are not to believe that he was either possessed or forced by the devil here, nor that any mountain, taken in the literal sense, is high enough to show him an entire hemisphere. What, then, can this passage mean, except that he went into the wilderness of his own accord, and that this carrying of him up and down, from the wilderness to the city and from there to a mountain, was a vision? St. Luke's phrasing agrees with this reading. He says that Jesus was led into the wilderness not *by* the Spirit but *in* the Spirit, while about his being taken up to the mountain and onto the pinnacle of the temple he speaks as St. Matthew does. And this suits the nature of a vision.

Again, St. Luke says of Judas Iscariot that "Satan entered into him," and that he then went and conferred with the chief priests and captains about how he might betray Christ to them. It may be answered that the entering of Satan, that is, of the Enemy, into him means the hostile and treacherous intention of selling his Lord and Master. Scripture frequently uses "the Holy Ghost" to mean the graces and good inclinations the Holy Ghost bestows. In the same way, "the entering of Satan" may be understood as the wicked thoughts and designs of the adversaries of Christ and his disciples. It is hard to say that the devil had entered into Judas before he had any such hostile design, and it is beside the point to say that he first became Christ's enemy in his heart and that the devil entered into him afterward. The entering of Satan and his wicked purpose were therefore one and the same thing.

But if there is no immaterial spirit, and no possession of men's bodies by any corporeal spirit, it may again be asked why our Saviour and his apostles did not teach the people so, and in words clear enough that they could no longer doubt it. Questions like these, however, are more curious than necessary for a Christian's salvation. One might just as well ask why Christ, who could have given all men faith, piety, and every kind of moral virtue, gave them to some only and not to all. One might ask why he left the search into natural causes and the sciences to men's natural reason and industry, rather than revealing it supernaturally to everyone, or to anyone, and one might ask many other such questions. Probable and pious reasons may nevertheless be offered for all of them. When God brought the Israelites into the Promised Land, he did not secure them there by subduing all the nations around them. He left many of those nations as thorns in their sides, to rouse their piety and industry from time to time. In the same way, our Saviour, in leading us toward his heavenly kingdom, did not remove all the difficulties of natural questions but left them to exercise our industry and reason. The aim of his preaching was only to show us the plain and direct way to salvation, namely belief in this article: "that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God, sent into the world to sacrifice himself for our sins, and at his coming again to reign gloriously over his elect and save them from their enemies eternally." The opinion that men are possessed by spirits or phantasms is no obstacle on that way, though for some it becomes an occasion to stray from it and follow their own inventions. If we demand that Scripture account for every question that might be raised to trouble us as we carry out God's commands, we might as well complain that Moses did not record when such spirits were created, as he recorded the creation of the earth and the sea, of men and of beasts.

To conclude: I find in Scripture that there are angels and spirits, good and evil, but not that they are incorporeal, as the apparitions are that men see in the dark, or in a dream or vision, which the Latins called *spectra* and took for daemons. I find that there are corporeal spirits, though subtle and invisible, but not that any man's body was ever possessed or inhabited by them. And I find that the bodies of the saints shall be of this kind, spiritual bodies, as St. Paul calls them.

### The Power of Casting Out Devils Is Not What It Was in the Early Church

Nevertheless, the contrary doctrine, that there are incorporeal spirits, has prevailed in the Church so thoroughly that the practice of exorcism, the expulsion of devils by conjuration, has been built upon it. That practice, though now carried on rarely and half-heartedly, has not yet been entirely abandoned. In the early Church there were many demoniacs and few madmen or sufferers from other such singular diseases, whereas in our own time we hear of and see many madmen and few demoniacs. This difference comes from a change not in nature but in names. Formerly the apostles, and after them for a time the pastors of the Church, cured those singular diseases, which they are no longer seen to do. Likewise, it is no longer in the power of every true believer to do all that the faithful did then, as we read in the sixteenth chapter of Mark: "in Christ's name to cast out devils, to speak with new tongues, to take up serpents, to drink deadly poison without harm, and to cure the sick by the laying on of hands," and all this with no other words than "in the name of Jesus." How all this has come about is another question. It is probable that those extraordinary gifts were given to the Church only for as long as men trusted wholly in Christ and looked for their happiness only in his kingdom to come. It follows that when they sought authority and riches, and trusted in their own cunning to win a kingdom of this world, these supernatural gifts of God were taken from them again.

### Another Relic of Paganism, the Worship of Images, Was Left in the Church, Not Brought into It

Another relic of paganism is the worship of images. It was not instituted by Moses in the Old Testament, nor by Christ in the New, nor was it brought in from the Gentiles. It was left among them after they had given their names to Christ. Before our Saviour preached, the general religion of the Gentiles was to worship as gods those appearances that remain in the brain after external bodies have impressed themselves on the organs of sense. These appearances are commonly called ideas, idols, phantasms, or conceits, because they are representations of the external bodies that cause them, and they contain no more reality than the things that seem to stand before us in a dream. That is why St. Paul says, "We know that an idol is nothing." He did not think that an image of metal, stone, or wood was nothing. He meant that the thing men honored or feared in the image, and held to be a god, was a mere figment, with no place, dwelling, motion, or existence except in the motions of the brain. To worship these figments with divine honor is what Scripture calls idolatry and rebellion against God. God was king of the Jews, and his lieutenant was first Moses and afterward the high priest. Had the people been permitted to worship and pray to images, which are representations of their own fancies, they would no longer have depended on the true God, of whom there can be no likeness, nor on his chief ministers, Moses and the high priests. Every man would then have governed himself according to his own appetite, to the utter overthrow of the commonwealth and to the people's own destruction for want of union. Therefore the first law of God was that "they should not take for gods *alienos deos*, that is, the gods of other nations, but only that one true God who condescended to speak with Moses, and through him to give them laws and directions for their peace and for their salvation from their enemies." And the second was that "they should not make for themselves any image of their own invention to worship." To submit to another king is the same deposing of one's own king, whether that other king is set up by a neighboring nation or by ourselves.

### An Answer to Certain Texts That Seem to Support Images

The passages of Scripture claimed to sanction setting up images in order to worship them, or setting them up at all in places where God is worshipped, fall into three groups. The first consists of two examples: the cherubim over the Ark of God, and the brazen serpent. The second consists of certain texts in which we are commanded to worship particular creatures because of their relation to God, as when we are told to worship his footstool. The last consists of other texts that authorize a religious honoring of holy things. But before I examine whether these passages prove what is claimed for them, I must first explain what is meant by worshipping, and what by images and idols.

### What Worship Is

I have already shown, in the twentieth chapter of this discourse, that to honor is to value highly the power of a person, and that such value is measured by comparing him with others. But because nothing can be compared with God in power, we do not honor him, but dishonor him, by valuing him at anything less than infinite. Honor, then, is by its own nature properly secret and internal, held in the heart. But men's inward thoughts appear outwardly in their words and actions, and these outward appearances are the signs of our honoring. They go by the name of WORSHIP, in Latin *cultus*. To pray to, to swear by, to obey, to be diligent and dutiful in serving, and in short all words and actions that betoken fear of offending or desire to please, are therefore worship, whether those words and actions are sincere or feigned. And because they appear as signs of honoring, they are ordinarily also called honor.

### The Distinction Between Divine and Civil Worship

The worship we show to those we take to be only men, such as kings and men in authority, is civil worship. But the worship we show to whatever we think to be God is divine worship, whatever the words, ceremonies, gestures, or other actions may be. For a man who thinks a king is only a man, falling prostrate before him is merely civil worship. Yet the man who simply takes off his hat in church, because he thinks it the house of God, worships with divine worship. Those who look for the distinction between divine and civil worship in the words *douleia* and *latreia*, rather than in the intention of the worshipper, deceive themselves. There are two sorts of servants. The first sort are absolutely in their masters' power, such as slaves taken in war and their offspring. Their bodies are not their own, their lives depend on their masters' will so completely that they forfeit them at the slightest disobedience, and they are bought and sold like beasts. These were called *douloi*, properly slaves, and their service *douleia*. The second sort serve voluntarily, for wages or in hope of some benefit from their masters. These are called *thetes*, that is, domestic servants, and their masters have no further right to their service than is contained in the agreements made between them. These two kinds of servant have this much in common: their labor is assigned to them by another. The word *latris* is the general name for both, signifying one who works for another, whether as a slave or as a voluntary servant. *Latreia* therefore signifies service of every kind, while *douleia* signifies only the service of bondmen and the condition of slavery. Scripture uses both words indiscriminately to signify our service of God: *douleia* because we are God's slaves, *latreia* because we serve him. And every kind of service contains not only obedience but also worship, that is, actions, gestures, and words that signify honor.

### What an Image Is; Phantasms

An IMAGE, in the strictest sense of the word, is the resemblance of something visible. In this sense, only the fantastical forms, apparitions, or seemings of visible bodies to the sight are images. Examples include the appearance of a man or some other thing in water, by reflection or refraction, and the appearance of the sun or stars seen directly through the air. These appearances are nothing real, either in the things seen or in the place where they seem to be. Their sizes and shapes are not the same as those of the object, but change as the organs of sight vary or as the object is viewed through glasses. They are often present in our imagination and in our dreams when the object is absent, and they change into other colors and shapes, as things that depend wholly on the fancy. These are the images that are originally and most properly called ideas and IDOLS, words derived from the language of the Greeks, in which the word *eido* means "to see." They are also called PHANTASMS, which in the same language means apparitions. And it is from these images that one of the faculties of human nature is called the imagination. From this it is clear that there neither is nor can be any image made of an invisible thing.

It is also evident that there can be no image of an infinite thing. All the images and phantasms produced by the impression of visible things have shape, and shape is a quantity bounded on every side. There can therefore be no image of God, nor of the soul of man, nor of spirits, but only of visible bodies, that is, bodies that either have light in themselves or are lit by bodies that do.

### Fictions; Material Images

A man can imagine shapes he has never seen, composing a figure from the parts of different creatures, as the poets make their centaurs, chimeras, and other monsters that no one has ever seen. In the same way he can give those shapes matter and make them in wood, clay, or metal. These too are called images, not because they resemble any bodily thing, but because they resemble certain fantastical inhabitants of their maker's brain. The idol as it first exists in the brain and the idol as it is painted, carved, molded, or cast in matter resemble each other. Because of this likeness, the material body made by art may be called the image of the fantastical idol made by nature.

In a broader use of the word, however, an image also includes any representation of one thing by another. In this sense an earthly sovereign may be called the image of God, and a lesser magistrate the image of an earthly sovereign. Often in the idolatry of the Gentiles little attention was paid to whether the material idol resembled the idol in their fancy, and yet it was still called its image. An unhewn stone has been set up for Neptune, and various other shapes far different from the shapes in which they conceived their gods. And today we see many images of the Virgin Mary and other saints that are unlike one another and correspond to no single person's fancy. Yet they answer well enough the purpose for which they were erected, which was simply to represent by their names alone the persons mentioned in the history. To each of those persons every man attaches a mental image of his own making, or none at all. An image in the broadest sense, then, is either the resemblance or the representation of some visible thing, or, as most often happens, both together.

But in Scripture the name of idol is extended still further, to signify also the sun, or a star, or any other creature, visible or invisible, when it is worshipped as a god.

### What Idolatry Is

Having shown what worship is and what an image is, I will now put the two together and examine what that IDOLATRY is which is forbidden in the Second Commandment and in other places of Scripture.

To worship an image is voluntarily to perform the outward acts that signify honor toward one of three things. The first is the material of the image, whether wood, stone, or metal, or some other visible creature. The second is the phantasm, or mental picture in the brain, which the material was shaped and figured to resemble or represent. The third is both together, conceived as a single living body composed of matter and phantasm, as a body is joined to a soul.

To bare one's head before a man of power and authority, or before a prince's throne, or in any other place the prince appoints for that purpose in his absence, is to worship that man or prince with civil worship. It is a sign of honoring not the chair or the place but the person, and it is not idolatry. But if the one who did it supposed that the prince's soul resided in the chair, or presented a petition to the chair, that would be divine worship, and idolatry.

To pray to a king for things he is able to do for us, even if we prostrate ourselves before him, is only civil worship, because we acknowledge no power in him except human power. But to pray to him voluntarily for fair weather, or for anything that God alone can do for us, is divine worship, and idolatry. On the other hand, if a king compels a man to do so by the terror of death or some other severe bodily punishment, it is not idolatry. When a sovereign uses the terror of his laws to command worship of himself, the obedience of his subjects is no sign that they inwardly honor him as a god. It signifies only that they wish to save themselves from death or from a miserable life. What is not a sign of inward honor is not worship, and therefore not idolatry. Nor can it be said that a person who does this gives scandal, or lays a stumbling block before his brother. However wise or learned he may be, no one else can infer from his conduct that he approves of it. They can infer only that he acts out of fear, and that the act is not his but the sovereign's.

To worship God in some particular place, or while turning one's face toward an image or a fixed place, is not to worship or honor the place or the image. It is to acknowledge it as holy, which means acknowledging that the image or place has been set apart from common use. That is what the word "holy" means. It implies no new quality in the place or image, only a new relation: its appropriation to God. Such worship is therefore not idolatry. It was not idolatry to worship God before the bronze serpent, nor for the Jews, when they were outside their own country, to turn their faces toward the Temple in Jerusalem as they prayed. Nor was it idolatry for Moses to take off his shoes when he stood before the burning bush. That ground belonged to Mount Sinai, which God had chosen as the place where he would appear and give his laws to the people of Israel, and it was therefore holy ground. Its holiness came not from any inherent sanctity but from its being set aside for God's use. In the same way, it is not idolatry for Christians to worship in churches that have been solemnly dedicated to God for that purpose by the authority of the king or of some other true representative of the Church. But to worship God as if he animated or inhabited such an image or place, treating an infinite substance as though it were contained in a finite place, is idolatry. Such finite gods are only idols of the brain and have no reality, and Scripture commonly calls them Vanity, Lies, and Nothing. Another form of idolatry is to worship God through a place or image, not as though he animated it or were present in it, but in order to be reminded of him or of some of his works, when the place or image has been dedicated or set up by private authority rather than by the authority of our sovereign pastors. For the commandment says, "Thou shalt not make to thyself any graven image." God commanded Moses to set up the bronze serpent. Moses did not make it for himself, and so it was not against the commandment. But the making of the golden calf by Aaron and the people was idolatry because it was done without authority from God. It was idolatry not only because they took the calf for God but also because they made it for religious use without warrant either from God, their sovereign, or from Moses, who was his lieutenant.

The Gentiles worshipped Jupiter and others as gods, though these were perhaps only men who, while alive, had performed great and glorious deeds. They also worshipped various men and women as children of God, supposing them to have been begotten between an immortal deity and a mortal human. This was idolatry, because they made these gods for themselves, with no authority from God either in his eternal law of reason or in his positive and revealed will. Our Saviour, too, was a man, whom we also believe to be immortal God and the Son of God. Yet this is not idolatry, because we build that belief not on our own fancy or judgment but on the word of God revealed in the Scriptures. The adoration of the Eucharist must be judged by the same rule. Christ's words "This is my body" may mean that he himself, and the apparent bread in his hand, and every apparent morsel of bread that has since been or shall hereafter be consecrated by priests, are so many bodies of Christ and yet all one body. If they mean this, the adoration is not idolatry, because our Saviour authorized it. If the text does not mean this, then the adoration is a worship of human institution, and therefore idolatry, since no other text can be cited in its support. It is not enough to say that God can transubstantiate the bread into Christ's body. The Gentiles also held God to be omnipotent. On that ground they could just as well excuse their idolatry by claiming, as others do, that their wood and stone had been transubstantiated into God Almighty.

Some claim that divine inspiration is a supernatural entry of the Holy Ghost into a man, rather than an acquisition of God's grace through doctrine and study. These people, I think, are caught in a very dangerous dilemma. If they do not worship the men they believe to be so inspired, they fall into impiety, since they fail to adore God's supernatural presence. If they do worship them, they commit idolatry, for the apostles would never permit themselves to be worshipped in that way. The safest course, therefore, is to understand three things as signs: the descent of the dove upon the apostles, Christ's breathing on them when he gave them the Holy Ghost, and the conferring of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands. God has been pleased to use these signs, or has ordained them to be used, to mark his promise to assist those persons in their study to preach his kingdom, and in their conduct, so that their conduct might edify others rather than give scandal.

### Scandalous Worship of Images

Besides the idolatrous worship of images, there is also a scandalous worship of them, which is likewise a sin, though not idolatry. Idolatry is worship expressed through signs of inward and real honor, whereas scandalous worship is only apparent worship. It may sometimes coexist with a deep, heartfelt loathing of both the image and the imaginary demon, or idol, to which the image is dedicated, and it may proceed solely from fear of death or some other severe punishment. It is nonetheless a sin in those whose actions others watch as lights to guide them, because people who follow their example cannot help stumbling and falling on the path of religion. The example of people we do not regard, by contrast, has no effect on us at all. It leaves us to our own diligence and caution, and so such people are no cause of our falling.

Suppose, then, that a pastor lawfully called to teach and direct others, or anyone else whose knowledge is highly esteemed, pays outward honor to an idol out of fear. Unless he makes his fear and reluctance as evident as his worship, he scandalizes his brother by appearing to approve of idolatry. His brother reasons from the conduct of his teacher, or of someone whose knowledge he holds in high regard, and concludes that the practice is lawful in itself. This scandal is a sin, and it is a scandal given. But suppose someone who is neither a pastor nor eminent for knowledge of Christian doctrine does the same, and another person follows him. Then no scandal is given, for the follower had no reason to imitate such an example. The scandal he claims is a pretense, which he takes upon himself as an excuse before others. An unlearned man under the power of an idolatrous king or state, if commanded on pain of death to worship before an idol, does well if he detests the idol in his heart, though he would do better if he had the fortitude to suffer death rather than worship it. But a pastor, as Christ's messenger, has undertaken to teach Christ's doctrine to all nations. If he did the same, it would be not only a sinful scandal with respect to the consciences of other Christians but a treacherous desertion of his charge.

To sum up what I have said so far about the worship of images: a person commits idolatry if he worships in an image or in any creature either its material, or some fancy of his own that he thinks dwells in it, or both together. He also commits idolatry if he believes that such things hear his prayers or see his devotions, though they have no ears or eyes. A person who counterfeits such worship for fear of punishment commits a sin, if he is a man whose example carries weight among his brethren. But a person does not commit idolatry if he worships the Creator of the world before an image, or in a place, that he has not made or chosen for himself but has taken from the command of God's word. The Jews did this when they worshipped God before the cherubim, and for a time before the bronze serpent, and in or toward the Temple of Jerusalem, which was also only for a time.

As for the worship of saints, images, relics, and other things practiced at this day in the Church of Rome, I say that the word of God does not permit them, nor were they brought into the Church of Rome by the doctrine taught there. Rather, they were partly left in it at the first conversion of the Gentiles, and the bishops of Rome afterward tolerated, confirmed, and expanded them.

### Answer to the Argument from the Cherubim and the Bronze Serpent

The defenders of these practices cite proofs from Scripture, namely the images that God himself appointed to be set up. But these were not set up for the people or for anyone to worship. They were set up so that people might worship God himself before them, as before the cherubim over the Ark and before the bronze serpent. We do not read that the priest or anyone else worshipped the cherubim. On the contrary, we read in the Second Book of Kings that Hezekiah broke into pieces the bronze serpent Moses had set up, because the people burned incense to it. Moreover, these examples are not offered for our imitation, as if we too should set up images on the pretext of worshipping God before them. The words of the second commandment, "Thou shalt not make to thyself any graven image," distinguish between the images God commanded to be set up and those we set up for ourselves. The argument therefore does not hold when it moves from the cherubim or the bronze serpent to images of human devising, or from the worship God commanded to a worship of men's own choosing. Something further should also be considered. Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent into pieces because the Jews worshipped it, so that they would do so no more. Christian sovereigns ought likewise to break down the images their subjects have been accustomed to worship, so that there may be no further occasion for such idolatry. For at this day, the ignorant people in places where images are worshipped really do believe there is a divine power in the images. Their pastors tell them that some of the images have spoken, have bled, and have worked miracles. The people take these miracles to have been performed by the saint, whom they think either is the image itself or dwells within it. When the Israelites worshipped the calf, they thought they were worshipping the God who had brought them out of Egypt. Yet it was idolatry, because they thought the calf either was that God or had him in its belly. Some may think it impossible that people could be so stupid as to take an image for God or a saint, or to worship it on that understanding. But Scripture plainly shows the contrary. When the golden calf was made, the people said, "These be thy gods, O Israel," as recorded in the thirty-second chapter of Exodus; and in the thirty-first chapter of Genesis the images of Laban are called his gods. We see daily by experience, among every sort of people, that men who care for nothing but their food and comfort are content to believe any absurdity rather than trouble themselves to examine it. They hold their faith as if it were an entailed estate, the kind of inherited property that the law forbids its holder to sell or transfer, which can be released only by an express new law.

### The Painting of Fancies Is No Idolatry; Abusing Them to Religious Worship Is

Defenders of images also argue from certain other passages that it is lawful to paint angels, and even God himself. They point to God's walking in the garden, to Jacob's seeing God at the top of the ladder, and to other visions and dreams. But visions and dreams, whether natural or supernatural, are only phantasms. Whoever paints an image of any of them makes an image not of God but of his own phantasm, and that is the making of an idol. I do not say that drawing a picture from one's imagination is a sin. But once it is drawn, to hold it as a representation of God is against the second commandment, and it can serve no purpose except worship. The same may be said of images of angels and of the dead, unless they are kept as memorials of friends or of people worthy of remembrance. Such use of an image is not worship of the image but a civil honoring of the person, not as he is, but as he was. But sometimes we honor the image we make of a saint for no other reason than that we think he hears our prayers and is pleased with the honor we do him, though he is dead and without sense. In doing so we attribute to him more than human power, and that is idolatry.

Neither the law of Moses nor the Gospel gives any authority for the religious worship of images or other representations of God that men set up for themselves, or for the worship of the image of any creature in heaven, on earth, or under the earth. Moreover, Christian kings, who are living representatives of God, are not to be worshipped by their subjects through any act that signifies a greater estimation of their power than the nature of a mortal man can admit. It therefore cannot be supposed that the religious worship now in use was brought into the Church through a misunderstanding of Scripture. The only remaining explanation is that it was left there because the images themselves were not destroyed when the Gentiles who had worshipped them were converted.
