### How Idolatry Was Left in the Church

The cause of this was the excessive esteem in which the craftsmanship of these images was held, and the high prices set upon them. The owners had been converted from worshipping them religiously as demons, as they once had. Yet they still kept the images in their houses, on the pretext of doing so in honor of Christ, the Virgin Mary, the apostles, and the other pastors of the early Church. It was easy to give them new names. What had perhaps been called an image of Venus and Cupid could become an image of the Virgin Mary and her son our Saviour, a Jupiter could become a Barnabas, a Mercury a Paul, and so on. Worldly ambition crept by degrees into the pastors. It drew them to try to please the newly made Christians, and it also gave them a taste for this kind of honor, which they too might hope to receive after their deaths, just as those who had already gained it. In this way the worship of the images of Christ and his apostles grew more and more idolatrous. Some time after the reign of Constantine, various emperors, bishops, and general councils did notice its unlawfulness and opposed it, but too late, or too weakly.

### The Canonizing of Saints

The canonizing of saints is another relic of paganism. It is neither a misunderstanding of Scripture nor a new invention of the Roman Church, but a custom as ancient as the Roman commonwealth itself. The first person ever canonized at Rome was Romulus. Julius Proculus swore before the Senate that he had spoken with Romulus after his death, and that Romulus had assured him that he dwelt in heaven, was called Quirinus there, and would look with favor on the state of their new city. On the strength of this account the Senate gave public testimony of his sanctity. Julius Caesar and later emperors received the same testimony, which is to say they were canonized as saints. Canonization, as it is now defined, is the same thing as the apotheosis of the heathens.

### The Name of Pontifex

It is also from the Roman heathens that the popes received the title and power of Pontifex Maximus. In the ancient Roman commonwealth this was the title of the official who held supreme authority, under the Senate and people, to regulate all ceremonies and doctrines concerning their religion. When Augustus Caesar changed the state into a monarchy, he took for himself nothing more than this office and that of Tribune of the People, which together gave him supreme power in both state and religion, and the emperors who succeeded him held the same. Later the emperor Constantine became the first to profess and authorize the Christian religion, and it was consistent with his profession to have religion regulated, under his authority, by the bishop of Rome. It does not appear, however, that the bishops held the title of Pontifex so early. It seems rather that later bishops assumed it of their own accord, to lend credit to the power they exercised over the bishops of the Roman provinces. That authority over other bishops came not from any privilege of St. Peter but from the privilege of the city of Rome, which the emperors were always willing to uphold. This is evident from what happened when the emperor made Constantinople the seat of the empire: the bishop of Constantinople then claimed to be the equal of the bishop of Rome. In the end, though not without contention, the pope prevailed and became Pontifex Maximus. But he held that position only by right of the emperor. It did not extend beyond the boundaries of the empire, and it held nowhere at all once the emperor had lost his power in Rome, even though it was the pope himself who took that power from him. From this we may observe in passing that the pope's superiority over other bishops has no basis except in territories where he is himself the civil sovereign, or where the emperor, holding sovereign civil power, has expressly chosen the pope as the chief pastor of his Christian subjects under himself.

### The Procession of Images

Carrying images about in procession is another relic of the religion of the Greeks and Romans. They too carried their idols from place to place in a kind of chariot reserved specially for that purpose, which the Latins called the *thensa* or *vehiculum deorum*, "the vehicle of the gods." The image was set in a frame or shrine they called a *ferculum*, and what they called a *pompa* is the same thing now called a procession. Accordingly, among the divine honors the Senate granted to Julius Caesar was the right to have a *thensa* and a *ferculum*, a sacred chariot and a shrine, in the procession at the games of the Circus. This amounted to being carried about as a god, just as the popes today are carried under a canopy by their Swiss Guards.

### Wax Candles and Lighted Torches

Among both Greeks and Romans, these processions also included the carrying of burning torches and candles before the images of the gods. Later the Roman emperors received the same honor. We read that when Caligula acceded to the empire, he was carried from Misenum to Rome amid a throng of people, with the roads lined with altars, animals for sacrifice, and burning torches. We read also that Caracalla was received into Alexandria with incense, the scattering of flowers, and *dadouchiai*, that is, with torches. Among the Greeks, the *dadouchoi* were the torchbearers who carried lighted torches in the processions of their gods. In the course of time, devout but ignorant people often honored their bishops with the same pomp of wax candles, and they honored the images of our Saviour and the saints in this way continually within the church itself. That is how the use of wax candles came in, and some of the ancient councils also established it.

The heathens also had their *aqua lustralis*, that is, holy water. The Church of Rome imitates them in its holy days as well. They had their Bacchanalia, and we have our wakes, the parish festivals that correspond to them. They had their Saturnalia, and we have our carnivals and the license granted to servants on Shrove Tuesday. They had their procession of Priapus, and we have our fetching in, raising, and dancing around maypoles, and dancing is a kind of worship. They had the procession called the Ambarvalia, and we have our procession around the fields in Rogation Week. Nor do I think these are all the ceremonies left in the Church from the first conversion of the Gentiles; they are only all that I can recall at present. If anyone were to study carefully what the histories record of the religious rites of the Greeks and Romans, I have no doubt he would find many more of these old empty wineskins of paganism. Through negligence or ambition, the doctors of the Roman Church have filled them again with the new wine of Christianity, and in time that wine will not fail to burst them.

## Chapter XLVI. Of Darkness from Vain Philosophy, and Fabulous Traditions

### What Philosophy Is

By philosophy we mean "the knowledge acquired by reasoning from the way anything is generated to its properties, or from its properties to some possible way of generating it, so that we may produce, as far as matter and human strength permit, such effects as human life requires." The geometer, for example, reasons from the construction of figures to many of their properties, and from those properties to new ways of constructing them, so that he can measure land and water and serve countless other uses. The astronomer, observing the rising, setting, and movement of the sun and stars in different parts of the heavens, discovers the causes of day and night and of the changing seasons, and by these he keeps an account of time. The same holds for the other sciences.

### Prudence Is No Part of Philosophy

This definition makes it plain that we should not count as any part of philosophy that original knowledge called experience, in which prudence consists. Experience is not attained by reasoning. It is found in brute beasts as well as in human beings, and it is nothing more than a memory of how events have followed one another in the past. Because the omission of any small circumstance can alter the outcome, even the most prudent person's expectations are often frustrated. Correct reasoning, by contrast, produces nothing but general, eternal, and unchangeable truth.

### No False Doctrine Is Part of Philosophy

Nor should we give the name of philosophy to any false conclusion, for a person who reasons correctly with words he understands can never arrive at an error.

### Nor Is Supernatural Revelation

Nor does the name belong to anything a person knows by supernatural revelation, since that knowledge is not acquired by reasoning.

### Nor Learning Taken on the Authority of Authors

Nor does it belong to anything we arrive at by reasoning from the authority of books. Such reasoning does not proceed from cause to effect or from effect to cause, and what it yields is not knowledge but faith.

### The Beginnings and Progress of Philosophy

Since the faculty of reasoning follows from the use of speech, there must have been some general truths discovered by reasoning almost as early as language itself. The native peoples of America are not without some sound moral maxims, and they have a little arithmetic for adding and dividing numbers that are not too large; but that does not make them philosophers. Before people understood the value of grain and grapevines, those plants grew in small quantities, scattered through fields and woods. No one yet ate or drank from them, or cultivated them separately in fields and vineyards; people lived on acorns and drank water. In the same way, a number of true, general, and useful ideas have existed from the beginning, as the natural growth of human reason. At first, though, they were few. People lived on crude experience, and there was no method, which is to say no sowing or planting of knowledge in its own ground, separated from the weeds and common plants of error and conjecture. The cause was a lack of leisure, since people were occupied in securing the necessities of life and defending themselves against their neighbors, and until great commonwealths were established it could not have been otherwise. Leisure is the mother of philosophy, and the commonwealth is the mother of peace and leisure. Wherever great and flourishing cities first arose, there the study of philosophy first appeared. The Gymnosophists of India, the Magi of Persia, and the priests of Chaldea and Egypt are counted the most ancient philosophers, and those countries were the most ancient kingdoms. Philosophy had not yet arisen among the Greeks and the other peoples of the West. Their commonwealths, perhaps no larger than Lucca or Geneva, never enjoyed peace except when their fears of one another happened to be equal, and they had no leisure to observe anything but each other. Eventually, when war had merged many of the smaller Greek cities into fewer and larger ones, seven men from different parts of Greece began to acquire a reputation for wisdom. Some earned it through moral and political maxims, others through the learning of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, namely astronomy and geometry. But we hear nothing yet of any schools of philosophy.

### The Schools of Philosophy Among the Athenians

After the Athenians defeated the Persian armies, they won command of the sea, and with it control of all the islands and coastal cities of the Aegean, in Asia as well as in Europe. They grew wealthy, and those who had no occupation at home or abroad had little to do except, as St. Luke says in Acts 17:21, "telling and hearing news," or lecturing publicly on philosophy to the young men of the city. Each master chose a place for the purpose. Plato taught in certain public walks called the Academia, named after a man called Academus; Aristotle in the walk of the temple of Pan, called the Lyceum; others in the Stoa, the covered walkway where merchants' goods were brought ashore; and still others elsewhere. There they spent their leisure teaching and disputing their opinions, and some would talk anywhere they could gather the city's youth to listen. Carneades did the same at Rome when he came as an ambassador, which led Cato to advise the Senate to send him away quickly, for fear he would corrupt the morals of the young men who delighted in hearing him say what they took to be fine things.

This is why the place where any of these philosophers taught and disputed was called a *schola*, which in Greek means leisure, and why their disputations were called *diatribae*, meaning ways of passing the time. Some of the philosophical sects even took their names from these schools. Plato's followers were called Academics; Aristotle's were called Peripatetics, from the walk where he taught; and Zeno's were called Stoics, from the Stoa. It is as if we in London were to name groups of men after Moorfields, the open grounds outside the city walls where people stroll, or after St. Paul's Church, whose nave is a common place for gossip and business, or after the Exchange, where merchants gather, simply because they meet there often to chatter and idle away the time.

Nevertheless, people were so taken with this custom that in time it spread across all of Europe and the greater part of Africa, until almost every commonwealth had schools publicly established and maintained for lectures and disputations.

### The Schools of the Jews

There were also schools among the Jews in ancient times, both before and after the time of our Savior, but they were schools of their law. They were called synagogues, meaning congregations of the people. Yet because the law was read, explained, and debated in them every Sabbath, they differed from public schools in name only, not in nature. They existed not only in Jerusalem but in every Gentile city where Jews lived. There was such a school at Damascus, which Paul entered in order to persecute; others at Antioch, Iconium, and Thessalonica, which he entered in order to dispute. Such too was the synagogue of the Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians, and those from Asia, which is to say the school of freedmen and of Jews who were foreigners in Jerusalem. It was members of this school who disputed with St. Stephen.

### The School of the Greeks Was Unprofitable

But what has been the use of those schools? What science do we possess today that was acquired through their lectures and disputations? Geometry is the mother of all natural science, and what we have of it we do not owe to the schools. Plato, the best of the Greek philosophers, barred entry to his school to anyone who was not already something of a geometer. Many people studied geometry to the great benefit of mankind, yet there is no record of their having schools, there was never a sect of geometers, and in those days geometers were not called philosophers. The natural philosophy of the schools was more a dream than a science, expressed in senseless and meaningless language, and this cannot be avoided by anyone who tries to teach philosophy without first acquiring a thorough knowledge of geometry. Nature works by motion, and the ways and degrees of motion cannot be understood without knowing the proportions and properties of lines and figures. Their moral philosophy is nothing but a description of their own passions. Where there is no civil government, the rule of conduct is the law of nature; where there is, it is the civil law, which determines what is honest and dishonest, just and unjust, and in general what is good and evil. These philosophers, however, made the rules of good and bad according to their own likes and dislikes. Since tastes vary so widely, nothing is generally agreed upon, and everyone does, as far as he dares, whatever seems good in his own eyes, to the ruin of the commonwealth. Their logic, which ought to be the method of reasoning, is nothing but verbal traps and devices for confounding anyone who tries to question them. In short, there is nothing so absurd, as Cicero observed (and he was one of them), that some of the old philosophers have not maintained it. I believe scarcely anything more absurd can be said in natural philosophy than what is now called Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, nothing more hostile to government than much of what he says in his *Politics*, and nothing more ignorant than a great part of his *Ethics*.

### The Schools of the Jews Were Unprofitable

The school of the Jews was originally a school of the law of Moses. In Deuteronomy 31:10, Moses commanded that at the end of every seventh year, at the Feast of Tabernacles, the law should be read to all the people so that they might hear and learn it. The reading of the law every Sabbath, which became the practice after the Babylonian captivity, should therefore have had no other purpose than to acquaint the people with the commandments they were bound to obey and to explain the writings of the prophets to them. But it is clear from our Savior's many rebukes that they corrupted the text of the law with false commentaries and empty traditions, and that they understood the prophets so poorly that they recognized neither Christ nor the works he performed, though these were exactly what the prophets had foretold. Through the lectures and disputations in their synagogues, they turned the doctrine of their law into a fantastical kind of philosophy concerning the incomprehensible nature of God and of spirits. They compounded it from the empty philosophy and theology of the Greeks, mixed with their own fancies drawn from the more obscure passages of Scripture, those most easily twisted to their purpose, and from the fabulous traditions of their ancestors.

### What a University Is

What we now call a university is a union and incorporation, under a single government, of many public schools in the same town or city. Its principal schools were established for three professions: the Roman religion, Roman law, and the art of medicine. Philosophy has a place there only as a handmaid to the Roman religion. And since the authority of Aristotle is the only authority accepted there, that study is not properly philosophy, whose nature does not depend on authors, but "Aristotelity." Geometry, until very recently, had no place in the universities at all, since it serves nothing but rigorous truth. If anyone, through his own natural talent, attained any degree of mastery in it, he was commonly thought a magician and his art diabolical.

### Errors Brought into Religion from Aristotle's Metaphysics

Turning now to the particular tenets of empty philosophy that have passed into the universities and from there into the Church, partly from Aristotle and partly from sheer blindness of understanding, I shall first consider their principles. There is a certain *philosophia prima*, or first philosophy, on which all other philosophy ought to depend. It consists chiefly in correctly limiting the meanings of the most universal names and terms. These limitations prevent ambiguity and equivocation in reasoning, and they are commonly called definitions. Examples are the definitions of body, time, place, matter, form, essence, subject, substance, accident, power, act, finite, infinite, quantity, quality, motion, action, passion, and various others needed to explain one's conceptions of the nature and generation of bodies. The explanation of these and similar terms, meaning the settling of their sense, is commonly called metaphysics in the schools, because it forms part of the philosophy of Aristotle that bears that title. But the schools use the word in a different sense. In Aristotle the title means "books written, or placed, after his natural philosophy," whereas the schools take it to mean books of supernatural philosophy, since the word *metaphysics* can bear either meaning. And indeed, most of what is written there is so far beyond any possibility of being understood, and so contrary to natural reason, that anyone who thinks there is something to understand in it must suppose it to be supernatural.

### Errors Concerning Abstract Essences

From this metaphysics, mixed with Scripture to produce scholastic divinity, we are told that there exist in the world certain essences separate from bodies, which they call abstract essences and substantial forms. Interpreting this jargon requires somewhat more than ordinary attention at this point, and I ask the pardon of readers unused to this kind of discussion for addressing myself to those who are. The world, by which I mean not just the earth, whose admirers we call worldly men, but the universe, the whole mass of everything that exists, is corporeal, that is, body. It has the dimensions of magnitude, namely length, breadth, and depth. Every part of body is likewise body and has the same dimensions. Consequently every part of the universe is body, and whatever is not body is no part of the universe. And because the universe is everything, whatever is no part of it is nothing, and therefore nowhere. It does not follow that spirits are nothing, for they have dimensions and are therefore really bodies, even though in ordinary speech the name *body* is given only to things that can be seen or touched, things that have some degree of opacity. Spirits, however, people call incorporeal. This is a more honorable name, and so it may be applied with greater piety to God himself. In speaking of God we consider not which attribute best expresses his nature, which is incomprehensible, but which best expresses our desire to honor him.

To learn on what grounds they claim that abstract essences or substantial forms exist, we must consider what those words properly signify. Words exist to record our thoughts and conceptions for ourselves and to make them known to others. Some words are names of the things conceived, such as the names of all the kinds of bodies that act on the senses and leave an impression in the imagination. Others are names of the imaginations themselves, that is, of the ideas or mental images we have of everything we see or remember. Others again are names of names, or of different kinds of speech: *universal*, *plural*, *singular*, *negation*, *true*, *false*, *syllogism*, *question*, *promise*, and *covenant* are names of certain forms of speech. Still others serve to show that one name follows from another or conflicts with it. When someone says, "A man is a body," he means that the name *body* necessarily follows from the name *man*, since they are simply different names for the same thing, a man; and this consequence is signified by joining the two names with the word *is*. We use the verb *is*, the Latins use their verb *est*, and the Greeks their *esti* in all its inflected forms. Whether every other nation in the world has a word corresponding to it in its own language, I cannot say, but I am sure they have no need of one. Simply placing two names in order could signify that one follows from the other just as well as the words *is*, *be*, *are*, and the like, if custom made it so, for it is custom that gives words their force.

Suppose there were a language with no verb corresponding to *est*, *is*, or *be*. The people who used it would be not one bit less capable of inferring, concluding, and every other kind of reasoning than the Greeks and Latins were. But what would then become of the terms derived from that verb, *entity*, *essence*, *essential*, *essentially*, and the many others that depend on them, as they are most commonly used? These are therefore not names of things. They are signs by which we make known that we conceive one name or attribute to follow from another. When we say, "A man is a living body," we do not mean that the man is one thing, the living body another, and the *is*, or being, a third. We mean that the man and the living body are the same thing, because the consequence "If he is a man, he is a living body" is true, and that truth is signified by the word *is*. Accordingly, *to be a body*, *to walk*, *to be speaking*, *to live*, *to see*, and similar infinitives, as well as *corporeity*, *walking*, *speaking*, *life*, *sight*, and the like, which signify exactly the same, are names of nothing, as I have explained more fully elsewhere.

Someone may ask what purpose such subtlety serves in a work like this one, where I claim to offer nothing beyond what is necessary to the doctrine of government and obedience. The purpose is this: that people may no longer let themselves be deceived by those who, with this doctrine of separated essences built on the empty philosophy of Aristotle, would frighten them out of obeying the laws of their country with empty names, as farmers frighten birds from the grain with an empty doublet, a hat, and a crooked stick set up in the field. It is on this basis that they claim that when a man is dead and buried, his soul, which is to say his life, can walk about separated from his body and be seen at night among the graves. On the same basis they claim that the shape, color, and taste of a piece of bread exist in a place where, they say, there is no bread. On the same basis they claim that faith, wisdom, and other virtues are sometimes poured into a person and sometimes breathed into him from heaven, as if virtuous people and their virtues could exist apart, along with a great many other notions that serve to weaken subjects' dependence on the sovereign power of their country. For who will try to obey the laws if he expects obedience to be poured or breathed into him? Who will not obey a priest who can make God, rather than his sovereign, or even rather than God himself? And who, if he is afraid of ghosts, will not show great respect to those who can make the holy water that drives them away? This will suffice as an example of the errors brought into the Church from Aristotle's entities and essences. Aristotle may well have known them to be false philosophy, yet written them as something consistent with, and supportive of, the Greek religion, fearing the fate of Socrates.

Once they have fallen into this error of separated essences, they are necessarily entangled in the many other absurdities that follow from it. Since they insist that these forms are real, they are obliged to assign them some place. But they hold them to be incorporeal, without any dimension of quantity, and everyone knows that place is dimension and can be filled only by something corporeal. So they are driven to protect their credit with a distinction: these forms, they say, are not anywhere *circumscriptively* but *definitively*. These terms are mere words, meaningless in this context, and they pass current only in Latin so that their emptiness may stay hidden. For the circumscription of a thing is nothing other than the determining or defining of its place, so both terms of the distinction mean the same. In particular, concerning the essence of a man, which they say is his soul, they affirm that the whole of it is in his little finger, and the whole of it in every other part of his body, however small, and yet that there is no more soul in the whole body than in any one of those parts. Can anyone think God is served by such absurdities? Yet all this must be believed by anyone who would believe in the existence of an incorporeal soul separated from the body.

And when they come to explain how an incorporeal substance can be capable of pain and be tormented in the fire of hell or purgatory, they have no answer at all, except that it cannot be known how fire can burn souls.

Again, since motion is change of place, and incorporeal substances are incapable of place, they struggle to make it seem possible that a soul can travel from here, without the body, to heaven, hell, or purgatory, and that the ghosts of men (and, I might add, of the clothes they appear in) can walk at night in churches, churchyards, and other burial places. I do not know what they can say in reply, unless they claim that ghosts walk definitively and not circumscriptively, or spiritually and not temporally, for such remarkable distinctions apply equally well to any difficulty whatever.

### Nunc-stans

As for the meaning of eternity, they will not allow it to be an endless succession of time. If it were, they could not explain why God's will and his preordaining of future things should not come before his foreknowledge of them, as an efficient cause comes before its effect or an agent before its action, nor could they defend many of their other bold opinions about the incomprehensible nature of God. Instead they teach that eternity is the standing still of the present time, a *nunc-stans*, or "standing now," as the schools call it. Neither they nor anyone else understands this, any more than they would understand a *hic-stans*, a "standing here," offered as an account of infinite magnitude of place.

### One Body in Many Places, and Many Bodies in One Place at Once

When we divide a body in our thoughts, we do so by counting its parts, and in counting those parts we also count the parts of the place it filled. It follows that in making many parts we also make many places for those parts, so that no one can conceive of more parts, or fewer, than there are places to hold them. Yet they would have us believe that by the almighty power of God one body may be in many places at the same time, and many bodies may be in one place at the same time, as though it honored divine power to say that what is, is not, or that what has been, has not been. These are only a small part of the incongruities they are driven to by disputing philosophically, instead of admiring and adoring the divine and incomprehensible nature. The attributes we give to God cannot signify what he is. They ought to signify our desire to honor him with the best titles we can think of. Those who venture to reason about his nature from these attributes of honor lose their understanding in the very first attempt, and they fall from one difficulty into another, without end and without number. They resemble a man ignorant of the ceremonies of court who comes into the presence of a far greater person than he is used to addressing. He stumbles as he enters, and to save himself from falling he lets slip his cloak; to recover the cloak he drops his hat; and with one blunder after another he betrays his bewilderment and his rustic manners.

### Absurdities in Natural Philosophy, as Gravity the Cause of Heaviness

As for physics, which is the knowledge of the subordinate and secondary causes of natural events, they offer no causes at all, only empty words. Suppose you want to know why some kinds of bodies naturally sink down toward the earth while others naturally rise away from it. The Schools will tell you, on the authority of Aristotle, that the bodies that sink are heavy, and that this heaviness is what makes them descend. But if you ask what they mean by heaviness, they will define it as an endeavor to go toward the center of the earth. So the cause of things sinking downward is an endeavor to be below, which amounts to saying that bodies descend or ascend because they do. Or they will tell you that the center of the earth is the place of rest and preservation for heavy things, and that heavy things therefore strive to be there. This is as if stones and metals had desires, or could pick out the place they wanted to be, as a man does; or loved rest, as a man does not; or as if a piece of glass were less safe in the window than falling into the street.

### Quantity Put into Body Already Made

If we want to know why the same body seems larger at one time than at another, though nothing has been added to it, they say that when it seems smaller it is condensed, and when larger, rarefied. And what do condensed and rarefied mean? Condensed, they say, is when the very same matter contains less quantity than before, and rarefied is when it contains more. This is as if there could be matter without some determinate quantity, when quantity is nothing other than the determination of matter, that is, of body, by which we say that one body is greater or smaller than another by such and such an amount. Or it is as if a body were first made without any quantity at all, and more or less were afterward put into it, according to how dense the body was meant to be.

### The Pouring In of Souls

For the cause of the human soul, they say *Creatur infundendo* and *creando infunditur*: "It is created by being poured in," and "It is poured in by being created."

### The Ubiquity of Appearances

For the cause of sense, they offer a ubiquity of *species*, that is, of the "shows" or appearances of objects. When these appearances present themselves to the eye, they say, the result is sight; to the ear, hearing; to the palate, taste; to the nostril, smell; and to the rest of the body, touch.

### Will, the Cause of Willing

For the cause of the will to perform some particular action, which they call *volitio*, they assign the faculty, that is, the general capacity people have to will sometimes one thing and sometimes another, which they call *voluntas*. In this way they make the power the cause of the act, as if one were to name, as the cause of men's good or evil acts, their ability to perform them.

### Ignorance an Occult Cause

On many occasions they put forward their own ignorance, disguised in other words, as the cause of natural events. They say, for instance, that fortune is the cause of contingent things, meaning things whose cause they do not know. They attribute many effects to occult qualities, meaning qualities unknown to them, and therefore, as they suppose, unknown to anyone else. And they attribute others to sympathy, antipathy, antiperistasis, specific qualities, and similar terms, none of which signifies either the agent that produces the effect or the operation by which it is produced.

If metaphysics and physics of this sort are not vain philosophy, there never was any, and St. Paul had no need to warn us against it.

### One Makes the Things Incongruent, Another the Incongruity

Their moral and civil philosophy contains the same absurdities, or greater ones. If a man commits an act of injustice, that is, an act contrary to the law, they say that God is the prime cause of the law, and also the prime cause of that act and of all other acts, but no cause at all of the injustice, which is the act's failure to conform to the law. This is vain philosophy. One might as well say that one man draws both a straight line and a crooked one, and another man makes the incongruity between them. Such is the philosophy of everyone who settles on his conclusions before he knows his premises, who claims to comprehend what is incomprehensible, and who turns attributes of honor into attributes of nature. This particular distinction was devised to uphold the doctrine of free will, that is, of a human will not subject to the will of God.

### Private Appetite the Rule of Public Good

Aristotle and other pagan philosophers define good and evil by the appetites of men. That definition is adequate so long as we consider people each governed by his own law, for among people who have no law but their own appetites there can be no general rule of good and evil actions. In a commonwealth, however, this measure is false. There the measure is not the appetite of private individuals but the law, which is the will and appetite of the state. Yet this doctrine is still put into practice. People judge the goodness or wickedness of their own actions, of other people's actions, and of the actions of the commonwealth itself, by their own passions. No one calls anything good or evil except what appears so in his own eyes, with no regard at all for the public laws. The only exceptions are monks and friars, who are bound by vow to that simple obedience to their superior which every subject ought to consider himself bound, by the law of nature, to render to the civil sovereign. This private measure of good is a doctrine not only vain but harmful to the public state.

### And That Lawful Marriage Is Unchastity

It is also vain and false philosophy to say that the act of marriage is contrary to chastity or continence, and so to make it a moral vice. Those who cite chastity and continence as grounds for denying marriage to the clergy do exactly this. They admit that the rule is nothing more than an ordinance of the Church, requiring those in holy orders who continually attend the altar and administer the Eucharist to abstain from women continually, under the name of perpetual chastity, continence, and purity. They therefore call the lawful relations of husbands with their wives a want of chastity and continence, and so make marriage a sin, or at least something so impure and unclean as to render a man unfit for the altar. If the law was made because relations with a wife are incontinent and contrary to chastity, then all marriage is a vice. If it was made because such relations are too impure and unclean for a man consecrated to God, then the other natural, necessary, daily functions that everyone performs should all the more render men unworthy to be priests, since they are more unclean.

The hidden foundation of this prohibition on priestly marriage, however, is unlikely to have been laid so lightly as on errors of moral philosophy like these. Nor was it laid on the preference for single life over matrimony. That preference came from the wisdom of St. Paul, who saw how burdensome it was for those who preached the Gospel in those times of persecution, and who were forced to flee from one country to another, to be weighed down with the care of a wife and children. The real foundation was the design of the popes and priests of later times to make themselves the clergy, that is, the sole heirs of the kingdom of God in this world. For that purpose it was necessary to deny themselves marriage, because our Savior says that at the coming of his kingdom the children of God shall "neither marry, nor be given in marriage, but shall be as the angels in heaven," that is, spiritual. Since they had taken on themselves the name of spiritual, it would have been an incongruity to allow themselves the possession of wives when there was no need for it.

### And That All Government but Popular Is Tyranny

From Aristotle's civil philosophy they have learned to call every kind of commonwealth except the popular kind, such as the state of Athens was in his time, a tyranny. The Athenians called all kings tyrants, and they called the aristocracy of thirty governors, installed by the Spartans who conquered them, the Thirty Tyrants. Likewise they called the condition of the people under democracy liberty. Originally, "tyrant" meant simply a monarch and nothing more. But when that form of government was later abolished in most parts of Greece, the word came to signify not only what it had meant before but also the hatred that the popular states bore toward it. In the same way the name of king became hateful in Rome after the kings were deposed. It is natural for everyone to imagine some great fault signified by any title given in spite, and to a great enemy. And when these same people are displeased with those who administer a democracy or an aristocracy, they are never at a loss for insulting names to express their anger, but readily call the one anarchy and the other oligarchy, or the tyranny of a few. What offends the people is nothing other than this: they are governed not as each of them individually would like, but as the public representative, whether one man or an assembly of men, thinks fit, that is, by an arbitrary government. For this they give evil names to their superiors, never realizing, until perhaps shortly after a civil war, that without such arbitrary government war of that kind would be perpetual, and that it is men and arms, not words and promises, that give the laws their force and power.

### That Not Men, but Law, Governs

It is therefore another error of Aristotle's *Politics* to hold that in a well-ordered commonwealth not men but the laws should govern. What man in possession of his natural senses, even one who can neither read nor write, does not find himself governed by those he fears and believes can kill or harm him if he disobeys? Who believes that the law can harm him, that is, words and paper, without the hands and swords of men? This belongs among the harmful errors, because such doctrines lead people, whenever they dislike their governors, to side with those who call those governors tyrants, and to think it lawful to make war against them. And yet these errors are often nourished from the pulpit by the clergy.

### Laws over the Conscience

There is another error in their civil philosophy, one they never learned from Aristotle, or Cicero, or any other of the pagans. It is the extension of the law's power, which is properly a rule of actions only, to people's very thoughts and consciences, through examination and inquisition into what they believe, even when their speech and actions conform. As a result, people are either punished for answering truthfully about their thoughts, or compelled to answer falsely for fear of punishment. It is true that a civil magistrate who intends to employ a minister in the office of teaching may ask him whether he is willing to preach such and such doctrines, and may refuse him the post if he declines. But to force a man to accuse himself of opinions when his actions are not forbidden by law is against the law of nature. It is especially so on the part of those who teach that a man will be damned to eternal and extreme torment if he dies holding a false opinion about an article of the Christian faith. Knowing that an error carries so great a danger, who would not be driven by natural concern for himself to stake his soul on his own judgment rather than on that of another man who has no stake in his damnation?

### Private Interpretation of Law

For a private person to interpret the law by his own spirit, without the authority of the commonwealth, that is, without permission from its representative, is another error in their politics, though this one is not drawn from Aristotle or any other pagan philosopher. None of those philosophers denies that the power of making laws also includes the power of explaining them when necessary. And are not the Scriptures, wherever they are law, made law by the authority of the commonwealth, and therefore part of the civil law?

Of the same kind is the error committed when anyone other than the sovereign restrains in any person a power that the commonwealth has not restrained. This is what they do who reserve the preaching of the Gospel to one particular order of men in places where the laws have left it free. If the state gives me leave to preach or teach, that is, if it does not forbid me, no one can forbid me. If I find myself among the idolaters of America, should I, a Christian though not ordained, consider it a sin to preach Jesus Christ until I have received orders from Rome? And once I have preached, should I not answer their doubts and expound the Scriptures to them, that is, should I not teach? Someone may reply that in such a case, as also for administering the sacraments to them, necessity will be counted as a sufficient commission. That is true. But it is also true that whatever would require a dispensation in case of necessity requires no dispensation at all when no law forbids it. To deny these functions to those whom the civil sovereign has not denied them is therefore to take away a lawful liberty, which is contrary to the doctrine of civil government.

### The Language of the School Divines

More examples of vain philosophy brought into religion by the doctors of scholastic divinity could be produced, but others may observe them for themselves if they wish. I will add only this: the writings of the school divines are, for the most part, nothing but meaningless strings of strange and barbarous words, or of words used otherwise than in the common usage of the Latin tongue, such as would have baffled Cicero, Varro, and all the grammarians of ancient Rome. Anyone who wants to see this proved should, as I have said before, try to translate any school divine into one of the modern languages, such as French or English or any other rich language. Whatever cannot be made intelligible in most of these languages is not intelligible in Latin either. Although I cannot classify this meaningless language as false philosophy, it has the property not only of hiding the truth but of making people believe they already possess it, so that they give up any further search.

### Errors from Tradition

Finally, there are the errors introduced from false or uncertain history. What are the legends of fictitious miracles in the lives of the saints, and all the stories of apparitions and ghosts cited by the doctors of the Roman Church to support their doctrines of hell and purgatory, the power of exorcism, and other doctrines that have no warrant in either reason or Scripture, together with all the traditions they call the unwritten word of God, but old wives' tales? Some of these may be found scattered through the writings of the ancient Church Fathers. But the Fathers were men who could too easily believe false reports. Those who follow the counsel of St. John, in the fourth chapter of his first epistle, to test the spirits will find that citing the Fathers' opinions as evidence for what they believed has one effect only, in all matters touching the power of the Roman Church, whose abuse the Fathers either did not suspect or profited from: it discredits their testimony, on account of their overly ready belief in reports. The most sincere people, when they lack a broad knowledge of natural causes, as the Fathers did, are commonly the most prone to such belief, for the best people are naturally the least suspicious of fraudulent designs. Pope Gregory and St. Bernard tell certain stories of ghosts who appeared and said they were in purgatory, and so does our own Bede, but nowhere, I believe, except on the report of others. If they, or anyone else, relate such stories from their own knowledge, they do nothing to strengthen these vain reports. They only expose their own weakness, or their own fraud.

### The Suppression of Reason

Alongside the introduction of false philosophy we may also place the suppression of true philosophy by men who are competent judges of the truth neither by lawful authority nor by sufficient study. Our own voyages have made it plain, and all who are learned in the human sciences now acknowledge, that there are Antipodes, people living on the opposite side of the globe. And it becomes clearer every day that years and days are determined by the motions of the earth. Nevertheless, men who in their writings have merely supposed such a doctrine, as an occasion to set out the reasons for and against it, have been punished for it by ecclesiastical authority. But on what grounds? Is it because such opinions are contrary to true religion? That cannot be, if they are true. Let the truth, then, first be examined by competent judges, or refuted by those who claim to know the contrary. Is it because they are contrary to the established religion? Then let them be silenced by the laws of those to whom their teachers are subject, that is, by the civil laws, for disobedience may lawfully be punished in those who, against the laws, teach even true philosophy. Is it because they tend to disorder in government, by encouraging rebellion or sedition? Then let them be silenced, and their teachers punished, by the power of the one entrusted with the care of public peace, which is the civil authority. For whatever power churchmen assume in their own right, in any place where they are subject to the state, is nothing but usurpation, even if they call it God's right.

## Chapter XLVII. Of the Benefit That Proceeds from Such Darkness, and to Whom It Accrues

### He Who Receives Benefit from a Deed Is Presumed to Be Its Author

Cicero speaks with honor of a member of the Cassius family, a severe judge among the Romans, for a practice he followed in criminal cases. When the testimony of the witnesses was insufficient, he would ask the accusers *Cui bono?*, that is, what profit, honor, or other satisfaction the accused had gained or expected from the deed. Among all presumptions, none points to the author of an act so clearly as the benefit of the act. By the same rule I intend here to examine who it may be that has so long possessed the people in this part of Christendom with these doctrines, which are contrary to the peaceable societies of mankind.

### That the Church Militant Is the Kingdom of God Was First Taught by the Church of Rome

First, consider the error that the present Church, now militant on earth, is the kingdom of God, meaning the kingdom of glory, or the Promised Land, and not the kingdom of grace, which is only a promise of that land. Certain worldly benefits are attached to this error. The first is that it entitles the pastors and teachers of the Church, as God's public ministers, to a right of governing the Church, and consequently, since the Church and the commonwealth are the same persons, to be the rulers and governors of the commonwealth. It was by this title that the pope persuaded the subjects of all Christian princes to believe that to disobey him was to disobey Christ himself, and, in every dispute between him and other princes, to abandon their lawful sovereigns, spellbound by the words "spiritual power." This amounts in effect to a universal monarchy over all Christendom. The popes were first invested with the right to be supreme teachers of Christian doctrine by and under the Christian emperors, within the bounds of the Roman Empire, as they themselves acknowledge, under the title of *Pontifex Maximus*, an officer subject to the civil state. But after the empire was divided and dissolved, it was not hard to impose another title on peoples already subject to them, namely the right of St. Peter. This served not only to keep their claimed power intact but to extend it over the same Christian provinces, even though those provinces were no longer united in the Roman Empire. Considering how much people desire to rule, this benefit of a universal monarchy is a sufficient presumption that the popes who claimed it, and long enjoyed it, were the authors of the doctrine by which it was obtained, namely that the Church now on earth is the kingdom of Christ. For once that is granted, it must be understood that Christ has some lieutenant among us, through whom we are to be told what his commandments are.

After certain churches had renounced this universal power of the pope, one would reasonably expect the civil sovereigns in all those churches to have recovered as much of it as had been their own right, and in their own hands, before they carelessly let it go. In England this happened in effect, except that those through whom the kings administered the government of religion, by maintaining that they held their office by God's right, seemed to usurp, if not a supremacy, then at least an independence from the civil power. Yet they only seemed to usurp it, since they acknowledged the king's right to deprive them of the exercise of their functions whenever he pleased.

### And Maintained Also by the Presbytery

But in those places where the Presbyterians took over that office, although many other doctrines of the Church of Rome were forbidden to be taught, this one was still retained: that the kingdom of Christ has already come, and that it began at the resurrection of our Savior. But *cui bono*? Who benefits, and what profit did they expect from it? They expected the same profit the popes expected: sovereign power over the people. For what does it mean for men to excommunicate their lawful king, except to bar him from every place of public worship in his own kingdom, and to resist him by force when he tries to correct them by force? And what does it mean to excommunicate anyone without authority from the civil sovereign, except to take away his lawful liberty and so usurp an unlawful power over their brethren? The authors of this darkness in religion, therefore, are the Roman and the Presbyterian clergy.

**Infallibility**

Under this same heading I also place all the doctrines that help them keep possession of this spiritual sovereignty once they have acquired it. The first is that the pope, acting in his public capacity, cannot err. For who, believing this to be true, would not readily obey him in whatever he commands?

**The Subjection of Bishops**

The second is the doctrine that all other bishops, in whatever commonwealth they reside, derive their right neither directly from God nor indirectly from their civil sovereigns, but from the pope. Because of this doctrine, every Christian commonwealth comes to contain many powerful men, for bishops are powerful, who depend on the pope and owe him obedience, even though he is a foreign prince. Through them he is able, as he has done many times, to stir up civil war against any state that will not submit to being governed according to his pleasure and interest.

**The Exemptions of the Clergy**

The third is the exemption of these bishops, and of all other priests, monks, and friars, from the power of the civil laws. By this means a large part of every commonwealth enjoys the benefit of the laws and the protection of the civil state while paying no share of the public expense. Nor are these people liable, as other subjects are, to the penalties their crimes deserve. Consequently they fear no one but the pope, and they cling to him alone, to uphold his universal monarchy.

**The Names "Sacerdotes" and "Sacrifices"**

The fourth is the practice of calling their priests *sacerdotes*, meaning sacrificers, when in the New Testament they are nothing more than *presbyters*, meaning elders. Among the Jews, while God was their king, *sacrificer* was the title of the civil sovereign and his public ministers. Likewise, turning the Lord's Supper into a sacrifice serves to make the people believe that the pope holds the same power over all Christians that Moses and Aaron held over the Jews: all power, both civil and ecclesiastical, such as the high priest possessed in that era.

**The Making of Marriage a Sacrament**

Fifth, the teaching that matrimony is a sacrament gives the clergy the right to judge which marriages are lawful. From that follows the right to judge which children are legitimate, and from that, in turn, who has the right of succession to hereditary kingdoms.

**The Celibacy of Priests**

Sixth, denying priests the right to marry serves to secure the pope's power over kings. For if a king is a priest, he cannot marry and pass his kingdom on to his descendants; and if he is not a priest, then the pope claims ecclesiastical authority over him and over his people.

**Auricular Confession**

Seventh, auricular confession, the private confession spoken into the priest's ear, secures their power by giving them better intelligence of the plans of princes and great men in the civil state than those men can obtain of the plans of the ecclesiastical state.

**The Canonization of Saints and the Declaring of Martyrs**

Eighth, they secure their power by canonizing saints and declaring who are martyrs. In this way they induce simple people to resist the laws and commands of their civil sovereigns stubbornly, even to the point of death, whenever the pope's excommunication has declared those sovereigns heretics or enemies of the Church, which, as they interpret it, means enemies of the pope.

**Transubstantiation, Penance, and Absolution**

Ninth, they secure it further by the power they attribute to every priest of making Christ, that is, of turning the bread and wine of the sacrament into his body and blood. They secure it as well by the power of imposing penance, and of forgiving sins or withholding forgiveness.

**Purgatory, Indulgences, and External Works**

Tenth, the clergy enrich themselves through the doctrines of purgatory, of justification by external works, and of indulgences.

**Demonology and Exorcism**

Eleventh, through their demonology, their use of exorcism, and the other practices that go with them, they keep the people in greater awe of their power, or believe they do.

**Scholastic Divinity**

Lastly, the metaphysics, ethics, and politics of Aristotle, together with the frivolous distinctions, barbarous terms, and obscure language of the Schoolmen, are taught in the universities, all of which were founded and regulated by the pope's authority. This teaching helps the clergy keep these errors from being detected. It also leads people to mistake the *ignis fatuus* of vain philosophy, the will-o'-the-wisp or false marsh-light that leads travelers astray, for the true light of the Gospel.

**Who the Authors of Spiritual Darkness Are**

If these were not enough, one could add other dark doctrines of theirs. The benefit of each plainly goes toward establishing an unlawful power over the lawful sovereigns of Christian peoples, or toward sustaining that power once established, or toward the worldly riches, honor, and authority of those who sustain it. Applying the rule already stated, *cui bono*, we may therefore justly name the authors of all this spiritual darkness. They are the pope and the Roman clergy, along with everyone else who strives to fix in people's minds the erroneous doctrine that the Church now on earth is the kingdom of God spoken of in the Old and New Testaments.

Yet the emperors and other Christian sovereigns may nonetheless be counted accessories to their own injury and to the public's. Under their rule these errors, and similar encroachments of churchmen upon their office, first crept in, disturbing the sovereigns' own possessions and their subjects' peace. They tolerated these things for lack of foresight into what would follow and of insight into the designs of their teachers. But without their authority, no seditious doctrine could have been publicly preached in the first place. I say they could have stopped it at the outset. Once the people were in the grip of those spiritual men, however, there was no human remedy that anyone could devise. As for the remedies God might provide, we must wait upon his good pleasure, for he never fails in his own good time to destroy all the schemes of men against the truth. He often allows the prosperity of his enemies, together with their ambition, to rise so high that its very violence opens the eyes their predecessors had cautiously sealed shut. Their grasping at too much then makes them let go of everything, just as Peter's net broke under the struggling of too great a multitude of fish. By contrast, those who impatiently tried to resist such encroachment before their subjects' eyes were opened only increased the power they resisted. I therefore do not blame the Emperor Frederick for holding the stirrup for our countryman Pope Adrian, steadying the pope's horse as a groom would for his master. Such was the disposition of his subjects at the time that, had he refused, he would probably not have succeeded to the Empire. But I do blame those rulers who, in the beginning, when their power was still whole, allowed such doctrines to be forged in the universities of their own dominions. In doing so they held the stirrup for all the popes who came after, while those popes mounted the thrones of every Christian sovereign, to ride and exhaust both the sovereigns and their people as they pleased.

But as the inventions of men are woven, so too are they unraveled. The method is the same, but the order is reversed. The web begins with the first elements of power, which are wisdom, humility, sincerity, and the other virtues of the apostles. The people they converted obeyed them out of reverence, not obligation. Their consciences were free, and their words and actions were subject to no one but the civil power. Later, as the flocks of Christ grew, the presbyters began to assemble to consider what they should teach. By binding themselves to teach nothing contrary to the decrees of their assemblies, they made it appear that the people were bound to follow their doctrine as well. When people refused, the presbyters refused to keep company with them, which was then called excommunication. They shunned them not as unbelievers but as the disobedient, and this was the first knot tied upon their liberty. Then, as the number of presbyters grew, the presbyters of the chief city or province acquired authority over the parish presbyters and claimed for themselves the title of bishops. This was a second knot on Christian liberty. Finally, the Bishop of Rome, on account of the imperial city, took upon himself an authority over all the other bishops of the Empire. He gained it partly by the will of the emperors themselves and by the title of *Pontifex Maximus*, the chief priesthood of pagan Rome that the emperors had held. At last, when the emperors had grown weak, he claimed it by the privileges of Saint Peter. This was the third and last knot, which completed the whole synthesis and construction of papal power.

The analysis, or undoing, therefore follows the same path, but it begins with the knot that was tied last. We can see this in the dissolution of the church government in England that had stood outside and beyond the civil order.

First, Queen Elizabeth completely dissolved the power of the popes. The bishops, who had previously exercised their functions by the pope's right, thereafter exercised them by right of the queen and her successors. Because they kept the phrase *jure divino*, "by divine right," they were thought to claim their authority directly from God, but the first knot was untied all the same. After this, the Presbyterians in England recently secured the abolition of episcopacy, and so the second knot was dissolved. At almost the same time, power was taken from the Presbyterians as well. We are thus brought back to the independence of the primitive Christians, each free to follow Paul, or Cephas, or Apollos, as he likes best. This is perhaps the best arrangement, provided it involves no contention, and provided we do not measure the doctrine of Christ by our affection for the person of his minister, the fault the Apostle rebuked in the Corinthians. It is best for two reasons. The first is that there ought to be no power over the consciences of men except that of the Word itself. The Word works faith in each person, not always according to the purpose of those who plant and water, but according to the purpose of God himself, who gives the increase. The second is that some teachers hold that there is great danger in every small error. It is unreasonable for them to require a man endowed with reason of his own to follow the reason of some other man, or the majority vote of many other men, which is little better than staking his salvation on the toss of a coin. Nor should those teachers resent this loss of their ancient authority. No one should know better than they that power is preserved by the same virtues through which it was acquired: wisdom, humility, clarity of doctrine, and sincerity of conduct. It is not preserved by suppressing the natural sciences and the morality of natural reason. Nor is it preserved by obscure language, or by claiming more knowledge than they can demonstrate, or by pious frauds. It is not preserved by any of the other faults that in the pastors of God's Church are more than faults. They are scandals, stumbling blocks likely to lead people sooner or later to overthrow their authority.

**Comparison of the Papacy with the Kingdom of Fairies**

Then the world accepted the doctrine "that the Church now Militant is the kingdom of God spoken of in the Old and New Testaments," the Church Militant being the Church on earth as distinguished from the Church triumphant in heaven. After that, the ambition and campaigning for the offices belonging to this kingdom became evident by degrees. The scramble was fiercest for the great office of Christ's lieutenant, and the pomp of those who won its principal public positions was plain to see. In the end it all became so evident that the clergy lost the inward reverence owed to the pastoral function. The wisest of the men who held any power in the civil state needed nothing more than the authority of their princes to refuse the clergy any further obedience. For from the time the Bishop of Rome succeeded in being acknowledged as universal bishop, on the pretext of succession to Saint Peter, their whole hierarchy, or kingdom of darkness, may fairly be compared to the kingdom of fairies. By this I mean the old wives' tales in England about ghosts and spirits and the tricks they play at night. And anyone who considers the origin of this great ecclesiastical dominion will readily see that the papacy is nothing other than the ghost of the deceased Roman Empire, sitting crowned upon its grave. For in just this way the papacy sprang up suddenly out of the ruins of that heathen power.

Their language, too, both in their churches and in their public acts, is Latin, which no nation in the world now commonly speaks. What is it but the ghost of the old Roman language?

The fairies, in whatever nation they dwell, have only one universal king. Some of our poets call him King Oberon, but Scripture calls him Beelzebub, prince of demons. The churchmen likewise, in whatever dominions they are found, acknowledge only one universal king: the pope.

The churchmen are spiritual men and "ghostly fathers," the old name for confessors. The fairies are spirits and ghosts. Fairies and ghosts inhabit darkness, solitary places, and graves. The churchmen walk in obscurity of doctrine, in monasteries, churches, and churchyards.

The churchmen have their cathedral churches. In whatever town one is built, it has the power, by virtue of holy water and certain charms called exorcisms, to make that town a city, that is, a seat of empire. The fairies, too, have their enchanted castles, and certain gigantic ghosts that lord it over the regions around them.

The fairies cannot be seized and brought to answer for the harm they do. So too the churchmen vanish from the tribunals of civil justice.

The churchmen take from young men the use of reason by certain charms compounded of metaphysics, miracles, traditions, and misused Scripture. Afterward these young men are good for nothing except carrying out what they are commanded. The fairies likewise are said to take young children from their cradles and change them into natural fools. The common people call such children elves, and they are prone to mischief.

The old wives have never settled in what shop or workroom the fairies make their enchantments. But the workshops of the clergy are well enough known. They are the universities, which received their discipline from papal authority.

When the fairies are displeased with someone, they are said to send their elves to pinch him. The churchmen, when displeased with any civil state, likewise make their elves pinch their princes. These elves are superstitious, enchanted subjects, and they do their pinching by preaching sedition. Sometimes, instead, the churchmen enchant one prince with promises and make him pinch another.

The fairies do not marry, but among them are incubi, who have intercourse with flesh and blood. The priests also do not marry.

The churchmen take the cream of the land through tithes and through the donations of ignorant men who stand in awe of them. So too in the fable of the fairies, who enter the dairies and feast on the cream they skim from the milk.

The story does not record what kind of money is current in the kingdom of the fairies. But the churchmen accept the same money we do when they receive payment. When they have to make a payment of their own, however, they pay in canonizations, indulgences, and Masses.

To these and similar resemblances between the papacy and the kingdom of fairies, one more may be added. The fairies have no existence except in the imaginations of ignorant people, which arise from the traditions of old wives or old poets. In the same way, the spiritual power of the pope beyond the bounds of his own civil dominion consists only in the fear of his excommunication. That fear grips people who have been led astray by false miracles, false traditions, and false interpretations of Scripture.

It was therefore not very difficult for Henry VIII, by his exorcism, or for Queen Elizabeth, by hers, to cast them out. But this spirit of Rome has now gone out, and it walks by missions through the dry places of China, Japan, and the Indies, which yield it little fruit. Who knows whether it may not return? Or rather, as in the Gospel parable of the unclean spirit, who knows whether an assembly of spirits worse than it may not enter and inhabit this clean-swept house, and make its end worse than its beginning? For the Roman clergy are not the only ones who claim that the kingdom of God is of this world, and who therefore claim a power within it distinct from that of the civil state. And this is all I intended to say concerning the doctrine of politics. When I have reviewed it, I shall willingly submit it to the judgment of my country.

## A Review, and Conclusion

Some have argued that no single person can be adequately fitted for every kind of civic duty. They draw this conclusion from the way certain natural faculties of the mind pull against one another, as certain passions also do, and from how each of these bears on our dealings with other people. Severity of judgment, they say, makes people censorious and slow to forgive the errors and weaknesses of others; quickness of imagination, on the other hand, makes thought less steady than it must be to distinguish precisely between right and wrong. Again, in every deliberation and every pleading, the capacity for solid reasoning is necessary, for without it people's resolutions are rash and their verdicts unjust. And yet unless there is also powerful eloquence to win attention and consent, reason will accomplish little. But these are opposing faculties. Reason rests on principles of truth, while eloquence rests on opinions already received, whether true or false, and on the passions and interests of men, which differ from person to person and shift over time.

Among the passions, too, courage, by which I mean contempt for wounds and violent death, inclines people toward private revenge, and sometimes toward attempts to unsettle the public peace. Timidity, meanwhile, often disposes them to desert the public defense. These two, they say, cannot exist together in the same person.

And when they consider how widely people's opinions and manners differ in general, they conclude that it is impossible to maintain a steady civil friendship with everyone the business of the world obliges us to deal with, since that business consists almost entirely of a perpetual contest for honor, riches, and authority.

To this I answer that these are indeed great difficulties, but not impossibilities, for education and discipline can reconcile them, and sometimes do. Judgment and imagination can both find a place in the same person, though they take turns, as the purpose he is pursuing requires. The Israelites in Egypt were sometimes bound to the labor of making bricks and at other times sent roaming across the country to gather straw. In the same way, the judgment may at one time be fixed on a single consideration, and the imagination at another time wander about the world. Reason and eloquence, likewise, can coexist very well, if not perhaps in the natural sciences, then certainly in the moral ones. For wherever there is room to adorn error and recommend it, there is far more room to adorn and recommend truth, provided one has the truth to adorn. Nor is there any conflict between fearing the laws and not fearing a public enemy, or between refraining from injuring others and forgiving the injuries others do. Human nature, therefore, is not as incompatible with civic duty as some think. I have known clarity of judgment and breadth of imagination, strength of reason and graceful speech, courage for war and fear of the laws, all present to an eminent degree in a single man. He was my most noble and honored friend, Mr. Sidney Godolphin, who hated no one and was hated by no one, and who was unfortunately killed at the beginning of the late civil war, in the public quarrel, by a hand unseen and itself unseeing.

To the laws of nature set out in the fifteenth chapter, I would add this one: "That every man is bound by nature, as far as it lies in his power, to protect in war the authority by which he is himself protected in time of peace." For anyone who claims a natural right to preserve his own body cannot also claim a natural right to destroy the one whose strength preserves him. That would be a plain contradiction of himself. And although this law may be derived as a consequence from some of those already listed there, the times require that it be pressed home and kept in mind.

I find from various English books recently printed that the civil wars have not yet sufficiently taught people at what point in time a subject becomes obligated to a conqueror, what conquest is, or how it comes to oblige people to obey the conqueror's laws. For their further satisfaction on these points, I say this: the moment at which a person becomes the subject of a conqueror is the moment at which, being at liberty to submit to him, he consents to be his subject, either in explicit words or by some other sufficient sign. When a person has the liberty to submit I showed earlier, at the end of the twenty-first chapter. For someone who owes his former sovereign no obligation beyond that of an ordinary subject, the liberty begins when the means of his livelihood fall within the enemy's guards and garrisons. At that point he no longer receives protection from his former sovereign, but is protected instead by the opposing side in return for his contribution. Paying such contributions is everywhere regarded as lawful, being unavoidable, even though it aids the enemy. Total submission, which likewise amounts to nothing more than aiding the enemy, therefore cannot be regarded as unlawful either. Besides, if one considers that those who submit aid the enemy with only part of their estates, whereas those who refuse aid him with the whole, since he simply seizes everything, there is no reason to call their submission, or their coming to terms, an assistance to the enemy. It is rather a loss to him. But if a person has taken on, beyond the obligation of a subject, the further obligation of a soldier, then he does not have the liberty to submit to a new power for as long as the old one keeps the field and provides him with a livelihood, whether in its armies or its garrisons. In that case he cannot complain that he lacks protection or the means to live as a soldier. When that support also fails, however, a soldier too may seek protection wherever he has the best hope of finding it, and may lawfully submit himself to his new master. So much for the time at which a person may lawfully submit, if he chooses to. If he does submit, he is unquestionably bound to be a loyal subject, for a contract lawfully made cannot lawfully be broken.

From this one can also understand when people may properly be said to be conquered, and in what the nature of conquest and the right of a conqueror consist, since this act of submission implies them all. Conquest is not the victory itself but the acquisition, through victory, of a right over the persons of men. A man who is killed is therefore overcome, but not conquered. A man who is captured and thrown into prison or chains is not conquered either, though he is overcome, for he is still an enemy and may save himself if he can. But a man who, on his promise of obedience, is granted his life and liberty is then conquered and a subject, and not before. The Romans used to say that their general had "pacified" a certain province, which is to say, in English, conquered it, and that a country was pacified by victory when its people had promised *imperata facere*, that is, to do what the Roman people commanded them. This was what it meant to be conquered. Such a promise may be either explicit or tacit: explicit when made in words, tacit when indicated by other signs. Consider, for example, a man who has not been called upon to make an explicit promise, perhaps because his power is too slight to matter. If he lives openly under the conqueror's protection, he is understood to have submitted himself to the government. But if he lives there secretly, he is liable to anything that may be done to a spy and enemy of the state. I do not say that he commits any injustice, for acts of open hostility are not called by that name; I say only that he may justly be put to death. Likewise, if a man is abroad when his country is conquered, he is neither conquered nor a subject. But if on his return he submits to the government, he is bound to obey it. Conquest, then, to define it, is the acquiring of the right of sovereignty by victory. That right is acquired through the people's submission, by which they contract with the victor, promising obedience in exchange for life and liberty.

In the twenty-ninth chapter I listed, among the causes that bring about the dissolution of commonwealths, their imperfect generation: a commonwealth born without an absolute and arbitrary legislative power, for lack of which the civil sovereign is forced to wield the sword of justice inconsistently, as though it were too hot for him to hold. One reason for this, which I did not mention there, is that sovereigns all want to justify the war by which their power was first won, believing that their right depends on that war and not on their actual possession of power. It is as if, for example, the right of the kings of England depended on the goodness of William the Conqueror's cause and on their own lineal and most direct descent from him. On that reasoning, there would perhaps be no tie binding any subject in the world today to obey his sovereign. And while rulers needlessly try to justify themselves in this way, they justify every successful rebellion that ambition may at any time raise against them and their successors. I therefore count as one of the most effective seeds of death in any state the practice whereby conquerors demand not only that people submit their actions to them in the future, but also that they approve all the conquerors' past actions, when there is scarcely a commonwealth in the world whose beginnings can in good conscience be justified.

The word "tyranny" means neither more nor less than the word "sovereignty," whether it resides in one person or in many, except that those who use the former are understood to be angry with the rulers they call tyrants. I therefore think that tolerating an openly professed hatred of tyranny is tolerating hatred of commonwealth in general, and is another evil seed, not much different from the first. For justifying the conqueror's cause usually requires condemning the cause of the conquered, yet neither is necessary to establish the obligation of the conquered.
