This is as much as I have thought fit to say in reviewing the first and second parts of this discourse.

In the thirty-fifth chapter I showed sufficiently from Scripture that in the commonwealth of the Jews, God himself was made sovereign by a covenant with the people, who were therefore called his peculiar people, to set them apart from the rest of the world, over whom God reigned not by their consent but by his own power. I also showed that in this kingdom Moses was God's lieutenant on earth, and that it was he who told the people what laws God had laid down. I did not, however, explain there whom God appointed to carry out those laws, especially in capital punishments, since I did not then regard the matter as requiring as much consideration as I have since found it does. We know that in commonwealths generally, the carrying out of corporal punishments has been assigned either to the guards or other soldiers of the sovereign power, or to people in whom poverty, contempt for honor, and hardness of heart combined to make them seek such an office. Among the Israelites, however, it was a positive law of God, their sovereign, that a person convicted of a capital crime should be stoned to death by the people, with the witnesses casting the first stone and the rest of the people following after. This law designated who the executioners were to be. It did not mean that anyone might throw a stone at the accused before conviction and sentence, where the congregation was the judge. The witnesses still had to be heard before the execution proceeded, unless the deed had been committed in the presence of the congregation itself or in sight of the lawful judges, for then no witnesses were needed beyond the judges themselves. This procedure, however, has not been thoroughly understood, and the misunderstanding has given rise to a dangerous opinion: that any person may, in certain cases, kill another by a right of zeal, as though the executions carried out on offenders in the kingdom of God in ancient times proceeded not from the sovereign's command but from the authority of private zeal. If we examine the texts that seem to support this opinion, they show quite the contrary.

First, when the Levites fell upon the people who had made and worshipped the golden calf and killed three thousand of them, they acted on the command of Moses, delivered from the mouth of God, as Exodus 32:27 makes plain. And when the son of an Israelite woman blasphemed God, those who heard him did not kill him. They brought him before Moses, who held him in custody until God should pass sentence on him, as appears in Leviticus 25:11–12. Again, in Numbers 25:6–7, when Phinehas killed Zimri and Cozbi, he did not act by a right of private zeal. Their crime was committed in full view of the assembly, so no witnesses were needed; the law was known; Phinehas was heir apparent to the sovereignty; and, most important of all, the lawfulness of his act depended entirely on its subsequent ratification by Moses, which he had no reason to doubt. Such a presumption of future ratification is sometimes necessary to the safety of a commonwealth. In a sudden rebellion, for instance, anyone able to suppress it by his own power in the region where it breaks out may lawfully do so, and arrange to have his action ratified or pardoned while it is under way or after it is done. Numbers 35:30, moreover, says expressly, "Whosoever shall kill the murderer, shall kill him upon the word of witnesses." But witnesses presuppose a formal court of judgment, and so condemn the claim to a *jus zelotarum*, a right of zealots. The law of Moses concerning anyone who entices others to idolatry, which in the kingdom of God amounted to renouncing allegiance to him, forbids concealing such a person and commands the accuser to have him put to death and to cast the first stone at him, as Deuteronomy 13:8 shows; but it does not permit killing him before he is condemned. And in Deuteronomy 17:4–6 the procedure against idolatry is set down exactly. There God speaks to the people as a judge and commands them, when a man is accused of idolatry, to inquire diligently into the facts and, finding the charge true, then to stone him; even so, it is the hand of the witness that throws the first stone. This is not private zeal but public condemnation. In the same way, when a father has a rebellious son, the law in Deuteronomy 21:18 is that he must bring the son before the judges of the town, and all the people of the town shall stone him. Lastly, it was on the pretext of these laws, and not on any pretext of private zeal, that Saint Stephen was stoned, for before he was taken away to execution he had pleaded his case before the high priest. Nothing in all this, nor in any other part of the Bible, supports executions carried out by private zeal. Such zeal is often nothing more than ignorance joined with passion, and it is contrary to both the justice and the peace of a commonwealth.

In the thirty-sixth chapter I said that Scripture does not declare in what manner God spoke supernaturally to Moses. I did not mean that God never spoke to him through dreams and visions and by a supernatural voice, as he did to other prophets. The manner in which he spoke to Moses from the mercy seat is set down explicitly in Numbers 7:89, in these words: "From that time forward, when Moses entered into the tabernacle of the congregation to speak with God, he heard a voice which spake unto him from over the mercy seat, which is over the ark of the testimony; from between the cherubims he spake unto him." What Scripture does not declare is what made God's manner of speaking to Moses superior to his manner of speaking to other prophets, such as Samuel and Abraham, to whom he also spoke by a voice, that is, by a vision, unless the difference lies in the clarity of the vision. For "face to face" and "mouth to mouth" cannot be understood literally of a divine nature that is infinite and incomprehensible.

As to the doctrine as a whole, I do not yet see any reason to doubt that its principles are true and fitting and its reasoning sound. I ground the civil right of sovereigns, and both the duty and the liberty of subjects, on the well-known natural inclinations of mankind and on the articles of the law of nature, of which no one who claims even enough reason to manage his own household ought to be ignorant. And I ground the ecclesiastical power of those same sovereigns on texts of Scripture that are both clear in themselves and consistent with the purpose of Scripture as a whole. I am therefore persuaded that anyone who reads this work solely in order to be informed will be informed by it. Those, however, who have already committed themselves, whether in writing, in public speech, or by conspicuous actions, to maintaining contrary opinions will not be so easily satisfied. In such cases it is natural for people to go on reading while, at the same moment, their attention drifts away as they hunt for objections to what they read earlier. And in a time when people's interests have shifted, such objections are bound to be very numerous, since much of the doctrine that helps establish a new government must necessarily run contrary to the doctrine that helped dissolve the old one.

In the part of the work that deals with a Christian commonwealth there are certain new doctrines. In a state where the contrary positions had already been fully settled, it might perhaps be a fault for a subject to publish them without permission, since doing so would usurp the place of a teacher. But at this present time, when people are calling not only for peace but also for truth, to offer doctrines that I believe to be true, and that plainly tend toward peace and loyalty, for the consideration of those who are still deliberating is nothing more than offering new wine to be put into new casks, so that both may be preserved together. And I suppose that at a time when novelty can cause no trouble or disorder in a state, people are not generally so inclined to revere antiquity as to prefer ancient errors to new and well-proven truth.

There is nothing I distrust more than my own style. Even so, I am confident that, apart from the printer's errors, it is not obscure. I have neglected the ornament of quoting ancient poets, orators, and philosophers, contrary to the custom of recent times, and whether I have done well or badly in this, the choice proceeds from a judgment grounded on many reasons. First, all truth of doctrine depends either on reason or on Scripture, both of which lend credit to many writers but never receive credit from any. Second, the questions at issue here are not matters of fact but matters of right, where there is no place for witnesses. Third, there is hardly a single one of those old writers who does not sometimes contradict both himself and others, which makes their testimony insufficient. Fourth, opinions accepted solely on the authority of antiquity are not, in themselves, the judgment of those who cite them, but merely words that pass from mouth to mouth, the way a yawn spreads from one person to the next. Fifth, people often have a fraudulent purpose when they stud their corrupt doctrine with the cloves of other men's wit. Sixth, I do not find that the ancients whom these writers cite considered it an ornament to do the same with those who wrote before them. Seventh, it is a sign of indigestion when Greek and Latin sentences come back up unchewed and unchanged, as they usually do. Lastly, although I revere those men of ancient times who either wrote the truth clearly or set us on a better path to discover it for ourselves, I think nothing is owed to antiquity itself. If we are to revere age, the present is the oldest age of the world. If we are to revere the age of the writer, I am not sure that those to whom such honor is given were generally older when they wrote than I am now as I write. Properly considered, the praise of ancient authors proceeds not from reverence for the dead, but from the rivalry and mutual envy of the living.

To conclude: so far as I can perceive, there is nothing in this whole discourse, nor in what I wrote earlier on the same subject in Latin, that is contrary to the word of God or to good morals, or that tends to disturb the public tranquility. I therefore think it may profitably be printed, and still more profitably taught in the universities, if those to whom the judgment of such matters belongs think so too. The universities are the fountains of civil and moral doctrine. From them the preachers and the gentry draw whatever water they find and sprinkle it on the people, both from the pulpit and in their conversation. Great care ought certainly to be taken, then, to keep that water pure, both from the venom of pagan political writers and from the incantations of deceiving spirits. By that means most people, knowing their duties, will be less liable to serve the ambitions of a few discontented persons in their designs against the state. They will be less aggrieved by the contributions necessary for their own peace and defense. And the governors themselves will have less reason to maintain, at the common expense, any larger army than is needed to defend the public liberty against the invasions and encroachments of foreign enemies.

And so I have brought to an end my discourse on civil and ecclesiastical government. It was occasioned by the disorders of the present time, and I have written it without partiality, without aiming it at any particular person, and with no other purpose than to set before people's eyes the mutual relation between protection and obedience, which the condition of human nature and the divine laws, both natural and positive, require to be observed without violation. In a revolution of states, truths of this kind can hardly be born under a favorable star. Those who dissolve an old government regard them with an angry eye, while those who are erecting a new one have their backs turned to them. Even so, I cannot think that this work will be condemned at present, either by the public judge of doctrine or by anyone who wishes the public peace to continue. In that hope I return to my interrupted study of natural bodies, in which, if God gives me the health to finish it, I hope the novelty will please as much as novelty usually offends in a doctrine concerning this artificial body, the commonwealth. For a truth that stands in the way of no one's profit or pleasure is welcome to everyone.

FINIS
